title: Heparin Allergic Skin Reactions in Pregnancy
summary: This small community captures a single, narrow clinical theme: cutaneous allergic reactions as an adverse effect of heparin thromboprophylaxis or treatment in pregnancy, and the substitution strategy used when they occur. Two relations define it. First, heparin increases the risk of allergic skin reaction, with the population explicitly scoped to pregnant women receiving heparin treatment. Second, an alternative LMWH treats (i.e., is the recommended management for) allergic skin reaction, scoped to women who are unable to tolerate heparin, and conditioned on the reaction being an allergic skin reaction without evidence of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. The practical teaching point for nursing staff is therefore: pregnant women on heparin should be monitored for skin reactions at injection sites and elsewhere; if a skin reaction occurs and HIT has been excluded, the response is to switch to an alternative low molecular weight heparin rather than to abandon anticoagulation. The HIT caveat is the key safety discriminator — the alternative-LMWH switch is only endorsed in the absence of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, implying that suspected HIT is a different pathway not described here. Only one guideline body contributes: the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG), with both relations traced to the same source location (RCOG T1, p17). There is consequently no inter-body disagreement to reconcile and no comparison of specificity between organisations; this theme rests on a single-source recommendation. Several things the community does not establish. It does not name a specific alternative LMWH (no product, dose, unit or frequency is given), nor a heparin dose or formulation that carries the risk. It gives no incidence or risk magnitude for allergic skin reaction, no timing (onset window, duration of monitoring, or when to switch), no platelet count threshold or test to exclude HIT, and no description of what an allergic skin reaction looks like clinically. It also says nothing about non-pregnant populations, perioperative gynecologic surgery specifically, alternatives beyond LMWH (e.g., fondaparinux or danaparoid), or outcomes after switching.

title: High-Alert Medications and Adverse Drug Events
summary:
This community represents the theme of high-alert or high-risk medications in the perioperative setting and the adverse drug events (ADEs) they can produce. Six drug classes are flagged by WHO (T1 p242) as increasing the risk of adverse drug events without further population qualifiers: insulin, oral anticoagulants, neuromuscular blocking agents, digoxin, chemotherapeutic agents, intravenous potassium, and aminoglycoside antibiotics. Nurse educators can use this list as the core content for a high-alert medication safety module.

Two drugs carry more specific, conditional guidance. Oral anticoagulants treat deep venous thrombosis in the patient following an ankle fracture, where the intended treatment course is three to six months; in patients taking oral anticoagulants, the risk shifts to bleeding when therapy is continued beyond the planned duration of treatment — making review of stop dates a concrete QI target. Neuromuscular blocking agents increase the risk of anaphylaxis specifically in patients who have previously reacted to one type of neuromuscular blocking drug, when another drug in the same class is given, so cross-reactivity within the class must be documented and heeded.

Contributing bodies are WHO (T1 pp. 46, 242) and the ERAS Society (T1 p7). WHO supplies all the risk and treatment relations; ERAS Society contributes only indication context for neuromuscular blocking agents, which apply to laparoscopic surgery and to open surgery when used to facilitate surgical exposure. The two do not conflict: ERAS describes appropriate use, WHO describes the hazard, and WHO is far more specific about populations, timing and reaction mechanisms.

The community does not establish dosing regimens, monitoring parameters, thresholds (e.g., INR or potassium concentrations), infusion rates for intravenous potassium, reversal or rescue protocols, or gynecologic-specific populations. No frequency or severity estimates for adverse drug events are given, no comparative ranking of the seven drug classes, and no relations linking insulin, digoxin, chemotherapeutic agents, intravenous potassium or aminoglycosides to any specific adverse outcome beyond the generic adverse drug event node.

title: Preventing Anaesthetic Mishap Through Equipment Checks
summary:
This community represents the theme of anaesthesia safety assurance through monitoring and equipment verification, with the shared endpoint of preventing anaesthetic mishap. Two distinct safeguards converge on that outcome. First, pulse oximetry is recommended as a preventive monitoring measure against anaesthetic mishap in surgical patients (WHO Tool 1, p22); the relation attaches no further condition, timing or saturation threshold. Second, a formal anaesthesia system check prevents anaesthetic mishap in patients undergoing anaesthesia, conditional on the items on the checklist being available and functioning correctly before every anaesthetic (WHO Tool 1, p25). The same anaesthesia system check is located explicitly in the preoperative phase for patients undergoing anaesthesia, with a clearly specified timing: before each anaesthetic, before the start of each operating day, and after any repairs, maintenance or introduction of new equipment (WHO Tool 1, p25). For a nurse educator, the practical teaching points are that the system check is not a once-daily task but a repeated, event-triggered one (per-case, per-day start, and post-maintenance/new-equipment), and that its protective effect is contingent on items being both present and functional, not merely on the checklist being completed. Pulse oximetry is framed as a continuous safeguard for the broader population of surgical patients, i.e. wider than the anaesthesia-specific population of the system check.

All relations in this community derive from a single guideline body, the WHO (Tool 1, pages 22 and 25); there are therefore no inter-body disagreements to reconcile, and no second source corroborates or contradicts these statements. The community does not establish who performs or documents the anaesthesia system check, what specific items the checklist contains, target oxygen saturation thresholds or alarm limits for pulse oximetry, escalation actions when a check fails or an item is unavailable, intraoperative or postoperative monitoring requirements, definitions or severity grading of anaesthetic mishap, drugs, doses, or any gynecologic-procedure-specific tailoring.

title: Anaphylaxis, Shock and Fluid Resuscitation Agents
summary:
This community covers acute perioperative haemodynamic and hypersensitivity emergencies: drug/agent triggers of anaphylaxis, its treatment, and fluid/oxygen/vasopressor resuscitation for shock and sepsis, plus antibiotic choice and cross-allergy constraints.

Triggers of anaphylaxis (WHO T1 p46): antibiotics, cephalosporin and imipenem (specifically in patients who have had an anaphylactic reaction to penicillin), opioids, hypnotics, anaesthetics, neuromuscular blocking agents (when another drug of the same class is given to a prior reactor), latex and colloid. Treatment: adrenaline 0.3–0.5 mg intramuscularly (WHO T1 p242), plus antihistamine, intravenous fluid, oxygen, ventilation and general supportive measures for cardiovascular collapse, airway occlusion and bronchospasm (WHO T1 p46).

Shock/sepsis: OpenRN (T2 p663) advises, for clients with early signs of shock, immediate oxygen to keep saturation >90%, with IV fluid and vasopressors as may be required. NICE is more population- and threshold-specific: oxygen for 16–18-year-olds with suspected sepsis, and for under-18s who are or have recently been pregnant, if signs of shock or SpO2 <92% on air (T1 p42, p27); IV fluid for people 16+ at moderate risk of severe illness/death after clinical assessment when there is no evidence of hypoperfusion (T1 p36); broad-spectrum antibiotic for NEWS2 3–4 with a single parameter contributing, managed as high risk, if the likely cause is current infection (T1 p36). NICE also flags fluid volume overload after 1,000 ml with no/limited change in hypoperfusion indicators (T1 p69); OpenRN frames the same hazard generically as fluid volume excess (T2 p1111), and IV fluid also treats fluid volume deficit, hypotension/tachycardia and diarrhoea.

Antibiotic/allergy nuances: RCOG contraindicates cephalosporins and carbapenems (incl. ceftriaxone) with anaphylaxis to penicillins or severe beta-lactam allergy (T1 p7, p11), yet recommends a cephalosporin for group B streptococcal prophylaxis in beta-lactam-allergic women in labour as a clindamycin substitute given rising resistance; ceftriaxone raises C. difficile risk. CDC (T1 p13) addresses patients unable to receive a cephalosporin. WHO (T1 p60) requires regimens active against staphylococci and β-haemolytic streptococci (cephalosporin or antistaphylococcal penicillin). Colloid: RCOG allows up to 1.5 L for postpartum haemorrhage until blood arrives, while NICE links colloid to coagulopathy, acute kidney injury and mortality in adults undergoing surgery — an unresolved tension. Oxytocin IV causes dose-related tachycardia and hypotension at caesarean (observational data).

Not established: no adrenaline dosing for children, no vasopressor agents or doses named, no fluid type/rate for shock, no antihistamine drug or dose (only sedation risk), no monitoring intervals, and no gynaecologic-surgery-specific anaphylaxis pathway.

title: Preoperative Anemia and Modifiable Risk Screening
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: detection of anemia (alongside other modifiable risk factors) during the preoperative phase of gynecologic surgery. All four relations converge on 'anemia' as the target condition, and all are anchored explicitly in the preoperative phase.

The recommendations are: (1) preoperative assessment of tobacco, alcohol and anemia, which is located in the preoperative phase and is stated to detect anemia when 'assessed routinely preoperatively' — i.e., anemia screening is bundled with tobacco and alcohol assessment as part of routine preoperative work-up rather than being ordered selectively; (2) preoperative screening for anemia, which detects anemia specifically for the population of patients undergoing elective surgery, with the timing condition 'before elective surgery'; and (3) anemia investigation, which detects anemia with the condition 'pre-operatively'. Together these describe a graded sequence: routine bundled assessment, targeted screening in elective surgical candidates, and further investigation once anemia is suspected — all completed before the operative date so that findings can influence planning.

Only one guideline body contributes: the ERAS Society (Text 1, pages 1–2). There are therefore no inter-body disagreements to reconcile. Within ERAS, the specificity varies: the anemia-screening statement is the most precise, naming both a population (elective surgery patients) and a timing (before elective surgery), whereas the bundled tobacco/alcohol/anemia assessment and the 'anemia investigation' entity carry only a generic preoperative timing without a defined population.

What this community does NOT establish: no hemoglobin, hematocrit or ferritin thresholds define anemia; no specific laboratory tests are named for screening or investigation; no interval is given between screening and surgery (e.g., number of weeks); and no treatment pathway is specified — iron (oral or intravenous), erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, transfusion triggers and postponement criteria are all absent. Likewise, no interventions are attached to the tobacco or alcohol findings, no emergency/non-elective population is addressed, and no intraoperative or postoperative anemia management, outcome measures or documentation standards are included.
key_entities: preoperative assessment of tobacco, alcohol and anemia

title: RAAS-Blocking Antihypertensives: Indications and Contraindications
summary:
This community covers renin-angiotensin system blockade for hypertension management — ACE inhibitors and angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) — including indications, contraindications, adverse effects and one monitoring test. All relations derive from a single guideline body, RNAO Nursing Management of Hypertension (Theme 2, pp. 71, 128, 141).

Indications: ACE inhibitors are recommended as first-line therapy for hypertension in people with diabetes, post-myocardial infarction, systolic dysfunction, or renal disease. ARBs are first line for hypertension without compelling indications for specific agents, and specifically when a client cannot tolerate ACE inhibitors.

Contraindications: ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy (pregnant women), women of child-bearing potential, hypersensitivity, salt and/or volume depletion, impaired renal function, chronic renal disease caused by bilateral renal artery stenosis, severe congestive heart failure, and concurrent use with an ARB. ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy, women of child-bearing potential, lactation (lactating women), and hypersensitivity.

Adverse effects/risks: ACE inhibitors increase risk of hyperkalemia, dry cough, proteinuria, angioedema (specifically in black clients when used as initial monotherapy), and renal failure in susceptible clients — bilateral renovascular disease, volume depletion, or concurrent non-steroidal anti-inflammatory use. ARBs increase risk of angioedema and upper respiratory infection; notably no cough or hyperkalemia risk is attached to ARBs here.

Monitoring: an annual urine test detects proteinuria in clients on antihypertensive medication therapy, as part of annual follow-up of medication therapy.

Internal consistency: p128 and p141 largely duplicate each other; p141 is more specific on drug–drug and clinical contraindications (ACEI–ARB combination, severe congestive heart failure, impaired renal function, hypersensitivity), while p128 is more specific on indications and populations (diabetes, post-MI, systolic dysfunction, renal disease; bilateral renal artery stenosis).

Not established: no dosing, titration, blood-pressure targets, or timing beyond "annual"; no potassium or creatinine monitoring thresholds or intervals; no perioperative or gynecologic-surgery-specific guidance (e.g., hold/continue instructions before anesthesia); no comparison with other antihypertensive classes; no severity grading of adverse events; and no second guideline body offering a differing or corroborating position.

title: Antenatal VTE Prophylaxis and Preventive Care
summary:
This community centres on antenatal and postpartum risk assessment and prevention — dominated by venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis (RCOG), with adjacent WHO antenatal preventive care and infection topics.

Core RCOG recommendations: VTE/thrombotic risk assessment for all women in early pregnancy or prepregnancy and at each hospital admission, detecting thrombotic risk factors. Pharmacological thromboprophylaxis antenatally is decided by weighing absolute VTE risk against bleeding risk; it should begin early in pregnancy for women with previous VTE, and applies to women with persistent antiphospholipid antibodies plus other risk factors. LMWH thromboprophylaxis runs throughout the antenatal period for women with previous VTE (except a single event related to major surgery with no other risk factors), and postpartum for 10 days after caesarean section; high-dose LMWH is used antenatally and for 6 weeks postpartum (or until return to oral anticoagulation) where previous VTE is linked to antithrombin deficiency, antiphospholipid syndrome, or recurrent VTE. For asymptomatic thrombophilia (heterozygous factor V Leiden or prothrombin gene mutation, or antiphospholipid antibodies), prophylaxis is indicated only with additional risk factors — three other risk factors, or from 28 weeks with two; women without previous VTE and no first-trimester risk factors or hospital admission may start at 28 weeks. Anti-Xa monitoring is not routine on therapeutic LMWH but is considered at extremes of body weight (<50 kg, ≥90 kg), renal disease, recurrent VTE, and antenatally with antithrombin deficiency (with a haematologist). Acute DVT/PE: therapeutic subcutaneous LMWH for the remainder of pregnancy and ≥6 weeks postnatally, ≥3 months total; V/Q lung scan for antenatal PE; LMWH self-injection allows outpatient management until delivery. Warfarin/vitamin K antagonists increase stillbirth and low birth weight risk; stillbirth, preterm birth and multiple pregnancy increase VTE risk. Also: anaemia screening, CMV-seronegative products and leucocyte depletion to prevent CMV transmission in elective antenatal transfusion, and sepsis risk-factor recognition antenatally and postpartum.

WHO contributes antenatal influenza vaccination at any stage, nutritional education (preterm birth, low birth weight — low/very low certainty), healthy-eating/activity counselling against excessive weight gain, antenatal information on uterotonics for PPH prevention, and chorioamnionitis treatment with once-daily gentamicin plus ampicillin (RCOG offers metronidazole with e.g. cefotaxime intrapartum for non-severe penicillin allergy). WHO also flags oxytocin given in error instead of a tocolytic, and re-used syringes/needles transmitting hepatitis and HIV.

Not established: specific LMWH agents, doses, units or weight-band regimens; how many risk factors constitute “risk factors” beyond the counts cited; intrapartum/neuraxial anaesthesia timing; outcome data for most prophylaxis; and no guidance linking the OpenRN anthelmintic/worm-infection item to pregnancy.
key_entities: high dose low molecular weight heparin thromboprophylaxis

title: Antiphospholipid Antibodies and VTE Risk
summary:
This community represents a single thematic thread: the detection of antiphospholipid antibodies (aPL) and their role as a risk factor for venous thromboembolism (VTE) and thrombosis in women, as framed by RCOG guidance on thrombosis and embolism (Green-top thromboprophylaxis material, RCOG T1, pages 3, 16, 17, 18).

Two recommendation strands appear. First, testing: antiphospholipid antibody testing is indicated to detect antiphospholipid antibodies in women who have had an unprovoked venous thromboembolism (stated at RCOG T1 p3 as 'unprovoked VTE' and repeated at p16 as 'unprovoked venous thromboembolism'). The population trigger is therefore an unprovoked event, not a provoked or situational one. Second, risk attribution: antiphospholipid antibodies increase the risk of VTE in women without previous VTE, with the condition specified as persistent antiphospholipid antibodies — that is, lupus anticoagulant and/or anticardiolipin antibodies and/or beta-2-glycoprotein 1 antibodies (RCOG T1 p18). Separately, antiphospholipid antibodies increase the risk of thrombosis in asymptomatic women (RCOG T1 p17), extending the concern beyond those who have already presented with an event.

Only one guideline body contributes here: RCOG. There is no cross-body disagreement to reconcile, but there are differences in specificity within the corpus. Page 18 is the most precise, naming the three antibody types and requiring persistence for risk to be counted; pages 3 and 16 state the testing indication in general terms only; page 17 uses the broader outcome term 'thrombosis' in asymptomatic women rather than VTE specifically.

What this community does not establish: no thresholds or titre cut-offs, no timing or interval for repeat testing to confirm persistence, and no definition of what counts as unprovoked. It names no drugs, doses, or thromboprophylaxis regimens (no heparin, LMWH, or aspirin), and specifies no antenatal, intrapartum, or postpartum duration of prophylaxis. It does not quantify the magnitude of risk increase, does not address perioperative or gynaecologic surgical management, and gives no guidance on who should interpret results or refer onward.

title: Preoperative Antiseptic Bathing for SSI Prevention
summary:
Clinical theme: This small, tightly focused community represents preoperative patient skin preparation by whole-body antiseptic bathing (antiseptic shower or bath) as a surgical site infection (SSI) prevention measure. It links a single intervention to a single outcome and situates that intervention firmly within the preoperative phase of care.

Recommendations, populations and conditions: For surgical patients, an antiseptic shower or bath is directed at preventing surgical site infection, with the timing condition that it be performed on at least the night before the operative day. The same intervention is explicitly assigned to the preoperative phase of care, again for surgical patients, with the condition 'at least the night before the operative day.' The phrase 'at least' indicates the night-before bath is a minimum expectation rather than a ceiling, so additional or repeat bathing (for example, also on the morning of surgery) is not excluded by these relations — but it is also not specified here.

Contributing bodies and differences: Only one guideline body contributes to this community: the CDC (CDC T1, p21), supplying both relations. Because there is a single source, there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile and no instance of one body being more granular than another; the CDC statement is the sole level of specificity available.

What this community does NOT establish: It does not name a specific antiseptic agent, concentration, or product (for example, no chlorhexidine gluconate versus povidone-iodine comparison), does not specify volume, contact time, application technique, or number of baths beyond the night-before minimum, and does not define whether a bath or a shower is preferred. It does not stratify by procedure type, wound class, anatomic site, age group, or SSI risk factors such as diabetes, obesity, colonization status, or immunosuppression. It gives no strength-of-evidence or recommendation grade, no outcome magnitude (no SSI rate reduction figure), no guidance on hair removal, intranasal decolonization, intraoperative skin prep, or antimicrobial prophylaxis, and no documentation, audit, or patient-education requirements.

title: Antithrombin deficiency testing and VTE risk
summary:
This community covers thrombophilia screening — specifically antithrombin deficiency testing — and the elevated venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk that antithrombin deficiency confers in pregnancy. All relations derive from a single guideline body, RCOG (Tranche 1, pages 3, 11, 14, 16, 17, 38); no other body contributes, so no inter-guideline disagreement can be identified.

Testing recommendations: antithrombin deficiency testing detects antithrombin deficiency in women with a family history of VTE who have either known antithrombin deficiency in the family or where the specific thrombophilia has not yet been identified (p3, p16). Thrombophilia screening is indicated more specifically for women with a previous VTE plus a family history of VTE and either antithrombin deficiency or an undetermined thrombophilia, because detection will alter the dose of thromboprophylaxis offered in pregnancy (p16) — the clearest statement of clinical purpose in the community.

Timing and interpretation cautions: in pregnant women presenting with suspected VTE, thrombophilia screening is contraindicated prior to commencing anticoagulant treatment (p11); results in pregnancy may also be influenced by the physiological changes of pregnancy and by acute thrombus (p11). Screening therefore should not delay or precede therapy.

Risk relations: antithrombin deficiency increases the risk of VTE in pregnant women, where it is classed as very high risk (p38), and in women with one or more symptomatic first-degree relatives (p17). It increases risk of pregnancy-related VTE in pregnant women (p17), and of VTE recurrence in women with previous VTE, particularly type 1 antithrombin deficiency with a family history (p14).

What is NOT established here: no specific anticoagulant agent, dose, intensity (e.g., prophylactic versus intermediate or treatment dose), duration, or postpartum timing is named; "anticoagulant treatment" is referenced only generically. No laboratory thresholds or assay types for antithrombin levels are given, no guidance on screening asymptomatic women without family history, and no monitoring, patient-education or multidisciplinary referral pathway is specified. Other thrombophilias beyond antithrombin deficiency are not individually characterised.

title: Antithrombin replacement around delivery timing
summary:
This community represents a narrow, high-acuity perioperative theme: the use of antithrombin replacement therapy in pregnant women with antithrombin deficiency and a history of venous thromboembolism (VTE), specifically timed around delivery and caesarean section.

The recommendations are twofold. First, the timing of antithrombin replacement is explicitly tied to the mode and onset of delivery: for women with previous VTE associated with antithrombin deficiency, replacement is given at the initiation of labour or prior to caesarean section. This timing relation appears twice in the corpus (RCOG Top Tip/table content at p2 and p14), indicating it is a reinforced, consistent message rather than an isolated statement. Second, antithrombin replacement is framed as a VTE-prevention intervention for women with antithrombin deficiency, but only around the time of delivery and only in individual cases — i.e., it is not a routine prophylactic measure but an individualised decision.

Only one guideline body contributes here: RCOG. There is therefore no cross-body disagreement to reconcile, but there is an internal difference in specificity between the two relation types. The timing relation is more specific in its population (previous VTE associated with antithrombin deficiency) and its trigger points (initiation of labour; before caesarean section), whereas the prevention relation uses a broader population (antithrombin deficiency, without requiring prior VTE) but constrains use to "individual cases only."

What this community does NOT establish: no doses, units, target antithrombin activity levels, or laboratory monitoring thresholds are given; no duration of therapy or postpartum continuation is specified; no concomitant or alternative agents (e.g. low-molecular-weight heparin regimens) are linked here; no criteria are provided for deciding which "individual cases" warrant replacement, and no responsible clinician, haematology referral pathway, or neuraxial anaesthesia interaction is described. It also says nothing about non-obstetric gynaecologic surgery, other thrombophilias, or outcomes/efficacy data supporting the practice.

title: Preemptive and Scheduled Acute Pain Analgesia
summary:
This community represents the theme of proactive analgesic timing in acute pain management — specifically, giving analgesia before pain escalates and dosing on a fixed schedule in the early post-injury period, balanced against sedation and respiratory safety.

Two recommendations dominate. First, prompt analgesic care treats both acute pain and pain generally in clients with pain, on the condition that it is given before the pain becomes severe or before activities anticipated to be pain-inducing (e.g., anticipatory dosing ahead of mobilisation or procedural activity). The graph records this twice, once framed to 'acute pain' and once to the broader 'pain' entity, indicating the principle is not restricted to the postoperative case.

Second, around-the-clock (scheduled rather than PRN) analgesic administration treats acute pain in clients after surgery, trauma, or injury, and is specified for the first 24 to 48 hours. This same intervention carries an explicit temporary contraindication relative to sedation: it should be withheld or reconsidered in clients after surgery, trauma, or injury when sedation or respiratory status indicates otherwise. Sedation assessment and respiratory status therefore function as the gating safety check on scheduled dosing — a clear teaching point for handoff and reassessment protocols.

Only one guideline body contributes here: OpenRN (Nursing Skills, Volume 2, p. 844) supplies all four relations. There are consequently no cross-body disagreements to reconcile; the corpus is single-sourced and internally consistent, with the around-the-clock recommendation being the more specific of the two (it names a population, a 24–48 hour window, and a suspension criterion, whereas prompt analgesic care states only a timing principle).

The community does not establish: any named drug, drug class, route, dose, or ceiling; any numeric sedation scale, respiratory rate, or oxygen saturation threshold defining when to hold a dose; who is authorised to withhold; what to do after 24–48 hours (taper, transition to PRN, or multimodal adjuncts); non-pharmacologic adjuncts; pediatric, obstetric, opioid-tolerant, or gynecologic-specific qualifications; or any monitoring frequency or documentation requirement.
key_entities: clients after surgery, trauma, or injury

title: Arterial Blood Sampling Risk Profile
summary:
This community is narrowly focused on the comparative safety of arterial blood sampling (arterial puncture, e.g. for blood gas analysis) relative to venipuncture. All three relations originate from a single node — arterial blood sampling — and describe a risk cascade: arterial puncture increases the risk of bleeding and of arterial occlusion when compared with venipuncture, and, where arterial occlusion has occurred, it increases the risk of ischemia in the tissue distal to the puncture site. The practical teaching point is therefore twofold: (1) arterial sampling is not equivalent to a venous draw in risk terms and should be reserved for indications that require arterial blood; and (2) post-procedure surveillance must extend beyond the puncture site to the distal limb, because the clinically important harm (distal ischemia) is conditional on occlusion rather than on puncture alone. Assessment of distal perfusion and of bleeding/hematoma at the site is the implied nursing action.

Only one guideline body contributes: OpenRN (Nursing Skills, Textbook 2, p1329). Because the community is single-sourced, there are no inter-body agreements, contradictions, or differences in specificity to reconcile; there is no second corpus statement to corroborate or refine the OpenRN risk claims.

The community does not establish: the population in which these risks apply (no age, obstetric/gynecologic, perioperative, anticoagulated, or comorbidity qualifiers are attached); any numeric magnitude of risk, incidence, or relative risk versus venipuncture; the anatomical site (radial, brachial, femoral) or whether risk varies by site; any threshold for compression time, duration of pressure, or monitoring interval after puncture; the role of an Allen test or other pre-procedure perfusion check; contraindications; anticoagulant or antiplatelet drug interactions; and management or escalation pathways once bleeding, occlusion, or distal ischemia is detected. It also makes no recommendation about who may perform arterial sampling or about documentation. These gaps should be filled from primary procedure guidance before the theme is used to build competency or QI criteria.

title: Asymptomatic Bacteriuria Screening and Treatment in Pregnancy
summary:
This community represents the detection and management of asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) in pregnant women — a screening-and-treat theme spanning diagnostic method selection and antibiotic duration. All three relations derive from WHO antenatal care guidance (WHO T1, pp. 10 and 12), so the community is single-source rather than multi-body; there are no competing recommendations from other guideline bodies represented here, and therefore no documented disagreements.

Diagnosis: midstream urine culture is the recommended method for diagnosing ASB in pregnant women. Where urine culture is not available, midstream urine gram-staining is the recommended alternative, and is explicitly preferred over dipstick tests — a resource-stratified conditional that a QI lead can operationalise as a two-tier testing pathway (culture as default; gram-stain as the fallback in culture-less settings; dipstick discouraged).

Treatment: pregnant women identified with ASB should receive an antibiotic regimen, specified as a seven-day regimen. The guideline content captured here is specific about duration (seven days) but not about drug choice.

What this community does NOT establish: no specific antibiotic agents, doses, or routes are named; no bacterial colony-count threshold (e.g. CFU/mL) defining a positive culture is given; no gestational-age window, screening frequency, or timing of screening within antenatal visits is specified. It does not state outcomes or the rationale (e.g. prevention of pyelonephritis, preterm birth or low birth weight), nor does it address follow-up or test-of-cure after the seven-day course, management of recurrent or persistent bacteriuria, penicillin allergy alternatives, or symptomatic urinary tract infection and pyelonephritis. Non-pregnant populations are out of scope — every relation is conditioned on pregnancy. Dipstick testing appears only as a comparator that is deprioritised, with no threshold or performance data attached. Educators should supplement with local antimicrobial formulary guidance and laboratory criteria, since this theme fixes the pathway and duration but leaves drug selection and diagnostic thresholds to other sources.

title: Aortic Area Auscultation for Valvular Murmurs
summary:
Clinical theme: this is a very small, single-source community covering one focused cardiovascular assessment skill — auscultation of the aortic area using the diaphragm of the stethoscope — and the two valvular abnormalities it is credited with detecting. It sits at the physical-assessment end of the perioperative knowledge graph rather than the intervention or medication end.

Recommendations captured: the graph asserts two DETECTS relations — auscultation of the aortic area with the diaphragm of the stethoscope detects (1) aortic stenosis and (2) aortic regurgitation. Both relations are recorded without any narrowing population qualifier and without a stated condition, trigger, or timing; in the graph as given they apply generally rather than to a defined subgroup such as pregnant patients, preoperative gynecologic surgical patients, or patients with known murmurs. No threshold values (e.g., murmur grade, valve area, gradient), no listening sequence, no positioning manoeuvres, no bell-versus-diaphragm comparison for other sites, and no drugs or doses are attached.

Guideline bodies: only one contributor is present — OpenRN Nursing Skills (Open Resources for Nursing), Text 2, page 562, supplying both relations. Because the community is single-source and single-page, there are no inter-body agreements, disagreements, or differences in specificity to reconcile; nothing here can be cross-validated against a second corpus, and no body is more granular than another.

What this community does NOT establish: it does not state sensitivity, specificity, or diagnostic accuracy of aortic auscultation; it does not distinguish systolic (stenosis) from diastolic (regurgitation) timing, radiation, or murmur character; it does not say when in the perioperative pathway to auscultate, who should perform it, or what escalation, referral, echocardiography, or anaesthetic-risk action should follow a detected murmur. It does not link either valvular lesion to gynecologic surgical risk, anticoagulation, endocarditis prophylaxis, or haemodynamic management. Educators should treat it as an isolated assessment-skill node requiring supplementation from cardiology or preoperative-evaluation guidance before use in QI or competency documentation.
key_entities: auscultation of the aortic area with the diaphragm of the stethoscope

title: Abdominal Surgery: VTE and Bowel Recovery
summary:
This community centres on abdominal surgery as a perioperative risk hub, linking two distinct concerns: thromboprophylaxis and postoperative gastrointestinal recovery. Three guideline bodies contribute. NICE (T1, p27) recommends venous thromboembolism prophylaxis for patients undergoing abdominal surgery, with the population explicitly narrowed to people at increased risk of VTE rather than all abdominal surgical patients. The ERAS Society (T1, p6) contributes a distinct enhanced-recovery recommendation: avoidance of drains and nasogastric tubes after abdominal surgery, stated without a risk-stratified qualifier, so it reads as a default practice for the abdominal surgical population. OpenRN (T2, p1173) supplies the assessment rationale, identifying abdominal surgery as increasing the risk of both paralytic ileus and hypoactive bowel sounds, and separately identifying opioids as an independent contributor to hypoactive bowel sounds. Opioid exposure and surgery therefore converge on the same GI finding, which supports bundling bowel-sound assessment with opioid stewardship in postoperative gynecologic care.

The bodies operate at different levels of specificity rather than in conflict. NICE is the only source applying a population condition (increased VTE risk); ERAS is the only source applying a timing condition (after abdominal surgery); OpenRN is descriptive/pathophysiologic and issues no intervention recommendation.

Importantly, the community does not establish: any named anticoagulant, dose, threshold or duration for VTE prophylaxis; any specified risk-assessment tool or scoring cut-off for defining increased VTE risk; which opioid agents, doses or routes carry greater ileus risk; any timing for resuming diet, mobilisation or bowel-sound auscultation frequency; any recommendation that avoiding drains or nasogastric tubes reduces ileus or hypoactive bowel sounds (no such relation is asserted); and no gynecologic-procedure-specific qualifiers such as laparoscopic versus open approach, hysterectomy type, or malignancy status. It also does not link VTE prophylaxis to the GI outcomes, nor address bleeding risk as a counterweight to prophylaxis. Educators should treat this as a scaffold requiring local protocol detail for agents, doses and monitoring intervals.
key_entities: avoidance of drains and nasogastric tubes

title: Hand hygiene agent selection and skin safety
summary:
This community centres on hand hygiene product selection, its skin-tolerance trade-offs, and adjunct barrier measures for interrupting disease transmission. Core recommendation: alcohol-based hand rub prevents disease transmission when hands are not visibly soiled (OpenRN T2 p263) and prevents infection among health-care workers when embedded in a program with ongoing educational and motivational activities (CDC T1 p27). It is temporarily contraindicated when hands are visibly soiled, with soap and water recommended until hands are clean (OpenRN T2 p239; WHO T1 p211; CDC T1 p29), and contraindicated for patients with Clostridioides difficile infection (OpenRN T2 p239) and where Bacillus anthracis exposure is suspected or proven, because alcohols have poor activity against spores (CDC T1 p34). Product-sequencing cautions: soap and chlorhexidine are contraindicated together (WHO T1 p57); soap concomitantly with alcohol-based hand rub is contraindicated (WHO T1 p211); and handwashing with soap and water after each use of an alcohol hand rub is contraindicated because it may cause dermatitis (CDC T1 p22). Adverse effects: alcohol-based hand rub increases risk of hand irritation when used on wet hands (WHO T1 p211), transient stinging at broken skin such as cuts and abrasions even with emollient-containing preparations (CDC T1 p10), skin dryness with frequent use unless emollients, humectants or other skin-conditioning agents are added, and flash fire if alcohol has not evaporated and static electricity is generated — prevented by rubbing hands together until all alcohol has evaporated (CDC T1 p10). Regular soap use increases risk of skin damage (CDC T1 p23); donning gloves on wet hands increases hand irritation (WHO T1 p211). Complementary transmission barriers: personal protective equipment (OpenRN T2 p263), barrier devices for rescue breathing (OpenRN T2 p788), safe handling/transport/laundering of soiled textiles (OpenRN T2 p203), and special disinfecting process after client discharge including mattress disinfection for C. difficile (OpenRN T2 p642). Ceftriaxone increases C. difficile risk (RCOG T1 p11).

CDC is most specific on adverse effects and sequencing; WHO on wet-hand and glove issues; OpenRN on environmental and organism-specific measures. The community establishes no contact times, product concentrations, volumes, frequencies, comparative efficacy between agents, or gynecologic/perioperative-specific hand hygiene thresholds.

title: Preoperative and Anticoagulation-Timed Diagnostic Testing
summary:
This community centres on diagnostic testing and screening — when it is offered, what it detects, and how its timing is constrained by anticoagulant therapy — spanning elective surgical preassessment (NICE) and obstetric venous thromboembolism/haemorrhage care (RCOG).

NICE (T1 pp8–9) covers preoperative risk stratification. Nutritional screening is a preoperative activity for people having intermediate, or major or complex, surgery, to detect malnutrition. Full blood count is offered routinely to ASA grade 1–4 patients before elective major or complex surgery, and applies to intermediate surgery in ASA grade 3–4 patients with cardiovascular or renal disease if symptoms have not recently been investigated. Electrocardiogram is only to be considered before intermediate surgery in ASA grade 2 patients with cardiovascular, renal or diabetes comorbidities. Haemostasis testing is only considered before intermediate surgery in ASA grade 3–4 patients with chronic liver disease.

RCOG (T1 pp3, 6, 7, 11, 20, 41) governs timing relative to anticoagulation. Baseline blood investigations, full blood count, coagulation screen and liver function tests should be taken before anticoagulant therapy is commenced in pregnant women with suspected venous thromboembolism. Thrombophilia screening is contraindicated prior to commencing therapy in pregnant women with suspected VTE; thrombophilia testing in women who develop VTE in pregnancy or the puerperium is performed once anticoagulant therapy has been discontinued. Anticoagulant treatment is continued until pulmonary embolism is definitively excluded, and treats VTE/DVT when compression ultrasonography or repeat testing confirms thrombosis; in confirmed pregnancy VTE it continues for the pregnancy and until at least 6 weeks postpartum, total duration at least 3 months. Liver function tests showing an anicteric pattern (markedly raised ALT with normal bilirubin) suggest herpetic hepatitis. In major obstetric haemorrhage, a coagulation screen detects clotting abnormality and fresh frozen plasma treats it during resuscitation.

Not established: no ASA- or surgery-graded thresholds for obstetric testing, no anticoagulant drug names, doses or agents, no specific nutritional screening tool or malnutrition criteria, no FFP volumes, and no link between preoperative NICE tests and obstetric VTE pathways.

title: Antihypertensive Cautions and Procedural Bradycardia Risk
summary:
This community links cardiovascular drug safety (antihypertensive contraindications and side effects) with procedure-induced bradycardia and dysrhythmia surveillance. Two distinct strands converge on bradycardia as a shared endpoint.

Drug strand (RNAO T2, pp.140-141, clients with hypertension): beta-blockers are contraindicated with congestive heart failure, peripheral vascular disease, sinus bradycardia, asthma or reversible airway obstruction, and heart block in the absence of a pacemaker. For clients taking beta-blockers, the drugs increase risk of bradycardia and erectile dysfunction. Long-acting calcium channel blockers are contraindicated with bradycardia in hypertensive clients. Thiazide diuretics increase risk of erectile dysfunction in patients treated with them. Nurse educators should note beta-blockers and long-acting CCBs converge on bradycardia, and that erectile dysfunction is a shared, adherence-relevant effect of both thiazides and beta-blockers.

Procedural strand (OpenRN T2): nasotracheal suctioning increases risk of bradycardia (p.1293); rectal medication administration increases risk of bradycardia in some patients if unintended vagal stimulation occurs (p.905). Monitoring is specified by procedure: for patients undergoing airway suctioning, electrocardiogram monitors for dysrhythmia if available, during and following the procedure (p.1293); for patients undergoing tracheostomy suctioning, assessment of patient response monitors for dysrhythmia and bradycardia, with instruction to stop the procedure if either occurs (p.1307). Pulse equality assessment detects peripheral vascular disease and arterial obstruction (p.63), and peripheral vascular disease increases risk of peripheral neuropathy (p.510).

Contributors differ in specificity: RNAO supplies drug-level contraindications and side effects for hypertensive clients but no monitoring procedure; OpenRN supplies procedural triggers, timing (during and following suctioning) and a stop rule, plus the physical-assessment route to detecting peripheral vascular disease that RNAO names only as a beta-blocker contraindication.

Not established: no numeric heart-rate, blood-pressure or dose thresholds; no drug doses, titration or discontinuation guidance; no gynecologic- or perioperative-specific population; no stated interaction between antihypertensive therapy and suctioning- or vagal-induced bradycardia; no management or treatment steps once bradycardia, dysrhythmia or erectile dysfunction occurs; and no evidence grading.
key_entities: assessment of patient response to suctioning

title: Assessing Bladder Fullness and Distention
summary:
This community represents bedside assessment of urinary bladder volume — specifically the detection of bladder fullness and bladder distention — as a precursor to decisions such as catheterization. Two modalities appear: non-invasive ultrasound bladder scanning and manual palpation (including the suprapubic approach).

Recommendations and their attached populations/conditions:

1) Ultrasound bladder scanner detects bladder fullness for patients being assessed for catheterization, with the explicit condition that it be used per agency policy (OpenRN Nursing Skills, T2 p1241). The guideline therefore defers thresholds, device selection and competency requirements to local institutional policy.

2) Bladder palpation detects bladder fullness in the same population — patients being assessed for catheterization (OpenRN T2 p1241) — positioning manual assessment alongside, not instead of, the scanner.

3) Bladder palpation detects bladder distention when performed by palpating gently from the umbilicus down toward the pelvis (OpenRN T2 p719). This is the most technique-specific statement in the community, naming both the direction of palpation and the requirement that it be gentle.

4) Suprapubic palpation detects bladder distention when performed during abdominal assessment (OpenRN T2 p736), framing the finding as part of routine systematic abdominal examination rather than a catheterization-specific step.

Guideline contributors: all four relations derive from a single body of source material, the OpenRN open-access nursing texts (Tome 2, pages 719, 736, 1241). There is thus no cross-body disagreement; instead the differences are in granularity and framing. Page 1241 is population-specific (catheterization assessment) and pairs scanner with palpation; page 719 is technique-specific (umbilicus toward pelvis, gentle); page 736 embeds suprapubic palpation in general abdominal assessment.

What this community does NOT establish: no residual-volume thresholds (e.g., no mL cut-off) triggering catheterization; no timing or frequency of scanning or palpation; no gynecologic or perioperative population specifics such as post-operative or post-anesthesia patients; no drugs; no comparative accuracy or preference between scanner and palpation; no documentation, competency or escalation requirements; and no link from these findings to retention diagnosis or catheter type.

title: Antibiotic Prophylaxis and Sepsis Recognition
summary:
This community links two connected threads: perioperative antimicrobial prophylaxis and the recognition/treatment of infection and sepsis, especially maternal sepsis.

Prophylaxis: CDC and WHO agree that prophylactic antimicrobials for surgical patients must be timed so a bactericidal serum and tissue concentration exists at incision. WHO is more specific on windows — optimally within 30 minutes of incision, or initiated in the 60 minutes before incision and stopped within 24 hours of the end of the operation. CDC adds agent selection based on efficacy against the most common pathogens for the specific operation, use only when indicated, and for high-risk caesarean section dosing immediately after umbilical cord clamping. WHO applies preoperative prophylaxis to laparoscopic cholecystectomy; the shared endpoint is prevention of surgical site infection. Antibiotics are contraindicated in patients with prior immediate/anaphylactic reactions to that specific agent (WHO), and antibiotics themselves carry anaphylaxis risk.

Sepsis: RCOG and NICE both mandate rapid broad-spectrum IV antibiotics. RCOG: within 1 hour for women at high risk of sepsis with or without septic shock, as part of a sepsis bundle; urgent serum lactate with ≥4 mmol/l prompting immediate escalation; obstetric (modified) early warning scoring for monitoring; clindamycin with piperacillin/tazobactam or meropenem as empirical therapy for life-threatening puerperal sepsis; GBS-covering regimens for women pyrexial ≥38°C in labour; treatment of both woman and baby for postpartum iGAS plus barrier nursing. RCOG risk flags: amber for diabetes, caesarean birth or cervical cerclage within 6 weeks, membranes ruptured 18–24 hours; red for repeated presentation. NICE stratifies by NEWS2 (score 3–4 with a single parameter driving points managed as high risk), permits deferral of antibiotics at low/moderate risk while gathering diagnostic information but no delay once decided, and allows pre-hospital antibiotics when transfer/handover exceeds 1 hour. OpenRN adds culture-guided therapy (blood cultures before antibiotics; susceptibility testing) and antibiotics within an hour of shock diagnosis.

Not established: specific drugs or doses for surgical prophylaxis, gynecologic-procedure-specific regimens, redosing rules, duration of sepsis therapy, or comparative outcome data.

title: Post-Exposure Management of Blood-Borne Pathogens
summary:
This community represents the occupational health theme of managing health care worker exposure to blood-borne pathogens after a needlestick injury or splashing of body fluids in the perioperative/clinical setting. It describes a four-step sequence: immediate first aid, testing, prophylaxis, and follow-up surveillance.

Recommendations, with populations and conditions: (1) Washing or flushing the exposure site prevents blood-borne pathogen infection in health care workers exposed via needlestick injury or splashing of body fluids, and is conditioned on being performed immediately after exposure. (2) Blood-borne pathogen testing detects infection and is applied to both the exposed health care worker and the source client, conditioned on the source of the exposure being known. (3) Medical prophylaxis prevents infection in the exposed health care worker, with the condition that it depends on the results of testing. (4) Repeat testing monitors for infection in the exposed health care worker, again depending on the results of initial testing. The logic is therefore sequential and conditional: immediate decontamination is unconditional, whereas testing scope depends on source identifiability, and both prophylaxis and surveillance are contingent on test results.

Guideline contribution: all four relations derive from a single source, OpenRN Nursing Skills (Volume 2, p620). Because only one guideline body contributes, there are no points of disagreement, and no comparison of specificity between bodies is possible; this theme is uncorroborated by any second corpus source and would benefit from cross-referencing occupational health or infection-control standards.

What the community does NOT establish: it does not name specific pathogens (e.g., HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C), does not specify particular prophylactic drugs, doses, or regimens, and gives no numeric time windows for initiating prophylaxis or intervals for repeat testing. It does not define what testing modality is used, what constitutes a positive threshold, the action to take when the source is unknown, reporting or documentation requirements, or counseling, work restriction, and confidentiality obligations. Primary prevention (sharps safety, PPE) is likewise outside this community.
key_entities: washing or flushing the exposure site

title: Bowel Sound Assessment and Obstruction Detection
summary:
This community centres on gastrointestinal surveillance — using abdominal auscultation as the primary detection tool for bowel obstruction, with a secondary link to gastroenteritis, plus one pharmacologic prevention measure (laxatives) for a specific post-procedural population.

Main recommendations: (1) Auscultation of bowel sounds detects bowel obstruction when bowel sounds are absent or other signs of obstruction are present (OpenRN T2 p1183). (2) Auscultation of the abdomen detects both bowel obstruction and gastroenteritis when hyperactive bowel sounds are heard (OpenRN T2 p719). Together these establish that the assessment finding cuts both ways: absent sounds point toward obstruction, while hyperactive sounds may indicate either obstruction or gastroenteritis, so auscultation alone cannot discriminate between the two. (3) A laxative prevents bowel obstruction in clients who have received barium, applied in the post-procedural period (OpenRN T2 p1183) — the only preventive, population-specific intervention in the community, and the only one tied to a defined procedural trigger.

Contributing bodies: all four relations derive from a single source, OpenRN Nursing Skills/Fundamentals (Textbook 2), drawn from two separate pages. There is therefore no cross-body disagreement to reconcile; however, the two pages differ in specificity. Page 1183 is more specific in two respects: it names an intervention (laxative), a population (barium recipients), a timing (post-procedural), and it ties detection to absent bowel sounds plus corroborating signs of obstruction. Page 719 is broader, attaching hyperactive bowel sounds to two differential conditions without naming a population or timing.

What this community does NOT establish: no specific laxative agent, dose, route, or interval after barium administration; no auscultation technique details (quadrants, duration of listening, stethoscope placement) or frequency of reassessment; no thresholds defining "hyperactive," "hypoactive," or the time required to declare sounds absent; no escalation pathway, imaging, or surgical referral criteria once obstruction is suspected; no gynecologic- or perioperative-specific population, and no link to opioid use, anesthesia, or postoperative ileus; and no treatment recommendations for gastroenteritis.

title: Bowel Involvement in Gynecologic Pelvic Surgery
summary:
This community centres on the implications of bowel involvement during gynecologic/pelvic surgery, spanning two distinct concerns: antimicrobial prophylaxis when the bowel is entered, and postoperative functional and route-of-administration consequences of bowel surgery.

Antibiotic prophylaxis: the ERAS Society guidance (T1) recommends anaerobic coverage for pelvic surgery for cancer specifically when the bowel is entered (p5), and more broadly states that anaerobic antibiotic coverage applies to both bowel surgery and pelvic surgery for cancer as an addition to standard antibiotic prophylaxis chosen according to the planned procedure (p6). ERAS is thus the only contributor on prophylaxis, and it is more specific at p5 (the intraoperative trigger of bowel entry) than at p6 (a general 'add anaerobic coverage to prophylaxis for the planned procedure' statement).

Postoperative consequences: OpenRN (T2) contributes the nursing-care side. Bowel surgery increases the risk of bowel incontinence (p1179), which is relevant to continence assessment, skin integrity and discharge teaching. OpenRN also establishes that rectal medication administration is contraindicated after bowel surgery (p854) — a concrete safety rule for nurses selecting an alternative route for antiemetics, analgesics or laxatives in these patients.

Contributing bodies and differences: ERAS Society addresses intraoperative prevention in the oncologic pelvic surgery population; OpenRN addresses postoperative nursing risk and medication-route safety in patients who have had bowel surgery. They do not conflict; they cover different phases of care and are complementary rather than overlapping.

What this community does NOT establish: no specific anaerobic agent is named (e.g., no drug, dose, timing, redosing interval or duration of prophylaxis), and no threshold for when bowel entry is deemed to have occurred. It does not quantify the magnitude or duration of bowel incontinence risk, nor specify assessment tools, pelvic floor or continence interventions, or bowel-preparation practices. It also gives no alternative route recommendation to replace contraindicated rectal administration, and no time limit on how long that contraindication persists after surgery.

title: Antiseptic Safety Harms and Burn Prevention
summary: This community centres on the safety profile of skin/mucosal antiseptics and related agents, balancing infection prevention against chemical, thermal and ototoxic harm. Efficacy: chlorhexidine prevents surgical site infection and is first choice for urogynecological procedures, using alcohol-based preparations on skin and aqueous-based on mucous membranes (AUGS). Hand hygiene, supported by purchasing more effective or acceptable products, prevents nosocomial infection (CDC), and chlorhexidine itself can cause nosocomial infection if solutions are contaminated. Harms: chlorhexidine is contraindicated in hypersensitivity (NICE) and in inner/middle ear surgery due to ototoxicity (CDC; WHO notes ototoxicity when instilled into the middle ear); severe hypersensitivity including anaphylaxis is reported though incidence is low; eye damage occurs with high concentrations or preparations containing alcohols/surfactants, and CDC is more specific — conjunctivitis and severe corneal damage with >1% chlorhexidine on eye contact. NICE adds severe chemical injury in preterm babies from both alcohol-based and aqueous solutions, and burns from skin antiseptics in babies. WHO lists chlorhexidine, isopropanol and iodine 3% as contraindicated on mucous membranes and chlorhexidine as incompatible with soap; NICE contraindicates alcohol-based solutions on mucous membranes because of burn risk — a tension with AUGS's aqueous-mucosal allowance is not resolved. Diathermy/burn bundle (NICE): dry preparation by evaporation, avoid pooling of solution, and remove soaked materials, drapes or gowns before diathermy, since alcohol-based solutions are flammable. Hexachlorophene is contraindicated for bathing patients with burns or extensive sensitive skin and causes systemic blood absorption in surgical personnel after repeated use (CDC). Ototoxic antibiotics vancomycin and gentamicin are flagged by RCOG, with serum vancomycin level monitoring for ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity in patients receiving vancomycin. OpenRN adds burn prevention for impaired tactile sensation (safe water-heater temperature; thermometer-checked bath water) and conjunctivitis care (antibiotic eye drops for bacterial conjunctivitis; hand-hygiene education because it is highly contagious). Not established: numeric concentrations beyond >1% chlorhexidine, vancomycin target levels, evaporation/drying times, safe water temperatures, monitoring intervals, or comparative antiseptic effectiveness.

title: Hypotonic Fluid Therapy and Hypernatremia Monitoring
summary: This community centers on hypotonic IV fluid selection for hypernatremia and intracellular dehydration, the populations in whom those fluids are unsafe, and the monitoring required when sodium-containing hypertonic solutions are used instead. Two agents dominate: 0.45% sodium chloride (half-normal saline) and 5% dextrose in water. Both are indicated to treat hypernatremia, and 0.45% sodium chloride is additionally indicated for intracellular dehydration. Both are contraindicated in clients with trauma, burns, and liver disease, with the stated rationale that these hypotonic fluids would worsen hypovolemia in such clients. Liver disease appears twice in the graph: as a contraindication to both hypotonic fluids, and separately as a factor that increases the risk of maternal sepsis in women during pregnancy or the postpartum period — the only obstetric link in this cluster. Trauma likewise appears both as a fluid contraindication and as a procedural risk, with suctioning identified as increasing the risk of trauma. On the monitoring side, close monitoring is recommended for hypernatremia in clients receiving hypertonic solutions, and serum sodium level monitoring is specified for patients given hypertonic solutions containing sodium, conditioned on such solutions actually being administered. Contributing bodies are unevenly represented: OpenRN (Nursing Skills/Fundamentals, T2 pp. 1070, 1296, 1329) supplies all fluid, contraindication, and monitoring content and is the more granular source, distinguishing generic 'close monitoring' from specific serum sodium measurement; RCOG (T1 p. 4) contributes only the liver-disease-to-maternal-sepsis risk relation. There is no contradiction between them, but no integration either — RCOG does not address fluid choice, and OpenRN does not address pregnancy or postpartum populations. The community does NOT establish numeric sodium thresholds for diagnosing or correcting hypernatremia, correction rate limits, monitoring frequency or timing intervals, infusion volumes or rates, alternative fluids for trauma/burn/liver-disease clients, perioperative gynecologic-specific fluid protocols, or any causal link between hypotonic fluid use and maternal sepsis.

title: Anesthetic Choice, Cancer Recurrence, Chronic Pain
summary:
This community represents an anesthetic-technique theme within enhanced recovery care: the hypothesis that intraoperative and adjunct anesthetic choices may influence long-term oncologic and pain outcomes rather than only immediate recovery. All relations come from a single source, the ERAS Society guideline (Table 1, p7), so the theme is drawn from one guideline body with no competing or more specific recommendation from another society to compare against.

Four agents/strategies are linked to prevention of cancer recurrence: propofol, ketamine, lidocaine, and avoidance of inhalational anesthetic agents. In every one of these four cases the attached condition is identical and explicitly cautionary — 'evidence suggestive only.' No population is narrowed beyond the guideline's perioperative gynecologic surgical context, and no dose, infusion rate, timing, or duration is specified for propofol, lidocaine, or the inhalational-avoidance strategy.

Ketamine carries a second, separate indication: prevention of chronic postoperative pain, qualified as a 'potential benefit; optimum treatment duration and dose not yet identified.' This is the only relation in the community addressing a pain outcome, and it is notable that the guideline explicitly concedes that dose and duration remain undefined — so educators should not teach a specific ketamine regimen from this material.

For QI purposes, the practical takeaway is that total intravenous or opioid-sparing techniques built on propofol, ketamine, and lidocaine, with reduced reliance on volatile agents, are described as plausibly beneficial but not established. This community does NOT establish: any dose, concentration, infusion duration, or administration timing; any patient subgroup (tumour type, stage, age, comorbidity) in whom benefit is greater; any comparative ranking among propofol, ketamine, lidocaine, and volatile avoidance; any effect on survival, recurrence-free interval magnitude, or acute postoperative pain; and any safety, contraindication, or monitoring requirement. It also provides no corroboration or dissent from other guideline bodies, and no strength-of-recommendation or evidence-grade label beyond the qualitative 'suggestive only' and 'potential benefit' wording.

title: Caesarean Uterotonic Prophylaxis and Thromboprophylaxis Timing
summary:
This community covers pharmacological prevention of two major perioperative risks around caesarean and vaginal birth: postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) and venous thromboembolism (VTE).

Uterotonics: WHO states oxytocin, carbetocin, misoprostol and the fixed drug combination of oxytocin and ergometrine all prevent severe PPH when compared with placebo or no uterotonic in women giving birth. WHO positions carbetocin 100 µg IM/IV for all births where its cost is comparable to other effective uterotonics, and specifically in settings where oxytocin is unavailable or its quality cannot be guaranteed (vaginal birth or caesarean section); it must be given by skilled health personnel trained to administer injectable uterotonics, as the single uterotonic for PPH prevention. RCOG is more procedure-specific: carbetocin 100 micrograms as an intravenous bolus over 1 minute for women undergoing elective caesarean delivery, is licensed for the caesarean indication, and reduces the need for further uterotonics compared with oxytocin.

Thromboprophylaxis: RCOG advises that for women receiving antenatal LMWH having an elective caesarean section, the thromboprophylactic dose is given on the day prior to delivery and the morning dose is omitted on the day of delivery; for women on treatment doses of LMWH, treatment doses are omitted for 24 hours prior to surgery. RCOG also notes elective caesarean section at least doubles postpartum VTE risk compared with vaginal birth.

Contributing bodies: WHO (population-level uterotonic choice, availability/cost and skilled-personnel conditions) and RCOG (caesarean-specific dosing, licensing and LMWH timing). They do not conflict; RCOG adds route, dose-timing and comparative-efficacy detail, WHO adds resource-setting framing.

Not established here: no relations link uterotonics to VTE risk or to LMWH management; no postoperative LMWH restart timing, no regional-anaesthesia interval, no mechanical prophylaxis, no risk-scoring thresholds. Oxytocin dose, route and comparative superiority are not specified, misoprostol dose and route are absent, and no contraindications, adverse effects, or outcomes beyond severe PPH prevention are defined.
key_entities: fixed drug combination of oxytocin and ergometrine

title: Preoperative carbohydrate drink in abdominal surgery
summary:
Clinical theme: this small community captures a single element of preoperative preparation — the use of a carbohydrate drink (carbohydrate loading) as part of readiness for abdominal surgery within enhanced recovery-style care. It links one intervention entity (carbohydrate drink) to one surgical population (abdominal major or complex surgery) and to one care phase (preoperative).

Recommendations and their populations/conditions: the graph records that a carbohydrate drink APPLIES_TO abdominal major or complex surgery, with the population condition stated as 'people having abdominal major or complex surgery'. The same intervention is placed OCCURS_IN_PHASE preoperative, for the identical population. In practice, this means the guidance in this community concerns offering a carbohydrate drink before surgery to adults undergoing major or complex abdominal procedures — relevant to gynecologic services performing open or complex abdominal operations. Educationally, the teaching points are the population trigger (major/complex abdominal surgery, not minor or day-case procedures as far as this community states) and the timing anchor (preoperative phase).

Contributing bodies: only NICE contributes here, via a single source location (NICE T1, p9). There are therefore no cross-body agreements or disagreements to reconcile in this community, and no instance where one organisation is more specific than another; the entire theme rests on one guideline passage.

What this community does NOT establish: it gives no dose, volume, carbohydrate concentration or product name; no timing threshold (e.g. hours before induction or before anaesthesia), and no relationship to fasting rules for clear fluids or solids. It states no exclusions or cautions (for example diabetes, delayed gastric emptying, emergency surgery, or aspiration risk), no outcomes claimed (insulin resistance, length of stay, nausea, thirst or hunger), and no strength-of-evidence or recommendation grading. It does not address non-abdominal or minor gynecologic surgery, paediatric patients, intraoperative or postoperative nutrition, or who is accountable for administration and documentation. Local protocols must supply these operational details.

title: Prostaglandin uterotonics for postpartum haemorrhage
summary:
This community covers prostaglandin uterotonics — carboprost, sulprostone and misoprostol — used in postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) management and prevention, together with their shared gastrointestinal side-effect profile. The therapeutic core is carboprost for PPH: RCOG states carboprost treats postpartum haemorrhage generally, and specifically treats atonic haemorrhage in women with PPH at 250 micrograms intramuscularly, repeated every 15 minutes to a maximum total dose of 2 mg (eight doses). A second RCOG entry, for women with major postpartum haemorrhage, expresses the same regimen as 0.25 mg IM every 15 minutes up to 8 times, and adds an alternative route of 0.5 mg intramyometrial — a route and dose not mentioned in the first RCOG statement. Nurse educators should note these two RCOG passages are consistent in the IM dose/interval/ceiling but differ in specificity about the intramyometrial option and about whether the population is all PPH or 'major' PPH.

The safety strand comes from WHO, which links injectable prostaglandins — carboprost and sulprostone — to increased risk of diarrhoea in women receiving them for PPH prevention, and separately links misoprostol to increased risk of diarrhoea in women receiving misoprostol for PPH prevention. Practically, this means counselling and monitoring for diarrhoea whenever prostaglandins are given, whether by injection or as misoprostol, in the prevention context.

The two bodies contribute different angles rather than conflicting advice: RCOG supplies treatment dosing, timing and route for carboprost; WHO supplies the adverse-effect signal across the prostaglandin class in prevention.

What this community does NOT establish: no dose, route, timing or indication is given for misoprostol or sulprostone; no first-line ranking of carboprost against oxytocin, ergometrine or tranexamic acid; no contraindications (e.g. asthma), monitoring parameters, or management of the diarrhoea; no efficacy claim that sulprostone or misoprostol treats PPH; and no adverse-effect data for carboprost in the treatment (as opposed to prevention) population.

title: Cardiac Risk: Nicotine Therapy and Bereavement
summary:
This community centres on myocardial infarction (MI) as a shared node linking two otherwise distinct concerns: pharmacologic safety of smoking-cessation therapy in recently infarcted clients, and the cardiac consequences of bereavement in surviving family members.

Recommendation 1 (RNAO, Tobacco/smoking cessation guideline, T2 p54): nicotine replacement therapy (NRT) is temporarily contraindicated in clients in the immediate post-MI period. The stated condition is within 2 weeks of MI, where NRT should be used with caution. The contraindication is explicitly temporary and time-bounded rather than absolute, so the practical teaching point is timing: defer or cautiously individualise NRT during the first 2 weeks after infarction, then reassess.

Recommendation 2 (OpenRN, T2 p1221): bereavement increases the risk of both cardiomyopathy and myocardial infarction in surviving family members of the deceased. No time window, age band, or grief severity threshold is attached, so this is framed as a general risk association applicable to bereaved relatives.

Contributing bodies: RNAO supplies the medication-safety, time-specific guidance (a defined 2-week post-MI window and a named drug class, NRT); OpenRN supplies the psychosocial/bereavement-care perspective and is the only source naming cardiomyopathy. RNAO is the more specific of the two on timing and drug detail; OpenRN is broader in scope but vaguer in operational thresholds. The two sources do not contradict each other — they converge only on MI as an outcome/context, not on any shared intervention.

What this community does NOT establish: it gives no alternative cessation strategy (e.g., non-nicotine pharmacotherapy or behavioural support) for post-MI clients within the 2-week window, no dose, route, or formulation guidance for NRT, and no criteria for resuming NRT after 2 weeks. It does not state that bereaved clients require cardiac screening, nor any monitoring interval, follow-up duration, or intervention to mitigate bereavement-related cardiomyopathy or MI risk. It does not link the two recommendations — nothing here addresses NRT use in bereaved clients or smoking behaviour after bereavement — and it offers no incidence figures, mortality data, or strength-of-evidence grading.
key_entities: surviving family members of the deceased

title: Smoking Cessation for Perioperative Risk Reduction
summary:
This community centres on tobacco use as a modifiable perioperative and cardiovascular risk factor, and on smoking cessation as the principal preventive intervention, with antihypertensive therapy appearing as an adjacent cardiovascular risk-reduction measure.

Risk relations: smoking increases the risk of poor wound healing (OpenRN T2 p696) and of cardiovascular disease (RNAO T2 p16).

Recommendations and their populations/conditions: (1) Smoking cessation should occur in the preoperative phase, timed at least four weeks before surgery (ERAS Society T1 p1) — the only source specifying a timing threshold. (2) For clients who smoke, cessation prevents poor wound healing (OpenRN T2 p696) and infection (OpenRN T2 p663). (3) For smokers, cessation prevents target organ damage and vascular disease, and for those who stop smoking, cardiovascular disease risk declines by as much as 50% after 1 year, taking up to 10 years to reach the risk level of never-smokers (RNAO T2 p53). (4) For clients with uncomplicated hypertension, antihypertensive therapy prevents cardiovascular disease (RNAO T2 p59).

Contributing bodies and differences in emphasis: ERAS Society contributes the surgical timing anchor (four weeks preoperatively) but no outcome specifics; OpenRN frames cessation around surgical wound outcomes (healing, infection); RNAO is the most granular on chronic vascular outcomes, quantifying risk decline and time-to-parity, and is the only source linking hypertension pharmacotherapy to cardiovascular prevention. There is no contradiction between sources — they are complementary, differing in outcome focus (wound/infection versus cardiovascular/target organ) rather than in advice.

What is not established: no named smoking-cessation pharmacotherapy, nicotine replacement product, dose, counselling model, or follow-up interval; no named antihypertensive drug, class, or blood-pressure threshold defining "uncomplicated hypertension"; no gynecologic-procedure-specific populations; no guidance for clients who cannot stop four weeks before surgery or who quit intraoperatively/postoperatively; no cessation effect on other perioperative outcomes such as pulmonary complications, length of stay, or mortality; and no relapse-prevention or postoperative-phase recommendations.

title: Antihypertensive Therapy for Cardiovascular Risk Reduction
summary:
This community represents a small, tightly focused theme on pharmacological blood pressure management: antihypertensive medication as both a treatment for high blood pressure and a means of preventing cardiovascular events. Both relations derive from a single guideline body, RNAO (Registered Nurses' Association of Ontario), Tool 2, at pages 59 and 116.

Two recommendations anchor the community. First, antihypertensive medication prevents cardiovascular events in hypertensive clients, with the stated condition that protection is broadly similar across the five drug classes — that is, the guideline emphasises class-equivalent cardiovascular benefit rather than privileging any one agent. For a nurse educator, the teaching point is that the outcome driver is blood pressure lowering and adherence, not the specific class chosen. Second, antihypertensive medication treats high blood pressure in people already taking medication to control it, with the explicit condition that medication should not be stopped while following the DASH eating plan. This is a patient-safety and counselling message: dietary intervention (DASH) is adjunctive, not a substitute for pharmacotherapy, and clients beginning DASH should be advised to continue their prescribed antihypertensives unless a prescriber directs otherwise. This is directly relevant to perioperative gynecologic nursing where patients may self-modify medication regimens around lifestyle change or surgery.

Because only RNAO Tool 2 contributes, there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile; the two entries are complementary rather than conflicting, with p116 being the more specific and actionable (naming DASH and a do-not-stop instruction) and p59 the more general risk-reduction statement.

What this community does NOT establish: it names none of the five drug classes, gives no specific drugs, no blood pressure thresholds or targets, no dosing, no timing of initiation, titration, or perioperative hold/resume instructions, and no monitoring parameters. It does not define which cardiovascular events are prevented or quantify effect size, does not address gynecologic-surgery-specific populations, pregnancy, or contraindications, and offers no guidance on when medication may legitimately be tapered or discontinued.

title: IV Therapy Complications: Pulmonary Edema, Air Embolism
summary:
This community represents the assessment, prevention, and emergency management of two vascular/respiratory complications of intravenous therapy: fluid volume excess progressing to pulmonary edema, and air embolism.

Monitoring: For clients receiving intravenous fluids, auscultate lung sounds for crackles and ask about dyspnea to detect fluid volume excess.
