For clients already in excess fluid volume, respiratory status monitoring targets pulmonary edema — watch for increasing anxiety, dyspnea, orthopnea, rising respiratory rate, and falling oxygen saturation; auscultation should detect new or worsening fine crackles, which warrant notifying the provider. Hypertonic solutions are flagged as increasing the risk of pulmonary edema.

Pulmonary edema response (patients receiving IV therapy, when pulmonary edema is suspected): raise the head of the bed and administer oxygen.

Air embolism: catheter insertion is identified as the risk-increasing event in patients receiving IV therapy. Prevention measures are concrete and mechanical — fill the drip chamber one-third to one-half, ensure all intravenous connections are tight, and use clamps on the intravenous system when it is not in use. If air embolism is suspected: occlude the source of air entry, administer oxygen at 100%, and place the patient in Trendelenburg position on the left side when that position is not contraindicated.

Guideline contribution: all relations derive from a single source, OpenRN Nursing Skills/Fundamentals (Tier 2), across three passages — p1111 (assessment and monitoring for fluid volume excess), p1329 (hypertonic solution risk), and p1363 (IV complication prevention and emergency management). Because there is only one contributing body, there are no inter-guideline disagreements; p1363 is the most operationally specific (positions, oxygen concentration, drip chamber fill fraction), while p1111 is most specific on assessment findings.

Not established: no numeric thresholds for respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, infusion rate, or fluid volume; no named diuretics or other drugs; no specified reassessment interval or duration of oxygen therapy; no gynecologic- or perioperative-specific population qualifiers; and no guidance on which hypertonic solutions or concentrations carry greatest risk.
key_entities: trendelenburg position on the left side
raising the head of the bed
filling the drip chamber one-third to one-half
ensuring all intravenous connections are tight
use of clamps on the intravenous system
occlusion of the source of air entry

title: Preventing Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infection Perioperatively
summary: This community centres on indwelling urinary catheters as a modifiable source of harm, principally catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI), and the bundle of insertion, maintenance, removal and program-level controls that prevent it. Risk factors named are female sex, older age, impaired immunity (CDC T1 p10, p36) and a history of prior UTI (OpenRN T2 p1241); catheters also increase risk of transmission of harmful microorganisms (WHO T1 p211), falls in clients tethered to equipment (OpenRN T2 p395), and infection with longer-term catheterization (AUGS T2 p11). Core recommendations: avoid catheterization whenever possible and never for incontinence management in patients or nursing home residents; verify CDC-approved indications before insertion and advocate an alternative (e.g. female external urinary catheter for women) if unmet; use aseptic insertion technique with sterile gloves/equipment by properly trained persons in acute care; perform hand hygiene before and after insertion and during any device manipulation; select the smallest appropriate catheter (typically 14 French) to prevent CAUTI and urinary tissue trauma; maintain a closed, preconnected sealed catheter-tubing junction drainage system with unobstructed urine flow. Removal should occur as soon as possible postoperatively, preferably within 24 hours, unless continued indications exist; ERAS Society (T1 p2) concurs for gynecologic oncology surgery (<24 h postop). Systemic antimicrobials are advised only where clinical indications exist (e.g. bacteriuria at catheter removal after urologic surgery), not routinely; antimicrobial/antiseptic-impregnated catheters are reserved for when rates are not falling despite a comprehensive strategy. System-level levers include facility risk-assessment-based quality improvement programs, standardized CAUTI surveillance in high-use units, unit-specific rate feedback to nursing staff, and nurse-directed removal protocols permitting RN removal without a physician order. CDC contributes the most granular thresholds and program elements; OpenRN adds bedside technique detail (French size, external catheters); WHO addresses broader transmission and disposable filters; RCOG covers hourly urometer output monitoring and impaired immunity as a maternal sepsis risk. The community does not establish CAUTI incidence rates, antibiotic agents/doses, catheter materials beyond impregnation, or comparative effectiveness of individual bundle elements, though CDC estimates 17–69% of CAUTIs may be preventable.
key_entities: CAUTI surveillance and quality improvement program
female sex, older age, impaired immunity, prior UTI

title: IV Fluid, Electrolyte and Drug Safety in Cardiorenal Risk
summary: This community covers safe intravenous fluid selection, glycemic control, and drug-related cardiorenal risk, converging on three vulnerable states: heart failure, renal failure, and cellular dehydration. OpenRN T2 p1070 is the most granular source on fluids: hypertonic 3% sodium chloride treats severe hyponatremia and cerebral edema but is contraindicated in heart failure, renal failure, and conditions caused by cellular dehydration; 5% dextrose/0.45% sodium chloride and 5% dextrose/lactated Ringer's treat hypoglycemia but carry the same three contraindications. OpenRN T2 p1329 adds that hypertonic solutions increase risk of pulmonary edema, fluid volume overload, and cellular dehydration, and are contraindicated in diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), where hypotonic solutions are instead used to push fluid back into dehydrated cells (DKA, hyperosmolar hyperglycemia). Heart failure history itself increases risk of fluid volume excess (OpenRN T2 p1111). NICE T1 p69 flags intravenous fluid administration as contraindicated with renal failure in patients aged 16+ at high sepsis risk by NEWS2 — the only sepsis-specific, age-bounded statement. Drug safety: all NSAIDs except aspirin increase heart failure and renal failure risk, with risk higher above directed dose or duration (OpenRN T2, p825); ketorolac requires renal function monitoring, with dose reduction at age 65 and over. RNAO T2 contributes cardiology-specific cautions: non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are cautioned against (not absolutely contraindicated) in heart failure (p127), and ACE inhibitors increase renal failure risk in susceptible clients — bilateral renovascular disease, volume depletion, or concurrent NSAID use (p128, p141). RNAO also specifies monitoring: sodium, potassium and creatinine bloodwork every 6–12 months for thiazide diuretic patients (electrolyte imbalance, p140), and for ACE inhibitor clients to detect hyperkalemia and renal failure (p128). Glycemia: OpenRN T2 p1078 recommends blood glucose monitoring, often hourly per agency policy, for insulin infusions, and IV dextrose to prevent hypoglycemia when insulin is given for potassium reduction; ERAS_Society T1 (p2, p4) echoes regular monitoring during insulin infusions and links hypoglycemia to mortality (p6). Not established: specific fluid rates or volumes, glucose or sodium numeric thresholds, gynecologic-surgery-specific populations, NSAID dose limits, or how these cautions interact perioperatively.
key_entities: bloodwork monitoring of sodium, potassium and creatinine

title: Waist Circumference Screening for Central Obesity
summary:
This community represents a small, tightly focused theme: the use of waist circumference measurement as a bedside anthropometric screening tool to detect central (abdominal) obesity, and the cardiovascular significance of that finding. It is the assessment-and-risk-stratification node of the corpus rather than a treatment pathway.

Three relations define the theme. First, waist circumference measurement detects central obesity (RNAO Toolkit 2, p45). Second, the same measurement detects abdominal obesity (RNAO T2, p119) — the graph treats these as two separately sourced statements, appearing in different sections of the same document, with 'central' and 'abdominal' obesity recorded as distinct entities rather than explicitly reconciled as synonyms. Third, central obesity increases the risk of adverse cardiovascular outcome (RNAO T2, p45), which is the only downstream clinical consequence captured here and the reason the measurement is recommended.

Only one guideline body contributes: the Registered Nurses' Association of Ontario (RNAO), via Toolkit 2. There is therefore no inter-body disagreement to reconcile; the only internal variation is terminological (central vs. abdominal obesity) and the fact that the p45 material links the finding to cardiovascular risk while the p119 material records detection alone, without attaching a risk statement. For educators, p45 is the more specific of the two citations.

What this community does NOT establish is substantial and should be stated plainly in any teaching or QI use. No population is specified — there is nothing here restricting or extending the recommendation to gynecologic surgical patients, any age band, or any comorbidity group. No condition or trigger for measurement is attached. No numeric thresholds are given: no centimetre cut-points for men or women, no BMI comparison, no waist-to-hip ratio. No measurement technique, anatomical landmark, timing (preoperative, day-of-surgery, postoperative), or frequency is specified. The 'adverse cardiovascular outcome' is unelaborated — no named events, no perioperative complication such as myocardial infarction or venous thromboembolism, and no effect size or risk magnitude. No drugs, interventions, referrals, or perioperative management changes follow from a positive finding in these relations. Local protocols must supply all thresholds and technique.

title: Preventing Medication Dose Calculation Errors
summary: This small community centres on medication dose calculation safety: the causal link between a calculation error and patient harm, and the two practical safeguards the corpus attaches to it. The single risk relation states that a calculation error increases the risk of a major adverse event, with the population explicitly narrowed to patients receiving medications with narrow therapeutic windows — i.e. agents where a small arithmetic slip translates directly into toxicity or subtherapeutic dosing. Two preventive recommendations are offered. First, clinicians performing drug calculations should use a calculator, with the condition specified as high-stress and/or high-risk situations — relevant to perioperative settings where cognitive load is high. Second, the calculated dose should be checked, with the condition given as at the point of dispensing drugs; no population is specified for this relation, so it reads as a general dispensing practice rather than one limited to a patient subgroup. Together the three relations form a simple hazard–barrier model useful for teaching: identify the high-consequence drug class, then apply a computational aid plus an independent verification step. Only one guideline body contributes here: the WHO (WHO Patient Safety curriculum, Topic 1, p242), and all three relations derive from that same page, so there are no inter-body disagreements or differences in specificity to reconcile; equally, there is no corroboration from a second source. Important limits: the community names no specific drugs, no numeric thresholds (no mg/kg limits, no concentration or infusion-rate cut-offs), no timings or frequencies for re-checking, and no definition of what constitutes a 'narrow therapeutic window' or a 'major adverse event'. It does not specify who should perform the check (independent double-check versus self-check), does not distinguish nurse from pharmacist or prescriber roles, does not address electronic prescribing, smart pumps, or standardised concentrations, and contains no gynecologic- or perioperative-specific population qualifiers. Quality-improvement leads should therefore treat this as a high-level principle requiring local operationalisation.

title: Chemical Phlebitis Prevention and Management
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: the prevention and management of chemical phlebitis in patients receiving intravenous infusion therapy — a vein-irritation complication relevant to perioperative gynecologic patients who commonly receive IV medications and fluids.

Prevention: adherence to parenteral drug therapy guidelines is identified as the preventive measure for patients receiving intravenous medications, with the condition specified as including the appropriate amount of solution and the appropriate rate of infusion. In other words, the graph attributes prevention to correct dilution volume plus correct infusion rate, applied to all patients on IV medications rather than to any narrower subgroup.

Treatment: for patients who already have chemical phlebitis, three interventions are given, each conditioned on evaluation of the infusion therapy and applied 'if indicated': (1) slowing the rate of infusion; (2) using a more dilute infusate; and (3) removing the vascular access device. The structure implies a graded approach anchored in reassessment of the infusion itself, with device removal being the most invasive option, but the graph does not rank or sequence them.

Contributing bodies: all four relations derive from a single source, OpenRN (Open Resources for Nursing) Nursing Skills, Tier 2, p. 1363. There is therefore no cross-guideline comparison possible here — no competing or more specific recommendation from a professional infusion-therapy or surgical society appears in this community, and no divergence or conflict can be documented.

What this community does NOT establish: it names no specific drugs, vesicants, irritants, or pH/osmolarity thresholds; no numeric infusion rates, dilution ratios, or time limits; no assessment scale or phlebitis grading criteria; no dwell-time or site-rotation intervals; and no signs/symptoms or diagnostic definition of chemical phlebitis. It does not distinguish peripheral from central vascular access devices, does not address mechanical, bacterial, or post-infusion phlebitis, and specifies no gynecologic- or perioperative-specific population, dosing, or monitoring frequency. Educators should supplement it with dedicated infusion-therapy standards before building competency or QI metrics.
key_entities: adherence to parenteral drug therapy guidelines

title: Chest Palpation for Air Leak, Crepitus
summary:
This community is narrow and tightly focused: the use of manual chest palpation as a bedside assessment technique to detect two specific findings around a chest tube site — air leak and crepitus (subcutaneous emphysema). Both relations share an identical population and condition, making this a single, coherent recommendation rather than a set of competing ones.

Main recommendation: perform chest palpation to detect air leak and crepitus in patients who currently have a chest tube in place or who have recently had a chest tube removed. The stated condition for both detections is that palpation be carried out near the tube insertion site — i.e., the assessment is site-directed rather than a general chest exam. The clinical implication for educators is that a single palpation maneuver at the insertion site yields two distinct assessment data points, and that the assessment window extends beyond the dwell time of the tube into the post-removal period.

Guideline contribution: only one source underpins this community — OpenRN (Nursing Skills, Open RN, Volume 2, p616) — supplying both relations. Because there is a single contributing body, there are no inter-guideline disagreements, no differences in specificity, and no conflicting populations or conditions to reconcile within this theme.

What this community does NOT establish: it gives no frequency or timing for palpation (no shift-based, hourly, or post-removal interval), no duration for how long after removal assessment should continue, and no definition of "recently removed." It does not specify technique details (pressure, hand position, extent of the area palpated), nor grading or documentation standards for crepitus extent. It does not state escalation thresholds, notification criteria, or any intervention for a detected air leak or crepitus (for example dressing reinforcement, occlusive dressing, imaging, or provider notification). No drugs, doses, oxygenation targets, drainage volumes, or water-seal chamber findings are referenced, and no adjunctive or confirmatory assessments (auscultation, chest radiograph, bubbling in the drainage system) are linked here. It is also silent on pediatric, obstetric, or gynecologic-surgery-specific variation despite the corpus context.
key_entities: patients with a chest tube or recently removed chest tube

title: Nonpharmacologic Approaches to Pain Management
summary:
This community represents nonpharmacologic, complementary and physical approaches to pain management, spanning two distinct pain populations: musculoskeletal pain in pregnancy and chronic pain in general nursing clients.

For pregnant women, WHO (T1 p14) addresses low back and pelvic pain with two different relation types. Regular exercise is recommended as prevention of low back and pelvic pain, to be sustained throughout pregnancy. For treatment of existing low back and pelvic pain, WHO names acupuncture and physiotherapy, explicitly conditioned on the woman's preferences and the options available in the setting — i.e., offered as preference-sensitive options rather than mandated therapy.

For clients with chronic pain, OpenRN (T2 p825) groups a broad set of complementary health approaches as treatments: acupuncture, massage therapy, meditation, relaxation techniques, spinal manipulation, tai chi, and yoga. The umbrella entity 'complementary health approach' is itself linked to chronic pain treatment (OpenRN T2), signalling that these modalities are taught as a category rather than as individually indicated therapies.

Contributing bodies and differences: WHO is pregnancy-specific and narrower — only acupuncture and physiotherapy for treatment, plus exercise for prevention — but is more specific about timing (throughout pregnancy) and decision-making (based on preferences and availability). OpenRN is broader in modality list but non-specific about condition, frequency, dose, or duration, and attaches no preference or availability caveat. Acupuncture is the sole modality shared by both bodies, bridging the pregnant and chronic pain populations.

What this community does NOT establish: no drugs, doses, thresholds, session counts, or treatment durations are specified; no comparative effectiveness or ranking among the modalities; no evidence-strength grading. It does not state that complementary approaches replace pharmacologic analgesia, nor address safety, contraindications, or use of yoga, tai chi, massage, meditation, spinal manipulation or relaxation in pregnancy specifically. Perioperative or postoperative gynecologic pain is not addressed, and physiotherapy is not extended to chronic pain, nor exercise to chronic pain prevention.

title: Catheter Route, Drainage and Duration Choices
summary: This community covers strategies to prevent catheter-associated bacteriuria and symptomatic UTI (SUTI) by choosing the catheter route, maintaining closed drainage, and minimising catheterisation duration. CDC (T1) supplies nearly all recommendations. Maintain a sterile closed urinary drainage system in all catheterised patients to prevent bacteriuria (p23). For male patients who need a urinary collection device but lack an indication for an indwelling catheter (e.g. no urinary retention or bladder outlet obstruction), external (condom) catheters reduce a composite outcome of SUTI, bacteriuria or death — low-quality evidence, with differences most pronounced in men without dementia; in cooperative men without retention or obstruction, external catheters are also an alternative to indwelling urethral catheters alongside intermittent catheterisation (p37). Suprapubic catheters, in selected populations (primarily postoperative and spinal cord injury patients), reduce urethral stricture and bacteriuria (low-quality evidence) versus indwelling urethral catheters, but carry a trade-off: prolonged duration of catheterisation (p37). Duration matters: shorter postoperative catheterisation — specifically 1 day rather than 3 or 5 days — prevents bacteriuria in postoperative patients (p39). A clamp-and-release (bladder training) strategy increases bacteriuria compared with free drainage over 72 hours and should not be used (p39). OpenRN (T2 p1241) contributes a single, procedure-level link: urethral stricture, or obstruction/scar tissue in the bladder or urethra, causes failure of catheter advancement during catheterisation — complementing CDC's epidemiological framing of stricture as an outcome to be prevented. CDC is more specific on populations, comparators and evidence quality; OpenRN is more specific about bedside insertion difficulty. The community does NOT establish gynecologic- or female-specific guidance (external catheter evidence is male-only), does not define catheter materials, lubricants, antiseptics or antimicrobial agents, gives no insertion technique, securement, meatal care or bag-emptying details, no criteria for selecting suprapubic placement, no mortality or stricture-rate thresholds, and no management pathway once catheter advancement fails.

title: Cefazolin Prophylaxis Timing and Dosing
summary:
This community represents preoperative antibiotic prophylaxis for gynecologic and urogynecologic surgery, centred on cefazolin as first-choice agent, its weight-based dosing, its timing relative to skin incision, and its role in preventing surgical site and postoperative infection.

Core recommendations: AUGS (T2) states cefazolin 2 gm intravenously prevents postoperative infection in women undergoing hysterectomy, and applies to urogynecological surgery as 2 gm IV within 1 hour of skin incision, increased to 3 g for patients over 120 kg. AUGS also credits both cefazolin and amoxicillin-clavulanic acid with preventing surgical site infection when given within 60 minutes of skin incision. The ERAS Society (T1) applies cefazolin to gynecologic interventions where antibiotic prophylaxis is mandatory, names amoxicillin-clavulanic acid an equivalent alternative, and recommends an increased antibiotic dose for obese patients (BMI > 35 or > 100 kg). CDC (T1) frames cefazolin as agent of first choice for clean operations and as providing adequate coverage for many clean-contaminated operations, and ties dosing to skin incision timing: a full therapeutic dose (1–2 g) in adult patients no more than 30 minutes before incision.

Points of difference and specificity: the three bodies diverge on the timing window — AUGS allows within 60 minutes / 1 hour of incision, whereas CDC is stricter at no more than 30 minutes before incision. Dose statements also differ: CDC cites 1–2 g for adults generally, while AUGS specifies 2 gm for hysterectomy/urogynecologic surgery with a 3 g escalation above 120 kg. ERAS acknowledges obesity-based dose increase but sets its thresholds as BMI > 35 or > 100 kg without naming the resulting dose, making AUGS the more concrete source on weight-based dosing.

Not established here: no redosing intervals or intraoperative repeat dosing, no guidance for beta-lactam allergy or non-cefazolin/non-amoxicillin-clavulanate alternatives, no duration of postoperative prophylaxis, no reconciliation of the 30- versus 60-minute windows, no pediatric population, and no outcome or infection-rate data supporting these choices.

title: Inner Cannula Care Prevents Tracheostomy Obstruction
summary:
Clinical theme: this community addresses routine inner cannula care (cleaning or replacement) as the core airway-maintenance intervention for patients with a tracheostomy tube, and how that care is sequenced with tracheostomy dressing changes.

Main recommendations and their populations/conditions:
1) Cleaning or replacement of the inner cannula prevents tracheostomy tube obstruction in patients with a tracheostomy, conditional on the care being performed regularly — at least every 12–24 hours (OpenRN T2 p1314). This is the only explicit numeric interval in the community.
2) The same intervention prevents airway occlusion by secretions in patients with a tracheostomy tube, when performed frequently according to agency policy (OpenRN T2 p1285). Here the frequency is delegated to local policy rather than a fixed threshold.
3) Sequencing: the timing of inner cannula cleaning/replacement determines the timing of the tracheostomy dressing change — the inner cannula should be replaced prior to changing the dressing, to prevent secretions from soiling the new dressing (OpenRN T2 p1314).

Contributing guideline bodies: all three relations derive from a single source corpus, OpenRN (Nursing Skills, Textbook 2), across two pages (p1285 and p1314). There is no cross-organisational disagreement; the difference is one of specificity. Page 1314 is more prescriptive (a concrete 12–24 hour minimum frequency, plus explicit ordering relative to the dressing change), whereas page 1285 states only "frequently according to agency policy." Educators should reconcile these by teaching the 12–24 hour floor while deferring to institutional policy where it is more frequent.

What the community does NOT establish: it names no drugs, cleaning solutions, disinfectants, or suction parameters; no cuff pressure, humidification, or tube size specifications; no criteria distinguishing when to clean versus replace a disposable inner cannula; no post-operative or gynecologic-surgery-specific populations, and no pediatric versus adult differentiation. It does not define dressing change frequency itself, outcomes such as infection or decannulation risk, competency/credentialing requirements, or escalation steps if obstruction occurs despite cannula care.
key_entities: cleaning or replacement of the inner cannula

title: Fall Risk Factors and Prevention Precautions
summary:
This community is a comprehensive fall risk-and-prevention map centred on the single outcome 'fall', drawn entirely from OpenRN Nursing Skills/Fundamentals (Tome 2). Risk factors cluster into: (1) medications — polypharmacy in clients on several prescriptions, sedating and high-risk medications causing sedation, confusion, impaired balance, orthostatic BP change or frequent urination, benzodiazepines (especially the frail elderly), anticholinergics in older adults (dizziness, drowsiness), gabapentin (sleepiness, weakness, unsteadiness), lecanemab, sleep aids in hospitalized clients; (2) cognition/behaviour — dementia, delirium, psychosis when agitated and confused, cognitive impairment; (3) mobility/physiology — gait and mobility problems, generalized weakness, need for an assistive device, orthostatic hypotension with light-headedness or dizziness on standing, loss of balance during position changes in older adults; (4) sensory — impaired/decreased visual acuity (including clients needing but not wearing glasses, compounded by an unfamiliar hospital environment), sensory impairment; (5) elimination — urinary frequency, frequent toileting needs; (6) environment/process — indwelling urinary catheters and IV poles tethering clients to equipment, inadequate handoff communication, and recent falls (e.g., a fall within the past three months).

Prevention recommendations are population-matched: universal fall precautions for all clients; scheduled hourly rounding integrating fall prevention with care; scheduled rounding/regular toileting for frequent toileting needs; call light within reach with demonstrated accurate use, and using it to request ambulation assistance; clearing room obstacles when leaving the room (including after dressing changes); properly fitting, securely fastened non-skid footwear during ambulation; gait belts and well-maintained assistive devices within safe reach for impaired gait/mobility; intense supervision for cognitively impaired clients who are agitated or wandering; clean corrective lenses within reach; changing positions slowly in older adults; assisting a dizzy client to sit on a chair or floor; medication review by a pharmacist (or prescriber if unavailable) to taper, stop or substitute safer alternatives; medication-related fall risk evaluation on admission and at regular intervals; client and caregiver education; and home safety adaptation after discharge (toilet seat height, grab bars, rubber shower mat).

Only one guideline body contributes, so no cross-body disagreement is demonstrable; page-level entries vary in specificity (p395 most granular). Notably absent: any validated fall-risk scoring tool or threshold, bed-alarm or restraint guidance, post-fall management, injury outcomes, and any gynecologic or perioperative-specific fall content.

title: Client Education Preventing Antibiotic Resistance
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: nurse-delivered client education on antibiotic adherence as the intervention that prevents antibiotic resistance. All three relations converge on the same causal claim, differing only in how specifically they describe the adherence behaviour.

Main recommendations and their populations/conditions:
1) Client education prevents antibiotic resistance for clients prescribed antibiotic therapy, with the condition that the teaching explicitly addresses behaviours such as stopping the medication early (OpenRN Tome 2, p639). This is the broadest framing and names the education itself as the preventive act.
2) Completion of the entire antibiotic course prevents antibiotic resistance in clients prescribed an antibiotic, with the added instruction that clients contact their provider if they are unable to complete the course (OpenRN T2 p639). This adds a concrete escalation pathway rather than leaving non-completion unaddressed.
3) Completing the prescribed length of antibiotic therapy prevents antibiotic resistance in clients prescribed antibiotics, specifically even if they feel better in a few days (OpenRN T2 p663). This is the most specific about the trigger for premature discontinuation — symptomatic improvement — which is the teachable moment for the nurse.

Contributing bodies: only one source corpus contributes here, OpenRN (Nursing Pharmacology/Skills, Tome 2, pages 639 and 663). There is therefore no inter-body disagreement; the two page-level entries are mutually reinforcing, with p639 supplying the education framing plus the "contact provider" fallback, and p663 supplying the "even if you feel better" rationale. For teaching purposes these can be merged into one message without conflict.

What this community does NOT establish: it names no specific antibiotic agents, doses, or classes; no course lengths, day thresholds, or timing windows; no gynecologic or perioperative population specifics (no surgical prophylaxis, no pre- or post-operative timing); no documentation, audit, or stewardship-program requirements; and no outcome data quantifying resistance reduction. It also does not describe how to assess adherence, what to do about missed doses, or any pediatric, pregnancy, or renal/hepatic modifications.
key_entities: completing prescribed length of antibiotic therapy

title: IV Fluid Tonicity Monitoring and Complications
summary:
This community centers on tonicity-based intravenous fluid therapy and the surveillance required to catch its neurologic, hemodynamic, and respiratory complications. The core recommendation is close monitoring, differentiated by fluid type: for clients receiving hypertonic solutions, monitor for hypervolemia, hypernatremia, and respiratory distress (with hypervolemia monitoring specifically indicated while hypertonic fluids are being administered); for clients receiving 5% dextrose in water, monitor for hypovolemia, hypotension, and cerebral edema; for clients receiving 0.9% normal saline, monitor for hypervolemia, especially in those with heart failure or renal failure. For patients receiving hypotonic solutions, patient status monitoring for hypotension and cerebral edema should occur while the infusion runs, because hypotonic IV solutions increase the risk of cerebral edema if too much fluid shifts out of the intravascular compartment into the cells. Conversely, hypertonic solutions — named specifically as hypertonic 3% sodium chloride — are treatments for cerebral edema in patients with cerebral edema, making tonicity both a cause and a therapy depending on direction of fluid shift.

A secondary respiratory thread connects to this: respiratory distress increases the risk of respiratory arrest; a baseline respiratory assessment prior to suctioning detects respiratory distress in patients requiring airway suctioning; and mechanical ventilation treats severe respiratory distress and treats respiratory acidosis when noninvasive interventions are unsuccessful.

All relations derive from a single guideline body, OpenRN Nursing Skills/Advanced Skills (Textbook 2, pages 1070, 1093, 1285, 1293, 1329), so there are no cross-body disagreements. Internally, p1070 is the most fluid-specific (naming 5% dextrose in water, 0.9% normal saline, 3% sodium chloride), while p1329 adds the mechanistic rationale for hypotonic-solution risk.

The community does not establish infusion rates, volume limits, sodium or osmolality thresholds, monitoring frequencies or durations, escalation criteria, or any gynecologic/perioperative-specific populations. It offers no treatment for hypervolemia, hypernatremia, hypovolemia, or hypotension, and no link between fluid therapy and respiratory arrest prevention beyond distress recognition.

title: Coagulopathy Recognition and Management in Haemorrhage
summary:
This community centres on coagulopathy as a complication of major haemorrhage — its causes, detection, treatment, and the drug it temporarily contraindicates — drawing chiefly on obstetric haemorrhage guidance plus general surgical and transfusion advice.

Risk factors: NICE (T1 p24) notes colloid administration increases coagulopathy risk in adults undergoing surgery. RCOG (T1 p20) identifies placental abruption and amniotic fluid embolism as conditions associated with EARLY coagulopathy.

Treatment: because of that early onset, RCOG advises fresh frozen plasma transfusion earlier than standard timing for women with placental abruption or amniotic fluid embolism. WHO (T1 p42) gives a ratio-based rule for a broader population — patients receiving packed red blood cells for haemorrhage should receive fresh-frozen plasma, when available, for each one or two units of packed red cells. These are complementary rather than conflicting: RCOG modifies timing for specific obstetric triggers, WHO sets a general dosing proportion.

Monitoring: RCOG (T1 p18) recommends repeated coagulation testing in women with continued bleeding, explicitly interpreting trends rather than single measurements. Post-event, RCOG (T1 p32) recommends testing for coagulopathies in women who have experienced a major postpartum haemorrhage, but only if there are other indicators — i.e. not routinely.

Thromboprophylaxis: RCOG (T1 p27) states low molecular weight heparin is temporarily contraindicated in women with coagulopathy, delayed while the coagulopathy persists — a key nursing handover point when VTE prophylaxis is withheld.

What this community does NOT establish: no numeric laboratory thresholds (no PT/APTT, fibrinogen, platelet or INR triggers), no FFP volumes or mL/kg doses, no testing intervals or definition of "repeated", no named alternative products (cryoprecipitate, fibrinogen concentrate, tranexamic acid, platelets), no criteria for what counts as an "other indicator" prompting coagulopathy testing, and no timeframe for restarting low molecular weight heparin once coagulopathy resolves. Which colloid, and whether crystalloid is preferred, is also not specified here.

title: Cerclage, PPROM and Maternal Sepsis Risk
summary:
This community represents the theme of obstetric infection risk arising from cervical instrumentation and loss of membrane integrity — specifically how cervical cerclage and preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM) predispose pregnant and postpartum women to sepsis, maternal sepsis and coliform (Gram-negative enteric) infection. All relations derive from a single guideline body, RCOG (Table 1, pp. 3–4), so the theme is internally consistent rather than contested.

Key content: (1) Cervical cerclage increases the risk of sepsis in patients with suspected sepsis where the cerclage constitutes an invasive procedure within the last 6 weeks — an explicitly time-bounded criterion flagged as an amber flag denoting moderate risk. This is the most specific statement in the community, giving both a window (6 weeks) and a triage colour/severity (amber, moderate). (2) Cervical cerclage increases the risk of maternal sepsis in women during pregnancy or the postpartum period — a broader, condition-free population statement. (3) Cervical cerclage increases the risk of coliform infection in pregnant women. (4) PPROM likewise increases the risk of coliform infection in pregnant women, making coliform infection the shared downstream outcome linking an iatrogenic/procedural risk factor and a spontaneous obstetric event.

Practical implication for educators: a recent cerclage should be actively sought in the history of any pregnant or recently delivered woman being assessed for suspected sepsis, and treated as an amber (moderate-risk) trigger if performed within 6 weeks; coliform organisms should be anticipated in both cerclage and PPROM presentations.

What this community does NOT establish: no antibiotic agents, doses, routes or timings; no observation thresholds (temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, lactate, white cell count); no escalation pathway, red-flag criteria, or sepsis-bundle timing; no guidance on cerclage removal, prophylaxis before or after cerclage, or PPROM latency management; no perioperative nursing tasks or monitoring frequency; and no comparison with other guideline bodies (e.g. NICE, WHO) since only RCOG contributes. Risk magnitude is qualitative only — no incidence figures or relative risks are given.

title: VTE Risk Assessment and Multimodal Prophylaxis
summary:
This community covers hospital-wide venous thromboembolism (VTE) prevention: risk assessment, pharmacological thromboprophylaxis, and mechanical measures (anti-embolism stockings, intermittent pneumatic compression), plus basic care such as maintaining hydration and early mobilisation for anyone admitted at increased VTE risk (NICE p9).

Assessment: NICE requires VTE risk assessment for all medical patients as soon as possible after admission or by first consultant review (or in A&E if not admitted within 12 hours of arrival), and for all surgical and trauma patients using a tool published by a national UK body, professional network or peer-reviewed journal.

Pharmacological prophylaxis: NICE conditions it on individual VTE risk balanced against bleeding risk — for medical patients started within 14 hours of the decision to admit; for surgical/trauma patients only when risk favours it. RCOG is more specific for obstetric populations: 6 weeks postnatally for women with a family history of VTE plus identified thrombophilia; extension up to 6 weeks or until resolution for persistent risk factors (prolonged admission, wound infection, puerperal surgery); and use in persistent antiphospholipid antibodies without prior VTE only if other risk factors exist, with risk stratification required.

Mechanical prophylaxis: stockings and/or IPC where pharmacological agents are contraindicated or bleeding risk is high — RCOG for women at high haemorrhage risk (major antepartum haemorrhage, coagulopathy, progressive wound haematoma, suspected intra-abdominal bleeding, postpartum haemorrhage) and stockings for travel over 4 hours; NICE by procedure: cranial and elective spinal surgery (30 days or until mobile/discharged), elective hip replacement (until discharge), elective knee replacement (stockings with LMWH, or IPC until mobile), abdominal (including gynaecological), thoracic, cardiac, bariatric, ENT, oral/maxillofacial, varicose vein, upper limb surgery (>90 minutes general anaesthesia or impaired mobilisation), lower limb amputation (contralateral leg), endovascular aneurysm repair, major trauma, immobile acute stroke (IPC within 3 days), spinal injury (specialist unit, MDT only), and pregnancy/postpartum within 6 weeks with reduced mobility (IPC first-line; stockings if IPC contraindicated). AUGS recommends IPC until ambulation for low-risk vaginal/laparoscopic urogynaecological procedures; ERAS endorses IPC generally.

Not established: specific drugs, doses, contraindication criteria, named risk-assessment tools, bleeding-risk thresholds, or comparative effectiveness between stockings and IPC.

title: Colour Flow Doppler in Postpartum Uterine Evaluation
summary:
This community represents a narrow diagnostic-imaging theme: the use of colour flow Doppler imaging as an adjunct when assessing the postpartum uterus, specifically to identify vascular lesions that can underlie abnormal or secondary postpartum bleeding. Two relations sit at its core, both drawn from the same source and both sharing an identical population and condition: colour flow Doppler imaging detects arteriovenous malformation, and colour flow Doppler imaging detects pseudoaneurysm, in postpartum women, when used in the evaluation of the postpartum uterus. Critically, both relations carry the explicit qualifier that there is no strong evidence to support its use — so the recommendation is descriptive of what the modality can show, not an endorsement of routine deployment.

Only one guideline body contributes here: RCOG (Table 1, p30). Because a single source underpins both relations, there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile and no instance of one guideline being more specific than another. Nurse educators should therefore present this as single-source, low-certainty guidance rather than cross-corpus consensus, and quality-improvement leads should not build audit standards or mandatory imaging pathways on it.

The community does not establish: any timing or gestational/postpartum day threshold for when Doppler should be performed; any numeric thresholds (for example vessel diameter, peak systolic velocity, resistance index, or blood-loss volume triggering imaging); which practitioner or setting should perform or interpret the scan; sensitivity, specificity or comparative accuracy against greyscale ultrasound, CT or angiography; and any management, escalation or referral pathway once an arteriovenous malformation or pseudoaneurysm is detected (no embolisation, surgical, or drug therapies such as uterotonics, tranexamic acid or antibiotics are named anywhere in these relations). It also does not address non-postpartum populations, women with retained products of conception as a distinct group, or any subgroup stratification by parity, mode of delivery, or prior uterine surgery. Practically, teaching should stress recognition of these two vascular diagnoses as possible causes of postpartum bleeding while stating openly that the evidence base for Doppler in this role is weak.

title: Enhanced recovery pathways in colorectal surgery
summary:
This community represents enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) principles as applied to colorectal resection, together with two specific pathway elements: pre-operative oral antibiotic bowel preparation and pre-operative complex carbohydrate loading. The anchor claim (ERAS Society) is that an enhanced recovery pathway prevents postoperative complications in patients undergoing colorectal surgery, conditional on systematic implementation of an evidence-based perioperative care protocol — i.e. the benefit is attributed to protocolised, whole-pathway delivery rather than to isolated interventions. The pathway is explicitly scoped to colorectal surgery.

Oral antibiotics are the most granularly specified element. They apply to colorectal surgery as pre-operative bowel preparation, and specifically to patients in whom a colon resection is planned, conditioned on the surgeon judging bowel preparation necessary, and may be given alone or combined with mechanical bowel preparation. Prevention claims are condition-dependent: reduction of surgical site infection is stated for patients undergoing colorectal surgery when oral antibiotics are combined with mechanical bowel preparation; reduction of post-operative infectious morbidity and of anastomotic leak is stated for oral antibiotics alone versus no bowel preparation, and is explicitly based on retrospective data — a weaker evidence tier that educators should flag.

RCOG contributes a complex carbohydrate drink applied to colorectal surgery, without further population or timing qualifiers here. AUGS extends the ERAS protocol to colorectal resection specifically in older patients, making it the only source that names an age-related population; ERAS Society and RCOG do not stratify by age. There is no contradiction between bodies — rather, differing specificity: ERAS Society details bowel-preparation conditions, AUGS names the older population, RCOG names the carbohydrate drink.

Not established: no specific antibiotic agents, doses, routes or timing windows; no volume, carbohydrate concentration or fasting interval for the carbohydrate drink; no components, duration or audit thresholds for the pathway itself; no outcomes such as length of stay, mortality or readmission; and no gynecologic-surgery population despite the perioperative gynecologic context — all relations here are colorectal.

title: Monitoring and Repositioning to Prevent Complications
summary:
This community centres on complication prevention and surveillance across the perioperative and inpatient course, combining systems-level programmes (enhanced recovery, clinical surveillance), haemodynamic monitoring, and hands-on nursing measures (repositioning, frequent monitoring).

Key recommendations by population and condition: (1) NICE recommends an enhanced recovery programme to prevent complications for patients having major or complex elective surgery (NICE T1 p20). (2) NICE states cardiac output monitoring may prevent complications in adults having surgery, but only 'considered on a case-by-case basis', explicitly noting the evidence base is one small study plus older studies of unclear relevance (NICE T1 p24) — a notably weaker, more hedged recommendation than the enhanced recovery programme. (3) OpenRN specifies repositioning at least every two hours to minimise pressure in patients with pressure injuries, preventing further pressure injury (OpenRN T2 p1145); repositioning is also used as a nonpharmacologic measure to treat musculoskeletal discomfort (OpenRN T2 p958). (4) For clients in physical restraints, OpenRN pairs repositioning with frequent monitoring after restraints have been applied, following agency policy, to prevent and detect complications (OpenRN T2 p405). (5) WHO assigns independent clinical surveillance to Member States that have the resources and capability to conduct risk-adjusted evaluations, when extending outcome measures beyond mortality to include morbidity by defining complications (WHO T1 p99).

Contributing bodies differ in altitude: OpenRN is the most concrete at the bedside (two-hourly repositioning; restraint monitoring deferred to local agency policy), NICE addresses surgical pathway and haemodynamic technology with explicit evidence caveats, and WHO operates at health-system/registry level with an explicit resource-capability precondition.

What this community does NOT establish: no drugs, doses, or pharmacologic agents; no numeric thresholds or targets for cardiac output monitoring, and no named device or technique; no defined interval or content for 'frequent monitoring' of restrained clients (left to agency policy); no components, duration, or outcome metrics for the enhanced recovery programme; no list of which complications count; no gynecologic- or obstetric-specific population, and no paediatric, pregnancy, or emergency-surgery guidance.

title: Anaesthesia Risk and Monitoring Standards
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused theme: the intrinsic risk of general anaesthesia and the role of structured intraoperative monitoring in preventing anaesthetic complications. It consists of two relations drawn from the same source, WHO Topic 1, page 8, and centres on one shared outcome entity: complications of anaesthesia.

The first relation establishes that general anaesthesia increases the risk of complications of anaesthesia, and the population attached is explicitly broad: healthy patients undergoing general anaesthesia. This is a key teaching point for perioperative nursing education, because the risk is framed as applying even to patients without comorbidity, not only to high-risk or ASA-elevated cases.

The second relation is the mitigating counterpart: anaesthesia monitoring standards prevent complications of anaesthesia. Its stated population and condition is narrower, surgical patients in industrialized countries, which situates the preventive claim in settings where such monitoring standards are in place and resourced. The contrast between the two populations is the most instructive feature of this community: the risk statement is universal across healthy patients, while the protective effect is documented in a specific resource context.

Only one guideline body contributes here, the WHO (Topic 1, p8). There are therefore no inter-body disagreements, no competing thresholds, and no instance of one organisation being more specific than another within this community.

What this community does NOT establish is substantial and should be stated plainly to learners. It names no specific anaesthetic agents or drugs, no dosing, no monitoring modalities or parameters (for example no oxygen saturation, capnography, blood pressure or temperature thresholds), no monitoring frequency or timing intervals, and no recovery-phase requirements. It does not quantify the magnitude of risk increase or the size of the preventive benefit, does not enumerate which complications are meant, does not address regional versus general anaesthesia comparisons, and offers no guidance for low-resource settings, obstetric or gynecologic subpopulations, or patients with comorbidity. Any local protocol detail must therefore come from other communities or sources.

title: Compromised airway risk and anaesthetic assistance
summary:
This community centres on the compromised airway as a shared perioperative concern, linking two distinct contributions: an intervention pathway and a set of predisposing respiratory/sleep conditions.

The single management recommendation comes from RCOG (T1 p15): anaesthetic assistance is indicated to treat a compromised airway in women with postpartum haemorrhage, specifically when the airway is compromised owing to an impaired conscious level. The population is therefore narrow (obstetric patients with PPH) and the trigger is explicitly a reduced level of consciousness rather than airway compromise from any cause. For nurse educators, the practical implication is that in PPH escalation, deteriorating conscious level should prompt immediate involvement of anaesthetic support for airway protection.

The risk side is contributed by WHO (T1 p35), which identifies two comorbidities that increase the risk of a compromised airway: sleep apnoea and asthma. These are stated without a restricted population or qualifying condition, so they read as general preoperative risk factors relevant to any surgical patient, supporting their inclusion in preoperative screening and airway-risk flagging.

The two bodies are complementary rather than conflicting. RCOG is more specific in population and trigger (PPH, impaired conscious level) and is the only source naming a responder or intervention (anaesthetic assistance). WHO is more specific in naming individual patient-level risk factors but offers no accompanying action, threshold or timing.

What this community does NOT establish: no drugs, doses, oxygen saturation thresholds, GCS or conscious-level cut-offs, monitoring intervals, or timings for calling anaesthetic help; no airway devices or techniques (no intubation, supraglottic airway or bag-mask guidance); no guidance on whether sleep apnoea or asthma patients require anaesthetic review preoperatively, or how their risk should be graded or documented; no link between the WHO risk factors and the RCOG PPH pathway; and no outcomes, escalation hierarchy, staffing or competency requirements. Any local protocol combining preoperative airway-risk screening with PPH escalation would need thresholds and techniques drawn from sources outside this community.

title: CTPA for Pregnancy-Related Pulmonary Embolism Imaging
summary: This community centres on computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA, also recorded as 'computerised tomography pulmonary angiogram') as the diagnostic test for suspected pulmonary embolism (PE) in pregnancy and the puerperium, and the trade-off between its diagnostic yield and maternal breast radiation exposure. Diagnostic recommendations: CTPA detects PE in pregnant women with clinical suspicion of PE, and is the indicated test where the chest X-ray is abnormal. In collapsed, shocked women who are pregnant or in the puerperium, and in women presenting with suspected massive PE, CTPA should be arranged within 1 hour of presentation to detect massive PE — an explicit, time-critical threshold nurses can build into escalation pathways. Risk recommendations: CTPA increases the risk of maternal breast cancer in pregnant women/women with suspected PE, attributed to the relatively high radiation dose of up to 20 mGy to maternal breast tissue; the risk is stated to be greater in younger women and higher than with V/Q scanning, which is associated with a lower risk. The guideline qualifies that the absolute risk is very small and that estimates are based on modelling or extrapolated data. Mitigation: bismuth shields placed over the breasts during CTPA reduce breast dose by 20–40%, framed as preventing breast cancer risk in women undergoing CTPA. Contributing body: all relations derive from a single source, RCOG Thromboembolic disease guidance (RCOG T1, pp. 2, 3, 7, 8, 14); there is therefore no cross-body disagreement here, though the corpus repeats the CTPA-versus-V/Q breast cancer comparison at differing levels of specificity (p8 quantifies the ≤20 mGy dose and younger-woman gradient, while pp. 2 and 7 only state the comparative risk is very small). What is NOT established: no anticoagulant drugs, doses, contrast agents, renal or fetal radiation thresholds, gestational age limits, sensitivity/specificity figures, or criteria for choosing V/Q over CTPA are specified; no nursing preparation, consent, or post-scan monitoring steps are given; and the shielding benefit is expressed only as dose reduction, not as a measured reduction in cancer incidence.

title: Confusion and Disorientation: Causes and Interventions
summary:
This community centers on acute confusion/disorientation — its physiologic contributors and the non-pharmacologic nursing interventions used to prevent or treat it. Two etiologic relations identify infection and electrolyte imbalance as risk factors that increase confusion (OpenRN Nursing Advanced Skills, T2 p521); these are stated without population or condition qualifiers, so they read as general risk statements applicable to any client presenting with new confusion.

The intervention arm is more tightly scoped. For people with Alzheimer's disease experiencing sundowning, two environmental measures are recommended specifically during the evening hours: maintaining adequate lighting in the evening, and reducing stimulation during evening hours — both framed as preventing confusion (OpenRN T2 p468). Reality orientation appears twice with differing scopes: it treats disorientation in older adults experiencing a change in environment or a stressful situation, conditioned on the use of environmental cues such as clocks, calendars, and whiteboards; and it treats confusion in clients with cognitive impairments who are cognitively able (OpenRN T2 p491). The latter qualifier is the key clinical nuance — reality orientation is reserved for those with sufficient cognitive capacity to benefit, whereas the sundowning recommendations rely on environmental modification rather than client cognitive participation.

All content derives from a single guideline body, OpenRN (Nursing Skills, Tome 2), across three page-level sources (p468, p491, p521). There is therefore no cross-body disagreement; the differences are in specificity — p468 is time-of-day and diagnosis specific, p491 is population- and readiness-specific, p521 is unqualified.

The community does not establish: any pharmacologic agents, doses, or drug-related causes of confusion; laboratory thresholds defining electrolyte imbalance; specific infection types or sites; delirium screening tools or scoring cutoffs; frequency or duration of reality orientation sessions; measurable light levels for "adequate lighting"; outcomes such as fall risk, length of stay, or mortality; and any explicitly perioperative or gynecologic-surgery context. Contraindications to reality orientation in clients who are not cognitively able are implied by the qualifier but not stated.
key_entities: clients with cognitive impairments who are cognitively able

title: Contamination prevention across PPE and medication administration
summary:
This community centers on a single outcome node — contamination — and the discrete nursing techniques that prevent it, spanning two domains: personal protective equipment (PPE) doffing/use and aseptic medication administration. All seven relations derive from one source, OpenRN Nursing Skills (Table 2), across pages 203, 922, and 1006, so the theme is internally consistent rather than contested between bodies.

PPE recommendations (p203): proper glove removal prevents contamination, stated without population or conditional qualifier. Discarding a gown into a designated container prevents contamination, conditional on the outer contaminated side being turned inward and the gown rolled into a bundle. A respirator prevents contamination for healthcare personnel exposed to patients with suspected or confirmed tuberculosis and other airborne diseases, conditional on being applied, worn, and removed appropriately; the same respirator also prevents inhalation of aerosolized infectious droplets for health care personnel during airborne transmission-based precautions. The respirator entries are the most specific in the community, naming both a pathogen (tuberculosis), a precaution category (airborne), and a second distinct outcome.

Medication administration recommendations: for patients receiving ear drops, avoiding contact with the dropper or the inside of the cap when removing the cap prevents contamination (p922). For patients receiving nasal medication instillation, keeping the bottle compressed as it is removed from the nose prevents contamination (p922). For patients receiving injections, use of new sterile equipment for each injection prevents contamination (p1006).

What this community does NOT establish: no infection or transmission rates, no drug names, doses, or concentrations, no time thresholds (e.g., duration of respirator wear, fit-test intervals, hand hygiene timing), and no sequencing of full PPE donning/doffing beyond gloves and gown. It does not address masks, eye protection, or face shields; does not specify respirator type (e.g., N95) or fit-testing; and offers no comparative effectiveness among these measures. Because a single guideline body contributes all statements, no inter-guideline disagreement can be assessed.
key_entities: avoiding contact with the dropper or inside of the cap
keeping the bottle compressed during removal from the nose
use of new sterile equipment for each injection

title: Body Positioning Prevents Sterile Field Contamination
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused theme in perioperative gynecologic nursing practice: the nurse's own body and clothing as a vector for contamination of the sterile field, and the behavioural controls that prevent it. Both relations in the community converge on one outcome entity — contamination of the sterile field — and both identify preventive nursing behaviours rather than pharmacologic or device-based interventions.

The two recommendations are: (1) attention to the position of body and clothing relative to the sterile field prevents contamination of the sterile field, with the condition explicitly attached that this applies when removing parts of the sterile kit; and (2) maintaining distance of body and clothing from the sterile field prevents contamination of the sterile field, stated without a narrowing condition and therefore applying generally whenever a sterile field is in use. Together they describe a paired awareness-plus-distance behaviour: the nurse must consciously monitor where the torso, arms and garments sit in relation to the field, and must keep that mass physically separated from it, with the moment of unpacking or withdrawing items from the sterile kit flagged as the specific high-risk step.

Only one guideline body contributes: OpenRN (Nursing Skills, Chapter 2, p247), which is the source of both relations. There is therefore no inter-body disagreement to reconcile, and no instance where one authority is more specific than another; the only internal difference in specificity is that the positional-attention recommendation is conditioned on sterile-kit removal while the distance recommendation is unconditioned and broader.

The community does not establish any quantitative threshold — no minimum distance in centimetres or inches, no defined boundary or margin around the field. It names no population beyond the implied sterile-procedure context (no age, procedure type, gynecologic subgroup, or staff role is specified), no timing or duration, no drugs or antiseptic agents, no gowning or draping requirements, and no consequence, infection rate, or remediation step should contamination occur. It also does not address other contamination routes such as airflow, talking, reaching over the field, or moisture strike-through.
key_entities: attention to position of body and clothing relative to the sterile field
maintaining distance of body and clothing from the sterile field
removal of parts of the sterile kit

title: Surveillance Practices Detecting Clinical Deterioration
summary:
This community represents the theme of ongoing patient surveillance for early detection of clinical deterioration, spanning obstetric wards, the anaesthetised surgical patient, and general nursing assessment. Five distinct monitoring practices all converge on the single outcome of detecting deterioration.

Recommendations by population and condition: (1) RCOG advises recording vital sign observations on an early warning system for pregnant women, with the explicit condition that the early warning system be modified for obstetrics to account for the physiological changes of pregnancy. (2) WHO specifies, for patients under anaesthesia, the continuous presence of a trained anaesthetist, and (3) continuous clinical observation in addition to equipment monitoring — i.e. monitors do not substitute for human observation. (4) OpenRN advises a primary survey for all patients, performed at the beginning of every shift or patient visit. (5) OpenRN also identifies respiratory rate assessment in adult patients, assessed against the patient's own baseline normal values rather than a fixed population cut-off.

Contributing bodies: RCOG (obstetric-specific), WHO (intraoperative/anaesthetic safety), and OpenRN (foundational nursing assessment). They are complementary rather than conflicting. RCOG is the most population-specific, requiring obstetric modification of scoring tools; WHO is the most specific about who must be present and that equipment monitoring alone is insufficient; OpenRN is the most specific about timing (every shift or visit) and about individualised baseline comparison for respiratory rate.

What this community does NOT establish: no numeric thresholds or trigger scores are given (no respiratory rate values, no early warning score cut-offs), no observation frequency or interval beyond "beginning of every shift or patient visit" and "continuous" during anaesthesia, and no named early warning tool (e.g. MEOWS, NEWS). It specifies no escalation pathway, responder, or response time once deterioration is detected, no drugs or treatments, no equipment list for anaesthetic monitoring, and no guidance for paediatric patients or for postoperative recovery-area surveillance.
key_entities: recording of vital sign observations on an early warning system
continuous presence of a trained anaesthetist

title: Needle Length Selection Prevents Injection Complications
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: safe injection technique, specifically the selection of correct needle length as a preventive intervention against local injection-site complications. All three relations in the community share one causal actor (correct needle length selection) and one qualifying condition, and differ only in the adverse outcome averted.

Main recommendation: for patients receiving injections, select needle length according to the type of injection being administered. When this condition is met, the graph asserts three preventive effects — prevention of bruising, prevention of abscess formation, and prevention of pain. The population is stated broadly as 'patients receiving injections'; no narrower subgroup (e.g., obstetric, gynecologic surgical, obese, pediatric, or anticoagulated patients) is specified, and no perioperative timing window is attached, so the recommendation should be read as generally applicable within the guideline corpus rather than procedure-specific.

Guideline contribution: the community is supported by a single source, OpenRN Nursing Skills (Volume 2, p. 1006). There is therefore no inter-body disagreement to reconcile and no instance of one body being more specific than another; conversely, there is no independent corroboration from a second guideline body, professional society, or perioperative standard. Educators should note the evidence base here is narrow and rests on one textbook page.

What this community does NOT establish: it gives no concrete needle length values in gauge or inches, and no mapping of specific lengths to specific injection routes (intramuscular, subcutaneous, intradermal) — 'type of injection' is left unspecified. It does not address needle gauge, injection site selection, volume limits, aspiration, Z-track technique, skin preparation, or patient body habitus/BMI thresholds that commonly drive length choice. It names no drugs, doses, or timings. It offers no risk magnitude, incidence, or strength-of-evidence grading for the prevented outcomes, and does not describe how to recognise or manage bruising, abscess, or pain once they occur. Quality-improvement leads wanting auditable criteria will need to source explicit length thresholds elsewhere.

title: Corticosteroid and antihistamine premedication risks
summary:
This community centres on two pharmacologic agents used prophylactically and symptomatically in perioperative and diagnostic-imaging contexts — corticosteroids and diphenhydramine — and on the adverse-effect profile that corticosteroids carry.

The convergent recommendation is allergy prophylaxis for contrast media: both corticosteroids and diphenhydramine prevent allergic reaction to contrast in clients who have had a previous allergic reaction, and both must be administered before the client receives the contrast (OpenRN Nursing Pharmacology/Skills, T2 p1183). Diphenhydramine is additionally indicated to treat pruritus (OpenRN T2). Corticosteroid harms are documented in three ways: increased risk of impaired wound healing (OpenRN T2 p1113) — directly relevant to surgical incision care and postoperative gynecologic recovery; increased risk of gastrointestinal bleeding specifically in clients taking nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs concurrently (OpenRN T2 p825); and a contraindication in women with HELLP syndrome when the corticosteroid is given for the specific purpose of treating HELLP syndrome (WHO Tier 1 p29).

Two guideline bodies contribute. WHO supplies the only obstetric-population statement and is the more population-specific source, naming women with HELLP syndrome and narrowly qualifying the contraindication to the treatment indication rather than to corticosteroid use generally. OpenRN supplies the general pharmacology and safety content — premedication timing, drug–drug interaction with NSAIDs, and wound-healing risk. They do not contradict each other; they operate at different levels of specificity, so WHO's HELLP restriction should be read as narrowing, not negating, OpenRN's broader corticosteroid guidance.

What this community does NOT establish: no doses, routes, frequencies, or time intervals before contrast administration; no comparison of corticosteroid versus diphenhydramine efficacy, nor whether they should be combined; no statement on which corticosteroid agent to use; no threshold for wound-healing risk (duration, dose, or surgical type); no guidance on gastrointestinal bleeding prophylaxis or NSAID substitution; no alternative HELLP therapy; and no monitoring parameters, sedation cautions for diphenhydramine, or gynecologic-surgery-specific protocols.

title: Pharmacologic cough management in advanced disease
summary:
This community represents a single, narrow clinical theme: pharmacologic suppression of cough as a symptom-management (palliative) intervention for clients with advanced disease. All three relations in the community converge on the same target symptom (cough) and the same qualifying population (clients with advanced disease), so the theme is best read as a small menu of interchangeable antitussive options rather than a stepwise algorithm.

The recommendations are: (1) opioids TREAT cough in clients with advanced disease; (2) dextromethorphan TREATS cough in clients with advanced disease; and (3) benzonatate TREATS cough in clients with advanced disease. In each case the population/condition qualifier is identical — 'clients with advanced disease' — and no other population (e.g., perioperative gynecologic surgical clients specifically, pediatric, obstetric, or opioid-naive clients) is attached to any of the three drug relations.

Only one guideline body contributes here: OpenRN, from a single locus (OpenRN Text 2, p. 1269). Because all three statements come from the same page of the same source, there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile, no instance of one body being more specific than another, and no conflicting population qualifiers within this community. For a QI lead, this means the theme currently rests on a single-source foundation and would benefit from cross-referencing against a second authority before being used as a standalone practice standard.

What this community does NOT establish: it gives no doses, dose ranges, routes, frequencies, maximum daily limits, or titration schedules; no timing relative to surgery or to other perioperative events; and no preference ranking or sequencing among opioid, dextromethorphan, and benzonatate. It does not define 'advanced disease' or state a threshold of disease severity, prognosis, or performance status that triggers treatment. It specifies no contraindications, monitoring parameters (e.g., respiratory depression or sedation surveillance with opioids), adverse effects, drug interactions, non-pharmacologic adjuncts, or outcome measures for cough relief, and it makes no statement about combining these agents.

title: Perioperative aspiration risk prevention and mitigation
summary: This community centres on pulmonary aspiration risk across the perioperative continuum: who is at risk, and which airway, fasting, pharmacologic and positioning measures reduce it. Risk factors named are general anaesthesia itself, symptomatic active reflux, a full stomach, obesity, emergency surgery in nonfasting patients, use of a laryngeal mask airway, and opioid-induced lethargy (OpenRN), which raises aspiration risk specifically in the presence of nausea and vomiting. Preventive recommendations from WHO include: rapid induction technique and assistant-applied cricoid pressure during induction for patients with symptomatic active reflux or a full stomach (cricoid pressure is credited with preventing passive regurgitation only if applied correctly); rapid sequence induction and intubation with preoxygenation; gastric decompression before induction; and appropriate selection of patients and method of airway control. Pharmacologic prophylaxis is differentiated by urgency: proton pump inhibitors or H2 antagonists prior to elective surgery, and oral sodium citrate prior to emergency surgery, for patients at risk of aspiration. Preoperative fasting is recommended for elective surgery (WHO notes it is not usually feasible in emergencies); AUGS and the ERAS Society specify overnight or 8-hour fasting for patients with delayed gastric emptying, with AUGS noting that urogynecological guidance is extrapolated from oncological, abdominal and gynecological surgery protocols. ERAS also states oral carbohydrate-rich drinks are contraindicated in emergency surgery. OpenRN contributes postoperative/ward-level positioning: head-of-bed elevation of at least 30–45 degrees, preferably high Fowler's, for patients receiving enteral tube medication. Contributors are WHO (airway and pharmacologic management), ERAS Society and AUGS (fasting and carbohydrate loading), and OpenRN (opioid sedation and positioning); WHO is most specific on induction technique, ERAS/AUGS on fasting duration, OpenRN on degrees of elevation. The community does not establish dosing, timing intervals for PPIs/H2 antagonists/sodium citrate, clear fluid fasting windows, comparative effectiveness of these measures, incidence or outcomes of aspiration, obesity thresholds, or gynecologic-surgery-specific airway protocols.
key_entities: rapid sequence induction and intubation with preoxygenation

title: Preventing Clogged Enteral Feeding Tubes
summary:
This community represents a narrow but practically important theme in perioperative and general nursing practice: preparing medications for administration through an enteral feeding tube so that the tube does not become clogged. Both relations in the community converge on a single adverse outcome to be prevented — a clogged enteral tube — and both are indexed to the same population: patients receiving medication via an enteral feeding tube.

The two recommendations form a clear decision hierarchy. First, use a liquid form of the medication whenever a liquid form is available; liquid formulations are stated to prevent clogging of the enteral tube. Second, only if a liquid form is not available AND the medication is safe to crush, crush the medication finely and dissolve it in water; this preparation likewise prevents tube clogging. The conditional wording is important for teaching and audit: the crush-and-dissolve pathway is explicitly a fallback, gated both on liquid unavailability and on a medication-specific safety determination that the drug may be crushed. The emphasis on crushing 'finely' and dissolving in water — rather than simply crushing — is the concrete technique element to reinforce in competency checks.

Only one guideline body contributes here: OpenRN (Nursing Skills, Table 2, p854). Because there is a single source, there are no inter-body disagreements, no competing thresholds, and no instance of one organisation being more specific than another; any apparent hierarchy comes from the internal conditional logic of the OpenRN text itself.

The community does not establish several things a QI lead would need elsewhere: it names no specific drugs, formulations, or classes that must never be crushed (e.g., no enteric-coated or extended-release exclusions are enumerated); it specifies no water volume, temperature, flush volume, or flush timing before, between, or after doses; it gives no tube sizes, tube types, or syringe sizes; it does not address what to do once a tube is already clogged; and it makes no perioperative-specific timing statements (e.g., preoperative fasting or postoperative resumption of enteral medications).
key_entities: crushing medication finely and dissolving in water
patients receiving medication via an enteral feeding tube

title: Airway Planning Prevents Anaesthesia Airway Deaths
summary:
This community represents a single, narrowly scoped clinical theme: the preventive value of appropriate planning for airway management in patients undergoing anaesthesia. Both relations in the community assert the same causal claim — that appropriate planning PREVENTS death from airway loss (one relation specifies 'death from airway loss during anaesthesia', the other the more general 'death from airway loss'). In both cases the population attached by the guideline is identical: patients undergoing anaesthesia. No additional qualifying condition, comorbidity, procedure type, or urgency category is attached.

The only contributing guideline body is the WHO, via two separate locations in the same volume (Tool 1, p107 and Tool 1, p10). These two citations are concordant rather than divergent: p107 is marginally more specific in that it situates the airway loss temporally 'during anaesthesia', whereas p10 states the outcome generically as 'death from airway loss'. There is no second guideline body (e.g. no professional anaesthesia or perioperative nursing society) in this community, so no cross-body disagreement or differential specificity can be assessed beyond that wording difference. The repetition across an introductory page (p10) and a later operational page (p107) suggests the message is framed both as a headline safety principle and as a working recommendation.

Importantly, this community does NOT establish what 'appropriate planning' consists of. It names no airway assessment tool, no predictive scoring threshold (e.g. Mallampati class, thyromental distance), no equipment requirements (laryngoscopes, supraglottic airways, capnography), no difficult-airway or failed-intubation algorithm, no drugs (no induction agents, neuromuscular blockers, or reversal agents such as sugammadex), no timing or checklist step, no staffing or skill-mix requirement, and no escalation or rescue pathway. It also gives no effect size, incidence, or risk stratification distinguishing higher-risk subgroups (e.g. obesity, obstetric, paediatric, or emergency cases). Educators should therefore treat this community as a high-level justification for structured pre-anaesthetic airway planning, and source the operational detail from other parts of the corpus.
key_entities: death from airway loss during anaesthesia

title: Preoperative decolonisation to prevent SSI
summary:
