This community represents preoperative staphylococcal decolonisation as a targeted surgical site infection (SSI) prevention strategy. Only two relations define the theme: decolonisation is placed in the preoperative phase of care, and it is linked to prevention of surgical site infection.

The two recommendations carry distinct populations and conditions. First, decolonisation occurs in the preoperative phase for people identified as carriers of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) or methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA), with the condition that it is undertaken before certain types of surgery, for example orthopaedic surgery. Second, decolonisation prevents surgical site infection in people undergoing surgical procedures for which the consequences of an infection are severe, such as cardiac surgery, with the condition that it be considered for those people who are likely to benefit the most — i.e. a risk-stratified rather than universal intervention. Together these imply two selection criteria that a quality-improvement lead should operationalise: documented S. aureus carriage status, and the severity of consequences should infection occur (orthopaedic and cardiac surgery are the named exemplars).

Only one guideline body contributes here: NICE (surgical site infection guidance, T1 p21). Because there is a single source, there are no inter-body disagreements, no competing thresholds, and no instance of one organisation being more specific than another within this community.

Important gaps: the relations do not name any decolonisation agent (no nasal mupirocin, chlorhexidine body wash, or antiseptic is specified), no dose, frequency, duration, or number of days before incision, and no timing relative to induction or antibiotic prophylaxis. Screening methods for identifying MRSA/MSSA carriage, re-screening or clearance confirmation, and management of persistent carriage are absent. No effect size, absolute or relative risk reduction, or outcome definition for SSI is given, and no contraindications, resistance monitoring, paediatric/obstetric-specific direction, or gynaecologic-surgery-specific application is established. Local protocols must supply these operational details.

title: Pharmacological VTE Prophylaxis: Risk-Based Timing Decisions
summary: This community centres on pharmacological venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis: who receives it, for how long, and how its timing is governed by risk reassessment, regional anaesthesia and concurrent chemotherapy. NICE (T1) supplies nearly all recommendations, structured procedure-by-procedure around the pivot judgement that VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk. Minimum 7-day courses are recommended after cardiac surgery (people not on other anticoagulation therapy, p31), bariatric surgery (p28), thoracic surgery (p29), and in serious or major trauma (p27, given as soon as possible after risk assessment). Extended prophylaxis to 28 days postoperatively is advised after major cancer surgery in the abdomen (p27). Foot or ankle surgery warrants prophylaxis when surgery requires immobilisation, total anaesthesia time exceeds 90 minutes, or VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk (p24). Special populations include people already on antiplatelet agents for other conditions (prophylaxis if VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk, based on condition or procedure, p13) and palliative care patients, where the decision weighs temporary increases in thrombotic risk factors, bleeding risk, likely life expectancy and the views of the person and family/carers (p16). In cancer, prophylaxis continues for as long as chemotherapy is being received (p16). For patients receiving regional anaesthesia, timing must be planned to minimise epidural haematoma risk (p19). Risk reassessment for VTE and bleeding monitors both outcomes at least daily and whenever clinical condition changes in serious or major trauma (p27), and at consultant review or clinical change for all people admitted to an acute psychiatric ward (p18). OpenRN (T2) contributes only chemotherapy-related symptom risks — nausea, vomiting and decreased appetite in clients receiving cancer treatment (p979), diarrhea in clients receiving chemotherapy and constipation in clients at end of life (p1269) — so the two bodies intersect at chemotherapy without conflicting: NICE is procedural and time-specific, OpenRN symptom-focused. The community does not name any specific drug, dose, route, or agent class, gives no numeric risk-assessment tool or bleeding thresholds, no gynecologic-surgery-specific durations, and no mechanical prophylaxis alternatives or interval rules for neuraxial catheter removal.
key_entities: risk reassessment for venous thromboembolism and bleeding

title: Cardiac Arrhythmia Risk, Monitoring, Contraindications
summary:
This community centres on cardiac arrhythmia as a perioperative hazard, linking three distinct strands: electrolyte-driven risk, intraoperative electrophysiologic monitoring, and a route-of-administration contraindication.

Risk factors: two electrolyte derangements are named as increasing arrhythmia risk — elevated potassium (hyperkalaemia) and decreased magnesium (hypomagnesaemia), both from OpenRN Nursing Skills (T2 p1425). No numeric thresholds, units, or reference ranges are attached to either, and no population or condition qualifier is given, so these are stated as general physiological associations rather than surgery-specific triggers.

Monitoring: the WHO Surgical Safety guidance (T1 p31) specifies the electrocardiograph as the device that monitors for cardiac arrhythmia, with an explicit population — patients under anaesthesia — and an explicit condition — continuous monitoring of heart rate and rhythm. This is the most specific recommendation in the community, because it names both who is monitored and the required continuity of monitoring.

Contraindication: OpenRN (T2 p854) states that rectal suppository administration is contraindicated in patients with a history of cardiac arrhythmias, i.e. the population is defined by arrhythmia history rather than an active rhythm disturbance.

Contributing bodies: WHO (T1) contributes only the intraoperative ECG monitoring standard; OpenRN (T2) contributes the electrolyte risk factors and the suppository contraindication. There is no disagreement between them — they address non-overlapping aspects (device-based surveillance versus aetiology and medication route safety). WHO is more specific on population and monitoring conditions; OpenRN is more specific on the drug-route restriction.

Not established: the community does not give potassium or magnesium threshold values, correction protocols, replacement drugs or doses; it does not state monitoring frequency, alarm limits, or duration beyond "continuous" while anaesthetised; it does not identify who performs or interprets the ECG; it offers no alternative route to rectal suppositories; it links no gynecologic procedure, anaesthetic agent, or postoperative timeframe to arrhythmia; and it specifies no escalation or treatment pathway once arrhythmia is detected.

title: Airway clearance, suctioning risks, oxygenation safeguards
summary:
This community covers pulmonary hygiene and airway suctioning safety: preventing and detecting atelectasis, hypoxemia, arrhythmia and pneumonia, plus management of hyperventilation-driven respiratory alkalosis. Core recommendations: (1) Deep breathing and coughing exercises prevent atelectasis in clients at risk for pneumonia due to immobility (p958). (2) Percussion detects atelectasis and pneumonia when dull sounds are heard over high-density areas (p616). (3) Suctioning generally, and nasotracheal suctioning specifically, increase risk of hypoxemia and atelectasis; general suctioning is additionally linked to arrhythmia (p1293, p1296). (4) Hyperoxygenation and hyperventilation performed prior to nasal and tracheal suctioning prevent atelectasis, hypoxemia and arrhythmia; hyperoxygenation applies to nasal and tracheal suctioning before the procedure, and to open tracheostomy suctioning before and during the procedure based on the patient's oxygenation status (p1296, p1307). For ventilated patients, ventilation with an ambu bag is applied prior to tracheal suctioning (p1296). (5) For hyperventilating clients, breathing retraining focused on abdominal (diaphragmatic) breathing treats respiratory alkalosis in acute management and treats hyperventilation with continuation of the exercise; lorazepam treats hyperventilation only if breathing retraining is unsuccessful and severe symptoms persist; continuous oxygen saturation monitoring monitors for hypoxemia if rebreathing is used (p1093).

All relations derive from a single corpus, OpenRN Nursing Skills/Fundamentals (Volume T2), so there is no cross-body disagreement; differences are in granularity across pages. Page 1296 is most specific about pre-procedure oxygenation and its three prevented complications, while page 1293 lists nasotracheal risks without arrhythmia and without preventive measures; page 1307 uniquely allows intra-procedural hyperoxygenation for open tracheostomy suctioning.

Not established: no numeric thresholds (SpO2 targets, suction pressures, catheter sizes, suction duration or number of passes), no lorazepam dose, route or frequency, no defined duration or frequency for deep breathing/coughing or breathing retraining, no rebreathing technique details, no gynecologic or perioperative population specificity, and no evidence grading or outcome data supporting these interventions.

title: VTE prophylaxis, diagnosis and treatment
summary: This community centres on venous thromboembolism (VTE) — chiefly deep venous thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE) — spanning risk factors, mechanical and pharmacological prophylaxis, diagnostic imaging, and treatment. Prevention: ERAS Society is most specific for gynecologic surgery, recommending prophylactic/preoperative anticoagulation initiated pre-operatively rather than post-operatively in gynecologic oncology patients, combined medical and mechanical prophylaxis; graduated/well-fitting compression stockings and pneumatic compression devices for perioperative prophylaxis and patients at risk of VTE (greatest VTE reduction in the first 5 post-operative days when pneumatic compression is combined with heparin); and low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) as extended prophylaxis for 28 days. NICE supports intermittent pneumatic compression in people admitted with acute stroke. RCOG addresses alternatives with caveats: aspirin ≥300 mg daily in surgical inpatients gives only modest benefit compared with heparin, and postoperative dextran in non-pregnant patients has weak evidence and is less effective than LMWH. Risk factors: lower limb immobilisation (NICE; DVT risk approximately 4–40%, and VTE after immobilisation for non-major orthopaedic surgery), general immobility (OpenRN), and antiphospholipid syndrome in pregnancy (RCOG: DVT, PE and VTE recurrence in women with prior VTE), diagnosed only if lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and β2-glycoprotein 1 antibody testing is positive on two occasions 12 weeks apart. Untreated DVT increases PE risk. Diagnosis/monitoring: RCOG makes compression duplex ultrasound the primary test, with bilateral leg studies in suspected PE (only a positive result is of value; negative does not exclude PE) and serial/repeat ultrasound on days 3 and 7 when initial imaging is negative but suspicion is high. OpenRN adds bedside inspection of lower extremities (unilateral warmth, redness, tenderness, calf swelling, sharp pain on dorsiflexion) and structured assessment for immobility complications (skin breakdown, constipation, pneumonia, DVT). Treatment: RCOG — LMWH immediately in pregnant women with clinically suspected DVT until objectively excluded unless strongly contraindicated; therapeutic subcutaneous LMWH for the remainder of pregnancy plus ≥6 weeks postnatally, minimum 3 months total; plus mobilisation with graduated elastic compression stockings. WHO cites oral anticoagulant for 3–6 months after ankle fracture. Nursing note: avoid peripheral IV placement in an extremity with DVT, fracture, contracture or extensive scarring (OpenRN). Not established: no comparative dosing of LMWH agents, no risk-assessment scoring tools, no thresholds for choosing mechanical versus pharmacological prophylaxis, no bleeding-risk or reversal guidance, and no gynecologic-surgery-specific diagnostic pathway.
key_entities: serial compression ultrasonography with doppler imaging

title: Dehydration risk, monitoring, prevention and treatment
summary:
This community centres on dehydration across the perioperative and general inpatient continuum: who is at risk, how it is detected, how it is prevented, and how it is corrected. Risk factors named are age-related impairment in thirst perception in older individuals (OpenRN T2 p1056) and intravenous diuretics in clients receiving them (OpenRN T2 p1111). Consequence: preoperatively, dehydration increases the risk of hypovolaemia (WHO T1 p41), linking fluid status directly to surgical safety.

Monitoring recommendations: monitor for signs of dehydration in clients with fever/hyperthermia (OpenRN T2 p663); assess urine output in at-risk clients, since decreased urine production is an early sign of both dehydration and kidney dysfunction (OpenRN T2 p1056); and in hospitalized patients experiencing diarrhoea, assess and monitor for signs of dehydration or electrolyte imbalance (OpenRN T2 p719).

Treatment: intravenous isotonic fluid administration as prescribed, with monitoring of the client's response, and encouraging oral fluid intake as tolerated unless contraindicated (both OpenRN T2 p1111).

Prevention: RCOG (T1 p3) specifies reducing the fluid fasting period to 2 hours before the anaesthetic for patients undergoing surgery. WHO (T1 p86) contributes an obstetric prevention measure — acustimulation therapy at the P6 point in pregnant women, RR 0.24 (0.07–0.83), graded low-certainty evidence.

Contributing bodies: OpenRN (nursing fundamentals) supplies almost all assessment and management detail; WHO supplies the preoperative dehydration–hypovolaemia link and the pregnancy-specific P6 acustimulation evidence; RCOG supplies the concrete perioperative fasting threshold. They are complementary rather than conflicting, but differ in specificity: only RCOG gives a timing threshold (2 hours), only WHO gives an effect size and certainty grading.

Not established: no volumes, rates or specific isotonic solutions; no defined urine-output thresholds (e.g. mL/kg/hr) or vital-sign/laboratory cut-offs; no frequency of monitoring; no gynecologic-surgery-specific fluid protocol; no guidance on contraindications to oral intake; and no evidence on whether reduced fasting or P6 acustimulation alters hypovolaemia, kidney dysfunction or surgical outcomes.
key_entities: reduced fluid fasting to 2 hours before anaesthetic

title: Combined Oxytocin and Amniotomy for Labour Delay
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: the augmentation of labour once delay in labour has been confirmed. It links two interventions — oxytocin (a pharmacologic uterotonic) and amniotomy (artificial rupture of membranes) — to one clinical target condition, delay in labour.

The recommendations are conditional and, importantly, interdependent. Oxytocin is indicated as a treatment for delay in labour in women with confirmed delay in labour, with the stated condition that it is used in combination with amniotomy. Amniotomy is likewise indicated for treating delay in labour in the same population — women with confirmed delay in labour — when combined with oxytocin, and the guideline explicitly records that amniotomy is NOT recommended when used alone. The practical teaching point for nursing staff is therefore that the two interventions form a package for confirmed delay; amniotomy as a standalone augmentation strategy is not endorsed, and the population qualifier "confirmed" delay should be respected before either intervention is initiated.

Only one guideline body contributes to this community: the WHO intrapartum/labour care guidance (WHO T1, p21). Because there is a single source, there are no inter-body disagreements, no divergent thresholds, and no instance of one organisation being more granular than another within this theme. Both relations carry identical population framing and mirrored conditions, so the two statements are internally consistent rather than competing.

What this community does NOT establish is substantial and should be flagged in any protocol built from it. There is no oxytocin dose, starting infusion rate, titration increment, maximum dose, or infusion route specified; no timing or duration criteria; no definition of what constitutes "confirmed" delay in labour (no cervical dilatation rate, partograph threshold, or time-in-stage cut-off); no distinction between first and second stage of labour; and no parity, gestational age, or membrane-status eligibility criteria. It also says nothing about monitoring requirements (fetal heart rate, uterine activity), contraindications, adverse effects such as hyperstimulation, alternatives to augmentation, or what to do if augmentation fails. These gaps must be filled from other sections of the corpus or local policy.
key_entities: women with confirmed delay in labour

title: Partograph Four-Hour Action Line Monitoring
summary:
This community represents a narrow but operationally important theme: use of the partograph with a four-hour action line as the labour-monitoring instrument for detecting delayed progress during the active phase of labour. Two relations define the theme. First, the active phase partograph with a four-hour action line is situated within the intrapartum phase of care, applying to women in labour specifically when they are in the active phase of labour. Second, that same tool is used to monitor for delay in labour progress, again for the population of women in labour and under the condition of the active phase. Together these establish the partograph as a phase-specific surveillance artefact rather than a general antenatal or postpartum record: its trigger threshold is the four-hour action line, and the clinical outcome it is designed to surface is delayed progress.

Only one guideline body contributes here: the WHO source (WHO Table 1, p20). Because there is a single contributing body, the community contains no inter-organisational disagreement, no divergence in thresholds, and no instance of one body being more specific than another. Educators should therefore present this as WHO-derived guidance without implying corroboration or contradiction from other corpora.

What the community does NOT establish is substantial. It does not state what action should be taken when the four-hour action line is crossed — no augmentation regimen, no oxytocin or amniotomy instruction, no escalation or referral pathway, and no caesarean threshold. It does not define the active phase (no cervical dilatation cut-off), does not specify how frequently the partograph should be plotted, and does not name which parameters (cervical dilatation, descent, contractions, fetal heart rate) are recorded. It offers no alternative action-line intervals (for example two- or three-hour lines) for comparison, no accuracy or outcome evidence, no exclusions such as multiple pregnancy or previous caesarean, and no guidance for the latent phase or for women not in labour. Quality-improvement leads should treat this as a documented monitoring requirement, sourcing response protocols elsewhere.
key_entities: active phase partograph with four-hour action line

title: Preventing Postoperative Ileus and Bowel Recovery
summary:
This community represents the theme of promoting return of gastrointestinal function after gynecologic surgery, i.e., prevention and management of postoperative ileus and delayed return of bowel function. All relations derive from a single guideline body, the American Urogynecologic Society (AUGS) enhanced recovery statement, Table 2 (pages 9, 11, and 14), so the community reflects one corpus voice rather than competing recommendations.

Four interventions are recommended as treatments for delayed return of bowel function (AUGS T2 p11): early feeding, coffee drinking, opioid-sparing analgesia, and maintenance of euvolemia. Two of these — opioid-sparing analgesia and euvolemia — are additionally framed on p14 as preventing ileus outright, making them the most strongly supported, dual-purpose measures in this cluster. The nuance worth teaching is that p11 positions these measures as treatments for slow bowel recovery while p14 positions the same two as preventive; this is a difference in framing/specificity within the same table rather than a disagreement between bodies.

One risk relation is documented: poorly controlled pain increases the risk of delayed return of bowel function in postoperative patients (AUGS T2 p9). This is the only relation in the community that carries an explicit population qualifier, and it links pain management quality directly to GI outcomes — reinforcing the rationale for opioid-sparing analgesia.

What the community does NOT establish: no specific drugs or drug classes are named within opioid-sparing analgesia (no agents, doses, or routes); no timing thresholds are given for "early" feeding; no volume, rate, or hemodynamic targets define euvolemia; and no dose, strength, timing, or frequency is specified for coffee drinking. Populations are unstated except for the pain relation, so applicability to specific gynecologic procedures, surgical approaches (open vs minimally invasive), or comorbid groups is not defined. No relative effect sizes, no ranking among the four interventions, no pharmacologic prokinetic agents, and no outcome measures or monitoring parameters for bowel recovery are provided. No second guideline body contributes.

title: Host Risk Factors Impairing Wound Healing
summary:
This community centres on patient-level (host) risk factors for delayed or impaired wound healing and surgical site infection, plus the assessment and correction strategies that mitigate them. Delayed wound healing is the hub: contributing factors named are diabetes/diabetes mellitus (especially poorly managed disease with elevated blood glucose or hemoglobin A1C), obesity, smoking, alcohol use, oral steroids, stress, advanced age, impaired mobility, nutritional deficiency (specifically vitamin C and zinc deficiency) and elevated blood urea nitrogen (OpenRN pp.696, 753, 1113). Recommended monitoring: wound assessment every shift documenting size, stage, location, exudate, granulation tissue and epithelialization for all clients with wounds, and reassessment at every dressing change; laboratory testing when a chronic wound is not healing as expected, including blood glucose and HbA1c testing to detect poorly managed diabetes. Interventions: blood sugar management for patients with diabetes mellitus, nutrition and hydration promotion for all patients with wounds, and for pressure injuries 30–35 kcal/kg/day with 1.25–1.5 g/kg protein plus micronutrients (OpenRN pp.1113, 1145). A linked fluid/electrolyte strand covers diabetes mellitus and diuretics as causes of fluid, electrolyte and acid–base imbalance, monitored by daily weights on the same scale, same time of day, similar clothing (report change >1 kg in 24 hours), 24-hour intake/output, and laboratory work (OpenRN p.1111).

Contributors: OpenRN provides nearly all detail; WHO (p.55) specifies diabetes as an SSI risk after cardiac operations and CDC (p.7) only for "certain kinds of operations" — neither is gynecology-specific. NICE (p.16) frames diabetes more broadly as increased morbidity in people needing surgery; RCOG (p.4) treats diabetes and oral steroids as amber sepsis flags (steroids via impaired immunity); ERAS links advanced age to prolonged stay after laparoscopic gynecologic surgery; RNAO sets waist circumference ≥102 cm (men)/≥88 cm (women) as a risk marker for diabetes, heart disease and hypertension.

Not established: no gynecologic-specific wound-healing thresholds, no glycemic targets or timing for perioperative glucose control, no antibiotic or dressing choices, no smoking/alcohol cessation intervals, and no quantified effect sizes or comparison between risk factors.

title: Delirium, Dementia and Depression in Older Adults
summary:
This community centres on acute and chronic neurocognitive vulnerability in older and hospitalized adults — delirium, dementia, depression and their shared consequences (falls, functional decline, medication-related harm).

Risk factors for delirium are the densest cluster: pre-existing dementia in hospitalized older adults, hospitalization itself, major elective surgery, hip fracture repair and cardiac surgery in older adults; infection, hypoxia, electrolyte imbalance, acute brain injury, sensory overload, excess stress and sleep deprivation; unavailable glasses/hearing aids in hospitalized older adults; and drugs — benzodiazepines (especially the frail elderly) and sedatives (older adults, clients already delirious). Depression risk is tied to dementia, diabetes, heart disease, cancer and kidney disease in older adults, and to functional decline in self-care/ADLs. Dementia also predisposes to functional incontinence, delayed sepsis diagnosis when history/symptoms cannot be communicated (NICE), medication-related harm (RNAO, Ontario), and falls in agitated, confused inpatients — as does delirium and cognitive impairment generally.

Recommended actions: prevent delirium in older adults with environmental control (quiet, well-lit room, clocks/calendars in view, family visits — also used as treatment), assistive sensory devices (glasses, hearing aids in place), and consistent staff assignment when possible; ERAS Society adds bispectral index monitoring in elderly surgical patients to reduce inhalational anesthetic dose, preventing delirium and postoperative cognitive dysfunction. Detection: trained nurse/physician delirium assessment for new altered mental status, delirium evaluation tools in hospitalized adults, cognitive function and mental status monitoring against baseline with prompt reporting, early detection at end of life (reversible causes may resolve), and the mini-mental status examination (24–30 no impairment, 18–23 mild, <18 severe) for hospital patients and long-term care residents. Depression: screening in older adults, watching for signs in clients with pain, treatment with medication, psychotherapy, or SSRIs first-line in palliative care.

Granularity differs: OpenRN supplies almost all delirium content; ERAS is uniquely intraoperative; NICE and RNAO contribute only dementia-specific harms. Not established: no gynecologic- or perioperative-nursing-specific pathways, no drug doses, screening intervals, tool names/cut-offs beyond MMSE, no comparative effectiveness of preventive measures, and no antipsychotic or delirium-treatment pharmacology.

title: Postpartum anticoagulation timing relative to delivery
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: how the timing of postpartum anticoagulation is anchored to the event of delivery. Both relations in the community are TIMING_DEPENDS_ON links pointing at 'delivery', making childbirth the pivotal reference point for restarting or switching anticoagulant therapy.

Two recommendations are captured. First, for postpartum women receiving thromboprophylaxis, low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) should be given as soon as possible after delivery, conditional on two safety criteria being met: there is no postpartum haemorrhage, and regional analgesia (e.g. epidural/spinal) has not been used. Second, for women who are on maintenance warfarin outside of pregnancy, conversion from LMWH back to warfarin should be delayed for at least 5–7 days after delivery, explicitly to minimise the risk of haemorrhage. Together these describe a sequence: prompt LMWH cover early postpartum, with deferred re-establishment of oral vitamin K antagonist therapy.

Only one guideline body contributes here: the RCOG (Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists), from a single source document (RCOG T1, pages 5 and 25). There is therefore no inter-body disagreement to reconcile; however, the two statements differ in specificity. The warfarin conversion recommendation gives a concrete numeric window (at least 5–7 days), whereas the LMWH recommendation is qualitative ('as soon as possible') and instead specifies clinical preconditions rather than a fixed hour or day threshold.

What this community does NOT establish: no LMWH doses, dose bands, weight-based dosing or brand names; no specific number of hours to wait after regional analgesia or after removal of an epidural catheter; no definition or volume threshold for what constitutes postpartum haemorrhage; no INR target or overlap/bridging protocol for the warfarin switch; no duration of postpartum thromboprophylaxis; no guidance for caesarean versus vaginal delivery, for breastfeeding, or for antenatal/intrapartum management. It also does not address alternative agents (e.g. unfractionated heparin, direct oral anticoagulants) or monitoring and risk-assessment tools, nor does it identify who should make these timing decisions.
key_entities: conversion from lmwh back to warfarin

title: Communication barriers delaying sepsis diagnosis
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused equity-and-recognition theme: cognitive and mental health conditions that impair a patient's ability to give a history or describe symptoms are recognised risk factors for DELAYED DIAGNOSIS OF SEPSIS. Three parallel relations are asserted, all from the same source (NICE, Tier 1, p58): dementia increases risk of delayed sepsis diagnosis for people with dementia; learning disability increases risk for people with learning disabilities; and severe mental health condition increases risk for people with severe mental health conditions. In every case the attached condition is identical and explicit — the risk applies 'when they find it challenging to communicate their history or symptoms.' The practical implication for perioperative gynecologic nursing is that these three populations warrant heightened vigilance and a lower threshold for objective assessment, because the usual reliance on patient-reported symptoms is unreliable; carers, family or support staff and observable signs become the primary information source.

Only one guideline body contributes here: NICE. There is therefore no cross-body agreement or disagreement to reconcile, and no more-specific competing statement from another organisation within this community. NICE's specificity lies in naming three discrete populations and a shared triggering condition (communication difficulty) rather than describing generic 'vulnerable patients.'

Importantly, the community does NOT establish: any numeric thresholds (no NEWS/NEWS2, lactate, temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate or blood pressure values); no timings for escalation, review, antibiotic administration or the sepsis six; no named drugs or antibiotic regimens; no screening tool, checklist or documentation requirement; no defined roles for who must assess or escalate; and no gynecologic- or perioperative-specific qualifiers such as post-hysterectomy or post-caesarean context. It also does not quantify the magnitude of increased risk, nor does it address other communication barriers (for example language, delirium, sedation, intubation or age extremes), and it makes no statement about outcomes such as mortality or ICU admission. Educators should treat this as a risk-awareness statement requiring local operational detail.

title: Lymphedema Risk Factors and Symptom Management
summary:
This community represents a single clinical theme: the etiology of lymphedema and its symptomatic (non-curative) management, as relevant to gynecologic oncology and perioperative nursing. All content derives from one source, OpenRN Nursing Care of Patients with Cancer/lymphatic content (OpenRN Textbook 2, p817); no second guideline body contributes, so there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile and no comparative specificity to weigh.

Four risk relationships are established, all as risk-increasing (not causal-deterministic) links to lymphedema: (1) infection; (2) cancer itself; (3) surgical removal of lymph nodes — directly relevant to perioperative gynecologic patients undergoing lymphadenectomy or nodal sampling; and (4) radiation therapy, with the stated condition that risk arises from scar tissue produced by radiation. None of these four relations attaches a narrower population, laterality, node count threshold, radiation dose, or time window, so they should be taught as general risk awareness applicable to any patient with cancer, prior nodal surgery, prior radiation, or intercurrent infection.

One management recommendation is present: massage TREATS lymphedema, with the population specified as patients who already have lymphedema, and an explicit qualifying condition that it helps manage symptoms only. Educators should stress this limitation — massage is framed as symptom management, not resolution or cure.

What the community does NOT establish: no drugs or pharmacologic agents are named; no dosing, frequency, duration, or timing of massage; no numeric thresholds (e.g., limb circumference or volume difference, number of nodes removed, radiation Gy); no compression garments, pneumatic pumps, complete decongestive therapy, exercise, skin care, or elevation protocols; no screening, surveillance, or baseline-measurement schedule; no prophylaxis or prevention strategy for at-risk perioperative patients; no severity staging; no criteria for referral to lymphedema therapy; and no infection-prevention guidance despite infection being listed as a risk factor. It also does not quantify relative risk among the four factors or address gynecologic-specific (e.g., lower-extremity or genital) lymphedema distinctly. Local protocols would be needed to operationalize prevention and escalation.

title: Preoperative Surgical Hand Antisepsis Agents
summary:
This community represents preoperative surgical hand antisepsis — specifically which antiseptic agents surgical personnel use for the surgical hand scrub, and one recognised skin-related adverse effect of repeated antiseptic exposure. All relations derive from a single source, CDC Table 1 (pages 10 and 20); no other guideline body contributes, so there are no inter-organisational disagreements to reconcile here.

Main recommendations. (1) Chlorhexidine gluconate applies to the surgical hand scrub for surgical personnel, specified as detergent-based formulations containing 2% or 4% chlorhexidine gluconate (CDC T1 p20). (2) Alcohol-based preparations also apply to the surgical hand scrub for surgical personnel, but with a sequencing condition: they are used following an initial 1- or 2-minute scrub with an antiseptic detergent (CDC T1 p20). (3) The surgical hand scrub itself is situated in the preoperative phase for surgical staff (CDC T1 p20). (4) Safety caveat: chlorhexidine gluconate increases risk of dermatitis, with the condition attached to products containing 4% used frequently for antiseptic handwashing (CDC T1 p10).

Where the corpus is more or less specific. The CDC content is precise on concentration thresholds (2% vs 4% CHG), on the alcohol sequencing timing (1–2 minute detergent scrub first), and on tying the 4% dermatitis risk to frequent antiseptic handwashing rather than to CHG generally. That gives an educator a concrete teaching point: 4% CHG used frequently carries a skin-integrity trade-off, which may argue for the 2% detergent option or the detergent-then-alcohol sequence.

What this community does NOT establish. It does not state total scrub duration for the CHG scrub, the specific alcohol concentration or product type, drying or nail/brush technique, or how many scrub cycles per shift constitute "frequent" use. It makes no claim of superiority between chlorhexidine gluconate and alcohol-based preparations, gives no surgical-site-infection outcome data, and says nothing about patient skin preparation, intraoperative or postoperative phases, glove use, or management of established dermatitis. Non-surgical staff and patient populations are out of scope.

title: Dextran thromboprophylaxis risks in pregnancy
summary:
This community centres on a single agent — dextran — used as pharmacological thromboprophylaxis, and the sharp divide between its limited role in non-pregnant surgical patients and its contraindication in pregnancy. All relations derive from RCOG Green-top guidance on thromboprophylaxis (RCOG T1, pages 7 and 26); no other guideline body contributes, so no inter-body disagreement can be demonstrated.

Key points by population and condition. In non-pregnant patients, dextran is credited with preventing deep venous thrombosis in the postoperative setting, but the guideline explicitly qualifies this: the evidence is weak and dextran is less effective than low molecular weight heparin (LMWH). Independently of pregnancy status, dextran increases the risk of bleeding. In pregnant women, dextran is contraindicated both antenatally and intrapartum, because it increases the risk of anaphylactoid reaction in that window — the only relation duplicated across two pages (p7 and p26), indicating it is stated both as a summary recommendation and in the detailed text. In the specific setting of anaphylaxis to dextran in pregnant women, the guideline links the reaction to a cluster of fetal and uterine harms: uterine hypertonus, fetal distress, and fetal neurological abnormality. Page 26 is the more granular source, carrying the mechanism-level detail and the non-pregnant DVT-prevention statement, while page 7 restates only the pregnancy anaphylactoid risk.

What this community does not establish: no dose, infusion rate, duration, timing thresholds, or monitoring parameters for dextran; no numeric incidence or relative risk for anaphylactoid reaction, bleeding, or the fetal outcomes; no guidance on postpartum or breastfeeding use (only antenatal and intrapartum are specified); no management pathway for a dextran anaphylactoid reaction once it occurs; and no direct comparison with agents other than the stated inferiority to LMWH. Mechanical prophylaxis, aspirin, unfractionated heparin and fondaparinux are absent. Educators should therefore use this theme to teach why dextran is avoided in obstetric care and why LMWH is preferred, not how to administer dextran.

title: Diarrhea, Fluid Loss, and Rehydration Management
summary: This community centres on diarrhea as a symptom driver of deficient fluid volume, its causes, monitoring and treatment. Causes named: chemotherapy and pelvic radiation (clients receiving these therapies), medication as an adverse effect in hospitalized patients, gastrointestinal irritation, and high fibre intake in some persons following the DASH eating plan (RNAO), which also risks bloating. RNAO's preventive recommendation is to increase fruit, vegetable and whole grain intake gradually rather than abruptly, preventing both diarrhea and bloating. Deficient fluid volume is driven by diarrhea, vomiting, fever, uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, and diuretic therapy (clients receiving diuretics). Monitoring: assess signs of deficient fluid volume in at-risk clients — poor skin turgor, delayed capillary refill, weak/thready pulse, severe thirst, dry mucous membranes, decreased urinary output; hemodynamic status every 15 minutes to one hour for unstable clients with deficient fluid volume. Assess stool characteristics in clients receiving laxatives and stool softeners, before administering them. Treatment: oral fluid intake, promoting hydration early with water or fluids that improve electrolyte status, intravenous hydration as ordered, and intravenous fluids based on the client's disease stage and goals for care; antidiarrheals as appropriate for clients with deficient fluid volume, withholding antidiarrheal medication if diarrhea resolves or constipation develops; medication to slow intestinal motility as ordered and appropriate; and, for chemotherapy/radiation-related diarrhea, loperamide, psyllium, or an anticholinergic agent may be prescribed to decrease incidence. One perioperative caveat comes from WHO: oral fluid intake is temporarily contraindicated in volume-depleted surgical patients when a general anaesthetic is impending — the only guideline here linking rehydration to anaesthetic timing. OpenRN supplies nearly all pathophysiology, monitoring parameters and drug specifics; RNAO contributes only dietary-fibre prevention; WHO only the anaesthesia contraindication. The community does not establish doses, frequencies or durations for loperamide, psyllium, anticholinergics or antidiarrheals, IV fluid types or volumes, diarrhea severity grading, fasting intervals before anaesthesia, or any gynecologic-surgery-specific thresholds; no comparative effectiveness among the antidiarrheal options is stated.
key_entities: gradual increase of fruit, vegetable and whole grain intake

title: Preoperative Airway and Aspiration Risk Assessment
summary:
This community centres on preoperative airway evaluation: identifying the difficult airway and aspiration risk before anaesthesia, and the equipment/technique responses that follow. Core recommendation: every patient should undergo airway assessment in the preoperative phase (WHO T1 p35, p36), using objective evaluation with a valid grading method — the Mallampati score, thyromental distance, or Bellhouse-Doré score — with a Mallampati score of 3 or 4 flagged as indicating a difficult airway (p107, p10). The same assessment is used to evaluate risk of aspiration in patients undergoing anaesthesia (p10, p107); a distinct 'airway and aspiration risk evaluation' is specified to occur before induction of anaesthesia (p117). Where the airway is only questionably difficult, a radiograph may help detect difficulty (p35). For patients whose airway is expected to be difficult, fibre-optic intubation is described as the gold standard for management, and can also be diagnostic in patients at high risk of airway failure — but only when used by anaesthetists experienced with it, in carefully selected cases (p36). Critically, induction of anaesthesia is temporarily contraindicated in patients recognised as having a difficult airway or aspiration risk until the anaesthetist confirms adequate equipment and assistance are present at the bedside (p107). Radiograph also appears in a separate safety role: detecting a retained surgical item in surgical patients when a count ought to be performed but is not, taken at completion of the procedure (p79).

All relations derive from a single guideline body (WHO, Tool 1), so there are no inter-body disagreements; differences are only in specificity — p107 and p10 name concrete grading tools and thresholds, whereas p35/p36 state the universal requirement generically.

Not established: no drugs (e.g. aspiration prophylaxis agents), fasting intervals, NPO thresholds, videolaryngoscopy or supraglottic alternatives, gynecology-specific or obstetric populations, paediatric criteria, documentation/handover requirements, or outcome data on whether assessment reduces failed intubation or aspiration.

title: Patient Risk Factors for Difficult Mask Ventilation
summary:
This community represents a single, narrowly scoped airway-safety theme: patient-level predictors of difficult mask ventilation, drawn from the WHO surgical safety guidance (Table 1, p36) as applied within perioperative gynecologic nursing practice. Both relations in the community are risk-attribution statements rather than intervention recommendations.

The two established points are: (1) age over 55 years increases the risk of difficult mask ventilation, and (2) body mass index over 26 increases the risk of difficult mask ventilation. Both carry the same population qualifier — adults — and neither is restricted to a particular procedure, anaesthetic technique, or phase of care beyond that. For a nurse educator, the practical takeaway is that these two objective, pre-anaesthetic data points (chronological age >55 years; calculated BMI >26 kg/m2) should be captured and flagged during preoperative assessment and handover of adult gynecologic surgical patients, so that airway difficulty is anticipated before induction.

Only one guideline body contributes here: WHO (Table 1, p36). Because there is a single source, the community contains no inter-guideline disagreement, no competing thresholds, and no instance of one body being more specific than another. The WHO thresholds themselves are precise and numeric, which makes them directly auditable in a QI checklist.

What this community does NOT establish is substantial. It gives no recommended action, escalation pathway, or equipment standard — no mention of two-person mask technique, oral or nasopharyngeal airways, supraglottic devices, videolaryngoscopy, or awake intubation. It names no drugs, doses, or induction agents, and specifies no timings (for example, when assessment must occur relative to induction). It does not address other commonly cited predictors such as beard, edentulousness, snoring or obstructive sleep apnoea, Mallampati class, thyromental distance, or limited neck extension, nor does it quantify the magnitude of risk conferred by age >55 or BMI >26, or whether the two factors are additive. It also says nothing about difficult intubation as distinct from difficult mask ventilation, nor about paediatric, obstetric, or emergency populations.

title: Routine Four-Hourly Vaginal Examination Intrapartum
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: the use of routine digital vaginal examination as a labour-progress assessment during the intrapartum phase. Both relations in the community centre on the same intervention (digital vaginal examination) and the same population (women in active labour), and both are drawn from WHO Table 1, page 20.

The recommendations are: (1) digital vaginal examination is situated within the intrapartum phase of care, performed for women in active labour at intervals of four hours; and (2) when performed at four-hourly intervals as a routine assessment, digital vaginal examination serves to detect delay in active labour. The practical implication for practice is that the four-hour interval is the specified timing for routine assessment in active labour, and that identification of delayed progress is the stated diagnostic purpose of that routine schedule.

Only one guideline body contributes here: WHO (source WHO T1 p20). Because there is a single contributing source, this community contains no cross-body agreement or disagreement, and no instance where one organisation is more specific or more permissive than another. Nurse educators should therefore treat the four-hourly interval as WHO-attributed rather than as a corroborated multi-guideline consensus, and should check other communities in the corpus for any competing or supplementary guidance.

The community does not establish: who should perform the examination or the required competency; aseptic technique, consent, or documentation requirements; findings to be recorded (for example cervical dilatation, effacement, station, or membrane status); any numeric threshold or rate of dilatation that defines delay in active labour; the actions or escalation pathway once delay is detected (no augmentation agent, oxytocin regimen, amniotomy, or caesarean threshold is named); indications for examination outside the four-hourly routine (such as suspected rupture of membranes, bleeding, or fetal heart rate concerns); applicability to latent-phase labour, preterm labour, or women with ruptured membranes; alternative or adjunct assessment methods; and any statement of recommendation strength or evidence certainty.

title: Preventing Bloodborne Virus Exposure in Staff
summary:
This community represents occupational protection of health-care personnel from bloodborne virus transmission in the perioperative setting, combining two complementary strategies: engineering/work-practice control of sharps and active immunization against hepatitis B.

Sharps-related recommendations (WHO Tool 1, p211) apply to health-care workers generally. First, keep handling of sharps to a minimum — an unconditioned, general work-practice control stated to prevent bloodborne virus infection. Second, discard the needle directly into a sharps container, with the explicit condition that this occurs immediately after use and at the point of use (i.e., no transport, recapping step, or intermediate placement is contemplated).

Immunization recommendations come from two bodies. WHO Tool 1 (p211) recommends hepatitis B immunization for students and all health-care workers, timed so that they are immunized as soon as they start seeing patients; WHO links this both to prevention of bloodborne virus infection broadly and, for students specifically, to prevention of hepatitis B. OpenRN (Tool 2, p203) makes the narrower statement that hepatitis B vaccination prevents hepatitis B in workers exposed to blood-borne pathogens.

Contributing bodies are WHO (Tool 1, p211) and OpenRN (Tool 2, p203). WHO is the more specific source: it names the population inclusively (students plus all health-care workers), attaches a timing condition (immunize at the start of patient contact), and adds the sharps-handling controls. OpenRN contributes only vaccination, with an exposure-based population framing ("workers exposed to blood-borne pathogens") rather than a role- or timing-based one. The two do not conflict; OpenRN is a subset of WHO's broader position.

The community does NOT establish: any vaccine schedule, dose, number of doses, or product name; anti-HBs titre thresholds or post-vaccination serologic testing; management of non-responders; any post-exposure prophylaxis, reporting, or follow-up pathway after a needlestick; protection against HIV or hepatitis C specifically (only the generic "bloodborne virus infection" node); safety-engineered device selection; sharps container specifications or disposal; personal protective equipment; and any effectiveness, incidence, or compliance data.
key_entities: keep handling of sharps to a minimum
discard needle directly into sharps container at point of use

title: Gowns and Aprons Preventing Clothing Contamination
summary:
This community covers protective body coverings — gowns and disposable plastic aprons — as barrier PPE that prevents contamination of health-care workers' clothing, either with feces (enteric precautions) or with blood and body fluids generally.

Main recommendations: (1) Wearing a gown prevents fecal contamination of clothing for health care workers entering the room of clients on enteric precautions; the condition attached is that the gown is always worn in the client room (OpenRN Text 2, p642, restated in OpenRN T2 as 'worn in the client room when enteric precautions are in place'). (2) A gown prevents contamination of clothing with blood and body fluids for health-care workers, with the type of gown selected according to the nature of the patient interaction and the potential for blood and body fluid penetration (WHO Text 1, p211). (3) A disposable plastic apron prevents contamination of clothing with blood and body fluids for health-care professionals and students, indicated when in close contact with patients, material or equipment, or whenever there is a risk that clothing may become contaminated (WHO T1, p211).

Contributing bodies: WHO (Text 1) and OpenRN (Text 2). They emphasise different triggers. OpenRN is transmission-based and room-based: the trigger is enteric precautions and the boundary is the client room, with an absolute 'always' condition. WHO is risk-assessment based: garment choice is graded to the anticipated interaction and fluid-penetration risk, and WHO uniquely names the disposable plastic apron and uniquely extends the population to students as well as qualified professionals.

What the community does not establish: no gown material specifications, sterility requirements, fluid-resistance standards or sizes; no donning/doffing sequence, duration of wear, or change frequency; no disposal, laundering or reuse guidance; no linkage to gloves, masks, eye protection or hand hygiene; no gynecologic- or perioperative-specific indications (e.g., surgical versus isolation gowns); and no outcome data, compliance thresholds or evidence grading supporting either approach.
key_entities: contamination of clothing with blood and body fluids

title: Dizziness Monitoring Across Medication Routes
summary:
This community centres on dizziness as a shared nursing assessment endpoint across several medication administration routes, together with the closely linked findings of orthostatic hypotension and nausea. Four concrete recommendations appear. First, monitoring for dizziness upon standing is directed at patients receiving rectal medication, where dizziness is the monitored outcome (OpenRN Table 2, p905); the same monitoring practice is also linked, without a stated population, to detection of orthostatic hypotension (p1111). Second, for patients receiving cardiac medication, the cardiac medication is treated as temporarily contraindicated if the patient suddenly becomes dizzy, and administration is postponed until further assessments are performed (p895) — this is the only relation in the community that changes a drug decision rather than only prompting observation. Third, for patients receiving ear instillation, monitoring for side effects is required when instilling medication or fluids into the ear, with both dizziness and nausea named as the side effects to watch for (p922). Taken together, the theme instructs educators that dizziness is a cross-route red flag: after rectal administration it is assessed positionally (on standing), during otic instillation it is assessed as an immediate side effect, and in cardiac medication administration it functions as a hold criterion.

All relations derive from a single guideline body, the OpenRN nursing skills corpus (Table 2, pages 895, 905, 911/1111, 922); there are therefore no inter-organisational disagreements to reconcile. Specificity differs internally: the ear-instillation and cardiac-medication entries carry both a population and a timing/trigger condition, the rectal-medication entry carries a population only, and the orthostatic hypotension link carries neither population nor condition.

The community does not establish any numeric thresholds (no blood pressure drop values, heart rate limits, or time intervals for reassessment), does not name specific drugs or classes within "cardiac medication," does not define what "further assessments" comprise or who authorises resumption, and offers no perioperative or gynecologic-specific population, no fall-prevention interventions, and no treatment for nausea or documentation requirements.

title: Cholinesterase Inhibitors and Memantine for Alzheimer Cognition
summary:
This community represents pharmacologic management of cognitive symptoms in Alzheimer disease, centred on four agents: the cholinesterase inhibitors donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine, plus the NMDA-receptor antagonist memantine. All four are linked to two targets in the corpus: Alzheimer disease itself and, more generally, cognitive symptoms.

Stage-specific recommendations come from OpenRN Nursing Pharmacology (Volume/Text 2), p1408. Donepezil is indicated across all stages of Alzheimer's disease, making it the broadest-spectrum agent in this set. Rivastigmine and galantamine are both restricted to mild-to-moderate stages. Memantine is positioned for moderate to severe Alzheimer's. Together these staging conditions form a near-continuous coverage: mild-to-moderate (rivastigmine, galantamine), moderate to severe (memantine), and all stages (donepezil).

A second, less specific set of statements from OpenRN T2 p468 records that each of the same four drugs treats cognitive symptoms, with no population or stage qualifier attached. The p1408 material is therefore the more specific source: it supplies the disease label and the stage thresholds that p468 omits. There is no contradiction between the two passages — p468 is simply a symptom-level restatement, and a nurse educator should teach from p1408 for staging decisions while using p468 to frame the shared therapeutic goal of cognitive symptom control.

Only one guideline body contributes here (OpenRN), so no inter-organisational disagreement can be assessed from this community.

Important gaps: the community establishes no dosing, titration schedules, routes, or timings; no monitoring parameters, adverse effects, contraindications, or drug interactions; no comparative efficacy or preference ranking among the three cholinesterase inhibitors; and no guidance on combination therapy (for example donepezil plus memantine). It also says nothing about perioperative or gynecologic-surgical considerations — such as whether these agents should be continued or withheld before surgery, anesthetic interactions, or postoperative delirium risk — despite the perioperative framing of the wider corpus. Non-pharmacologic cognitive interventions, caregiver education, and treatment of behavioural (non-cognitive) symptoms are likewise absent.

title: Sterile Technique and Obstetric Haemorrhage Safeguards
summary: This community links intraoperative infection-prevention practice with obstetric haemorrhage management across vaginal delivery and caesarean section. Two strands emerge. First, sterile barrier and hand hygiene practice: WHO states sterile gloves apply to surgical procedures, vaginal delivery, and invasive procedures or any task requiring sterile conditions (health-care professionals), and that gloves worn by the operating team during the operation prevent surgical site infection. CDC adds mechanism-level detail: sterile gloves prevent contamination of surgical team members' hands with blood and body fluids and prevent transmission of microorganisms to patients (all scrubbed team members), and double-gloving further reduces hand contamination compared with a single pair. CDC also specifies surgical hand antisepsis for surgical personnel in the preoperative phase, before donning sterile gloves, using either an antimicrobial soap or an alcohol-based hand rub with persistent activity. NICE contributes the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist, applied to each surgical procedure, including dental procedures. Second, haemorrhage care: RCOG recommends prophylactic oxytocin after vaginal delivery, noting higher doses of 40 IU or 80 IU did not reduce overall PPH treatment compared with 10 IU. RCOG also recommends considering intraoperative cell salvage for emergency use in women with PPH associated with caesarean section or vaginal delivery, occurring in the intrapartum phase. RCOG further notes that vaginal delivery increases risk of hysterectomy in women treated with a uterine compression suture to control PPH. Contributing bodies: WHO (glove indications, SSI prevention), CDC (most specific on hand antisepsis agents, timing, double-gloving), NICE (checklist scope), RCOG (obstetric haemorrhage). They are complementary rather than conflicting; CDC is more granular than WHO on technique, and NICE alone extends checklist use to dental procedures. Not established: any causal link between glove or hand-antisepsis practice and obstetric haemorrhage outcomes; specific glove-change intervals, scrub durations, or which double-gloving indication applies; oxytocin route, timing, or dose for caesarean section; cell salvage eligibility criteria, volumes, or filtration requirements; and quantified hysterectomy risk after compression suture.

title: Pre-procedural analgesia timing for painful interventions
summary: This community represents a single, coherent theme: timing analgesia around painful nursing and rehabilitation activities so that pain control is in place before the intervention rather than after it. Two procedure clusters are covered. First, physical therapy/rehabilitation: PRN pain medication treats pain in a client with fractures undergoing rehabilitation, given before physical therapy so the client can participate in the exercises; in the specific case of a client refusing pain medication for cultural reasons, the documented timing was administration one hour before the scheduled physical therapy session. Second, wound care: PRN pain medication should be offered in advance of a dressing change for clients with pain; analgesic medication treats wound pain in patients with painful wounds when administered before the dressing change; and premedication treats wound pain in patients undergoing dressing changes when the wound is painful, given before the dressing change. A related but distinct dressing recommendation appears in the same cluster: for patients with nonadherent or petroleum-impregnated gauze dressings, changing the dressing every 24–28 hours prevents adherence to the wound bed. All relations derive from a single guideline body, OpenRN Nursing Skills/Fundamentals (Textbook 2, pp. 771, 788, 1145, 1151, 1165); there are no competing or conflicting bodies here. Specificity varies within that source: only p788 supplies a concrete interval (one hour pre-therapy), while pp. 771, 1145 and 1165 state only 'before' or 'in advance of' the dressing change. Terminology also varies (PRN pain medication, analgesic medication, premedication) without the source distinguishing them pharmacologically. The community does NOT establish drug names, doses, routes, or maximum frequencies; it does not specify a pre-dressing-change lead time; it gives no pain-score threshold that should trigger premedication; it does not address non-pharmacologic adjuncts, pediatric, obstetric or perioperative gynecologic subpopulations specifically; and it does not describe how to manage patients who decline analgesia beyond noting the cultural-refusal scenario. Reassessment and documentation expectations after administration are absent.

title: Controlled Substance Safeguards Against Drug Diversion
summary:
This community represents a narrow but high-stakes theme: institutional safeguards that protect controlled substances from diversion in the perioperative/gynecologic nursing setting. It contains only two relations, both drawn from OpenRN Nursing Skills (Text 2, p. 854), and both converge on a single adverse outcome entity — drug diversion.

The first recommendation is general: controlled substance safety measures prevent drug diversion. No population restriction, unit, drug class, or triggering condition is attached to this relation, so it should be read as a baseline expectation applying wherever controlled substances are stocked or administered.

The second recommendation is the operational specific: a two-nurse controlled substance count is used to monitor for drug diversion. Its conditions are explicit — it is performed at every shift change, and the physical count is compared against the controlled substance administration record. This is the more concrete of the two statements and is the one a QI lead can audit directly: the observable metrics are shift-change completion rate, two-nurse participation, and count-versus-record reconciliation/discrepancy rate.

Only one guideline body contributes (OpenRN), so there is no inter-body disagreement to reconcile; there is instead a difference in specificity within the same source, where the broad "safety measures" statement is operationalised by the two-nurse shift-change count. Educators should note the distinct verbs: safety measures are framed as preventive, while the count is framed as detective/monitoring — the count identifies discrepancies rather than stopping diversion at the point of access.

What this community does NOT establish: it names no specific controlled drugs (no opioid, benzodiazepine, or anaesthetic agents), no dose or quantity thresholds, and no acceptable discrepancy tolerance. It does not specify who the two nurses must be (e.g. licensure level, outgoing versus incoming), how to document or escalate a discrepancy, reporting timelines, or regulatory/board notification duties. It defines no gynecologic- or perioperative-specific population, no wastage or witnessing procedure, no automated dispensing cabinet or e-record requirement, and gives no evidence grade, sanction pathway, or outcome data on diversion rates.
key_entities: two-nurse controlled substance count at shift change

title: NSAID GI Side Effects: Food Administration
summary:
This community represents a narrow but practically important theme in perioperative gynecologic nursing: the gastrointestinal tolerability of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and the use of administration with food as a simple nursing countermeasure.

The core risk statement is that NSAIDs increase the risk of dyspepsia (OpenRN Table 2, p. 825). The corresponding nursing recommendation is that administration with food prevents dyspepsia and prevents nausea. Both preventive relations are conditioned on a specific population: clients taking NSAIDs (stated in one instance as 'clients taking nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs' at p. 825, and as 'clients taking NSAIDs' in the other instances). The practical teaching point is therefore consistent and actionable — when an NSAID is administered or dispensed, pair the dose with food to reduce dyspepsia and nausea.

Only one guideline body contributes here: OpenRN, via its Table 2 medication content, with the more granular citation being OpenRN T2 p. 825. There is no cross-body disagreement to reconcile. The only variation is in specificity of expression: the p. 825 entries state the risk relation and spell out the population using the full drug-class name, whereas the unpaginated OpenRN T2 entries extend the same food-with-dose advice to nausea as well as dyspepsia. Educators can treat these as a single coherent recommendation rather than competing guidance.

What the community does not establish: it names no individual NSAID agents (no ibuprofen, ketorolac, naproxen, or aspirin), no doses, no thresholds, and no timing beyond the general instruction to give with food. It does not specify whether food should precede, accompany, or follow the dose, nor any minimum quantity or type of food. It says nothing about more serious NSAID gastrointestinal harms such as ulceration or bleeding, nothing about acid-suppression co-therapy, and nothing about renal, bleeding, or cardiovascular risk. No gynecologic- or surgery-specific population (e.g., post-hysterectomy clients) is attached, and no duration of therapy, monitoring plan, or contraindicated group is defined.

title: Post-Stroke Dysphagia Screening in Nursing
summary:
This small community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: recognition of dysphagia as a consequence of cerebrovascular accident (stroke), and the nurse's role in detecting it through direct observation of swallowing. Two relations anchor the theme. First, cerebrovascular accident is identified as increasing the risk of dysphagia, with the population explicitly scoped to patients who have experienced a cerebrovascular accident. Second, assessment of swallowing of pills, liquid, or food is identified as a means of detecting dysphagia in that same population. The practical implication for education and quality improvement is that any patient with a stroke history should be considered at elevated risk for impaired swallowing, and that a structured bedside observation of how the patient manages pills, liquids, and solid food serves as the detection method named in the corpus.

Only one guideline body contributes here: OpenRN (Nursing Skills / fundamentals text), specifically Table 2 material on page 719. Because there is a single source, there are no inter-organizational disagreements, no competing thresholds, and no instance of one body being more specific than another; the corpus offers one consistent statement of risk and one consistent detection modality.

Importantly, the community does not establish a great deal that a QI lead would need for protocol design. It specifies no timing for screening (for example, no requirement to screen within a set number of hours of admission or before first oral intake), no validated screening tool or scoring threshold, no pass/fail criteria, and no frequency of reassessment. It names no drugs, no thickened-liquid or diet-texture levels, and no NPO orders. It does not identify who must perform or escalate the assessment (nurse versus speech-language pathologist), specifies no referral pathway, and does not link dysphagia to downstream outcomes such as aspiration, aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition, dehydration, or medication administration route changes. Other dysphagia risk factors beyond stroke are absent, as are perioperative or gynecologic-specific applications, despite the wider corpus context.
key_entities: assessment of swallowing of pills, liquid, or food
patients who have experienced a cerebrovascular accident

title: Dysphagia identification and treatment prevent aspiration
summary:
Clinical theme: this small community centres on swallowing impairment (dysphagia) as a modifiable risk factor for two downstream harms — aspiration pneumonia and unintended weight loss — in neurologically injured patients. It links a screening/assessment action (early identification) and a management action (treatment) to preventive outcomes, making it a useful anchor for pneumonia-prevention and nutrition bundles even though the source corpus is general nursing rather than gynecologic-specific.

Recommendations, with populations and conditions: (1) Early identification of dysphagia prevents aspiration pneumonia, specified for patients who have experienced a cerebrovascular accident (stroke) or other head injury (OpenRN Textbook 2, p471). (2) Treatment of dysphagia prevents aspiration pneumonia in patients with difficulty swallowing after a cerebrovascular accident (OpenRN Textbook 2, p719). (3) The same treatment relation, for the same post-CVA dysphagia population, also prevents unintended weight loss (OpenRN T2 p719).

Contributing bodies and differences: all three relations derive from a single source corpus, OpenRN (Open Resources for Nursing) Textbook 2, at two distinct locations. The p471 statement is broader in population — it includes 'other head injury' alongside cerebrovascular accident — and is narrower in scope of action, addressing only early identification and only aspiration pneumonia. The p719 statement is narrower in population (post-CVA difficulty swallowing only) but broader in outcome, adding unintended weight loss as a second prevented harm. There is no contradiction between them; they are complementary, with p719 extending the benefit of intervention beyond respiratory risk to nutritional risk.

What this community does NOT establish: no screening tool, bedside swallow test, or timing/threshold for 'early' identification is named; no specific treatments are described (no diet-texture levels, thickened-liquid grades, positioning protocols, speech-language pathology referral criteria, enteral feeding indications, or drugs); no frequency of reassessment, no weight-loss percentage or BMI threshold defining 'unintended weight loss', and no incidence or effect-size data are given. It also does not address perioperative or gynecologic surgical populations, postoperative nausea, sedation, or anaesthesia-related aspiration risk, and provides no guidance for non-neurologic causes of dysphagia.

title: Neonatal infection risk assessment after maternal sepsis
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: structured assessment of the newborn for risk factors and clinical indicators of infection when the mother has been treated with antibiotics for sepsis or invasive bacterial infection around the time of birth. Both relations in the community are detection relations, linking one intervention (assessment for risk factors and clinical indicators of neonatal infection) to two outcome entities (neonatal infection; early-onset neonatal infection).

The recommendations, with their populations and conditions, are: (1) perform assessment for risk factors and clinical indicators of neonatal infection in babies of women treated for sepsis during labour, or in the 24-hour period before or after birth (RCOG T1 p1); and (2) perform the same assessment to detect early-onset neonatal infection in babies of women who receive parenteral antibiotic treatment for confirmed or suspected invasive bacterial infection at any time during labour, or in the 24-hour periods before and after the birth (RCOG T1 p15). The practical trigger for both is therefore a maternal antibiotic-treated infection episode within a window spanning labour plus 24 hours pre- and post-birth.

Only one guideline body contributes: RCOG (Table 1, pages 1 and 15). There is no cross-body disagreement to reconcile. The two statements differ in specificity: the p15 version is more precise, naming the route and indication of maternal therapy (parenteral antibiotics for confirmed or suspected invasive bacterial infection), explicitly covering "any time during labour," and naming the outcome as early-onset neonatal infection; the p1 version uses the broader term "sepsis" and the general outcome "neonatal infection."

What this community does NOT establish: it names no specific antibiotic agents, doses or durations for mother or baby; no numeric thresholds (temperature, heart rate, CRP, white cell count) or scoring tools; no frequency, duration or documentation standard for the neonatal observations; no escalation, blood-culture, lumbar-puncture or treatment pathway if indicators are present; no discharge criteria; and no evidence grading, outcome data or applicability to babies whose mothers received oral or prophylactic-only antibiotics.
key_entities: assessment for risk factors and clinical indicators of neonatal infection
maternal sepsis treated during labour or within 24 hours before/after birth
parenteral antibiotic treatment for confirmed or suspected invasive bacterial infection

title: Edema Assessment and Fluid Overload Risk
summary:
This small community centres on edema as a clinical finding in perioperative gynecologic care: how it is detected and graded at the bedside, and one identified antecedent risk state. Two guideline sources contribute, and they address different halves of the theme.

Assessment recommendation (OpenRN Nursing Fundamentals/Skills, T2 p1111): edema should be assessed using the graded 1+ to 4+ scale. The relation is stated twice — once unconditionally, and once with an explicit population and timing qualifier: for clients with fluid and electrolyte imbalances, the graded assessment is to be performed prior to implementing interventions. Practically, this establishes edema grading as a baseline measurement that precedes and therefore informs treatment, rather than a finding documented after intervention. The OpenRN material is the more specific of the two contributors, in that it names the actual scoring instrument (1+ through 4+) and the timing (pre-intervention).

Risk recommendation (AUGS, T2 p5): fluid volume overload increases the risk of edema, with the population narrowed to the geriatric population. AUGS thus supplies the etiologic/risk framing and the age-specific population, while OpenRN supplies the measurement method. The two do not conflict; they are complementary, and together they support a workflow in which older patients receiving fluids are screened for volume overload and have edema graded on the 1+ to 4+ scale before interventions begin.

What the community does NOT establish: it names no drugs (no diuretics, no specific fluids or infusion rates), no numeric thresholds for intake, output, weight change, or serum electrolytes, and no volume or duration limits that would define "fluid volume overload." It does not specify reassessment frequency, which grade (e.g., 2+ vs 3+) should trigger escalation, who documents the finding, or what interventions follow. It also does not define edema anatomic site (pedal, sacral, periorbital), does not extend the geriatric risk statement to non-geriatric adults, and offers no outcome data linking graded assessment to improved perioperative results.
key_entities: edema assessment using the 1+ to 4+ scale
clients with fluid and electrolyte imbalances

title: Fluid, Electrolyte and Diuretic Monitoring
summary:
This community covers assessment, treatment and monitoring of fluid volume and electrolyte disturbances, with diuretic therapy as the central risk driver. Treatment: for clients with excess fluid volume, prescribed diuretics (monitoring for effect), prescribed fluid restriction and prescribed dietary sodium restriction; for fluid volume deficit, intravenous fluid and isotonic IV solution (to replace extracellular fluid lost to bleeding, dehydration, shock, burns, trauma or GI loss); IV fluid with electrolytes treats electrolyte imbalance. Isotonic solutions must be used with caution in hypertension, heart failure and renal disease because they can cause fluid volume overload, and excessive infusion causes excess fluid volume.

Diuretics increase risk of electrolyte imbalance, acid-base imbalance, orthostatic hypotension, and deficient fluid volume/fluid volume deficit in clients receiving them, and hypovolemia with excessive use; monitoring for fluid volume deficit is indicated in clients on diuretic therapy. Diabetes mellitus history also raises electrolyte imbalance risk. Electrolyte imbalance in turn increases risk of paralytic ileus, confusion and delirium.

Monitoring specifics: daily weights at consistent times with trending, notifying the provider for gain >1 kg in 24 hours; intake and output with 24-hour trends, notifying for urine output <30 mL/hour (0.5 mL/kg/hour, monitored for kidney injury in deficient fluid volume); vital signs (decreased BP with elevated heart rate and weak/thready pulse = deficit; elevated BP with bounding pulses = excess); serum osmolarity (elevated = deficit, decreased = excess) and urine osmolarity (increased/concentrated = deficit); close electrolyte monitoring of sodium, potassium, calcium, phosphorus, magnesium in at-risk clients; calcium and potassium with magnesium supplementation; dehydration/electrolyte assessment in hospitalized patients with diarrhea; and home monitoring for medication-related imbalance.

Contributions: OpenRN Nursing Fundamentals/Skills supplies nearly all bedside parameters and thresholds. RNAO adds the only drug-class-specific laboratory interval — sodium, potassium and creatinine every 6 to 12 months for patients on thiazide diuretics — which OpenRN does not specify.

Not established: no gynecologic or perioperative population is named, no specific diuretic drugs or doses, no numeric electrolyte or osmolarity cut-offs, no fluid-restriction volumes or sodium limits, and no evidence grading or outcome data.
key_entities: bloodwork monitoring of sodium, potassium and creatinine

title: Preventing Airway Disaster in Difficult Airways
summary: This community represents a single coherent clinical theme: prevention of airway disaster (failed or catastrophic airway management) in surgical patients, centred on identifying the difficult airway before induction and preparing accordingly.
