Three interventions converge on the same outcome. First, pre-induction airway evaluation prevents airway disaster when it is coupled with appropriate planning and careful preparation of both the patient and the equipment (WHO T1 p37) — this recommendation is stated for surgical patients generally, without a risk-stratified population. Second, regional anaesthesia prevents airway disaster in patients at high risk for a difficult airway, to be used 'if possible' as an adjustment to the planned approach to anaesthesia; one statement is more specific, defining high risk by example as a Mallampati score of 3 or 4 (WHO T1 p10), while the parallel statement leaves 'high risk' undefined (WHO T1 p107). Third, emergency airway equipment prevents airway disaster in the same high-risk population when it is kept accessible; here again one source is more specific, additionally requiring that a capable assistant be physically present at induction (WHO T1 p10), whereas the other requires only accessible equipment (WHO T1 p107). All relations derive from a single guideline body, the WHO (Tool/Table 1, pages 10, 37 and 107); there are therefore no cross-organisation disagreements, only differences in granularity between pages — p10 supplies the assessment threshold (Mallampati 3–4) and the staffing requirement, p107 gives the general form, and p37 supplies the assessment-and-planning step that identifies the population the other two recommendations act on. The community does NOT establish what the pre-induction evaluation should consist of beyond appropriate planning and preparation, nor which specific items constitute 'emergency airway equipment', nor the qualifications defining a 'capable assistant'. It names no drugs, no induction agents, no regional technique or block type, no monitoring parameters, and no timing beyond 'at induction'. It also does not specify a gynecologic or obstetric population, does not address awake or postoperative extubation risk, and gives no effect sizes, evidence grades or escalation pathway if regional anaesthesia is not possible.

title: Endometritis prevention, detection, and treatment
summary:
This community centres on postpartum/post-surgical endometritis — its risk factors, prophylaxis, surveillance detection, and antimicrobial treatment — with related invasive group A streptococcal sequelae.

Prevention (WHO T1): prophylactic antibiotics prevent endometritis in women undergoing both elective and non-elective caesarean section; vaginal swabbing with povidone-iodine solution, applied before caesarean section, also prevents endometritis in women undergoing caesarean section. WHO additionally names vaginal surgery as a risk factor for endometritis (no population or qualifier given).

Risk (RCOG T1 p11): perineal colonisation with group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus in pregnant women, on ascending vaginally, increases risk of endometritis as well as streptococcal toxic shock syndrome, myonecrosis and peritonitis — useful for teaching why perineal colonisation is not a trivial finding.

Detection: RCOG (T1 p30) specifies high vaginal and endocervical swabs when endometritis is suspected, and high vaginal swab plus routine vaginal microbiology assessment in women presenting with secondary postpartum haemorrhage. CDC (T1 p19) contributes a surveillance rather than bedside method: chart review triggered by a computer-generated report of antibiotic orders detects endometritis in postcaesarean section patients — relevant to QI case-finding.

Treatment: RCOG recommends antimicrobial therapy when endometritis is suspected, and appropriate use of antimicrobial therapy in women presenting with secondary postpartum haemorrhage. OpenRN (T2 p1172) adds a practical sequencing rule: for patients undergoing wound culture, obtain the specimen before antimicrobial therapy is started if possible — the only timing dependency stated here, and it reinforces RCOG's swab-then-treat logic.

Differences in specificity: WHO is most specific on prophylaxis agents/procedures (povidone-iodine, caesarean subgroups); RCOG is most specific on diagnostic specimens and the secondary PPH population; CDC addresses only surveillance detection; OpenRN only specimen timing.

Not established: no named antibiotic drugs, doses, routes, or durations for treatment or prophylaxis; no timing thresholds (e.g. minutes before incision), no diagnostic criteria, temperature or laboratory thresholds; no outcome or effectiveness data; nothing on vaginal-surgery prophylaxis, breastfeeding, or non-obstetric populations.
key_entities: chart review triggered by a computer-generated report of antibiotic orders
perineal colonisation with group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus

title: Airway and Oxygenation Monitoring During Anaesthesia
summary:
This community represents the theme of continuous physiological monitoring of oxygenation and ventilation during anaesthesia, and its role in preventing catastrophic hypoxic injury. Two monitoring modalities anchor the theme: pulse oximetry and capnography, both linked to the prevention of hypoxic brain damage in patients undergoing anaesthesia (WHO Surgical Safety Guidelines, Table 1, p22). Capnography carries two additional, more specific functions: it monitors for hypoxia in patients undergoing anaesthesia (p22), and it detects endotracheal tube misplacement, with the stated condition that detection occurs by displaying the expired carbon dioxide waveform and concentration (p25). For educators, the practical message is that pulse oximetry and capnography are complementary rather than interchangeable — pulse oximetry appears here only as a preventive measure against hypoxic brain damage, whereas capnography additionally provides ventilation-specific and airway-position-specific information, making it the more richly specified modality in this corpus.

Only one guideline body contributes to this community: the WHO, via Table 1 (p22) and p25. There are therefore no inter-body disagreements to reconcile here; the differences are internal to the WHO material, where p25 is more specific than p22 — p22 states the outcome (prevention of hypoxic brain damage, monitoring for hypoxia) while p25 specifies the mechanism of detection (expired CO2 waveform and concentration) and a distinct clinical target (endotracheal tube misplacement).

Importantly, this community does NOT establish: any numeric thresholds (no SpO2 percentage, no end-tidal CO2 value or range), any timing or frequency of monitoring (no interval for observation, no duration of monitoring post-anaesthesia), any device alarm settings, or any escalation/response algorithm once hypoxia or tube misplacement is detected. It names no drugs, no reversal agents, and no airway rescue techniques. It does not narrow the population beyond "patients undergoing anaesthesia" — there is no gynecologic-specific, paediatric, obstetric, or ASA-class stratification, and no distinction between general, regional, or sedation cases. Nor does it assign responsibility to a specific role (anaesthetist versus circulating or scrub nurse), or specify documentation requirements. Local protocols must supply these operational details.
key_entities: expired carbon dioxide waveform and concentration

title: ERAS Protocols in Urogynecologic Surgery
summary:
This community represents enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) as an integrated perioperative care pathway for urogynecologic surgery, together with two of its concrete intraoperative components: goal-directed fluid management and minimally invasive port strategy.

Main recommendations. (1) An ERAS protocol should be applied to urogynecologic surgical patients across all approaches described: vaginal surgery, open surgery, and laparoscopic/vaginal surgery with or without robotic assistance (AUGS T2 p7). The population is explicitly 'urogynecologic surgical patients' rather than a single procedure type. (2) ERAS is credited with preventing postoperative morbidity in older patients when compared with non-ERAS standard of care, with the supporting application in older patients undergoing colorectal resection (AUGS T2 p3) — i.e., the morbidity-reduction evidence cited is extrapolated from a colorectal population and applied to older surgical patients. (3) Intravenous fluid administration in laparoscopic and vaginal urogynecologic surgery should be given at rates of 2 mL/kg/h with the goal of euvolemia (AUGS T2 p5). (4) Surgeons should use the smallest sized and minimum number of laparoscopic ports in laparoscopic and vaginal urogynecologic surgery — specifically the number needed to efficiently perform the procedure (AUGS T2 p7).

Contributing bodies. All relations derive from a single source, the AUGS (American Urogynecologic Society) Table 2 material (pages 3, 5, 7). There are therefore no cross-society disagreements captured here. Internal specificity varies: the fluid recommendation is quantitative (2 mL/kg/h, euvolemia endpoint), whereas the port recommendation is qualitative/judgment-based, and the ERAS-to-approach recommendations state applicability without listing component elements.

What this community does NOT establish. It does not enumerate the individual ERAS bundle elements (no analgesic, antiemetic, antibiotic, VTE-prophylaxis, carbohydrate-loading or feeding specifics appear), gives no timings, no age threshold defining 'older patients', no fluid type or upper limit, no port size in millimetres or maximum port count, and no outcome data for urogynecologic patients themselves — the morbidity benefit is tied to colorectal resection in older patients. No nursing workflow, monitoring parameters, or contraindications are specified.
key_entities: use of smallest sized and minimum number of laparoscopic ports

title: Enhanced Recovery for Major Elective Surgery
summary:
This community represents the theme of enhanced recovery programmes (ERPs) and associated baseline assessment for people undergoing elective major or complex surgery — the population most relevant to major gynaecologic procedures. The organising principle is that enhanced recovery is not a single postoperative intervention but a pathway spanning all three perioperative phases.

Core recommendations: an enhanced recovery programme applies to people having elective major or complex surgery, and should span the preoperative, intraoperative and postoperative phases; the guideline explicitly states the programme should cover all 3 stages of perioperative care 'for optimum effectiveness'. The stated purpose is prevention: ERPs are linked to preventing complications and specifically postoperative complications in this same population (NICE T1 p20, with the phase-spanning structure restated at p6).

Two supporting assessments sit alongside the programme for the same broad surgical population. Nutritional screening applies to people having major or complex surgery. A full blood count should be offered routinely to people of ASA grade 1 to 4 having elective major or complex surgery — this is the only relation in the community carrying an explicit patient-stratification threshold (ASA 1–4) and the only one specifying 'offer the test routinely'.

Contributing bodies: all relations derive from a single source, NICE T1 (pages 6, 8, 9, 20). There is therefore no cross-body disagreement to reconcile here; the only variation is in granularity — p20 adds the conditional qualifiers ('for optimum effectiveness', 'all 3 stages') and the complication-prevention rationale, whereas p6 states the phase coverage and applicability plainly without conditions.

What this community does NOT establish: no drugs, doses, fluid or carbohydrate-loading regimens, mobilisation or feeding timings, length-of-stay targets, or discharge criteria are specified. It does not define which complications are prevented, quantify effect size, or state who delivers or coordinates the programme. Nutritional screening tools, thresholds and referral triggers are unspecified, as are FBC timing relative to surgery, target values, and what to do for ASA grade 5. No gynaecology-specific tailoring is given.

title: Postpartum Sexual Health and Dyspareunia Enquiry
summary:
This community represents a narrow but clinically important theme: routine enquiry about resumption of sexual intercourse and dyspareunia as an element of postpartum well-being assessment. It comprises a single practice (enquiry about sexual intercourse and dyspareunia), the care phase in which it belongs (postpartum), and the finding it is intended to identify (dyspareunia).

The recommendations are: (1) enquiry about sexual intercourse and dyspareunia occurs in the postpartum phase, for all women, timed at two to six weeks after birth; and (2) this enquiry serves to detect dyspareunia, again for all women, and specifically when conducted as part of an assessment of overall well-being two to six weeks after birth. The population is unrestricted — all postpartum women, not only those with perineal trauma, operative delivery, or caesarean — and the condition attached is the timing window plus the framing of the enquiry within a broader well-being assessment rather than as an isolated question.

Only one guideline body contributes: WHO (WHO T1 p23). Because a single source and a single page underpin both relations, there are no inter-body disagreements, no competing timing windows, and no instance of one organisation being more specific than another within this community. The specificity that does exist comes from WHO alone: the two-to-six-week window and the requirement that the enquiry sit inside an overall well-being assessment.

The community does not establish: any management, treatment, or pharmacological intervention for dyspareunia (no lubricants, topical oestrogen, analgesia, or pelvic floor physiotherapy are named); no screening tool, scripted wording, or scoring threshold; no referral criteria or escalation pathway; no follow-up interval beyond six weeks; no link to perineal trauma severity, mode of birth, breastfeeding status, or contraception counselling; and no documentation standard or quality indicator. It also says nothing about who should perform the enquiry, in what setting, or about privacy and consent considerations. Educators should therefore treat this as a case-finding prompt only, and source management guidance elsewhere.
key_entities: enquiry about sexual intercourse and dyspareunia

title: Managing Anorexia at End of Life
summary:
This community represents a narrow but clinically important theme: the management of anorexia (loss of appetite/reduced intake) in clients at the end of life, as addressed in palliative/end-of-life content within the perioperative gynecologic nursing corpus. All three relations converge on a single target condition — anorexia — and all specify the same population: clients at the end of life.

The recommendations fall into two modalities. Pharmacologic: mirtazapine and olanzapine are each identified as treatments for anorexia in end-of-life clients, with the stated condition that they are prescribed specifically to increase intake. Neither agent is differentiated from the other in the source material — no dosing, thresholds, sequencing, comparative efficacy, or timing of initiation is attached, and no preference between mirtazapine and olanzapine is expressed. Non-pharmacologic/nutritional: enteral nutrition treats anorexia in the same end-of-life population, but with a more specific qualifying condition — it is indicated for clients who continue to have an appetite but cannot swallow. This is the most precisely scoped recommendation in the community, as it hinges on preserved appetite plus impaired swallowing rather than on appetite loss alone.

All three relations derive from a single guideline body and location: OpenRN (Open Resources for Nursing), Text 2, page 1269. Because the corpus contribution is uniform, there are no inter-body disagreements, no conflicting populations, and no instances where one organisation is more specific than another; the only variation in specificity is internal, between the two appetite-stimulant entries (condition: prescribed to increase intake) and the enteral nutrition entry (condition: appetite present but swallowing impossible).

What this community does not establish: no doses, routes, frequencies, or titration for mirtazapine or olanzapine; no monitoring parameters, adverse-effect profiles, or contraindications; no thresholds for weight loss, caloric intake, or duration of anorexia that would trigger treatment; no guidance on when to withhold or withdraw enteral nutrition; no goals-of-care, consent, or ethical decision-making framing; and no linkage to gynecologic surgical populations, cancer cachexia specifically, or non-end-of-life anorexia.
key_entities: clients at the end of life

title: Enterococcal Endocarditis Prophylaxis in GI/GU Procedures
summary:
This community represents antibiotic prophylaxis against enterococcal infectious endocarditis in patients undergoing or affected by gastrointestinal and genitourinary tract procedures or infections — a directly relevant theme for perioperative gynecologic nursing, since GU procedures fall within the operative field. All three relations derive from a single source, WHO Technical Series 1, page 60.

Main recommendations: ampicillin and amoxicillin are both identified as the preferred agents for enterococcal prophylaxis. The population is explicitly defined as patients with the cardiac conditions listed in the guideline who either (a) have an established gastrointestinal or genitourinary tract infection, or (b) are receiving antibiotic therapy in connection with a gastrointestinal or genitourinary tract procedure. Vancomycin is named as the alternative agent, indicated specifically for patients who do not tolerate ampicillin; its role is framed as a substitute rather than a first-line choice.

Guideline bodies: only WHO contributes here (WHO Technical Series 1, p60). Because there is a single contributing body, no inter-guideline disagreement can be identified, and no cross-corpus comparison of specificity is possible. Within the WHO material itself, the ampicillin and amoxicillin entries are the more specific ones — they carry a fully described population and the "preferred agent" designation — whereas the vancomycin entry is specified only by the tolerance-based condition and does not restate the cardiac or GI/GU population.

What this community does NOT establish: no doses, routes, weight-based calculations, timing relative to incision, redosing intervals, or duration of therapy are given for ampicillin, amoxicillin, or vancomycin. The specific "cardiac conditions listed" are referenced but not enumerated in these relations. There is no guidance distinguishing ampicillin from amoxicillin (for example by route or setting), no criteria defining ampicillin intolerance, no pediatric or pregnancy-specific provisions, and no statement on whether prophylaxis is recommended for routine gynecologic procedures in patients without the listed cardiac conditions. Monitoring, adverse-effect surveillance, and outcome data are also absent.

title: Ergometrine-Oxytocin for Third-Stage PPH Prevention
summary:
This community centres on ergometrine-oxytocin as a uterotonic for active management of the third stage of labour, weighing its haemorrhage-prevention benefit against its side-effect and blood-pressure risks. All relations derive from a single guideline body, the RCOG (Top Tier document 1, pages 3 and 11), so no cross-body comparison or disagreement can be demonstrated here.

Recommendations and populations: For women in the third stage of labour, ergometrine-oxytocin prevents postpartum haemorrhage, with the guideline specifying a small reduction in risk compared with oxytocin alone when PPH is defined as blood loss of at least 500 ml (RCOG T1 p11). A more targeted statement applies to women at increased risk of haemorrhage: ergometrine-oxytocin prevents minor postpartum haemorrhage, but only in the absence of hypertension (RCOG T1 p3). Correspondingly, ergometrine-oxytocin is contraindicated with hypertension in this same increased-risk population (RCOG T1 p3) — the key screening point for nurses preparing third-stage prophylaxis.

Harms: For women receiving ergometrine-oxytocin in the third stage, and compared with oxytocin alone, the drug carries a five-fold increased risk of nausea and vomiting and a five-fold increased risk of elevation of blood pressure (RCOG T1 p11). Page 3 (risk-stratified guidance) is thus more specific about contraindication and the minor-PPH endpoint, while page 11 is more specific about comparative magnitude of benefit and harm.

What is not established: the community gives no dose, route, timing of administration, or number of doses; no absolute event rates, numbers needed to treat/harm, or blood-pressure thresholds defining the hypertension contraindication; and no statement about severe or major PPH, transfusion, retained placenta, or maternal mortality. It does not address alternatives beyond the oxytocin comparator (e.g. misoprostol, carbetocin, tranexamic acid), nor management of nausea/vomiting or hypertension if they occur, nor applicability to caesarean birth, pre-eclampsia specifically, or preterm populations.
key_entities: women at increased risk of haemorrhage

title: Aciclovir for suspected disseminated HSV sepsis
summary:
This community addresses recognition and empirical treatment of disseminated herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection as a cause of maternal sepsis that does not respond to first-line antibacterial therapy. The unifying clinical logic is that antibacterials will not treat a viral cause, so escalation of sepsis therapy must include an antiviral and a confirmatory virological test.

Main recommendations: (1) Intravenous aciclovir treats disseminated HSV infection in women in whom first-line antibacterial medication has failed, and the benefit is tied to starting it early. (2) Its timing depends explicitly on the antibacterial escalation decision: aciclovir should ideally be started at the same time as the first change in antibacterial regime, rather than after further deterioration. (3) In women with suspected maternal sepsis, intravenous aciclovir forms part of the second-line regimen when a change in antibiotic regimen is being considered because of deterioration despite first-line treatment. (4) Diagnostically, an ethylenediamine tetra-acetic acid (EDTA) blood sample for HSV polymerase chain reaction should be sent when disseminated HSV and hepatitis is suspected, to detect disseminated HSV infection.

Contributing bodies: all four relations derive from a single RCOG source document (RCOG T1, pages 4, 7 and 11), so there is no inter-body disagreement to reconcile. Within the RCOG material there is a difference in specificity: page 4 frames aciclovir around failure of first-line antibacterial medication and links timing to the first antibacterial change, while page 11 frames it more broadly as second-line therapy in suspected maternal sepsis with deterioration. Page 7 adds the specific trigger of suspected disseminated HSV with hepatitis for EDTA HSV PCR.

What this community does NOT establish: no aciclovir dose, infusion rate, frequency, duration or renal-adjustment guidance; no numeric thresholds for "deterioration" or time limits defining "early"; no named first- or second-line antibacterial agents; no turnaround time, sensitivity or action-on-result pathway for the HSV PCR; no neonatal, breastfeeding, or postoperative gynecologic-specific guidance; and no monitoring, de-escalation or stopping criteria if PCR is negative.
key_entities: ethylenediamine tetra acetic acid blood sample for herpes simplex virus polymerase chain reaction

title: Alcohol-Based Antiseptic Risks and Contraindications
summary:
This community centres on alcohol as a perioperative agent — principally as a skin antiseptic, but also as a substance with systemic perioperative risk — and catalogues four distinct harms or limits on its use.

Main recommendations and their conditions: (1) Alcohol is contraindicated for surgery at or in close proximity to mucous membranes or the eyes; the population is surgical patients and the condition is an operative site at or close to mucous membranes or the eyes (WHO, Tool 1 p57). (2) Alcohol increases the risk of skin irritation when alcoholic antiseptics are applied repeatedly (WHO T1 p56) — relevant to repeated prepping or serial applications. (3) Alcohol increases the risk of fatal clostridium infection when used to sterilise surgical instruments, because alcohols do not destroy bacterial spores (WHO T1 p56); alcohol is therefore not an instrument steriliser. (4) Alcohol increases the risk of excess morbidity in the perioperative period (ERAS Society, Tool 1 p1).

Contributing bodies: WHO supplies the three antiseptic/instrument-specific statements and is the more granular source, naming the anatomical exclusion (mucous membranes, eyes), the mechanism of failure (no sporicidal activity), and the exposure pattern that causes irritation (repeated use). ERAS Society contributes a single, broader statement linking alcohol to excess perioperative morbidity without specifying route, dose or patient subgroup. The two do not conflict; they operate at different levels of specificity — WHO on product handling and site selection, ERAS on patient-level perioperative risk.

What this community does not establish: no concentrations, contact times, drying times, volumes or product formulations (e.g. no alcohol-chlorhexidine or alcohol-iodine comparisons) are given; no thresholds for alcohol consumption, no cessation interval before surgery, and no screening or counselling pathway for the ERAS morbidity signal. It defines no gynecologic-specific population, no alternative antiseptic for mucous-membrane or ocular sites, no validated sterilisation substitute for instruments, and no management of alcohol-induced skin irritation once it occurs. Fire risk from alcohol prep, though clinically well known, is absent here.
key_entities: surgery at or in close proximity to mucous membranes or the eyes

title: Compression Wrap Contraindications in Wound Care
summary:
This small community represents a single, narrowly scoped clinical theme: absolute contraindications to the application of compression wraps in wound and lower-extremity care. Both relations in the community are of the CONTRAINDICATED_WITH type, and both originate from one source, OpenRN Nursing Skills (Table/Section T2, p. 1423).

The two recommendations are: (1) do not apply a compression wrap when there is exposed bone or organ at or near the intended wrap site; and (2) do not apply a compression wrap over an infected area. In practice this means that before wrapping, the nurse must inspect the wound bed and surrounding tissue and defer compression if deep structures (bone, viscera/organ) are visible or if signs of local infection are present, escalating instead to the provider or wound care specialist.

Contributing guideline bodies: OpenRN is the only contributor here, so there is no cross-body agreement or disagreement to reconcile, and no instance where one body is more granular than another. Educators should note that the specificity of these statements is limited to the two named conditions — the graph records the contraindication categorically, without qualifiers.

What this community does NOT establish is substantial. It attaches no specific patient population (e.g., no gynecologic, postoperative, diabetic, or venous-insufficiency cohort is named), no age or comorbidity criteria, and no timing, frequency, or duration parameters for compression. It names no drugs, no pressure thresholds (e.g., mmHg of compression), no wrap products or layering techniques, and no assessment intervals or perfusion checks (such as ankle-brachial index cutoffs) that would ordinarily gate compression therapy. It does not describe alternative dressings or interventions for the excluded situations, does not address relative contraindications (e.g., arterial disease, uncompensated heart failure), and does not state consequences of violating the contraindications. Nor does it define "infected area" or specify how exposed bone or organ should be managed instead. Any local protocol built from this theme will need supplementary sources for population targeting, compression pressures, and monitoring.

title: Preventing and Managing Vesicant Extravasation Injury
summary:
This community addresses extravasation — the inadvertent leakage of an infused medication into surrounding tissue — as a hazard of intravenous drug delivery in the perioperative setting, together with its causative agents, preventive routes of administration, and immediate management steps.

Two agent classes are named as risk drivers. NICE (T1, p71) identifies vasopressors as increasing extravasation risk specifically when given peripherally, and is the more specific source on modifiers: risk is affected by cannula dwell time, dosage and concentration. OpenRN (T2, p1363) frames the risk more generically at the level of vesicants, which cause extravasation when administered and inadvertently leaking into surrounding tissue. The two bodies are complementary rather than contradictory — NICE narrows to a drug class and quantitative-ish determinants (dwell time, dose, concentration) without stating thresholds, while OpenRN supplies the prevention and treatment pathway.

Prevention recommendations, all from OpenRN: use central line administration for patients receiving known vesicant medications, thereby avoiding peripheral delivery; and, for patients receiving vesicant medication through an intravenous catheter, detach all administration sets and aspirate from the catheter hub prior to removing the catheter. Management recommendations, also OpenRN: stop the infusion, and aspirate from the catheter hub prior to catheter removal — aspiration therefore appears in both a preventive and a treatment role, positioned before the catheter is pulled.

What the community does not establish: no numeric thresholds for cannula dwell time, infusion dose or concentration; no named individual vasopressor or vesicant drugs; no antidotes, warm/cold compress, hyaluronidase, surgical consultation or escalation criteria; no monitoring frequency, site-assessment schedule, or documentation/reporting requirements; no grading of extravasation severity or outcomes; and no gynecologic- or perioperative-phase-specific population qualifiers — populations are defined only as "patients receiving known vesicant medications" or receiving them via an IV catheter, and "peripheral administration." NICE offers no prevention or treatment relation here, so the preventive/therapeutic guidance rests on a single source and page.

title: Arterial Ulcer Dressing and Positioning Care
summary:
This community represents a small, focused theme: local wound management and limb positioning for patients with arterial (ischemic) ulcers. Only two relations are present, both drawn from OpenRN Nursing Skills (Textbook 2), and together they pair one recommended intervention with one contraindicated intervention for the same population.

Recommendation 1: moist wound dressing treats arterial ulcers. Population: patients with arterial ulcers. Condition: dressings must maintain a moist wound environment. This positions moisture maintenance as the operative requirement of dressing selection, rather than naming any specific product, frequency, or duration (OpenRN T2 p1113).

Recommendation 2: extremity elevation is contraindicated with arterial ulcers. Population: patients with arterial ulcers. Condition: 'in most cases' — i.e., the guideline states a general rather than absolute prohibition, implicitly leaving room for clinician judgement in exceptional situations that the corpus does not enumerate (OpenRN T2 p1145).

Contributing bodies: a single source, OpenRN (Open Resources for Nursing), contributes both statements, from two different pages of the same textbook (p1113 and p1145). There is therefore no inter-organisational disagreement to reconcile. The two pages are complementary rather than conflicting: p1113 is more specific about the therapeutic goal (moist environment), while p1145 is deliberately hedged ('in most cases') and is the less absolute of the two statements. Educators should note that the contraindication and the dressing guidance appear in separate sections, so learners encountering only one page may miss the paired message that arterial ulcers require moist dressings but not elevation.

What this community does NOT establish: no specific dressing products, materials, or change intervals; no drugs, antibiotics, or analgesics; no perfusion thresholds (e.g., ankle-brachial index values, toe pressures) to define arterial etiology or to justify the elevation exception; no alternative positioning (such as dependent positioning) as an affirmative recommendation; no guidance on venous versus arterial ulcer differentiation, debridement, compression therapy, revascularisation, offloading, infection surveillance, healing timelines, or outcome measures. No perioperative or gynecologic-specific qualifiers are attached to either statement.

title: PPE Barriers Against Blood/Fluid Splash Exposure
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: the use of personal protective equipment (PPE) as a barrier to prevent health-care worker exposure to blood and bodily fluids during procedures where splashing is anticipated — the standard-precautions core of perioperative and intrapartum infection control. All three relations share the same population (health-care workers) and the same outcome entity (exposure to blood and bodily fluids), differing only in the anatomical/exposure risk that triggers each item.

Specific recommendations and their conditions:
1) Shoe covers are indicated for health-care workers in situations in which splashing of blood or fluid is likely or expected — the guideline gives the labour room during delivery as the exemplar setting.
2) A full-body fluid-repellent gown is indicated when there is a risk of extensive splashing of blood, bodily fluids, secretions or excretions; perspiration is explicitly excluded from this trigger.
3) A face mask together with eye protection is indicated when there is a risk of blood, bodily fluids, secretions and/or excretions splashing into the face and eyes.

Guideline contributions: all three statements derive from a single source, WHO (Table 1, p211). There is therefore no inter-body disagreement to reconcile within this community; the WHO text is notable for being risk-triggered and site-specific rather than blanket — the gown recommendation is the most tightly qualified ("extensive" splashing, perspiration excluded), while the shoe-cover recommendation is the only one anchored to a named clinical setting (labour room delivery).

What this community does NOT establish: it specifies no gloves, caps, respirators or double-gloving; no material standards, fluid-resistance ratings, or sterility requirements; no donning/doffing sequence, timing, or duration of use; no disposal, reuse or decontamination pathway. It does not address patient protection, surgical-site infection, or airborne/aerosol transmission, and it offers no evidence grading, effect sizes, or compliance thresholds. No paediatric, immunocompromised or specific surgical subpopulations are differentiated, and no alternative recommendations exist for resource-limited settings.
key_entities: exposure to blood and bodily fluids

title: Fall Risk Assessment Detects Perioperative Falls
summary:
Clinical theme: this small community centres entirely on fall risk assessment as a screening/detection activity, and the two things it detects — 'fall risk' itself and discrete 'risk factors for falls'. It represents the safety-screening strand of the perioperative gynecologic nursing corpus rather than any treatment or intervention pathway.

Main recommendations as stated: (1) Fall risk assessment detects fall risk in clients with sensory impairments — the population is specified narrowly here (sensory impairment, e.g. as a contributing vulnerability), with no stated frequency or trigger condition. (2) Fall risk assessment detects risk factors for falls in all clients, with the condition that it is performed per agency policy. The second relation is broader in population (universal rather than sensory-impaired) but conditions timing and method on local institutional policy rather than a fixed interval.

Contributing guideline bodies: both relations derive from a single source body, OpenRN, specifically OpenRN Tome 2 (p521 for the sensory-impairment statement, p910 for the all-clients/agency-policy statement). There is therefore no cross-body disagreement to reconcile; the difference is internal and one of specificity. Page 521 is more specific about population (sensory impairments) but silent on timing; page 910 is more specific about the governing condition (agency policy) and about the object of detection (individual risk factors, not just aggregate risk), while generalising the population to all clients. Educators can present these as complementary: universal screening per policy, with heightened attention where sensory impairment is present.

What this community does NOT establish: no named assessment tool or scale, no numeric score thresholds or cut-offs, no assessment frequency, timing relative to surgery (preoperative, intraoperative, postoperative, discharge), and no reassessment triggers. It names no drugs, no sedation or anaesthesia agents as fall contributors, and no specific gynecologic procedures or postoperative states. It specifies no interventions following a positive screen (no bed alarms, gait belts, toileting rounds, or handoff communication), no documentation requirements, no responsible role, and no outcome or quality measures linking assessment to reduced falls.

title: Fecal Impaction: Prevention, Treatment, Complications
summary:
This community centers on fecal impaction — its causation, prevention, treatment, and downstream complication — as described in bowel elimination content of the OpenRN Nursing Skills corpus (Volume 2, pp. 1173, 1179, 1183).

Treatment: Two interventions are named. A mineral oil enema and digital removal of impacted stool are both indicated for fecal impaction, with the more specific population qualifier appearing on p. 1173: clients with large balls of hard stool. On p. 1183 the same two interventions are restated without population qualification, so p. 1173 is the more specific of the two passages regarding which clients warrant enema or digital disimpaction.

Prevention: A laxative prevents fecal impaction specifically in clients who have received barium, given post-procedurally. This pairs with the causal claim that barium increases risk of fecal impaction in clients who received barium, making post-barium laxative administration the one clearly populated, clearly timed prophylactic recommendation in this theme.

Complication: Fecal impaction increases the risk of bowel incontinence, conditioned on the mechanism that a lump of hard stool partly blocks the large intestine — i.e., liquid stool passing around the obstruction, framed here as a risk relationship rather than a treatment target.

Guideline bodies: All relations derive from a single source, OpenRN (Nursing Skills, Volume 2). There are therefore no cross-organization disagreements; the only variation is granularity between pages, with p. 1173 attaching the "large balls of hard stool" population and p. 1183 attaching the barium/post-procedural conditions.

Not established: no drug names, doses, volumes, or oil quantities for the mineral oil enema; no named laxative agent, dose, route, or interval after barium administration; no sequencing rule (enema before or after digital removal); no contraindications or cautions for digital disimpaction; no diagnostic thresholds defining impaction; no perioperative or gynecologic-surgery–specific population despite the corpus framing; and no relation addressing treatment of the resulting bowel incontinence.

title: Timing of birth in maternal sepsis
summary:
This small community addresses a single, focused perioperative decision point: whether and when to expedite birth in a pregnant woman who is haemodynamically or physiologically unstable because of sepsis. The graph contains two parallel relations, both drawn from RCOG (Trimester 1 document, page 14): birth INCREASES_RISK_OF maternal mortality, and birth INCREASES_RISK_OF fetal mortality. Both relations carry the identical population qualifier — women with maternal instability due to sepsis — and the identical condition qualifier — unless the source of infection is intrauterine.

The practical teaching point is therefore that in the septic, unstable parturient, proceeding to birth is not a neutral or automatically therapeutic act: it adds risk to both mother and fetus. The implied recommendation is to stabilise the mother first rather than deliver reflexively, with one explicit exception — if the intrauterine contents are the source of infection, the risk calculus described here does not apply, and the guideline's caveat allows birth to be pursued as source control. Educators can frame this for theatre and labour-ward teams as: confirm or exclude an intrauterine source of sepsis before treating delivery as the intervention of choice.

Only one guideline body contributes to this community — RCOG — so there are no inter-body agreements, disagreements, or differences in specificity to reconcile; no NICE, WHO, AAGBI, ACOG or nursing-body counterpart appears here.

Importantly, this community does not establish: any numeric threshold or score defining "maternal instability" (no blood pressure, lactate, temperature, heart rate, qSOFA or MEOWS values); any timing window for stabilisation or for delivery; any antibiotic, vasopressor, fluid or other drug regimen; any mode-of-birth guidance (vaginal versus caesarean); any gestational-age limits; any magnitude of the mortality risk conferred; and any criteria for diagnosing an intrauterine source. It also says nothing about postoperative, anaesthetic, monitoring, or neonatal care pathways. Those details must be sourced from other communities or the full RCOG text.

title: Acetaminophen-centred multimodal analgesia and fever management
summary: This community centres on non-opioid antipyretic-analgesic therapy, with acetaminophen as the hub, spanning perioperative multimodal pain control, fever/hyperthermia treatment, and hepatic safety monitoring. Recommendations: ERAS Society (T1 p9) advises routine pre-operative oral acetaminophen, gabapentin and celecoxib for post-operative pain in patients undergoing gynecologic surgery. AUGS (T2 pp8-9) recommends acetaminophen for postoperative pain in urogynecological surgery as part of perioperative multimodal analgesia, and applies it specifically to vulvar and vaginal surgery patients unless contraindicated. OpenRN (T2, p825) frames acetaminophen more generally as treatment for mild pain and fever across all ages, with NSAIDs also treating fever, and acetaminophen used for hyperthermia in clients with fever/hyperthermia as appropriate (p663). Safety thresholds come only from OpenRN: hepatotoxicity risk in adult clients if more than 4,000 mg is taken in 24 hours (3,200 mg for older adults, 2,000 mg for chronic alcoholics), or if three or more alcoholic drinks are consumed daily while using acetaminophen; liver dysfunction risk in clients taking acetaminophen daily for chronic osteoarthritis pain, for whom liver function monitoring is indicated. Fever itself increases risk of deficient fluid volume (OpenRN p1111). One obstetric link: misoprostol increases risk of fever in women receiving it for postpartum haemorrhage prevention (WHO T1 p26). Differences: ERAS is most specific on route and timing (routine oral, pre-operative) and names the full triple regimen; AUGS names only acetaminophen but adds the contraindication caveat and surgical subpopulations; OpenRN contributes dosing ceilings, populations at hepatic risk, and monitoring, which the surgical guidelines do not. The community does NOT establish acetaminophen doses or dosing intervals for surgical patients, comparative efficacy among acetaminophen, gabapentin and celecoxib, gabapentin or celecoxib adverse effects or contraindications, which NSAID agents to use, whether perioperative acetaminophen requires liver function monitoring, management of misoprostol-induced fever, or how fever-related deficient fluid volume should be treated.

title: Fibre-optic intubation for anticipated difficult airway
summary:
This community centres on a single airway-management technology: fibre-optic (flexible endoscopic) intubation, and its role, limits and complications in patients with a difficult airway. All relations derive from one source, WHO Table 1, p36 — no other guideline body contributes, so there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile, and no gynecologic- or perioperative-specific population qualifiers beyond airway risk are attached.

Main recommendations: fibre-optic intubation TREATS the difficult airway and is described as the gold standard for expected difficult airway management, in patients whose airway is anticipated to be difficult. It also serves a diagnostic/assessment function (DETECTS difficult airway) in patients at high risk of airway failure, but only when performed by anaesthetists experienced with the technique and in carefully selected cases — the operator-experience and case-selection caveat is the most specific condition in the community. A stated benefit is prevention of dental damage.

Relative contraindications (all flagged explicitly as relative, i.e. temporary/conditional rather than absolute) are: acute life-threatening airway obstruction; an airway-obstructing abscess or friable tumour; distortion of anatomy limiting airway space; and copious secretions or blood in the airway. Educators should teach these four as the triggers to consider an alternative airway plan.

Recognised complications to monitor for: hypoxia, bacteraemia, airway and laryngeal cord trauma, and alteration in blood pressure and heart rate.

What this community does NOT establish: no drugs, doses, sedation or topical anaesthesia regimens, no timings, no numeric thresholds (e.g. SpO2 limits, scope size, time-to-desaturation), no comparison with videolaryngoscopy, awake tracheostomy or supraglottic devices, no competency or training volume requirements, no antibiotic prophylaxis guidance despite the bacteraemia risk, and no monitoring frequency or escalation pathway. It also does not define how 'expected difficult airway' or 'high risk for airway failure' is assessed, nor any obstetric, gynecologic, paediatric or pregnancy-specific adaptations.
key_entities: distortion of anatomy limiting airway space
copious secretions or blood in the airway
alteration in blood pressure and heart rate

title: Fluid resuscitation timing in haemorrhage
summary:
This community centres on fluid resuscitation as the pivotal intervention for volume loss in perioperative and obstetric care, and specifically on the question of *when* fluid should be given versus withheld. All four relations derive from a single guideline body, WHO (Technical/Training module T1, pp. 19, 41, 42), so the theme is best read as one organisation's internally nuanced position rather than a comparison across bodies.

The therapeutic recommendations are twofold. First, fluid resuscitation TREATS postpartum haemorrhage in women with postpartum haemorrhage (WHO T1 p19). Second, it TREATS hypovolaemia in hypovolaemic patients, with the condition that it is delivered during definitive intervention (WHO T1 p41) — i.e. resuscitation is coupled to, not a substitute for, definitive control of bleeding.

The timing recommendations qualify this. Fluid resuscitation OCCURS_IN_PHASE preoperative for patients who present for surgery in a volume-depleted state, and the guideline attaches the condition "whenever possible" — a permissive rather than absolute instruction (WHO T1 p42). Counterbalancing this, fluid resuscitation is TEMPORARILY_CONTRAINDICATED relative to definitive care in patients with uncontrolled and ongoing blood loss in prehospital management, with the note that some advocate fluid restriction until definitive care begins (WHO T1 p41). Educators should highlight this apparent tension: the same guideline urges preoperative correction of volume depletion where feasible, yet flags restraint in the prehospital patient who is still actively and uncontrollably bleeding. The p41 statement is explicitly hedged ("some advocate"), so it is a reported position, not a firm directive.

What this community does NOT establish: no fluid types (crystalloid, colloid, blood products), no volumes, rates or weight-based dosing, no haemodynamic or laboratory thresholds (blood pressure, heart rate, haemoglobin, lactate) for starting or stopping fluids, no monitoring or endpoint criteria, no paediatric or comorbidity-specific modifications, and no defined duration of the "temporary" contraindication beyond "until definitive care begins." Nor does any second guideline body corroborate or contest the WHO position here.

title: Fluid Volume Overload Risk and Monitoring
summary: This community centers on fluid volume overload as a hub complication in perioperative and IV therapy care: what causes it, who is vulnerable, how it is detected, and what it in turn causes. Risk contributors include intravenous fluids generally (NICE flags overload risk in suspected sepsis once 1,000 mL has been given with no or limited change in indicators of hypoperfusion), isotonic IV solutions (use with caution in patients with hypertension, heart failure, or renal disease), and hypertonic solutions. Patient-level risks are known congestive heart failure and known chronic kidney disease in patients receiving IV infusion therapy. Monitoring recommendations are population-specific: daily weight assessment for patients receiving IV fluids; weight monitoring generally; monitoring for signs of fluid overload whenever hypertonic fluids are administered; assessment and documentation of infused volumes plus overload signs frequently per agency policy in children; frequent IV infusion monitoring in older adults; auscultation over the apex with the bell of the stethoscope in the left lateral position to detect an S3, as in acute heart failure exacerbation; and electrolyte monitoring in clients with diarrhea for electrolyte disturbance. Downstream, AUGS attributes electrolyte disturbance, congestive heart failure, ileus, and edema to overload in the geriatric population, and ERAS links salt and fluid overload in the postoperative period to postoperative morbidity in surgical patients. RNAO contributes drug-level cardiac cautions: beta-blockers are contraindicated with congestive heart failure in clients with hypertension, and long-acting calcium channel blockers increase CHF risk in clients taking calcium channel blockers. Bodies differ in specificity: NICE alone gives a volume threshold (1,000 mL); OpenRN supplies the concrete assessment techniques and age-specific monitoring frequencies; AUGS and ERAS describe consequences without monitoring detail. The community does not establish target fluid volumes or infusion rates, defined weight-gain or urine-output thresholds for diagnosing overload, treatment or de-resuscitation strategies, monitoring intervals beyond "daily" and "per agency policy", or any gynecologic-procedure-specific fluid regimen.
key_entities: auscultation over the apex with the bell of the stethoscope in the left lateral position

title: Bladder Emptying in Postpartum Haemorrhage Management
summary:
This small community represents the theme of bladder management as an adjunctive measure in the treatment of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH). It links a single intervention (bladder emptying), a single device (Foley catheter), and a single clinical condition (postpartum haemorrhage).

The two recommendations captured are: (1) bladder emptying TREATS postpartum haemorrhage, with the population specified as women with postpartum haemorrhage; and (2) a Foley catheter APPLIES_TO bladder emptying for the same population, with the explicit condition that the catheter is left in place rather than removed after a single drainage. Practically, for a nurse educator this means that in the woman actively bleeding after birth, emptying the bladder is part of the therapeutic bundle, and the preferred method is an indwelling Foley catheter that remains in situ (supporting ongoing drainage and, by implication, continued monitoring of the bladder as a source of uterine displacement or atony contribution).

Only one guideline body contributes here: the RCOG (Tier 1, page 25). Because there is a single source, there are no inter-body disagreements, no competing thresholds, and no instance of one body being more specific than another; the RCOG statement is the sole level of specificity available in this community.

Important gaps: the community does not establish any timing (when in the PPH sequence to catheterise, or how long to leave the Foley in place), any catheter size, balloon volume, or fluid-instillation detail, and no urine-output threshold or monitoring frequency. It does not state a mechanism (e.g. facilitating uterine contraction or fundal assessment) and does not rank bladder emptying against or alongside other PPH treatments — no uterotonics (oxytocin, ergometrine, misoprostol, carboprost), tranexamic acid, uterine massage, balloon tamponade, or surgical measures appear in these relations. It also does not address antepartum or intrapartum haemorrhage, non-obstetric bleeding, catheter-associated urinary tract infection prevention, or criteria for catheter removal. Any local protocol or teaching built from this theme must draw those specifics from other sections of the corpus.

title: Antihypertensive Therapy and Follow-Up Timing
summary:
This small community represents the pharmacologic management of hypertension and the follow-up interval that flows from it. Two relations, both drawn from RNAO (Registered Nurses' Association of Ontario) Tool/Table 2 (pages 59 and 70), anchor the theme.

First, antihypertensive drug therapy is identified as a treatment for hypertension, with the population specified as hypertensive clients and the condition specified as vigorous therapy (RNAO T2 p59). The graph names no individual agent, drug class, dose, or blood pressure threshold that would define 'vigorous' therapy.

Second, the timing of the follow-up visit is stated to depend on antihypertensive drug therapy: for treated clients with hypertension, follow-up occurs at one-month intervals until the blood pressure goal is reached (RNAO T2 p70). This is the only concrete timing in the community and it is explicitly conditional on the client already being on drug therapy and on the blood pressure goal not yet being attained.

Only one guideline body contributes here, so there are no inter-organisational disagreements to reconcile; RNAO is the sole source and the two pages are complementary rather than conflicting. The p70 relation is the more specific of the two, supplying a population qualifier ('treated clients') and an explicit interval, whereas p59 remains at the level of a general treatment assertion.

What this community does NOT establish: it does not name any specific antihypertensive drug or class; it does not define the numeric blood pressure goal or any diagnostic/treatment threshold; it does not state what 'vigorous therapy' means operationally or when to escalate, add, or de-prescribe agents; it does not specify follow-up frequency once the blood pressure goal is reached, nor intervals for untreated or newly diagnosed hypertensive clients. It says nothing about non-pharmacologic management, monitoring parameters, adverse effects, or perioperative/gynecologic-specific considerations, and it offers no pregnancy-, age-, or comorbidity-specific tailoring. Educators should treat it as a skeleton for follow-up scheduling that must be supplemented from fuller hypertension guidance.

title: Perioperative VTE prophylaxis across surgical specialties
summary: Theme: procedure-specific venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in surgical and immobilised patients, with a smaller strand on other surgical risks. Mechanical prophylaxis (NICE) is started on admission and continued until mobility is no longer significantly reduced relative to normal or anticipated mobility, for abdominal, thoracic, bariatric, cardiac (increased VTE risk), cranial (30 days or until mobile/discharged, whichever is sooner), lower limb amputation, spinal injury, and ENT or oral/maxillofacial surgery patients at increased VTE risk plus high bleeding risk; also on admission for open vascular or major endovascular procedures when pharmacological prophylaxis is contraindicated, and where antiplatelet therapy for other conditions means bleeding risk outweighs VTE risk. Pharmacological options: LMWH where VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk — cranial surgery (last preoperative dose no less than 24 hours before surgery; postoperative dosing 24–48 hours after), bariatric and ENT surgery for a minimum of 7 days, and fragility fractures of pelvis/hip/proximal femur (last dose no less than 12 hours before surgery). Fondaparinux sodium is the alternative when LMWH is contraindicated (thoracic, cardiac without other anticoagulation, acutely ill medical patients and acute psychiatric admissions, palliative care), for a minimum of 7 days in abdominal, bariatric and acute medical patients; 28 days subcutaneously in fragility fractures, or a month starting 6 hours after surgery with low bleeding risk; last preoperative dose no less than 24 hours before surgery; consider stopping in lower limb immobilisation beyond 42 days. RCOG adds obstetric specificity: fondaparinux for pregnant women intolerant of heparin/danaparoid needing continuing anticoagulation or with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, used with a consultant haematologist expert in haemostasis and pregnancy (UK licence is outside pregnancy), and regional anaesthesia deferred 36–42 hours after the last fondaparinux dose. NICE also flags surgery increasing sepsis risk (16+), WHO infection risk from invasive procedures, OpenRN bariatric nutritional deficiency and surgery for bowel incontinence. Not established: dose amounts, device types, thresholds for risk-assessment tools, gynecologic-specific prophylaxis, or comparative effectiveness.

title: Preoperative Counseling to Prevent Fatigue
summary:
This community centres on fatigue as a perioperative outcome and on preoperative counseling as the principal preventive intervention, with opioid analgesia framed as a contributing risk. ERAS Society (T1) links opioids to increased fatigue specifically in patients relying on opioid alone for post-operative analgesia, i.e. when an opioid is the sole post-operative analgesic — an argument for multimodal analgesia, though no alternative agents or doses are named here. ERAS Society (T1 p1) recommends preoperative counseling as a preventive measure against fatigue, pain and fear, without restricting the population or timing. WHO (T1 p154) shifts the focus from patients to staff, noting that fatigue in health-care practitioners increases the risk of medical error — a patient-safety and staffing consideration relevant to QI leads. OpenRN (T2 p653) offers the only symptom-management action: frequent rest periods between activities to treat fatigue in patients experiencing hypoxia.

On timing and population, AUGS (T2 pp3, 12, 14) is the most specific contributor: preoperative counseling is placed in the preoperative phase and initiated at the time of the preoperative visit, and it applies to urogynecological surgery for patients being planned for same-day discharge. ERAS Society is broader, situating counseling in the preoperative phase for all patients (T1 p11) without procedure restriction. The bodies do not conflict; AUGS narrows ERAS's universal recommendation to a defined surgical population and a concrete trigger point (the preoperative visit), while ERAS uniquely attaches outcome claims (fatigue, pain, fear prevention) to counseling.

The community does not establish counseling content, format, duration, or who delivers it; no fatigue screening tools, severity thresholds, or measurement instruments; no opioid dose thresholds or named alternative analgesics; no evidence grading or strength of recommendation; and no causal link between patient fatigue and patient harm (the medical-error pathway applies only to practitioners). It also does not state whether rest periods help non-hypoxic patients, nor whether counseling reduces fatigue in same-day-discharge urogynecology patients specifically.

title: Agitation, Friction and Pressure Injury Risk
summary:
This community links behavioural agitation to mechanical skin injury: agitation is itself a driver of friction during movement in bed, and friction in turn increases the risk of both skin damage and pressure injury. It therefore joins dementia/end-of-life symptom management with skin integrity and safe-handling practice.

Agitation prevention: for clients with dementia who ask about a hallucination or delusion, responding honestly prevents agitation (OpenRN T2 p468); for clients with dementia where reduced lighting creates shadows and misinterpretation of the environment, turning on lights prevents agitation (p468). Conversely, suctioning increases the risk of agitation in clients with terminal secretions (p1288), implying suctioning should be weighed against its agitating effect in that population.

Friction and skin protection: friction increases risk of pressure injury (p718, p731) and of skin damage specifically when skin is rubbed against a hard object such as the bed or the arm of a wheelchair (p718). Three client factors increase friction: spasticity, contracture, and agitation (p731). The stated preventive measure is use of two assistants plus a draw sheet when pulling the client up in bed, for clients requiring moderate to maximum assistance in moving (p731).

Contributing bodies: all relations derive from a single source, OpenRN (Nursing Skills/Fundamentals, Tier 2), across three page clusters — p468 (dementia communication and environment), p718 and p731 (friction, pressure injury, safe transfer), and p1288 (terminal secretions). No cross-organisation comparison is possible; p718 is more specific about the mechanism and contact surfaces of friction, while p731 is more specific about client-level risk factors and the two-assistant/draw-sheet technique.

Not established: no drugs, doses, sedation thresholds, repositioning intervals, timings, or risk-assessment scores (e.g. Braden) are specified; no staging of pressure injury; no evidence that preventing agitation reduces pressure injury incidence; no guidance on shear versus friction, alternatives to suctioning for terminal secretions, or management of spasticity and contracture themselves; and nothing specific to perioperative or gynecologic surgical populations.
key_entities: use of two assistants plus a draw sheet when pulling the client up in bed

title: Anaemia Screening and Iron Treatment in Pregnancy
summary:
This community covers the detection and initial pharmacological management of anaemia in pregnancy, plus one recognised treatment side effect. Three detection pathways are represented, all for the population 'pregnant women': generic screening for anaemia (RCOG T1 p10), full blood count (FBC) testing as the laboratory method (WHO T1 p10), and on-site haemoglobin testing with a haemoglobinometer, which WHO attaches an explicit condition to — it is the detection route 'in settings where full blood count testing is not available' (WHO T1 p10). This conditional substitution is the most operationally specific statement in the community and is the point where WHO is more granular than RCOG: RCOG contributes only the general principle that screening detects anaemia in pregnant women, without naming an assay, whereas WHO names both FBC and point-of-care haemoglobinometry and ranks them by resource availability. There is no contradiction between the bodies — the difference is specificity, not direction.

On treatment, WHO (T1 p103) recommends an iron supplement for the narrower population of a 'pregnant woman with mild anaemia'. The same source flags a consequence of that therapy: iron supplementation increases the risk of constipation in a pregnant woman taking iron supplements for mild anaemia. For teaching or QI purposes, this pairs an intervention directly with its anticipated adverse effect, supporting counselling and bowel-care follow-up whenever iron is initiated in this group.

What the community does NOT establish: no haemoglobin or ferritin thresholds define anaemia or 'mild' anaemia; no iron formulation, dose, route (oral versus parenteral), frequency or duration is given; no timing or gestational interval for screening or rescreening is specified. Management of moderate or severe anaemia, transfusion, and non-pregnant or postoperative gynaecologic populations are absent, as are perioperative implications. No preventive or treatment measure for the iron-related constipation is provided, and no outcome data (maternal or fetal) link screening or supplementation to improved results.
key_entities: on-site haemoglobin testing with a haemoglobinometer

title: Magnesium Sulfate, Eclampsia, and Neuroprotection
summary:
This community centres on hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and maternal sepsis, with magnesium sulfate as the pivotal drug linking seizure prophylaxis, seizure treatment, and fetal/neonatal neuroprotection.

WHO recommendations (WHO T1 p29) position magnesium sulfate as the agent of choice, in preference to other anticonvulsants, both to PREVENT eclampsia in women with severe pre-eclampsia and to TREAT eclampsia in women who have seized. Full intravenous or intramuscular regimens are specified for both prevention and treatment. Where the full regimen cannot be administered, WHO is more operationally specific: give a magnesium sulfate loading dose followed by immediate transfer to a higher-level health-care facility for women with severe pre-eclampsia and eclampsia. Separately (WHO T1 p17), magnesium sulfate PREVENTS cerebral palsy in the infant and child when given to women at risk of imminent preterm birth before 32 weeks of gestation — a distinct neuroprotective indication with its own gestational threshold.

RCOG contributes the risk and monitoring side. Pre-eclampsia and eclampsia both INCREASE the risk of pulmonary oedema in women receiving fluid resuscitation (RCOG T1 p11), which is a caution for volume management. In women with sepsis, magnesium sulfate increases the risk of hypotension, and additional monitoring is advised (RCOG T1 p14). RCOG also flags that intrauterine infection, in neonates of women with maternal sepsis, increases the risk of neonatal encephalopathy and cerebral palsy (RCOG T1 p14) — note cerebral palsy appears here as an infection-mediated outcome, separate from the preterm-birth pathway WHO addresses.

The bodies are complementary rather than conflicting: WHO defines drug choice, regimen and referral logic; RCOG defines the adverse-effect and comorbidity context.

Not established here: actual doses, infusion rates, durations, or serum magnesium targets; specific monitoring parameters or frequencies; fluid volume limits or restriction thresholds; antihypertensive agents; antibiotic choices for intrauterine infection or sepsis; whether magnesium sulfate mitigates infection-related cerebral palsy; timing of delivery; and any anaesthetic or perioperative-specific nursing actions.
key_entities: full intravenous or intramuscular magnesium sulfate regimen
magnesium sulfate loading dose followed by immediate transfer to a higher level health-care facility
imminent preterm birth before 32 weeks of gestation

title: Gastric decompression in laparoscopic/robotic surgery
summary:
Clinical theme: intraoperative gastric decompression as a safety measure during minimally invasive gynecologic surgery. The community is small and tightly focused, linking a single intervention — gastric decompression achieved by oro- or nasogastric intubation — to one surgical population and one specific harm it is intended to avert.

Main recommendations: (1) Gastric decompression by oro- or nasogastric tube applies to patients undergoing laparoscopic or robotic surgery, with the explicit condition that the tube should be removed at extubation — i.e., it is an intraoperative-only device, not a postoperative one. (2) The stated purpose is prevention of gastric perforation in patients undergoing laparoscopic or robotic surgery, specifically during trochar or Veress needle insertion, when a distended stomach lies in the path of entry. Practically, this frames decompression as an entry-safety step tied to the abdominal access phase, and removal as an emergence/extubation-phase task — two concrete handoff points that nurse educators can build into pre-incision briefing and end-of-case checklists.

Contributing bodies: only the ERAS Society (Table 1, p1) contributes to this community. Because there is a single source, there are no inter-guideline disagreements to reconcile and no instance of one body being more specific than another; the ERAS Society statement itself supplies the population (laparoscopic or robotic surgery), the timing condition (removal at extubation), the mechanism-relevant moment (trochar or Veress needle insertion), and the outcome prevented (gastric perforation).

What this community does NOT establish: it does not specify tube size, route preference between oral and nasal placement, insertion timing relative to induction, confirmation-of-placement technique, suction settings, or documentation requirements. It gives no guidance for open or vaginal gynecologic approaches, no exceptions for patients at aspiration risk or with difficult airways, and no direction on postoperative nausea, vomiting, ileus, or reinsertion criteria. No quantitative effect size, incidence of gastric perforation, or strength/quality-of-evidence grading is attached, and no alternative or adjunct decompression strategies are named.
key_entities: gastric decompression by oro- or nasogastric intubation

title: General aseptic field for simple procedures
summary:
This community represents a single, narrow theme in perioperative/procedural nursing practice: selecting the appropriate level of aseptic technique — specifically, when a *general* aseptic field (rather than a critical aseptic field) is sufficient for a clinical procedure. Two relations define the theme, both drawn from OpenRN Nursing Skills (Chapter/Table 2, p. 239).

Main recommendations: A general aseptic field APPLIES_TO (1) intravenous irrigation and (2) dry dressing change. For both, the stated condition is identical and is the decisive criterion: the procedure's key parts and key sites are easily protected. In other words, the population is patients undergoing these two comparatively simple procedures, and the qualifying condition is the ease with which key parts (e.g., the elements that must remain sterile) and key sites can be protected during the procedure; where that is true, a general aseptic field is the appropriate standard rather than a more stringent field.

Contributing bodies: only one source contributes here — OpenRN (Open Resources for Nursing), Table 2, page 239. Because the corpus segment is single-source, there are no inter-organisational disagreements to reconcile, and no instance where one body is more specific or more permissive than another. The OpenRN entry is itself fairly specific in naming the two example procedures and the protective condition, but it does not stratify by patient risk group.

What this community does NOT establish: it gives no drug names, no antiseptic agents or concentrations, no timings (e.g., scrub or dry times), no thresholds or numeric criteria, and no equipment lists (gloves, drapes, gown type). It does not define what constitutes a "key part" or "key site," nor does it describe the alternative (critical) aseptic field or when to escalate to it. It says nothing about gynecologic- or perioperative-specific procedures, immunocompromised or surgical populations, infection outcomes, competency assessment, or audit measures. Educators should treat it as a decision rule fragment requiring supplementation from other guideline sections.

title: Cardiac Surgery Perioperative Risk Reduction Bundle
summary:
This community centres on cardiac surgery as a high-risk index procedure and the perioperative measures clustered around it, chiefly infection prevention, plus VTE prophylaxis and delirium risk. Cardiac surgery is characterised as increasing risk of surgical site infection (SSI) caused by Staphylococcus aureus (NICE T1 p20, where high-risk status is determined locally by joint decisions between surgical and infection control teams) and, in older adults, of postoperative delirium (OpenRN T2 p451).

Main recommendations: a gentamicin-collagen implant may be considered for patients undergoing cardiac surgery, applied to the wound before skin closure, to prevent SSI, with benefit framed at 1 month and 2 months after surgery (NICE T1 p12 and p24; p12 explicitly frames this as 'consider only'). Antimicrobial prophylaxis for cardiac surgery should be directed primarily against staphylococci and be of short duration (WHO T1 p60) — consistent in target organism with NICE's S. aureus risk statement, though WHO is the more specific source on agent spectrum and duration. Chlorhexidine mouth rinse is recommended for patients undergoing cardiac surgery to prevent postoperative pneumonia (WHO T1 p57). For VTE, NICE T1 p31 specifies pharmacological prophylaxis for a minimum of 7 days in people not receiving other anticoagulation therapy, and mechanical prophylaxis for people at increased risk of VTE.

Contributing bodies: NICE (implant, VTE prophylaxis, S. aureus SSI risk), WHO (antimicrobial prophylaxis spectrum/duration, chlorhexidine mouth rinse), and OpenRN (delirium risk in older adults). They are complementary rather than contradictory; NICE is more specific on timing/duration thresholds, WHO on prophylaxis characteristics.

Not established: no specific antibiotic agents, doses, concentrations, chlorhexidine strength or rinse frequency; no gentamicin-collagen implant dose or size; no named pharmacological VTE agent or upper duration limit; no criteria defining 'increased risk of VTE' or 'high risk' for S. aureus SSI; no delirium prevention or screening intervention; and no gynecologic-surgery-specific application of these cardiac surgery recommendations.
key_entities: surgical site infection caused by staphylococcus aureus

title: Gloves, Gowns, and Hand Decontamination
summary:
This community covers personal protective equipment (examination gloves, isolation gowns) and hand decontamination as complementary barriers against contamination in perioperative and inpatient care. Two guideline bodies contribute: the CDC hand hygiene guidance (T1, pp. 29-34) and OpenRN nursing fundamentals (T2, pp. 203, 642).

Core recommendations: For health-care workers, gloves worn during patient contact prevent hand contamination, prevent personnel acquiring infection from patients, prevent bloodborne pathogen transmission, and prevent transmission of health-care worker flora to patients (CDC T1 p31). Gloves also prevent hand contamination among the majority of personnel having direct contact with patients colonized or infected with C. difficile or vancomycin-resistant enterococcus (CDC T1 p31). OpenRN adds the isolation gown and gloves as a pair: when contact transmission-based precautions are in place, both are donned upon room entry to prevent contamination of clothing (T2 p203).

Gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene. CDC specifies that examination gloves increase the risk of hand contamination in health-care workers as a result of small, undetected holes or during glove removal (T1 p29); accordingly, hand decontamination after removing gloves prevents hand contamination (T1 p32). CDC is the more procedurally specific body on timing, indicating hand decontamination before insertion of an indwelling urinary catheter and before donning sterile gloves for central intravascular catheter insertion (T1 p34).

OpenRN uniquely names an occupational harm CDC does not address here: repeated glove use increases the risk of contact dermatitis in nurses (T2 p642). The two bodies do not conflict; they differ in emphasis, CDC on pathogen transmission and procedure-linked hand hygiene timing, OpenRN on isolation-precaution donning sequence and skin health.

Not established: no glove material (latex, nitrile, vinyl), thickness, or double-gloving guidance; no hand hygiene agent, alcohol concentration, scrub duration, or volume thresholds; no glove-change frequency or wear-time limits; no gown type or sterile-gown criteria; no gynecologic-surgery-specific populations, no pediatric or immunocompromised specifications; no dermatitis prevention or treatment measures; and no quantified effect sizes or infection-rate outcomes.
key_entities: transmission of health-care worker flora to patients

title: Glove Use and Hand Hygiene Interplay
summary: This community centres on gloves as a double-edged infection-prevention control: protective when used correctly, a vector for transmission when substituted for hand hygiene. WHO (T1 p211) is procedure-focused: sterile gloves, and gloves generally, are indicated for health-care professionals performing invasive procedures or any contact requiring sterile conditions. CDC (T1 p4) attaches the complementary hand-hygiene condition — handwashing with antimicrobial soap by health-care workers before and after invasive procedures or care of high-risk patients. CDC (T1 p31) is the most specific on pathogen-level benefit: routine wearing of vinyl gloves when handling any body substances prevented Clostridium difficile diarrhoea on wards where personnel did so; gloves prevented hand contamination in the majority of personnel having direct contact with patients with C. difficile or vancomycin-resistant enterococcus, and prevented VRE hand colonisation in personnel touching contaminated environmental surfaces. OpenRN (T2, p642) supplies the harm side: gloves prevent infection only when used properly; used improperly they increase risk of infection, notably through missed hand-hygiene opportunities caused by glove overuse. Cross contamination of clients occurs when gloves used in client care are not removed before touching other surfaces or the client; secondary infection occurs when gloves are not removed and hand hygiene is not performed before the next procedure. Repeated glove use also increases contact dermatitis risk in nurses — an occupational-health point unique to OpenRN. For nonsterile gloves, OpenRN specifies they prevent transmission of microorganisms according to agency policy (p1192) and prevent exposure to blood when applied after performing hand hygiene (p1021), while still carrying cross-contamination risk in client care (p642). Points of emphasis differ rather than conflict: WHO defines indications, CDC quantifies organism-specific protection and pairs gloves with antimicrobial soap, OpenRN details failure modes.
