The community does NOT establish glove material choice beyond CDC's vinyl example, donning/removal technique steps, glove-change frequency or timing thresholds, specific antimicrobial soap agents or contact times, gynecologic- or perioperative-specific glove protocols, sterile versus nonsterile decision criteria, or dermatitis mitigation strategies.

title: Checklists and Communication Prevent Hypersensitivity Errors
summary:
This community represents a narrow but high-stakes patient-safety theme: preventing adverse drug reactions in patients with a known hypersensitivity (documented allergy) by means of system-level safeguards rather than drug-specific pharmacology. Two paired recommendations sit at its core, both drawn from the same guideline passage. First, the use of checklists prevents adverse drug reaction in the population of patients with known hypersensitivity, under the condition of errors of commission — that is, a drug the patient is already known to react to is nonetheless administered. Second, good communication among the clinical care team prevents adverse drug reaction in the same population and under the same condition. The implied mechanism is that the allergy is already known and documented; the failure is one of transmission and verification at the point of care, so structured verification (checklist prompts, read-backs, explicit team-wide sharing of allergy status) is the barrier that closes the gap. For a nurse educator or QI lead, the practical translation is to embed allergy confirmation into perioperative checklist steps and into team briefings/handovers, and to audit errors of commission as the outcome measure.

Only one guideline body contributes here: the WHO surgical safety guidance (WHO T1, p46). There is therefore no cross-body comparison, no point of divergence, and no instance of one organisation being more specific than another; both relations are equally general.

What this community does not establish: it names no specific drugs, drug classes, doses or thresholds; no timing (for example, when in the perioperative pathway the checklist or communication should occur, or how far in advance allergy status must be verified); no checklist format, content, or required items; no definition or grading of severity of the adverse drug reaction; no guidance for patients without a known hypersensitivity, nor for errors of omission; and no effect size, evidence grade, or recommendation strength. It also does not specify roles, accountability, or documentation standards, nor any gynecologic-procedure-specific tailoring.
key_entities: good communication among the clinical care team

title: Bereavement Surveillance for Complicated Grief
summary:
This community represents a narrow but clinically important theme: surveillance for complicated grief among the bereaved during the bereavement period. It contains two parallel monitoring relations, both drawn from OpenRN Textbook 2, page 1260. First, formal grief assessment is directed at monitoring for complicated grief in survivors — explicitly defined as bereaved family members and significant others — with the condition that this occurs during the bereavement period. Second, general nurse monitoring is directed at the same outcome, complicated grief, for the population of bereaved clients, again during the bereavement period. Taken together, the theme positions the nurse as an active screener rather than a passive comforter after a patient death or loss, and frames complicated grief as a detectable, monitorable phenomenon rather than an inevitable consequence of loss.

Only one guideline body contributes here: OpenRN (Open Resources for Nursing), and both relations originate from the same page, so there is no cross-body disagreement to reconcile. There is, however, a difference in specificity between the two relations. The grief assessment relation is more precise about population, naming survivors as bereaved family members and significant others; the nurse monitoring relation uses the broader, less delimited term bereaved clients. The timing condition is identical and equally non-specific in both: 'during the bereavement period.'

What this community does not establish is substantial and should temper any protocol built from it. It specifies no screening instrument, no scoring threshold or cut-off for identifying complicated grief, and no interval, frequency, or duration of monitoring — the bereavement period is never bounded in days, weeks, or months. It names no pharmacologic agents, no psychotherapy modality, and no referral criteria or escalation pathway once complicated grief is suspected. It does not identify risk factors, does not distinguish complicated grief from normal or anticipatory grief, and offers no perioperative or gynecologic-specific tailoring despite the wider corpus context. Quality-improvement leads should treat this as an assessment mandate awaiting operational detail from other sources.
key_entities: survivors (bereaved family members and significant others)

title: Group A Streptococcal Infection in Pregnancy
summary:
This community represents the detection, treatment, containment and post-exposure prevention of group A streptococcal (GAS) infection in the maternity setting, drawn entirely from RCOG Top Tips (T1, pages 7 and 15).

Detection: a throat swab for bacterial culture is recommended for any woman who is unwell with symptoms of tonsillitis or pharyngitis; the same swab serves to identify both GAS and tonsillitis. This is the only diagnostic step named.

Treatment: where any group A streptococcus is identified during pregnancy, aggressive treatment — specifically aggressive antibiotic treatment — is indicated. In women with known GAS infection in pregnancy, aggressive antibiotic treatment is also framed as a measure to prevent maternal death, making prompt escalation a mortality-reduction intervention rather than simply symptom control.

Containment: pregnant women with identified GAS require infection control precautions, including barrier nursing as per local guidelines. For women suspected of, or diagnosed with, GAS sepsis, barrier nursing with protective clothing in a single room is specified to minimise spread to other women and to staff.

Staff and neonatal considerations: antimicrobial prophylaxis should be considered for healthcare workers following exposure to the respiratory secretions of women with GAS infection. Maternal GAS infection increases the risk of neonatal sepsis in babies, so identification has implications for newborn surveillance.

Guideline bodies: only RCOG contributes here, so no inter-body disagreement can be assessed. Within RCOG, page 15 is more specific than page 7 — page 7 covers only swab-based detection, while page 15 layers treatment, isolation, staff prophylaxis and outcomes.

What is not established: no antibiotic agent, dose, route or duration is named for either maternal treatment or staff prophylaxis; "aggressive" is undefined. No timing thresholds (e.g. hours to first dose), no exposure window for staff prophylaxis, no duration of isolation or de-isolation criteria, and no neonatal screening or treatment pathway are given. Nothing addresses non-pregnant surgical patients, intrapartum antibiotic choice, or GAS carriage screening in asymptomatic women.
key_entities: barrier nursing with protective clothing in a single room

title: Respiratory Droplet Precautions and Barrier Nursing
summary:
This community represents source-control and transmission-based precautions against respiratory and droplet-spread infection in perioperative/obstetric-gynecologic settings, combining hand hygiene, masking, spatial separation, staff contact avoidance, and barrier nursing.

Core recommendations: (1) Hand hygiene, performed frequently, prevents respiratory infection and its transmission among health care personnel caring for patients with signs and symptoms of respiratory infection (OpenRN T2, p203). (2) Masks prevent respiratory infection and block entry of large infectious droplets through mucous membranes: worn by personnel when examining/caring for clients with respiratory signs and symptoms, and worn by infected personnel when avoiding direct patient contact is not possible (OpenRN T2 p203). (3) Surgical masks applied as source control on coughing persons contain secretions and prevent transmission (OpenRN T2 p203). (4) Spatial separation of persons with respiratory infections in common waiting areas — ideally greater than 3 feet, when possible (OpenRN T2, p203). (5) Health care personnel who have a respiratory infection should avoid direct client contact, especially with high-risk clients (OpenRN T2). (6) Barrier nursing applies to women suspected of having influenza while awaiting PCR results (RCOG T1 p7), and barrier nursing plus masks protect other patients and healthcare workers from group A streptococcus infection (RCOG T1 p11).

Contributing bodies: OpenRN (Nursing Skills, Tier 2) supplies the generic respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette bundle with the most operational specificity — the >3 foot threshold, source-control masking of coughers, and the conditional hierarchy (avoid contact first, mask if unavoidable). RCOG (Tier 1) is population-specific rather than technique-specific: it names influenza (pending PCR) and group A streptococcus in women, and prescribes barrier nursing as the organizing intervention without stating distance, mask type, or duration. They are complementary, not conflicting.

Not established: no respirator/N95 versus surgical mask distinction, no antiviral or antibiotic therapy (no oseltamivir, no penicillin/clindamycin for GAS), no isolation room or negative-pressure requirements, no duration of barrier nursing or de-escalation criteria after negative PCR, no eye protection, gown or glove specifications, no vaccination guidance, and no outcome or effectiveness data quantifying risk reduction.
key_entities: entry of large infectious droplets through mucous membranes

title: Monitoring-Induced Sleep Disruption and Care Grouping
summary: This community represents a small but practically important theme: iatrogenic sleep disruption in hospitalized clients caused by the nursing care process itself, and the clustering of care activities as the countermeasure. Two relations define it. First, therapeutic monitoring is identified as increasing the risk of disturbed sleep pattern in the hospitalized client, with the condition specified as monitoring that interrupts rest at least hourly — i.e., the hazard is tied to frequency of interruption, not to monitoring per se. Second, grouping of care tasks is presented as a treatment for disturbed sleep pattern in the hospitalized client already experiencing that problem, with the operational condition being that lab draws, vital signs and assessments are grouped together rather than performed as separate, sequentially disruptive encounters. Read together, the pair forms a single risk-and-mitigation dyad usable in quality-improvement work: audit how often overnight monitoring contacts occur (the at-least-hourly threshold is the only stated trigger), then bundle phlebotomy, vital sign measurement and assessment into consolidated rounds. Only one guideline body contributes here — OpenRN Nursing Fundamentals, Volume 2, page 900 — supplying both the risk statement and the intervention statement; there is therefore no cross-body disagreement, no competing threshold, and no instance of one source being more specific than another within this community. What the community does not establish: it names no drugs, no pharmacologic or non-pharmacologic sleep aids beyond task grouping, and no perioperative- or gynecology-specific population despite the surrounding corpus — the population is simply "hospitalized client." It gives no permissible monitoring interval (e.g., no recommendation to move from hourly to 2- or 4-hourly checks), no protected sleep window or clock times, no criteria for when monitoring frequency may safely be reduced, no acuity or safety exclusions where hourly monitoring must be maintained, and no outcome measures, sleep assessment tools, or effect sizes demonstrating that grouping care resolves disturbed sleep pattern. Educators should present it as a directional principle requiring local protocol to operationalize.

title: PONV Risk and Enhanced Recovery Gynaecology
summary:
This community links gynaecological surgery to postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) risk and situates that risk within an enhanced recovery (ERAS) framework. Two risk-elevating factors are named repeatedly: gynaecological surgery itself and laparoscopic procedures, both flagged by the ERAS Society (T1 p1, p7) as increasing PONV risk. Nitrous oxide is a third risk factor, but with an explicit population qualifier — it increases PONV risk in patients with a high baseline risk (ERAS_Society T1 p7).

Two preventive recommendations follow. First, omission of nitrous oxide prevents PONV, conditioned specifically on laparoscopic gynecologic surgery. Second, prophylaxis with a combination of at least two anti-emetics prevents PONV and, per ERAS, 'should be standard' — i.e. multimodal rather than single-agent prophylaxis is the default, not a rescue strategy. No individual anti-emetic drugs, doses or timings are named in these relations.

A separate ERAS relation notes gynaecological surgery increases risk of bowel incontinence (OpenRN T2 p1179), which sits alongside PONV as a postoperative morbidity but is not linked to any prophylaxis here.

Contributing bodies: ERAS Society supplies all PONV risk and prevention content and is the most specific (baseline-risk stratification, laparoscopic condition, two-agent threshold). RCOG (T1 p1) contributes the programme-level framing: enhanced recovery applies to gynaecological surgery for patients undergoing elective procedures, described as being implemented across the NHS in four specialties, and spans the preoperative, perioperative and postoperative phases for patients undergoing major surgery. OpenRN contributes only the bowel incontinence risk. The bodies do not conflict; they operate at different granularity — RCOG defines scope and phases, ERAS defines the intervention detail.

Not established: no named anti-emetic agents, doses, routes or administration timing; no validated PONV risk score or numeric definition of 'high baseline risk'; no explicit link between enhanced recovery pathways and PONV outcomes; no management (as opposed to prevention) of established PONV; no prevention or nursing management pathway for bowel incontinence; and no paediatric, emergency or non-elective populations.
key_entities: prophylaxis with a combination of at least two anti-emetics

title: Balancing haemorrhage risk against thromboprophylaxis
summary:
This community represents the bidirectional tension between bleeding and clotting in the peripartum period: anticoagulants used to prevent venous thromboembolism (VTE) can precipitate or worsen haemorrhage, while haemorrhage itself is identified as a factor that increases VTE risk in women after delivery (RCOG T1 p21). All relations derive from a single guideline body, RCOG (Reducing the Risk of Thrombosis and Embolism, Green-top-style guidance), pages 5, 14, 20, 21, 23 and 24, so there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile; differences are only in specificity between statements.

Key recommendations: (1) Pharmacological thromboprophylaxis is only temporarily contraindicated in postpartum women at risk of haemorrhage — it should be started or reinstituted as soon as the immediate risk of haemorrhage is reduced (p5). (2) For women already on low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) who develop a haemorrhagic problem, LMWH is stopped until expert haematological advice is obtained and the immediate risk of haemorrhage has fallen (p5); p20 is more concrete on process, naming stopping LMWH as the treatment and directing the clinician to seek advice from a haematologist. (3) Unfractionated heparin (UFH) increases haemorrhage risk in pregnant women, particularly in late pregnancy, when apparent heparin resistance leads to unnecessarily high doses being used (p14). (4) Protamine sulfate is the reversal/treatment agent for haemorrhage in women receiving unfractionated heparin (p24). (5) A central line is used to monitor for haemorrhage when the cardiovascular system is compromised by haemorrhage or disease (p23).

What this community does not establish: no numeric thresholds are given for platelet count, haemoglobin, blood loss volume, anti-Xa level or protamine dose; no defined time interval for how long to withhold or when exactly to reinstitute LMWH or prophylaxis; no antidote is specified for LMWH (only stopping it); no mechanical prophylaxis alternatives, transfusion triggers, tranexamic acid, or regional anaesthesia timing rules appear. Monitoring is limited to central line use, with no stated frequency or observation set.

title: Nonpharmacologic management of dementia-related hallucinations
summary:
Theme: this small community addresses non-drug, environmental and interpersonal nursing interventions for hallucinations in clients with dementia — a relevant concern in perioperative gynecologic settings where older clients with cognitive impairment may experience perceptual disturbance. Both relations are TREATS links directed at the single clinical target 'hallucination'.

Recommendations as stated: (1) Gentle patting is indicated as a therapeutic response for clients with dementia who are experiencing hallucinations — the population condition is explicitly 'clients with dementia experiencing hallucinations', i.e. an active-symptom trigger rather than prophylaxis. (2) A well-lit environment is indicated for clients with dementia, with the more specific situational condition 'in well-lit areas where other people are present' — combining illumination with social presence as the operative circumstance. Note the difference in specificity: the patting recommendation is conditioned on the symptom being present, while the lighting recommendation is conditioned on the setting/environment and adds a second element (presence of other people) that the patting entry does not.

Contributing body: only one source contributes here — OpenRN (Open Resources for Nursing), Text 2, page 468. Because there is a single contributing guideline and a single page, there are no cross-body disagreements to reconcile and no competing or contradictory recommendations to arbitrate; the two interventions appear complementary rather than alternative.

What this community does NOT establish: no drugs, doses, or pharmacologic alternatives (no antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, or anything else) are named; no thresholds, frequencies, durations, or timings for patting or for lighting levels are specified; no perioperative phase (pre-, intra-, post-operative) is attached; no gynecologic-surgical population is specified beyond 'clients with dementia'; no severity grading of hallucinations, no escalation or de-escalation pathway, no contraindications (e.g., when touch may worsen agitation), no outcome measures or evidence grade, and no ranking of the two interventions relative to one another. It also says nothing about delirium versus dementia differentiation.

title: Preventing genital tract infection through hygiene education
summary:
This community represents a small, tightly focused patient-education and hygiene theme: primary prevention of genital tract infection (notably invasive group A streptococcal, GAS, disease) in the peripartum period. Both relations converge on a single outcome entity, genital tract infection, and both are preventive rather than diagnostic or therapeutic.

Recommendations. (1) Hand washing before and after using the lavatory or changing sanitary towels prevents genital tract infection. Population: all pregnant women and those who have recently given birth. Condition: this is emphasised especially when the woman herself, her family, or close contacts have symptoms of GAS infection — i.e. household contact with symptomatic GAS raises the priority of the advice, though the advice applies universally. (2) Provision of verbal AND written information about GAS prevention and about the signs and symptoms of GAS prevents genital tract infection. Population: all pregnant women and those who recently gave birth; no additional qualifying condition is attached, so this is a blanket antenatal/postnatal counselling expectation rather than a risk-triggered one.

Contributing bodies. Only one body contributes here: RCOG (Tier 1, p15). Both statements come from the same page, so there is no inter-guideline disagreement, corroboration, or conflict to reconcile. Within the corpus fragment, the hand-washing item is the more specific of the two — it names the exact behaviours (lavatory use, sanitary towel changes) and a modifying circumstance (symptomatic woman, family, or close contacts) — whereas the information-giving item specifies the format (verbal plus written) and content domain (prevention, signs and symptoms) but no trigger or timing.

What is not established. The community gives no timing or frequency for delivering the education (e.g. which antenatal visit, or before discharge), no named antiseptics, soaps, alcohol gels, antibiotics or prophylactic drugs, no thresholds, no screening or swabbing pathway, no escalation or treatment steps once GAS is suspected, no contact-tracing or household decolonisation guidance, and no documentation, audit or competency standard. It also does not quantify effect size or grade the strength of evidence for either intervention.
key_entities: hand washing before and after using the lavatory or changing sanitary towels
verbal and written information about gas prevention, signs and symptoms
all pregnant women and those who recently gave birth
family or close contacts with symptoms

title: Stimulant laxatives preventing barium-related hardened stool
summary:
Clinical theme: prevention and treatment of hardened stool/constipation arising from two iatrogenic sources — retained barium contrast media and opioid therapy — with stimulant laxatives as the shared pharmacologic intervention.

Risk relation: barium contrast diagnostic procedures increase the risk of hardened stool in clients who have recently undergone such procedures; the stated condition is failure to expel the barium within a day or two of the procedure. This gives educators a concrete post-procedure surveillance window: confirm barium passage within 1–2 days.

Recommendations: (1) A stimulant laxative prevents hardened stool in clients after barium contrast diagnostic procedures, when prescribed specifically to promote barium expulsion following the procedure. (2) A stimulant laxative treats constipation in clients taking opioids, added on an as-needed basis to maintain a normal bowel pattern, with the explicit caveat that it is not intended for long-term use.

Contributing guideline body: all three relations derive from a single source, OpenRN (Nursing Skills/Pharmacology, Text 2), at p1183 (barium and post-procedure laxative use) and p825 (opioid-induced constipation). Because only one corpus contributes, there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile; however, the two passages differ in specificity and framing. The p1183 material is procedure-anchored and preventive, tying the laxative to a defined event and a 1–2 day expulsion threshold, and requires a prescription. The p825 material is symptom-driven and therapeutic, PRN-titrated to bowel pattern rather than to a time threshold, and uniquely adds a duration limitation (avoid long-term use).

Not established: the community names no specific stimulant laxative agent, dose, route, or frequency; no defined interval for "long-term"; no alternative or adjunct agents (e.g., stool softeners, osmotics), fluid or fiber measures, or bowel regimen escalation steps. It does not address pediatric, pregnant, obstructive, or perioperative gynecologic-specific populations, does not state contraindications or adverse effects, and provides no monitoring, imaging follow-up, or escalation pathway if barium is still not expelled after laxative administration.

title: Hand hygiene prevents healthcare-associated infection
summary:
This community centers on hand hygiene as the core intervention for preventing health care associated infection (HAI), plus the system-level conditions that erode adherence. Three guideline sources contribute: CDC (T1, pp. 8 and 29), WHO (T1 p211), and OpenRN (T2 p203).

Main recommendations: Hand hygiene prevents HAI, stated unconditionally by both CDC (p29) and WHO (p211), and specifically for hospitalized patients when adherence to recommended hand-hygiene practices improves (CDC p29). CDC p8 adds a dose-response framing: HAI rates fall as adherence to recommended hand-hygiene measures improves. CDC is the most product-specific source: for health-care personnel, antiseptic handwashing prevents HAI compared with handwashing with plain soap and water, and antiseptic handwashing with a chlorhexidine-containing detergent prevents HAI compared with handwashing with plain soap or use of an alcohol-based hand rinse. OpenRN contributes a broader behavioural frame: standard precautions prevent HAI for all patients, regardless of suspected or confirmed infection status.

Risk side: poor adherence to hand hygiene increases HAI risk for hospitalized patients during periods of understaffing and overcrowding; understaffing and overcrowding are each independently listed as increasing HAI risk, and both are described as consistently linked with poor hand-hygiene adherence. For a QI lead, this makes staffing and census pressure legitimate targets of an HAI reduction bundle, not just individual technique training.

Differences in emphasis: WHO and CDC p29 assert the general preventive effect; only CDC p8 differentiates agents and ranks chlorhexidine-containing detergent above plain soap and above alcohol-based hand rinse in the comparisons stated. Only OpenRN frames prevention through standard precautions applied universally.

Not established here: no numeric adherence thresholds, staffing ratios, occupancy limits, scrub durations, chlorhexidine concentrations, or product contact times; no perioperative- or gynecologic-surgery-specific populations; no surgical hand antisepsis, glove, or skin-prep relations; no infection-type breakdown (e.g., surgical site vs. bloodstream); and no outcome data on how much HAI risk falls per unit of improved adherence.

title: Preventing health care-associated infection in surgery
summary:
This community centres on prevention of health care-associated infection (HAI), including surgical site infection (SSI), and the environmental and system-level factors that drive it. All relations derive from a single source, WHO Table 1 p211 — no other guideline body contributes, so no inter-body disagreement can be assessed.

Core protective recommendations: hand hygiene prevents HAI and is directed at *everyone working in health care* (not just nurses or surgeons); standard precautions prevent HAI for *health-care staff*; and compliance with infection prevention and control guidelines prevents HAI, conditional on health-care workers actually complying. Early hospital discharge is also framed as preventive — patients should leave hospital as soon as possible, reducing exposure time. Note that the population framing differs subtly: hand hygiene is the broadest (all health-care workers), while standard precautions are specified for health-care staff, and the compliance relation is explicitly conditional rather than absolute.

Risk factors: a developing country setting increases risk of both SSI (for surgical patients in developing countries) and HAI generally (for patients in developing countries) — the only relation set that stratifies risk by geography/resource level. Environmental sources — contaminated food, contaminated water, and contaminated medication (e.g. intravenous fluids) — each increase HAI risk and are noted to *usually cause outbreaks* rather than sporadic cases, which is an important epidemiological distinction for QI investigation: cluster detection, not individual case review.

What this community does NOT establish: no antimicrobial agents, antiseptics or prophylactic antibiotics are named; no thresholds (e.g. hand hygiene compliance rates, timing of surgical prophylaxis, duration of scrub); no specific timing for "early" discharge; no device- or procedure-specific measures (catheters, ventilators, drains); no gynecologic- or obstetric-specific populations despite the perioperative gynecologic context; and no quantified effect sizes or relative contribution of each risk factor. It also does not describe surveillance methods, isolation practices, sterilisation/decontamination standards, or how outbreak investigation of contaminated food, water or medication should proceed.
key_entities: compliance with infection prevention and control guidelines

title: Central Adiposity and Waist Circumference Risk
summary:
Clinical theme: this small community addresses body-fat distribution as an independent risk marker in nursing assessment, distinguishing central (abdominal) adiposity from peripheral (hip and thigh) fat deposition. Rather than treating weight alone as the risk variable, the relations position where fat is carried, and waist circumference as its bedside proxy, as the driver of health-problem risk relevant to perioperative gynecologic patient assessment.

Main recommendations and their populations/conditions: (1) Excess abdominal fat increases risk of health problems, with the stated condition being a comparison — abdominal fat carries greater risk than fat located in the hip and thigh area. No specific population restriction is attached to this relation. (2) High waist circumference increases risk of health problems specifically for individuals whose BMI falls in the 'normal weight' range, under the condition of a high waist circumference. This second relation is the more clinically pointed of the two: it directs assessors not to be reassured by a normal BMI, because waist circumference can independently flag risk in that group. Practically, this supports routinely measuring waist circumference alongside BMI rather than substituting one for the other.

Contributing guideline bodies: both relations derive from a single source, the Registered Nurses' Association of Ontario (RNAO), Tool 2, page 119. There is therefore no cross-body disagreement to reconcile in this community; the two RNAO statements are complementary, with the waist-circumference statement being the more population-specific (normal-weight BMI) and the abdominal-fat statement the more general comparative claim.

What this community does NOT establish: it names no numeric threshold for 'high' waist circumference (no cm or inch cut-points, and no sex- or ethnicity-specific values), no BMI numeric boundaries for 'normal weight', and no measurement technique, landmark or timing (e.g. preoperative versus postoperative assessment). It does not specify which health problems are increased, quantify the magnitude of risk, name any drug, intervention, or perioperative management change, and does not link adiposity to gynecologic surgical outcomes, anesthesia, wound or thromboembolic risk. No follow-up interval or documentation requirement is defined.
key_entities: fat located in the hip and thigh area

title: Health Teaching as Cross-Population Intervention
summary:
This small community represents a single unifying clinical theme: nurse-delivered health teaching (patient education) as an active therapeutic and preventive intervention rather than merely supportive communication. Two relations anchor the theme, each tied to a distinct population and condition.

First, health teaching is identified as TREATING anxiety in clients receiving palliative care (OpenRN Nursing Fundamentals/Management, Textbook 2, p. 1269). Here education is framed as a symptom-directed intervention for psychological distress in the palliative population.

Second, health teaching is identified as PREVENTING diabetes complications in clients with diabetes (OpenRN T2, p. 696). Here the same intervention is framed prospectively, as risk reduction in a chronic-disease population.

The combined message for educators is that health teaching functions across both the treatment and prevention axes of care, and that its documented indications in this corpus span acute psychological symptom relief (palliative anxiety) and long-term complication avoidance (diabetes). For QI purposes, this supports auditing whether structured teaching is documented for both palliative clients reporting anxiety and all clients with diabetes.

Only one guideline body contributes: OpenRN, in the same volume (Textbook 2). There is therefore no inter-body disagreement, no competing recommendation, and no more-specific versus more-general pairing to reconcile; the two entries differ only in population, condition, and relation type (TREATS vs PREVENTS), with the diabetes prevention entry appearing earlier in the text (p. 696) than the palliative anxiety entry (p. 1269).

Critically, this community does NOT establish: any teaching content, curriculum, or topic list; any dose, frequency, session length, or timing (including preoperative versus postoperative delivery); any threshold, screening cut-off, or outcome measure for anxiety or for glycemic control; any named drug or pharmacologic comparator or adjunct; any specific diabetes complication (e.g., retinopathy, neuropathy, foot ulceration); any perioperative or gynecologic-surgery-specific application; any evidence grading, strength of recommendation, or effect size; and any statement about who should deliver the teaching, in what setting, or with what documentation requirements.

title: Postoperative Mobility and Pulmonary Prophylaxis
summary:
This community represents non-pharmacologic, nursing-driven postoperative prophylaxis: simple mobility and pulmonary hygiene measures aimed at preventing two complications of immobility after gynecologic/urogynecologic surgery — healthcare-acquired respiratory infection and venous thromboembolism (VTE).

Four interventions converge on prevention of healthcare-acquired respiratory infection: incentive spirometry, coughing and deep breathing, positional changes, and early ambulation (the latter qualified as 'as appropriate,' i.e., contingent on patient readiness and safety). These are drawn from OpenRN (T2, p663) and are stated without a narrowed population, so they read as general postoperative/inpatient nursing care rather than procedure-specific directives.

Early ambulation is the bridging node: in addition to its respiratory benefit, AUGS (T2, p13) credits it with preventing venous thromboembolism, and here the guideline is markedly more specific about population — inpatients with a low risk profile undergoing vaginal or laparoscopic urogynecological procedures. That specificity matters for QI work: AUGS positions early ambulation as the VTE strategy for the low-risk inpatient undergoing minimally invasive or vaginal urogynecologic surgery, while OpenRN treats it as one element of a broader pulmonary-hygiene bundle.

The two bodies do not conflict; they differ in scope and granularity. OpenRN contributes the pulmonary bundle with no population qualifiers; AUGS contributes a risk-stratified, procedure-specific VTE indication.

What this community does NOT establish: no timing, frequency, duration, or dose parameters are given — nothing on how soon after surgery ambulation should begin, how far or how often, or how many incentive spirometry breaths/repetitions per hour. No thresholds or risk-scoring tools are named to define the 'low risk profile.' No pharmacologic prophylaxis (e.g., heparin or low-molecular-weight heparin) or mechanical prophylaxis (compression devices) appears, so this community cannot be read as the complete VTE prevention pathway, nor does it address moderate/high-risk patients, open or abdominal procedures, or outpatients. It also does not state that the pulmonary measures prevent VTE, or that positional changes, coughing/deep breathing, or incentive spirometry have any VTE effect.
key_entities: inpatients with low risk profile undergoing vaginal or laparoscopic urogynecological procedure

title: Hand Hygiene and Perioperative Infection Prevention
summary: This community centres on infection prevention in perioperative and general patient care, with hand hygiene as the dominant hub intervention, supported by antibiotics, aseptic technique, gloves, catheter management and normothermia. Hand hygiene is stated to prevent healthcare-associated/nosocomial infection, transmission of infectious agents and pathogenic microorganisms, MRSA transmission, bloodborne pathogen transmission, colonization, respiratory infection transmission, catheter-associated UTI and integumentary harm — for all patients, hospitalized patients, health-care workers, students, relatives and visitors, and all visitors/staff/clients of a neutropenic client. Named timings: immediately before any clean/aseptic task including preparing sterile medications; before and after preparing and administering parenteral injections; before and after urinary catheter insertion and any device/site manipulation; immediately after glove removal or exposure to body fluids; after touching a patient; when preparing food, medications and dressings; frequently when caring for patients with respiratory infection signs/symptoms. Handwashing is also specified immediately prior to and during invasive procedures. Hand hygiene is preferred over gloves when exposure risk is minimal; gloves prevent infection when used properly but increase risk if used improperly, and gloves prevent bloodborne pathogen transmission in health-care workers. Alcohol-based hand rub prevents infection when embedded in ongoing educational/motivational programs, but is temporarily contraindicated when hands are visibly soiled (use soap and water until clean); hand hygiene itself is temporarily contraindicated for students/workers with dermatitis or eczema until resolved. Other prevention: prophylactic antibiotics for surgical patients with appropriate administration; antimicrobial prophylaxis in preterm prelabour rupture of membranes; surgical scrubbing before theatre entry; aseptic technique; normothermia maintenance perioperatively (AUGS); urinary catheter removal preferably within 3–8 h, since longer-term catheterization raises risk. Risk factors: surgery/invasive procedures, colonization, diabetes. Culture detects infection in surgical personnel with draining skin lesions; antibiotics treat infection when selected by susceptibility testing. Contributors: WHO (broadest role/population detail), CDC (adherence, products, MRSA, program design), OpenRN (task-level nursing moments), AUGS (catheter and normothermia specifics). Not established: specific antibiotic agents, doses, timing windows for prophylaxis, scrub agents, durations of hand hygiene, effect sizes, or gynecologic-procedure-specific thresholds.

title: Hearing Loss Detection and Anxiety Risk
summary:
This community represents a small, coherent theme: nursing assessment for hearing loss/impairment and its psychological consequence, anxiety. It links two assessment techniques (informal conversational assessment and the whispered voice test) to the detection of hearing loss and hearing impairment, and links hearing loss itself to increased anxiety risk.

Main content and its stated populations/conditions: (1) Basic hearing assessment during conversation detects hearing loss, with the condition that findings are based on patient cues observed during normal conversation — i.e., the nurse uses ordinary interaction as a screening opportunity rather than a formal test. (2) The whispered voice test detects hearing loss when the patient reports fewer than three out of a possible six numbers or letters correctly for both ears; this is the only explicit numeric threshold in the community. (3) The whispered voice test also detects hearing impairment, conditioned on the test being performed accurately — signalling that technique fidelity, not just the score, governs interpretation. (4) For individuals experiencing hearing loss, hearing loss increases the risk of anxiety, giving a psychosocial rationale for screening and for communication accommodations.

Contributing bodies: all statements derive from a single source, OpenRN (Open Resources for Nursing) Textbook 2, at pages 521 (hearing loss → anxiety) and 539 (both assessment methods). There is therefore no cross-body disagreement to reconcile. Within this single source, the whispered voice test is the more specific recommendation (explicit <3/6 correct threshold, both ears), while conversational assessment is described only qualitatively via patient cues.

What the community does NOT establish: no perioperative or gynecologic-surgery-specific population is named; no timing (preoperative, intraoperative, post-anaesthesia) or frequency of screening is given; no drugs, ototoxic agents, or treatments are mentioned; no audiometry referral pathway, sensitivity/specificity, or age-based criteria appear. It does not specify how anxiety should be screened, measured, or managed once hearing loss is identified, nor does it link hearing assessment to consent, sedation, or discharge teaching.

title: Detecting and monitoring fluid volume excess
summary:
This community centres on the recognition, risk stratification and ongoing surveillance of fluid volume excess (hypervolemia) in patients, with a secondary strand on skin inspection as both a fluid and a pressure-damage assessment tool. Risk factors named are a history of kidney disease, a history of heart failure, and receipt of intravenous fluids; these populations are the explicit targets of heightened monitoring.

Detection recommendations (all OpenRN, Tab 2 p1111) pair an assessment with its positive finding: skin inspection detects excess when skin is tight, edematous and shiny; vital signs assessment when blood pressure is elevated with bounding pulses; lung auscultation when crackles are present, often first heard in the lower posterior lung fields; and serum osmolarity when it is decreased, i.e. the blood is more dilute than normal. Laboratory monitoring of serum osmolarity, serum sodium, blood urea nitrogen and hematocrit is recommended, with decreased levels indicating fluid volume excess. For clients receiving intravenous fluids specifically, nurses should undertake general monitoring for excessive fluid volume and auscultate lung sounds for crackles while asking about dyspnea. Intake and output monitoring should be performed over a 24-hour period, noting trends of decreasing urine output in relation to fluid intake.

Two guideline bodies contribute. OpenRN supplies the entire fluid-balance pathway. NICE (Tab 1 p11) contributes only the skin-damage element, and is more population- and frequency-specific than OpenRN: inspect skin 2 or 3 times a day, particularly over the heels and bony prominences, in people with a significant reduction in mobility, poor skin integrity or any sensory loss. Skin inspection is thus shared between the two bodies but serves different endpoints (hypervolemia vs pressure damage); the sources do not conflict, they simply address different questions.

The community does not establish any treatment: no diuretics, fluid-restriction volumes, drugs or infusion rates are named. No numeric thresholds are given for blood pressure, osmolarity, sodium, BUN, hematocrit or urine output, no escalation or notification criteria, and no perioperative or gynecologic-surgery-specific application despite the corpus context.
key_entities: laboratory monitoring of serum osmolarity, serum sodium, blood urea nitrogen and hematocrit

title: Antenatal Heartburn: Lifestyle Advice Then Antacids
summary:
This community represents the stepped management of heartburn (physiological reflux) during pregnancy, a common antenatal discomfort addressed within routine antenatal care rather than in the intraoperative or postoperative setting. All four relations derive from a single guideline body, WHO (antenatal care guidance, T1 p13), so the theme is uniform in provenance and there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile.

The recommendations form a clear two-step sequence. First line: diet and lifestyle advice for pregnant women, which the guideline frames both as PREVENTING heartburn and as TREATING it once present; this advice is explicitly situated in the antenatal phase of care. Second line: an antacid, indicated specifically for pregnant women with troublesome symptoms, and conditioned on symptoms not being relieved by lifestyle modification. The escalation trigger is therefore symptom persistence plus symptom burden ('troublesome'), not a numeric threshold.

For educators, the teachable point is that non-pharmacological counselling is the default first intervention for every pregnant woman, and pharmacotherapy is reserved for treatment failure — a useful anchor for antenatal counselling checklists and for QI audits of whether lifestyle advice was documented before an antacid was offered.

What this community does NOT establish: it names no specific diet or lifestyle measures (no foods, meal timing, posture, or weight guidance are specified); it names no specific antacid agent, dose, formulation, frequency, or maximum duration; and it gives no gestational-age window, trimester restriction, or timing of review after starting an antacid. It does not address alternatives or later steps such as alginates, H2-receptor antagonists, or proton-pump inhibitors, nor any safety, contraindication, iron/nutrient-interaction, or referral criteria. It says nothing about heartburn in the perioperative, intrapartum, or postpartum periods, nor about non-pregnant gynecologic surgical patients, and provides no outcome or effectiveness data to support the prevention claim.

title: Surgical Risk Factors for Heavy Blood Loss
summary:
This community centres on anticipating and mitigating heavy intraoperative blood loss in gynecologic and obstetric surgery, plus one adjacent thromboembolic risk. Four procedural or intraoperative factors are named as increasing the risk of heavy blood loss: caesarean section, reoperation, major vascular surgery, and difficult dissection (all WHO Tier 1, p42). These are stated as general surgical risk factors, without a specified population qualifier, threshold volume for 'heavy' loss, or numeric risk estimate.

The single preventive recommendation is correction of coagulation deficits: for patients with known coagulation deficits, this should be undertaken before surgery, whenever clinically possible, and is explicitly located in the preoperative phase (WHO T1 p42). The condition 'whenever clinically possible' allows for urgent or emergency cases where correction cannot be completed; the guideline does not describe what to do in that situation.

Two guideline bodies contribute. WHO (Tier 1, p42) supplies all of the blood-loss risk factors and the preoperative correction recommendation, and is the more general source — its risk statements carry no population restriction. RCOG (Tier 1, p22) is the more specific contributor on a different outcome: it links reoperation to increased risk of venous thromboembolism specifically for women after caesarean section. Reoperation is therefore the bridging entity, flagged by WHO for bleeding risk and by RCOG for VTE risk in the post-caesarean population. The two bodies do not contradict one another; they address complementary complications, and no relation reconciles the tension between bleeding risk and thromboprophylaxis.

What this community does NOT establish: no drugs, agents, doses or blood products are named (no tranexamic acid, no specific factor concentrates, plasma, or anticoagulants); no thresholds define 'heavy' blood loss; no timing beyond 'before surgery'; no intraoperative or postoperative interventions; no monitoring, transfusion triggers, or escalation pathways; and no VTE prophylaxis regimen for the RCOG post-caesarean reoperation population. Educators should treat this as a risk-recognition and preoperative-optimisation theme requiring local protocols to operationalise.

title: IV Catheter Dislodgement Bleeding Control
summary:
Clinical theme: this small community addresses a single, focused peripheral IV access complication in the perioperative gynecologic nursing context — accidental dislodgement of an intravenous catheter and the resulting bleeding at the insertion site. It links a causal risk relation to a corresponding immediate nursing intervention, making it a natural teaching unit for IV site monitoring and first-response skills.

Main content and populations: (1) Intravenous catheter dislodgement increases the risk of hemorrhage; the population attached to this relation is patients with intravenous access. No subgroup qualifiers (e.g., anticoagulated patients, specific gauges, central vs. peripheral lines, intraoperative vs. postoperative phase) are specified. (2) Application of pressure with gauze treats hemorrhage in the same population, with the condition stated as 'if dislodgement occurs, until the bleeding stops.' The endpoint is therefore clinical (cessation of bleeding) rather than time-based — no minimum number of minutes of pressure is given.

Contributing guideline bodies: the entire community derives from a single source, OpenRN Nursing Skills (Open Resources for Nursing, Text 2, p. 1363). Both relations come from the same page, so there is no cross-body corroboration, no disagreement to reconcile, and no instance of one body being more granular than another. Educators should note that the specificity here is at the level of a basic skills text, not a specialty perioperative or gynecologic surgical standard.

What this community does NOT establish: it gives no thresholds for defining or grading hemorrhage (no volume, hemoglobin, or vital-sign criteria), no duration for holding pressure, no guidance on dressing, elevation, tourniquet use, escalation, or physician notification, and no drugs — no hemostatic agents, topical or systemic tranexamic acid, or reversal agents are mentioned. It does not address prevention of dislodgement (securement devices, tubing management, patient education), documentation, re-siting the catheter, or downstream complications such as infiltration, phlebitis, hematoma, or infection. It also says nothing about gynecologic-procedure-specific bleeding risks despite the corpus context, and offers no evidence grading or strength-of-recommendation rating.

title: Heparin VTE Prophylaxis and Epidural Timing
summary: This community centres on pharmacologic thromboprophylaxis with heparin/low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) and the timing interlock between anticoagulant dosing and neuraxial (epidural) catheter management. Prophylaxis recommendations: the ERAS Society advises heparin to prevent venous thromboembolism (VTE) in all gynecologic oncology patients undergoing major surgery lasting >30 minutes, and in patients at risk of VTE it should be commenced preoperatively, combined with mechanical methods, and continued post-operatively. WHO states heparin prevents VTE in surgical patients 'when indicated' (less specific than ERAS) and also notes heparin's application in cardiopulmonary bypass. RCOG contributes obstetric specificity: heparin prevents VTE in women with obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome without prior VTE, with antenatal therapy typically stopped between 35 weeks and delivery; heparin is continued until the INR is >2.0 for at least 24 hours when transitioning to warfarin; heparin is contraindicated in women with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, where danaparoid can be considered instead; and heparin increases the risk of allergic skin reaction in pregnant women receiving treatment. Epidural timing: RCOG repeatedly specifies that an epidural catheter should not be removed within 12 hours of the most recent LMWH injection, and that LMWH should not be given for at least 4 hours after catheter removal. ERAS states more generally that both epidural catheter placement and removal should be timed according to the last heparin dose in patients receiving prophylactic anticoagulation — the same principle, but without numeric thresholds, so RCOG's 12-hour/4-hour windows are the operational detail for practice. Points not established: no dose, drug-specific unit, or duration of postoperative prophylaxis is given; no guidance on mechanical method type, renal impairment or weight-based adjustment, spinal (versus epidural) anaesthesia, platelet monitoring for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, or danaparoid dosing; timing thresholds for unfractionated heparin (as distinct from LMWH) are absent; and no bleeding-risk or contraindication list for surgical patients, nor any resolution of whether ERAS intends the same 12-hour/4-hour intervals.

title: Acetaminophen dosing limits preventing hepatotoxicity
summary:
This community centers on a single safety theme: acetaminophen-induced hepatotoxicity and the nursing calculations and risk screening that prevent it, including risk carried by combination opioid-acetaminophen products such as Percocet.

Main relations and their populations/conditions: (1) Acetaminophen increases hepatotoxicity risk in adult clients when more than 4,000 mg is taken in 24 hours, with lower ceilings of 3,200 mg for older adults and 2,000 mg for chronic alcoholics. (2) Acetaminophen also increases hepatotoxicity risk in clients using acetaminophen who consume three or more alcoholic drinks every day; the same threshold is expressed independently as daily alcohol consumption (three or more drinks per day) increasing hepatotoxicity risk in acetaminophen users. (3) Percocet increases hepatotoxicity risk in geriatric clients when two tablets are administered every four hours across a 24-hour period. (4) The protective action is calculation of the cumulative 24-hour acetaminophen dose in clients receiving combination or as-needed (PRN) acetaminophen products, performed before administering an additional dose.

Contributing guideline bodies: all relations derive from OpenRN Nursing Pharmacology (Text 2), with two entries localized to page 825. No competing or second body is represented, so there are no cross-body disagreements; the page-specific citations simply restate the cumulative-dose calculation and alcohol-related risk in more granular, locatable form, while the unpaginated OpenRN T2 entries supply the numeric ceilings (4,000/3,200/2,000 mg) and the Percocet geriatric scenario.

What this community does NOT establish: it gives no perioperative or gynecologic-surgery-specific dosing, no pediatric, pregnancy, hepatic- or renal-impairment thresholds, and no weight-based dosing. It does not specify monitoring parameters (e.g., LFT/AST-ALT values), signs of hepatotoxicity, antidote or N-acetylcysteine treatment, timing of dose intervals other than the Percocet every-four-hours example, or a safe alcohol quantity below three drinks daily. It also does not quantify Percocet acetaminophen content, address other combination products by name, or define documentation/handoff processes for cumulative dose tracking.

title: Intestinal Obstruction Prevention, Detection, Management
summary:
This community centres on intestinal obstruction (with hernia as a related abdominal finding) across three nursing functions: prevention during medication administration, physical-assessment detection, and management once obstruction is suspected.

Prevention: bulk-forming fiber medications must be mixed in a full eight-ounce glass of water. The population is clients taking methylcellulose or psyllium, and the condition is at the time these medications are administered; adequate fluid volume is what prevents the fiber from causing intestinal obstruction.

Detection: abdominal inspection detects hernia when masses or bulges are present, and detects intestinal obstruction when visible intestinal peristalsis is observed. Broader abdominal assessment is the monitoring activity for intestinal obstruction, positioning inspection findings (bulges, visible peristalsis) as the concrete cues within ongoing abdominal surveillance.

Management: nil per os (NPO) status is identified as a treatment for intestinal obstruction, i.e., withholding oral intake as part of care once obstruction is present.

Contributing bodies: all relations derive from a single guideline corpus source, OpenRN (Open Resources for Nursing), across two page locations — OpenRN T2 p1173 (fiber medication and water volume) and OpenRN T2 p719 (abdominal inspection findings) and OpenRN T2 p1183 (NPO status, abdominal assessment monitoring). There is therefore no inter-body disagreement to reconcile. The differences are in specificity: p1173 is highly specific (named drugs methylcellulose and psyllium, a stated eight-ounce water volume, and an administration-time condition), whereas p1183 is generic, attaching no population or condition to NPO status or abdominal assessment. p719 sits between these, specifying observable trigger findings but no population.

Not established: the community does not specify perioperative or gynecologic-surgery populations, timing or duration of NPO status, criteria for resuming oral intake, frequency of abdominal assessment, auscultation or bowel-sound parameters, imaging or laboratory confirmation, escalation or surgical referral pathways, nasogastric decompression, or any relationship between hernia and subsequent obstruction. No thresholds beyond the eight-ounce fluid volume are given, and no outcome or effectiveness data are attached to any recommendation.
key_entities: mixing fiber medication in a full eight-ounce glass of water

title: PCR-Based Detection of Herpes Simplex Virus
summary:
This community represents a narrow but clinically important theme: laboratory confirmation of herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection in the perioperative/peripartum gynecologic setting using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing. Two diagnostic modalities converge on the single target condition, HSV infection.

Main recommendations: (1) A viral swab for PCR detects HSV infection in women with suspected HSV cutaneous infection, or in women presenting with vulval or sacral pain/paraesthesia even when no visible lesion is present; the sample should be taken directly from the lesion, or as a vaginal sample where no lesion is available to swab. (2) An HSV PCR blood sample also detects HSV infection and is to be used 'if indicated' — the guideline does not further specify what constitutes an indication, so this remains a clinician-judgement trigger rather than a protocolised test.

The swab-based recommendation is markedly more specific than the blood-based one: it names the eligible population (suspected cutaneous HSV; vulval/sacral pain or paraesthesia with no visible lesion) and the sampling site options (lesion or vagina), whereas the blood PCR carries only a conditional 'if indicated' qualifier. Educators should emphasise that absence of a visible lesion does not exclude testing — prodromal or neuropathic vulval/sacral symptoms alone justify a PCR swab.

Guideline contribution: all relations derive from a single source, RCOG (Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists), Table 1, page 7. There is therefore no inter-body disagreement captured here, and no corroborating or conflicting guidance from other colleges in this community.

What this community does NOT establish: it specifies no antiviral therapy (no aciclovir or other drug, dose or duration), no timing or turnaround thresholds for results, no serology or type-specific antibody testing, no criteria for the 'if indicated' blood sample, no infection-control or theatre precautions, no mode-of-delivery or surgical implications, and no neonatal or partner management. It is purely a detection/diagnostic node awaiting linkage to treatment and perioperative pathways.
key_entities: herpes simplex virus polymerase chain reaction blood sample
viral swab for polymerase chain reaction

title: Hexachlorophene Bathing Risks in Neonates
summary:
This small community captures a single, sharply bounded clinical theme: the use of hexachlorophene bathing as an antiseptic skin practice in newborns, and the tension between its demonstrated anti-staphylococcal benefit and its neurotoxic risk. Two relations, both sourced to CDC (T1, p10), define the theme.

First, hexachlorophene bathing is documented as PREVENTING health-care-associated Staphylococcus aureus infection, with the population specified as infants in hospital nurseries and the condition specified as settings where routine hexachlorophene bathing is in use. This is a nursery-level, population-based infection-prevention observation rather than an endorsement of individual patient use.

Second, and directly counterbalancing it, hexachlorophene bathing is CONTRAINDICATED WITH the neonate. The population is neonates and the condition is routine bathing, with the stated rationale being potential neurotoxic effects. Practically, this means the graph frames routine hexachlorophene bathing of neonates as something to avoid, even though the same agent is associated with reduced S. aureus transmission in nurseries.

Only one guideline body contributes here: the CDC, and both relations trace to the same page (T1 p10), so there is no inter-body disagreement to reconcile. The internal contrast is within a single source: the contraindication statement is the more specific and more actionable of the two, because it names the population (neonates), the practice pattern (routine bathing), and the mechanism of harm (neurotoxicity). The prevention statement is more descriptive and epidemiological, tied to nursery-wide use.

What this community does NOT establish: no dose, concentration, frequency, duration, or timing of bathing; no age, weight, or gestational-age threshold separating "neonate" from other infants; no alternative antiseptic agents (for example chlorhexidine) or comparative effectiveness; no guidance for non-routine or outbreak-driven use; no monitoring parameters or signs of neurotoxicity to assess; and no perioperative or surgical-site-specific recommendation. Educators should present this as a cautionary agent-specific teaching point, not a bathing protocol.

title: Staffing and Device-Related Bloodstream Infection Risk
summary:
This small community represents the theme of catheter-associated bloodstream infection (BSI) risk, framed from two angles: the device itself and the nursing workforce caring for it. Both relations converge on a single outcome entity, bloodstream infection.

The WHO contribution is the broader, unconditioned statement: an intravascular device increases the risk of bloodstream infection. No population restriction, threshold, or timing is attached — it is a general risk assertion applicable wherever intravascular devices are in use (WHO T1 p211).

The CDC contribution is more specific and is the actionable quality-improvement point: a high patient-to-nurse ratio increases the risk of bloodstream infection. Its population is explicitly narrower — patients with central venous catheters — and its condition is methodological and situational: the association was observed during an outbreak investigation and persisted after adjustment for confounding factors (CDC T1 p8). For a nurse educator or QI lead, this means nurse staffing should be treated as a modifiable infection-prevention variable for CVC-bearing patients, not merely a workload or satisfaction issue, and staffing data are relevant evidence during outbreak review.

The two bodies do not conflict; they operate at different levels of specificity. WHO identifies the device as the hazard; CDC identifies a care-delivery factor that modulates risk in the subset of patients with central venous catheters, and is the only source here that qualifies its claim with adjustment for confounders.

What this community does NOT establish: no numeric threshold defines a "high" patient-to-nurse ratio; no target ratio, staffing model, or skill-mix recommendation is given. There is no dwell-time or catheter-duration threshold, no insertion-site preference, no specification of catheter type beyond "central venous catheter" and the generic "intravascular device," and no antiseptic, dressing, flush, or antimicrobial agent (no drug is named). Causality is not asserted beyond association, no effect size or attributable-risk figure is provided, and no perioperative or gynecologic-specific population is specified despite the corpus context. Prevention bundles, surveillance definitions, and outcomes other than bloodstream infection are absent.

title: Preventing Hip Dislocation After Hip Replacement
summary: This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: prevention of prosthetic hip dislocation through positioning precautions in patients who have undergone hip replacement. The causal anchor is that hip replacement itself increases the risk of hip dislocation, because a man-made hip is smaller than the original joint, so the ball may easily come out of its socket. Two positioning precautions are named as preventive measures for patients after hip replacement during the recovery period: (1) avoidance of crossing the legs or ankles, specified as applying when sitting, standing, or lying down; and (2) avoidance of hip flexion greater than 90 degrees, which both applies to the hip replacement population and prevents dislocation during recovery. The 90-degree flexion limit is the only numeric threshold in the community; the leg-crossing precaution is the more positionally specific of the two, being explicitly extended across all three postures rather than a single activity. The only contributing guideline body is OpenRN (Nursing Skills, Tab 2, p763), so no cross-body agreement or disagreement can be characterised from this material; all four relations derive from one page of one source, meaning the theme is corroborated by a single authority rather than triangulated. Notably, the community does not establish a defined duration for the 'recovery period,' does not specify when precautions may be relaxed, and gives no follow-up or reassessment interval. It names no other precautions (for example nothing about abduction pillows, adduction limits, internal or external rotation limits, elevated seating, transfer technique, or weight-bearing status), no surgical approach distinctions (anterior versus posterior), and no drugs, doses, anticoagulation, or analgesia. It does not quantify dislocation incidence or risk reduction, identify patient-level risk modifiers (age, BMI, revision surgery, neuromuscular disease), or describe signs of dislocation, escalation pathways, or management once dislocation occurs. It also does not address perioperative gynecologic populations despite the wider corpus context, nor patient-education documentation or adherence monitoring.
key_entities: avoidance of crossing legs or ankles
avoidance of hip flexion greater than 90 degrees

title: Eating Disorder History in Nutritional Assessment
summary:
This community represents a narrow but clinically important theme: the significance of a documented history of anorexia nervosa or bulimia as a risk marker identified during nursing nutritional assessment. Both relations in the community originate from a single entity — history of anorexia or bulimia — and both apply to the same population and condition: clients undergoing nutritional assessment. No perioperative or gynecologic-specific qualifier is attached in these relations.

The two recommendations are: (1) a history of anorexia or bulimia increases the risk of body image disturbance, and (2) the same history increases the risk of vitamin, mineral, and electrolyte disturbance. The practical implication for a nurse educator is that eating disorder history should be elicited as part of routine nutritional assessment and should trigger attention to both a psychosocial domain (body image, self-perception) and a physiological domain (micronutrient and electrolyte status). Both risks are flagged with equal weight; the graph gives no priority ordering between them.

Only one guideline body contributes: OpenRN (Nursing Fundamentals/Management, Tome 2, p1015). Because the corpus contribution is single-source, there are no points of disagreement, no competing thresholds, and no instance of one body being more specific than another for this theme.

What this community does NOT establish is substantial. It names no specific laboratory tests, no numeric thresholds (for example, no potassium, magnesium, phosphate, albumin, prealbumin, BMI or weight-loss percentage cut-offs), and no timing for assessment or reassessment relative to surgery. It names no drugs, supplements, or repletion regimens, and no referral pathway (dietitian, psychiatry, eating disorder service). It does not distinguish anorexia nervosa from bulimia nervosa in terms of differing risk profiles, does not state whether the history must be active or remote, and does not address refeeding syndrome, perioperative fasting, anesthesia risk, wound healing, or gynecologic procedure–specific outcomes. Any local protocol built on this theme must draw thresholds and interventions from sources outside this community.

title: Preventing HIV transmission at delivery
summary:
This community represents the theme of preventing HIV transmission in the intrapartum/perinatal setting, and it operates on two complementary levels: protection of health care workers and infection-control practice on the one hand, and pharmacologic prevention of mother-to-child transmission on the other.

The first recommendation is that universal precautions be applied to prevent HIV transmission, with the population specified as health care workers at all deliveries — explicitly including deliveries involving mothers known to be HIV-positive. The framing is important for educators: precautions are not selectively applied to known-positive women but are used universally at every birth, so that unknown or unrecorded serostatus does not create a gap in protection.

The second recommendation is antiretroviral drug therapy to prevent HIV transmission, for women testing positive for HIV and their children. The stated conditions are that it be given in accordance with current treatment recommendations, and that extended prophylaxis to the infant be considered. Both mother and infant are therefore within scope, with the infant component described as an option to consider rather than a fixed requirement.

Only one guideline body contributes here: WHO (Tool 1, p31) is the source of both relations, so there is no cross-body agreement or disagreement to reconcile in this community. The two recommendations differ in specificity: the universal-precautions statement is unconditional and applies to all deliveries, whereas the antiretroviral statement deliberately defers detail to "current treatment recommendations."

What this community does not establish: it names no specific antiretroviral agents, doses, regimens, or routes; it gives no timing for initiation or duration of maternal therapy or of infant extended prophylaxis; it defines no CD4, viral load, or gestational-age thresholds; and it specifies no criteria for deciding when extended infant prophylaxis should be used. It also does not describe the content of universal precautions (barriers, sharps handling, post-exposure management), nor does it address HIV testing pathways, mode of delivery, or infant feeding. Local protocols and current WHO treatment guidance must supply these operational details.
key_entities: health care workers at all deliveries
women testing positive for HIV and their children

title: Blood Pressure Monitoring and Elevation Triggers
summary:
This community centres on detection and monitoring of elevated blood pressure, and on the iatrogenic and pharmacologic factors that raise it. Two guideline sources contribute: RNAO (Tab 2, pp. 35, 38, 59), which frames home/self blood pressure monitoring as a hypertension detection and surveillance tool, and OpenRN (Tab 2, p. 1293), which contributes a single procedural risk.

Main points: (1) Home blood pressure monitoring detects hypertension, but only when properly assessed (RNAO p35). (2) Home monitoring is used to monitor for elevated blood pressure, and readings should be checked more frequently in persons with diabetes and in clients having difficulty following a treatment plan (RNAO p38). (3) Elevated blood pressure increases risk of mortality when self/home values exceed 135/85 mmHg or clinic readings exceed 140/90 mmHg (RNAO p38) — note the deliberately lower home threshold versus the clinic threshold. (4) Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs increase the risk of elevated blood pressure, flagged specifically for clients taking over-the-counter medications, supplements or herbal remedies (RNAO p59), making medication reconciliation including OTC/herbal products a screening step. (5) Nasotracheal suctioning increases the risk of elevated blood pressure (OpenRN p1293), an acute procedural spike rather than chronic hypertension.

Divergence and specificity: RNAO is far more specific, supplying numeric thresholds, at-risk populations (diabetes, adherence difficulty) and monitoring frequency guidance; OpenRN contributes only an unqualified procedural risk with no population, threshold, or mitigation condition attached.

What this community does NOT establish: no antihypertensive drug regimens, doses, or titration; no specified monitoring intervals (only "more frequently"); no technique standard defining "properly assessed"; no NSAID agent names, doses, or duration of exposure; no guidance on suctioning technique, duration, or preoxygenation to prevent BP rise; no perioperative or gynecologic-specific thresholds; and no stated causal link between monitoring itself and improved mortality outcomes.
key_entities: clients having difficulty following a treatment plan
over-the-counter medications, supplements or herbal remedies

title: Discharge Education Preventing Hospital Readmission
summary:
This community centres on preventing hospital readmission and unplanned hospital visits after discharge through structured patient education and coordinated transitional care. Three interventions converge on the same outcome. First, ERAS Society (T1 p12) recommends post-operative patient education delivered in the postoperative phase, to patients before discharge; it prevents readmission specifically when combined with closer follow-up, and the guideline attaches the concrete estimate that 50% of readmissions are preventable. The same ERAS education, directed at patients and caregivers before discharge, also prevents unplanned hospital visits during the immediate post-discharge period — the only relation in this community that names caregivers explicitly and that separates unplanned visits from formal readmission. Second, OpenRN (T2 p788) is the most content-specific contributor: discharge education on home pain management for clients and families at discharge, on the condition that unmanaged pain at home may otherwise drive readmission. Third, RNAO (T2 p54) works at the system rather than teaching level, recommending a formal interprofessional cross-sectoral approach for adults transitioning from hospital to home or to a rehabilitation facility, with readmission within 30 days of discharge as the defined outcome window; RNAO itself flags that the evidence is inconsistent across studies.

Differences worth noting for QI planning: RNAO supplies the measurable threshold (30-day readmission) and the transition destinations (home, rehabilitation facility) but is candid about inconsistent evidence; ERAS supplies the quantified preventable fraction and the requirement for paired follow-up; OpenRN supplies the clinical topic (home pain management) and the family audience.

The community does not establish any drug, dose, analgesic regimen, or pain threshold; it does not specify education format, duration, timing intervals, or who delivers it; it does not define the composition of the interprofessional team or what "closer follow-up" entails. Nothing here is gynecologic- or procedure-specific, no preoperative or intraoperative phase links exist, and no relation quantifies effect size beyond the 50%-preventable estimate.
key_entities: discharge education on home pain management

title: Hand hygiene practices causing occupational dermatitis
summary:
This community centres on occupational skin damage (irritant/contact dermatitis) in health-care workers as an adverse consequence of hand hygiene practice — an important theme for perioperative nurses, who perform frequent antisepsis and surgical scrubbing. Three distinct exposures are linked to dermatitis risk. First, chlorhexidine gluconate: products containing 4% CHG increase dermatitis risk when used frequently for antiseptic handwashing (CDC). Second, handwashing with plain soap and water increases dermatitis risk in health-care workers specifically when performed after each use of an alcohol hand rub (CDC) — i.e. the practice of routinely 'double washing' after alcohol-based rub is discouraged on skin-tolerance grounds. Third, hot water increases dermatitis risk with repeated exposure during hand washing; this is asserted by both WHO (for hand washing generally) and CDC (twice, framed for 'health-care workers washing hands' and 'health-care personnel washing hands'), making avoidance of hot water the single most redundantly supported point in the community.

Contributing bodies are CDC (hand hygiene guideline, pages 10, 22, 34) and WHO (page 211). They agree fully on hot water: WHO states the risk as a general hand-washing condition, while CDC is slightly more specific in naming the exposed population (health-care workers/personnel). CDC alone contributes the two more granular, product- and sequence-specific risks — the 4% chlorhexidine gluconate concentration threshold and the alcohol-rub-then-soap-and-water sequence. No contradictions exist between the bodies here; the difference is one of specificity, with CDC supplying concentrations and behavioural sequences that WHO does not.

The community does not establish quantitative risk magnitudes, incidence rates, water-temperature thresholds in degrees, or a frequency threshold defining 'frequent' use. It offers no protective or mitigating interventions — no emollients, moisturisers, glove recommendations, alternative antiseptic concentrations, or lower-irritancy agents — and no diagnostic criteria, severity grading, or management pathway for established dermatitis. It also says nothing about antimicrobial efficacy trade-offs, patient outcomes, surgical-site infection, or whether dermatitis in turn reduces hand hygiene compliance.

title: Preventing HIV Transmission in Childbirth
summary:
This community centres on preventing HIV transmission in the perioperative/intrapartum and immediate newborn period, plus generic occupational and patient protection through universal precautions. The pivotal risk relation is that labour and delivery itself increases the risk of HIV transmission for pregnant women living with HIV, framing intrapartum care as the key window for intervention.

Recommendations, with their stated populations and conditions:
- Universal precautions prevent HIV transmission for both health-care workers and patients, applied whenever first aid or health care is administered (i.e., not restricted to known-positive patients).
