- Reinforcing recommended antenatal clinic visits prevents transmission in pregnant women with HIV, with the guideline specifically flagging high-risk management in the late third trimester.
- Avoiding unnecessary instrumentation prevents transmission in pregnant women with HIV during labour and delivery.
- For the newborn of a woman with HIV: non-invasive suction of nasogastric secretions, and washing away blood on the newborn, both prevent transmission.

Guideline contribution: all six relations derive from a single body, WHO (WHO T1). The occupational/universal precautions statement sits at p211, while the pregnancy-, labour- and newborn-specific measures cluster at p31. Because only one guideline body contributes, there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile; the differences are in granularity — p31 is population-specific (pregnant women with HIV, their newborns) and time-specific (late third trimester; during labour and delivery), whereas p211 is deliberately universal and condition-agnostic, applying regardless of known HIV status.

What this community does NOT establish: no antiretroviral drugs, regimens, doses, or maternal/infant prophylaxis schedules are named; no viral-load, CD4 or other numeric thresholds are given; no mode-of-delivery recommendation (e.g., caesarean vs vaginal) is specified; no guidance on infant feeding, cord clamping timing, episiotomy, membrane rupture duration, or post-exposure prophylaxis after occupational exposure appears. It also does not define what counts as 'unnecessary' instrumentation, quantify the effect size of any measure, specify HIV testing or retesting protocols, or address transmission routes other than perinatal and health-care contact.
key_entities: washing away blood in the newborn
pregnant women with human immunodeficiency virus
newborn of women with human immunodeficiency virus

title: ARV Therapy Preventing Breastfeeding HIV Transmission
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: the use of antiretroviral (ARV) medicines to prevent mother-to-child transmission of HIV through breastfeeding. Both relations in the community converge on the same outcome entity — HIV transmission through breastfeeding — and identify two distinct pharmacological strategies for preventing it.

The recommendations are: (1) lifelong antiretroviral therapy prevents HIV transmission through breastfeeding, and (2) antiretroviral prophylaxis prevents HIV transmission through breastfeeding. For both, the population is explicitly the same: mothers known to be HIV-infected. For both, the attached condition is identical: the intervention must be provided according to WHO recommendations. The distinction the graph draws is therefore between sustained, lifelong maternal treatment and a prophylactic ARV course, offered as alternative routes to the same preventive endpoint for the same population.

Only one guideline body contributes here: WHO (WHO T1, p32). Because the community is single-sourced, there are no inter-body disagreements, no competing thresholds, and no points where one organisation is more specific than another. The two relations are equally specific and mutually consistent, differing only in the ARV strategy named.

What the community does NOT establish is substantial and should be flagged in any teaching or QI use. It names no specific ARV drugs, regimens, doses, or drug classes. It gives no timings — no gestational or postpartum start point, no duration of prophylaxis, and no defined breastfeeding duration or weaning point. It sets no laboratory thresholds (no CD4 count, viral load, or maternal clinical staging criteria) to decide between lifelong therapy and prophylaxis. It does not state whether the prophylaxis is maternal or infant, nor does it compare the effectiveness of the two strategies against each other. It also says nothing about mothers of unknown or negative HIV status, about replacement feeding alternatives, or about perioperative or intrapartum management. Users must consult the full WHO source for the actual regimens and eligibility criteria.
key_entities: human immunodeficiency virus transmission through breastfeeding

title: Surgical Wound Dressings for SSI Prevention
summary:
This community covers postoperative surgical wound dressing selection, centred on sterile dressings as a barrier against surgical site infection (SSI) and on dressing choices for incisions managed by delayed primary closure. Two distinct clinical situations are represented: (1) primarily closed incisions, and (2) incisions deliberately left open at the skin level for a few days before closure.

Main recommendations: For incisions closed primarily, a sterile dressing should be maintained over the wound to prevent SSI for 24-48 hours postoperatively (CDC T1 p21; WHO T1 p68 states the same 24-48 hour window). For delayed primary closure, three options are attached to the same population/condition - the incision left open at skin level for a few days before closure: sterile dressing, sterile moist gauze packing, and hydrofiber dressing (WHO T1 p55). Hydrofiber dressing carries an additional, exudate-specific indication: in wounds with large amounts of exudate it prevents maceration of surrounding tissue (OpenRN T2 p1145).

Contributing bodies: WHO (T1 pp. 55, 68) is the broadest contributor, covering both the 24-48 hour sterile dressing recommendation and the full menu of delayed primary closure dressings. CDC (T1 p21) converges with WHO on timing but is more specific about population, explicitly limiting the recommendation to incisions closed primarily. OpenRN (T2 p1145) contributes the only wound-characteristic-based criterion (large exudate volume) and the only non-infection outcome (maceration prevention). There is no contradiction between the sources; the difference is one of scope and specificity rather than conflict.

What this community does NOT establish: it gives no preference ranking or comparative effectiveness among sterile dressing, sterile moist gauze packing, and hydrofiber dressing for delayed primary closure; no dressing change frequency, technique, or duration beyond the 24-48 hour figure; no guidance on what to do after 48 hours; no gynecologic- or procedure-specific populations, no antimicrobial or antiseptic dressing agents, no drugs, and no exudate volume threshold defining "large amounts".

title: Hyperkalemia: Drug Risks, Monitoring, Treatment
summary:
This community centres on hyperkalemia as a medication- and disease-related electrolyte risk, spanning causation, laboratory surveillance, and escalating treatment. Causative factors named are potassium-sparing diuretics (amiloride, triamterene, spironolactone), ACE inhibitors, oral or intravenous potassium supplements, kidney failure, and metabolic acidosis. The same potassium-sparing agents are also framed protectively: RNAO states they prevent hypokalemia in clients treated with diuretics for hypertension and specifically in patients already on thiazide diuretics — a deliberate dual-edged message (prevents hypokalemia while increasing hyperkalemia risk) that educators should teach together rather than separately.

Monitoring recommendations are population-specific. RNAO directs bloodwork for sodium, potassium and creatinine in clients taking ACE inhibitors (p128), and potassium plus creatinine monitoring for ACE-inhibitor clients on p141; potassium monitoring is specified for clients using potassium-sparing diuretics (amiloride, triamterene, spironolactone).

Treatment, from OpenRN, is graded by severity: decreased dietary potassium intake for mild symptoms; sodium polystyrene sulfonate orally or rectally for severe symptoms; insulin to help decrease potassium in clients with hyperkalemia or a patient with elevated potassium; and hemodialysis for severe symptomatic hyperkalemia as temporary use to lower potassium quickly. A key preventive nursing action is stopping any potassium contained in IV fluids in a patient with elevated potassium. WHO contributes only that insulin increases risk of an adverse drug event — a high-alert-medication caution that should accompany its use as a potassium-lowering therapy.

Contributors differ in emphasis: RNAO is more specific about who to monitor and which analytes to draw (antihypertensive-treated clients, thiazide co-therapy), OpenRN is more specific about treatment sequencing and severity triggers, and WHO addresses only medication-safety risk.

Not established: any numeric potassium threshold, ECG criteria, monitoring frequency or timing intervals, dosing of insulin/dextrose, calcium or bicarbonate therapy, and any perioperative or gynecologic-surgery-specific application. No relations address pregnancy, anesthesia timing, or which clinician acts, and no evidence grades or strength-of-recommendation levels are attached.
key_entities: bloodwork monitoring of sodium, potassium and creatinine

title: Rare Alcohol Hand Rub Hypersensitivity Reactions
summary: This small community represents a single, narrowly scoped safety theme in hand hygiene practice: true hypersensitivity to alcohol itself, or to additives (e.g., fragrances, emollients, preservatives) present in alcohol-based hand rubs, as a cause of adverse skin reactions in health care personnel. Two relations, both drawn from CDC Table 1, p10, link this hypersensitivity to two distinct outcomes: contact urticaria syndrome (an immediate, IgE-type reaction) and allergic contact dermatitis (a delayed, type IV reaction). Both relations carry the same explicit qualifying condition — these reactions 'occur only rarely.' The practical takeaway for perioperative nurse educators is therefore twofold: alcohol-based hand rub remains the expected product, and genuine allergy is an uncommon explanation for skin complaints; but when a worker reports hives/wheals immediately after application, or eczematous, delayed-onset dermatitis, hypersensitivity to alcohol or an additive should be considered and the specific product formulation reviewed. Only one guideline body contributes here — the CDC — so no inter-guideline disagreement or difference in specificity can be demonstrated within this community; there are no competing WHO, AORN, or professional-society statements represented, and no cross-body corroboration of the 'rarely' qualifier. Importantly, the community does NOT establish: any named population beyond the implicit user of alcohol hand rubs (no perioperative-specific, pregnant, pediatric, or atopic subgroup is specified); any numeric incidence, prevalence, or threshold for 'rarely'; any timing of onset for either reaction; any named culprit alcohol (ethanol, isopropanol, n-propanol) or named additive; any diagnostic pathway such as patch or prick testing; any management, substitution, or work-restriction recommendation; and any comparison with the far more common irritant contact dermatitis or with soap-and-water handwashing. It also does not link these reactions to surgical hand antisepsis practice, glove use, or infection outcomes. Educators should treat this as an awareness/differential-diagnosis point rather than an actionable protocol, and seek additional guideline sections for product selection, skin-care programs, and occupational health follow-up.
key_entities: hypersensitivity to alcohol or additives in alcohol hand rubs

title: Hypertension Detection, Lifestyle and Drug Management
summary: This community centres on hypertension across the perioperative/peripartum continuum: its detection, lifestyle and pharmacological treatment, risk factors, and limb-specific measurement cautions. Detection: blood pressure measurement detects hypertension in all adults at all appropriate visits (RNAO T2 p16, p30), with diagnosis based on an average of two or more readings on two or more occasions (OpenRN T2 p178). Office measurement remains the 'gold standard'; home and ambulatory monitoring also detect hypertension when properly assessed (RNAO T2 p35). Self/home monitoring requires educated clients and validated, properly calibrated equipment (RNAO T2 p16, p37). Ongoing monitoring should also cover client engagement, general health status and medication side effects (RNAO T2 p70). WHO adds a postpartum timing: BP shortly after birth, repeated within six hours if normal (WHO T1 p23). Treatment: lifestyle interventions treat and possibly prevent hypertension and, when optimal BP is achieved, prevent heart attack and stroke (RNAO T2 p27, p41, p51, p70). Specific targets: DASH diet; sodium 65-100 mmol/day with dietitian collaboration; weight reduction of -4.5 kg; alcohol reduction of -2.7 drinks/day; exercise 3 times/week; BMI 18.5-24.9 kg/m2; waist circumference below 102 cm (men)/88 cm (women) (RNAO T2 p16, p42, p43, p45). BMI >30, weight gain (per 4.5 kg), increased waist circumference, and cocaine, marijuana, amphetamine and MDMA increase risk (RNAO T2 p45, p59, p119). Exercise training's effect persists only while training continues. Pharmacology: ACE inhibitors first line for diabetes, post-MI, systolic dysfunction, renal disease; ARBs first line if ACE inhibitors are not tolerated (RNAO T2 p128); vigorous antihypertensive therapy plus combination pharmacological-lifestyle therapy for most clients (p59); nurse-delivered home/clinic interventions treat hypertension (p59). WHO advises continuing antenatal antihypertensives postpartum (T1 p29). Obstetric caution: RCOG contraindicates ergometrine and ergometrine-oxytocin in hypertension (T1 p25, p3), and WHO notes ergometrine raises BP when used for PPH prevention (T1 p26). Procedural cautions: avoid BP measurement in an arm with prior mastectomy or fistula (OpenRN T2 p190) and venipuncture in a lumpectomy/mastectomy extremity (p1329). Not established: BP diagnostic thresholds, specific drug doses, target BP values, preeclampsia/gestational hypertension pathways, or intraoperative hypertension management.

title: Ergot Uterotonics for Postpartum Haemorrhage
summary:
This community covers ergot-alkaloid uterotonics — ergometrine, methylergometrine, and the fixed oxytocin/ergometrine combination — as second-line agents for preventing and treating postpartum haemorrhage (PPH), plus their contraindications and adjuncts.

Prevention (WHO): for women undergoing vaginal birth or caesarean section, ergometrine 200 µg IM/IV, or the fixed combination 5 IU/500 µg IM, may be used as the single uterotonic for PPH prevention in settings where oxytocin is unavailable or its quality cannot be guaranteed; methylergometrine is likewise an option in such settings 'if appropriate'. All are conditional on hypertensive disorders being safely excluded beforehand; the combination is also credited with preventing severe PPH versus placebo/no uterotonic. WHO adds a practical caveat: these agents are temporarily unsuitable where the heat-sensitive drug has been transported/stored under the same compromised cold-chain conditions as the suspect oxytocin. Screening for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy detects such disorders in women who may receive ergometrine/methylergometrine, where screening capacity exists.

Treatment: WHO recommends ergometrine or the fixed combination when IV oxytocin is unavailable or bleeding does not respond to oxytocin. RCOG is more specific on dosing — ergometrine 0.5 mg by slow IV or IM for women with PPH, including major PPH, with oxytocin preferred initially and ergometrine used alongside it; contraindicated in women with hypertension. For secondary PPH, RCOG notes ergometrine and misoprostol have limited supporting evidence, and lists balloon tamponade and transcatheter arterial embolisation for ongoing bleeding.

Safety: ergometrine increases risk of hypertension, nausea, vomiting, headache and abdominal pain when used for PPH prevention; the fixed combination increases nausea and vomiting. In retained placenta, ergometrine is contraindicated because it may cause tetanic uterine contraction and delay placental expulsion.

Not established: no comparative efficacy ranking against oxytocin (benefit only 'assumed similar'), no dosing for methylergometrine or for prevention timing, no blood-pressure thresholds defining the contraindication, no paediatric/anaemia or other population qualifiers, and no evidence base for ergometrine or misoprostol in secondary PPH.
key_entities: fixed drug combination of oxytocin and ergometrine
screening for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

title: Perioperative temperature monitoring and thermal management
summary:
This community centres on perioperative thermoregulation: detecting and treating abnormal body temperature, plus the overlapping analgesic/antipyretic role of ibuprofen and acetaminophen.

Monitoring: WHO (T1 p25) recommends body temperature measurement to detect BOTH hyperthermia and hypothermia, at frequent intervals where clinically indicated — explicitly citing prolonged operations and young children as triggers. The ERAS Society (T1 p1) frames temperature monitoring functionally rather than by patient group: monitoring is used to titrate warming devices (hypothermia) and to guide warming therapy (hyperthermia). WHO is more specific about who and when to monitor; ERAS is more specific about the purpose — closing the loop between measurement and active warming intervention.

Treatment of hyperthermia: OpenRN (T2 p663) supports three interventions for clients with fever/hyperthermia — ibuprofen 'as appropriate', acetaminophen 'as appropriate', and external cooling 'as needed'. No doses, routes, temperature thresholds or intervals are given; the conditions are left to nursing judgement.

Analgesia overlap: NICE (T1 p13) recommends ibuprofen for postoperative pain in adults having surgery, including dental surgery, for immediate postoperative pain of all severities, with one explicit exclusion — patients who have had surgery for hip fracture. Ibuprofen is therefore the bridging entity between the antipyretic and analgesic strands; educators should note the differing populations (febrile clients generally vs. adult postoperative patients) and that only NICE states a contraindication.

What this community does NOT establish: no numeric temperature thresholds defining hyperthermia or hypothermia; no doses, routes, frequencies or maximum daily limits for ibuprofen or acetaminophen; no named warming devices or specified external cooling methods; no monitoring-interval numbers (only 'frequent... where clinically indicated'); no gynecologic- or pregnancy-specific guidance; no treatment pathway for hypothermia beyond implied warming therapy; no evidence grades, no malignant hyperthermia pathway, and no statement that acetaminophen treats postoperative pain.

title: Preoperative carbohydrate loading and metabolic optimization
summary:
This community centers on preoperative metabolic conditioning — chiefly oral carbohydrate loading — within ERAS-style gynecologic and urogynecologic pathways, plus the modifiable risk factor of alcohol abuse and the high-risk surgical populations in which these measures matter most.

Core recommendations: Carbohydrate loading is a preoperative-phase intervention, given as clear fluids including oral carbohydrate drinks up until 2 hours before initiation of anesthesia (AUGS). AUGS is the more specific on dose and population, recommending routine use of a ≤ 50-g clear liquid carbohydrate drink for patients undergoing urogynecologic surgery, while explicitly noting this is extrapolated from non-gynecological surgery data. The ERAS Society frames the benefit mechanistically: routine oral carbohydrate loading before major abdominal surgery prevents/attenuates postoperative insulin resistance, and preoperative carbohydrate treatment has this effect in patients undergoing abdominal, orthopedic and cardiac surgery. For the highest-acuity gynecologic oncology populations — patients undergoing total pelvic exenteration or hyperthermic intra-peritoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC) — ERAS states carbohydrate loading "should be considered," as it may attenuate increased insulin resistance; these procedures are themselves flagged as risk-elevating (total pelvic exenteration increases postoperative morbidity in gynecologic oncology patients; HIPEC increases perioperative morbidity in patients with gynecologic cancer). ERAS also identifies alcohol abuse as increasing both perioperative mortality and perioperative morbidity.

Contributing bodies: ERAS Society (T1) supplies the physiologic rationale, the oncologic/high-risk populations, and the alcohol risk signal; AUGS (T2) supplies the concrete threshold (≤ 50 g), the 2-hour clear-fluid cutoff, and the urogynecologic population. They do not conflict; AUGS is more prescriptive on dose and timing, ERAS more explicit about conditional ("should be considered") use in exenteration/HIPEC and about evidence in non-gynecologic surgery.

Not established here: no alcohol cessation protocol, duration, or screening tool; no guidance for diabetic patients, gastroparesis, or aspiration risk; no specified carbohydrate product, concentration, or volume beyond ≤ 50 g; no timing rule for the oncology populations; no stated effect of carbohydrate loading on morbidity, mortality, length of stay, or infection; and no link between alcohol abuse and insulin resistance or carbohydrate loading.

title: Fibrinogen replacement in postpartum haemorrhage
summary:
This community centres on fibrinogen monitoring and replacement during ongoing postpartum haemorrhage (PPH), linking hypofibrinogenaemia to bleeding progression and naming two replacement products: cryoprecipitate and fibrinogen concentrate.

Rationale: in women with PPH, hypofibrinogenaemia increases the risk of progression of bleeding, with risk flagged when fibrinogen falls below 3 g/l and especially below 2 g/l (RCOG T1 p21). This makes fibrinogen a distinct laboratory trigger rather than something inferred from routine clotting screens.

Recommendations by population and condition:
- Cryoprecipitate treats PPH in women with postpartum haemorrhage when haemorrhage is ongoing and fibrinogen is less than 2 g/l (RCOG T1 p16).
- Cryoprecipitate treats PPH empirically in women who have received 8 or more units of red blood cells and continue to bleed, in rare cases of massive bleeding when no coagulation results or platelet counts are available (RCOG T1 p20) — i.e. a fallback when laboratory data cannot guide therapy.
- Both cryoprecipitate and fibrinogen concentrate treat hypofibrinogenaemia in women with continuing PPH, with the stated goal of maintaining fibrinogen at least 2 g/l, even if PT and APTT are normal (RCOG T1 p21). The explicit "even if PT/APTT are normal" caveat is an important teaching point: normal PT/APTT does not exclude a clinically significant fibrinogen deficit.

Contributing bodies: all relations derive from a single guideline source, RCOG (Tranche 1, pages 16, 20, 21). There is therefore no inter-organisational disagreement captured here; the only variation is in specificity, where p21 gives the target level and the PT/APTT caveat, p16 gives the treatment trigger (<2 g/l with ongoing bleeding), and p20 covers the no-results massive transfusion scenario.

Not established: doses, volumes or units of cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate; infusion timing or repeat intervals; any preference between cryoprecipitate and fibrinogen concentrate; frequency of fibrinogen re-testing; neonatal, antepartum or non-obstetric populations; and any nursing administration, monitoring or adverse-effect guidance.
key_entities: red blood cell transfusion (8 or more units)

title: Diuretic-Induced Electrolyte Imbalance and Alkalosis
summary:
This community centers on diuretic-associated electrolyte disturbances — chiefly hypokalemia and hyponatremia — and their downstream acid-base consequence, metabolic alkalosis. Two guideline bodies contribute: RNAO (Tool 2, pp. 127, 140) frames risk and prevention in hypertension management, while OpenRN (Tool 2, pp. 895, 1093, 1111) supplies medication-administration safety checks and alkalosis management.

Risk: thiazide diuretics increase the risk of both hypokalemia and hyponatremia in patients treated with thiazides (RNAO p140). Hypokalemia in turn increases the risk of metabolic alkalosis when hydrogen ions shift into cells as potassium shifts out (OpenRN p1093).

Prevention and monitoring: potassium-sparing diuretics prevent hypokalemia both in clients treated with diuretics for hypertension (RNAO p127) and specifically in patients on thiazide diuretics (RNAO p140). RNAO p127 is the most specific on surveillance timing: bloodwork monitoring for hypokalemia every 6–12 months for clients on diuretic therapy for hypertension. OpenRN p1111 recommends monitoring for electrolyte imbalance — both hypokalemia and hyponatremia — in clients receiving diuretic therapy, but without a stated interval; RNAO names an interval but only for potassium, not sodium.

Point-of-administration safety (OpenRN p895): review the laboratory potassium level before administering a diuretic such as furosemide to detect hypokalemia; if the potassium level is lower than normal range, furosemide is temporarily contraindicated until the provider is notified.

Metabolic alkalosis management (OpenRN p1093), guided by ABG results and the suspected cause: stop gastrointestinal suctioning, stop diuretic administration, stop bicarbonate administration if bicarbonate is being administered, and dialysis for clients with kidney disease.

Not established: no numeric potassium or sodium thresholds, no named potassium-sparing agent, no dosing or potassium-replacement regimens, no monitoring interval for hyponatremia, and no explicit perioperative or gynecologic-surgery-specific guidance. The community also does not address hyperkalemia, other diuretic classes beyond thiazides and furosemide, or outcomes of the recommended interventions.

title: Perioperative Hypotension: Causes, Fluids, Vasopressors
summary: This community centres on recognition, causation and treatment of hypotension/hypovolemia and shock in perioperative and obstetric care. Iatrogenic and clinical causes are well represented: anesthetic drugs cause hypotension via arteriolar and venous dilatation in surgical patients (ERAS Society); intravenous oxytocin causes dose-related hypotension at caesarean section (WHO); magnesium sulfate in women with sepsis warrants additional monitoring (RCOG); hypotonic IV solutions can precipitate hypotension, hypovolemia and cerebral edema if too much fluid shifts intracellularly, although they legitimately treat cellular dehydration in DKA/hyperosmolar hyperglycemia (OpenRN); diuretics with excessive use and severe bleeding cause hypovolemia; nasotracheal suctioning also risks hypotension. Treatment recommendations: crystalloid fluid resuscitation for sepsis-related hypotension or lactate ≥4 mmol/L — RCOG specifies both rapid 30 ml/kg and an early 500 ml bolus that may need repeating; vasopressors for sepsis when hypotension persists during/after fluid resuscitation, targeting MAP ≥65 mmHg (RCOG), postoperatively if required, and once intravascular volume is normalised during surgery to maintain MAP and thereby prevent fluid excess (ERAS Society); NICE endorses peripheral vasopressor for septic shock/hypotension in people at high risk of severe illness or death from sepsis when fluids are not working, and is uniquely explicit that peripheral administration risks extravasation, influenced by cannula dwell time, dose and concentration. Epinephrine treats hypotension and vasodilation in anaphylaxis after allergen elimination (WHO). Monitoring: vital signs before cardiac/blood pressure medication, with blood pressure medication temporarily withheld if systolic <100 per MAR parameters; close monitoring of clients on hypotonic solutions or 5% dextrose in water; blood pressure and heart rate re-evaluated for return to normal within eight hours after IV fluid; mental status monitoring for septic shock, especially older adults. RCOG links major postpartum haemorrhage hypotension to postpartum hypopituitarism, detected by screening. Not established: choice between specific vasopressor agents, crystalloid type, reconciliation of RCOG's 30 ml/kg versus 500 ml bolus approaches, extravasation management, or outcome evidence for any strategy.

title: Perioperative normothermia maintenance and temperature monitoring
summary:
This community centres on preventing perioperative hypothermia and the monitoring needed to detect it. Hypothermia is framed as a modifiable harm: ERAS Society links it to bleeding, wound infection and cardiac morbidity, while WHO specifies hypocoagulation and infection in patients under anaesthesia. ERAS also identifies the mechanism of risk — anaesthesia plus major surgery causes hypothermia through exposure and impairment of normal thermoregulatory response.

Recommendations cluster around active warming. ERAS Society advises routine use of an active warming device to maintain normothermia intraoperatively, with named modalities: forced air blanket devices during surgery, underbody warming mattresses (particularly useful in robotic surgery or wherever a blanket would interfere with surgical access), prewarming to avoid the initial drop in body temperature, and warming of intravenous fluids using a suitable device. AUGS concurs, recommending active warming for adult surgical patients maintained throughout the intraoperative phase. WHO recommends a patient warming device for surgical patients. RCOG contributes a distinct population: keeping the woman warm to prevent hypothermia in women with postpartum haemorrhage.

Monitoring is the paired intervention. WHO recommends body temperature measurement at frequent intervals where clinically indicated — explicitly citing prolonged operations and young children. ERAS frames temperature monitoring functionally, as the means to titrate warming devices. Separately, ERAS recommends advanced hemodynamic monitoring in the perioperative phase for high-risk patients with large blood loss (>7 ml/kg) or a SIRS response undergoing major open surgery, to individualise fluid therapy and optimise oxygen delivery.

Bodies are complementary rather than conflicting: ERAS is most granular on device selection and surgical-access trade-offs; WHO is most specific on when to measure temperature; AUGS specifies the duration and adult population; RCOG extends the principle to obstetric haemorrhage.

Not established here: any numeric temperature target or threshold defining hypothermia, timing or duration of prewarming, fluid or blanket temperature settings, monitoring site (core vs peripheral), specific frequency intervals, paediatric or postoperative-phase protocols, comparative effectiveness between forced air and underbody devices, or drug-based warming adjuncts.

title: Hypovolaemia recognition, resuscitation, and respiratory failure risk
summary:
This community covers perioperative circulatory-volume management and its overlap with acute respiratory failure. The dominant thread (WHO Surgical Safety guidance, T1 pp41-42) is that hypovolaemia in surgical patients increases the risk of avoidable mortality and morbidity, so it must be identified early: identification of hypovolaemia detects current or potential volume depletion in surgical patients. Named precipitants are preoperative dehydration, sepsis and spinal cord injury — the latter two through vasodilation producing a relative hypovolaemic state. Treatment recommendations for hypovolaemic patients include fluid resuscitation during definitive intervention, crystalloid solution for patients with fluid deficits, volume resuscitation for patients with haemorrhage coupled with surgery to stem the bleeding, and control of haemorrhage, which WHO stresses must be paired with a resuscitation plan. Prevention is explicitly timed: intravenous access placement belongs in the preoperative phase, before skin incision, whenever loss of a large volume of blood is expected or is a major risk. Ongoing monitoring of fluid status should occur wherever feasible and be tailored to the clinical situation in volume-depleted surgical patients, using urinary catheterization and central venous cannulation as situation-dependent adjuncts.

A second, smaller thread from OpenRN (T2) addresses acute respiratory failure, listing pneumonia, stroke, spinal cord injury and opioid overdose as risk factors, and naloxone as the treatment for opioid overdose in women and the elderly who are found unresponsive. Spinal cord injury is the only entity bridging the two threads.

Contributors differ in specificity: WHO is granular about volume status — fluid types, timing relative to skin incision, and monitoring modalities — while OpenRN contributes aetiological lists and one drug indication without dosing or route. Notably, the community establishes no numeric thresholds (no blood loss volumes, urine output targets, CVP values, naloxone doses or repeat intervals), no gynecologic- or obstetric-specific populations, no crystalloid-versus-colloid comparison, and no explicit link between hypovolaemia and respiratory failure or airway management.

title: Preventing Hypovolaemic Shock from Major Blood Loss
summary:
This community represents the theme of anticipating and preventing hypovolaemic shock in surgical patients at risk of major intraoperative blood loss, and it centres on securing adequate vascular access before the operation begins. The single causal relation is that major blood loss increases the risk of hypovolaemic shock in surgical patients, with the guideline attaching a concrete threshold: blood loss exceeding 500 ml, or 7 ml/kg in children. This paediatric weight-based qualifier is the only population-specific refinement in the community and is important for educators teaching that a volume that seems modest in an adult may be catastrophic in a child.

Two preventive interventions are recommended, both for surgical patients and both under the same condition: where there is a significant risk of greater than 500 ml blood loss, access should be established prior to skin incision. The named options are (1) a large bore intravenous line and (2) a central venous catheter. Timing is explicit and clinically actionable for perioperative nursing checklists and briefings: access is a pre-incision task, not a rescue measure.

All three relations derive from a single guideline body, the WHO (WHO T1, p108); no other body contributes here, so there are no inter-guideline conflicts or differences in specificity to reconcile within this community. The WHO source is more specific about thresholds (500 ml; 7 ml/kg paediatric) than about how to choose between access routes.

What this community does NOT establish: it does not state a preference or selection criteria between a large bore intravenous line and a central venous catheter, nor gauge size, catheter site, or number of lines. It specifies no fluid or blood product regimen (no crystalloid, colloid, tranexamic acid, or transfusion trigger), no monitoring parameters or shock recognition criteria, no estimated blood loss measurement method, no gynecologic-procedure-specific risk stratification, and no post-incision or postoperative escalation pathway. It also gives no operational definition of "significant risk."

title: Hypoxia detection and prevention perioperatively
summary:
This community centres on hypoxia — its risk factors, monitoring, detection and prevention — across the intraoperative and postoperative course, with hypercapnia and delirium as linked concerns. Hypoxia is framed as a driver of harm: it increases the risk of delirium (OpenRN T2 p451). Two risk contributors are named: obstructive sleep apnea, in patients/clients with OSA while sleeping or when unable to maintain an open airway while sleeping (OpenRN T2 p545, p653), and fibre-optic intubation (WHO T1 p36).

WHO (Tier 1) supplies the anaesthesia monitoring recommendations: pulse oximetry continuously during surgery and for all patients undergoing anaesthesia, functioning both as detection and as a secondary safeguard against hypoxia (WHO T1 pp22, 25); capnography for patients undergoing anaesthesia (p22); inspired oxygen concentration monitoring throughout anaesthesia using an instrument fitted with a low-oxygen concentration alarm, the alarm itself being preventive (p31); continuous monitoring with careful planning (p25); and adequate illumination and exposure of the patient so the lips or nail beds can be observed (p25).

OpenRN (Tier 2) contributes bedside nursing assessment and procedural safeguards: assessment of level of consciousness detects hypoxia when excessive drowsiness, restlessness or irritability is present, and as part of respiratory assessment with the patient seated if tolerated — the same assessment also detects hypercapnia (pp562, 638); continuous pulse oximetry while the patient is sleeping for patients with suspected OSA (p653); and limiting tracheostomy suctioning to no longer than 15 seconds at a time (p1307).

The bodies are complementary rather than conflicting: WHO is more specific about equipment and alarms during anaesthesia, OpenRN about sleep-related OSA screening, neurological signs, and the 15-second suction threshold.

Not established: no oxygen saturation or PaCO2 numeric thresholds, no FiO2 targets, no oxygen delivery devices, drugs, or escalation/rescue algorithms; no gynecologic-specific populations; no stated frequency for consciousness assessment; and no evidence that any single monitor eliminates hypoxia or that preventing hypoxia prevents delirium.
key_entities: adequate illumination and exposure of the patient
limiting suction to 15 seconds at a time

title: Hysterectomy Prophylaxis and PPH Uterus-Sparing Measures
summary:
This community links two converging threads: infection prevention for hysterectomy/vaginal surgery, and uterus-sparing management of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) where hysterectomy is the outcome to be avoided.

Infection prevention: WHO (T1 p60) and AUGS (T2 p6) both attach antibiotic/antimicrobial prophylaxis to hysterectomy, with AUGS specifying the population as women undergoing hysterectomy. ERAS Society (T1 p6) is the most specific on agent and dosing — a first generation cephalosporin, with weight-based dosing. AUGS (T2 p14) adds preoperative vaginal cleansing with chlorhexidine gluconate or povidone-iodine before hysterectomy or vaginal surgery (explicitly a preoperative-phase intervention), and states it prevents surgical site infection in patients undergoing vaginal surgery, using a 4% aqueous solution.

PPH and hysterectomy avoidance (RCOG T1, WHO T1): Balloon tamponade treats PPH in women with PPH — WHO frames it as a means to potentially avoid surgery or as a temporizing measure while awaiting transfer to a higher-level facility; RCOG frames it as PPH treatment in combination with haemostatic suturing, as treatment for secondary PPH with ongoing bleeding, and as preventing hysterectomy. RCOG uniquely uses it diagnostically: a 'negative test' (continued PPH after balloon inflation) detects PPH requiring laparotomy. Haemostatic brace suture treats severe PPH and prevents hysterectomy. RCOG identifies three risk factors for proceeding to hysterectomy in women treated with a uterine compression suture for PPH: increasing age, vaginal delivery, and prolonged delay between delivery and suture placement (2–6 hours). AUGS separately links increasing age to small bowel obstruction.

Not established: no antibiotic timing, redosing interval, or specific dose/weight threshold; no balloon type, inflation volume, or dwell time; no comparative effectiveness of balloon versus brace suture; no sequencing rule between vaginal cleansing and antibiotics; no evidence that vaginal cleansing prevents infection after abdominal hysterectomy specifically; and no quantified hysterectomy risk for age or vaginal delivery.
key_entities: vaginal cleansing with chlorhexidine gluconate or povidone-iodine

title: Positioning Measures Preventing Perioperative Iatrogenic Neuropathy
summary:
This community is a narrowly focused, single-source theme on intraoperative positioning as a means of preventing iatrogenic (positioning-related) nerve injury in gynecologic surgery. It contains two preventive relations, both drawn from AUGS Table 2, p7: (1) padding of bony prominences prevents iatrogenic neuropathy, and (2) anatomic positioning of the lower extremities prevents iatrogenic neuropathy. Practically, this frames neuropathy prevention as a nursing-controllable, mechanical intervention bundle — protecting pressure points where nerves lie superficially over bone, and keeping the legs in neutral, physiologic alignment rather than in extremes of flexion, abduction, or external rotation.

Only one guideline body contributes here: AUGS (American Urogynecologic Society), via its Table 2 summary at p7. Because there is no second contributing body, the graph shows no points of agreement, disagreement, or differing levels of specificity between organizations; AUGS is by default the most specific and the only source. Both relations are stated as unqualified preventive statements — the graph attaches no restricting population beyond the perioperative gynecologic surgical context of the corpus, and no conditional trigger such as case length, lithotomy versus supine positioning, BMI, diabetes, or pre-existing neuropathy.

What this community does NOT establish: it names no specific padding materials, devices, or stirrup types; no thresholds for degrees of hip flexion, abduction, or knee angle; no time limits for operative duration or intervals for repositioning; no documentation, handoff, or assessment requirements; and no postoperative surveillance or escalation pathway if numbness, weakness, or foot drop appears. It does not identify which nerves are at risk (e.g., common peroneal, femoral, obturator, brachial plexus), does not quantify effect size or incidence reduction, and cites no drugs or pharmacologic adjuncts. It also does not address other positioning harms such as pressure injury, compartment syndrome, or venous stasis. Educators should therefore treat this as a high-level principle requiring locally developed procedural detail and competency criteria.

title: Preventing Postoperative Ileus After Gynecologic Surgery
summary:
This community centers on postoperative ileus as a shared adverse outcome in gynecologic perioperative care, its two named risk drivers (opioid analgesia and fluid volume overload), and a bundle of five preventive measures. Two guideline bodies contribute risk relations: the ERAS Society states that opioid analgesics increase the risk of ileus (no population or condition qualifier attached), and AUGS states that fluid volume overload increases ileus risk specifically in the geriatric population. OpenRN contributes the parallel opioid safety concern, linking opioid analgesics to respiratory depression in clients treated with opioids — the only non-ileus outcome in the community and the only one framed as a monitoring/safety issue rather than a bowel-function issue.

AUGS supplies all five preventive recommendations, clustered on a single guideline page: early feeding, opioid-sparing analgesia, euvolemia, drinking coffee, and gum chewing all prevent ileus. Notably, the AUGS prevention statements carry no population or condition restrictions, so they are stated as general recommendations even though the same body's fluid-overload risk statement is narrowed to geriatric clients. The preventive set mirrors the risk set: opioid-sparing analgesia counters the ERAS opioid–ileus link, and euvolemia counters the AUGS fluid-overload link, giving educators a clean risk-to-countermeasure pairing for teaching.

Differences in specificity: AUGS is the more granular source, naming discrete interventions (coffee, gum chewing) and one at-risk population (geriatric); ERAS contributes only the broad opioid–ileus association; OpenRN is the only source addressing respiratory depression surveillance.

What this community does not establish: no drug names beyond the generic class "opioid analgesic"; no doses, opioid-sparing agents, or alternative analgesics; no timing for early feeding, no coffee or gum-chewing quantities, frequencies, or start times; no fluid-volume thresholds or euvolemia targets; no age cutoff defining "geriatric"; no effect sizes, evidence grades, or monitoring parameters for respiratory depression; and no relation between ileus and respiratory depression themselves.

title: Imaging for Suspected Iliac Vein Thrombosis
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused diagnostic theme: the imaging modalities used to confirm or exclude iliac vein thrombosis when it is clinically suspected. All three relations converge on one target condition (iliac vein thrombosis) and all three carry the same triggering condition — clinical suspicion of iliac vein thrombosis, which the guideline characterises by the presenting features of back and buttock pain together with swelling of the entire limb (this symptom detail is attached specifically to the Doppler ultrasound relation).

The recommendations are: (1) Doppler ultrasound of the iliac vein detects iliac vein thrombosis when iliac vein thrombosis is suspected on the basis of back and buttock pain and swelling of the entire limb; (2) magnetic resonance venography detects iliac vein thrombosis when it is suspected; and (3) conventional contrast venography detects iliac vein thrombosis when it is suspected. For teaching purposes, the practical message is that the symptom triad of back/buttock pain plus whole-limb swelling should prompt dedicated iliac vein imaging rather than reliance on standard leg assessment alone, and that three modalities are recognised as capable of making the detection.

Only one guideline body contributes here: the RCOG (RCOG T1, p7). There are therefore no inter-body disagreements or overlaps to reconcile in this community. The only difference in specificity is internal: the Doppler ultrasound relation is more specific because it names the clinical features that constitute suspicion, whereas the MR venography and contrast venography relations state the indication only in general terms.

What this community does NOT establish: it gives no hierarchy, preferred first-line choice, or sequencing among Doppler ultrasound, magnetic resonance venography and conventional contrast venography; no sensitivity, specificity or accuracy thresholds; no timing targets for when imaging must be performed; no population restrictions (e.g. pregnant, postpartum, or postoperative gynecologic patients are not differentiated); no contraindications or safety considerations (such as contrast or radiation issues); and no anticoagulant drugs, doses, or treatment or prophylaxis pathways following a positive or negative result.
key_entities: doppler ultrasound of the iliac vein
back and buttock pain with swelling of the entire limb

title: Bowel Management Plans Prevent Constipation, Impaction
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: the use of an individualized bowel management plan as a preventive nursing intervention against constipation and its downstream complication, fecal impaction. All three relations converge on one intervention (bowel management plan) and two outcomes prevented (constipation, impaction).

The core recommendation is that a bowel management plan be implemented on an as-needed basis with the explicit target of achieving a bowel movement every one to three days. That frequency threshold is the only quantitative parameter the community supplies, and it is attached consistently to all three edges. Population specification is minimal: two edges are unpopulated (implicitly any client under nursing care), while the third narrows to hospitalized clients for the constipation-prevention claim. Thus the constipation relation is stated at two levels of specificity — a general form and a hospitalized-client form — whereas the impaction relation appears only in the general, unpopulated form. The impaction edge is therefore the less specific of the two outcomes with respect to population.

Only one guideline body contributes: OpenRN (Nursing Skills, Volume/Tier 2), and all evidence traces to a single locus, page 1183. Consequently there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile, no competing thresholds, and no independent corroboration within this community; the apparent redundancy of the constipation edges reflects differing population granularity from the same source rather than convergent evidence from multiple guidelines.

What the community does NOT establish: no drugs, agents, or classes are named (no stool softeners, osmotic or stimulant laxatives, suppositories, or enemas); no dosing, route, or timing of administration; no non-pharmacologic components such as fluid volume, fibre intake, mobility, or toileting schedules; no assessment tools, documentation standards, or escalation criteria if the one-to-three-day target is not met. It also makes no claim specific to perioperative or gynecologic surgical patients, opioid-related constipation, postoperative ileus, or paediatric, obstetric, or long-term-care populations, and offers no contraindications or safety cautions.
key_entities: bowel movement every one to three days

title: Host Risk Factors Impairing Wound Healing
summary: This community centres on modifiable and non-modifiable host factors that impair wound healing and raise perioperative infection risk, plus the few interventions offered against them. Impaired wound healing is the hub outcome, driven by diabetes, obesity, smoking, alcohol use/consumption, corticosteroids, venous insufficiency, biofilm, older age, and nutritional problems (nutritional deficiency in clients with chronic wounds unless deficiencies are addressed; poor nutrition in the elderly; malnutrition in surgical patients with severe protein-calorie malnutrition, for some operations, noted by CDC as a crude association only). Smoking is the most heavily documented factor: OpenRN links it to infection (including clients who smoke), delayed/poor wound healing, necrosis and wound dehiscence; ERAS Society ties it to postoperative morbidity and complications; AUGS specifies surgical site infection in patients undergoing urogynecologic surgery; RCOG links smoking to post-thrombotic syndrome in women following DVT in pregnancy; RNAO to cardiovascular disease. Older age broadens the theme beyond wounds: skin tears with fragile, nonelastic skin and skin injury in older adults (OpenRN), medication-related harm in Ontario populations (RNAO), suicide in older adults (OpenRN), and CDC's catheter-specific risks — CAUTI in patients with urinary catheters and mortality in patients with indwelling catheters, highest over 70 years of age. Interventions named: exercise to prevent impaired wound healing in older adults/older clients as appropriate, positioned preoperatively for surgical patients (AUGS); exercise also treats hypertension in hypertensive adults 3 times per week (RNAO) and low back pain in pregnant women in addition to usual antenatal care (WHO); protein and micronutrient supplementation for clients with pressure injuries at 30–35 kcal/kg with 1.25–1.5 g/kg protein daily (OpenRN); and applying a gait belt on top of clothing or gown to prevent skin injury in clients requiring gait belts. Specificity differs: CDC and AUGS give population/threshold detail, OpenRN gives breadth without thresholds. The community does NOT establish smoking-cessation timing or protocols, quantified risk magnitudes, diabetes/obesity thresholds, corticosteroid drugs or doses, alcohol limits, or biofilm management.

title: Handoff Communication Failures Drive Perioperative Harm
summary:
Clinical theme: this community is a single, tightly focused hazard cluster centred on inadequate handoff (hand-off/report) communication as an upstream cause of perioperative patient harm. All four relations radiate from one causal node, framing communication failure at transitions of care — the kind occurring between pre-op, intra-op (OR), and post-op/PACU phases and at shift change — as a risk multiplier rather than an isolated event.

Recommendations and asserted risks: inadequate handoff communication is documented to INCREASE the RISK OF four distinct adverse outcomes: (1) falls, (2) wrong-site surgery, (3) medication error, and (4) delay in treatment. The practical implication for educators and QI leads is that structured, standardised, verified handoff is a shared control for all four outcomes simultaneously — meaning fall-prevention, correct-site verification, medication-safety, and timeliness programmes should not be audited as unrelated silos but should share a common handoff intervention and metric.

Populations and conditions: notably, the corpus attaches NO specific population qualifier and NO conditional trigger to any of the four relations; they are stated as general, unconditioned risk associations. Educators should therefore treat them as applicable across the perioperative gynecologic nursing population described by the source, without narrowing to a subgroup (e.g., no distinction by age, procedure type, anaesthesia class, or ASA status is supplied).

Contributing guideline bodies: the sole contributor is OpenRN (Nursing Skills, Topic 2, p.159). Because only one body and one page underpin the community, there is no inter-guideline disagreement to reconcile and no instance where one body is more specific than another; equally, there is no corroboration from a second source.

What this community does NOT establish: it specifies no handoff tool or format (no SBAR, I-PASS, or checklist named), no timing, frequency, or duration requirements, no personnel or competency requirements, no thresholds or measurable criteria for adequacy, no effect sizes or incidence rates, no directionality evidence that improved handoff reduces these outcomes, and no drugs, doses, or condition-specific exceptions.

title: Preventing Adverse Events Across Perioperative Care
summary:
This community centres on the shared outcome 'adverse event' and the structural, procedural and pharmacological factors that either prevent or increase it across the perioperative pathway. Four distinct levers converge on the same endpoint: postoperative placement, team verification, organisational leadership, and patient self-medication.

Main recommendations with their populations and conditions: (1) NICE (T1 p26) recommends care in a non-ward-based specialist recovery area during the postoperative phase for people with a high risk of complications or mortality, stating this prevents adverse events — the phase is explicitly postoperative, and the population is risk-stratified rather than all surgical patients. (2) WHO (T1 p228) attaches a verification process to surgical patients, which prevents wrong site surgery outright, and prevents adverse events only if the tool is followed consistently by the entire team without skipping steps — a conditional, fidelity-dependent claim that is more specific than a blanket endorsement of checklists. (3) OpenRN (T2 p383) locates risk at the organisational level: inadequate leadership increases the risk of adverse events for health care organisations, conditioned on the absence of an effective culture of safety. (4) WHO (T1 p242) identifies over-the-counter drugs as increasing adverse event risk for consumers who self-prescribe, particularly when taken with other medications.

Contributing bodies: NICE, WHO (two separate passages) and OpenRN. They differ in level of analysis rather than conflict — NICE addresses physical care setting and patient risk stratification, WHO addresses both intraoperative team process and community/consumer medication safety, and OpenRN addresses leadership and safety culture. WHO is the most specific about the condition under which a preventive intervention actually works (complete, unskipped team execution).

What this community does not establish: no named drugs, doses, thresholds, timings, monitoring intervals or lengths of stay in the recovery area; no criteria defining 'high risk of complications or mortality'; no description of the verification tool's steps; no gynecologic-specific populations; and no causal link between leadership, verification and recovery-area care with one another.

title: Modifiable Barriers to Same-Day Discharge
summary: This community represents a narrow but operationally important theme: the two clinical problems most often responsible for failure to discharge on schedule after gynecologic minimally invasive surgery managed on an Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) pathway. Both mapped relations are of the same type (INCREASES_RISK_OF) and converge on a single outcome node, delayed discharge, from two upstream causes: urinary retention and inadequate pain control. Both edges carry the identical population qualifier — patients undergoing gynecologic minimally invasive surgery on an ERAS pathway — and the identical condition qualifier: 30% of delayed discharges are attributed to the factor. The only contributing guideline body in this community is the ERAS Society (ERAS_Society T1, p8); no other corpus body appears here, so there are no inter-society disagreements to reconcile and no instance of one body being more granular than another within this theme. The practical implication for educators and QI leads is that discharge-readiness teaching and audit for this population should be built around two trackable domains — postoperative voiding status and analgesic adequacy — because together they account for the stated share of delayed discharges. What this community does NOT establish is substantial. It contains no recommended interventions, no drugs, doses, routes or analgesic regimens, and no bladder-management protocol; catheter removal timing, post-void residual thresholds, trial-of-void criteria, pain-score cut-offs and reassessment intervals are all absent. It specifies no discharge criteria, no length-of-stay target, and no definition of what counts as a “delay.” It does not state whether the two 30% attributions are independent or overlapping, nor whether they sum to a total proportion of delayed discharges; it also does not identify the remaining causes. No risk factors for urinary retention or for inadequate pain control are represented, no directional relation between the two causes is asserted, and no data are given for open or non-ERAS gynecologic surgery, obstetric patients, or other surgical specialties. Any protocol built on this theme must draw its thresholds and drug choices from other sections of the corpus.

title: Surgical Site Hematoma as Wound Complication Risk
summary:
This small community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: the hematoma as a driver of postoperative wound complications in gynecologic surgical patients. It captures the causal reasoning nurses need when assessing an operative site — that a collection of blood in the tissues is not merely a cosmetic or comfort issue but an active risk factor for two distinct downstream outcomes.

The two relations both originate from the same entity and share the same condition. First, a hematoma increases the risk of infection, and second, a hematoma increases the risk of incisional dehiscence (separation of the wound edges). In both cases the guideline attaches the qualifying condition that the hematoma develops at a surgical site; the corpus does not extend these risk statements to hematomas arising elsewhere. No narrower population is specified beyond the surgical-site context — the statements are framed generally rather than restricted by age, procedure type, comorbidity, or approach (open versus laparoscopic).

Only one guideline body contributes here: OpenRN (Nursing Skills, Volume 2, page 1113) supplies both relations. Because there is a single source, the community contains no points of disagreement, no competing thresholds, and no instance of one body being more specific than another. The consistency is therefore internal rather than corroborated across organisations.

Importantly, the community does not establish a great deal that a quality-improvement lead might want. It gives no magnitude of risk — no relative risk, absolute rate, or hematoma size threshold at which risk rises. It specifies no timing (when after surgery hematomas most often form, or when infection or dehiscence typically presents). It names no drugs, anticoagulation practices, prophylactic antibiotics, or reversal agents, and no drain, pressure-dressing, or evacuation interventions. It does not describe assessment technique, documentation standards, escalation criteria, or which clinician should be notified. Nor does it state whether infection and dehiscence are independent outcomes or sequential, with infection precipitating dehiscence. Educators should treat this as a foundational rationale statement requiring supplementation from other corpus sections for actionable protocol content.

title: Fluids and antipyretic-analgesic supportive measures
summary:
This community groups low-cost, non-invasive supportive interventions — increased oral fluid intake, paracetamol, tepid sponging and lowering the environmental temperature — used for symptom control (pyrexia, pain), for prevention of constipation, for treating urinary tract infection, and for post-procedure contrast clearance.

Key recommendations by population and condition: RCOG (T1 p11) bundles four measures for pyrexia in women in labour — paracetamol, increased fluid intake, tepid sponging, and lowering the environmental temperature. NICE (T1 p27) recommends paracetamol for pain in adults having surgery, specifically alongside opioid analgesia, with the oral route preferred for people able to take oral medicines. OpenRN (T2) covers increased fluid intake most broadly: to prevent constipation generally (p1173), in clients taking opioids, and in older adults (both 'as appropriate'); to treat urinary tract infection in clients with a UTI (p1159); and in clients who have received contrast, applied after a contrast imaging procedure and situated in the postoperative phase (p1183).

Contributing bodies and differences: RCOG is the only source addressing intrapartum pyrexia and is the only one combining physical cooling measures with drug and fluid therapy. NICE is the most specific on paracetamol's role in surgical pain — it frames it as adjunctive to opioids and states a route preference, which RCOG does not do for its antipyretic use. OpenRN is the most granular on fluids, naming distinct populations (opioid users, older adults, UTI, post-contrast) and hedging with 'as appropriate' rather than mandating intake.

What this community does not establish: no doses, frequencies, maximum daily limits or durations for paracetamol; no fluid volumes, targets or timing intervals for increased intake; no temperature threshold defining pyrexia and no target temperature for cooling; no specified environmental temperature; no criteria for what 'as appropriate' means, nor contraindications (e.g. fluid restriction, hepatic impairment). It also does not rank these measures, define escalation if pyrexia or pain persists, or extend the labour bundle to surgical or postoperative gynecologic patients.

title: Reducing perioperative mortality through risk modification
summary:
This community centres on identifying and modifying modifiable perioperative risk in order to reduce perioperative mortality and postoperative complications. Two levers appear: (1) structured preoperative risk assessment, and (2) individualised goal-directed fluid therapy intraoperatively. A patient-level risk factor, alcohol abuse, is named as increasing the risk of perioperative mortality (ERAS Society, T1 p1), giving a concrete target for preoperative screening and optimisation.

RCOG (T1 p2) recommends preoperative risk assessment for all patients undergoing surgery, situating it explicitly in the preoperative phase. Its stated benefit is conditional: assessment prevents postoperative complications and perioperative mortality only 'if possible, organised so that problems identified can be addressed' — i.e. assessment alone is insufficient unless services can act on findings before surgery. For quality-improvement purposes this is the key process measure: a referral/optimisation pathway attached to the assessment, not merely a completed form.

RCOG (T1 p3) also recommends individualised goal-directed fluid therapy in patients undergoing colorectal surgery, to prevent bowel hypo-perfusion and perioperative mortality, with the mortality benefit specified for the condition of using stroke volume to guide intraoperative fluid management. This is the most technically specific recommendation in the community, naming both the target population (colorectal surgery) and the monitoring variable (stroke volume).

Contributing bodies are RCOG (both process recommendations, with populations and conditions) and the ERAS Society (the alcohol-abuse risk association only, stated without population or condition). RCOG is markedly more specific; ERAS here supplies risk-factor context rather than an intervention. The two do not conflict.

The community does not establish: any alcohol screening tool, cessation interval, or abstinence duration before surgery; any numeric stroke-volume, fluid-volume or haemodynamic thresholds; which risk-assessment instrument or scoring system to use; timing of preoperative assessment relative to surgery; whether goal-directed fluid therapy benefits gynaecologic (as opposed to colorectal) surgery; who performs the assessment; or any drug, anaesthetic or transfusion recommendation.

title: Induction of Labour: Indications, Agents, Anticoagulant Timing
summary:
This community centres on induction of labour (IOL) — when it is indicated, which agents to use, when it is contraindicated, and how it interacts with maternal anticoagulation. WHO (T1 pp19, 29) supplies the clinical indications and methods; RCOG (T1 pp19, 4) contributes anticoagulant timing and a sepsis risk flag.

Indications (WHO T1 p29/p19): IOL treats mild gestational hypertension at term; mild pre-eclampsia at term; severe pre-eclampsia at a gestational age when the fetus is not viable or unlikely to achieve viability within one or two weeks; and prelabour rupture of membranes at term.

Contraindications (WHO T1 p19): IOL is not recommended for suspected fetal macrosomia in women at term, and is temporarily contraindicated before 41 weeks of gestation in women in whom gestational diabetes is the only abnormality.

Methods (WHO T1 p19): low-dose vaginal prostaglandin; low-dose vaginal misoprostol 25 µg 6-hourly; misoprostol by oral or vaginal route for women with a dead or anomalous fetus in the third trimester; balloon catheter combined with oxytocin when prostaglandins (including misoprostol) are unavailable or contraindicated; and sweeping of membranes to reduce the need for formal IOL.

Anticoagulation timing (RCOG T1 p19): low molecular weight heparin should be stopped 24 hours before induction in women on LMWH maintenance therapy; subcutaneous unfractionated heparin should be discontinued 12 hours before induction or regional anaesthesia. RCOG is the more specific source here, whereas WHO does not address anticoagulant interruption. Separately, RCOG (T1 p4) flags gestational diabetes as an amber-flag factor increasing sepsis risk in patients with suspected sepsis — note gestational diabetes appears in both a sepsis-risk and an IOL-timing context, with no direct link drawn between the two.

Not established: no dosing for oxytocin or balloon catheter protocols, no comparative effectiveness ranking between methods, no guidance on IOL in preterm hypertensive disease other than non-viable severe pre-eclampsia, no monitoring or failed-induction pathways, and no restart timing for LMWH or unfractionated heparin postpartum.

title: Preventing Urethral Traction in Indwelling Catheters
summary:
This community centres on a single, tightly focused maintenance theme: protecting the urethra from mechanical traction in patients with an indwelling urinary catheter. Two distinct nursing actions converge on the same preventive outcome. First, securing the indwelling catheter (e.g., to the patient) prevents traction on the urethra; the population is patients with indwelling catheters and the condition is after insertion, making this an immediate post-insertion task rather than an ongoing one. Second, emptying the urine collection bag also prevents urethral traction, with the specified threshold that the bag be emptied when it is half to two-thirds full, in patients with an indwelling catheter. The same emptying action is additionally linked as applying to indwelling catheterisation generally, situating bag management within routine catheter care rather than as an isolated intervention.

Two guideline bodies contribute. The CDC (T1 p12) supplies the securement recommendation and anchors it to the post-insertion period. OpenRN (T2 p1208) supplies both statements about emptying the collection bag and is the more specific source here, because it attaches a concrete volume threshold (half to two-thirds full) rather than an unquantified instruction. There is no conflict between the two bodies: they address complementary mechanisms of traction (device fixation versus bag weight) and are consistent in identifying urethral traction as the harm to be avoided.

Important limits: the community does not state how securement should be achieved (no device, tape, strap, leg-versus-abdomen positioning, or laterality is named), nor how often securement should be reassessed. No drugs are involved and none are named. It does not quantify catheter dwell time, removal criteria, or indications for catheterisation, and it does not specify frequency of bag emptying beyond the fill threshold. It does not describe downstream consequences of traction (such as trauma, bleeding, bladder spasm, dislodgement, or catheter-associated urinary tract infection), nor does it address gynecologic-surgery-specific populations, drainage-bag positioning below bladder level, closed-system integrity, or hand hygiene. Any teaching built on this theme must draw those details from elsewhere in the corpus.

title: Injection Site Tissue Integrity and Absorption
summary:
This community centres on a single clinical theme: how the condition of the tissue at an injection site determines whether parenteral medication is actually absorbed. All four relations converge on one adverse outcome node, 'ineffective medication absorption,' with tissue-level risk factors as upstream drivers and site selection as the protective intervention.

Risk relations: both intramuscular and subcutaneous injection are flagged as increasing the risk of ineffective medication absorption in patients with muscle atrophy or decreased blood flow to the tissue, conditioned explicitly on reduced muscle mass and reduced blood flow being present at the chosen injection site (OpenRN T2 p1053). Scar tissue is a parallel risk factor for any patient receiving an injection, conditioned on the site being scarred or atrophied (same source and page). The single preventive recommendation is to avoid sites with atrophied muscle, specified for patients receiving intramuscular injections (OpenRN T2 p1040). Practically, this yields one teachable rule: palpate and inspect before injecting, and reject sites that are scarred, atrophied, or poorly perfused for both IM and subcutaneous routes.

Contributing bodies: all content derives from a single corpus, OpenRN (Nursing Skills, Textbook 2), across two pages. There is therefore no inter-organisational disagreement to reconcile. There is a difference in specificity within the source: p1040 states the preventive action but restricts its stated population to IM injections, whereas p1053 extends the risk framing to subcutaneous injections and to scar tissue for injections generally. Educators should note the preventive guidance is narrower than the risk statement it addresses.

Not established: no named drugs, no needle lengths or gauges, no volume limits, no anatomical site list (e.g., ventrogluteal versus deltoid), no thresholds defining 'atrophy' or adequate perfusion, no timing or rotation schedules, and no alternative route recommendations when all candidate sites are compromised. No populations beyond 'patients receiving injections' with atrophy, scarring, or decreased blood flow are addressed, and no perioperative gynecologic specifics, outcomes data, or monitoring strategies for suspected non-absorption are provided.
key_entities: decreased blood flow to the tissue

title: Breastfeeding: Drug Contraindications and Immune Benefit
summary:
This community centres on breastfeeding as a clinical decision point that both restricts maternal drug choice and confers infant benefit. Two distinct medication classes are flagged as temporarily contraindicated during lactation. RCOG (T1 p26) states that non-vitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulants (NOACs/DOACs) are temporarily contraindicated in women who are breastfeeding, for the duration of breastfeeding — implying an alternative anticoagulant is needed while lactation continues, though no substitute is named in these relations. WHO (T1 p33) states that primaquine is temporarily contraindicated in women who are pregnant or breastfeeding, with the restriction lasting until delivery and breastfeeding are completed; WHO is the more specific of the two in that it extends the population to pregnancy as well as lactation and defines the endpoint as completion of both delivery and breastfeeding. Both bodies frame the contraindication as temporary rather than absolute, so the practical nursing implication is timing and counselling rather than permanent avoidance.

Counterbalancing these restrictions, OpenRN (T2 p663) identifies breastfeeding as protective against infectious disease in infants, on the mechanism that it provides passive immunity until the infant's own immune system matures. This supplies the rationale for why clinicians should preserve breastfeeding and adjust maternal pharmacotherapy around it, rather than stopping lactation to accommodate a drug.

The bodies do not conflict; they address different drugs and different sides of the same decision (RCOG anticoagulation, WHO antimalarial, OpenRN infant immunology).

What this community does NOT establish: no dosing thresholds, washout intervals, or milk-transfer data for either drug; no named alternative anticoagulant or antimalarial; no guidance on expressing and discarding milk; no duration or exclusivity threshold for the infant immune benefit; no specific infectious diseases prevented; and no perioperative-specific instructions on when to restart NOACs or primaquine after weaning. Local protocols and full guideline text are required for those details.

title: Aseptic Breaches Driving Infectious Phlebitis
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: the contamination-related causes of infectious (septic) phlebitis in patients with vascular access devices. All three relations converge on one outcome entity — infectious phlebitis — and identify three modifiable upstream risk factors: (1) poor aseptic technique, explicitly scoped to the population of patients with vascular access devices; (2) emergent vascular access device insertion, i.e. lines placed under urgent/emergency conditions where full aseptic preparation may be compromised; and (3) a contaminated dressing at the access site. The practical implication for perioperative gynecologic nursing education and QI work is that infectious phlebitis prevention rests on insertion-time asepsis, recognition that emergently placed devices carry elevated risk (and therefore warrant heightened surveillance or early reassessment/replacement consideration), and ongoing integrity and cleanliness of the site dressing.

Contributing guideline material is limited to a single source: OpenRN Nursing Skills (Volume 2, p.1363). There is therefore no cross-body comparison available — no AORN, CDC/HICPAC, INS, or professional society statement is represented in this community, and no point of disagreement or differing specificity between bodies can be identified. The one population qualifier present ('patients with vascular access devices') attaches only to the poor-aseptic-technique relation; the emergent-insertion and contaminated-dressing relations carry no stated population or condition, so their scope is implicitly the same device-bearing population but is not formally narrowed.

What this community does NOT establish: it gives no numeric thresholds, no dwell-time or dressing-change intervals, no timing for site assessment, no catheter type, gauge, or site preferences, and no antiseptic agents (e.g. no chlorhexidine or alcohol concentrations) or antimicrobial therapy. It does not grade or quantify the relative magnitude of risk among the three factors, does not define diagnostic criteria or severity staging for infectious phlebitis, and does not specify management once phlebitis occurs (line removal, culturing, or treatment). It also says nothing about non-infectious phlebitis mechanisms (mechanical or chemical) or about gynecologic-surgery-specific modifiers.

title: Peripheral IV Site Assessment and Infiltration Prevention
summary:
This community centers on surveillance, risk reduction, and management of peripheral intravenous site complications — specifically infiltration and vein irritation — in patients with venous access devices.

Assessment recommendations: IV site assessment monitors for IV site complications in any patient with a venous access device, and should occur every time the nurse interacts with the patient. For patients in inpatient and nursing facilities with peripherally inserted IVs, catheter assessment should occur at least every 4 hours, and every 1 to 2 hours for patients who are critically ill or sedated. For patients receiving primary IV solution administration, the site is assessed for both vein irritation and infiltration before initiating fluids and again after the infusion begins. Before administering IV push medications, checking patency of the IV site is used to detect infiltration.

Risk and prevention: In patients receiving infusion therapy, the IV catheter itself increases infiltration risk; additional risk factors are excessive patient movement, a dislodged or incorrectly placed catheter, and rapid infusion of fluids or medications into a fragile vein. Prevention for patients with a peripheral IV catheter includes avoiding insertion sites at areas of flexion.

Management: IV fluid administration is temporarily contraindicated at a venipuncture site showing signs or symptoms of vein irritation or infiltration — the site should not be used if there are any concerns. When infiltration occurs, treatment is stopping the infusion and removing the cannula.

Contributing body: all relations derive from a single source, OpenRN Nursing Skills (Volume 2, pages 1359, 1363, 1376); no cross-organizational comparison or disagreement is available, though the frequency guidance (p1359) is more specific for inpatient/critical-care populations than the general "every interaction" rule.
