Not established: no named drugs, vesicants, or antidotes; no infiltration staging scale or measurable thresholds (e.g., swelling size, temperature, dressing standards); no guidance on extravasation, phlebitis grading, catheter dwell-time limits, restart-site selection, warm/cold compresses, elevation, or documentation and escalation requirements; and nothing specific to perioperative gynecologic populations.
key_entities: dislodged or incorrectly placed intravenous catheter
rapid infusion of fluids or medications
avoiding insertion sites at areas of flexion
stopping the infusion and removing the cannula

title: Suspected Influenza: Testing, Antivirals, Complications
summary:
This community represents the recognition, diagnostic confirmation and empirical treatment of suspected influenza, together with the respiratory complications that make influenza clinically urgent in the population addressed by the guideline (women suspected of having influenza, in a perioperative gynecologic/obstetric care context).

Two linked recommendations define the care pathway. First, diagnostic confirmation: a viral nasal or throat swab sent for influenza polymerase chain reaction (PCR) detects influenza, and the condition attached is that the swab be taken immediately in women suspected of having influenza — testing is not deferred pending clinical deterioration. Second, treatment is empirical and does not wait on the laboratory: antiviral therapy treats influenza and is given while awaiting PCR results in the same population of women with suspected influenza. Together these establish a 'swab immediately, treat immediately' approach where the diagnostic test and therapy run in parallel rather than in sequence.

The community also frames why this urgency matters by naming two complications. Influenza increases the risk of secondary bacterial infection, which typically follows influenza and other viral respiratory infections; and influenza increases the risk of pulmonary haemorrhage, specified as a feature of primary influenza. The distinction is useful for educators: secondary bacterial infection is a later, post-viral event, whereas pulmonary haemorrhage is attributed to primary influenza itself.

Only one guideline body contributes here — RCOG (Tier 1, p7) — so there is no cross-body disagreement, no divergent thresholds, and no instance where one organisation is more specific than another. All four relations derive from the same page, making this a single-source, internally consistent theme.

What the community does NOT establish: no specific antiviral agent, dose, route, duration or timing window is named; no antibiotic regimen or prophylaxis for the secondary bacterial infection is specified; no PCR turnaround time, sensitivity, or repeat-testing rule is given; no management of pulmonary haemorrhage is described; and no gestational age, pregnancy stage, perioperative timing, isolation/infection-control measures, or vaccination guidance is attached to any relation. Risk magnitudes are qualitative only, with no quantified incidence.
key_entities: viral nasal or throat swab for influenza polymerase chain reaction

title: Maternal Vaccination to Prevent Sepsis Deaths
summary:
This community represents antenatal immunisation as a primary prevention strategy against infection-related maternal mortality, linking two vaccines (influenza and COVID-19) to the outcomes they avert in pregnant and recently pregnant women.

Main recommendations: (1) Influenza vaccination should be offered during the antenatal phase and, per WHO (T1 p12), may be given to pregnant women at any stage of pregnancy — i.e. no trimester restriction is imposed. (2) RCOG attaches three preventive claims to influenza vaccination in pregnant women: prevention of influenza A infection (T1 p2), prevention of infection-related maternal death (T1 p7), and prevention of maternal death from sepsis (T1 p2, population stated more broadly as pregnant OR recently pregnant women). (3) COVID-19 vaccination is likewise credited with preventing maternal death from sepsis in pregnant or recently pregnant women (RCOG T1 p2).

Contributing bodies: WHO and RCOG. Their contributions are complementary rather than conflicting. WHO is the only source specifying timing/phase (antenatal, any stage of pregnancy) and does so only for influenza. RCOG is the only source specifying outcomes and is more granular about them (organism-level — influenza A infection — as well as mortality endpoints), and is the only source extending the target population beyond pregnancy to recently pregnant women, and the only source naming COVID-19 vaccination.

What this community does NOT establish: no dose, product, brand, adjuvant status, or number of doses for either vaccine; no schedule or timing for COVID-19 vaccination (no antenatal-phase or gestational-age link is asserted); no definition of the interval covered by "recently pregnant"; no contraindications, cautions, or adverse-event guidance; no effect sizes, absolute risk reductions, or thresholds for benefit; no statement on breastfeeding, postpartum catch-up, or neonatal/infant protection; no linkage of COVID-19 vaccination to influenza A or to infection-related maternal death as a distinct outcome; and no perioperative-specific guidance (e.g. vaccination status checks before gynecologic surgery). Educators should treat these as gaps requiring other corpus sections or local policy.

title: Injection Technique to Prevent Site Pain
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: nursing technique measures that reduce or prevent injection site pain in patients receiving injections. All three relations converge on the same outcome entity (injection site pain) and all derive from one source, OpenRN Nursing Skills (Volume 2, p1006), so the theme reflects a foundational nursing-skills text rather than a multi-body consensus.

Three preventive recommendations are asserted, each for the population 'patients receiving injections':
1) Needle selection — use a larger diameter needle to prevent injection site pain. No gauge numbers, injection routes (IM, subcutaneous, intradermal), anatomic sites, or drug-specific viscosity thresholds are specified in the community.
2) Needle change — change the needle after medication is withdrawn from a vial and before administration. The condition is explicitly timed: withdrawal first, then needle exchange, then administration.
3) Patient positioning — position the patient properly, with limbs relaxed and comfortable, so that muscle tension is reduced at the injection site.

Guideline bodies: only OpenRN contributes; there are no competing or corroborating recommendations from surgical, anesthesia, or perioperative societies in this community, and therefore no points of disagreement or differing specificity to reconcile. Within OpenRN itself, the needle-change and positioning recommendations carry explicit conditions (timing relative to vial withdrawal; relaxed, comfortable limbs), whereas the larger-diameter-needle recommendation is stated without any qualifying condition — making it the least operationally specific of the three.

What this community does not establish: it names no drugs, no needle gauges or lengths, no volume limits, no injection sites or routes, and no patient subgroups (e.g., gynecologic surgical patients, obese patients, pediatric or anticoagulated patients). It offers no effect sizes, pain scales, or evidence grades, and does not address related outcomes such as tissue injury, bleeding, nerve damage, medication leakage, or needlestick safety. Nor does it link these techniques to perioperative gynecologic workflows specifically; the applicability is generic to any patient receiving an injection. Educators should treat it as basic technique reinforcement requiring local specification of needle sizes and routes.

title: Injury and Fall Prevention Through Education
summary:
This community centers on injury- and fall-risk reduction in vulnerable patients, achieved chiefly through targeted patient/family education, protective footwear and skin care, and environmental or ergonomic design. Risk drivers named are sensory impairment (increases risk of both falls and injury in individuals with sensory impairments) and unsafe behavior (increases risk of injury in individuals with dementia).

Concrete recommendations, with their attached populations/conditions: (1) education about room layout and tactile boundary cues prevents injury in clients with altered visual acuity; (2) patient education prevents injury in patients with neuropathy and decreased sensation; (3) well-fitting shoes prevent injury in patients with diabetes, with the explicit condition of never going barefoot; (4) fragile skin protection prevents injury in patients with skin tears; (5) ergonomic design prevents injury when it considers physical layout, work-process flow, and use of technology. Separately, patient education is anchored to the preoperative phase for patients undergoing gynecologic surgery, with the condition that it stress non-opioid alternatives as first-line therapy.

Contributing bodies: OpenRN (Nursing Skills/fundamentals content, pp. 434, 451, 521, 910, 1145) supplies all of the population-specific injury- and fall-prevention statements, including the sensory, dementia, diabetes, neuropathy and skin-tear populations plus the systems-level ergonomic design item. The ERAS Society (T1 p9) contributes only the perioperative gynecologic-surgery education item and is narrower in scope but more specific about content (non-opioid alternatives as first-line) and timing (preoperative). Thus the two sources converge on education as the common intervention but differ in target: OpenRN on sensory/skin/foot safety, ERAS on analgesic expectation-setting.

What is not established: no drug names, doses, or opioid-sparing agents are specified; no fall-risk scores, screening thresholds, timing intervals, or reassessment frequencies are given; no linkage is made between the OpenRN injury-prevention measures and the gynecologic perioperative population, nor between ergonomic design and patient falls specifically. Effectiveness magnitude, staff-injury outcomes, and post-discharge follow-up are absent.
key_entities: education regarding room layout and tactile boundary cues

title: Wound packing choice protects granulation tissue
summary:
This community represents a narrow but practically important theme in perioperative gynecologic wound care: how the choice and condition of packing material at dressing change determines whether granulation tissue is preserved or damaged. Two relations, both from the OpenRN corpus (Nursing Skills, Text 2), anchor the theme around a single shared outcome entity, injury to granulation tissue.

The first recommendation is protective: easily removable packing material prevents injury to granulation tissue. Its stated population is patients with deep or tunneling wounds, and its condition is at each dressing change — i.e., the protective effect is tied to the repeated act of removal, not to initial placement alone. Practically, this frames packing selection as a decision made with removal in mind for cavity and tunneling wounds.

The second relation is the counterpoint and is a risk statement: sterile gauze increases the risk of injury to granulation tissue, conditioned specifically on the gauze being unmoistened and adhering to the wound base. No population qualifier is attached to this relation — it is stated as a property of the material and its moisture state rather than of a wound type. Note that sterile gauze is not framed as inherently harmful; the hazard is conditional on dryness and adherence.

Both statements come from a single guideline body, OpenRN (pages 1145 and 1151), so there is no inter-body disagreement to reconcile. The two entries differ in specificity: p1145 specifies population (deep or tunneling wounds) and timing (each dressing change) but not material identity; p1151 names the material (sterile gauze) and its physical state but omits population and timing.

The community does not establish any moistening agent, solution, or drug; no thresholds for moisture, packing volume, or dressing-change frequency; no named alternative packing products; no evidence grades or outcome rates; and no gynecologic-surgery-specific indication, despite the corpus context. It also says nothing about infection, bleeding, dehiscence, or healing time.

title: Inspired Oxygen Monitoring Preventing Hypoxic Mixtures
summary:
This community represents intraoperative anaesthetic gas safety: continuous monitoring of inspired oxygen concentration, coupled with alarm-equipped equipment, to detect and prevent hypoxia, hypoxic gas mixtures and oxygen supply failure in patients under anaesthesia.

Core recommendations. (1) Monitor inspired oxygen concentration throughout anaesthesia in all patients under anaesthesia, using an instrument fitted with a low-oxygen-concentration alarm; this monitoring is explicitly placed in the intraoperative phase (WHO T1 p31) and serves to detect both hypoxia and a hypoxic gas mixture (WHO T1 p25, p31). (2) The same alarm-equipped monitoring is framed as preventive, not merely detective: it prevents delivery of a hypoxic gas mixture and prevents unrecognised oxygen supply failure (WHO T1 p25). (3) Nitrous oxide increases the risk of a hypoxic gas mixture unless it is used together with oxygen via a machine specifically designed to prevent hypoxic mixtures (WHO T1 p25) — the only named agent in this community. (4) A dedicated oxygen supply failure alarm should be present to monitor for oxygen supply failure in patients under anaesthesia (WHO T1 p31), giving a second, independent safeguard alongside inspired oxygen monitoring.

Contributing bodies. All relations derive from a single source, WHO Tier 1 (pages 25 and 31); no other guideline body contributes, so there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile. Within WHO, p25 is more explicit about mechanism and prevention (nitrous oxide risk, hypoxic-mixture-proof machines), while p31 is more explicit about timing (throughout anaesthesia), phase (intraoperative) and the separate oxygen supply failure alarm.

What is not established. No numeric thresholds are given — no minimum FiO2, no alarm set-point, no SpO2 target, and no sampling interval beyond "throughout anaesthesia." The population is generic "patients under anaesthesia"; nothing is specified for gynecologic surgery, obstetric, paediatric, obese or pregnant subgroups. No escalation or response algorithm for a triggered alarm is described, no equipment-check or pre-anaesthesia calibration step, no documentation requirement, no role assignment (who monitors), and no link to capnography, pulse oximetry or other monitors. Nitrous oxide dosing and alternatives are not addressed.

title: Perioperative Hyperglycemia Prevention, Monitoring, and Treatment
summary:
This community centers on perioperative glycemic control in gynecologic surgery, linking the risk factors for hyperglycemia, its prevention through metabolic-stress reduction, its detection by glucose monitoring, and its treatment with insulin.

Prevention: The ERAS Society (T1 p2) positions ERAS elements that reduce metabolic stress as preventive for both insulin resistance and hyperglycemia — making hyperglycemia a modifiable consequence of surgical stress rather than only a comorbidity issue.

Risk: RNAO (T2 p140) identifies thiazide diuretics as increasing hyperglycemia risk in patients treated with thiazide diuretics, flagging a medication-review point during preoperative assessment.

Monitoring: AUGS (T2 p7) recommends perioperative glucose measurement to monitor for hyperglycemia in both diabetics and non-diabetics, with levels maintained under 200 mg/dL. This is the most explicit statement that non-diabetic patients also require surveillance.

Treatment: ERAS Society (T1 p2 and p4) recommends insulin infusion for hyperglycemia when blood glucose exceeds 180–200 mg/dL, stated consistently across two pages.

Contributors and differences: Three bodies contribute distinct pieces — ERAS Society (prevention plus treatment thresholds), AUGS (monitoring population and target ceiling), RNAO (drug-related risk). They are complementary rather than conflicting, but the thresholds are not identical in framing: AUGS specifies maintaining levels under 200 mg/dL, while ERAS triggers insulin infusion above 180–200 mg/dL, leaving the 180–200 mg/dL band ambiguous as to whether it is a target or a treatment trigger. AUGS is more specific about who to monitor; ERAS is more specific about what to do once a threshold is crossed.

Not established: the relations do not specify glucose measurement frequency or timing (preoperative, intraoperative, postoperative intervals), insulin infusion dosing, titration, or duration, hypoglycemia thresholds or rescue treatment, which specific ERAS elements reduce metabolic stress, whether thiazides should be withheld perioperatively, alternative agents (e.g., subcutaneous insulin or oral agents), or any gynecologic-procedure-specific or outcome data linking control to infection or length of stay.
key_entities: eras elements that reduce metabolic stress

title: Intermittent Catheterisation: Techniques and Indications
summary:
This community centres on intermittent catheterisation (IC) as an alternative to indwelling urethral catheterisation, covering both its clinical indications and the adjuncts/techniques that support it. Two indication clusters appear. First, prevention: IC is recommended to prevent urinary tract deterioration in children with myelomeningocele and neurogenic bladder (CDC T1 p11, p35 - stated twice, indicating emphasis rather than two distinct populations). Second, treatment: IC treats postoperative urinary retention in catheterized surgical/postoperative patients, specifically when delivered under nurse-directed protocols for management of postoperative urinary retention (CDC T1 p16, p45) - a directly actionable target for QI work on nurse-led bladder management pathways.

Four modifiers attach to how IC is performed. Clean, non-sterile technique applies to patients requiring chronic intermittent catheterization in the non-acute care setting (p12). A portable ultrasound device applies to patients undergoing IC to assess urine volume and reduce unnecessary catheter insertions (p12). Hydrophilic catheters apply generically to patients requiring intermittent catheterization (p39). External (condom-type) catheters are positioned as an alternative to indwelling urethral catheters in cooperative male patients without urinary retention or bladder outlet obstruction (p37).

All relations derive from a single guideline body - CDC (T1) - so there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile; differences are only in specificity. The chronic/non-acute clean-technique statement (p12) and the male-specific external catheter criteria (p37) are narrowly conditioned, whereas the hydrophilic catheter recommendation (p39) carries no setting, frequency, or comparative condition.

The community does NOT establish: catheterisation frequency or timing intervals; bladder-volume thresholds at which ultrasound should trigger or withhold catheterisation; duration of nurse-directed protocols or criteria for escalation to indwelling catheterisation; whether hydrophilic or clean technique reduces infection or trauma versus alternatives; use of sterile technique in acute care; any drugs; and any gynecologic- or obstetric-specific population. Female patients are addressed only implicitly, since the external catheter recommendation is limited to cooperative males.
key_entities: children with myelomeningocele and neurogenic bladder

title: Wound haematoma risk with peripartum anticoagulation
summary: This community addresses caesarean section wound complications in women receiving anticoagulation, and the two surgical measures recommended to mitigate them. The risk signal: low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) increases the risk of wound haematoma in women following caesarean section, quantified at around 2%; more broadly, peripartum anticoagulation increases the risk of both wound haematoma and wound complications generally in women receiving it. Two mitigations are recommended, both restricted to the narrower population of patients receiving therapeutic (not prophylactic) doses of LMWH undergoing caesarean section. First, wound drains — specifically abdominal and rectus sheath drains — should be considered, to allow drainage of any haematoma and thereby prevent wound haematoma. Second, skin closure with interrupted sutures rather than a continuous technique, again to allow drainage of any haematoma; this is framed both as preventing wound haematoma and as treating haematoma once formed. RCOG (Thrombosis/thromboembolism guidance, T1) is the sole contributing body here, so there are no inter-organisational disagreements to reconcile. There is, however, a difference in granularity within the document: page 5 (the summary/recommendation list) specifies the drain sites (abdominal and rectus sheath) and the permissive wording "should be considered", while page 20 states the same interventions in the fuller text and page 23 supplies the ~2% haematoma incidence figure. Educators should teach the p5 specificity alongside the p20 rationale. The community does not establish: any timing or dosing thresholds for LMWH administration relative to surgery, when drains should be removed, which suture material or gauge to use, whether prophylactic-dose LMWH warrants the same measures, whether these measures apply to non-caesarean gynaecologic surgery, the incidence of wound complications other than haematoma, any nursing surveillance protocol (observation frequency, escalation triggers, blood loss thresholds), management of an established haematoma beyond drainage, or comparative effectiveness/evidence grading for drains versus interrupted closure. Regional anaesthesia considerations, unfractionated heparin, and other anticoagulants are absent.

title: Perioperative SSI Prevention and Enhanced Recovery
summary: This community covers perioperative bundles that span preoperative, intraoperative and postoperative phases: enhanced recovery, preoperative nutrition/fluids, multimodal analgesia, and above all surgical site infection (SSI) prevention. Enhanced recovery programmes should span preoperative and intraoperative phases for people having elective major or complex surgery, for optimum effectiveness (NICE). Preoperatively: nutritional screening for intermediate, major or complex surgery; clear fluids permitted until 2 hours before operation (all surgery, including dental); a carbohydrate drink for abdominal major or complex surgery; preoperative assessment for people undergoing surgery (NICE). Intraoperatively: intravenous crystalloid fluid maintenance for adults undergoing surgery; maintain optimal oxygenation (sufficient oxygen during major surgery and recovery to keep haemoglobin saturation >95%) and adequate perfusion (NICE). Multimodal analgesia treats postoperative pain when analgesics from different classes are combined and prevents opioid-related complications (NICE); AUGS applies it to urogynecologic surgery beginning preoperatively and continuing intraoperatively and postoperatively; ERAS Society applies it to laparoscopic gynecologic/oncology surgery. SSI prevention: nasal mupirocin plus chlorhexidine body wash before procedures where S. aureus is a likely cause (locally determined by procedure type, risk factors, impact of infection); decolonisation for identified MRSA/MSSA carriers before e.g. orthopaedic surgery, and where infection consequences are severe (e.g. cardiac surgery) — but nasal decolonisation should not be offered to all surgical patients. Razors increase SSI risk; use electric clippers with single-use head on the day of surgery. Non-iodophor-impregnated incise drapes used routinely increase risk. Skin antisepsis/antiseptic skin preparation immediately before incision (CDC: concentric circles toward periphery; WHO: rapid reduction with persistent efficacy, including before caesarean section); chlorhexidine in alcohol usually first choice, not on mucous membranes — AUGS specifies alcohol-based chlorhexidine for skin, aqueous for mucous membrane, povidone-iodine only if chlorhexidine contraindicated. Antimicrobial prophylaxis when indicated by published guidelines, within one hour prior to incision (WHO), and for clean operations with prosthetic material or catastrophic-risk SSI (CDC). Triclosan-coated sutures: NICE notes clear benefit only in paediatric surgery; CDC gives a weak recommendation (moderate-quality evidence, benefit–harm trade-off). Topical povidone-iodine, ampicillin powder, cephaloridine before wound closure rest on dated studies; gentamicin-collagen implant applies to cardiac surgery. Antibiotics treat suspected SSI presenting with cellulitis, covering likely organisms per local resistance and microbiology. Not established: doses, agent concentrations, specific analgesic drugs, glycaemic/temperature targets, outcome magnitudes, or gynecology-specific prophylaxis regimens.
key_entities: hair removal with electric clippers with a single-use head

title: Intraoperative Fluid Management Technology Indications by Surgical Risk
summary:
This community represents a single, narrow theme: the clinical situations in which intraoperative fluid management technology (i.e. cardiac output/flow-guided fluid monitoring to direct intraoperative fluid administration) is indicated, stratified by the risk of the surgery and the risk of the patient.

Two recommendations are captured, both from RCOG (Table 1, page 3). First, intraoperative fluid management technology applies to patients undergoing major or high-risk surgery; the condition attached specifies this includes major surgery with an anticipated blood loss greater than 500 ml, and major abdominal surgery. Second, the technology also applies in intermediate-risk surgery, but only for high-risk patients, with the example population given as patients aged over 80 years. The practical teaching point is therefore a two-axis trigger: either the procedure itself is major/high-risk (with the 500 ml anticipated blood loss threshold and major abdominal surgery as concrete qualifiers), or the procedure is intermediate-risk but the patient carries elevated risk, such as age over 80.

Only one guideline body contributes here: RCOG, via a single table entry. There are consequently no cross-body agreements or disagreements to reconcile, and no instance where one guideline is more specific than another — the specificity in this community (the >500 ml blood loss threshold, major abdominal surgery, age >80 years) comes entirely from RCOG's own qualifying conditions.

What this community does NOT establish: it names no specific device, monitor or brand, no particular fluid (no crystalloid, colloid or blood product is specified), and no dosing, volume or infusion rate. It gives no timings for when monitoring should start or stop, no haemodynamic targets or thresholds (e.g. stroke volume variation, cardiac index) to guide boluses, and no other patient-level risk factors beyond age over 80. It does not define "intermediate-risk" or "high-risk" surgery beyond the examples given, states no outcome or evidence grading, and makes no recommendation about postoperative fluid management, transfusion triggers, or nursing documentation and competency requirements.
key_entities: anticipated blood loss greater than 500 ml

title: Intrapartum care bundle and postpartum haemorrhage prevention
summary:
This community covers intrapartum (labour and birth) care and the immediate postpartum transition, spanning routine labour support, third-stage management, haemorrhage prevention/treatment, infection and sepsis surveillance, HIV testing, and thromboembolism risk assessment.

Third stage: WHO and RCOG both place active management of the third stage in the intrapartum phase; RCOG specifies it prevents postpartum haemorrhage in women delivering vaginally, and prevents primary PPH in women at mixed levels of bleeding risk where blood loss exceeds 1000 ml at birth. WHO adds prophylactic uterotonic administration during the third stage for all women giving birth, plus uterine tone assessment during the third stage. Early umbilical cord clamping is displaced: WHO temporarily contraindicates it in favour of late cord clamping for all births unless the neonate is asphyxiated and must be moved for resuscitation (late clamping after 1–3 minutes, classed postpartum); delayed clamping applies to both vaginal and caesarean births; RCOG states early clamping is no longer recommended as part of active management. Postpartum uterine atony increases risk of primary PPH; RCOG names oxytocin infusion as first-line treatment for primary PPH, 40 iu in 500 ml isotonic crystalloids at 125 ml/hour unless fluid restriction is necessary. RCOG also situates intraoperative cell salvage during caesarean or vaginal delivery, and perimortem caesarean section for pregnant women beyond 20 weeks with unsuccessful resuscitation.

Sepsis/infection: RCOG recommends continuous electronic fetal monitoring for maternal pyrexia, suspected or confirmed sepsis, and critically ill pregnant women, with CTG changes as an early warning sign of maternal organ dysfunction; intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for maternal pyrexia or signs of sepsis prevents group B streptococcal infection. WHO is more specific for colonisation, recommending intrapartum antibiotics for women with group B Streptococcus colonization to prevent early neonatal GBS infection.

WHO uniquely supplies labour-process and person-centred items: midwife-led continuity of care where midwifery programmes function well, continuous companionship, mobility/upright position and oral fluid and food intake for low-risk women, four-hourly digital vaginal examination, active-phase partograph with four-hour action line, male involvement respecting women's autonomy, provider-initiated HIV testing and counselling and re-testing during labour in generalized epidemic settings, and rapid HIV testing for unknown status in labour or immediately postpartum to detect HIV infection. RCOG adds repeat VTE risk assessment intrapartum and immediately postpartum, monitoring for venous thromboembolism if admitted for any reason or if intercurrent problems develop.

Not established: no drug doses or agents for prophylactic uterotonics, no antibiotic names/doses, no thresholds for cell salvage or CTG interpretation, no second-line PPH escalation, no outcome or effectiveness data, and no explicit conflict resolution between WHO and RCOG.
key_entities: active management of the third stage of labour
early neonatal group b streptococcus infection

title: Oxytocin IV bolus injection rate safety
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused safety theme: the haemodynamic risk associated with the route and speed of oxytocin administration when it is given as an intravenous bolus, principally in the context of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) prevention. Both relations in the community converge on the same causal claim — that oxytocin, and specifically oxytocin given by intravenous bolus injection, increases the risk of adverse haemodynamic effect. The populations attached are women receiving oxytocin by intravenous bolus injection, and more specifically women receiving oxytocin for the prevention of postpartum haemorrhage. The governing condition in both cases is the injection rate: the risk is stated to arise if a rapid injection rate is used, and a slow injection rate is preferred. The practical, teachable message for perioperative and intrapartum nursing staff is therefore that when the IV bolus route is used for oxytocin in PPH prophylaxis, the bolus should be delivered slowly rather than rapidly, in order to mitigate adverse haemodynamic effects.

Only one guideline body contributes to this community: WHO (WHO T1 p19). Because there is a single contributing source, the community contains no inter-body disagreement and no instance of one organisation being more or less specific than another; the two relations are complementary restatements, with the second narrowing the population from 'any woman receiving IV bolus oxytocin' to 'women receiving oxytocin for prevention of postpartum haemorrhage' and naming the route explicitly as the risk-bearing entity.

What this community does not establish: it gives no numeric dose of oxytocin, no defined injection duration or mL/min threshold that distinguishes 'slow' from 'rapid', and no definition or grading of the 'adverse haemodynamic effect' (e.g. hypotension, tachycardia, arrhythmia are not named). It does not compare IV bolus with IV infusion or intramuscular administration, does not address other uterotonics, does not identify higher-risk subgroups such as women with cardiac disease or those under regional or general anaesthesia, and specifies no monitoring, treatment or escalation pathway if a haemodynamic effect occurs.

title: IVIG and clindamycin for streptococcal toxic shock
summary:
This community represents adjunctive immunomodulatory and antimicrobial therapy for severe Gram-positive infection in obstetric patients — specifically group A streptococcal (GAS) sepsis, toxic shock and Gram-positive necrotising infection. All relations derive from a single source, RCOG Top Tip / guidance page 11 (RCOG T1 p11); no other guideline body contributes, so no inter-body disagreement can be assessed.

Main recommendations: (1) Clindamycin treats GAS sepsis in pregnant women with suspected GAS sepsis, and is specified for use in combination with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). (2) IVIG treats GAS sepsis in the same population, in combination with clindamycin — the two entries are reciprocal, indicating a paired regimen rather than either agent alone. (3) IVIG treats toxic shock and Gram-positive necrotising infection, with two levels of population detail: 'the sickest women' when other measures are failing, and 'critically ill women with Gram-positive infections' in severe Gram-positive necrotising infections and toxic shock. IVIG is therefore positioned as rescue/adjunctive therapy after other measures fail, not first-line. (4) Administration detail: IVIG should be given in a critical care setting with a blood warming device — a concrete nursing/equipment requirement relevant to competency checklists and critical care transfer planning. (5) Contraindication: IVIG is contraindicated in congenital immunoglobulin A deficiency, stated twice, once explicitly for mothers with congenital IgA deficiency — so IgA status is a screening consideration before administration.

What this community does NOT establish: no doses, infusion rates, durations, or number of IVIG courses; no numeric thresholds (lactate, blood pressure, temperature) defining 'sickest' or 'critically ill'; no timing window from recognition to administration; no definition of which 'other measures' must have failed first; no alternative antibiotic if clindamycin is unsuitable; no monitoring parameters or adverse-event management for IVIG beyond the IgA contraindication; no postpartum versus antenatal differentiation; and no guidance on neonatal implications. It also does not address diagnosis or microbiological confirmation of GAS.
key_entities: pregnant women with suspected GAS sepsis
critical care setting with blood warming device

title: Ketamine as adjunct opioid-sparing analgesia
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused theme: the use of low-dose intravenous ketamine as an adjunct to intravenous opioid analgesia in the perioperative period, including its role in patients with opioid sensitivity or abnormal pain sensitivity. All relations concern one drug (intravenous ketamine) and three overlapping pain targets: moderate to severe pain, pain generally in adults receiving an IV opioid, and abnormal pain sensitivity.

Main recommendations: (1) For people whose pain is expected to be moderate to severe, where an intravenous opioid alone does not give adequate pain relief, or who have opioid sensitivity, give a single dose of intravenous ketamine 0.25 mg/kg to 1 mg/kg during or immediately after surgery, to supplement other types of pain relief (NICE T1 p14). (2) For adults receiving an intravenous opioid, ketamine may be added to the opioid if the opioid alone does not provide adequate pain relief or if the person is opioid sensitive (NICE T1 p28). (3) For people who are opioid sensitive specifically, a single dose of 0.25 mg/kg to 1 mg/kg may be considered for abnormal pain sensitivity (NICE T1 p28).

Guideline contribution: only NICE contributes here (T1, pages 14 and 28); there are no competing or corroborating bodies in this community, so no inter-body disagreement can be identified. The p14 statement is the most specific on timing (during or immediately after surgery) and on framing ketamine as supplementary; p28 statements are more specific about the population (adults on IV opioid; opioid-sensitive people) and about the indication of abnormal pain sensitivity. Dosing (single dose, 0.25–1 mg/kg) is consistent across pages.

What this community does NOT establish: it gives no infusion or repeat-dosing regimen, no route other than intravenous, no guidance for children or obstetric/gynecologic subgroups specifically, no monitoring requirements, contraindications, or adverse-effect management (e.g., psychomimetic effects), no comparative effectiveness versus other adjuncts, and no criteria defining "adequate pain relief" or "opioid sensitivity."

title: IV Site Surveillance for Infusion Complications
summary:
This community represents surveillance of peripheral/central intravenous infusion systems for the early detection of intravenous therapy complications during perioperative and general nursing care. Two related recommendations define a tiered monitoring frequency based on patient vulnerability and drug risk.

Baseline recommendation: assessment of the intravenous infusion system monitors for intravenous therapy complications in all patients receiving intravenous therapy, performed routinely throughout the course of treatment. The relation does not fix a numeric interval for this general population, only that assessment is recurrent for the duration of therapy.

High-risk recommendation: hourly intravenous site assessment monitors for intravenous therapy complications in two specified populations — neonatal and pediatric patients, and any patient receiving infusions of vesicant medications — with an explicit hourly frequency. This is the more specific of the two statements, converting 'routine' surveillance into a defined one-hour cadence where extravasation or tissue injury risk is greatest.

Guideline contribution: both relations derive from a single source, OpenRN Nursing Skills (Volume 2, p. 1359). There is therefore no cross-body disagreement to reconcile; rather, the corpus shows an internal escalation of specificity — the general 'infusion system assessment / routine' statement is refined by the 'site assessment / hourly' statement for neonates, children, and vesicant infusions. Educators can present these as one nested standard rather than competing guidance.

What this community does NOT establish: it names no specific vesicant drugs, no assessment findings or thresholds (no criteria for redness, swelling, pain, blanching, capillary refill, infusion pressure, or blood return), no definition or subtypes of intravenous therapy complication (infiltration, extravasation, phlebitis, infection, air embolus are not enumerated), and no interventions, escalation pathways, or documentation requirements once a complication is suspected. It does not quantify 'routinely' for adults on non-vesicant infusions, does not distinguish peripheral from central access, does not address dwell time or catheter replacement, and provides no outcome or quality-indicator data supporting hourly versus less frequent checks.

title: Iodine and iodophor antiseptic contraindications
summary:
This community represents the safety profile of iodine-based skin antiseptics (iodine and iodophors, e.g. povidone-iodine-type preparations) used for perioperative skin preparation in gynecologic surgery. Only three relations exist, and all concern patient-level tolerability rather than antimicrobial efficacy.

Main recommendations: (1) Iodine is contraindicated in patients with allergies to iodine preparations (WHO Tier 1, p57). (2) Iodophor is likewise contraindicated, with a slightly broader population statement — patients with allergies to iodophors OR to iodine (WHO T1 p57). This pairing implies that a documented iodine allergy should exclude both the elemental iodine agent and iodophor formulations, so an alternative antiseptic must be selected preoperatively. (3) Iodine increases the risk of skin irritation (CDC Tier 1, p10); this relation carries no population or conditional qualifier, so it is stated as a general hazard rather than one limited to allergic patients.

Contributing bodies: WHO supplies both contraindication relations and is the more specific source, naming the allergy population and distinguishing iodine from iodophor. CDC contributes the single adverse-effect relation (skin irritation) attached to iodine only. The two bodies do not conflict; they address different endpoints — WHO on absolute contraindication by allergy history, CDC on an irritant adverse effect. Notably, CDC does not extend the skin-irritation risk to iodophors in this community, and WHO does not quantify or grade the irritation risk.

What this community does NOT establish: no alternative antiseptic is named (no chlorhexidine-alcohol or alcohol-based comparator), no efficacy or surgical-site-infection outcome data, no application timing, contact/drying time, concentration threshold or volume, no frequency or severity estimate for skin irritation, no guidance on thyroid effects, iodine absorption, pregnancy, neonates or mucosal/vaginal use, and no screening or documentation process for identifying iodine allergy. It also does not address management if irritation or a reaction occurs intraoperatively or postoperatively. Educators should treat this as an allergy-screening and skin-tolerance theme only, and seek other communities for antiseptic selection and technique.

title: Iodophor Antisepsis Risks and Contraindications
summary:
This community represents a narrow but clinically important safety theme: the adverse-effect and contraindication profile of iodophor (povidone-iodine type) antiseptics used for skin preparation in perioperative gynecologic care. All three relations derive from a single source, WHO Technical/Guideline document T1, page 57; no other guideline body (e.g., professional nursing or surgical societies) contributes to this cluster, so there are no inter-organisational disagreements to reconcile — but equally no external corroboration.

Three points are established. First, iodophor increases the risk of allergic reaction; this is stated generally, without a qualifying population or triggering condition. Second, iodophor increases the risk of an increased serum iodine level; here WHO is more specific, attaching the population 'patients treated with iodine or iodophor solutions' and the condition 'especially when large areas were treated for a long period' — i.e., the systemic iodine-absorption hazard is framed as dose- and exposure-dependent (broad surface area plus prolonged application), which is directly relevant to extensive abdominal/perineal prepping and to prolonged gynecologic procedures. Third, iodophor is contraindicated with allergy to iodine preparations, for the population 'patients with allergies to iodophors or iodine' — supporting a pre-procedure allergy screen for iodine/iodophor sensitivity and substitution of an alternative agent when such allergy is documented.

Educationally, the actionable teaching points are: screen for iodine/iodophor allergy before prep; limit treated surface area and contact duration where feasible; and remain alert to systemic iodine effects after large-area, long-duration application.

What this community does NOT establish: no numeric thresholds (no serum iodine cut-off, no maximum body-surface area, no time limit defining 'long period'), no specified iodophor concentration or product, no named alternative antiseptic (e.g., chlorhexidine) for iodine-allergic patients, no monitoring protocol or laboratory testing schedule, no management pathway for allergic reaction, and no statements about neonatal, pregnant, thyroid-disease or mucosal-application subgroups. Comparative efficacy against other antiseptics and any surgical-site-infection outcomes are entirely outside this cluster.

title: Post-Prostate Surgery Bladder Irrigation and Continence
summary:
This small community centres on the postoperative care of patients undergoing prostate surgery, linking two distinct concerns: continence sequelae of the surgery itself, and the use of continuous bladder irrigation to keep the urinary tract patent afterwards.

Two substantive points are established. First, prostate surgery is identified as increasing the risk of bowel incontinence (OpenRN Nursing Skills Volume 2, p1179) — relevant to preoperative counselling, postoperative assessment, and skin/continence care planning. Second, an irrigation catheter applies to prostate surgery, described as typically used after surgery to flush the surgical area, and it prevents bladder blood clot formation in the population of patients after prostate surgery, under the condition that it is used to irrigate the bladder (p1208). The actionable nursing implication is monitoring irrigation flow and outflow characteristics so that clots do not obstruct the bladder in this specific postoperative population.

Only one guideline body contributes: the OpenRN open-access nursing skills text (Volume 2), drawing on two separate pages (p1179 for the continence risk, p1208 for the irrigation catheter). Because there is a single source, there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile; however, the two entries differ in specificity. The irrigation statement is the more specific of the two — it names the population (post-prostate-surgery patients), the intervention (irrigation catheter), the mechanism (flushing the surgical area/irrigating the bladder) and the outcome averted (bladder clot formation). The bowel incontinence statement is a bare risk association with no population subgroup, timeframe, or severity qualifier.

The community does not establish: any irrigation solution (e.g. normal saline), volume, flow rate, duration, or discontinuation criteria; no drugs, doses or thresholds of any kind; no timing for catheter removal; no distinction between prostate surgery types (e.g. TURP versus prostatectomy); no incidence figures or duration for bowel incontinence; no management or rehabilitation pathway for incontinence; no link between the incontinence risk and the irrigation catheter; and no complications of irrigation itself (e.g. infection, hyponatraemia, catheter blockage escalation).

title: Emollient Skin Protection Preventing Dermatitis and Cracking
summary:
This community centers on topical emollient use to protect skin integrity, split across two populations: health-care workers whose hands are repeatedly exposed to hand hygiene products, and patients whose skin is dry or at risk of breakdown.

For health-care personnel, the CDC hand hygiene guideline (Tab 1) offers a bundled approach to preventing irritant contact dermatitis: hand lotions or creams applied in association with handwashing or hand antisepsis (p34; also p29 listing lotion and cream separately), barrier creams as one element of a minimization strategy (p21), alcohol-based hand rubs containing emollients used specifically to reduce exposure to irritating soaps and detergents (p21), replacing products with high irritation potential (p21), and education of personnel about the risks of irritant contact dermatitis (p21). Notably, CDC frames dermatitis prevention as both a product-selection and an educational/behavioral intervention, not solely a moisturizer issue.

For patients, OpenRN (Tab 2) addresses skin cracking rather than dermatitis. Lotion is recommended for clients with rarely moist skin, explicitly at a Braden moisture subscale score of 4 (p731), and lotion application is recommended for clients with dry skin areas (p753). OpenRN is the more specific source on patient-level triggers, naming a concrete assessment threshold (Braden moisture = 4); CDC is the more specific source on occupational product choice (emollient-containing alcohol rubs, barrier creams, substituting high-irritation products).

The two bodies do not conflict; they address different populations and different outcomes (occupational irritant contact dermatitis vs. patient skin cracking), converging only on lotion/cream as the shared intervention.

What this community does NOT establish: no specific product brands, active ingredients, concentrations, application volumes, or dosing frequencies/timings; no evidence ranking among barrier cream, lotion, cream, emollient-containing rub, education, or product substitution; no guidance for Braden moisture scores below 4; no statement that lotions prevent infection, pressure injury, or dermatitis in patients; and no comment on compatibility of lotions with gloves or with alcohol-based rub efficacy.
key_entities: education of personnel regarding risks of irritant contact dermatitis
replacing products with high irritation potential
clients with rarely moist skin (Braden moisture score 4)

title: Jet Injector Flu Vaccine Local Reactions
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: the expected local (injection-site) adverse reaction profile of needle-free jet injector administration of influenza vaccine in adults. All six relations share one source entity (jet injector), one relation type (INCREASES_RISK_OF), one population (adults receiving jet injector flu vaccine), and one timing condition (up to seven days post-vaccination).

The practical takeaway for nurse educators is anticipatory guidance and documentation: adults who receive influenza vaccine by jet injector should be counselled that, for up to seven days after vaccination, they are at increased risk of injection-site tenderness, pain, redness, itching, swelling, and bruising. Because the same population and time window attaches to all six reactions, they can be taught as a single cluster of expected local effects rather than as separate risks, and a seven-day window is the concrete threshold for distinguishing expected local reactogenicity from a complaint warranting further assessment.

Only one guideline body contributes to this community: OpenRN (Nursing Skills, Volume 2, p. 1021). There is therefore no cross-corpus agreement or disagreement to reconcile, no competing specificity between bodies, and no second source corroborating the seven-day window or the six-symptom list.

Important limits: the community does NOT establish incidence or severity rates for any of the six reactions, nor does it rank them. It does not compare jet injector with needle-and-syringe intramuscular or intradermal administration, so no claim of relative risk can be drawn. It specifies no management or treatment (no cold compress, analgesic, or acetaminophen/ibuprofen recommendation), no escalation or referral criteria, and no contraindications to jet injector use. It says nothing about systemic reactions (fever, myalgia, syncope, anaphylaxis), nothing about children, pregnancy, immunocompromised, or perioperative gynecologic surgical patients specifically, nothing about vaccine brand, dose, or anatomic site, and nothing about efficacy or immunogenicity. Quality-improvement leads seeking those elements will need additional sources beyond this community.
key_entities: adults receiving jet injector flu vaccine

title: Joint stabilization device risks in children
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused safety theme: the iatrogenic harms associated with joint stabilization devices (arm boards/splints used to immobilize a joint) applied to secure intravenous access in pediatric patients. All three relations in the community share the same subject, the same population, and the same qualifying condition, so the theme is best read as one recommendation expressed through three distinct adverse outcomes.

Main content: In children with intravenous access, a joint stabilization device increases the risk of (1) circulatory constriction, (2) pressure injury, and (3) nerve damage. The stated condition for all three risks is identical and specific: the harm arises if the device exerts pressure in the area of flexion or under the device. The practical implication for education and QI work is that pediatric IV sites immobilized with a stabilization device require assessment of the flexion area and the skin/tissue beneath the device for signs of constricted circulation, pressure damage, and neurologic compromise, and that the device should not be applied so as to create pressure at those points.

Contributing bodies: only one source contributes to this community — OpenRN (Nursing Skills, Text 2, p1359). Because there is a single source, there are no inter-guideline disagreements, no competing thresholds, and no instance of one body being more specific than another; the corpus offers no corroborating or conflicting pediatric IV immobilization guidance here.

What this community does NOT establish: it gives no assessment frequency or timing (no interval for neurovascular checks), no duration limits for device use, no specific device types, sizes, or padding materials, and no anatomical sites beyond the general "area of flexion." It specifies no age or weight bands within the pediatric population, no severity grading or staging for the pressure injury or nerve damage, no treatment or escalation pathway once harm is detected, and no documentation requirements. It also does not address adults with intravenous access, nor does it weigh these risks against the benefit of maintaining IV patency or identify alternatives to joint stabilization.

title: Breakthrough Pain Management After Gynecologic Surgery
summary:
This community represents the pharmacologic management of breakthrough pain in the perioperative/postoperative setting, specifically what to add when baseline non-opioid analgesia is inadequate. Two agent classes converge on the same target concept (breakthrough pain): opioids and ketorolac.

Recommendations with their populations and conditions: (1) AUGS (T2 p9) directs that an opioid be used to treat breakthrough pain in postoperative patients, with the explicit condition that this occurs only when acetaminophen and NSAIDs are not sufficient — i.e., opioids are positioned as escalation therapy layered on a multimodal non-opioid base, not first-line. (2) OpenRN (T2; T2 p825) directs that ketorolac treats breakthrough pain in adults/clients with severe acute pain who are already being treated with opioids, and constrains duration to short-term management, up to five days in adults. The two OpenRN statements are duplicative in substance, differing only in wording ("adults" vs "clients") and in citation granularity.

Contributing bodies and differences: AUGS contributes the postoperative, stepped-analgesia framing but names no specific opioid, dose, route, or duration. OpenRN is more specific in two respects — it names a single drug (ketorolac) and it attaches a concrete duration threshold (up to five days in adults) plus a prerequisite (concurrent opioid therapy, severe acute pain). Notably, the two bodies describe reciprocal sequencing: AUGS adds an opioid when NSAIDs are insufficient, while OpenRN adds an NSAID (ketorolac) to patients already on opioids. Neither contradicts the other, but neither reconciles the sequence.

What this community does NOT establish: no specific opioid agents, doses, routes, intervals, or maximum opioid duration; no pain-score threshold defining "breakthrough" or "severe acute"; no pediatric, geriatric, renal, bleeding-risk, or pregnancy/lactation guidance; no ketorolac dosing or contraindications; no monitoring, de-escalation, or discharge-prescribing rules; and no gynecologic-procedure-specific tailoring beyond the general postoperative population.

title: Perioperative acute kidney injury risk detection
summary:
This community centres on acute kidney injury (AKI) as a perioperative risk in surgical and obstetric/gynaecologic patients, and on the two ways it is addressed: preoperative risk-based laboratory detection, intraoperative/postoperative urine output monitoring, and avoidance of a fluid choice that raises risk.

Detection: NICE recommends kidney function testing in the preoperative phase for patients undergoing elective surgery, but only on a considered, non-routine basis and only in people already at risk of AKI. Three risk-stratified populations are named: (1) ASA grade 1 patients at risk of AKI, where the test is considered rather than routinely offered; (2) patients at risk of AKI who are ASA grade 2 undergoing intermediate surgery, or ASA grade 1 undergoing major or complex surgery ("consider only"); and (3) ASA grade 3 or ASA grade 4 patients undergoing minor surgery, again only if at risk of AKI. The consistent conditional language means testing is a clinical judgement, not a blanket requirement.

Monitoring: RCOG specifies an hourly urometer to monitor for AKI in women receiving fluid resuscitation, used when indicated so that urine output is measured with precision — the obstetric/haemorrhage-facing counterpart to NICE's preoperative testing.

Risk factor: NICE states that colloid increases the risk of AKI in adults undergoing surgery, implying colloid avoidance in fluid strategy.

Contributing bodies: NICE (T1 pp9, 24) supplies preoperative testing thresholds by ASA grade and surgical severity plus the colloid risk statement; RCOG (T1 p11) is more specific about bedside monitoring technique in women receiving fluid resuscitation. They are complementary rather than conflicting, operating in different phases.

Not established: no AKI diagnostic criteria, creatinine or eGFR thresholds, urine-output cut-offs (e.g. mL/kg/h), or definitions of "at risk of AKI"; no named alternative fluids (crystalloid regimens, doses); no guidance for ASA 2 patients undergoing minor surgery, ASA 3–4 undergoing major surgery, or emergency surgery; no timing interval for preoperative testing; and no escalation, referral or treatment pathway once AKI is detected.

title: Needle Gauge Selection and Injection-Site Reactions
summary:
This community is narrow and single-sourced: it represents needle-selection technique for parenteral injections and its relationship to local injection-site reactions. All six relations originate from one node, 'larger diameter needle', and all point to local adverse effects of injection: pain, injection site pain, redness, injection site redness, swelling, and injection site swelling. Note that the graph pairs each generic symptom (pain, redness, swelling) with an explicitly site-localized duplicate, so the theme is effectively three distinct local reactions expressed twice.

Main recommendation as encoded: for the population 'patients receiving injections' (no age, procedure, drug, or route sub-population specified), selecting a larger diameter needle is asserted to PREVENT injection site pain, redness, and swelling. No condition beyond 'patients receiving injections' is attached to any edge, and no threshold gauge value, needle length, injection volume, medication, anatomical site, or timing is given.

Guideline contribution is homogeneous: every relation derives from a single source, OpenRN Tier 2, page 1006 (Open RN nursing textbook/clinical skills content). Because only one body contributes, there are no inter-guideline disagreements, no points of divergence, and no instance where one body is more specific than another; conversely, there is also no corroboration or triangulation from surgical, anesthesia, or perioperative gynecologic guideline bodies within this community.

What the community does NOT establish: it does not define what counts as 'larger' (no gauge numbers such as 18G vs 25G), does not distinguish intramuscular from subcutaneous or intradermal routes, and does not address gynecologic or perioperative populations specifically despite the corpus context. It does not link needle diameter to infection, bleeding, hematoma, tissue damage, drug absorption, or patient anxiety, nor to any medication class (e.g., anticoagulants, antibiotics, hormonal agents). It provides no dosing, timing, monitoring interval, or documentation guidance, and no evidence grade or strength-of-recommendation. Educators should treat it as a single technique claim requiring external corroboration before use in competency materials.

title: Lecanemab risks: falls and brain swelling
summary:
This community is very small and represents a single pharmacovigilance theme: adverse-effect risks associated with lecanemab, an anti-amyloid monoclonal antibody used in Alzheimer's disease. Two relations are captured, both drawn from the same source (OpenRN Nursing Pharmacology, Textbook 2, p. 468): lecanemab increases the risk of falls, and lecanemab increases the risk of brain swelling (cerebral edema, the ARIA-type toxicity clinicians commonly monitor). For a nurse educator, the usable teaching point is that a patient on lecanemab carries a dual safety burden — a neurologic risk (brain swelling) and a functional/injury risk (falling) — which together argue for fall-precaution bundling and neurologic status surveillance in any care setting, including perioperative gynecologic care where sedation, positioning, and post-anesthesia mobilization could compound fall risk.

Importantly, the community attaches no population qualifier, no condition or trigger, no dose, no threshold (e.g., no infusion dose, no MRI monitoring interval, no timing of onset), and no severity grading to either relation. The risks are stated as unconditional, drug-level associations only.

Only one guideline body contributes: OpenRN (open-access nursing pharmacology textbook content). There is therefore no cross-body comparison available — no specialty society, anesthesia, or perioperative gynecology guideline is represented, so no statement can be made about where bodies agree, differ, or where one is more granular than another.

What this community does NOT establish: it does not specify which patients are at greatest risk (age, frailty, ApoE4 status, anticoagulation, prior stroke); it does not give monitoring recommendations, MRI surveillance schedules, or criteria for holding or discontinuing lecanemab; it does not describe fall-prevention interventions, assessment tools, or perioperative management (whether to interrupt therapy before surgery); it does not quantify incidence or relative risk; and it does not link lecanemab to any gynecologic surgical outcome, bleeding risk, or anesthetic interaction. Any protocol built from this theme requires supplementation from external, more specific sources.

title: Managing Leg Cramps in Pregnancy
summary:
This community represents a single, narrow clinical theme: symptom relief for leg cramps as a common physiological complaint of pregnancy. Three intervention options converge on the same outcome entity (leg cramps) with identical population and conditional framing.

Main recommendations: For pregnant women, magnesium, calcium, or non-pharmacological treatment options may be used for the relief of leg cramps. Each of these three relations carries the same qualifying condition — the choice is to be made 'based on a woman's preferences and available options.' This makes the recommendation explicitly preference-sensitive and context-dependent rather than a fixed protocol: no one agent is positioned as first-line over the others, and the guideline defers to shared decision-making and local availability. Practically, this supports nurse-led counselling in which magnesium supplementation, calcium supplementation, and non-drug measures are presented as equivalent, discussable choices for the pregnant patient reporting leg cramps.

Guideline contribution: All three relations derive from a single source, the WHO antenatal care guidance (WHO T1, p13). There is therefore no cross-body comparison available in this community — no competing or more specific recommendation from another guideline body, and no point of disagreement or differing specificity to reconcile. The theme is entirely WHO-attributed.

What this community does NOT establish: it specifies no doses, salts/formulations, frequencies, durations, or timing by trimester for magnesium or calcium; it does not enumerate which non-pharmacological measures qualify (e.g., no named stretching, massage, heat, or exercise modality); it sets no severity thresholds or symptom criteria for initiating treatment. It gives no efficacy ranking, no comparative effect sizes, no safety warnings, contraindications, or interactions, and no monitoring or follow-up requirements. It does not address leg cramps outside pregnancy, nor does it link the theme to perioperative gynecologic care, anaesthesia, venous thromboembolism, or differential diagnosis of leg pain. Quality-improvement leads should treat this as a counselling and shared-decision-making prompt, and source dosing and non-pharmacological specifics from elsewhere.

title: Neonatal Jaundice Detection and Phototherapy
summary:
This small community represents neonatal hyperbilirubinemia (jaundice) as a two-step clinical theme: laboratory detection followed by treatment escalation. It sits somewhat outside the perioperative gynecologic focus of the wider corpus, connecting instead to newborn/postpartum care.

Detection: a serum bilirubin test is the recommended means of detecting jaundice in the newborn, with the specific stated context of being performed in the emergency room at 72 hours of age (WHO T1 p200). This is the more procedurally specific of the two relations, naming both the setting (emergency room) and the timing threshold (72 hours of life).

Treatment: light therapy (phototherapy) treats jaundice in newborn babies, and the stated condition for its use is when mild jaundice does not resolve on its own and additional treatment is required (OpenRN T2 p817). This frames phototherapy as second-line after expectant management of mild jaundice, rather than as an initial intervention.

Contributing bodies: two sources contribute, with no contradiction between them but different emphases. WHO (T1) supplies the diagnostic/timing element anchored to acute presentation at 72 hours. OpenRN (T2) supplies the therapeutic element and the escalation trigger (failure of spontaneous resolution of mild jaundice). Neither source is contradicted; they are complementary halves of a detect-then-treat pathway.

What the community does NOT establish: no numeric serum bilirubin thresholds (e.g., mg/dL or µmol/L cut-points) are given for either diagnosis or for initiating phototherapy; no gestational-age, birth-weight, or risk-factor stratification is provided. There is no mention of transcutaneous bilirubin screening, repeat or serial testing intervals, exchange transfusion, IVIG, pharmacologic agents, or feeding/hydration support. Duration of phototherapy, irradiance, eye protection, monitoring during therapy, discontinuation criteria, and follow-up are absent. The relations also do not define "mild" jaundice, do not address kernicterus risk, and do not link jaundice to maternal factors, blood group incompatibility, or any perioperative or gynecologic context. Local protocol should supply thresholds and monitoring detail.

title: IV Site Local Infection: Risk, Detection, Treatment
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: local infection at a peripheral intravenous access site in patients with intravenous access — its causative risk factors, its detection, and its management. All four relations converge on the entity 'local infection', making this a cause-detect-treat cluster rather than a broad infection-control framework.

Risk factors: (1) Nonadherence to aseptic technique increases the risk of local infection in patients with intravenous access, specifically during IV initiation or IV maintenance — i.e., the risk window spans both insertion and ongoing care, not insertion alone. (2) A contaminated or non-intact dressing increases risk in the same population, with the condition specified as when the dressing becomes contaminated or non-intact over the access site.

Detection: Culture of purulent drainage and of the catheter tip detects local infection in patients with intravenous access, conditioned on infection being suspected — that is, culturing is a suspicion-triggered diagnostic step, not routine surveillance.

Treatment: Cannula removal combined with sterile cleaning of the site treats local infection in patients with intravenous access; no condition is attached, implying it applies whenever local infection is identified in this population.

Guideline contribution: only one source contributes here — OpenRN Nursing Skills (Volume 2, p1363). There are therefore no inter-body disagreements, no competing recommendations, and no instance of one body being more specific than another; the entire theme rests on a single corpus location and should be treated as single-source evidence for QI purposes.

What the community does NOT establish: no antimicrobial agents, drugs, doses, or routes are named; no dressing type, dressing-change interval, catheter dwell-time threshold, or antiseptic (e.g., chlorhexidine concentration) is specified; no timing for obtaining cultures or for re-siting the cannula is given. Clinical signs defining 'suspected infection' beyond purulent drainage are not enumerated, and no distinction is drawn between peripheral and central access, phlebitis versus infection, or local versus bloodstream infection. Special populations (pediatric, immunocompromised, critical care) are not addressed.
key_entities: cannula removal and sterile site cleaning
culture of purulent drainage and catheter tip

title: Antihypertensive Cardiac Contraindications and Risks
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused theme: cardiac safety considerations when antihypertensive agents are used in clients with hypertension, specifically beta-blockers and long-acting calcium channel blockers (CCBs). All eight relations derive from one source, RNAO Best Practice Guideline Toolkit 2 (T2), p141, so the theme reflects the nursing-management/medication-review portion of that guideline rather than a cross-corpus consensus.

Main content: For clients with hypertension, beta-blockers are contraindicated with heart block, with the explicit qualifying condition 'in the absence of a pacemaker' — implying the contraindication is conditional rather than absolute if pacing is present. Long-acting calcium channel blockers carry a broader contraindication set for clients with hypertension: heart block, bradycardia, ventricular dysfunction, and pregnancy. Separately, for the population of clients already taking calcium channel blockers, long-acting CCBs are recorded as increasing the risk of heart block, peripheral edema, and congestive heart failure. Note the dual framing of heart block: it is both a contraindication (pre-existing condition screening in hypertensive clients) and an adverse outcome risk (monitoring in clients on therapy). Practically, this supports pre-prescribing screening for conduction disease, bradycardia, ventricular dysfunction and pregnancy status, and ongoing assessment for edema, heart-failure signs and new conduction abnormality in clients on CCB therapy.

Contributing bodies and differences: RNAO is the only contributing body; no other guideline body appears, so no agreement, conflict, or difference in specificity between organisations can be characterised. Within RNAO, the beta-blocker entry is more specific than the CCB entries because it names the pacemaker modifier.

What this community does NOT establish: no drug names within classes, doses, blood-pressure thresholds, heart-rate or PR-interval cut-offs, monitoring intervals, timing of assessment, or perioperative/gynecologic-surgery-specific instructions. It does not state alternative agents, pregnancy-safe substitutes, management of detected adverse effects, severity grading of heart block, or nursing accountability for prescribing decisions. It also gives no beta-blocker adverse-risk relations and no evidence grading.

title: LMWH thromboprophylaxis and bleeding contraindications in pregnancy
summary:
This community centres on low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) as the pivotal agent for venous thromboembolism (VTE) prevention and treatment in pregnancy, balanced against active bleeding as a temporary contraindication. All relations derive from a single guideline body, the RCOG (Trimester 1 document, pages 2, 7, 10, 23, 27), so no inter-body disagreement can be assessed.

Prevention: LMWH prevents VTE in pregnant women when used for thromboprophylaxis (p23). The most operationally specific statement (p2) extends this to women admitted to hospital when pregnant, explicitly including admissions to the gynaecology ward with hyperemesis gravidarum or ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, unless a specific contraindication such as risk of labour or active bleeding is present.

Treatment: LMWH treats VTE in any woman with symptoms and/or signs suggestive of VTE in pregnancy, and should be given until the diagnosis is excluded by objective testing, unless treatment is strongly contraindicated (p2, p7). This establishes empirical anticoagulation ahead of confirmatory imaging as the default nursing/medical expectation.

Contraindications: LMWH is temporarily contraindicated in active bleeding — described variously as women with active bleeding with dosing delayed while bleeding is active (p27), women admitted to hospital when pregnant while there is active bleeding (p10), and while active bleeding or risk of labour is present (p2). Pages 2 and 10 are population-specific (pregnant hospital admissions) and p2 adds risk of labour; p27 is the most explicit about timing, framing the contraindication as a delay rather than permanent avoidance.

Not established: the community specifies no LMWH agent names, doses, weight bands, renal thresholds, platelet counts, or duration of prophylaxis; no timing relative to neuraxial anaesthesia, surgery, or delivery; no risk-scoring tool or threshold that triggers prophylaxis; no alternatives (e.g. unfractionated heparin, mechanical prophylaxis) when LMWH is contraindicated; no definition of "active bleeding" or "risk of labour"; and no guidance on when to restart LMWH once bleeding settles, nor any monitoring or reversal pathway.

title: Advanced Wound Dressings Preventing Periwound Maceration
summary:
This community represents a single clinical theme: selection of advanced contact-layer and foam dressings to protect periwound skin and intact skin in patients with exuding wounds, with maceration prevention as the shared outcome. All relations derive from one source, OpenRN Nursing Skills (Table 2, p. 1423); no second guideline body contributes, so no inter-body disagreement can be assessed.

Three products are named. Adaptic contact layer dressing prevents maceration in wounds ranging from dry to heavily exuding, conditional on being applied directly to the wound as the primary wound contact dressing. Lyofoam foam dressing is indicated for patients with moderately to highly exuding wounds and is credited with two outcomes: preventing exudate leakage and preventing maceration. Mepilex Border foam dressing is indicated for patients with moderate to high exuding wounds, where maceration prevention is conditional on the Safetac layer sealing the wound edges; it additionally prevents pressure injury when used specifically for skin and pressure injury protection, and prevents additional pain when the condition is dressing change.

Notable specificity differences within the corpus: Adaptic has the broadest exudate range (dry through heavily exuding) but only one stated benefit and requires primary-contact placement; Lyofoam and Mepilex Border are restricted to moderate-to-high exudate; Mepilex Border is the most mechanistically specified (Safetac edge seal) and the only dressing linked to pressure injury prevention and to reduced pain at dressing change.

What this community does NOT establish: no dressing change frequency, wear time, dressing size, or duration of therapy; no comparative effectiveness or ranking among Adaptic, Lyofoam and Mepilex Border; no specification of wound type (surgical, gynecologic incision, ulcer) or perioperative timing; no contraindications, allergy cautions, or infected-wound guidance; no antimicrobial or drug component; and no thresholds defining "moderate," "high," or "heavy" exudate. Pressure injury prevention is asserted only for Mepilex Border and only when used for that purpose, with no anatomical site, risk score, or repositioning schedule attached.

title: Exudate Management to Prevent Periwound Maceration
summary: This community centers on a single clinical concern in wound care: protecting the periwound skin from maceration by controlling moisture, chiefly through absorbent dressing selection and drying technique during wound cleansing. Four interventions converge on the outcome 'maceration of surrounding tissue.' Hydrofiber dressings and alginate dressings are each indicated for wounds with large amounts of exudate; absorbent dressings more broadly are indicated for wounds with excessive exudate, specifically when excessive exudate must be managed. Distinct from dressing choice, drying the wound edges with sterile gauze — using sterile forceps to avoid excess moisture — is recommended for patients undergoing wound cleansing, making technique as well as product a maceration-prevention lever. The community also carries an explicit safety counterpoint: alginate dressing increases the risk of wound bed injury when used in dry wounds. Alginate is therefore the only entity here with both a benefit and a harm condition attached, and the moisture status of the wound (heavily exuding versus dry) is the decisive assessment that determines whether it helps or harms. All relations derive from a single guideline source, OpenRN Nursing Skills (Text 2, pages 1145, 1151, and 1185); no second guideline body contributes, so there are no inter-organizational disagreements to reconcile, though the corpus is internally more specific about alginate (with an explicit contraindication) than about hydrofiber or generic absorbent dressings, for which no dry-wound caution is recorded. The community does not establish quantitative thresholds for what counts as 'large' or 'excessive' exudate, dressing change frequency or wear time, comparative effectiveness among hydrofiber, alginate and other absorbent dressings, or any preference ordering. It says nothing about specific patient populations beyond 'patients undergoing wound cleansing' — notably no gynecologic, postoperative, or perioperative population is named — and nothing about barrier films, ointments, negative-pressure therapy, drugs, infection, or how to grade or document maceration once it occurs.
key_entities: drying wound edges with sterile gauze

title: Intact Skin as Infection Barrier
summary:
