This small community represents a single, foundational infection-prevention theme: the skin as the body's first-line mechanical barrier. Both relations in the community centre on one intervention concept — maintaining intact skin — and link it to two distinct protective outcomes, each attached to a different population.

Recommendation 1: maintaining intact skin prevents exposure to pathogens, with the population specified as nurses. This frames skin integrity as an occupational self-protection measure for the perioperative clinician — unbroken skin blocks pathogen entry during patient contact and procedural work. No condition beyond the nurse population is attached.

Recommendation 2: maintaining intact skin prevents infection, with the population specified as clients with an impaired immune system. Here the same intervention is applied to patient risk stratification: in immunocompromised gynecologic surgical clients, loss of skin integrity carries a heightened consequence, so preserving the barrier is an infection-prevention priority.

Guideline contribution: both statements come from a single source body, OpenRN. The general nurse-facing statement is cited to OpenRN Tier 2 without page localisation; the immunocompromised-client statement is cited more precisely to OpenRN Tier 2, page 696. The page-level citation is therefore the more specific of the two, and OpenRN is the only contributing body — there is no cross-body corroboration, contradiction, or divergence available within this community.

What this community does NOT establish: it names no specific skin-care products, antiseptics, dressings, moisturisers, or drugs; no assessment tools, risk scales, or scoring thresholds for skin breakdown; no timing, frequency, or duration for skin assessment or intervention; and no definition of what counts as "impaired immune system." It does not describe how to restore skin integrity once broken, does not specify hand-hygiene or glove practices, and does not quantify infection-risk reduction. It also does not extend the nurse-protection claim to patients, or the infection-prevention claim to immunocompetent clients — those populations are simply not addressed. Educators should treat this as a conceptual anchor requiring supplementation with operational skin-care protocols.
key_entities: clients with an impaired immune system

title: Continuous epidural for major open-torso surgery
summary:
Theme: this small, tightly focused community covers the role of continuous epidural analgesia in postoperative pain management, specifically as an alternative route when patients cannot take oral opioids and are undergoing major or complex open-torso surgery. All four relations link a single intervention (continuous epidural) to two clinical targets (pain, postoperative pain) and one procedural context (major or complex open-torso surgery).

Main recommendations and their populations/conditions: (1) Continuous epidural TREATS pain in people having major or complex open-torso surgery, with the stated purpose of early pain relief (NICE T1 p28). (2) Continuous epidural APPLIES_TO major or complex open-torso surgery in people who cannot take oral opioids, with the condition that clinicians should take into account the benefits of a continuous epidural (NICE T1 p13); p28 restates this more specifically for people who cannot take an oral opioid having major or complex open-torso surgery, on the grounds that they may benefit from early pain relief. (3) Continuous epidural TREATS postoperative pain in people who cannot take oral opioids — especially those having major or complex open-torso surgery, those expected to have severe pain, or those with cognitive impairment — and should be offered as a choice alongside patient-controlled analgesia (NICE T1 p13).

Guideline bodies: only NICE contributes (NICE T1, pages 13 and 28); there is no cross-body disagreement to reconcile. Internally, p13 is broader in population (adds patients expected to have severe pain and those with cognitive impairment) and adds the shared decision-making element of offering epidural as a choice with patient-controlled analgesia; p28 is narrower and emphasises the timing rationale of early pain relief.

What this community does NOT establish: no local anaesthetic or opioid agents, doses, concentrations, or infusion rates; no duration of epidural therapy or timing of removal; no catheter insertion level or technique; no monitoring, contraindications, anticoagulation rules, or complication management; no thresholds defining "severe pain" or "cognitive impairment"; no comparative effectiveness data versus patient-controlled analgesia; and no gynecologic-specific or paediatric/obstetric guidance beyond the generic open-torso surgery population.
key_entities: people who cannot take oral opioids

title: Early Urinary Catheter Removal After Pelvic Surgery
summary:
This community represents a narrow but practically important perioperative theme: the timing of urinary catheter removal as an infection-prevention measure in gynecologic and pelvic surgery. Only two relations anchor it, and together they pair an indication (which patients) with a rationale (why).

The first recommendation, from AUGS (T2, p11), applies early removal of the catheter specifically to women undergoing major pelvic reconstructive surgical procedures. This is the population-defining statement in the community: it names the surgical category rather than a generic surgical population, but it does not attach a numeric threshold, hour count, or postoperative day to 'early'.

The second recommendation, from RCOG (T1, p3), supplies the mechanism and the condition: early removal of the catheter prevents secondary infection when the catheter is removed 'as soon as possible'. RCOG is therefore the source of the temporal condition, while AUGS is the source of the population specificity. Neither body contradicts the other; they are complementary, and the only divergence is in granularity — AUGS scopes the practice to major pelvic reconstructive surgery, RCOG frames the timing qualitatively and ties it to an outcome (secondary infection) without restricting the population in the relation captured here.

For educators and QI leads, the actionable content is: in women having major pelvic reconstructive procedures, remove the indwelling catheter as soon as clinically possible, with reduction of secondary infection as the stated benefit.

What this community does NOT establish: no defined removal interval in hours or days; no criteria for what makes removal clinically possible (e.g., voiding trial protocols, residual volume thresholds, mobility or analgesia milestones); no guidance on management of post-removal urinary retention or re-catheterisation; no antibiotic prophylaxis, agents, or doses; no catheter type or care-bundle specification; no distinction between transurethral and suprapubic drainage; no risk stratification, quality metrics, or audit targets; and no evidence grading or strength-of-recommendation labels. Populations outside major pelvic reconstructive surgery are not addressed by these relations.

title: Preoperative airway assessment for difficult intubation
summary:
This community represents preoperative airway risk assessment: identifying patients at risk of difficult intubation before anaesthesia in gynecologic surgery, and the bedside screening tests used to predict it. Four relations converge on a single outcome entity, difficult intubation, from two directions — anatomical risk factors and clinical assessment tools.

Risk factors: obesity and a short immobile neck are each stated to increase the risk of difficult intubation. No population restriction or condition is attached to either of these two relations, so they are presented as general risk markers rather than qualified by BMI thresholds, neck circumference, or procedure type.

Assessment recommendations: thyromental distance measurement and the Mallampati classification are each described as detecting difficult intubation, both explicitly for apparently normal adult patients, and both conditioned on being used in combination with each other — thyromental distance when combined with the Mallampati classification, and Mallampati when combined with thyromental distance. The practical teaching point is that these two tests are recommended as a paired screen in adults who appear normal on casual inspection, not as standalone predictors.

Guideline contribution: all four relations derive from a single body and location, WHO Table 1, page 35 (WHO T1 p35). There is therefore no cross-body disagreement, no divergence in specificity, and no competing or corroborating recommendation from another society within this community.

What this community does not establish: it gives no numeric thresholds (no thyromental distance cut-off in centimetres, no Mallampati class boundary, no BMI or weight criterion for obesity), no sensitivity, specificity or predictive values, and no timing for when in the perioperative pathway assessment should occur. It does not name any airway equipment, drugs, induction agents, or rescue techniques, and does not describe management or escalation once difficult intubation is predicted. Paediatric, obstetric, and clinically abnormal-airway populations are outside the stated scope, since the detection relations are limited to apparently normal adults. Causal mechanisms linking obesity or a short immobile neck to airway difficulty are also not specified.

title: Perioperative malnutrition screening, risk, prevention
summary:
This community centres on malnutrition as a modifiable perioperative risk factor, linking its detection (screening), its consequences (infection and wound healing), a congenital cause in infants, and its prevention through preoperative dietary intervention.

Detection: NICE (T1 p8) recommends nutritional screening to detect malnutrition in people having intermediate surgery or major/complex surgery. No specific screening tool, threshold or timing is named in these relations.

Risk: CDC (T1 p9) states that malnutrition increases the risk of postoperative nosocomial infection and of impaired wound healing, but restricts this to surgical patients with severe protein-calorie malnutrition, and only for some types of operations; the guideline explicitly labels this a crude association only, i.e. not established as causal or adjusted for confounders. This is an important caveat for QI messaging.

A distinct pediatric pathway: OpenRN (T2 p471) notes that cleft palate in infants increases the risk of malnutrition, because the communication between the oral and nasal cavities makes suckling difficult — a structural feeding problem rather than a disease/treatment-related deficit.

Prevention: AUGS (T2 p3) places dietary intervention in the preoperative phase for surgical patients and states that it prevents malnutrition in patients undergoing prehabilitation, specifically disease and/or treatment-related malnutrition.

Contributing bodies and differences: NICE contributes surgical-magnitude-stratified screening; CDC contributes the (deliberately hedged) outcome associations and is the most specific about severity (severe protein-calorie malnutrition); AUGS is the most specific about phase and program context (preoperative prehabilitation); OpenRN alone addresses infants. They do not contradict each other but occupy different points of the pathway, and only CDC qualifies the evidence strength.

Not established: no screening instrument, cut-off score, timing interval, caloric/protein target, supplement or drug, or duration of prehabilitation is specified. There is no stated link from screening to a defined intervention pathway, no evidence that dietary intervention reduces infection or improves wound healing, no gynecologic-specific population, and no management pathway for infants with cleft palate.

title: Dressing choices for secondary-intention surgical wounds
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: topical wound care product selection for surgical wounds that are left to heal by secondary intention. All three relations converge on the same clinical target entity — management of surgical wound healing by secondary intention — and all apply to the same population, namely patients with surgical wounds healing by secondary intention (relevant perioperatively in gynecologic surgery where wounds are packed or left open rather than primarily closed).

There are two prohibitions and one positive recommendation. First, Eusol with gauze is contraindicated for this population and indication. Second, mercuric antiseptic solutions are likewise contraindicated. Third, an interactive dressing is the recommended option that applies to the management of these wounds. No dosing, frequency of change, timing interval, wound-size threshold, or duration of therapy is attached to any of the three relations; the conditions recorded are limited to the wound-healing mode (secondary intention).

Only one guideline body contributes: NICE (surgical site infection / wound management guidance, table T1, page 14). Because there is a single source at a single location, there is no inter-body disagreement to reconcile, no divergence in specificity between organisations, and no competing or more granular recommendation from another society within this community. Educators should therefore present these points as NICE-derived, and should not imply corroboration or contradiction from other guideline producers.

What the community does not establish: it does not name which specific interactive dressing types or brands to use, nor compare them head-to-head; it does not give a review or change schedule, expected healing timeframe, or criteria for escalation; it says nothing about systemic or topical antibiotics, antiseptic alternatives beyond Eusol/gauze and mercuric solutions, debridement, negative-pressure therapy, or packing technique. It also does not address wounds healing by primary intention, gynecologic-specific subpopulations (e.g. obesity, diabetes, immunosuppression), infection diagnosis, or outcome data supporting the contraindications.
key_entities: management of surgical wound healing by secondary intention
patients with surgical wounds healing by secondary intention

title: Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis in gynecologic-obstetric procedures
summary:
This community centres on single-dose antimicrobial prophylaxis for gynecologic and obstetric procedures, with a secondary thread on therapeutic and endocarditis-preventive uses of ampicillin. Two guideline bodies contribute: WHO (Tier 1, pp. 10, 18, 19, 28, 30, 60) and the ERAS Society (Tier 1, pp. 1, 5, 6).

WHO recommends antimicrobial/prophylactic antibiotics for women undergoing manual removal of the placenta, explicitly as a single dose. The named agents for that indication are ampicillin or a first generation cephalosporin, given as a single dose 'if manual removal of the placenta is practised' (repeated across pp. 10, 19, 28). For caesarean section, WHO recommends a single dose of a first generation cephalosporin in preference to other antibiotic classes. Beyond prophylaxis, WHO positions ampicillin as first-line treatment for chorioamnionitis in women with chorioamnionitis, in a simple regimen with once-daily gentamicin; and as the preferred agent for enterococcal prophylaxis to prevent enterococcal infectious endocarditis in patients with the listed cardiac conditions who have an established gastrointestinal or genitourinary tract infection or who receive antibiotic therapy for a GI/GU procedure.

ERAS adds surgical-timing and dosing specificity that WHO does not: a first generation cephalosporin administered within 60 minutes before skin incision for gynecologic oncology surgery, with weight-based dosing for hysterectomy and possible dose adjustment based on patient weight for simple hysterectomy. The two bodies converge on the first generation cephalosporin as the workhorse agent but differ in emphasis — WHO on obstetric single-dose events, ERAS on incision-relative timing and weight-based dosing in surgical oncology/hysterectomy.

The community does not establish specific drug doses in milligrams, weight thresholds or cut-offs, redosing intervals for long cases, alternatives for penicillin/cephalosporin allergy, gentamicin dosing details, duration beyond 'single dose', or prophylaxis for vaginal birth, episiotomy or other gynecologic procedures. No comparative effectiveness between ampicillin and cephalosporins for manual placental removal is stated.

title: Massive PE and IV Heparin in Pregnancy
summary:
This community represents the emergency recognition and management of massive pulmonary embolism (PE) with cardiovascular compromise in pregnant and puerperal women, plus the role of intravenous unfractionated heparin (UFH) as the manipulable anticoagulant around delivery, regional anaesthesia and haemorrhage risk.

Diagnosis: for collapsed, shocked women who are pregnant or in the puerperium, or any woman with suspected massive PE, both computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) and an urgent portable echocardiogram should be arranged within 1 hour of presentation.

Treatment: IV unfractionated heparin is the preferred initial treatment for massive PE with cardiovascular compromise in pregnant and puerperal women. Thrombolysis/thrombolytic therapy is indicated if massive PE is confirmed, or in extreme circumstances prior to confirmation; the decision is made on an individual basis by a multidisciplinary resuscitation team.

Peripartum anticoagulation: for women in whom venous thromboembolism (VTE) occurs at term, IV UFH is considered because it is more easily manipulated and, given its shorter half-life, minimises the time without anticoagulant therapy, thereby preventing VTE recurrence. IV UFH is stopped 6 hours before induction of labour or regional anaesthesia. At caesarean section, IV UFH may be used for women at high risk of haemorrhage in whom continued heparin treatment is essential, until the haemorrhage risk factors have resolved.

Contributing body: all relations derive from a single source, RCOG Thrombosis/VTE guidance (T1, pages 3, 5, 14, 19); no cross-body disagreement can be assessed. Internally, page 14 is the most population-specific ("collapsed, shocked women who are pregnant or in the puerperium"), while page 3 states the same actions more generally for "women presenting with suspected massive pulmonary embolism"; page 3 also names "echocardiogram" where page 14 specifies "portable echocardiogram."

Not established: no heparin dosing, infusion rates, APTT targets or monitoring thresholds; no thrombolytic agent, dose or contraindications; no restart timing for anticoagulation after delivery, neuraxial block or haemorrhage resolution; no guidance on non-massive PE, alternative imaging (e.g. V/Q), fetal or radiation considerations, low-molecular-weight heparin comparisons, or outcome/mortality data.

title: Epidural, Misoprostol, Hyperthermia and VTE
summary:
This community groups two perioperative/intrapartum concerns in obstetric care: (1) non-infectious causes of maternal hyperthermia, and (2) the timing of neuraxial anaesthesia in women receiving treatment for venous thromboembolism (VTE). All relations derive from a single guideline body, RCOG (Table/Trimester 1, pages 11 and 19).

On hyperthermia, the graph records two agents as risk-raising: misoprostol and epidural anaesthesia. In both cases the qualifying condition is identical and important — the attribution is a 'diagnosis of exclusion'. That is, epidural-related or misoprostol-related pyrexia should only be accepted after infective and other causes of maternal fever have been ruled out, not as a first-line explanation. For a nurse educator, the teaching point is that a temperature rise in a woman with an epidural in situ, or after misoprostol administration, still triggers a full sepsis/infection assessment before being labelled drug- or block-related.

On anaesthesia and VTE, epidural anaesthesia is listed as temporarily contraindicated in obstetric patients undergoing treatment for VTE. The stated condition is that it may proceed only after discussion with a senior anaesthetist and in keeping with local anaesthetic protocols. This makes escalation and local protocol adherence the operative safeguards; the contraindication is time-limited ("temporarily"), not absolute.

Differences between bodies cannot be assessed here: RCOG is the only contributing source, so there is no cross-guideline agreement or conflict to report, and no more- or less-specific alternative recommendation.

The community does not establish: any numeric thresholds (no temperature cut-off defining hyperthermia, no misoprostol dose or route, no interval in hours between last anticoagulant dose and epidural insertion or catheter removal); which anticoagulant agents constitute 'treatment for VTE'; the incidence or magnitude of hyperthermia risk; management or treatment of maternal hyperthermia once identified; neonatal consequences; whether spinal or other neuraxial techniques share the same contraindication; and whether prophylactic-dose (as opposed to treatment-dose) anticoagulation carries the same restriction.

title: Preventing Maternal Mortality: Anaesthesia, Hygiene, Timing
summary:
This community centres on maternal mortality as an outcome node, with four modifiable or contributory factors: anaesthetic technique, hand hygiene, and the timing of birth in sepsis.

Anaesthetic technique (RCOG, T1 p24) contributes two paired statements. General anaesthesia increases the risk of maternal mortality in obstetric patients when compared with regional anaesthesia; conversely, central neuraxial anaesthesia prevents maternal mortality in the obstetric population when used as the anaesthetic technique of choice. The practical message for perioperative gynecologic/obstetric nursing is that regional/neuraxial block should be the default, with general anaesthesia reserved as the higher-risk alternative.

Infection prevention (CDC, T1 p7) contributes the historical Semmelweis-type finding: hand cleaning with an antiseptic agent prevents maternal mortality among mothers who delivered in the First Obstetrics Clinic at the General Hospital of Vienna, specifically when compared with washing hands with plain soap and water. Note the narrowness of this population and the comparator — antiseptic versus plain soap and water, not versus no hand hygiene.

Timing of delivery in sepsis (RCOG, T1 p14): birth increases the risk of maternal mortality in women with maternal instability due to sepsis, unless the source of infection is intrauterine. This makes birth a conditional hazard — stabilise first, except where the uterus is the septic source and delivery is source control.

Contributing bodies: RCOG supplies three of four relations, all anaesthetic or obstetric-decision focused and stated at population level (obstetric patients, women unstable from sepsis). CDC supplies the single hand-hygiene relation and is far more specific about setting and comparator but least generalisable. The two bodies do not contradict each other; they address different causal pathways and are not cross-referenced.

Not established: no drugs, doses, thresholds (e.g., blood pressure, lactate, temperature), timings, or gestational ages are given; no quantified risk reduction or effect size; no guidance on which antiseptic agent, on neuraxial contraindications, on when general anaesthesia is nonetheless indicated, or on how to define/measure maternal instability. Perioperative gynecologic (non-obstetric) applicability is not addressed.

title: Maternal sepsis risk, detection, antibiotic management
summary:
This community covers recognition, risk stratification and urgent antimicrobial management of maternal sepsis in pregnant and recently pregnant women, plus its severe complication, necrotising fasciitis. Almost all content derives from RCOG (Green-top on maternal sepsis, T1 pp.1-11), with a single WHO contribution.

Risk factors for maternal sepsis in women during pregnancy/postpartum (RCOG p4) include obesity, caesarean birth, cervical cerclage, amniocentesis, prolonged rupture of membranes, vaginal trauma, retained pregnancy tissue, history of pelvic infection, contact with invasive group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus, intravenous drug use, multiple gestation, impaired immunity, immunosuppressant medication, renal, cardiac or liver disease, and ethnic minority background. RCOG is more specific for two of these when a sepsis risk stratification tool is applied to patients with suspected sepsis: prolonged rupture of membranes of 18-24 hours and any invasive procedure (e.g. amniocentesis) within the last 6 weeks are amber flags denoting moderate risk. WHO adds only that multiple gestation increases risk of postpartum haemorrhage in women who give birth — a different outcome, not sepsis.

Detection: a sepsis risk stratification tool for all women with suspected infection, and sepsis screening for women with fever during labour. Regular pain score assessment in postpartum women with suspected sepsis or wound infection monitors for necrotising fasciitis (escalating analgesia to opioids is the warning sign).

Treatment: intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour for women at high risk of sepsis, with or without septic shock, as part of a sepsis bundle; rapid broad-spectrum antibiotics for any unwell pregnant/recently pregnant woman after early diagnosis. Sepsis bundles apply to inpatients with red flag (high-risk) features. For life-threatening sepsis/puerperal sepsis with unknown organism sensitivity: piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem plus clindamycin (Gram-positive/anaerobic cover; switches off exotoxin production in necrotising fasciitis); add vancomycin with any MRSA history; intravenous aciclovir second-line if deterioration prompts regimen change. Piperacillin-tazobactam is contraindicated with beta-lactam allergy. Surgery to drain pus provides source control.

Not established: doses, durations, de-escalation criteria, alternative regimens for beta-lactam allergy, outcome data, or nursing workflow for bundle delivery.

title: Preoperative Bowel Preparation for Colorectal Surgery
summary:
This community centres on preoperative colon preparation before elective colorectal surgery, combining mechanical bowel preparation (MBP) with nonabsorbable oral antimicrobial agents to reduce infectious complications.

Main recommendations. CDC (T1 p21) advises that, for patients undergoing elective colorectal operations, the colon be mechanically prepared before the operation using enemas and cathartic agents, and that a nonabsorbable oral antimicrobial agent be administered in divided doses on the day before the operation. CDC (T1 p13) is the most specific on sequencing: for patients undergoing preparation of the colon, the oral agent is given in divided doses the day before surgery, after the enemas and cathartics — i.e. the antimicrobial timing is dependent on completion of the mechanical prep. ERAS Society (T1 p3) frames MBP as preventive of surgical site infection specifically when combined with oral antibiotics, and (T1 p1) reports that in rectal cancer patients undergoing low anterior resection MBP may reduce infectious morbidity, but explicitly qualifies this as a single RCT finding requiring further study. Both bodies place MBP in the preoperative phase (ERAS T1 p1; CDC T1 p21).

Contributing bodies and differences. CDC supplies the operational detail (agents used for mechanical prep, divided dosing, day-before timing, order relative to enemas/cathartics). ERAS supplies the outcome rationale and population nuance (SSI prevention only in combination with oral antibiotics; low anterior resection for rectal cancer) and is more cautious about strength of evidence. They do not conflict, but ERAS conditions benefit on the antibiotic combination rather than mechanical prep alone.

What is not established. No specific nonabsorbable oral antimicrobial drug is named, and no doses, number of divided doses, clock times, or enema/cathartic agents or volumes are specified. No thresholds, contraindications, laparoscopic-versus-open distinctions, paediatric or emergency-surgery guidance, or recommendations for MBP without oral antibiotics are provided. The rectal-cancer/low-anterior-resection benefit remains unconfirmed, and no intravenous prophylaxis, skin preparation, or postoperative elements are covered here.
key_entities: rectal cancer patients undergoing low anterior resection

title: Preventing mechanical phlebitis in IV therapy
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: nursing measures to prevent mechanical phlebitis — vein wall irritation caused by physical movement or friction of a peripheral intravenous catheter — in patients receiving intravenous therapy. All three relations converge on the same adverse outcome (mechanical phlebitis) and the same population (patients receiving IV therapy), making this a device-and-site management theme rather than a pharmacologic one.

Three preventive recommendations are captured. First, catheter selection: choose the smallest outer diameter catheter that will support the prescribed therapy; the stated condition is explicit — selection is made relative to the therapy being delivered, so gauge choice is therapy-driven rather than routine. Second, use catheter securement technology to stabilise the device at the insertion site; this is stated for all patients receiving IV therapy with no qualifying condition. Third, apply joint stabilisation, qualified as 'as needed' — i.e., an intermittent, assessment-triggered intervention rather than a standing order, implicitly relevant when a catheter sits at or near a flexion point.

Only one guideline body contributes here: OpenRN (Nursing Skills, Volume 2, p. 1363). Because the community draws on a single source and a single page, there are no inter-body disagreements, no competing thresholds, and no opportunity to compare specificity across corpora. Within the source, specificity varies: catheter sizing carries an explicit selection condition, joint stabilisation carries a conditional 'as needed' trigger, and securement is stated unconditionally.

The community does not establish several things a QI lead would need. It gives no catheter gauge numbers, no dwell-time or rotation intervals, no anatomical site preferences (e.g., avoiding the antecubital fossa), and no securement product types or brands. It defines no assessment scale, grading criteria, or monitoring frequency for phlebitis, and specifies no treatment or escalation pathway once mechanical phlebitis occurs. It does not address chemical or infective phlebitis, infiltration, extravasation, or thrombophlebitis, and contains no gynecologic- or perioperative-specific population qualifiers despite the surrounding corpus.

title: Clinician Fatigue, Stress and Error Risk
summary:
This community represents a single coherent theme: the human-factors contribution of practitioner state — fatigue, stress, illness, burnout and work-schedule design — to the occurrence of medical error, together with the one protective countermeasure the corpus names (structured self-monitoring). All seven relations converge on the same outcome node, 'medical error', and all derive from a single source, WHO Patient Safety Curriculum Guide (Multi-professional Edition), Topic 1, p154.

Risk-increasing factors, with their attached populations and conditions: fatigue increases risk of medical error in health-care practitioners generally (no threshold or hours-awake figure given); twelve-hour shifts and mandatory overtime increase risk specifically in nurses; burnout increases risk specifically in new nurses; and stress and illness increase risk in students, conditioned on 'when feeling unwell or stressed'. Note the population specificity: shift length and overtime are framed as nursing workforce/scheduling issues, burnout as a problem of the newly qualified, and stress/illness as a student self-awareness issue.

The single preventive recommendation is self-monitoring of status and well-being, directed at students, with the explicit condition that it be done using mnemonic aids such as HALT or IM SAFE. This is the only actionable intervention in the community, and it is framed as an individual-level practice rather than a system-level control.

Guideline bodies: only WHO contributes here (WHO Topic 1, p154); there are therefore no inter-body disagreements to reconcile, and no corroboration from other guidelines in the corpus. This is a notable gap for a QI lead seeking multi-source support.

What the community does NOT establish: no numeric thresholds (no maximum consecutive hours, no rest-interval or hours-awake cut-offs, no burnout inventory scores), no error rates or effect sizes, no employer- or system-level controls (rostering limits, fatigue-risk management systems, prohibitions on mandatory overtime), no specific error types or perioperative/gynecologic procedures, no drugs, and no evidence that self-monitoring or HALT/IM SAFE reduces error in qualified nurses, new nurses or practitioners generally — its stated population is students only.

title: Medication Error Risk Factors and Safeguards
summary:
This community maps medication safety: patient-, staff-, system- and product-level risk factors for medication error and harm, plus the nursing safeguards that prevent them.

Risk factors (WHO T1 p242) are patient-related — pregnancy, renal dysfunction, multiple health problems, polypharmacy (especially when medications are prescribed by more than one health-care provider), language barriers where the patient does not speak staff's language, and young age (children and babies, especially neonates, because of required drug-dose calculations) — and staff-related: inexperienced personnel, rushing (as in emergencies), and interruption mid-task. Product/system factors include look-alike, sound-alike drug names, inconsistent colour coding and look-alike labelling, and storage of similar-appearing ampoules together when they contain different drugs (WHO T1 p46); OpenRN adds inadequate handoff communication (p159), incorrect dosage calculation and work-arounds that bypass safe-administration policies (p895).

Recommendations: WHO advises colour-coding by class of drug for medications with similar-sounding names but different effects/mechanisms (p46), and monitoring for medication side-effects in every patient receiving medications you prescribe, dispense or administer (p242). OpenRN is most operationally specific: nurses should verify the rights of medication administration at least three times before administering (three checks / six rights completed three times, p378, p854), document immediately after administration (p854), double-check medication calculations (p895), and use a 'do not use' list of abbreviations (p378). RNAO frames polypharmacy as medication-related harm in Ontario populations and recommends informing persons and their support network of medication changes — what changed and why — with printed material during transitions in care (p61). OpenRN also links polypharmacy to side effects in persons with dementia taking multiple medications and to falls in clients on several prescription medications.

Not established: no specific drugs, doses, thresholds, error rates, or reporting/reconciliation processes; no gynecologic- or perioperative-specific populations; no evidence grading, comparative effectiveness of the checks, or guidance on interruption-free zones, staffing, or technology (barcoding, smart pumps). WHO, OpenRN and RNAO complement rather than contradict one another.
key_entities: three checks of the rights of medication administration
six rights of medication administration check
do not use list of abbreviations
informing persons and their support network of medication changes with printed material

title: Medication-related harm risk in care transitions
summary:
This community centres on medication-related harm during transitions in care, plus a closely linked outcome — non-attendance of follow-up appointments after hospital discharge. Its core content is a vulnerability profile: for populations in Ontario, older age, low health literacy, polypharmacy, dementia, disability, and low socio-economic status all increase the risk of medication-related harm (RNAO Transitions in Care, p61). For persons in Ontario after a transition from hospital, low health literacy and lack of social support increase the risk of non-attendance of a follow-up appointment (RNAO T2 p27) — so low health literacy is the single factor bridging both harms and is a natural screening priority.

Three interventions appear. Medication education prevents medication-related harm for persons in transitions in care, delivered during the transition. Enhanced support prevents medication-related harm specifically for persons identified as at high risk, and is timed before and after transitions in care — i.e. risk stratification should precede discharge, not follow it. Monitoring is recommended for patients receiving medication, to detect medication-related harm (WHO, p242).

Contributing bodies: RNAO supplies all risk-factor and prevention statements, with population framing anchored to Ontario and to hospital-to-community transitions; WHO contributes only the surveillance element, framed more broadly for any patient receiving medication and without a transition qualifier. RNAO is therefore more specific about who is at risk and when to intervene; WHO is broader in scope but silent on risk factors. There is no contradiction between them.

What this community does NOT establish: no named drugs or drug classes, no numeric thresholds (no definition of polypharmacy by medication count, no age cut-off for "older age", no health-literacy score), and no specified monitoring frequency, duration, or tool. It does not describe how to screen for or identify high-risk patients, what "enhanced support" concretely comprises, or who delivers it. No effect sizes, evidence grades, or outcomes such as readmission or mortality are attached. Interventions for lack of social support or for non-attendance itself are absent, as are gynecologic- or surgery-specific applications.

title: Avoiding finger milking during capillary sampling
summary:
This community represents a single, narrowly focused specimen-integrity theme: mechanical manipulation of the puncture site during capillary (fingerstick) blood collection and its effect on specimen quality. Both relations in the community assert the same causal claim — that milking or massaging the finger (described in one node as 'milking or massaging the finger' and in the other as 'milking or massaging the finger site') increases the risk of a hemolyzed specimen. The populations differ only in breadth: one relation is scoped to patients undergoing capillary blood glucose sampling, the other to the broader group of patients undergoing capillary blood sampling generally. Together they support a consistent practice recommendation: when obtaining capillary blood, whether for point-of-care glucose testing or other capillary specimens, the nurse should not milk or massage the finger to obtain or increase blood flow, because doing so risks hemolysis of the sample and therefore unreliable results.

Only one guideline body contributes here — OpenRN (Open Resources for Nursing), Text 2, at pages 1078 and 1095. There is no interbody disagreement to reconcile; the two entries are internally consistent and mutually reinforcing. The p1078 entry is the more specific of the two in terms of population (capillary blood glucose sampling), while p1095 generalises the same caution to all capillary blood sampling, which is the more useful framing for policy or checklist language.

What this community does not establish: it specifies no alternative techniques (e.g., warming the site, dependent positioning, puncture depth, lancet selection, or site rotation), no acceptable amount of gentle pressure, no timing or wait interval after puncture, no drop-discard practice, and no thresholds for repeat sampling. It does not quantify how much hemolysis risk increases, does not describe downstream consequences such as falsely altered glucose values or specimen rejection rates, and names no drugs, devices, or laboratory criteria. It also does not address venipuncture, arterial sampling, pediatric heel sticks, or documentation and quality-monitoring requirements. Educators should therefore treat this as a single discrete do-not-do point requiring supplementation from other guideline sections.
key_entities: milking or massaging the finger site
patients undergoing capillary blood glucose sampling

title: Uterotonic Prophylaxis and PPH Anticoagulation Timing
summary:
This community covers pharmacological prevention and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH), plus the timing of postpartum anticoagulation when PPH risk is present. Contributors are WHO (T1) and RCOG (T1).

Prevention: WHO recommends a uterotonic for all births during the third stage of labour, with only ONE effective uterotonic used, correct dosage, safe use and monitoring; it is the main intervention within the active management of the third stage package. Oxytocin 10 IU IM/IV is the drug of choice, including where multiple uterotonic options exist, and for vaginal or caesarean birth when given by skilled health personnel trained in injectable uterotonics. Carbetocin 100 µg IM/IV is an alternative for all births where cost is comparable to other effective uterotonics, or where oxytocin is unavailable or its quality cannot be guaranteed. Misoprostol 400–600 µg orally is recommended where skilled birth attendants are absent and oxytocin is unavailable, administered by community health workers, lay health workers or trained traditional birth attendants; it increases risk of diarrhoea. RCOG is more procedure-specific: oxytocin 5 IU by slow IV injection at caesarean section, oxytocin as agent of choice for third-stage prophylaxis (superior to misoprostol), and carbetocin 100 µg IV bolus over 1 minute for elective caesarean (licensed for this indication).

Treatment: WHO — IV oxytocin alone is first-line, including in women who already received prophylactic oxytocin; sublingual misoprostol 800 µg if IV oxytocin is unavailable or bleeding is unresponsive. RCOG — oxytocin 5 IU slow IV, repeated if necessary, or infusion 40 IU in 500 ml for major PPH; oxytocin preferred initially in hypertension or pre-eclampsia.

Anticoagulation (RCOG only): LMWH is temporarily contraindicated in postpartum women on thromboprophylaxis until immediate haemorrhage risk falls; warfarin is delayed while risk persists, avoided until at least day 5 postpartum and longer if at increased risk, as it increases PPH risk before day 5 and compared with LMWH.

Not established: no tranexamic acid, ergometrine, surgical/mechanical measures, blood-loss thresholds, transfusion triggers, or PPH definitions; WHO gives no anticoagulation guidance and RCOG no lay-worker misoprostol pathway.

title: Fluid restriction and drain avoidance reduce morbidity
summary:
This community represents a 'less is more' theme in perioperative gynecologic and abdominal surgical care: minimising both intravenous fluid excess and the routine use of surgical drains in order to reduce post-operative morbidity. Two distinct interventions converge on the single outcome entity 'morbidity'.

First, the ERAS Society (T1, p1) states that restrictive fluid therapy prevents morbidity in patients undergoing major intra-abdominal surgery, with an explicit condition: the benefit holds only if fluid restriction is not initiated solely in the post-operative period. In other words, the restrictive strategy must span the intraoperative (and pre/peri-operative) course; starting restriction only after the patient leaves theatre is not what the protective evidence supports. This is a conditional, mechanism-sensitive recommendation rather than a blanket instruction to limit fluids.

Second, the RCOG (T1, p3) contributes three parallel relations identifying nasogastric drains, abdominal drains and vaginal drains as each increasing the risk of morbidity. These are stated without population or conditional qualifiers in this community, so they read as general cautions against routine drain placement across the guideline's surgical population.

The two bodies are complementary rather than contradictory: ERAS is more specific in naming a population (major intra-abdominal surgery) and a timing condition, whereas RCOG is more specific in enumerating the exact devices (nasogastric, abdominal, vaginal) implicated. There is no disagreement between them in these relations.

What the community does NOT establish: no fluid volumes, rates, infusion types, or crystalloid/colloid choices are specified; no numeric thresholds or weight-based targets are given. It does not define 'morbidity' (no named complications such as ileus, infection, anastomotic leak or pulmonary oedema). It does not quantify effect sizes or risk magnitudes, nor state whether drains ever remain indicated for selected patients, how long they may stay, or removal timing. It does not link fluid strategy to drain use, address mortality, length of stay, or readmission, and provides no drug names, monitoring parameters or nursing escalation criteria.

title: Perioperative mortality risk factors and prevention
summary:
This community centres on mortality as a shared outcome node, linking modifiable perioperative exposures and deterioration markers to death (and, in sepsis, ICU admission). It spans fluid choice, physiologic monitoring, glycemic control, neuromuscular recovery, catheter-associated risk, and systems-level safety.

Protective interventions: the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist prevents mortality in surgical patients (NICE T1 p25). For intraoperative fluid management in adults undergoing surgery, intravenous crystalloid prevents mortality when used rather than colloid, while colloid increases mortality risk; the trade-off noted is that crystalloid increases risk of nausea and vomiting compared with colloid (NICE T1 p24). RCOG is more specific about a particular colloid: hydroxyethyl starch increases mortality risk in critically ill nonpregnant patients (burns, trauma, or following surgery) (RCOG T1 p16) — consistent in direction with NICE's colloid caution but restricted to a named agent and a critically ill, nonpregnant population.

Deterioration and physiologic risk markers: a NEWS2 score of 5 or more increases risk of both mortality and intensive care unit admission in people with suspected sepsis aged 16 and over (NICE T1 p59). Elevated blood pressure increases mortality risk at self/home values >135/85 mmHg or clinic readings >140/90 mmHg (RNAO T2 p38). Hypoglycemia increases mortality risk (ERAS Society T1 p6) and residual neuromuscular blockade increases mortality risk (AUGS T2 p4), though neither carries a population or threshold qualifier here. For patients with indwelling urinary catheters, CDC identifies older age (highest risk over 70 years) and higher severity of illness as mortality risk factors (CDC T1 p36).

What this community does not establish: no effect sizes, timings, dosing, or monitoring intervals; no defined glucose threshold for hypoglycemia, no quantitative measure of residual blockade, and no reversal agents. Guidance for pregnant patients on hydroxyethyl starch is explicitly outside the stated population, and no relation links checklist use, blood pressure control, or catheter care to each other.
key_entities: world health organization surgical safety checklist

title: Antiretroviral prevention of HIV mother-to-child transmission
summary:
This community represents pharmacological prevention of mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HIV, spanning both maternal antiretroviral therapy (ART) and infant post-exposure prophylaxis. All four relations are PREVENTS relations pointing at the single outcome 'mother-to-child transmission of human immunodeficiency virus', and all derive from one source: WHO Tier 1 (WHO T1, pp. 31-32).

Maternal recommendations: (1) Antiretroviral therapy is recommended for all pregnant and breastfeeding women infected with HIV, and should be maintained at least for the duration of the period in which MTCT risk persists. (2) The specific first-line regimen named is the fixed combination tenofovir disoproxil fumarate + lamivudine + efavirenz, for pregnant and breastfeeding women, explicitly including women in the first trimester and women of childbearing age; it applies whether the ART is lifelong or is initiated solely for MTCT prevention and then stopped.

Infant recommendations, both conditioned on infants receiving replacement feeding (not breastfeeding): (1) nevirapine given as daily infant prophylaxis for four to six weeks; (2) zidovudine given twice daily for four to six weeks as an alternative to nevirapine. The two infant agents are therefore interchangeable options for the same population and duration, differing in dosing frequency (daily vs twice daily).

Contributing bodies: only WHO contributes here, so no inter-body disagreement can be assessed; the finer specificity sits within WHO itself, where the general 'all pregnant and breastfeeding women' ART statement (p31) is operationalised by the named regimen on p32.

What this community does NOT establish: no doses, milligram strengths, or weight-band dosing; no viral load, CD4 or gestational-age thresholds for starting or stopping; no guidance for breastfed infants (only replacement-fed infants are covered); no infant or maternal HIV testing, monitoring or follow-up schedule; no efficacy or transmission-rate figures; no toxicity, teratogenicity or adverse-effect statements (despite first-trimester efavirenz use being explicitly included); and no perioperative, intrapartum or mode-of-delivery guidance linking these drugs to surgical or gynecologic care.
key_entities: mother-to-child transmission of human immunodeficiency virus
pregnant and breastfeeding women infected with HIV

title: Preventing Iatrogenic Fungal Infection Exposure
summary:
This small community centers on a single clinical theme: nurse-controlled prevention of iatrogenic fungal infection, approached from two directions — a protective self-care behaviour after inhaled medication delivery, and a device-related hazard from improvised equipment.

Recommendation 1: mouth rinsing with water prevents fungal infection in patients using metered dose inhalers (MDIs). The stated population is patients receiving inhaled corticosteroids via MDI, and the condition is explicit as to timing — the rinse is performed after inhalation. This makes the behaviour a teachable, discrete post-administration step that belongs in patient education and in medication administration checklists wherever inhaled corticosteroids are given.

Recommendation 2: a wooden tongue depressor increases the risk of fungal infection when used as a joint stabilization device. Here the population is narrower and higher-risk — preterm infants or immunocompromised individuals — and the condition is the off-label use of the wooden depressor for joint stabilization (e.g., improvised splinting) rather than oral examination. The implication for quality improvement is to substitute purpose-made, non-porous stabilization devices in neonatal and immunocompromised populations.

Guideline contribution: both relations derive from a single corpus source, OpenRN (Nursing Skills, Volume 2), at p922 for the MDI rinsing recommendation and p1359 for the tongue depressor caution. Because only one guideline body contributes, there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile. The two statements differ in specificity: the MDI recommendation is precise about timing (after inhalation) but broad about population (any MDI user of inhaled corticosteroids), whereas the tongue depressor caution is precise about population (preterm infants, immunocompromised) and use context but gives no exposure duration or threshold.

What this community does NOT establish: it names no specific fungal organism (e.g., no Candida species identified), no corticosteroid drug names, doses, or spacer use, no incidence or risk magnitude, no diagnostic criteria or treatment pathway for established fungal infection, no rinse volume, duration, or whether spitting versus swallowing matters, and no alternative stabilization products. It is also silent on perioperative gynecologic specifics despite the wider corpus context.

title: Broad-spectrum antimicrobials in maternal sepsis
summary:
This community centres on the double-edged role of broad-spectrum antimicrobials in pregnancy-related sepsis: they are the core time-critical treatment, yet prior exposure to them shapes the resistance risk clinicians must anticipate.

The principal recommendation comes from NICE (T1, p19): for people with suspected sepsis who are currently or recently pregnant and who meet one or more high risk criteria, give a broad-spectrum antimicrobial without delay — within 1 hour of identifying that they meet any high risk criterion — provided antibiotics have not already been given for this episode. The population is explicitly obstetric/postpartum, the trigger is the presence of any single high-risk criterion (not a composite score threshold), and the condition on the action is both a timing limit (1 hour) and an exclusion (no repeat dosing if already treated this episode). This is the operational, auditable element for a QI dashboard: door-to-antibiotic time ≤1 hour in pregnant or recently pregnant patients flagged high risk.

RCOG (T1, p7) contributes the counterbalancing caution: in women who have already been on broad-spectrum antimicrobials before developing signs of sepsis, that prior exposure increases the risk of multi-drug resistant infection. RCOG is therefore more specific about the prior-exposure subgroup and its microbiological consequence, while NICE is more specific about population definition, the high risk criteria trigger, and the 1-hour timing. The two do not conflict — NICE governs when to start, RCOG governs how to interpret risk in the previously treated woman.

What this community does NOT establish: no named agents, doses, routes, or combinations; no definition or list of the "high risk criteria"; no guidance on de-escalation, duration, review points, or culture-directed narrowing; no antimicrobial choice for suspected multi-drug resistant infection; no thresholds (lactate, blood pressure, temperature, NEWS/MEOWS scores) linked here; and no source-control, fluid, or escalation recommendations. Educators should source those elements from adjacent sepsis-recognition and antimicrobial-stewardship material rather than inferring them from this theme.
key_entities: people who are or have recently been pregnant with suspected sepsis

title: Polypharmacy and Comorbidity Drug Interaction Risk
summary: This small community represents a single, tightly focused theme: the elevated risk of drug interactions in perioperative gynecologic patients who arrive with chronic disease burden. Two relations converge on the same outcome entity, 'drug interaction'. First, use of multiple medications increases the risk of drug interaction, with the population explicitly scoped to patients with chronic disease who are taking multiple medications. Second, multiple co-morbidity increases the risk of drug interaction, scoped to patients with multiple co-morbidities. Both statements come from the same source, WHO Technical/Training document 1, page 242, so the theme is contributed by a single guideline body (WHO); no other corpus body (for example a national college or society guideline) appears here, and therefore no inter-body agreement, disagreement, or difference in specificity can be assessed from this community. The two WHO statements are complementary rather than competing: one frames the hazard around the drug regimen itself (polypharmacy), the other around the underlying disease profile (multimorbidity), which in practice frequently co-occur in the same preoperative patient. For educators, the usable message is that medication review and comorbidity assessment should both be treated as drug-interaction screening triggers in chronic-disease patients presenting for gynecologic surgery. Importantly, the community establishes only a risk association. It names no specific drugs, drug classes, or interacting pairs; it gives no numeric threshold for what counts as 'multiple' medications or 'multiple' co-morbidities; it specifies no timing (no preoperative interval, no intraoperative or postoperative window); and it identifies no route, dose, or monitoring parameter. It also does not state any recommended action — there is no relation prescribing medication reconciliation, pharmacist review, drug cessation or substitution, laboratory monitoring, or documentation. Nor does it link drug interaction onward to any downstream harm such as bleeding, hypotension, delayed recovery, or anaesthetic complication. Quality-improvement work using this theme should therefore treat it as a rationale for screening, not as a validated screening protocol, and should seek thresholds and interventions from other parts of the corpus.
key_entities: patients with chronic disease taking multiple medications

title: Nonpharmacologic Measures for Musculoskeletal Discomfort
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: the use of nonpharmacologic comfort measures to manage musculoskeletal discomfort in the perioperative gynecologic patient. Three interventions are named, each linked to the same target problem by the same relation type (TREATS) and the same qualifying condition — that they are applied 'as nonpharmacologic measure': (1) repositioning, (2) splinting, and (3) heat and cold application. The practical implication for nurse educators is that musculoskeletal discomfort should first prompt consideration of positioning changes, supported splinting of the affected or incisional area, and thermal therapy (heat or cold) before or alongside pharmacologic analgesia. All three are presented as parallel, co-equal options; no ranking, sequence, or preference among them is stated.

Only one guideline body contributes to this community: OpenRN, from a single locus in the corpus (Textbook 2, page 958). Because the evidence is drawn from one source and one page, there are no inter-guideline disagreements to reconcile, no instance of one body being more specific than another, and no competing or conflicting recommendations to adjudicate. Quality-improvement leads should treat this as a single-source, low-granularity cluster rather than a corroborated multi-guideline consensus.

The community does NOT establish several things a protocol would require. No specific population is attached to any of the three relations — there is no stated restriction by age, procedure type, comorbidity, or perioperative phase (preoperative, intraoperative, PACU, or discharge). No timing, frequency, or duration is given (for example, how long to apply heat versus cold, or how often to reposition). No thresholds are specified, such as a pain score that should trigger these measures or escalate to medication. No drugs are named anywhere in this community, and no relationship to pharmacologic analgesia, contraindications (for example, when heat should be avoided), documentation requirements, expected outcomes, or effectiveness evidence is described. Distinct guidance for heat versus cold is also not differentiated.

title: Preoperative Nasal MRSA Screening Detection
summary:
This community represents a single, narrow perioperative infection-prevention theme: preoperative nasal screening to detect methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) colonisation in women undergoing gynecologic surgery. Both relations in the community converge on the same clinical target entity — MRSA colonisation — reached by two closely related detection methods.

The recommendations are: (1) a nose swab for rapid MRSA screening detects MRSA colonisation, with the population specified as women whose MRSA status is unknown, conditioned on such testing being available; and (2) nasal molecular screening detects MRSA colonisation, conditioned on testing being available (no population restriction is attached to this second relation). The practical implication for nurse educators is that, where local laboratory capacity permits, nasal sampling is the recognised route to identify carriage status before surgery, and the trigger for testing is unknown MRSA status rather than any specific risk factor, comorbidity, or procedure type.

Only one guideline body contributes to this community: the RCOG (RCOG T1, p7). There is therefore no inter-body disagreement to reconcile here. Within the RCOG material, the nose-swab/rapid-screening statement is the more specific of the two — it names the population (women of unknown MRSA status) — whereas the molecular screening statement carries only the availability condition. Both share the identical availability caveat, indicating the recommendation is contingent on local resources rather than absolute.

What this community does NOT establish is substantial. It specifies no timing (how many days or hours before surgery to swab), no additional sampling sites beyond the nose (e.g. throat, groin, perineum), no sensitivity or turnaround-time thresholds, and no comparative preference between rapid culture-based swabbing and molecular screening. Critically, it does not link a positive result to any downstream action: no decolonisation agents (e.g. mupirocin, chlorhexidine), no antibiotic prophylaxis modification, no isolation or theatre-scheduling measures, no re-screening interval, and no outcome claims about surgical site infection reduction. It also gives no guidance for women with known MRSA status or where testing is unavailable.
key_entities: nose swab for rapid MRSA screening
women whose MRSA status is unknown

title: Preparatory Oxygenation and Positioning for Nasal Suctioning
summary:
This community represents a narrow procedural-safety theme: the preparatory steps taken immediately before nasal (nasopharyngeal) suctioning to protect the patient against suction-induced hypoxemia and to secure a patent airway. All three relations converge on the single procedure node 'nasal suctioning', framing it as an intervention that requires pre-procedure oxygenation and airway positioning rather than immediate instrumentation.

Main recommendations, with their stated conditions: (1) hyperoxygenation applies to nasal suctioning 'prior to the procedure'; (2) increasing supplemental oxygen applies to nasal suctioning 'for a few minutes prior to the procedure' — this is the most temporally specific element in the community, operationalising hyperoxygenation as a sustained several-minute pre-oxygenation window rather than a single breath; and (3) head extension to open the airway applies to nasal suctioning, stated without a timing or population qualifier. Read together, the pattern for a nurse educator is: pre-oxygenate for a few minutes, extend the head to open the airway, then suction.

Guideline contribution: a single source underpins the entire community — OpenRN Nursing Skills (Text 2, p. 1296). There is therefore no cross-body disagreement to reconcile, and no second guideline offering a competing or more granular version of these steps. The only internal gradation of specificity is between the general instruction to hyperoxygenate and the more concrete 'for a few minutes' framing of increased supplemental oxygen.

What this community does NOT establish: no patient population is specified (no age group, no gynecologic or perioperative subgroup, despite the corpus context), and no perioperative phase is attached. It gives no oxygen concentration, FiO2 target, litres-per-minute flow, delivery device, or SpO2 threshold that would define adequate pre-oxygenation or trigger the intervention. It does not define suction pressure, catheter size, suction duration, number of passes, or recovery intervals; does not address contraindications or cautions for head extension (for example suspected cervical spine injury); and provides no monitoring, documentation, or post-suction reoxygenation guidance.
key_entities: head extension to open the airway

title: Nasotracheal Suctioning Risks and Chest Assessment
summary:
This community centres on airway clearance safety — specifically the adverse-event profile of nasotracheal suctioning — paired with one bedside respiratory assessment technique. All relations derive from a single guideline body, OpenRN (Nursing Skills, Tab 2), from two locations: p1293 (suctioning complications) and p616 (chest expansion assessment).

The dominant recommendation-relevant content is that nasotracheal suctioning increases risk of a broad, multi-system set of complications, stated without population restriction or qualifying condition in the source: hypoxemia; cardiac arrest and respiratory arrest; cardiac dysrhythmia and bradycardia; hypotension and, conversely, elevated blood pressure; increased intracranial pressure; laryngospasm, bronchospasm and bronchoconstriction; atelectasis and pneumothorax; gagging, vomiting and uncontrolled coughing; pain; hospital-acquired infection; and direct mechanical trauma — nasal irritation, nasal bleeding, laceration of a nasal turbinate, and perforation of the pharynx. For educators, this supports teaching that suctioning is a high-risk procedure warranting pre-procedure assessment, cardiopulmonary and neurologic monitoring, and infection-prevention technique.

The assessment thread is narrower and explicitly conditional: chest expansion assessment detects pneumothorax and pneumonia, but only when the condition “chest expansion is unequal” is met (OpenRN T2 p616). Pneumothorax is the single node linking the two threads — it is both a suctioning complication and a finding detectable by unequal chest expansion — which is a useful teaching bridge between procedure risk and post-procedure surveillance.

Because only one guideline body contributes, there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile; the p616 assessment content is more specific (it carries an explicit triggering condition) than the p1293 risk list, which is unqualified.

The community does NOT establish: any population specification (no age, pregnancy, gynecologic-surgical or perioperative phase criteria), suction pressures, catheter sizes, suction pass duration or frequency, pre-oxygenation requirements, contraindications, incidence or likelihood of any listed complication, management or rescue steps once a complication occurs, or any drug therapy. It also does not state sensitivity, specificity, or alternatives (e.g., auscultation, imaging) for chest expansion assessment.

title: Perioperative nausea: risks, prevention, nonpharmacologic care
summary:
This community centres on nausea as a perioperative and general clinical symptom — its drug-related causes, multimodal prevention within ERAS pathways, and largely nonpharmacologic nursing management.

Risk factors: opioids increase nausea risk in patients receiving them (AUGS T2 p9) and specifically when relied on as the sole post-operative analgesic (ERAS Society T1 p9); NSAIDs (OpenRN T2 p825), chemotherapy in clients receiving cancer treatment (OpenRN T2 p979), medications generally as an adverse effect in hospitalised patients (OpenRN T2 p719), and ergometrine when used for postpartum haemorrhage prevention (WHO T1 p26).

Prevention: preoperative patient education, delivered in the preoperative phase (AUGS T2 p9; RCOG T1 p2) using leaflets, video and psychological preparation, prevents nausea, pain and anxiety when added to an existing ERAS protocol (ERAS Society T1 p2; AUGS T2 p3) and treats post-surgical nausea, pain and anxiety (ERAS Society T1 p1). An oral carbohydrate-rich drink given up to 2 h before surgery prevents nausea in surgical patients (AUGS T2 p3). RCOG (T1 p3) is more specific about population: early feeding combined with reduced volume of routine intravenous fluids prevents nausea in women undergoing routine gynaecological surgery. Administration with food prevents NSAID-related nausea (OpenRN T2).

Treatment: metoclopramide lowered mean nausea score (Rhodes Index) below placebo on day 3 in pregnant women (WHO T1 p95); OpenRN contributes nonpharmacologic measures — peppermint inhaler, relaxation techniques, music therapy, room-temperature meals and fluids, avoiding strong odours and high-bulk meals (T2 p100, p1269) — plus timing antiemetic/analgesic medication before mealtime for clients with nutritional deficit (T2 p1015), and monitoring for side effects including nausea during ear instillation (T2 p922).

Contributors: ERAS Society and AUGS (ERAS-aligned prevention bundles), RCOG (gynaecological surgery fluids/feeding), WHO (obstetric drugs), OpenRN (nursing comfort measures).

Not established: no doses, frequencies, PONV risk scores, or comparative efficacy between interventions; no guidance on prophylactic antiemetic agents such as ondansetron or dexamethasone; no evidence that the nonpharmacologic OpenRN measures were tested in surgical populations; and no resolution of how opioid-sparing analgesia should be constructed.

title: Perioperative nausea, vomiting and carbohydrate loading
summary: This community centres on postoperative/perioperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) — its drivers, prevention (notably preoperative carbohydrate loading), monitoring and drug treatment. Prevention: NICE (T1 p23) says a preoperative carbohydrate drink could be considered for people having major abdominal surgery, and reports it prevents postoperative headache and thirst in those who receive it. The ERAS Society (T1 p1, p6) is more directive and more specific: oral carbohydrate loading occurs in the preoperative phase, should be used routinely before major abdominal surgery, prevents nausea and vomiting when given preoperatively, and prevents insulin resistance/postoperative insulin resistance as part of the ERAS protocol. So NICE 'could be considered' vs ERAS 'should be used routinely' is the clearest divergence in strength, and only ERAS links carbohydrate loading to PONV and insulin resistance, while only NICE claims headache and thirst benefit. Risk factors named: intravenous crystalloid increases nausea and vomiting risk in adults undergoing surgery when compared with colloid for intraoperative fluid management (NICE T1 p24); opioids (OpenRN T2 p825) and elevated calcium (OpenRN T2 p1425); and uterotonics — WHO (T1 p26) flags the fixed combination of oxytocin and ergometrine for PPH prevention, with RCOG (T1 p11) quantifying a five-fold increased risk for ergometrine-oxytocin in the third stage compared with oxytocin alone. Management (OpenRN T2): antiemetics treat nausea/vomiting and vomiting in clients with deficient fluid volume as appropriate; prochlorperazine and ondansetron if prescribed; aromatherapy with essential oils such as peppermint oil for hospitalized and chemotherapy clients; oral administration of analgesia is temporarily contraindicated while the client is nauseated and vomiting. Clients receiving opioids need continual monitoring for nausea/vomiting, respiratory depression, constipation, urinary retention, oversedation and pruritus. WHO (T1 p95) supports doxylamine and pyridoxine in pregnant women (reduced PUQE score baseline to day 15, moderate certainty). Not established: carbohydrate drink composition, volume or timing before induction; specific antiemetic doses, routes or comparative efficacy; monitoring frequency; whether colloid should replace crystalloid; and any gynecologic-surgery-specific PONV thresholds or prophylaxis regimens.

title: Necrotic Wound Tissue Debridement Options
summary:
Clinical theme: management of necrotic (black) tissue in the wound bed, a barrier to healing in postoperative and other wounds. The community links two interventions to a single clinical target — necrotic tissue — representing the choice between surgical/mechanical-style debridement and enzymatic (chemical) debridement.

Recommendations as stated: (1) Wound debridement treats necrotic tissue in patients with necrotic (black) tissue in the wound bed; the guideline frames this as necessary 'in most circumstances, for the wound to heal,' i.e., removal of necrotic tissue is a general precondition of healing rather than an optional adjunct. (2) Collagenase ointment treats necrotic tissue when it is applied daily to the wound bed and covered with sterile gauze or a foam dressing — the only agent, dosing interval (daily) and dressing options (sterile gauze or foam) named in this community.

Contributing body/source: both relations derive from a single source, OpenRN Nursing Skills (Textbook 2, p. 1145). Because there is only one contributing guideline, there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile. The two statements differ in specificity: the debridement relation specifies the population (any patient with black/necrotic tissue in the wound bed) and a strong general rationale but no technique, setting, or operator; the collagenase relation specifies drug, frequency, and dressing but attaches no explicit population, leaving it implicitly applicable to the same necrotic-tissue population.

What the community does NOT establish: no criteria for selecting debridement versus collagenase; no debridement method (sharp, surgical, autolytic, mechanical, biologic); no treatment duration, endpoint, or reassessment interval for collagenase; no contraindications, cautions, adverse effects, or periwound skin protection guidance; no dressing change frequency beyond 'daily' application; no wound-type, anatomic-site, or gynecologic/perioperative-specific qualifiers; no pain management, anesthesia, or referral thresholds; and no outcome data or evidence grading. Exceptions to the 'most circumstances' debridement rule are acknowledged in wording but never enumerated — educators should not infer them.
key_entities: necrotic (black) tissue in the wound bed

title: Co-amoxiclav Avoidance in Preterm PROM
summary:
This small but clinically important community represents a single antibiotic-safety theme: the avoidance of co-amoxiclav (amoxicillin-clavulanate) in women with preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (PPROM), and the neonatal harm that drives that avoidance. Both relations converge on one drug and one obstetric population, making this a focused prescribing-safety cluster rather than a broad antimicrobial-stewardship theme.

The main recommendations are: (1) co-amoxiclav is contraindicated in women with preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (WHO, T1 p17); and (2) co-amoxiclav increases the risk of necrotising enterocolitis in babies exposed to the drug in utero (RCOG, T1 p11). The population for the contraindication is specifically women with PPROM; the population for the harm signal is specifically neonates with in-utero exposure. Nurse educators should teach these as a paired cause-and-effect message: the contraindication exists because of the neonatal necrotising enterocolitis risk, not because of maternal intolerance.

Two guideline bodies contribute. WHO states the directive prohibition — the actionable prescribing rule at the bedside. RCOG is more specific about mechanism and outcome, naming necrotising enterocolitis and identifying the exposed baby (rather than the mother) as the at-risk party. The two are complementary rather than conflicting: RCOG supplies the rationale that WHO's contraindication implies. For QI purposes, this supports a hard-stop or alert on co-amoxiclav orders where PPROM is documented, with the RCOG rationale surfaced in the alert text.

What this community does NOT establish: it names no alternative antibiotic, dose, route, duration, or gestational-age threshold for PPROM prophylaxis; it gives no timing window for exposure risk, no quantified magnitude of necrotising enterocolitis risk, and no monitoring or neonatal surveillance pathway. It says nothing about co-amoxiclav use in women with intact membranes, in term rupture of membranes, in chorioamnionitis, or in perioperative surgical prophylaxis, and nothing about maternal outcomes. Any protocol specifying what to give instead must draw on guidance outside this community.
key_entities: babies exposed to co-amoxiclav in utero

title: Sharps and Needle-Stick Injury Prevention
summary:
This community centres on preventing percutaneous sharps and needle-stick injuries and the blood-borne pathogen exposure that follows them. Two hazard relations anchor the theme: both needle-stick injury and sharps injury increase the risk of blood-borne pathogen exposure for nurses and other health care workers (OpenRN T2 p620).

Recommendations fall into programmatic and technique-level controls. Programmatically, a sharps injury prevention program prevents both sharps and needle-stick injuries for health care workers, while a community needle disposal program provides the same protection for community members (OpenRN T2 p620) — the only relation addressing non-clinical populations. WHO T1 p211 contributes generic "needle-stick injury precautions" with an explicitly broader population: patients and health-care workers, not staff alone.

Technique-level controls are all from OpenRN T2 and are more specific: immediate disposal of sharps in an FDA-cleared sharps disposal container when performing procedures that include needles or other sharps (p203); use of a sharps container and avoidance of recapping needles (p203); immediate disposal of the used syringe and needle in a sharps container after administration of the medication, with the safety device activated (p1006); the scoop-cap technique when recapping is unavoidable (p1006); removing the needle cap straight off with the nondominant hand (p1021); and shielded intravenous catheters, effective only when the safety mechanism is used as intended and not disabled or overridden (p1363).

Differences: WHO states the principle and widens it to patients; OpenRN supplies the operational detail, device specifications and conditions. Note an internal tension in OpenRN — p203 advises avoiding recapping, while p1006 endorses the scoop-cap technique when recapping the needle.

The community does not establish post-exposure management (no testing, prophylaxis drugs, timings or reporting pathways), specific pathogens, injury or seroconversion rates, container filling thresholds or disposal schedules, glove/PPE requirements, training frequency, or any gynecologic- or perioperative-specific application.
key_entities: immediate disposal of sharps in FDA-cleared sharps disposal container
removing the needle cap straight off with the nondominant hand
immediate disposal of used syringe and needle in sharps container

title: Neonatal Jaundice Surveillance After Late Cord Clamping
summary:
This community represents a narrow but operationally important theme: neonatal jaundice detection and management as a safeguard accompanying the adoption of late (delayed) umbilical cord clamping. It contains two linked clinical actions — identification of neonatal jaundice and treatment of neonatal jaundice — both directed at the single condition of neonatal jaundice.

The recommendations are population- and context-bound in the same way. Both apply to neonates cared for in health services that have adopted late cord clamping.
