Identification of neonatal jaundice is recommended specifically where late cord clamping is adopted, i.e. the practice change carries an accompanying requirement that services be able to detect jaundice in newborns. Treatment of neonatal jaundice is qualified as being provided 'if necessary' — that is, contingent on the outcome of identification rather than applied routinely to all neonates. For a QI lead, the practical implication is that a service cannot implement late cord clamping in isolation: capability for jaundice screening and, where indicated, treatment must be in place as a paired capacity.

Only one guideline body contributes to this community: the World Health Organization (WHO Technical/Guideline document 1, page 32). There is therefore no cross-body disagreement, no competing threshold, and no instance of one organisation being more specific than another within this theme; the entire theme rests on a single WHO source and a single page.

The community does not establish how jaundice should be identified — no visual inspection protocol, transcutaneous or serum bilirubin measurement, bilirubin thresholds, timing of assessment (e.g. hours of life), or repeat-screening intervals are specified. It does not name any treatment modality: phototherapy, exchange transfusion, and any drugs or doses are absent. It also does not define 'late cord clamping' in seconds or minutes, does not quantify the risk of jaundice attributable to late clamping, does not address preterm versus term neonates separately, and does not specify who performs identification, documentation requirements, escalation or referral pathways, or parent education content.
key_entities: neonates in health services adopting late cord clamping

title: Adjuvant Neuropathic Agents in Perioperative Analgesia
summary:
This community centres on non-opioid adjuvant analgesics — chiefly gabapentin, with amitriptyline as a related agent — used for neuropathic and post-operative pain, plus the safety burden that accompanies gabapentin.

Recommendations: The ERAS Society guideline (T1 p9) recommends gabapentin for post-operative pain in patients undergoing gynecologic surgery, specifying that it be given routinely by the oral route pre-operatively. The OpenRN nursing text (T2, p825) contributes the broader pharmacologic profile: gabapentin treats neuropathic pain and restless leg syndrome, and amitriptyline treats neuropathic pain in adults, with the population specified as adults with neuropathic pain such as diabetic neuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia, or post-stroke pain.

Safety: For clients taking gabapentin, OpenRN attaches risks of sleepiness, unsteadiness, weakness, falls, and suicidality. These are the practical monitoring and patient-education targets for perioperative nurses, particularly relevant when a pre-operative oral dose is given before ambulation, transfer, or discharge teaching.

Contributing bodies and differences: ERAS Society is the only source addressing the perioperative gynecologic surgical population and is the more specific on timing and route (routine, oral, pre-operative). OpenRN is the only source addressing indications beyond surgery (neuropathic pain, restless leg syndrome), the alternative agent amitriptyline, and adverse-effect risks. Notably, ERAS states no adverse-effect cautions for its surgical population, and OpenRN attaches no perioperative context to its gabapentin risks — so the fall/sedation/suicidality warnings must be carried across by the educator rather than read from a single guideline.

Not established: no doses, dose thresholds, dosing intervals, or duration of therapy for gabapentin or amitriptyline; no timing interval for the pre-operative dose; no comparative effectiveness between gabapentin and amitriptyline; no amitriptyline adverse effects or perioperative role; no contraindications, renal or age-based adjustments, or interactions (including with opioids or other sedatives); no monitoring schedule or fall-prevention protocol; and no outcome data (opioid sparing, pain scores, length of stay) supporting the ERAS recommendation.

title: Appointment Adherence Monitoring and Telephone Recall
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: appointment attendance as both a marker and a modifiable driver of adherence to prescribed regimens. The three relations form a coherent risk-monitor-intervene loop. First, a missed appointment increases the risk of non-adherence to the prescribed regimen for clients on prescribed regimens — i.e., attendance failure is treated as an early warning signal rather than an isolated administrative event. Second, monitoring adherence to medical appointments is identified as the surveillance activity that detects non-adherence to prescribed regimens (no population or condition qualifier is attached, so it is stated generically). Third, telephone recall of clients who miss appointments prevents non-adherence, specified for the population of clients who miss appointments and conditioned on the recall being undertaken as an effort to keep them in care — that is, the phone call is framed as a retention-in-care strategy, not merely rescheduling.

All three relations derive from a single guideline body, the Registered Nurses' Association of Ontario (RNAO), Tool 2, page 68. Because only one body contributes, there are no inter-organisational disagreements, no competing thresholds, and no instances where one guideline is more granular than another; the specificity gradient exists only within RNAO's own statements, where the intervention (telephone recall) carries both a population and a condition while the monitoring recommendation carries neither.

What this community does NOT establish: no timing or frequency is given for telephone recall (no interval after the missed visit, no number of attempts), no threshold for how many missed appointments constitutes risk, and no alternative contact modalities (text, mail, outreach visit) are named. No drugs, doses, or specific prescribed regimens are identified, and no gynecologic or perioperative population is specified despite the corpus context. It also does not quantify effect size, define who performs the recall, address documentation, or link non-adherence to downstream clinical outcomes such as surgical cancellation, complications, or readmission.
key_entities: telephone recall of clients who miss appointments

title: NSAID Analgesia Risks and Vomiting Management
summary:
Theme: pharmacologic symptom control — chiefly NSAIDs for pain/inflammation/fever — and the adverse-effect burden that follows, with vomiting as a shared hub linking many triggers and treatments.

Core recommendation (AUGS T2 p9): give an NSAID, unless contraindicated, for postoperative pain in patients after vulvar and vaginal surgery; AUGS also flags that opioids increase vomiting risk in patients receiving them. OpenRN T2 (esp. p825) supplies the pharmacology detail: NSAIDs treat mild-to-moderate pain, inflammation and fever but increase risk of nausea, vomiting, dyspepsia, renal failure, and GI bleeding — the latter specifically in older adults and those taking NSAIDs concurrently with warfarin or corticosteroids (warfarin and corticosteroids are each listed as raising GI bleed risk in that concurrent context). All NSAIDs except aspirin increase heart attack, heart failure and stroke risk, with risk higher if taken more than directed or longer than directed. OpenRN adds two concrete practice points: monitor for early signs of GI bleeding in older adults receiving NSAIDs, and withhold NSAIDs for seven days before a guaiac-based fecal occult blood test.

Other bodies contribute distinct angles. WHO T1 notes NSAIDs can precipitate a severe asthmatic response in susceptible patients (p46), that ergometrine used for postpartum haemorrhage prevention causes vomiting (p26), and that ginger treats vomiting in pregnant women (moderate certainty vs placebo, p88). RNAO T2 is blood-pressure focused: NSAIDs, sympathomimetics and herbal remedies raise blood pressure in patients not reaching target BP (p71) or taking OTC/supplement products (p59); combined lifestyle interventions achieving optimal BP prevent heart attack (p41).

Vomiting also arises from medications generally in hospitalized patients, chemotherapy, and nasotracheal suctioning, and can cause deficient fluid volume; antiemetics treat vomiting in clients with deficient fluid volume, as appropriate.

Not established: no NSAID drug names, doses, routes, durations, or age thresholds; no ranking of NSAID safety; no BP numeric targets; no antiemetic agents named; no guidance for pregnancy/renal impairment beyond the above.

title: Nutrient Deficiency Risk After Bowel Resection
summary:
This small community represents a single, focused clinical theme: the nutritional consequences of bowel resection and the corresponding need for nutrient supplementation in postoperative gynecologic/abdominal surgical patients whose intestine has been surgically shortened. Two relations define it. First, bowel resection increases the risk of nutrient deficiency, with the condition explicitly stated as circumstances in which all or parts of the intestine are removed — i.e., the loss of absorptive intestinal surface is the mechanism implied by the guideline. Second, nutrient supplementation applies to bowel resection, with the population qualified as 'many clients who have experienced bowel resection,' signalling a common but not universal indication that requires individual assessment rather than blanket ordering.

Only one guideline body contributes here: OpenRN (Nursing Skills / OpenRN Text 2, p979). Because the corpus provides a single source, there are no inter-body disagreements, no competing thresholds, and no instance of one organisation being more specific than another. The educator should therefore treat this as an OpenRN-derived teaching point rather than a multi-society consensus, and should look outside this community for corroborating nutrition or enhanced-recovery guidance.

Importantly, the community does not establish: which specific nutrients are at risk (no mention of vitamin B12, iron, fat-soluble vitamins, calcium or protein); which supplement formulations, routes (oral, enteral, parenteral) or doses are indicated; any timing, duration, or frequency of supplementation; any laboratory thresholds or monitoring intervals to trigger or titrate therapy; the proportion of patients meaning of 'many'; the extent or site of resection that predicts deficiency severity; and any outcomes data (wound healing, length of stay, readmission). It also does not link to perioperative fasting, ostomy care, malabsorption diagnosis, or dietitian referral pathways.

For quality improvement, this theme supports a simple screening prompt — flag every bowel-resection patient for nutritional deficiency risk and supplementation assessment — while acknowledging that operational detail must be sourced from local nutrition protocols, since the graph supplies none.

title: Nutritional Deficiency and Impaired Wound Healing
summary:
Clinical theme: this community links altered nutritional status to wound healing outcomes, with dietician collaboration as the shared detection and treatment pathway. Three nodes carry the causal chain: bariatric surgery increases risk of nutritional deficiency (condition: because bariatric procedures alter the anatomy and physiology of the gastrointestinal tract), and nutritional deficiency in turn increases risk of delayed wound healing and, specifically for clients with chronic wounds, impaired wound healing unless the deficiencies are addressed.

Main recommendations with populations and conditions: (1) Anticipate and screen for nutritional deficiency in post-bariatric-surgery patients on the basis of the anatomic/physiologic GI alteration. (2) For patients experiencing poor wound healing, collaborate with a dietician to detect nutritional deficiency. (3) For clients with poor wound healing, collaborate with a dietician to treat the identified deficiency, triggered when a client is experiencing poor wound healing. The chronic-wound population is the most specific target, where the guideline explicitly conditions continued impaired healing on deficiencies not being addressed.

Contributing bodies: all relations derive from a single corpus, OpenRN (Open RN nursing textbook series), Text 2, across three locations — p979 (bariatric surgery/nutritional risk), p1113 (delayed wound healing; dietician detection), and p696 (chronic wounds and poor wound healing; dietician detection and treatment). There is no cross-organisational disagreement, but granularity differs: p1113 states dietician collaboration only as a detection step for patients with poor wound healing, whereas p696 is more specific, adding a treatment role and naming clients with chronic wounds and the "unless deficiencies are addressed" caveat. p979 contributes the surgical-risk origin but does not connect bariatric patients directly to wound outcomes.

What this community does NOT establish: no named nutrients, supplements, drugs, or laboratory thresholds (e.g., albumin, prealbumin, BMI); no screening tool, timing, frequency, or perioperative window for dietician referral; no dosing or duration of nutritional therapy; no evidence grading; no gynecologic-surgery-specific population; and no direct causal link between bariatric surgery and delayed or impaired wound healing.

title: Obesity as Cross-Cutting Perioperative Risk Multiplier
summary:
This community is organised around a single hub entity, obesity, and maps the breadth of perioperative and obstetric complications it amplifies across five guideline bodies. No intervention or drug regimen is specified anywhere in these relations; every edge is a risk-association statement, so the theme is essentially risk stratification and heightened surveillance for patients with obesity.

Airway and respiratory risk: WHO (T1 p35, p37) links obesity to difficult intubation and aspiration, without stated thresholds. AUGS (T2 p4) is population-specific, attaching decreased chest wall compliance to patients undergoing robotic and laparoscopic hysterectomy — the only edge tied to a defined surgical approach.

Wound, skin and vascular risk: OpenRN (T2 p1113) contributes the densest cluster for obese individuals — venous injury, wound dehiscence, hematoma formation, impaired and delayed wound healing, wound infection, and pressure injury. OpenRN (T2 p719) also links obesity to generalized abdominal distention. CDC (T1 p7) is the most quantitatively specific source, citing surgical site infection risk in patients undergoing certain kinds of operations at greater than 20% ideal body weight.

Thromboembolic and infectious obstetric risk: RCOG (T1) provides the most finely populated conditions — venous thromboembolism after vaginal delivery (p21) and after caesarean section (p22); post-thrombotic syndrome (p21); maternal sepsis in women during pregnancy/postpartum (p4); and pulmonary embolism in overweight and obese pregnant women while receiving LMWH prophylaxis doses appropriate for women of weights 50–90 kg (p23) — i.e., a breakthrough-risk warning that standard-weight-band dosing may be insufficient.

Where sources differ in specificity: CDC alone gives a numeric adiposity threshold; RCOG alone stratifies by delivery mode and prophylaxis context; WHO and OpenRN state risk generically for all obese individuals.

Not established here: no BMI cut-points (other than CDC's >20% IBW), no alternative LMWH dose, no positioning, airway, pressure-redistribution, antibiotic or wound-closure interventions, no effect sizes, timings, or monitoring intervals, and no relations among the complications themselves.

title: LMWH timing in suspected VTE testing
summary:
This community represents a narrow but high-stakes theme: how anticoagulation with low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) is sequenced against objective diagnostic testing in women with clinically suspected venous thromboembolism (VTE), where bleeding risk complicates the usual 'treat first, confirm later' approach.

Two linked recommendations are captured. First, objective testing for VTE is the diagnostic step that detects (confirms or excludes) VTE, and it applies to women with clinically suspected venous thromboembolism. Second, LMWH is temporarily contraindicated — that is, treatment is withheld — specifically in the subgroup of women with clinically suspected VTE who are also at risk of bleeding. In that population, LMWH is postponed until objective testing has confirmed the diagnosis, and the guideline frames this as a deliberate judgement made after considering the balance of the risks of haemorrhage versus clotting. The contraindication is therefore conditional and time-limited, not absolute: it is tied to the pending diagnostic result and to an explicit individualised risk assessment, which is the practical teaching point for nurses triaging suspected VTE in women at bleeding risk (for example, perioperative or postpartum patients).

Only one guideline body contributes here: the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG), with both relations drawn from a single source page (RCOG T1 p11). There is therefore no inter-body disagreement to reconcile, and no point at which one body is more specific than another; the specificity that exists lies within the RCOG statement itself, which distinguishes women at bleeding risk from the broader suspected-VTE population.

What this community does not establish: it names no LMWH dose, weight band, dosing interval or duration; no specific test modality (no compression ultrasound, D-dimer, V/Q or CTPA), no test thresholds and no timeframe within which objective testing must occur. It does not define what constitutes 'at risk of bleeding', does not describe treatment of confirmed VTE, alternative anticoagulants, thromboprophylaxis, mechanical measures, reversal agents, or management for women without bleeding risk. It also gives no monitoring, escalation or documentation pathway.
key_entities: women with clinically suspected venous thromboembolism

title: MEOWS Charting for Sepsis and Haemorrhage
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: the use of the obstetric modified early warning system (MEOWS) as a structured bedside surveillance tool for detecting deterioration in two obstetric emergencies — maternal sepsis and ongoing (postpartum) bleeding.

Two recommendations are captured. First, MEOWS should be used to monitor for sepsis in women with suspected sepsis, and the condition attached is that such women are managed through a multidisciplinary approach with early escalation and senior input — i.e. the chart is not a stand-alone intervention but a trigger within an escalation pathway. Second, MEOWS should be used to monitor for continuous bleeding in patients with postpartum haemorrhage who require high dependency or intensive care, with the guideline emphasising its value especially in cases where bleeding is not apparent (e.g. concealed or intra-abdominal loss), where physiological trend data may be the earliest signal.

Only one guideline body contributes here: the RCOG (Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists), drawing on two separate parts of the corpus (T1 p7 for sepsis; T1 p24 for postpartum haemorrhage). Because the evidence is single-source, there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile; the two statements are complementary rather than conflicting. The PPH statement is the more specific of the two in terms of care setting, naming high dependency or intensive care patients, whereas the sepsis statement is more specific about process, naming multidisciplinary management with early senior escalation.

What this community does NOT establish: no numeric trigger thresholds or scoring cut-offs for MEOWS parameters (no blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, temperature or urine output values), no observation frequency or timing intervals, no escalation timeframes, no named drugs, antibiotics, uterotonics or fluid regimens, and no diagnostic or laboratory criteria for sepsis or estimated blood loss definitions of PPH. It also says nothing about MEOWS use in non-obstetric gynaecological surgery, postoperative populations, outcome evidence for MEOWS, or documentation and audit requirements. Educators should therefore pair this theme with local MEOWS trigger charts and sepsis/PPH bundles.
key_entities: multidisciplinary approach with early escalation and senior input

title: Venous Symptoms and Oedema in Pregnancy
summary:
This community centres on lower-limb venous problems in pregnancy — varicose veins, oedema and venous thromboembolism (VTE) — and the conservative, non-pharmacological measures used to relieve them.

Risk relationship: RCOG (T1 p12) states that varicose veins increase the risk of venous thromboembolism in pregnant women. This is the only causal/risk link in the community and the only entry point to VTE.

Treatment recommendations: WHO (T1 p14) recommends leg elevation for both oedema and varicose veins in pregnant women, and water immersion for the same two conditions in the same population; in both cases the stated condition is that the choice is made 'based on a woman's preferences and available options', i.e. an explicitly preference-sensitive, comfort-oriented recommendation rather than a mandated intervention. RCOG (T1 p16 and p4, repeated) recommends leg elevation for oedema specifically in pregnant women with deep vein thrombosis, and specifies timing: in the initial management of DVT.

Contributing bodies and differences: two bodies contribute — WHO and RCOG. WHO is broader in scope (general pregnant population; two interventions; two target symptoms) and frames use around maternal preference. RCOG is narrower but more clinically specific: it restricts leg elevation to pregnant women already diagnosed with DVT, names the timing (initial DVT management), and uniquely supplies the varicose-veins-to-VTE risk link. There is no contradiction between them; they address different populations and stages of care. Only leg elevation is endorsed by both bodies; water immersion is WHO-only.

What this community does NOT establish: no drugs, doses, anticoagulation regimens or thresholds (e.g. no heparin, LMWH, compression stocking pressures, gestational ages or duration of elevation). It does not state that leg elevation or water immersion prevents or treats VTE itself, does not quantify the varicose-veins VTE risk, gives no diagnostic criteria for DVT or oedema, no postoperative or gynecologic-surgery population, and no contraindications, monitoring or escalation criteria.

title: Analgesic Use: Benefits and Sedation Risk
summary:
This community centres on the analgesic as a class-level intervention, framed by three linked ideas drawn from a single guideline source (OpenRN Nursing Skills/Fundamentals, Volume 2): a specific therapeutic indication, a population-based caution, and an adverse-effect risk.

Recommendations and their populations/conditions: (1) Analgesics TREAT transient mechanical phlebitis — the stated population is patients with transient mechanical phlebitis (e.g., IV-site related), and the condition is 'as needed' (PRN) rather than scheduled dosing (OpenRN T2 p1363). (2) Analgesics are flagged as CONTRAINDICATED_WITH older adults — the population is older adults, with the qualifying condition that this applies specifically to those analgesics that may have adverse effects in older adults, i.e., it is a selective rather than blanket contraindication (OpenRN T2 p844). (3) Analgesics INCREASE_RISK_OF sedation, stated without population or conditional restriction, so it should be read as a general class risk applicable to any patient receiving an analgesic (OpenRN T2 p395).

Contributing bodies and differences: only one guideline body contributes here — OpenRN — so there is no cross-body disagreement to reconcile. However, the three source pages differ in specificity: p1363 is the most specific (named condition plus PRN timing), p844 adds a population qualifier plus a hedge ('may have adverse effects'), and p395 is the least specific, giving an unqualified risk statement. For teaching or audit purposes, the phlebitis indication and the sedation risk together imply the need to monitor sedation whenever PRN analgesia is given, including for a minor local complication.

What this community does NOT establish: no individual drug names, drug classes (opioid vs non-opioid), doses, dosing intervals, maximum daily limits, or age thresholds defining 'older adult'; no sedation assessment tool, monitoring frequency, or escalation/reversal pathway; no alternative or safer substitute analgesics for older adults; no route of administration; no perioperative-phase timing (pre-, intra-, post-operative); and no outcome, efficacy, or duration-of-treatment data for phlebitis.

title: Omitting Nitrous Oxide to Prevent PONV
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused anesthetic-technique theme: intraoperative omission of nitrous oxide as a PONV-prevention strategy in laparoscopic gynecologic surgery. All four relations converge on one intervention (omission of nitrous oxide), one population (patients undergoing laparoscopic gynecologic surgery), and one outcome (postoperative/post-operative nausea and vomiting, recorded under both spellings as separate outcome nodes).

Main recommendation: for patients having laparoscopic gynecologic surgery, nitrous oxide should be omitted from the anesthetic, with the stated condition that the omission applies during the laparoscopic gynecologic procedure itself; the expected benefit is prevention of postoperative nausea and vomiting. The intervention is also linked directly to the surgical population via APPLIES_TO relations, so the scope is procedure-specific rather than a general anesthesia recommendation.

Contributing guideline body: only the ERAS Society contributes here, via a single source document (T1), with the same content appearing on p1 (summary/recommendation level) and p7 (body/discussion level). Because there is one body and one document, there are no cross-society disagreements to reconcile; the p1 and p7 statements are consistent duplicates rather than differing positions. The only nuance in specificity is redundancy of outcome labelling ("postoperative" vs "post-operative nausea and vomiting"), which educators should treat as one clinical outcome when building teaching materials or audit definitions.

What this community does NOT establish: it names no alternative agents or carrier gases to substitute for nitrous oxide, no anesthetic depth, dosing, or duration thresholds, and no timing beyond "during" the procedure. It specifies no adjunctive antiemetic drugs, no risk-stratification tool or PONV risk score to select patients, and no baseline or target PONV rates. It does not address open, vaginal, or robotic gynecologic surgery, obstetric patients, pediatric patients, or non-gynecologic laparoscopy. It provides no recommendation strength or evidence grade, no statement on nitrous oxide effects on bowel distension, recovery time, length of stay, or pain, and no nursing monitoring, documentation, or rescue-treatment pathway for patients who still develop PONV.

title: Regional Analgesia for Open Gynecologic Surgery
summary:
This community represents the perioperative regional/neuraxial analgesia options recommended for patients undergoing OPEN general gynecologic surgery, as part of an enhanced recovery (ERAS) approach to opioid-sparing pain control. All four relations share the same population — open general gynecologic surgery — and differ only in the technique and the condition under which it applies.

Main recommendations, with populations/conditions:
1) Spinal anesthesia with intrathecal morphine applies to open general gynecologic surgery, stated without an attached qualifying condition — i.e., the baseline/first-line neuraxial option in this set.
2) Thoracic epidural analgesia applies to the same population as an alternative, specified to use a low-concentration local anesthetic plus opiates for 24–48 hours.
3) Truncal nerve block applies to open general gynecologic surgery specifically for patients who have undergone general anesthesia without neuraxial blockade — i.e., a rescue/substitute pathway when spinal or epidural was not used.
4) Continuous wound infiltration of local anesthetic applies to the same population, with the weaker conditional framing that it "can be considered."

Guideline bodies: only one source contributes — the ERAS Society (T1, p2). There are therefore no inter-society disagreements, no divergent thresholds, and no instance of one body being more specific than another within this community; the only gradation of strength is internal to ERAS, descending from unconditioned recommendation (intrathecal morphine), to a specified alternative (thoracic epidural with dose/duration detail), to a population-restricted option (truncal block), to a discretionary option (continuous wound infiltration).

What this community does NOT establish: no doses, concentrations, or volumes are given for intrathecal morphine, epidural local anesthetic/opiate, truncal block, or wound infiltration; no specific agents beyond "morphine," "local anesthetic," and "opiates" are named. No duration is specified except the 24–48 h epidural window. It does not address minimally invasive or laparoscopic gynecologic surgery, cesarean or oncologic subpopulations, contraindications, anticoagulation or catheter-removal timing, monitoring requirements, nursing assessment intervals, systemic multimodal adjuncts, or comparative outcome data ranking these techniques.
key_entities: continuous wound infiltration of local anesthetic

title: Perioperative Urinary Catheter Use and Timely Removal
summary:
This community represents perioperative urinary catheter stewardship: restricting indwelling catheter placement to genuine surgical indications and removing the catheter promptly after operation. Two recommendation strands appear. First, catheter use should be limited in operative patients: CDC guidance (T1 p10) states urinary catheters should be used in patients undergoing an operative procedure only as necessary, rather than routinely — i.e., placement is indication-driven, not a default element of surgical care. Second, for patients who do have an operative indication for an indwelling catheter, removal should be early. OpenRN (T2 p1230) states that patients who require an indwelling catheter for operative purposes typically have it removed within 24 hours or less. CDC (T1 p45) frames the same point by phase, tying removal to the postoperative period: for operative patients with an indication for an indwelling catheter, remove as soon as possible, preferably within 24 hours, unless there are appropriate indications for continued use.

Contributing bodies are CDC and OpenRN. They agree on the 24-hour benchmark and are complementary rather than conflicting. CDC is more specific in two ways: it explicitly addresses the upstream decision to place a catheter at all (only as necessary, not routine), and it anchors removal to the postoperative phase while naming an explicit exception clause ("unless there are appropriate indications for continued use") plus the stronger framing "as soon as possible." OpenRN describes the 24-hour-or-less removal as typical practice without stating exceptions.

What this community does not establish: it names no specific operative procedures, patient subgroups (e.g., urologic, gynecologic, obstetric, epidural or prolonged-anesthesia cases), or age/comorbidity criteria; it does not list what counts as an acceptable indication for placement or for continued use beyond 24 hours; it specifies no catheter type, size, insertion technique, drainage-system care, aseptic requirements, antimicrobial or drug measures, alternatives such as intermittent or external catheterization, voiding-trial or post-removal retention protocols, documentation or reminder/stop-order systems, and no CAUTI outcome thresholds or audit metrics.

title: Opioid Analgesia: Indications and Adverse Effects
summary: This community centres on opioids as perioperative and palliative analgesics and the adverse-effect burden nurses must anticipate, monitor and treat. Therapeutic claims: opioids treat moderate to severe pain, including via the IV route for rapid relief (OpenRN T2 p825); acute surgical pain in postsurgical clients, short-term use only (OpenRN p1416); breakthrough pain in postoperative patients when acetaminophen and NSAIDs are insufficient (AUGS T2 p9); and, in palliative care with end-stage disease, dyspnea using relatively small doses titrated to relief without oversedation, plus cough in advanced disease (OpenRN p1269). Adverse effects cluster into GI (nausea, vomiting, constipation, decreased bowel motility, hypoactive bowel sounds, paralytic ileus with chronic use), CNS/respiratory (sedation, somnolence, fatigue, lethargy, impaired stimuli perception, decreased respiratory rate, respiratory depression), genitourinary (urinary retention, especially in opioid-naive clients or spinal-route delivery), pruritus (especially spinal route), anaphylaxis (WHO T1 p46), and misuse outcomes—overdose, opioid use disorder, and addiction. One explicit safety threshold: withhold the opioid while a client (not receiving end-of-life care) is oversedated or the respiratory rate is under 12/minute (OpenRN p844). Continual monitoring for pruritus is advised for clients receiving opioids (p844); pruritus is treated with antihistamines, specifically diphenhydramine. Contributors: OpenRN (most granular, covering routes, opioid-naive status, chronic use, end-of-life populations, and the RR<12 hold rule); AUGS (multimodal framing—opioids reserved for breakthrough pain after acetaminophen/NSAIDs, listing nausea, vomiting, constipation, somnolence); ERAS Society (risks of fatigue, nausea, sedation, addiction specifically when opioids are the sole postoperative analgesic); WHO (anaphylaxis only). AUGS and ERAS converge on limiting opioid-only analgesia; neither specifies monitoring thresholds as OpenRN does. Constipation risk is also flagged for end-of-life clients (p1269) and respiratory depression for that group (p1288). The community does NOT establish doses, dosing intervals, specific opioid agents, gynecologic-surgery-specific protocols, naloxone or bowel-regimen prophylaxis, monitoring frequency, or comparative effectiveness against non-opioid analgesics.

title: Opioid disposal education at discharge
summary:
Clinical theme: This small, tightly focused community addresses discharge-phase opioid stewardship in the perioperative gynecologic setting — specifically, patient and family education on safe disposal of leftover opioid medication as a harm-reduction intervention. The two relations in the community both originate from a single node, opioid disposal education, and both are preventive in nature, framing unused take-home opioids as a residual community risk after the surgical episode ends.

Recommendations, with population and condition: (1) Provide opioid disposal education to prevent opioid diversion. Population: clients being discharged with an opioid medication, and their families. Condition/timing: delivered as part of the discharge plan. (2) Provide the same opioid disposal education to prevent accidental opioid exposure. Population as stated: someone other than the person for whom the opioid was prescribed — i.e., the protected party is a third party (household member, child, visitor) rather than the patient. Condition/timing: again, as part of the discharge plan. Practically, this means disposal instruction is not optional or ad hoc teaching but a scheduled element of the discharge process for every client leaving with an opioid prescription, and the teaching audience explicitly includes family, not the patient alone.

Contributing guideline bodies: Both relations derive from a single source, OpenRN (Nursing Skills / OpenRN Tome 2, p. 788). There is therefore no cross-body corroboration, no divergence, and no instance of one body being more specific than another within this community; the two edges differ only in the harm outcome specified (diversion vs. accidental exposure), not in population framing or timing.

What this community does NOT establish: it names no specific opioid agents, doses, quantities, or prescribing thresholds; no disposal method (take-back program, drug deactivation pouch, flushing, pharmacy return); no documentation, teach-back, or competency verification requirement; no follow-up interval or re-education timepoint; no gynecologic-procedure-specific tailoring; and no outcome data quantifying reduction in diversion or exposure. It also does not address opioid storage, naloxone co-prescribing, or in-hospital opioid waste.
key_entities: clients being discharged with an opioid medication and their families

title: ERAS Metabolic Stress and Insulin Resistance
summary:
This community centres on perioperative metabolic management within Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) pathways for gynecologic surgery, with insulin resistance as the pivotal intermediate outcome linking care processes to complications. Insulin resistance is stated to increase the risk of perioperative complications specifically in patients undergoing pelvic exenteration or HIPEC therapy (ERAS Society, T1 p11), which frames why metabolic-stress reduction matters.

Four interventions are credited with preventing insulin resistance: oral carbohydrate loading, thoracic epidural analgesia, and early feeding, each as part of the ERAS protocol (ERAS Society T1 p6), plus the general category of 'ERAS elements that reduce metabolic stress' (T1 p2). Early mobilisation is separately recommended to prevent perioperative complications in pelvic exenteration/HIPEC patients (T1 p11).

The oral carbohydrate-rich drink is the most fully specified element. Timing: preoperatively, up until 2 hours before initiation of anesthesia (ERAS Society T1 p4); AUGS (T2 p3) similarly supports administration up to 2 h before surgery in surgical patients and adds a benefit ERAS does not — prevention of nausea, alongside reduced insulin resistance. AUGS (T2 p13) is more explicit about population, placing the preoperative carbohydrate drink in diabetic and obese patients. ERAS Society is more explicit about limits: its insulin-resistance benefit in gynecologic surgery is extrapolated from non-gynecological surgery data, and the drink is contraindicated in gastrointestinal motility disorders, documented delayed gastric emptying, and emergency surgery (all T1 p4).

The two bodies are complementary rather than conflicting: AUGS broadens the outcome (nausea) and names at-risk populations; ERAS Society supplies the timing rule, contraindications and an evidence caveat.

Not established here: any carbohydrate dose, volume or concentration; fasting rules for solids; glucose thresholds or insulin/glycemic-control drug regimens; epidural agents, levels or dosing; what 'early' means for feeding or mobilisation in hours; whether these interventions reduce mortality, length of stay or infection; and whether reduced insulin resistance in non-exenteration/non-HIPEC populations translates into fewer complications.
key_entities: eras elements that reduce metabolic stress

title: Methamphetamine Use and Oral Health Risks
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: the oral health consequences of methamphetamine use, relevant to preoperative assessment and perioperative airway/oral care planning in gynecologic surgical patients who use stimulants. All three relations originate from one source, OpenRN Textbook 2, page 471, and all describe methamphetamine as a risk-increasing agent for oral pathology.

The recommendations, with their attached populations, are: (1) methamphetamine increases risk of oral tissue breakdown, for the population of methamphetamine users; (2) methamphetamine increases risk of tooth decay, for methamphetamine users; and (3) methamphetamine increases risk of oral lesions, with a narrower population condition — users who specifically smoke methamphetamine. The third relation is the most specific in the community, distinguishing route of administration (smoking) as the qualifying condition, whereas the tooth decay and oral tissue breakdown risks are attached to methamphetamine use generally, without route restriction. Practically, this means a nurse assessing any patient disclosing methamphetamine use should anticipate dental caries and mucosal/tissue breakdown, and should escalate suspicion of discrete oral lesions when the route is inhalational/smoked.

Only one guideline body contributes here — OpenRN — so there are no inter-body disagreements, no competing thresholds, and no corroborating or conflicting recommendations from professional societies (e.g., AORN, ACOG, ASA) within this community. The apparent specificity gradient is internal to the single source rather than a difference between organisations.

What this community does NOT establish: it gives no numeric thresholds (no dose, frequency, cumulative duration, or years of use), no timing for screening, no preoperative abstinence interval, and no perioperative management, referral, or dental-consultation pathway. It does not state prevalence, severity grading, or reversibility of the oral findings, nor does it link these oral findings to anaesthetic airway risk, intubation difficulty, surgical site infection, or gynecologic surgical outcomes. It also says nothing about other stimulants, other routes (injection, insufflation), pregnancy, or treatment of established oral disease.

title: Paracetamol route selection in surgical analgesia
summary:
This community represents the theme of baseline paracetamol analgesia for surgical patients, and specifically the choice of route (oral versus intravenous) as the defining clinical decision. All three relations derive from a single guideline source, NICE T1 (page 12), so this theme reflects one guideline body rather than a comparison across bodies.

The core recommendation is that oral paracetamol applies to adults having surgery, including dental surgery, and that it should be offered irrespective of pain severity. Dental surgery is captured as an explicitly named subset of surgery, making the dental population the more specific instance of the broader surgical recommendation; the condition attached is identical in both cases (irrespective of pain severity), so oral paracetamol is positioned as a routine, non-severity-stratified baseline rather than a rescue or step-up analgesic.

The second recommendation constrains the intravenous route: intravenous paracetamol is temporarily contraindicated in favour of oral paracetamol for adults having surgery, and is not to be used unless the person cannot take oral medicine. Inability to take oral medicine is therefore the only stated trigger for the IV route. For nurse educators and QI leads, this supports auditable practice points: confirming oral tolerance before IV paracetamol is prescribed or administered, documenting the reason when the IV route is used, and prompting IV-to-oral switch once oral intake is possible.

What this community does NOT establish: no doses, dose intervals, maximum daily limits, weight- or age-based adjustments, or timing relative to induction, incision or discharge are given. It says nothing about paediatric, obstetric, hepatic- or renal-impaired populations, or about paracetamol contraindications and hypersensitivity. It does not address combination or multimodal regimens (NSAIDs, opioids, local anaesthetic techniques), nor rectal or other alternative routes. No comparative or conflicting recommendation from a second guideline body is present, so cross-corpus agreement on paracetamol route selection cannot be assessed from these relations alone.

title: HIV Prevention and Testing in Pregnancy
summary:
This community represents HIV prevention and detection across the pregnancy-to-intrapartum continuum, drawing on WHO guidance (WHO T1, pages 13 and 31). Two distinct activities are captured: pharmacological pre-exposure prophylaxis for women who are HIV-negative but at risk, and point-of-care diagnosis for women whose status is unknown when they present in labour.

The prophylaxis recommendations: oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) prevents HIV infection in pregnant women at substantial risk of HIV infection, and should be offered as an additional prevention choice within a combination prevention approach rather than as a stand-alone measure (WHO T1 p13). The named agent is tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, also indicated to prevent HIV infection in pregnant women at substantial risk, again as part of combination prevention (WHO T1 p13). The conditional framing matters for practice: eligibility is risk-based ('substantial risk'), and the intervention is positioned as an offer/choice embedded in broader prevention services.

The detection recommendation: rapid HIV testing detects HIV infection in mothers presenting at labour with unknown HIV status, performed during labour or immediately postpartum (WHO T1 p31). This gives QI leads a concrete trigger — unknown status at admission in labour — and a concrete timing window — intrapartum or immediate postpartum.

Only one guideline body contributes here: WHO. There are therefore no inter-body disagreements to reconcile, though the corpus differs internally in specificity — page 13 names a specific drug (tenofovir disoproxil fumarate) alongside the generic modality (oral PrEP), while page 31 specifies a testing modality and timing without naming a test product.

What this community does NOT establish: no dosing, frequency, duration, or stopping rules for oral PrEP or tenofovir disoproxil fumarate; no definition or threshold for what constitutes 'substantial risk'; no list of the other components of 'combination prevention'; no antiretroviral prophylaxis or treatment pathway for mothers who test positive, and no infant post-exposure or feeding guidance; no test sensitivity, confirmatory algorithm, or repeat-testing interval; and no safety or monitoring statements for PrEP use in pregnancy.
key_entities: pregnant women at substantial risk of HIV infection
mothers presenting at labour with unknown HIV status

title: NEWS2 Single-Parameter Score and Organ Dysfunction
summary:
This small community represents one narrow but operationally important theme: the use of the National Early Warning Score 2 (NEWS2) as a bedside screening tool for organ dysfunction in suspected sepsis, and specifically the significance of a single physiological parameter scoring 3 points.

Two linked recommendations are captured. First, in people aged 16 or over with suspected sepsis, a single parameter contributing 3 points to the NEWS2 score is treated as increasing the risk of organ dysfunction; the guideline is explicit that this position rests on committee consensus based on clinical expertise, despite a lack of supporting evidence (NICE T1, p60). Second, NEWS2 score assessment is credited with detecting organ dysfunction in people with suspected sepsis, with the triggering condition stated as when a single parameter contributes 3 points to the NEWS2 score (NICE T1, p66). Practically, this means the aggregate NEWS2 total is not the only trigger: one extreme derangement in a single vital sign is itself an escalation cue for the perioperative gynecologic nurse who suspects sepsis.

Only one guideline body contributes here — NICE (Tier 1, pages 60 and 66). There is therefore no cross-body disagreement to reconcile. Internally, the two statements differ in specificity of population: the risk statement is restricted to people aged 16 or over, whereas the detection statement is generalised to people with suspected sepsis without an age qualifier. Educators should note this asymmetry rather than assume the 16-and-over threshold applies to both.

The community does not establish: which specific NEWS2 parameters (respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, pulse, consciousness, temperature) most often score 3; any aggregate NEWS2 threshold values; escalation timings, review intervals or who must be called; any diagnostic tests, antibiotics, fluids, drugs or doses; sensitivity, specificity or outcome data; paediatric, pregnant or immediate-postoperative gynecologic-specific criteria; or any definition or grading of organ dysfunction itself. It also provides no evidence base — the causal link is consensus-derived only.
key_entities: single parameter contributing 3 points to a NEWS2 score

title: Essential Imaging Display Before Procedures
summary:
THEME: This small, tightly focused community represents the intraoperative availability and display of essential imaging — the requirement that relevant films/studies be present and visibly displayed in the operating room for procedures where the surgical plan depends on them. It is a component of surgical safety checklist practice rather than a drug- or dose-based recommendation.

RECOMMENDATIONS AND POPULATIONS: A single recommendation — display of essential imaging — is applied to four procedure populations: (1) tumour resection, (2) thoracic procedures, (3) orthopaedic procedures, and (4) spinal procedures. In every case the attached condition is identical and conditional: the requirement applies 'when imaging is needed for the case.' The graph therefore does not mandate imaging display universally, but only where the case type makes imaging necessary to confirm site, side, level or lesion location. All four relations carry equal weight; no procedure category is prioritised over another, and no distinction is drawn between elective and emergency settings.

GUIDELINE BODIES: All four relations derive from a single source, WHO Table 1, page 110 (surgical safety checklist guidance). There is thus no inter-body disagreement, no competing or more specific parallel recommendation from another society, and no gynecologic-specialty-specific elaboration within this community — a notable gap for a perioperative gynecologic nursing corpus, since gynecologic tumour resection would fall under 'tumour resection' only by inference.

WHAT IT DOES NOT ESTABLISH: The community specifies no timing (e.g., before induction, before incision, or at time-out), no responsible role (surgeon, circulating nurse, radiographer), and no verification or documentation method. It defines no criteria for deciding when imaging 'is needed,' no imaging modalities (CT, MRI, plain film, PACS versus hard copy), no thresholds, and no escalation pathway if imaging is absent. It names no drugs, doses or monitoring parameters, and states no outcome benefit, audit metric or compliance target. Educators should treat it as a checklist prompt requiring local operationalisation.

title: Diuretic-Induced Orthostatic Hypotension and Fall Risk
summary:
This community represents a medication-related fall-risk pathway: diuretics (including thiazide diuretics specifically) increase the risk of orthostatic hypotension, which in turn increases fall risk in clients whose blood pressure drops on standing, particularly when light-headedness or dizziness occurs. The countermeasure theme is structured orthostatic blood pressure surveillance plus symptom monitoring.

Main recommendations with populations and conditions: (1) Recognise thiazide diuretics as raising orthostatic hypotension risk in patients treated with them (RNAO), and diuretics generally in clients receiving them (OpenRN). (2) Routinely monitor orthostatic blood pressure in clients taking any medication that can cause orthostatic hypotension. (3) For clients specifically at risk of falls, obtain daily orthostatic blood pressure measurement, notifying the provider as indicated. (4) Technique and threshold: measure lying and again after standing one to three minutes; a fall in systolic BP greater than 20 mm Hg or diastolic greater than 10 mm Hg is abnormal. (5) Monitor for dizziness upon standing as a clinical indicator of orthostatic hypotension.

Contributing bodies: RNAO (Tab 2, p140) contributes only the drug-class risk link, and is more specific at the drug level by naming thiazide diuretics. OpenRN (Tab 2, pp395, 436, 1111) supplies the whole monitoring and detection apparatus, the fall consequence, and the numeric diagnostic thresholds and 1–3 minute standing interval; it generalises the drug exposure to diuretics as a class. The two sources are complementary rather than contradictory, though they differ in monitoring frequency emphasis: routine monitoring for medication-exposed clients versus daily measurement for fall-risk clients.

What this community does not establish: no treatment or prevention interventions (no fluid, dosing-adjustment, deprescribing, ambulation-assistance, or patient-education measures), no fall-outcome or injury rates, no specific gynecologic or postoperative population, no age or comorbidity qualifiers, and no defined action threshold beyond notifying the provider. It also does not name other drug classes, other causes of orthostatic hypotension, or heart-rate criteria.

title: Osteoporosis risk, prevention, and treatment
summary: This community centres on osteoporosis as both a drug-related harm in pregnancy and a general bone-health problem requiring screening, prevention, and pharmacologic treatment. Two guideline bodies contribute. RCOG (T1 p17, p23) addresses anticoagulant-induced bone loss: prolonged use of unfractionated heparin during pregnancy increases osteoporosis risk in pregnant women, a point repeated across two pages. Low molecular weight heparin also increases risk, but RCOG is explicit that the risk is much less than with unfractionated heparin, reported as 0.04% — the only numeric threshold in the community and a concrete argument for LMWH over UFH when prolonged antenatal anticoagulation is needed. OpenRN (T2) supplies the general nursing content. Detection: a risk for injury assessment detects osteoporosis in clients with a history of frequent falls (p395). Consequence: osteoporosis increases risk of fracture in people with osteoporosis, including from minor injuries, because bones are weakened (p763). Prevention, for patients at risk and aimed at keeping bones strong: a diet rich in calcium and vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise, and smoking avoidance (p763). Treatment: bisphosphonates and calcitonin, both qualified as 'if needed, for severe osteoporosis' (p763). The two bodies differ in scope rather than conflict: RCOG is specific about drug exposure, population (pregnant women) and quantified incidence but offers no prevention or treatment guidance; OpenRN is specific about assessment, lifestyle prevention and drug therapy but does not address pregnancy or heparin at all. The community does NOT establish: any bone density screening test, threshold or interval; dosing, duration or route for bisphosphonates or calcitonin; a definition of 'severe' osteoporosis; calcium or vitamin D amounts; the type, frequency or intensity of weight-bearing exercise; whether prevention measures mitigate heparin-associated bone loss; whether osteoporosis prophylaxis is indicated during antenatal anticoagulation; any perioperative or gynecologic-surgery-specific management; and any fracture-risk magnitude or fall-prevention intervention beyond the risk for injury assessment.
key_entities: diet rich in calcium and vitamin d

title: Hearing Impairment Detection and Ototoxic Risk
summary:
This community represents a single clinical theme: identification of hearing impairment and one recognised contributor to it. Three relations tie two detection methods and one risk factor to the same outcome entity, hearing impairment.

Main recommendations, with populations and conditions: (1) Screening hearing testing detects hearing impairment in all newborns, with the condition that screening be completed before discharge — this is the only relation in the community that specifies both a defined population and a defined timing. (2) The whispered voice test detects hearing impairment, conditioned on being performed accurately; no population, age group, or setting is attached, so its applicability is left open. (3) Ototoxic medication increases the risk of hearing impairment; this relation carries no population and no condition, and no individual drug, dose, duration, or monitoring threshold is named.

Contributing guideline bodies: all three relations derive from a single source corpus, OpenRN Nursing Fundamentals Volume 2, at pages 510, 521, and 539. Because there is only one contributing body, there are no inter-guideline disagreements to reconcile. There is, however, a clear difference in specificity within the corpus: the newborn screening relation (p510) is the most operationally actionable, naming both a universal population and a discharge-linked deadline, whereas the ototoxicity relation (p521) is the least specified, and the whispered voice test relation (p539) sits in between, adding only an accuracy caveat.

What this community does NOT establish: it names no specific ototoxic agents (no aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, platinum agents or any other drug class), no dosing or cumulative-exposure thresholds, and no baseline or serial audiometric monitoring schedule for patients receiving ototoxic therapy. It does not state sensitivity, specificity, or pass/refer criteria for either the newborn screen or the whispered voice test, does not define what "performed accurately" requires, does not specify who performs or documents the tests, and gives no follow-up, referral, or rescreening pathway for a failed newborn screen. No perioperative or gynecologic-specific application is described.

title: Laboratory Monitoring for Anticoagulation Safety
summary:
This community centres on laboratory surveillance of therapeutic anticoagulation to detect over-anticoagulation, drawing on three related relations from RCOG guidance (Top Ten / thromboprophylaxis-anticoagulation material, pages 14, 19 and 20). All three edges converge on a single safety outcome — over-anticoagulation — monitored by coagulation assays rather than by clinical signs alone.

Main recommendations with populations and conditions:
• Activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) measurement monitors for over-anticoagulation in patients receiving intravenous unfractionated heparin, with a defined schedule: 4–6 hours after the loading dose, 6 hours after any dose change, and then at least daily once the patient is in the therapeutic range (RCOG T1 p14).
• APTT is again identified as the monitor for over-anticoagulation in pregnant women receiving unfractionated heparin, but the condition is flagged as problematic: there are recognised issues in monitoring unfractionated heparin in pregnancy using the APTT (RCOG T1 p19).
• International normalised ratio (INR) testing monitors for over-anticoagulation in women transferring from LMWH to warfarin postpartum, with daily testing during the transfer period (RCOG T1 p20).

Contributing bodies and differences: only RCOG contributes here, so there is no inter-body disagreement to reconcile; the variation is internal and population-driven. The non-pregnant IV unfractionated heparin recommendation (p14) is the most specific, giving explicit timing anchors (post-loading dose, post-dose change, daily at therapeutic range). The obstetric statement (p19) is deliberately more cautious, noting APTT limitations in pregnancy without substituting an alternative assay or threshold. The postpartum warfarin transition (p20) specifies frequency (daily) and a different test (INR).

What this community does NOT establish: no numerical target ranges or thresholds are given for APTT ratio or INR; no anti-Xa or alternative assay is named for pregnancy despite the acknowledged APTT problem; no LMWH monitoring recommendation, dose-adjustment algorithm, reversal agent, or action to take when over-anticoagulation is detected; no duration for postpartum INR monitoring; and no perioperative gynaecologic-surgery-specific timing.

title: Enlarged prostate as urinary retention risk
summary:
Clinical theme: This is a small, single-source community describing benign prostatic enlargement as an anatomic risk factor for lower urinary tract dysfunction in adult males. It sits at the intersection of perioperative bladder assessment and continence care, where obstructive outlet pathology predisposes patients to incomplete emptying.

Recommendations/assertions and their populations: Two relations, both scoped to adult males, both drawn from OpenRN Nursing Skills/Fundamentals (Textbook 2, p. 1150). (1) An enlarged prostate increases the risk of urinary retention. (2) An enlarged prostate increases the risk of overflow urinary incontinence — the leakage that follows chronic retention and bladder overdistension. No additional condition qualifiers (e.g., postoperative status, anesthesia type, opioid exposure, catheter presence) are attached to either relation; the population is simply adult males.

Contributing bodies and differences: Only one guideline body contributes — OpenRN, via a single page (T2 p1150). There is therefore no cross-corpus agreement, contradiction, or difference in specificity to reconcile: no professional society (e.g., AORN, ASA, urology or continence bodies) is represented here, and neither relation is corroborated or refined by a second source. Both relations share identical population, condition, and provenance, so the community is best treated as one textbook statement expressed as two risk edges.

What this community does NOT establish: It gives no screening or diagnostic thresholds — no post-void residual volume cutoffs, no bladder-scan timing, no interval after surgery or after catheter removal at which retention should be assessed. It names no drugs (no alpha-blockers such as tamsulosin, no 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors, no anticholinergics to avoid) and no interventions such as intermittent or indwelling catheterization. It does not quantify risk (no incidence, relative risk, or odds), does not stratify by prostate size, symptom score, or age band, and says nothing about female or pediatric patients, other retention causes (medications, neurologic disease, immobility), or management of overflow incontinence once present. Educators should pair it with procedure-specific retention protocols before operational use.

title: Preventing Opioid-Related Oversedation and Respiratory Depression
summary:
This community centres on sedation and respiratory safety in patients receiving analgesic and sedating medications, particularly opioids delivered by patient-controlled analgesia (PCA). Oversedation is the hub concept, with respiratory depression as the closely linked adverse outcome.

Risk factors and drug cautions: benzodiazepines increase the risk of oversedation, with the guideline specifically flagging the frail elderly as the population of concern. Opioids are temporarily contraindicated while a client is oversedated or the respiratory rate falls below 12 breaths/minute; the nurse withholds the dose in that situation, with an explicit exception for clients receiving end-of-life care.

Engineering and monitoring safeguards: for clients on PCA, pump settings themselves prevent oversedation when the pump is programmed to deliver medication only every set number of minutes and with a maximum hourly dose limit. Nursing assessment is the second layer: for clients receiving PCA medications, nurses monitor respiratory rate, SpO2, sedation level and mental status to detect both oversedation and respiratory depression. More broadly, any client receiving opioids requires continual monitoring for oversedation.

Contributing bodies: all relations derive from a single source, OpenRN Nursing Skills / Nursing Pharmacology (Textbook 2), cited at p825 (PCA monitoring), p844 (opioid withholding and continual monitoring), and p1269 (benzodiazepine risk in the frail elderly). Because only one corpus contributes, there are no inter-body disagreements; differences are only in granularity — the p844 material gives a concrete numeric threshold (respiratory rate <12/minute) and a population exception (end-of-life care), whereas the PCA monitoring statements name assessment parameters without specifying frequency or alert values, and the p1269 benzodiazepine statement names a vulnerable population without a threshold.

Not established: no specific drug names, doses, PCA lockout intervals or maximum hourly limits; no reversal agent (e.g., naloxone) or escalation pathway; no defined monitoring frequency or duration; no validated sedation scale; no guidance for non-PCA routes, epidural analgesia, or gynecologic/perioperative-specific populations despite the perioperative framing; and no combined benzodiazepine-plus-opioid interaction rule.
key_entities: nursing monitoring of respiratory rate, SpO2, sedation level and mental status

title: Oxybutynin and Urge Incontinence Management
summary:
This community represents a small, tightly focused theme: pharmacologic management of urge-type urinary incontinence and the behavioural factors that predispose to it. Three relations anchor it. First, oxybutynin is identified as a treatment for urge urinary incontinence, with the explicit condition that it be given 'as prescribed' — i.e., the nursing role is administration and monitoring within an existing prescription, not independent initiation. Second, the same drug and the same 'as prescribed' condition extend to mixed urinary incontinence, indicating that oxybutynin's applicability is not limited to pure urge presentations but also covers mixed patterns where an urge component is present. Third, ineffective toileting habits are flagged as increasing the risk of urge urinary incontinence, which positions patient toileting behaviour as a modifiable contributor and supports pairing drug therapy with behavioural assessment and education.

All three relations derive from a single guideline body, OpenRN (Nursing Fundamentals/Skills, Volume T2, pages 1162 and 1183). Because there is only one contributing source, this community shows no inter-body disagreement; the only internal distinction is one of specificity — p1162 is drug-specific and condition-qualified ('as prescribed'), while p1183 is a broader risk statement with no population or condition attached at all, making it the less specific of the two claims.

Important limits for educators and QI leads: the community does not state any dose, frequency, route, titration schedule, duration, or timing for oxybutynin; it names no anticholinergic side effects, contraindications, monitoring parameters, or drug alternatives. It specifies no patient population by age, sex, surgical status, or perioperative phase, and does not link oxybutynin to stress, overflow, functional, or transient incontinence. It does not define what constitutes 'ineffective toileting habits', nor does it establish that correcting toileting habits reduces urge incontinence — only that poor habits raise risk. No thresholds, outcome measures, or escalation criteria are present, so any protocol work would need supplementation from sources outside this community.

title: Triclosan-Coated Sutures for SSI Prevention
summary:
This community covers a single, narrowly scoped intervention: antimicrobial triclosan-coated sutures used in place of standard (uncoated) sutures to prevent surgical site infection (SSI). All relations in the community link one entity (antimicrobial triclosan-coated suture) to one outcome (surgical site infection), with paediatric surgery appearing as the population where benefit is best established.

Main recommendations. NICE states that triclosan-coated sutures prevent SSI in patients undergoing surgery — the condition attached is 'when using sutures', i.e. the choice applies at the point of wound closure when suture material is selected — and highlights paediatric surgery in particular (NICE T1 p12). NICE is more specific elsewhere: the comparison is explicitly against standard sutures, and clear benefit has been shown only in paediatric surgery (NICE T1 p25). A separate NICE relation confines applicability to paediatric patients on the same basis. The CDC also supports triclosan-coated sutures for SSI prevention, but grades this as a weak recommendation — 'consider use' — based on moderate-quality evidence suggesting a trade-off between benefits and harms (CDC T1 p3).

Contributing bodies and differences. Two bodies contribute: NICE and the CDC. They agree on direction of effect (SSI reduction versus standard sutures) but differ in framing. NICE differentiates by population, restricting the claim of clear benefit to paediatric surgery; the CDC does not specify a population here and instead qualifies strength of evidence, offering a weak/conditional 'consider' recommendation with an explicit benefit–harm trade-off. Educators should present this as a conditional, population-sensitive option rather than a mandate.

What this community does NOT establish. It gives no gynecologic- or obstetric-specific evidence, no adult surgical subgroup data, and no demonstrated benefit outside paediatric surgery. It specifies no triclosan concentration, suture gauge or material, no timing beyond the closure step, no cost-effectiveness threshold, no numerical SSI risk reduction, and does not name the specific harms behind the CDC trade-off. It also says nothing about bundling with other SSI measures such as skin antisepsis or antibiotic prophylaxis.

title: Perioperative Pain Assessment and Multimodal Management
summary:
This community covers perioperative and general pain management: assessment, multimodal pharmacology, nonpharmacologic measures, and procedural practices that provoke or prevent pain.

Assessment: RNAO (T2) mandates initial and ongoing pain screening/assessment for all people in the care of health providers, using a comprehensive, evidence-based, person- and family-centred approach. OpenRN adds concrete tools — a valid pain intensity rating scale, frameworks such as PQRST or OLDCARTES, and client self-monitoring for chronic pain.

Pharmacology: NICE (T1) recommends paracetamol alongside opioid analgesia for adults having surgery (oral route preferred if able to take oral medicines); pre-emptive analgesia for when local anaesthesia wears off; IV ketamine added to an IV opioid when the opioid alone is inadequate or the person is opioid sensitive; and patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) or continuous epidural as a choice for people who cannot take oral opioids, with continuous epidural for major/complex open-torso surgery for early pain relief. OpenRN grades therapy by severity: NSAIDs for mild-to-moderate pain, opioids for moderate-to-severe pain (IV for rapid relief), morphine for severe cancer/end-of-life pain (no ceiling effect) and morphine sulfate sublingually in dying clients for pain and dyspnea — while warning that higher morphine doses increase sedation and respiratory depression. PCA is self-administered via programmed pump; pressing the button by anyone other than the client is contraindicated. Analgesia should be prompt — before pain becomes severe, before pain-inducing activity, or before physical therapy in rehabilitating fracture clients.

ERAS Society and AUGS add perioperative specifics: preoperative counseling/education (added to an existing ERAS protocol) prevents and treats postoperative pain; PCA should be required in <5% of laparotomy patients; postoperative shivering increases pain; low insufflation pressure prevents pain; perineal ice packs treat pain. OpenRN details procedural pain prevention: correct needle length, ventrogluteal site for adult IM injections, larger diameter needles; nasotracheal suctioning and silver dressings (which prevent infection in moderate-to-high exuding wounds) may cause pain. WHO notes wrong-side surgery causes pain and anxiety.

Not established: doses, dosing intervals, comparative efficacy, opioid-sparing thresholds, epidural duration, or gynecologic-specific pain protocols beyond ERAS/AUGS items.

title: Postoperative Paralytic Ileus Risk and Monitoring
summary:
This community centers on postoperative paralytic ileus — its risk factors, bedside detection, and initial management — in gynecologic/abdominal surgical nursing care. Risk factors documented are abdominal surgery, general anesthesia, electrolyte imbalance, chronic opioid use (condition: chronic use, not single doses), bacterial or viral intestinal infections, decreased blood flow to the intestines, and kidney or liver disease. A second source states the combined exposure more specifically: clients who have recently had abdominal surgical procedures under general anesthesia are at increased risk, naming the population explicitly rather than listing surgery and anesthesia as separate factors.

The core nursing recommendation is assessment-driven surveillance. Bowel sound assessment discriminates by finding: hypoactive bowel sounds detect constipation, whereas absent bowel sounds detect paralytic ileus. Monitoring for symptoms of paralytic ileus is indicated for postoperative clients and is anchored to the postoperative phase; monitoring of bowel sounds is likewise a monitoring intervention for paralytic ileus. For treatment, strict NPO status treats paralytic ileus.

All relations derive from a single guideline body, OpenRN (Nursing Skills/Nursing Management text), drawn from two passages: Tome 2 p1173 (risk factors, bowel sound interpretation, postoperative symptom monitoring, strict NPO) and Tome 2 p1183 (the recently-postoperative abdominal/general-anesthesia population and bowel sound monitoring). There is no cross-body disagreement; p1183 is the more population-specific of the two, while p1173 is broader and the only source giving the auscultation thresholds and the NPO intervention. Because only one corpus contributes, apparent duplication ("monitoring for symptoms" vs. "monitoring of bowel sounds") reflects two passages rather than competing recommendations.

The community does NOT establish: any timing or frequency of bowel sound auscultation, duration of NPO status, criteria for resuming oral intake, specific opioid agents or dose thresholds defining "chronic use", electrolyte values, imaging or laboratory confirmation, pharmacologic or decompressive therapies (e.g., nasogastric suction, prokinetics), escalation criteria, or gynecologic-procedure-specific incidence or outcomes.
key_entities: abdominal surgical procedure under general anesthesia
decreased blood flow to the intestines
monitoring for symptoms of paralytic ileus

title: Preincision Antimicrobial Prophylaxis in Cesarean Section
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: the timing of parenteral antimicrobial prophylaxis in cesarean section as a surgical site infection (SSI) prevention measure. Two relations anchor it. First, parenteral antimicrobial prophylaxis applies to caesarean section when it is administered before skin incision. Second, in patients undergoing cesarean section, parenteral antimicrobial prophylaxis prevents surgical site infection under that same condition of administration before skin incision. The actionable recommendation for perioperative gynecologic/obstetric nursing practice is therefore: for the population of patients undergoing cesarean delivery, give the parenteral prophylactic antimicrobial prior to skin incision rather than after cord clamping or later in the procedure, because the preincision timing is the condition under which the SSI-prevention benefit is attached. For a QI lead, the measurable process element is documented administration of a parenteral prophylactic agent before incision, with the outcome measure being post-cesarean SSI rate.

Only one guideline body contributes here: the CDC (source CDC T1 p3), so there are no inter-body disagreements, no conflicting timing windows, and no instance of one organisation being more specific than another within this community. All content derives from a single page of a single source, which limits the breadth of corroboration.

Important gaps: the community does NOT name any specific antimicrobial agent (no cefazolin, azithromycin, or other drug is specified), nor any dose, route detail beyond "parenteral," redosing interval, weight-based adjustment, or a numeric time threshold such as 60 minutes before incision. It does not address duration or discontinuation of prophylaxis postoperatively, patients with beta-lactam allergy, laboring versus scheduled/elective cesarean, ruptured membranes, obesity thresholds, or non-cesarean gynecologic procedures (e.g., hysterectomy). It establishes no relation to other SSI bundle elements such as skin antisepsis, hair removal, glycemic control, or normothermia, and provides no evidence-strength grading. Those elements must be sought from other communities or source documents before building a complete protocol.

title: Artificial Nails and Nail Polish Hand Contamination
summary:
This community centres on a single, tightly focused hand-hygiene theme: fingernail condition among health-care personnel as a reservoir for pathogens and a driver of infection risk, even when hand hygiene or surgical scrub is performed correctly.

The core recommendations: (1) Artificial nails increase pathogen carriage on the hands of nurses despite hand hygiene (OpenRN T2, incl. p642). (2) Chipped nail polish carries the same risk for nurses, again despite hand hygiene (OpenRN T2, p642). (3) CDC adds organism- and setting-specific detail: artificial nails increase risk of Pseudomonas colonisation in nurses working in a neonatal intensive care unit, and of infection caused by gram-negative bacilli and yeast in health-care personnel wearing artificial nails (CDC T1 p31). (4) In the perioperative setting, artificial nails on surgical team members increase bacterial and fungal colonization of the hands despite an adequate hand scrub, and are linked to surgical site infection in cardiovascular surgery patients through an outbreak of Serratia marcescens associated with a surgical nurse wearing artificial nails (CDC T1 p11).

Two guideline bodies contribute. OpenRN is broader in scope of nail finish — it is the only source addressing chipped nail polish — but stays generic ("pathogen carriage on the hands," nurses as a population). CDC is markedly more specific, naming organisms (Pseudomonas, Serratia marcescens, gram-negative bacilli, yeast), populations (NICU nurses, surgical team members, cardiovascular surgery patients), and progressing from colonisation to a documented outbreak-associated surgical site infection. The two do not contradict one another; CDC extends OpenRN.

What this community does NOT establish: no explicit prohibition, policy wording, permissible nail length threshold, or re-polish/removal interval is stated; no antiseptic agent, scrub duration, or glove recommendation is specified; intact (non-chipped) polish is not assessed, nor is any risk quantified (no relative risk, incidence, or outbreak case counts). No monitoring, auditing, or remediation action is attached to any relation.
key_entities: infection caused by gram-negative bacilli and yeast
bacterial and fungal colonization of the hands

title: Hand Hygiene and Fomite Pathogen Transmission
summary:
This community represents basic infection-prevention practice: hand hygiene as the core protective action, and everyday fomites (gripper socks, mobile devices) as vectors for pathogen transmission in the patient care environment.
