Recommendations. (1) Handwashing prevents infection when performed routinely at appropriate moments (OpenRN Table 2, p203), and specifically prevents infection in patients undergoing invasive procedures when performed immediately prior to and during the procedure (OpenRN T2 p247). (2) Handwashing prevents transmission of pathogens in health-care facilities generally (CDC T1 p4). (3) Gripper socks increase the risk of pathogen transfer to bed linens, of pathogen transmission, and of infection for clients who ambulate in the hallway, specifically when the socks worn for walking are worn back into bed (OpenRN T2, p642). The stated countermeasure is removal of gripper socks before entering bed, for clients who used gripper socks for walking, performed before the client climbs into bed (OpenRN T2). (4) Mobile devices increase the risk of pathogen transmission (OpenRN T2), stated without a qualifying population or condition.

Contributing bodies. Two sources contribute: OpenRN (Table 2, pages 203, 247, 642) and CDC (Table 1, p4). CDC frames handwashing broadly at the facility level as preventing transmission of pathogens; OpenRN is more specific, naming infection as the outcome and attaching timing and population conditions (routine moments; immediately before and during invasive procedures). Only OpenRN addresses fomites — gripper socks and mobile devices — and only OpenRN supplies a concrete corrective action (sock removal before bed entry). There is no contradiction between the two bodies; the difference is granularity and scope.

What is not established. No hand-hygiene agent, technique, duration, or product (soap versus alcohol-based rub) is specified; no thresholds or contact times are given. No mitigation is offered for mobile devices (no cleaning or disinfection step). Nothing links these practices to surgical-site infection rates, perioperative phases, antibiotic prophylaxis, or specific gynecologic procedures, and no outcome or compliance metrics are quantified.
key_entities: removal of gripper socks before entering bed

title: Equipment Cleaning to Prevent Cross-Transmission
summary:
This community represents a single, narrow infection-prevention theme: reprocessing of medical equipment and instruments as the barrier to patient-to-patient transmission of infectious agents in the perioperative and general nursing environment. Both relations converge on the same outcome node, indicating that equipment hygiene is framed primarily as a cross-contamination control measure rather than, for example, a device-performance or sterility-assurance issue.

Two recommendations are captured. First, cleaning of medical equipment and instruments prevents patient-to-patient transmission of infectious agents; this statement is given without a qualifying population or condition, so it reads as a general expectation applicable to all patients and all reusable items. Second, and more specific, disinfection of shared equipment after each patient use prevents patient-to-patient transmission. This second recommendation carries explicit qualifiers: the population is patients requiring shared equipment, with the graph naming a unit-wide bedside blood glucose monitor as the concrete example; the condition is when dedicated (single-patient) equipment is not possible; and the manner of performance is according to agency policy. The implied hierarchy is therefore dedicated equipment first, and if that is unavailable, disinfection between every patient use.

Only one guideline body contributes here: OpenRN, from a single source location (OpenRN Textbook 2, p203). There is consequently no inter-body disagreement to reconcile, but there is an internal gradient of specificity: the general cleaning statement is unconditioned, while the disinfection statement adds population, contingency, and a deference to local agency policy, which effectively delegates the operational detail downward.

The community does not establish which disinfectant agents, concentrations, or contact/dwell times to use; it names no product, no wet-time threshold, and no drying or storage requirements. It does not distinguish cleaning from disinfection from sterilization, nor specify high-level versus low-level disinfection or Spaulding categories. It names no specific organisms, no monitoring or audit metrics, no documentation requirements, no staff training or competency expectations, and no accountable role. It offers no perioperative-specific instrument reprocessing pathway and no evidence grading or strength-of-recommendation rating.
key_entities: cleaning of medical equipment and instruments
disinfection of shared equipment after each patient use

title: Imaging to Detect Suspected Pelvic Abscess
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: the use of diagnostic imaging to identify pelvic abscess in women during the postpartum/post-pregnancy period and in women with suspected sepsis. Three imaging modalities are named — pelvic ultrasound scan, computed tomography (CT) scan, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan — and all are linked by a DETECTS relation to pelvic abscess.

The recommendations are conditional rather than routine: imaging is indicated only 'if pelvic abscess is suspected.' For women following pregnancy, all three modalities apply (pelvic ultrasound, CT, MRI). For women with suspected sepsis, pelvic ultrasound and CT are documented; MRI is recorded only for the post-pregnancy population, so the corpus is more specific about MRI's place in postpartum assessment than in the general suspected-sepsis pathway. Practically, this means a nurse or clinician escalating a woman with clinical suspicion of pelvic collection should anticipate ultrasound and/or cross-sectional imaging as the confirmatory step, and should ensure the suspicion is clearly documented, since the trigger for imaging is clinical suspicion rather than a numeric threshold.

Only one guideline body contributes: the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG), all from a single source location (RCOG T1, p7). There are therefore no inter-body disagreements to reconcile; the only internal variation is the population scope difference for MRI noted above.

The community does NOT establish: any preferred or first-line modality or diagnostic sequence; sensitivity, specificity or accuracy data; timing or urgency targets (e.g. hours from suspicion to scan); what clinical signs, observations, laboratory values or scoring thresholds should raise suspicion of a pelvic abscess; any antimicrobial regimen, drug, dose or route; indications for surgical or radiological drainage; contrast use, safety, or considerations for pregnancy or breastfeeding; nursing monitoring, escalation criteria, or handover responsibilities; and any outcome or follow-up imaging guidance. These gaps would need to be sourced from wider sepsis and postpartum infection guidance before building teaching or audit tools.

title: Constipation Risk, Prevention, and Bowel Management
summary: This community covers bowel elimination management: constipation risk factors, prevention, treatment escalation, and the overlap with bowel incontinence and fecal impaction. Risk factors include opioids (patients/clients receiving opioids, including end-of-life and palliative clients), chemotherapy at end of life, other medications as an adverse effect in hospitalized patients, immobility, and delayed bowel movements in school-aged children during school hours. Core prevention is nonpharmacologic: increased fluid intake, increased dietary fiber, and increased activity/ambulation for older adults and clients taking opioids 'as appropriate,' with adequate fluid intake and ambulation as part of a bowel regimen. Bulk agents psyllium and methylcellulose prevent constipation but must be mixed in a full eight-ounce glass of water to avoid intestinal obstruction. For all clients taking opioids, a bowel management program should start with the first opioid dose and continue until the opioid is discontinued, with docusate prescribed initially and stimulant laxatives/sennosides added as needed to maintain a normal bowel pattern, not long-term; continual monitoring for constipation is advised for clients receiving opioids. A bowel management program is also indicated if a client cannot achieve a soft, formed bowel movement every three days. When oral medications fail or can no longer be tolerated (palliative care), milk of magnesia, bisacodyl, rectal suppository, or enema are used; sennosides and docusate feature in palliative daily bowel regimens. Laxatives are withheld if loose stools or diarrhea occur, and are used for colonoscopy bowel prep the day before, and post-barium to prevent hard stools, fecal impaction, and bowel obstruction. Hypoactive bowel sounds on assessment may detect constipation. Conversely, chronic constipation, fecal impaction, long-term laxative use, colectomy, and bowel surgery increase bowel incontinence risk; psyllium adds bulk for loose stool/incontinence and reduces diarrhea, and scheduled laxatives every three days help neurogenic incontinence. Contributors: OpenRN Nursing Fundamentals (T2) supplies nearly all specifics; AUGS T2 notes only opioid-related constipation risk; RCOG T1 adds laxatives within an enhanced recovery protocol. No doses, gynecologic-surgery-specific regimens, comparative efficacy, or outcome data are established.

title: Bowel Function Optimization After Pelvic Reconstruction
summary:
This community represents postoperative bowel care as a discrete perioperative nursing theme in pelvic reconstructive surgery. Two linked ideas are captured: (1) bowel function optimization is a component of care applying to pelvic reconstructive surgery, specified for women undergoing reconstructive pelvic surgery for pelvic floor disorders (AUGS Table 2, p4); and (2) a laxative regimen applies to pelvic reconstructive surgery and prevents constipation, specified for patients after pelvic reconstructive surgery (AUGS Table 2, p11). The clinical logic implied is that straining and constipation are undesirable after repair of pelvic floor disorders, so bowel regimens are positioned as a preventive rather than reactive intervention, initiated in the postoperative period.

Only one guideline body contributes here: AUGS (American Urogynecologic Society), via two locations in the same Table 2 (p4 and p11). There is therefore no cross-society disagreement to reconcile, and no comparison with other perioperative bodies is available in this community. The two AUGS entries differ in granularity: the p4 entry is broad and population-specific (women having reconstructive pelvic surgery for pelvic floor disorders) but names no intervention, while the p11 entry is more specific about the intervention (a laxative regimen) and its target outcome (constipation prevention) and locates it in the postoperative phase ("after" surgery).

Importantly, the community does NOT establish: any named laxative agent or class (no osmotic, stimulant, softener, or fiber product specified), doses, frequency, or duration of therapy; no start time relative to surgery (preoperative bowel prep versus day-of-surgery versus discharge prescribing is not addressed); no thresholds or endpoints such as days without a bowel movement, stool consistency scales, or criteria for escalation or rescue therapy. It does not address bowel preparation before surgery, opioid-induced constipation management, defecatory dysfunction outcomes, contraindications, adverse effects, or patient education content. It also does not extend these recommendations to non-pelvic or non-gynecologic surgical populations, and provides no evidence grading or strength-of-recommendation information.

title: Beta-lactam prophylaxis and penicillin allergy
summary: This community represents perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis with beta-lactams and the constraint imposed by penicillin allergy in gynecologic/obstetric surgery. The positive recommendation comes from WHO (T1 p18): for women undergoing caesarean section, a single dose of penicillin is advised, in preference to other classes of antibiotics. Against this sits a repeated allergy caveat: WHO states penicillin is contraindicated in patients with penicillin allergy, with the qualifier that an alternative preoperative antibiotic is used instead (T1 p234), and separately in the patient allergic to penicillin (T1 p122) and the patient with a previous severe reaction to penicillin (T1 p48) — the latter being the most specific about reaction severity. CDC (T1 p13) contributes a parallel constraint on the alternative agent itself: cephalosporin is flagged as contraindicated/unsuitable for patients unable to receive a cephalosporin in the context of penicillin allergy, signalling that cross-reactivity or intolerance must be screened before defaulting to a cephalosporin substitute. Practically, the theme supports a workflow of documenting allergy history (including severity of any prior penicillin reaction), giving single-dose penicillin at caesarean section when no allergy exists, and substituting an alternative preoperative antibiotic when it does — verifying that a cephalosporin is itself acceptable. Contributions differ in emphasis rather than content: WHO supplies both the affirmative caesarean-section recommendation and most allergy statements; CDC addresses only the cephalosporin-ineligible subgroup. The community does not establish which specific alternative agent should be used, its dose or route, the timing relative to skin incision, redosing rules, or duration beyond the stated single dose. It gives no allergy-testing or cross-reactivity thresholds, no definition of "severe reaction," no guidance for non-caesarean gynecologic procedures, and no outcome data (infection rates, resistance) to justify the preference for penicillin over other classes. Local formulary and antimicrobial stewardship input remains necessary to operationalise the alternative-agent choice.

title: Perioperative Bundle: Normothermia, Glycemia, Infection Prevention
summary: This community represents the perioperative care bundle for gynecologic/major surgery, centering on temperature management, glycemic control, infection prophylaxis, catheter stewardship, safety checklists, analgesia, and hemodynamic optimization. Normothermia is the most heavily corroborated element: CDC recommends maintaining normothermia during surgery for all patients to prevent surgical site infection (SSI), placing it explicitly in the intraoperative phase; the ERAS Society is more specific, recommending warming 2 hours before and after surgery in addition to intraoperative warming for patients undergoing major abdominal surgery, and separately lists active warming as perioperative care; AUGS frames normothermia broadly as preventing infection when incorporated into perioperative care. Glycemic control is the second anchor, with striking cross-body agreement on a threshold: AUGS, ERAS Society, and CDC all recommend perioperative glucose below 200 mg/dL for patients with and without diabetes to prevent SSI (AUGS repeats the <200 mg/dL target as 'glucose control'). CDC adds a diabetes-specific recommendation for serum blood glucose control in all diabetic patients, particularly avoiding perioperative hyperglycemia. Other perioperative elements: WHO places antimicrobial prophylaxis in the perioperative phase for surgical patients, and recommends the surgical safety checklist for operating teams before induction of anaesthesia, before skin incision, and before the patient leaves the operating room. CDC addresses indwelling urethral catheter insertion for selected surgical procedures only when an appropriate indication is present, and urinary catheter management guided by guidelines and algorithms. AUGS recommends multimodal analgesia beginning preoperatively and continuing intraoperatively and postoperatively; ERAS recommends pain specialist evaluation for all patients using buprenorphine, and advanced hemodynamic monitoring for high-risk patients with large blood loss (>7 ml/kg) or a SIRS response undergoing major open surgery, to individualize fluid therapy and optimize oxygen delivery. RCOG contributes enhanced recovery for patients undergoing major surgery. Not established here: specific warming devices or temperature targets in degrees, insulin protocols or glucose monitoring frequency, named antibiotic agents/doses/timing, catheter duration limits, analgesic drug names or doses, and any outcome data beyond SSI/infection prevention.

title: Anti-embolism stockings for VTE prophylaxis
summary: This community centres on graduated anti-embolism stockings (AES) as mechanical VTE prophylaxis across surgical, obstetric and medical populations, plus their contraindications. NICE (T1) supplies the broad surgical map: AES prevent VTE in people admitted to hospital at increased VTE risk when correctly used; specific settings include cranial surgery (start on admission, continue 30 days or until mobile/discharged), elective spinal surgery (30 days or until mobile/discharged), abdominal, bariatric, thoracic, ENT, cardiac and oral/maxillofacial surgery (the latter two/three where increased VTE risk and, for ENT and maxillofacial, high bleeding risk; applied on admission and continued until mobility is no longer significantly reduced). For elective hip replacement, AES are used if pharmacological interventions are contraindicated, until hospital discharge; for elective knee replacement, combined with LMWH until discharge where VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk. In varicose vein surgery, AES are for those at increased VTE risk if pharmacological prophylaxis is contraindicated, fitted on admission and continued until mobility recovers, while LMWH timing is 6–12 hours after surgery. Spinal injury patients should receive AES only in a specialist spinal injury unit after MDT discussion. NICE also covers pregnancy: pregnant women or those within 6 weeks of birth, miscarriage or termination with significantly reduced mobility, if intermittent pneumatic compression is contraindicated. RCOG (T1) is more specific obstetrically: AES as an adjunct to anticoagulant thromboprophylaxis in surgical patients; combined with LMWH after caesarean section in hospitalised women at particularly high VTE risk; as an alternative to pharmacological prophylaxis in women at high haemorrhage risk (major antepartum haemorrhage, coagulopathy, progressive wound haematoma, suspected intra-abdominal bleeding, postpartum haemorrhage); after postpartum haemorrhage when chemical thromboprophylaxis is contraindicated; and for travel over 4 hours. Contraindications (NICE) are peripheral arterial disease (suspected or proven; temporarily contraindicated until expert opinion sought), major limb deformity or unusual leg size/shape preventing correct fit, and fragile skin or local conditions where damage may occur. The community does not establish stocking class/pressure, sizing or fitting technique, effectiveness comparisons with intermittent pneumatic compression, LMWH doses, monitoring or documentation requirements, or paediatric guidance.

title: Peripheral Edema: Causes, Monitoring, Management
summary:
This community centres on peripheral edema in the perioperative/inpatient setting — its contributing causes, its surveillance, and the simple mechanical interventions used to relieve it, plus an overlapping use of limb elevation for infusion-related phlebitis.

Two risk contributors are named. RNAO (T2 p141) identifies long-acting calcium channel blockers as increasing the risk of peripheral edema, with the population specified as clients taking calcium channel blockers. OpenRN (T2 p562) separately identifies thrombosis as increasing the risk of peripheral edema, without a narrowing population or condition attached.

For monitoring, OpenRN (T2 p1111) directs peripheral edema monitoring in clients with excess fluid volume, with the explicit condition that the provider be notified as indicated. The same OpenRN passage supplies two management recommendations for that population, both conditioned on 'if edema is present': limb elevation and compression. OpenRN (T2 p1363) additionally recommends limb elevation as treatment for patients with transient mechanical phlebitis — so elevation appears as a shared intervention across two distinct problems (fluid-volume edema and catheter-related mechanical phlebitis).

Contributing bodies are RNAO and OpenRN. Their roles are complementary rather than conflicting: RNAO contributes only the pharmacologic risk link (long-acting calcium channel blockers), while OpenRN is more specific and more operational, naming the population (excess fluid volume), the trigger condition (edema present), the interventions (elevation, compression), and the escalation step (notify provider). There is no point of disagreement in these relations.

What this community does NOT establish: no thresholds or grading scales for edema severity, no monitoring frequency or timing, no specific calcium channel blocker agents, doses, or whether substitution/discontinuation is advised, and no compression type, pressure, or duration. It does not state gynecologic- or surgery-specific applicability, does not link edema to VTE prophylaxis or anticoagulation, does not describe diuretic or fluid-restriction management, and does not define how thrombosis-related edema should be assessed or differentiated from fluid-overload edema. Outcomes and effectiveness data are absent.

title: Preventing Periwound Skin Maceration in Wound Care
summary:
This community centers on periwound skin maceration — breakdown of the intact skin surrounding a wound from prolonged moisture exposure — and the balance nurses must strike between keeping the wound bed moist and keeping the surrounding skin dry.

Three risk factors are named. Excess wound drainage increases maceration risk specifically in patients with venous ulcers (OpenRN T2 p1136). More generally, a heavily draining wound increases risk (p1145), and a moist dressing increases risk when used improperly (p1145) — i.e., the therapeutic moist-wound-healing dressing itself becomes the hazard if misapplied or allowed to contact periwound skin.

Preventive recommendations are all topical/technique-based. Careful dressing application prevents maceration while maintaining wound bed moisture (p1145) — the core teaching point that moisture control is selective, not global. Barrier products named explicitly are: skin barrier cream, skin protective wipe, and skin barrier wafer (all p1145), plus the broader category skin barrier/protectant (p1185), which carries the most specific guidance in the corpus — indicated for patients with wound packing or wound exudate, applied to the periwound skin as needed.

All relations derive from a single guideline body, OpenRN (Open Resources for Nursing, Nursing Skills), across three passages: p1136 (venous ulcer context), p1145 (general maceration risk and barrier product list), and p1185 (barrier/protectant with population and application site). There is no inter-body disagreement to reconcile; the differences are in granularity — p1145 enumerates specific product forms without stating population or frequency, while p1185 supplies population (wound packing or exudate), site (periwound skin), and timing (as needed) but not product form. Educators may wish to merge the two.

The community does NOT establish: any drainage volume or exudate threshold defining "excess" or "heavily draining"; dressing change intervals; comparative effectiveness among cream, wipe, and wafer; how to assess or stage maceration once present; treatment (as opposed to prevention) of established maceration; or any gynecologic- or perioperative-specific application, despite the corpus framing.

title: Analgesic Premedication Timing Before Physical Therapy
summary:
This community represents a single, consistent clinical theme: the timing of analgesic administration relative to scheduled physical therapy sessions, so that pain control is established before the client is mobilised. All three relations are TIMING_DEPENDS_ON links from an analgesic-administration entity to physical therapy, indicating that the dosing schedule is driven by the therapy schedule rather than the reverse.

Recommendations and their populations/conditions: (1) For clients with anticipated pain, pain medication administration should occur prior to physical therapy sessions (OpenRN T2 p958). (2) For clients attending physical therapy, premedication with analgesics should be given before the session (OpenRN T2 p1421). (3) The most specific instance concerns a client refusing pain medication for cultural reasons, where a PRN pain medication was administered one hour before the scheduled physical therapy session (OpenRN T2 p788) — this is the only entry that names a concrete interval (one hour) and the only one specifying a PRN rather than a scheduled order. It also uniquely flags a cultural-refusal context, implying that premedication timing must be negotiated with clients whose beliefs affect analgesic acceptance.

Guideline contribution: all three statements derive from the same corpus body, OpenRN (Textbook 2), at pages 788, 958 and 1421. There is no cross-body disagreement; the differences are in granularity — p958 and p1421 state the principle generically ("prior to"/"before the session"), while p788 operationalises it with a one-hour lead time in a PRN, culturally sensitive scenario.

What this community does NOT establish: no specific drugs, drug classes, doses, or routes are named; no pain-score thresholds (e.g., numeric rating scale cut-offs) trigger the premedication; no guidance on onset-of-action differences between oral, IV or transdermal analgesics; no acceptable timing window other than the single one-hour example; no gynecologic- or postoperative-specific population qualifiers; no outcome evidence that premedication improves therapy participation or function; and no direction on how to proceed if a client persistently declines analgesia.
key_entities: client refusing pain medication for cultural reasons

title: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia Surveillance in Obstetrics
summary:
This community covers heparin safety in pregnancy and the postpartum/post-caesarean period, centred on heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), platelet count thresholds, and alternative anticoagulants. All relations derive from a single guideline body, RCOG (Thromboprophylaxis document, pages 3-36); no other body contributes, so no inter-body disagreement can be assessed.

Key recommendations: LMWH is temporarily contraindicated in pregnant and postpartum women when the platelet count falls below 75 × 10⁹/L (p36), and is contraindicated outright in women with established HIT — for pregnant women requiring continuing anticoagulation, an alternative agent should be chosen under specialist advice (p17, p27). Named alternatives are fondaparinux sodium (pregnant women, as an alternative to LMWH when HIT occurs, p18) and danaparoid (considered instead of heparin in women with HIT, p17). Unfractionated heparin (UFH) increases HIT risk relative to LMWH, stated for pregnant women generally (p11), pregnant women receiving thromboprophylaxis where risk is 'substantially lower with LMWH' (p23), and for any exposure (p14, p24). Chemical thromboprophylaxis prevents thrombosis after postpartum haemorrhage once bleeding is arrested and coagulopathy corrected (p23), but is contraindicated in thrombocytopenia (p23).

Monitoring is the most specific element: platelet count every 2-3 days from days 4-14, or until heparin is stopped, for postoperative obstetric patients and women given UFH after caesarean section or other surgery (p3, p7, p14, p24), detecting both HIT and thrombocytopenia. For women on LMWH, platelet monitoring is indicated only with prior UFH exposure (p23), plus at outpatient follow-up for pregnant women on maintenance LMWH treatment (p4). A platelet count check after 24 hours of initiating treatment detects HIT in patients who received any heparin within the last 100 days (p14).

Not established: no platelet threshold for restarting LMWH, no dosing regimens for fondaparinux or danaparoid, no diagnostic testing (e.g. antibody assays), no management of confirmed HIT beyond drug substitution, and no lower platelet limit for chemical thromboprophylaxis.

title: Immobility Complications and Pneumonia Prevention
summary:
This community centres on the hazards of immobility in perioperative and postpartum patients, with pneumonia as the hub complication. OpenRN (Nursing Skills/Fundamentals) establishes that immobility increases risk of deep venous thrombosis, constipation, skin breakdown, and pneumonia in immobile clients (T2 p1421), with immobility-related pneumonia risk restated generically at p958. RCOG contributes an obstetric-specific parallel: immobility increases risk of venous thromboembolism in women after delivery (T1 p21) — more population-specific than OpenRN's generic 'immobile clients', though RCOG names VTE rather than DVT. WHO adds a device-related pathway: ventilator use increases pneumonia risk (T1 p211), a mechanism absent from the OpenRN immobility framing.

Preventive and monitoring recommendations: adequate fluid intake prevents constipation when delivered as part of a bowel regimen (OpenRN T2 p1416), and prevents pneumonia in clients at risk due to immobility, specifically to liquefy pulmonary secretions (OpenRN T2 p958). Ongoing assessment for signs of complications monitors for pneumonia in clients at risk of complications of immobility (OpenRN T2 p1421). Two focused physical-assessment techniques detect pneumonia: chest expansion assessment when chest expansion is unequal, and percussion when dull sounds are heard over high-density areas (OpenRN T2 p616). Once established, pneumonia increases risk of acute respiratory failure (OpenRN T2 p1285), and antibiotics treat pneumonia in patients with pneumonia (OpenRN T2 p1425) — no agent, dose, route or duration is named.

What this community does NOT establish: no mobilisation or ambulation intervention, no incentive spirometry, deep-breathing, positioning or turning schedule, and no pharmacologic or mechanical thromboprophylaxis (no LMWH, heparin, or compression devices) despite DVT/VTE being named risks. No fluid volume threshold, monitoring frequency, or timing for assessment is specified; no bowel regimen components beyond fluid; no ventilator-bundle measures; and no gynecologic-surgery-specific population or postoperative day thresholds. Diagnostic confirmation (imaging, cultures) and severity criteria for pneumonia or respiratory failure are absent, as is any antibiotic selection guidance.

title: Diagnostic testing for suspected lower respiratory infection
summary:
This small community represents the diagnostic confirmation step for suspected lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) — a concern in perioperative gynecologic care, where post-operative respiratory symptoms must be distinguished from other causes of fever or deterioration. Two distinct diagnostic modalities converge on the same target condition.

Recommendations: (1) Point-of-care C-reactive protein (CRP) testing is indicated to help detect LRTI in people with suspected lower respiratory tract infections (NICE, T1 p5). The population is defined by clinical suspicion alone, not by age, comorbidity or surgical status. (2) A chest x-ray is used to detect LRTI, conditioned on suspicion of a lower respiratory tract infection (OpenRN, T2 p663).

Contributing bodies: NICE contributes the point-of-care CRP recommendation; OpenRN (open nursing textbook material) contributes the chest x-ray pathway. The two do not conflict — they describe complementary tests for the same suspected condition. NICE is more specific about test modality and setting, naming point-of-care CRP as the biomarker approach, whereas OpenRN names conventional imaging. Neither source, as captured here, sequences the two tests, states which should come first, or indicates whether one obviates the other.

What this community does NOT establish: no CRP thresholds or cut-off values (e.g. mg/L bands) are given, so no guidance exists here on how a CRP result should influence antibiotic prescribing or escalation. No antibiotic agents, doses, routes or durations are named. No timings are specified — nothing on how soon after symptom onset or post-operative day CRP or chest x-ray should be obtained, nor on repeat testing intervals. No population qualifiers are provided for gynecologic surgical patients specifically, and no pregnancy or radiation-exposure caveats for chest x-ray appear. The community also omits other diagnostics (sputum culture, pulse oximetry, blood cultures), severity scoring, and any linkage to outcomes such as length of stay or readmission. Educators should treat this as a two-test recognition prompt requiring local protocol to supply thresholds and treatment actions.

title: Care Coordination Prevents Readmissions After Transitions
summary:
Clinical theme: this small community addresses continuity of care across transitions (e.g., hospital-to-home discharge after gynecologic surgery), framing coordination and follow-up as a safety intervention rather than a clerical task. The causal logic is bidirectional in effect: structured follow-up and care coordination after a transition PREVENTS unplanned hospital readmission, while poor coordination in care INCREASES the risk of both unplanned readmission and emergency department visits. The named population in every relation is uniformly 'persons undergoing transitions in care' — the graph does not narrow this to a gynecologic, oncologic, or age-specific subgroup.

Main recommendation and its condition: provide follow-up and care coordination after transitions in care to prevent unplanned readmission. The attached condition is an important caveat about expected effect size — not all readmissions can be prevented; approximately 25 per cent are retrospectively determined to be preventable. Quality-improvement leads should therefore set targets against that preventable fraction rather than treating all-cause readmission as a fully modifiable metric. The risk relations for poor coordination carry no additional qualifying condition beyond the transitions-in-care population, so both ED visits and readmissions should be tracked as coordination-sensitive outcomes.

Contributing bodies: only one source underpins this community — RNAO (Registered Nurses' Association of Ontario), Transitions in Care guideline material, page 27 (RNAO T2 p27). Because all three relations derive from the same page of the same body, there are no inter-organisational agreements or contradictions to reconcile, and no body here is more granular than another. Any perceived consensus should be reported as single-source.

What this community does NOT establish: it names no drugs, no doses, no follow-up timing (no interval such as 24–72 hours or 7/30 days), no readmission measurement window, no responsible discipline or handover tool, no specific coordination components (e.g., medication reconciliation, teach-back, discharge summary transmission), and no effect sizes or quality of evidence beyond the 25 per cent preventable estimate. It also does not define which surgical or gynecologic populations are highest risk, nor link coordination to mortality, complications, pain control, or patient experience.
key_entities: follow-up and care coordination after transitions

title: Preventing Post-operative Infectious Morbidity in Gynecologic Surgery
summary:
This community centres on post-operative infectious morbidity as a shared outcome node, linking two protective interventions (antisepsis and oral antibiotics) with one procedural risk factor (cytoreductive surgery involving colonic resection). It represents the perioperative infection-prevention theme: what nurses can do to reduce infectious complications, and which patients arrive at surgery already at elevated baseline risk.

Main recommendations and their populations/conditions:
- Antisepsis prevents post-operative infectious morbidity in surgical patients generally (CDC, T1 p5). The population is broad and unqualified — no specific agent, concentration, skin-prep technique, or timing is attached in this community.
- Oral antibiotics prevent post-operative infectious morbidity, but the condition is narrow and important: the effect is described for oral antibiotics alone compared with no bowel preparation, and the supporting evidence is retrospective (ERAS Society, T1 p3). No drug names, doses, or dosing schedule are specified.
- Cytoreductive surgery with colonic resection increases risk of post-operative infectious morbidity in ovarian cancer patients (ERAS Society, T1 p4). This is the most population-specific statement in the community and flags a group warranting heightened surveillance.

Contributing bodies: the CDC supplies the general, all-surgical-patients antisepsis principle; the ERAS Society supplies the gynecologic-oncology-specific content — both the bowel-preparation recommendation with its explicit comparator and evidence caveat, and the ovarian cancer/colonic resection risk relation. The two do not conflict; ERAS is simply more granular about population (ovarian cancer), comparator (no bowel preparation), and evidence quality (retrospective), while CDC is broader in scope.

What this community does NOT establish: no antiseptic agents, antibiotic drugs, doses, routes, or administration timings; no mechanical bowel preparation comparison beyond "no bowel preparation"; no combined oral-plus-mechanical regimen; no quantified risk magnitude, thresholds, or infection rates; no wound-class or surgical-site-infection subtypes; and no guidance on whether ovarian cancer patients undergoing colonic resection should receive intensified prophylaxis. Prospective evidence for the oral antibiotic benefit is absent.

title: Preventing post-thrombotic syndrome after DVT
summary:
This community centres on post-thrombotic syndrome (PTS) as a long-term complication of deep vein thrombosis (DVT), particularly in pregnancy and the postnatal period, and on the two preventive levers identified: prolonged low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) therapy and graduated compression stockings. All relations derive from a single guideline body, RCOG (Tier 1, pages 5, 16, 21 and 26), so the community reflects one consistent source rather than competing recommendations.

Pharmacological prevention: LMWH is stated to prevent PTS when used for a prolonged period — more than 12 weeks — in women with venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and in pregnant women treated for VTE; the same benefit is described for patients with proximal DVT, where the example given is tinzaparin for more than 12 weeks. Note the duration threshold (>12 weeks) is the defining condition, not simply any LMWH exposure.

Mechanical prevention: graduated compression stockings prevent PTS where they provide greater than 23 mmHg support at the ankle. For patients with proximal DVT, a below-knee stocking with ankle pressure >23 mmHg is specified, and it is explicitly not required on the unaffected leg. Graduated elastic compression stockings are also cited as preventive in nonpregnant patients — a more specific population qualifier than the general ankle-pressure statement on p26.

Risk factors for PTS after DVT in pregnancy include smoking, age greater than 33 years, and proximal postnatal thrombosis; obesity and recurrent ipsilateral DVT are listed as risk-increasing without a population qualifier.

What this community does not establish: no dose, intensity or monitoring regimen for LMWH; no stated duration of stocking wear; no evidence that stockings or LMWH prevent DVT recurrence itself (only PTS); no comparison of LMWH versus compression, or of the two used together; no guidance for distal or upper-limb thrombosis; and no PTS diagnostic criteria, severity grading, or treatment once established.
key_entities: graduated compression stocking providing greater than 23 mmhg support at the ankle

title: Post-Pelvic-Surgery Voiding Surveillance in Women
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: detection and monitoring of short-term voiding dysfunction in women after pelvic surgery, using post-void residual (PVR) measurement at the point of catheter removal. The causal claim is that pelvic surgery increases the risk of short-term voiding problems in women; the nursing action that follows is a post-void residual check, which is scoped specifically to women undergoing pelvic surgery and conditioned on the timing 'after catheter removal'. The same PVR check is the designated monitoring modality for the short-term voiding problem itself, again in the population of women following pelvic surgery and at the post-catheter-removal time point. Practically, for a quality-improvement lead this translates into one auditable step: every woman having pelvic surgery should have a documented PVR assessment once her catheter is out, on the rationale that her surgery has raised her baseline risk of transient voiding difficulty.

Only one guideline body contributes here: the RCOG (Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists), all three relations drawn from RCOG Table 1, page 3. Because the evidence is single-source, there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile and no instance of one organisation being more granular than another; the theme is uniformly specified at the level of population (women), procedure class (pelvic surgery), and timing (after catheter removal).

Important limits: the community does not define a numeric PVR threshold that constitutes an abnormal or actionable residual, does not state how PVR should be measured (bladder scan versus in-out catheterisation), and does not specify how many checks are required or over what interval. It does not name any drug, does not describe management if the PVR is elevated (for example re-catheterisation, intermittent catheterisation, or referral), and does not define what counts as resolution of the voiding problem or 'short-term'. It also does not distinguish among types of pelvic surgery, anaesthetic technique, or risk subgroups, nor does it address longer-term voiding dysfunction, urinary retention outcomes, or infection risk.

title: Aseptic Scrubbing Before Epidural Insertion
summary:
This community represents infection prevention and adverse-event detection surrounding neuraxial (epidural) anaesthesia in the perioperative gynecologic setting. Four relations link a single preventive practice (scrubbing) to a single procedure (epidural insertion) and to two serious central nervous system infections (epidural abscess, meningitis), with postmortem examination appearing as the modality by which those infections are detected.

Main recommendations: scrubbing applies to epidural insertion, with the explicit timing condition that it be performed prior to the epidural insertion; and scrubbing prevents epidural abscess when performed prior to epidural insertion, per evidence-based guidelines. The stated population is limited to patients undergoing epidural insertion — no age, parity, procedure type, ASA class, or immune-status subgroup is specified. Postmortem examination detects epidural abscess and detects meningitis; these are diagnostic/confirmatory relations attached to the fatal-outcome context, not to living patients.

Contributing guideline bodies: all four relations derive from a single source, WHO (T1, p93). Because only one body contributes, there are no inter-guideline disagreements, no competing thresholds, and no instance of one body being more specific than another. The most specific element supplied by WHO is the timing qualifier — scrubbing before, not after or during, epidural placement — and the qualifier that this rests on evidence-based guidelines.

What this community does NOT establish: no scrub agent is named (no chlorhexidine, alcohol, or povidone-iodine), no scrub duration, no hand-hygiene or glove/gown/mask/drape specification, and no skin-preparation dry time. It does not state that scrubbing prevents meningitis — only epidural abscess. It gives no incidence rates, no risk thresholds, no catheter dwell-time limits, no antibiotic prophylaxis, no surveillance interval, and no ante-mortem diagnostic pathway (no MRI, lumbar puncture, blood culture, or symptom triggers such as fever or back pain). It does not address epidural removal, contraindications, anticoagulation, or who should perform the insertion. Educators should therefore treat this as a narrow timing-of-asepsis message requiring local policy to fill in technique detail.

title: Postnatal Psychological Assessment for Depression Screening
summary:
This small community represents postpartum mental health surveillance — specifically, the routine assessment of psychological well-being after birth and its role in identifying postnatal depression. Two relations anchor the theme, both drawn from a single WHO source (WHO T1, p23).

The first recommendation places postnatal assessment of psychological well-being within the postpartum phase, applied to all women, with an explicit timing of 10–14 days after birth. This establishes a universal, time-specified touchpoint rather than a risk-targeted or symptom-triggered one.

The second recommendation narrows the population and adds a condition: for women whose maternal blues symptoms have not resolved at 10–14 days after birth, and specifically when symptoms have not resolved, the assessment functions as monitoring for postnatal depression. In other words, persistence of maternal blues beyond the 10–14 day window is the trigger that converts a routine well-being check into active surveillance for postnatal depression. The 10–14 day mark is the only threshold stated in this community.

Only one guideline body contributes here — WHO — and both relations come from the same page, so there are no inter-body disagreements, no competing timings, and no instance of one organisation being more specific than another. Educators should treat this as WHO-only guidance rather than a corroborated multi-source consensus.

The community does not establish: any named screening instrument or scoring cut-off; who should perform the assessment or in what setting; the frequency or number of assessments beyond the single 10–14 day timepoint; any drug, dose, or non-pharmacological treatment for postnatal depression; referral pathways, escalation criteria, or thresholds for specialist mental health input; risk factors or higher-risk subgroups warranting earlier or more intensive assessment; management of maternal blues itself; and any linkage to perioperative or gynecologic surgical care despite the wider corpus context. It also says nothing about outcomes, follow-up intervals after a positive finding, or assessment of partners, infants, or women beyond the immediate postpartum period.
key_entities: maternal blues symptoms not resolved at 10-14 days after birth

title: Postnatal Review After Pregnancy VTE
summary:
Clinical theme: this small community addresses postpartum follow-up of women who have had a venous thromboembolism (VTE) during pregnancy or the puerperium, specifically using the routine postnatal review as the point of care at which longer-term sequelae of that VTE are identified. The two relations position the postnatal review both temporally (it occurs in the postpartum phase) and functionally (it detects post-thrombotic venous damage).

Main recommendation with population and condition: for patients who develop venous thromboembolism during pregnancy or the puerperium, the postnatal review should be used to detect post-thrombotic venous damage; the stated condition/timing is 'at the postnatal review'. The only phase anchor given is the postpartum period. No other assessments, drugs, doses, durations or numeric thresholds are attached to these relations.

Contributing guideline bodies: only the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG) contributes here, from a single source location (RCOG T1, p21). Because a single body supplies both relations, there are no inter-society disagreements, no competing timings, and no instance of one guideline being more specific than another within this community. The RCOG statement is itself broad rather than operationalised.

What this community does NOT establish: it does not define what the postnatal review consists of, who performs it, or exactly when after delivery it should occur (no week or day interval is given). It does not specify how post-thrombotic venous damage is to be assessed (no clinical scoring, imaging such as duplex ultrasound, or referral pathway), nor what action follows a positive finding — for example compression stockings, anticoagulation continuation, thrombophilia testing, or vascular referral. It says nothing about anticoagulant agents (e.g. LMWH), duration of postpartum thromboprophylaxis, contraception advice, or counselling about recurrence risk in future pregnancies. It also excludes women whose VTE occurred outside pregnancy or the puerperium. Educators should therefore treat this as a single prompt to screen for post-thrombotic damage at postnatal review, and source management detail elsewhere in the corpus.
key_entities: venous thromboembolism in pregnancy or the puerperium

title: Postoperative recovery, prophylaxis and complication prevention
summary:
This community covers postoperative (and postpartum) care bundles aimed at preventing complications: enhanced recovery, thromboprophylaxis, catheter and wound management, mobilisation, nutrition and surveillance.

Enhanced recovery programmes are recommended postoperatively for people having elective major or complex surgery (NICE), with non-ward-based specialist recovery area care for those at high risk of complications or mortality. Early mobilisation is central: within 24 h of surgery (ERAS Society), postpartum as soon as appropriate after birth for all women (WHO), and encouraged by effective analgesia with reduced systemic opiates (RCOG). It is credited with preventing thromboembolism/VTE (NICE: hospital inpatients at increased VTE risk), thromboembolic events, pulmonary complications, muscle loss, and perioperative complications in pelvic exenteration or HIPEC. Thromboprophylaxis includes postoperative pharmacological prophylaxis (AUGS), VTE prophylaxis for gynecologic oncology surgery >30 min (ERAS), extension to 28 days after major abdominal cancer surgery (NICE), switching combined oral hormonal contraception to an alternative or oral to transdermal estrogen before surgery to prevent thromboembolism (ERAS), and platelet count monitoring every 2–3 days from days 4–14 or until heparin stopped in obstetric patients on unfractionated heparin (RCOG).

Catheter care: remove indwelling urinary catheters as soon as possible, preferably within 24 h unless indicated (CDC), in PACU for prolonged-surgery catheters, with shorter catheterisation duration; AUGS is more specific, favouring removal within 3–8 h to prevent infection. Wound care (CDC, WHO): appropriate incision management, sterile technique for dressing changes, sterile dressing packing for incisions left open for delayed primary closure/secondary intention, and postdischarge SSI surveillance. Other measures: increased fraction of inspired oxygen after extubation in patients with normal pulmonary function under general anaesthesia with endotracheal intubation (CDC); lung protective ventilation (tidal volume 6–8 ml/kg, PEEP 6–8 cm H2O) in open abdominal surgery; active warming until PACU discharge with temperature >36.0 °C; regular diet within 24 h and early oral intake; IV fluids until oral fluids tolerated (AUGS); increased fluid intake after contrast; ileus monitoring; drain monitoring/emptying; head-of-bed elevation; vascular access site monitoring for 24 h with catheter removal if phlebitis signs persist; post-procedure debriefing; discharge advice on sepsis symptoms (NICE); WHO postpartum counselling on pre-eclampsia, thromboembolism, haemorrhage and infection signs.

The community does not establish comparative effectiveness, drug doses/agents for prophylaxis, outcome magnitudes, or how measures should be sequenced or combined.

title: Preventing Postoperative Complications Across Perioperative Pathways
summary:
This community centres on the single outcome 'postoperative complication' and the bundle of structured, largely preoperative interventions guidelines recommend to prevent it. Five bodies contribute: NICE, WHO, ERAS Society, AUGS and RCOG.

Systems-level recommendations: NICE supports enhanced recovery programmes for people having elective major or complex surgery, and the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist for surgical patients generally. WHO adds a monitoring/surveillance system where results of surgical care are not routinely tracked and complications are not recorded. ERAS Society frames the enhanced recovery pathway for colorectal surgery, conditional on systematic implementation of an evidence-based perioperative care protocol, and reports observational evidence that increasing compliance with ERAS guidelines reduces complications in colorectal patients. AUGS is more quantitatively specific, citing ERAS protocol compliance greater than 70% in gynecological oncology patients.

Modifiable risk factors and preoperative optimisation: ERAS Society identifies smoking as increasing risk, and recommends intensive preoperative interventions aimed at complete alcohol cessation for at least four weeks. Prehabilitation is consistently placed in the preoperative phase (ERAS Society, AUGS for gynecology and general surgical patients). ERAS Society specifies its content — inspiratory muscle training, aerobic exercise and/or resistance training — for patients undergoing intra-abdominal operations in a traditional surgical care setting; AUGS endorses it for gynecologic surgery patients only as a weak recommendation on very low quality evidence, explicitly noting more high-quality studies are needed. This is the clearest divergence in strength of evidence.

RCOG contributes preoperative risk assessment for surgical patients, ideally organised so identified problems can be addressed, and avoidance of intraoperative hypothermia.

What this community does not establish: no drug names, doses, temperature thresholds, smoking-cessation durations, prehabilitation session frequency or duration, or timing of risk assessment are given. No mortality, length-of-stay or readmission outcomes appear, no complication types are specified, and no comparative effectiveness between checklist, prehabilitation, ERAS compliance or normothermia is stated. Gynecologic-specific evidence remains weakest.
key_entities: world health organization surgical safety checklist
compliance with enhanced recovery after surgery guidelines

title: Preoperative Clear Fluids Reduce Postoperative Symptoms
summary:
This community represents preoperative fasting liberalisation: allowing clear fluids (including water and carbohydrate drinks) up to a defined cut-off before surgery, and the symptom benefits attributed to that practice. All relations derive from NICE (T1, pages 9 and 23); no other guideline body contributes, so there are no inter-body contradictions to reconcile, only differences in specificity.

Core recommendations and their populations/conditions:

1. Clear fluid intake is placed in the preoperative phase for people having surgery, including dental surgery, with the condition that clear fluids may be drunk until 2 hours before the operation (NICE T1 p9). This is the broadest population statement and the only one that explicitly names dental surgery.

2. Clear fluid intake under that same 2-hour rule prevents postoperative nausea and vomiting and prevents postoperative headache in the same population (NICE T1 p9).

3. Drinking water until 2 hours before surgery prevents postoperative headache and postoperative nausea and vomiting, specified for adults having surgery (NICE T1 p23). This is narrower in population (adults) and more specific in the fluid named (water) than the p9 clear-fluid statements, while using the identical 2-hour threshold.

4. A preoperative carbohydrate drink prevents postoperative headache for people given a carbohydrate drink before surgery (NICE T1 p23). Notably, no timing threshold is attached to the carbohydrate drink, and no nausea/vomiting benefit is recorded for it.

What the community does not establish: it does not address solid food fasting, milk or milk-containing drinks, or paediatric-specific timings; it gives no volume limits, no guidance for patients at aspiration risk, delayed gastric emptying, diabetes or emergency surgery; and it names no drugs (no antiemetics, no analgesics). It does not state a timing window for carbohydrate drinks, nor whether carbohydrate drinks reduce postoperative nausea and vomiting. It offers no outcomes beyond postoperative headache and postoperative nausea and vomiting, no gynecologic-surgery-specific qualification, and no strength-of-evidence grading or effect sizes.
key_entities: drinking water until 2 hours before surgery

title: Preventing postoperative ileus and PONV
summary:
This community represents non-pharmacologic and simple pharmacologic measures used in the perioperative period to restore gastrointestinal function and prevent postoperative ileus, with a secondary benefit for postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV). Two interventions anchor the theme: chewing gum and postoperative laxatives.

Recommendations: (1) Chewing gum is recommended to prevent postoperative ileus. The ERAS Society (T1, p2) states that gum chewing 'should be considered,' without restricting it to a surgical subgroup. AUGS (T2, p11) is more population-specific, tying ileus prevention with chewing gum to patients undergoing colorectal surgery. (2) AUGS also extends chewing gum to prevention of postoperative nausea and vomiting, specifying the population as women undergoing laparoscopic surgery and the condition as sugar-free chewing gum given following surgery — the only place in this community where gum formulation (sugar-free) and timing (postoperatively) are stated. (3) A postoperative laxative 'should be considered' to prevent postoperative ileus (ERAS Society, T1, p2).

Contributing bodies: the ERAS Society and AUGS. They agree that chewing gum prevents postoperative ileus and neither contradicts the other. The difference is one of scope and granularity: ERAS frames both gum and laxatives as general 'should be considered' recommendations for its surgical population, while AUGS narrows the evidence to colorectal surgery (ileus) and to women having laparoscopic surgery (PONV), and alone specifies sugar-free gum used after surgery. Only ERAS mentions laxatives.

What this community does NOT establish: no specific laxative agent, dose, route, or start time is named; no frequency, duration, or number of chewing-gum sessions per day is given; ERAS does not state whether its gum recommendation is limited to colorectal or gynecologic laparoscopic cases; no laxative role in PONV prevention is claimed; and no thresholds, outcome measures (e.g., time to first flatus or bowel movement), contraindications, or comparative effectiveness between gum and laxatives are described. Educators should treat these as low-risk adjuncts to be operationalized locally.

title: Modifiable and disease-related morbidity risks
summary:
This community centres on the determinants of postoperative morbidity and mortality in gynecologic and gynecologic-oncology surgery, and the single protective intervention named against them. It groups patient-level modifiable risks (poor nutritional status, smoking, preoperative anemia), management-related risk (salt and fluid volume overload in the postoperative period), disease burden markers (ascites, peritoneal carcinomatosis), procedure-related risk (total pelvic exenteration), and one preventive care model (ERAS protocol).

Main content by population/condition: poor nutritional status increases postoperative morbidity in patients undergoing gynecologic/oncology surgery (ERAS Society) and increases surgical site infection risk in patients undergoing certain kinds of operations (CDC). Smoking increases postoperative morbidity, and preoperative anemia increases both postoperative morbidity and postoperative mortality (ERAS Society, general surgical framing). Fluid volume overload increases morbidity specifically in surgical patients when salt and fluid overload occurs in the postoperative period. Ascites and peritoneal carcinomatosis both increase morbidity in gynecologic/oncology patients; total pelvic exenteration increases morbidity in gynecologic oncology patients. AUGS states that an enhanced recovery after surgery protocol prevents postoperative morbidity in older patients when compared with non-ERAS standard of care.

Contributing bodies: the ERAS Society supplies most risk relations and is the most specific about oncologic and procedural context (ascites, carcinomatosis, exenteration, postoperative salt/fluid overload). CDC contributes only the nutrition–surgical site infection link, narrowing the outcome to SSI rather than global morbidity. AUGS is narrower still in population (older patients) but is the only source naming a prevention strategy. There is no contradiction between bodies; they differ in outcome granularity (SSI vs. composite morbidity) and population breadth.

What this community does NOT establish: no numeric thresholds (e.g., hemoglobin, albumin, BMI, pack-years), no timing for preoperative optimisation, no smoking-cessation interval, no named nutritional supplements, iron or transfusion regimens, no fluid volumes or targets, and no ERAS element-by-element specification. It also does not state that ERAS prevents mortality, or that correcting anemia, smoking or malnutrition reduces morbidity — only that these states raise risk.

title: Multimodal PONV Risk Reduction in Gynecologic Surgery
summary:
This community centres on prevention and treatment of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) in gynecologic and general surgical patients, spanning risk stratification, anaesthetic technique, pharmacologic prophylaxis and non-drug adjuncts.

Risk factors: gynaecological surgery itself and laparoscopic procedures raise PONV risk (ERAS Society). AUGS specifies the Apfel score components — female gender, non-smoking status and postoperative opioid use. Nitrous oxide increases risk in patients with high baseline risk of vomiting (ERAS Society); AUGS adds that in patients receiving general anaesthesia this risk is eliminated with aggressive PONV prophylaxis. WHO contributes a separate nitrous oxide hazard: risk of a hypoxic gas mixture in anaesthetised patients unless delivered with oxygen via a machine designed to prevent hypoxic mixtures.

Recommendations: ERAS Society advises multimodal antiemetic prophylaxis for patients undergoing gynecologic procedures, with prophylaxis using at least 2 antiemetics as standard and a multimodal approach with more than 2 agents; propofol-based total intravenous anaesthesia (continuous target-controlled infusion under general anaesthesia); omission of nitrous oxide during laparoscopic gynecologic surgery; regional anaesthesia added to general anaesthesia; and multimodal non-opioid analgesia. AUGS is drug- and population-specific: preoperative dexamethasone for women undergoing reconstructive vaginal surgery, sugar-free chewing gum after surgery for women undergoing laparoscopic surgery, propofol-based TIVA, and antiemetic prophylaxis given according to patient-specific risk. NICE addresses fasting: clear fluids may be drunk until 2 hours before the operation (people having surgery, including dental surgery) and water until 2 hours before surgery in adults. RCOG contributes only that anti-emetics treat PONV as part of an enhanced recovery protocol.

Differences/gaps: ERAS emphasises agent counts and technique; AUGS names specific drugs, timing and gynecologic subpopulations; NICE focuses on preoperative hydration; WHO on nitrous oxide safety rather than PONV. The community does not specify antiemetic drug classes beyond dexamethasone, doses, routes, timing schedules, Apfel score thresholds for escalation, rescue-treatment regimens, or outcome magnitudes. Propofol's suggested effect on cancer recurrence is explicitly evidence-suggestive only.
key_entities: clear fluid intake until 2 hours before surgery
Apfel score (female gender, non-smoking status, postoperative opioid)

title: Multimodal Postoperative Analgesia Across Perioperative Guidelines
summary:
This community represents multimodal postoperative pain management, spanning oral/IV non-opioid analgesics, opioids and opioid-sparing regional techniques, drawn from NICE, AUGS (urogynecologic) and ERAS Society guidance.

Foundation: multimodal analgesia treats postoperative pain in adults having surgery when analgesics of different classes are combined (NICE). ERAS advises regular scheduled acetaminophen plus NSAID for all patients unless contraindicated. AUGS names acetaminophen and NSAIDs as part of perioperative multimodal analgesia for urogynecological surgery, and after vulvar and vaginal surgery unless contraindicated; NICE also positions NSAIDs as additional analgesia alongside other analgesics.

NICE is most prescriptive on drug choice: ibuprofen for immediate postoperative pain of all severities in adults (including dental surgery) unless surgery was for hip fracture; IV NSAID only if the person cannot take oral medicine, and then a traditional NSAID rather than a COX-2 inhibitor; oral immediate-release opioid only when immediate pain is expected to be moderate to severe. For people who cannot take oral opioids, patient-controlled analgesia and continuous epidural are offered as a choice, with epidural especially for major/complex open-torso surgery, expected severe pain, or cognitive impairment.

ERAS contributes the regional/adjunct techniques: thoracic epidural analgesia for major abdominal surgery (analgesic effect up to 72 h), as an alternative in open general gynecologic surgery using low-concentration local anesthetic plus opiates for 24–48 h, and possibly in major oncologic surgery where additional IV opioids are frequently required; it also prevents insulin resistance within the ERAS protocol. Transversus abdominis plane block suits major abdominal surgery and patients not receiving neuraxial blockade (effect up to 24 h). Perioperative IV lidocaine infusion and incisional infiltration with bupivacaine (as a multimodal component) are also endorsed; AUGS supports incisional local anesthetic infiltration to reduce systemic medication needs.

Not established: comparative superiority or ranking between techniques, doses, dosing intervals, opioid tapering/discharge prescribing, pediatric or obstetric populations, contraindication details beyond hip fracture, monitoring requirements, and specific nursing assessment or pain-score thresholds.

title: Decontamination and Nasogastric Tubes: Pneumonia, SSI
summary:
This community centres on two levers affecting postoperative pneumonia and surgical site infection (SSI): pharmacologic decontamination of the aerodigestive tract, and avoidance of routine nasogastric (NG) tube use.

On the protective side, WHO (T1 p57) links selective decontamination of the digestive tract (SDD) to prevention of postoperative pneumonia in patients undergoing digestive-tract surgery, and — explicitly to a lesser extent — to prevention of SSI in that same population. WHO also credits chlorhexidine mouth rinse with preventing postoperative pneumonia, but the population attached is specifically patients undergoing cardiac surgery, not abdominal or gynecologic surgery.

On the risk side, the ERAS Society identifies nasogastric intubation as increasing the risk of postoperative pneumonia in patients undergoing elective abdominal surgery (T1 p1, restated for the nasogastric tube at T1 p6). AUGS (T2 p7) extends the harm to a different outcome, stating that the nasogastric tube increases the risk of surgical site infection in patients after abdominal surgery, with the explicit condition that systematic (routine) use should be avoided.

Contributing bodies are WHO, the ERAS Society, and AUGS. They are complementary rather than contradictory: WHO supplies the decontamination interventions and confines chlorhexidine rinse to cardiac surgery; ERAS is the most specific on NG tubes and pneumonia in elective abdominal surgery; AUGS is the only source tying NG tubes to SSI and the only one carrying an explicit practice directive to avoid systematic use.

The community does not establish: any drug, agent, concentration, dose, or timing/duration for SDD or chlorhexidine mouth rinse; any evidence grade or effect size; whether SDD or chlorhexidine rinse benefits gynecologic or non-cardiac, non-digestive-tract populations; whether chlorhexidine rinse affects SSI at all; and no threshold, duration, or indication defining when an NG tube is nonetheless appropriate (e.g., for therapeutic decompression). No mechanism, no interaction between the decontamination and NG-tube pathways, and no mortality or length-of-stay outcomes are asserted.
key_entities: selective decontamination of the digestive tract

title: Exogenous Estrogen and Postoperative Thromboembolism Risk
summary: This small community represents a single, focused perioperative theme: exogenous hormonal therapy as a contributor to venous thromboembolic risk in women undergoing gynecologic surgery. Two entities feed one shared outcome. First, combined oral hormonal contraception is identified as increasing the risk of postoperative thromboembolism. Second, hormone replacement therapy is likewise identified as increasing postoperative thromboembolism risk, with the qualifying condition that it is characterised as a 'relative' risk factor rather than an absolute or independent one. Both relations derive from the same source, ERAS Society (T1, p1), so the community is single-body and internally consistent; no competing or contradictory recommendation from another guideline body is present, and there is no cross-body comparison to be made. The only gradation of specificity within the community is the explicit 'relative risk factor' condition attached to hormone replacement therapy, which is absent from the combined oral hormonal contraception relation. For educators and QI leads, the practical takeaway is that preoperative assessment and thromboprophylaxis risk stratification should capture current use of combined oral hormonal contraception and of hormone replacement therapy as documented risk elements. Importantly, the community does NOT establish a great deal that clinicians often ask about: it specifies no population beyond the implicit perioperative gynecologic surgical patient (no age band, BMI threshold, procedure type, malignancy status, or personal/family VTE history stratum); no drug names, doses, estrogen or progestin types, or routes (oral versus transdermal or vaginal); no magnitude of risk (no relative risk, odds ratio, or absolute incidence); and no timing guidance whatsoever — there is no stated interval for stopping or restarting contraception or HRT before or after surgery. It also does not recommend any specific prophylaxis (no low-molecular-weight heparin, unfractionated heparin, mechanical compression, or duration of extended prophylaxis), nor does it link these agents to any outcome other than postoperative thromboembolism. Any local protocol on hormone cessation timing or agent-specific prophylaxis must be sourced outside this community.

title: Nurse-Directed Postoperative Urinary Retention Management
summary:
This community centres on the assessment and treatment of postoperative urinary retention (POUR) in surgical and pelvic reconstructive populations, and specifically on shifting that management into nurse-directed, protocol-driven, and patient-driven pathways rather than routine indwelling catheterisation or clinician-only decision-making.

Two core recommendations recur. First, intermittent catheterisation TREATS postoperative urinary retention: in catheterized surgical patients when used under a nurse-directed protocol (CDC T1 p45), and in postoperative patients generally as part of nurse-directed protocols for POUR management (CDC T1 p16). Second, a bladder ultrasound scanner DETECTS postoperative urinary retention in postoperative patients when embedded within POUR management protocols (CDC T1 p45 and p16) — i.e., non-invasive volume assessment is paired with intermittent catheterisation so that catheters are passed only when retention is objectively identified. Third, from a different body, patient-driven self-discontinuation of a transurethral catheter TREATS postoperative urinary retention in patients after pelvic reconstructive surgery, on the basis that it is not inferior to office-based discontinuation (AUGS T2 p11).

Two guideline bodies contribute. CDC (T1) is the more general and infrastructural voice: it names the personnel model (nurse-directed protocols), the detection technology (bladder scanner), and the therapeutic modality (intermittent catheterisation) across broad postoperative and catheterized surgical populations. AUGS (T2) is narrower but more population-specific, addressing women after pelvic reconstructive surgery and extending autonomy to the patient for catheter removal. They do not conflict; AUGS adds a self-management step downstream of the CDC detection/intermittent-catheterisation framework.

What this community does NOT establish: no bladder-volume thresholds (e.g., residual volume in mL) for scanning or catheterisation, no timing or frequency of intermittent catheterisation, no maximum duration of catheterisation, no drugs (no alpha-blockers or cholinergics named), no criteria for selecting patients suitable for self-discontinuation, no outcome data on catheter-associated urinary tract infection or reintervention rates, and no guidance for non-gynecologic or paediatric populations. It also does not specify who trains nurses or patients, or what escalation pathway applies when retention persists.

title: VTE Prophylaxis and Postpartum Haemorrhage Balance
summary: This community covers risk-assessed thromboprophylaxis across pregnancy, surgery and the puerperium, and the counterbalancing bleeding risk, including postpartum haemorrhage management. RCOG dominates: risk assessment in early pregnancy/prepregnancy (detecting VTE risk factors), repeated intrapartum and immediately postpartum, and at least once after delivery before discharge. Antenatal pharmacological prophylaxis is based on absolute VTE risk versus bleeding risk, beginning early in pregnancy for women with previous VTE, and for women with persistent antiphospholipid antibodies plus other risk factors. Postpartum thresholds are lower than antenatal. Specific durations: LMWH for 10 days after caesarean section; 6 weeks postpartum for prior confirmed VTE, family history plus identified thrombophilia, asymptomatic thrombophilia, low-risk thrombophilia with first-degree-relative VTE, and asymptomatic antithrombin, protein C or S deficiency or multiple defects (even without extra risk factors); high-dose LMWH for 6 weeks (or until return to oral anticoagulants) where previous VTE relates to antithrombin deficiency, APS or recurrent VTE; 10 days for asymptomatic factor V Leiden/prothrombin mutation or antiphospholipid antibodies with one other risk factor; 3–5 days only for primary APS without previous VTE; extension to 6 weeks with persistent risk factors (prolonged admission, wound infection, puerperal surgery). Therapeutic anticoagulation treats VTE for the pregnancy plus ≥6 weeks postnatally and ≥3 months total, but increases postpartum haemorrhage risk; prophylaxis is temporarily contraindicated until immediate haemorrhage risk falls. Low-dose aspirin gives modest recurrence reduction in non-pregnant first unprovoked VTE after warfarin but is contraindicated as obstetric thromboprophylaxis. NICE adds timing precision: LMWH within hours of completed risk assessment in pregnancy, continuing until risk resolves or discharge; medical patients within 14 hours of admission decision; surgical/trauma and medical prophylaxis only when VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk, with unnecessary prophylaxis increasing bleeding. ERAS covers preoperative prophylaxis and combined oral hormonal contraception continued to surgery. WHO contributes early mobilisation as soon as appropriate after birth and uterine massage to prevent (active third-stage management) and treat PPH, sustained until bleeding stops or the uterus contracts; RCOG names uterine atony as the commonest PPH cause. AUGS notes postoperative prophylaxis only. The community does not specify drug doses, weight-based regimens, mechanical prophylaxis, laboratory monitoring, neuraxial anaesthesia timing intervals, uterotonic agents, or comparative effectiveness between agents.
key_entities: high dose low molecular weight heparin thromboprophylaxis

title: Beta-lactam Alternative Antibiotics in Perioperative and Obstetric Infection
summary: This community centres on antibiotic selection for prophylaxis and treatment when beta-lactams cannot be used, plus the toxicities and monitoring that follow. Surgical prophylaxis: preoperative antimicrobial prophylaxis applies to laparoscopic cholecystectomy (WHO p234), and CDC (p5) states SSI prevention measures apply to open cholecystectomy and, where applicable to the corresponding open operation, to laparoscopic cholecystectomy. For penicillin/beta-lactam-allergic patients, WHO recommends clindamycin as an alternative preoperative antibiotic for laparoscopic cholecystectomy (p122) and clindamycin, vancomycin or teicoplanin for operations where risk is primarily from skin organisms (p60; clindamycin only if local susceptibility patterns are favourable). CDC (p13) endorses clindamycin or vancomycin for gram-positive cover when cephalosporins cannot be given, and restricts vancomycin otherwise to specific circumstances such as a detected cluster of MRSA mediastinitis or incisional SSI from methicillin-resistant coagulase-negative staphylococci. WHO specifies timing: vancomycin infusion completed within one hour of skin incision (pp60, 67). Both clindamycin and vancomycin treat known or suspected methicillin-resistant staphylococcal infection in beta-lactam-intolerant patients (WHO p60); vancomycin also substitutes for ampicillin in enterococcal infective endocarditis prophylaxis. Obstetric use (RCOG p11): clindamycin with piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem for life-threatening puerperal/maternal sepsis (Gram-positive and anaerobic cover, sensitivities unknown), with IVIG for suspected group A streptococcal sepsis, and in necrotising fasciitis to switch off exotoxin production; vancomycin is added if MRSA history or suspicion. For beta-lactam-allergic women needing intrapartum GBS prophylaxis, cephalosporin or vancomycin substitutes for clindamycin because of rising resistance; vancomycin is an option in severe penicillin allergy; broad-spectrum cover for GBS is advised for women pyrexial at ≥38°C in labour, and intrapartum prophylaxis for maternal pyrexia or signs of sepsis (p15). Endometritis: clindamycin plus gentamicin first-line (WHO p30, RCOG p30); gentamicin once-daily with ampicillin for chorioamnionitis (WHO p30); oral step-down adds no benefit once improved on IV therapy in uncomplicated cases.
