Harms: clindamycin–C. difficile; vancomycin–nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, red man syndrome if infused too rapidly; gentamicin–oto/nephrotoxicity, with serum vancomycin and gentamicin level monitoring (the latter for endocarditis on lower twice-daily dosing). Vaginal swabs just before birth detect GBS in preterm labour (WHO p103). Not established: specific doses, durations, gynecologic-surgery-specific regimens, comparative effectiveness, or resolution of the clindamycin-versus-vancomycin choice in GBS prophylaxis.

title: Second-line mechanical interventions for PPH
summary:
This community covers non-pharmacological, mechanical and radiological interventions for postpartum haemorrhage (PPH), chiefly where uterine atony is the cause, and their place in escalation after uterotonics. Four interventions appear: intrauterine balloon tamponade, bimanual uterine compression, external aortic compression, and uterine artery embolization.

Intrauterine balloon tamponade is recommended by WHO for women with PPH due to uterine atony when women do not respond to uterotonics or uterotonics are unavailable (WHO T1 pp19, 28). RCOG is more procedurally specific: tamponade (including a hydrostatic balloon catheter) is the first-line 'surgical' intervention for most women where uterine atony is the only or main cause of haemorrhage (RCOG T1 pp6, 26); it is also endorsed for resource-poor settings (p26) and, for women with continuing major obstetric haemorrhage, is placed in theatre after examination under anaesthesia and correction of clotting abnormality (p41).

Bimanual uterine compression and external aortic compression are both WHO recommendations framed as temporizing measures until appropriate/substantive care is available — bimanual compression for women with PPH due to uterine atony after vaginal delivery (pp19, 28) and generally for women with PPH (pp10, 19); external aortic compression likewise for atonic PPH after vaginal birth (pp10, 19, 28) and for PPH generally (pp10, 19).

Uterine artery embolization is a WHO recommendation for persistent bleeding when relevant resources are available (p10), and specifically for atonic PPH if other measures have failed and necessary resources exist (p19).

Contributing bodies are WHO (temporizing manual/aortic compression, embolization, tamponade after uterotonic failure) and RCOG (tamponade as first-line surgical step, device type, theatre sequencing). RCOG contributes nothing here on compression techniques or embolization; WHO contributes no device specifics.

The community does not establish balloon inflation volumes, dwell times, retention or removal criteria, success or failure thresholds, blood-loss triggers, transfusion or uterotonic drug regimens, nursing monitoring parameters, complications, caesarean-specific guidance, or interventions for non-atonic causes such as trauma or retained tissue.
key_entities: postpartum haemorrhage due to uterine atony

title: Povidone-iodine antisepsis for infection prevention
summary:
This community centres on a single agent, povidone-iodine, and its role as an antiseptic for infection prevention across three distinct guideline contexts. All three relations are preventive: two target surgical site infection (SSI) and one targets neonatal conjunctivitis.

Recommendations by population and condition: (1) AUGS (Tier 2, p6) positions povidone-iodine as a preventive agent against SSI in patients undergoing urogynecological procedures, but explicitly as a second-line option — it should be considered only if chlorhexidine is contraindicated. (2) NICE (Tier 1, p24) supports povidone-iodine for SSI prevention in the broader population of surgical patients, applied topically before wound closure; the guideline flags that this recommendation rests on dated studies. (3) WHO (Tier 1, p57) addresses a different population entirely — neonates — recommending a 2.5% ophthalmic solution as prophylaxis against neonatal conjunctivitis.

Contributing bodies and differences: AUGS, NICE and WHO all contribute. AUGS is the most specific on comparative preference, subordinating povidone-iodine to chlorhexidine for urogynecological skin/site preparation. NICE is the most specific on timing and technique (topical application before wound closure) but the least confident on evidence quality (dated studies). WHO is the most specific on formulation and strength (2.5% ophthalmic solution) and is the only source addressing an ocular, neonatal indication rather than a surgical wound. There is no direct contradiction between the three: they address different populations, sites and timings, though AUGS and NICE differ in enthusiasm for povidone-iodine as a general SSI measure — AUGS conditions its use on chlorhexidine contraindication while NICE does not state that restriction.

What this community does NOT establish: no comparative effectiveness data quantifying SSI reduction, no concentration or contact time for the surgical applications (only the neonatal 2.5% is specified), no guidance on adverse effects, iodine allergy, thyroid effects, or use in pregnancy; no repeat-dosing or re-application intervals; and no evidence grading beyond NICE's caveat about dated studies.

title: Pre-eclampsia: prevention and complication risks
summary:
This community centres on pre-eclampsia as both a preventable condition and a driver of downstream maternal complications, spanning antenatal prophylaxis and immediate postnatal surveillance.

Risk relations (all RCOG T1): pre-eclampsia increases risk of pulmonary oedema specifically in women receiving fluid resuscitation (p11), postpartum haemorrhage (p10), and venous thromboembolism in pregnant women (p12). These three sequelae frame why fluid balance, blood-loss and thromboprophylaxis vigilance matter in pre-eclamptic patients.

Prevention recommendations (all WHO T1): calcium supplementation prevents pre-eclampsia in pregnant women in populations with low dietary calcium intake, at a daily oral dose of 1.5–2.0 g elemental calcium (p9, p15). WHO extends the same recommendation to pregnant women with active tuberculosis, particularly those at higher risk of developing hypertension, in settings where calcium intake is low (p33), and locates this calcium supplementation in the antenatal phase (p33). Acetylsalicylic acid prevents pre-eclampsia in pregnant women, and should be initiated before 20 weeks of pregnancy (p15) — the only timing threshold given for aspirin.

Postnatal monitoring: counselling on signs and symptoms monitors for pre-eclampsia in all women after birth, in the first few days after birth (WHO T1 p23) — a reminder that risk does not end at delivery.

Contributing bodies differ in emphasis rather than conflicting: WHO supplies the prophylactic and counselling interventions with explicit doses, timing and population qualifiers (low dietary calcium intake, active tuberculosis, <20 weeks); RCOG supplies the complication profile, and is more specific in conditioning pulmonary oedema risk on fluid resuscitation.

Not established here: no aspirin dose, no upper gestational limit or stopping rule for either agent, no diagnostic criteria, blood-pressure thresholds or severity grading for pre-eclampsia, and no treatment pathway (e.g. antihypertensives, magnesium sulfate, delivery timing). The graph does not quantify effect sizes, does not state how the three complications should be monitored or managed, does not specify what signs and symptoms the postnatal counselling should cover or who delivers it, and offers no guidance for women with adequate dietary calcium.

title: Pregnancy as Risk State and Contraindication
summary: This community centres on pregnancy as both a risk-elevating physiological state and a pervasive contraindication that must be detected before surgery and before prescribing. Detection: WHO recommends a pregnancy status check in the immediate preoperative period for female surgical patients, to identify pregnancy before any surgery that could pose risks to mother or fetus. Risk elevation: RCOG states pregnancy raises venous thromboembolism risk four- to five-fold versus nonpregnant women of the same age, and raises recurrence risk in women with previous VTE (relative risk 3.5 versus the nonpregnant period); it also raises risk of invasive group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus infection compared with non-pregnant women. WHO links pregnancy to increased medication error risk in patients with specific conditions, and OpenRN links pregnancy to urinary incontinence in adult females. Contraindications: RCOG contraindicates warfarin and vitamin K antagonists antenatally for women requiring antenatal VTE treatment because of adverse fetal effects; non-vitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulants (DOACs) should be avoided antenatally as they likely cross the placenta with potential direct fetal effects, and are also temporarily contraindicated while breastfeeding; dextran is contraindicated antenatally and intrapartum; and D-dimer testing is not to be used in investigating acute VTE in pregnancy. RNAO adds cardiovascular contraindications: ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers, and long-acting calcium channel blockers (the latter specified for clients with hypertension). WHO contraindicates anthelminthic treatment in pregnant women in endemic areas until after the first trimester. Contributing bodies: RCOG (most granular—thrombosis drug-by-drug, with trimester/peripartum timing and quantified risks), RNAO (antihypertensives, no timing specified), WHO (preoperative screening, anthelminthics, medication error), OpenRN (continence). RCOG uniquely gives numeric risk magnitudes and distinguishes antenatal versus breastfeeding restrictions; RNAO and WHO state contraindications without such timing. The community does NOT establish safe alternative agents, dosing, gestational thresholds beyond the first trimester, how pregnancy status is tested, what to do when a check is positive, or outcomes of these interventions.

title: Inherited Thrombophilias and Pregnancy VTE Risk
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: high-risk inherited (heritable) thrombophilias as risk factors for venous thromboembolism (VTE) in pregnancy. All five relations are risk-attribution statements drawn from RCOG Green-top guidance (RCOG T1, pp. 17 and 38), and all are scoped to the population 'pregnant women'.

The named thrombophilias are: antithrombin deficiency; homozygous factor V Leiden; homozygous prothrombin gene mutation; and compound heterozygous factor V Leiden plus prothrombin gene mutation. Each is stated to increase the risk of pregnancy-related VTE in pregnant women (p17). One additional, more specific statement appears on p38: homozygous factor V Leiden increases VTE risk in pregnant women under the condition that the woman is 'classed as intermediate risk' — i.e. the guideline links the genotype to a risk-stratification category, not merely to a generic risk statement. This is the only relation in the community that carries a stratification condition, and it is the point where the corpus is most specific.

Only one guideline body contributes: the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RCOG). There is therefore no inter-body disagreement to reconcile here; the only internal variation is depth of specification between p17 (broad risk listing of four thrombophilias) and p38 (risk-category placement for homozygous factor V Leiden alone).

What this community does NOT establish: no thromboprophylaxis drug is named (no LMWH, heparin, aspirin or warfarin), no dose, no weight bands, and no duration or timing of prophylaxis (no antenatal start point, no intrapartum or postpartum interval, no six-week postnatal rule). No numeric risk magnitudes, odds ratios or absolute incidences are given. No screening or testing recommendations for thrombophilia are stated, no risk-category thresholds or scores are defined beyond the bare label 'intermediate risk', and risk categories are not assigned to antithrombin deficiency, homozygous prothrombin gene mutation or the compound heterozygous genotype. Acquired thrombophilias (e.g. antiphospholipid syndrome) and low-risk heritable variants (heterozygous factor V Leiden) are absent. Educators should pair this theme with the corresponding prophylaxis-dosing guidance before use in practice.
key_entities: compound heterozygous factor v leiden and prothrombin gene mutation

title: Preoperative Assessment for Wound Healing Risk
summary:
This small community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: the placement of preoperative assessment within the perioperative timeline and its role in identifying patients at risk of poor surgical wound healing. Two relations define it. First, preoperative assessment is situated in the preoperative phase for the population 'people undergoing surgery'. Second, preoperative assessment detects potential wound healing problems in that same population, with the explicit condition that it is carried out 'as part of a structured approach to care for surgical wounds'. The practical recommendation for educators and QI leads is therefore twofold: (1) ensure that every patient undergoing surgery receives an assessment before the operation, and (2) ensure that assessment is embedded in a structured, documented surgical wound care pathway rather than performed as an isolated task, so that identified wound healing risks can be carried forward into intraoperative and postoperative care.

The only contributing guideline body in this community is NICE (source: NICE T1, p15). Because a single body and a single page underpin both relations, there are no inter-guideline disagreements, no competing thresholds, and no instance of one body being more specific than another; any comparison with other corpora (e.g. specialty gynecologic surgical societies) would have to be drawn from outside this community.

What the community does NOT establish is substantial. It names no specific wound healing risk factors (no diabetes, smoking, obesity, BMI thresholds, albumin or glycaemic targets), no assessment tools or scoring systems, and no timing interval — it does not say how many days or weeks before surgery the assessment should occur, or who should perform it. It specifies no drugs, no antimicrobial or antiseptic prophylaxis, no dressing or skin-preparation choices, and no gynecology-specific population detail (the population is the generic 'people undergoing surgery'). It also defines no actions to take once a potential wound healing problem is detected, and no outcome or audit measures. Local protocols must supply these operational details.
key_entities: structured approach to care for surgical wounds

title: Preoperative Bathing to Prevent Surgical Infection
summary:
Clinical theme: This small, tightly focused community addresses preoperative patient skin preparation by whole-body bathing as a surgical site infection (SSI) prevention measure situated in the preoperative phase of care.

Main recommendation: For surgical patients, perform preoperative full body bathing with either soap (a non-antimicrobial agent) or an antiseptic agent, with the wash occurring at least the night before the operative day. The graph links this intervention directly to prevention of surgical site infection, and explicitly assigns it to the preoperative phase, with the same timing condition (at least the night before surgery) attached to both relations. Notably, the guideline language permits either soap or an antiseptic agent, i.e., an antiseptic product is not mandated over plain soap.

Contributing guideline bodies: Only the CDC contributes here (CDC Table 1, p. 4). Because a single source and a single population ('surgical patients') are represented, there are no inter-body disagreements, no competing timing windows, and no more- versus less-specific parallel recommendations to reconcile within this community.

What this community does NOT establish: It does not name a specific antiseptic agent (e.g., no chlorhexidine gluconate or povidone-iodine product, concentration, or formulation is specified), does not state a required number of baths or repeat wash on the morning of surgery, and does not define an upper limit or 'no earlier than' boundary—only a minimum of the night before. It does not stratify by procedure type, surgical site, wound class, or patient risk factors (e.g., diabetes, obesity, colonisation status), nor does it address gynecologic-specific considerations such as vaginal or perineal preparation. No effect size, SSI rate reduction, evidence grade, or strength of recommendation is captured, and no supervision, documentation, or patient-education requirements are specified. For QI purposes, the actionable, auditable element is simply: documented full-body soap or antiseptic bath completed on or before the night preceding the operative day for every surgical patient.
key_entities: preoperative full body bathing with soap or antiseptic agent

title: Preoperative Bathing to Prevent SSI
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused perioperative theme: preoperative whole-body bathing as a surgical site infection (SSI) prevention measure, situated squarely in the preoperative phase of care. All relations converge on one intervention — a full body shower or bath — and one outcome — prevention of surgical site infection.

The core recommendation is that surgical patients perform a full body shower or bath before surgery to prevent SSI. Two agent options are explicitly named at the same level: soap, which may be either antimicrobial or nonantimicrobial, or an antiseptic agent. No preference is expressed between antimicrobial and nonantimicrobial soap, and no specific antiseptic product is named. The timing condition is repeated across all four relations and is the most concrete parameter in the community: the wash should be performed on at least the night before the operative day. The phrase "at least" implies the night-before wash is a minimum rather than a ceiling, but no additional or repeat washes are specified. The population is stated broadly as surgical patients, with no narrowing to gynecologic, abdominal, or implant procedures, and no age, BMI, or comorbidity qualifiers.

Only one guideline body contributes here: the CDC (CDC T1 p1). Because there is a single source, there are no interbody disagreements, no competing thresholds, and no instance of one organization being more specific than another; the apparent redundancy in the relations reflects the same CDC statement expressed as both an SSI-prevention claim and a phase-placement claim.

What this community does NOT establish: the number of washes, the volume or duration of washing, whether chlorhexidine gluconate or povidone-iodine is preferred, any concentration or formulation (e.g., wipes vs. liquid), whether an operative-morning wash is required in addition to the night-before wash, documentation or patient-education requirements, effect sizes or SSI rate reductions, and any linkage to hair removal, skin antisepsis at the surgical site, antibiotic prophylaxis, or normothermia. It also does not address pediatric, emergency, or immunocompromised populations separately.
key_entities: preoperative full body shower or bath with soap or antiseptic agent

title: Anxiety, Dyspnea: Nonpharmacologic and Pharmacologic Management
summary:
This community centers on the anxiety–dyspnea cycle and its management, spanning perioperative preparation, pain care, and palliative/end-of-life care. Anxiety is shown to increase risk of dyspnea (OpenRN p545, p653), and hearing loss increases anxiety risk in individuals experiencing hearing loss (p521); wrong-side surgery is linked to anxiety when undertaken without supervision of a senior resident or consultant oral surgeon (WHO p234).

Nonpharmacologic recommendations dominate: relaxation techniques and relaxation with guided imagery, health teaching, spiritual support, and a stress diary for anxiety in palliative care clients; teaching enhanced breathing and coughing techniques for anxiety; and referral for psychiatric counseling for clients unable to cope with the experience of their illness (OpenRN p1269, p545, p653). Relaxation technique also treats anxiety-heightened pain in patients receiving injections (p1006), nausea (p1269), and chronic pain as a complementary health approach (p825). For dyspnea in palliative care, pursed-lip breathing, tripod positioning, energy conservation techniques and relaxation are recommended (p1269, p545). Monitoring: anxiety assessment for clients with dyspnea (p545) and watching for signs of anxiety or fear in clients with pain (p844).

Pharmacologic entries: benzodiazepines and antianxiety medication treat anxiety (as prescribed), but benzodiazepines increase risk of respiratory depression when taken concurrently with opioids or other sedatives (p825), and of falls, oversedation, delirium (especially the frail elderly, p1269) and impaired cognition (p395). Opioids treat dyspnea in palliative care clients with end-stage disease using relatively small doses titrated to relief without oversedation; morphine sulfate sublingually treats dyspnea in dying clients (p1288).

Guideline bodies: OpenRN supplies most clinical detail; ERAS Society states preoperative patient education and psychological preparation prevent anxiety (and education treats anxiety after surgery); AUGS is more specific, specifying educational leaflets, video, etc. including psychological preparation. OpenRN adds explanation of the procedure for patients undergoing staple removal.

Not established: benzodiazepine drug names, doses, thresholds or timing; opioid dose numbers; comparative effectiveness of relaxation versus pharmacotherapy; anxiety screening tools or scores; and any gynecologic-specific anxiety protocol.

title: Preoperative preparation preventing intra-operative hypovolaemia
summary:
Clinical theme: this is a small, single-source community centred on the preoperative phase of gynecologic surgical care, and specifically on the role of preoperative preparation as a preventive measure against intra-operative hypovolaemia. It links a process of care (preparation before surgery) to both a timing anchor (the preoperative phase) and an adverse intra-operative outcome (hypovolaemia), framing preparation as risk-reduction rather than as routine ritual.

Recommendations captured: only one substantive recommendation is represented — that preoperative preparation prevents intra-operative hypovolaemia, and that this preparation is situated in (occurs in) the preoperative phase. No population qualifier, no condition or trigger, no threshold and no timing window are attached to either relation in this community; the guideline text as extracted applies the statement generally, without narrowing to age group, comorbidity, procedure type (e.g. laparotomy versus laparoscopy), ASA class, or emergency versus elective status.

Contributing bodies: the World Health Organization is the sole contributor, via WHO Technical/Training material Tier 1, page 41. Because there is only one source, there are no inter-body agreements, disagreements, or differences in specificity to reconcile; nothing here can be compared against, for example, national surgical or anaesthetic society guidance, and no body is more granular than another within this community.

What the community does NOT establish: it does not specify what preoperative preparation consists of — no fluids, crystalloid or colloid volumes, no fasting duration or carbohydrate loading, no blood products, cross-matching, group-and-save, tranexamic acid, haemoglobin threshold, or vasopressor plan is named. It does not define or grade hypovolaemia (no blood-pressure, heart-rate, urine-output or estimated-blood-loss criteria), does not state who performs or documents the preparation, and does not describe monitoring, escalation, or intra-operative or postoperative management once hypovolaemia occurs. It also provides no evidence grade, strength of recommendation, or outcome data. Educators should therefore treat this as a conceptual anchor requiring local protocol detail, not an implementable bundle.

title: Preoperative Antiseptic Shower for SSI Prevention
summary:
This community covers a single, tightly focused perioperative theme: the preoperative antiseptic shower (bathing with antiseptic soap) as a patient-preparation measure situated in the preoperative phase and aimed at preventing surgical site infection (SSI).

Recommendations and populations: For surgical patients generally, a preoperative shower with antiseptic soap is linked to prevention of surgical site infection (WHO T1 p68). The same source places the intervention explicitly in the preoperative phase for surgical patients. The CDC source (T1 p11) also assigns the shower to the preoperative phase for surgical patients, but adds a product-specific condition: repeated showers are usually indicated when chlorhexidine gluconate-containing products are used. This is the only drug/agent named in the community, and the only dosing-frequency qualifier present.

Contributing bodies and differences: Two guideline bodies contribute — WHO and CDC. WHO carries the outcome claim (shower prevents SSI) and the phase placement; CDC is more specific about implementation, i.e. that chlorhexidine gluconate products typically require repeated showers rather than a single wash. Conversely, CDC in this community makes no explicit SSI-prevention claim, and WHO specifies no antiseptic agent, no number of showers, and no timing interval. The two are complementary rather than contradictory: WHO supplies the rationale, CDC the product-conditional application.

What this community does NOT establish: it does not specify how many hours before incision the shower(s) should occur, the number of showers required, chlorhexidine gluconate concentration, or an alternative agent (e.g. povidone-iodine or plain soap comparison). It does not define the surgical population any more narrowly than "surgical patients" — there is no gynecologic-specific, obstetric, diabetic, or colonized (e.g. MRSA) subgroup, and no exclusion criteria such as chlorhexidine allergy or pediatric/neonatal limits. No strength-of-evidence grade, no effect size or SSI rate threshold, and no documentation, patient-education, or adherence-monitoring requirement is captured. Quality-improvement leads should therefore treat local protocol details (timing, agent concentration, number of showers) as outside what these relations authorise.

title: Preoperative Chlorhexidine Shower for SSI Prevention
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: preoperative skin antisepsis by patient bathing as a component of surgical site infection (SSI) prevention in gynecologic surgery. It comprises one intervention (preoperative shower with a chlorhexidine-based antimicrobial soap), one outcome it is credited with preventing (surgical site infection), and one temporal anchor (the preoperative phase).

The main recommendation is that surgical patients perform a preoperative shower using chlorhexidine-based antimicrobial soap before surgery, positioned explicitly as part of SSI reduction bundles rather than as a stand-alone measure. The population attached to the recommendation is broad — 'surgical patients' — and the condition is bundle-based SSI reduction. The phase relation confirms the timing is preoperative, i.e. before the surgical procedure.

Only one guideline body contributes to this community: the ERAS Society (ERAS_Society T1, p6). Because there is a single contributing source, there are no inter-society disagreements, no competing thresholds, and no instance of one body being more granular than another within this theme. Any harmonisation work would therefore need to draw on sources outside this community.

Important limits: the community does NOT establish the number of showers, the interval between shower(s) and incision (e.g. night-before versus morning-of dosing), the chlorhexidine concentration or formulation (soap versus impregnated cloths versus alcohol-based preparations), or whether an alternative antiseptic (e.g. plain soap or povidone-iodine) is acceptable. It does not quantify the magnitude of SSI reduction, specify SSI subtype (superficial, deep, or organ/space), or define which other bundle elements must accompany the shower for the effect to hold. It does not address gynecology-specific subpopulations (e.g. laparotomy versus laparoscopy, obesity, diabetes, or vaginal hysterectomy), contraindications such as chlorhexidine allergy or pediatric skin, documentation or patient-education requirements, or who is accountable for verifying adherence on the day of surgery. Nurse educators should treat this as a bundle-level directive requiring local protocol specification.
key_entities: preoperative shower with chlorhexidine-based antimicrobial soap

title: Preoperative Surgical Scrub Prevents Site Infection
summary:
This small community represents a single, tightly scoped theme: the preoperative surgical hand/forearm scrub performed by the surgical team with an antiseptic agent, and its role in preventing surgical site infection (SSI). Both relations in the community concern the same actor population — members of the surgical team — rather than the patient, making this a team-practice (rather than patient-preparation) node within the perioperative corpus.

Main content: (1) The preoperative surgical scrub with an antiseptic agent PREVENTS surgical site infection. The attached population is the surgical team, and the stated condition is reducing resident skin flora for the duration of a procedure, specifically relevant if gloves become punctured or torn during surgery — i.e., the scrub provides a residual antiseptic effect on the hands that limits contamination when glove integrity is lost intraoperatively. (2) The scrub OCCURS_IN_PHASE preoperative, again for the surgical team, situating it before incision as part of pre-incision preparation.

Contributing bodies: only the CDC contributes here (CDC T1, p19); both relations derive from the same source and page. There is therefore no cross-body agreement or disagreement to reconcile, and no instance where one organization is more specific than another — a gap a QI lead should note if seeking corroborating or more granular guidance (e.g., from AORN or other perioperative bodies) in the wider corpus.

What this community does NOT establish: it names no specific antiseptic agent (no chlorhexidine gluconate, povidone-iodine, or alcohol-based product), no scrub duration or number of minutes, no brush-versus-brushless technique, no repeat-scrub interval between cases, and no drying or gowning/gloving sequence. It sets no patient-side skin antisepsis, hair-removal, or antibiotic-prophylaxis timing thresholds, and gives no outcome magnitude (no SSI rate reduction, relative risk, or evidence grade). It also does not address double-gloving, glove-change intervals, or management steps once a glove puncture is recognized — it only notes that residual flora reduction matters in that scenario.
key_entities: preoperative surgical scrub with antiseptic agent

title: Pressure injury prevention, assessment, and debridement
summary:
Theme: comprehensive pressure injury risk reduction, surveillance, and wound management, with an incidental link to mobility (ambulation) as both a skin and bowel intervention.

Risk factors named: obesity (in obese individuals), friction and shear, prolonged immobility in one position, decreased sensation, bladder or bowel incontinence, and — in children with intravenous access — joint stabilization devices that exert pressure at a flexion point or under the device.

Prevention: repositioning at least every two hours for patients with pressure injuries, and every two hours for clients with wounds while avoiding positioning directly on an injured area; ambulation to redistribute pressure points and increase blood/oxygen flow; pressure-relieving devices for at-risk clients; specialty mattress, bed, or chair pads for clients with wounds; keeping bed linens clean, dry, and wrinkle free (Braden friction/shear category; also prevents skin breakdown); transparent dressings on intact skin over elbows and heels for clients rated 2–Potential Problem for friction/shear; elbow and heel protectors for potential or actual friction/shear problems; silicone-based dressings in sacral and heel-shaped forms; Mepilex border foam dressing; protective skin barrier application and moisture barrier ointment (including clients with wounds).

Monitoring: head-to-toe skin assessment for hospitalised clients on admission, daily, and if condition deteriorates or per facility policy; skin checks each time the person is turned, cleaned, or the bed is changed; skin assessment every shift for clients rated 1–Problem for friction/shear and for patients very limited or completely immobile on the Braden mobility category (also for pressure ulcer); daily tube insertion site assessment for patients with enteral tubes; continual assessment of degree of tissue damage, since damage can worsen untreated. Diligent assessment itself is framed as preventive.

Treatment: wound debridement where slough or eschar is present and healing is required — specified for stage 3 and 4 injuries as required for accurate staging and healing — and for necrotic (black) tissue in the wound bed; chemical debridement agents for slough or eschar per provider orders.

Ambulation also prevents constipation as part of a bowel regimen, including clients taking opioids, but is temporarily contraindicated after a fall if the client remains weak or dizzy.

All relations derive from a single corpus (OpenRN Nursing Skills, Volume 2), so no inter-body disagreement can be assessed; page-level entries differ only in specificity (e.g., p718/p1113/p1145 on debridement staging, p731 on Braden-tiered interventions). The community does not establish comparative effectiveness between support surfaces or dressings, dosing/product brands beyond Mepilex, healing timelines, debridement method selection (sharp vs. enzymatic), or any gynecologic/perioperative-specific positioning thresholds despite the perioperative framing.
key_entities: skin assessment and inspection every shift

title: Braden-Stratified Pressure Ulcer Prevention and Surveillance
summary:
This community represents pressure injury prevention and surveillance for immobile or bedfast patients, with interventions tiered by mobility risk as scored on the Braden Scale. Two intervention classes appear: monitoring (skin assessment/inspection) and prevention (offloading, repositioning, support surfaces).

Surveillance recommendations are explicitly dose-stratified by Braden mobility category. For hospitalised patients with no mobility limitations or only slightly limited mobility, a daily skin check is indicated. For patients rated very limited or completely immobile on the Braden mobility category, skin assessment and inspection is escalated to every shift; the same every-shift frequency is specified for bedfast clients confined to bed.

Preventive interventions for bedfast clients confined to bed include heel protectors, applied with the heels elevated off the bed, and positioning with pillows to elevate pressure points. For patients rated very limited or completely immobile, the guideline adds turning and repositioning every 1–2 hours governed by a posted turning schedule, heel elevation, and consideration of a specialty bed (framed as an option rather than a requirement).

All relations in this community derive from a single source, OpenRN Nursing Skills (Volume 2, p. 731); no second guideline body contributes, so there are no inter-body conflicts to reconcile. Internally, the most specific guidance attaches to the very limited/completely immobile Braden group (explicit 1–2 hour turning interval plus posted schedule), whereas the bedfast-client statements specify the mechanism of heel offloading (heels elevated off bed) without a turning interval; low-risk patients receive only a monitoring frequency and no preventive measure.

The community does not establish any pharmacologic therapy, wound dressing, nutritional or moisture-management intervention, Braden numeric score cut-points, staging criteria for existing pressure ulcers, specialty bed type or selection criteria, escalation pathways when ulcers develop, documentation standards, or any perioperative/intraoperative gynecologic-specific positioning guidance. No outcome data, effect sizes, or evidence grading accompany the recommendations.
key_entities: skin assessment and inspection every shift
turning and repositioning every 1-2 hours with posted turning schedule
positioning with pillows to elevate pressure points

title: Primaquine deferral and chloroquine relapse prophylaxis
summary:
This community represents anti-relapse (radical cure) management of malaria in populations where primaquine cannot be given immediately — specifically pregnant or breastfeeding women and people with G6PD deficiency — and the substitute or modified regimens used to prevent relapse in the interim.

Main recommendations: (1) Primaquine is temporarily contraindicated in women who are pregnant or breastfeeding, and should be withheld until delivery and breastfeeding are completed (WHO T1 p33). (2) In place of primaquine during that period, weekly chloroquine chemoprophylaxis is recommended for pregnant or breastfeeding women to prevent malaria relapse, continued until delivery and breastfeeding are completed (WHO T1 p33). (3) Once delivery and breastfeeding are completed, primaquine may then be given to prevent relapse, with the decision conditioned on the woman's G6PD status (WHO T1 p33). (4) For people with G6PD deficiency, primaquine can still prevent relapse using an intermittent regimen of 0.75 mg/kg body weight once weekly for 8 weeks, administered with close medical supervision (WHO T1 p13).

Guideline contributions: all four relations derive from a single body, WHO (Table/section 1, pages 13 and 33). There is no inter-organisational disagreement in this community; the two pages are complementary rather than conflicting — p33 is specific about the obstetric timing (defer primaquine, bridge with weekly chloroquine, then reassess by G6PD status), while p13 is the more specific source for dosing in G6PD deficiency (0.75 mg/kg weekly × 8 weeks under close supervision).

What this community does not establish: no chloroquine dose, formulation, or route is specified (only "weekly"); no primaquine dose is given for non-G6PD-deficient patients or for post-partum use; no guidance on how or when G6PD testing should be performed, nor what constitutes "close medical supervision"; no haemolysis monitoring thresholds, adverse-event management, or infant safety data for breastfeeding; and nothing links these regimens to perioperative or gynecologic surgical care, anaesthesia, or transfusion decisions.

title: ECMO for Fulminant Viral Pneumonia
summary:
Clinical theme: this small community captures a single escalation-of-care pathway — the use of extra-corporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) as a rescue therapy for severe viral respiratory infection in the perioperative/obstetric-gynecologic context. It sits at the most acute end of the respiratory support spectrum, linking one advanced intervention to two viral diagnoses.

Main recommendations: ECMO is presented as a treatment for (1) primary influenza pneumonia and (2) SARS-CoV-2 infection. In both cases the attached condition is identical and explicit: ECMO 'should be considered in fulminant cases.' The graph therefore frames ECMO not as routine management of influenza or COVID-19, but as a consideration reserved for fulminant presentations — i.e. patients whose respiratory deterioration has progressed beyond conventional support. Both relations are drawn from the same guideline passage, indicating that the two infections are handled in parallel with the same threshold for ECMO consideration.

Contributing bodies: only one guideline body contributes here — the RCOG (RCOG T1, p7). Because a single source underpins both relations, there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile, and no instance where one body is more specific than another. The RCOG statement is uniform across influenza and SARS-CoV-2, with no differentiation of thresholds, timing, or criteria between the two pathogens.

What this community does NOT establish: it gives no definition or objective criteria for 'fulminant' (no PaO2/FiO2 ratio, oxygen saturation, ventilation duration, or lactate threshold); no timing for referral or initiation; no specification of the population beyond what the source guideline covers — notably no explicit statement about pregnancy stage, gestational age, postpartum status, or perioperative timing. It does not name ECMO modality (veno-venous vs veno-arterial), referral centre requirements, anticoagulation strategy, contraindications, or expected outcomes. It also does not describe the preceding rungs of escalation (oxygen, high-flow, non-invasive or invasive ventilation), antiviral therapy, or any relationship to delivery decisions. Educators should therefore treat this as a signpost to escalate and refer, not a protocol.

title: Transfusion and Blood Loss Drive Postoperative Risk
summary:
This community centers on perioperative blood transfusion as a shared risk exposure linking three adverse postoperative outcomes in gynecologic surgery: small bowel obstruction, prolonged length of stay, and surgical site infection. Two additional patient/operative factors — advanced age and intraoperative blood loss — converge on the same length-of-stay outcome, suggesting a theme of blood management and patient-level risk stratification rather than any single intervention.

Specific relations and their scope: AUGS (T2 p10) links perioperative blood transfusion to small bowel obstruction, stated without a restricting population or condition. ERAS Society (T1 p8) is the most population-specific contributor, identifying transfusion, advanced age, and blood loss as risk factors for prolonged length of stay specifically in patients undergoing laparoscopic gynecologic surgery. CDC (T1 p7) is the most condition-specific: transfusion increases surgical site infection risk for patients undergoing certain kinds of operations and when certain blood products are transfused, though neither the operation types nor the blood products are named here.

Contributing bodies: AUGS, ERAS Society, and CDC. They do not conflict; they differ in granularity and framing. ERAS frames transfusion within a multifactorial recovery/length-of-stay model, CDC frames it as an infection-control exposure qualified by product type and procedure, and AUGS states the bowel-obstruction association broadly. Practically, all three support minimizing avoidable transfusion and controlling operative blood loss, with heightened attention to older patients in laparoscopic gynecologic cases.

What this community does NOT establish: no transfusion thresholds (no hemoglobin trigger), no restrictive-versus-liberal strategy, no volume or unit counts, no timing windows (preoperative, intraoperative, postoperative), and no named blood products, drugs, or hemostatic/blood-conservation agents such as tranexamic acid or iron. It does not quantify effect sizes, define "advanced age" numerically, quantify "blood loss," or state that transfusion is causal rather than associated. It also offers no screening, consent, monitoring, or SSI-prophylaxis protocols, and no guidance for open or vaginal approaches.

title: Naloxone Reversal and Prolonged Opioid Monitoring
summary:
This small community represents the theme of opioid toxicity recognition and reversal in the perioperative setting, centred on two linked ideas: pharmacologic rescue with naloxone, and the duration of surveillance required after that rescue.

The first recommendation is that naloxone treats opioid toxicity, with the explicit condition that a second dose may be required because naloxone's duration of action is shorter than that of some opioids. Practically, this means a patient who responds to an initial dose can re-narcotise as naloxone wears off while the causative opioid is still active, so staff must be prepared to redose rather than assume one dose is definitive.

The second recommendation is that prolonged monitoring is indicated to detect (ongoing or recurrent) opioid toxicity, with the population specified as people who have overdosed on long-acting opioids — the example given is fentanyl patches. This is the more population-specific of the two statements: it names a mechanism of prolonged exposure (transdermal/long-acting formulations) that justifies extending observation beyond the immediate reversal window.

Only one guideline body contributes here: OpenRN (Nursing Pharmacology / Textbook 2, p788) supplies both relations. There is therefore no inter-body disagreement to reconcile, and no point where a second corpus source is more or less specific; the two statements are internally consistent and complementary, one addressing drug redosing and the other addressing observation duration for long-acting agents.

What this community does NOT establish is substantial and should be flagged for local protocol work: no naloxone dose, route, concentration, or dosing interval is given; no definition of "prolonged" monitoring in hours; no monitoring parameters or thresholds (respiratory rate, sedation score, SpO2, capnography); no criteria for escalation, infusion versus intermittent dosing, or safe discharge; no specific gynecologic or perioperative population, age group, or comorbidity qualifiers; and no guidance on naloxone-precipitated withdrawal or on opioid-tolerant patients.

title: Intraoperative Antibiotic Redosing in Prolonged Surgery
summary:
This community represents a single, narrowly scoped theme: intraoperative redosing of surgical antibiotic prophylaxis when an operation is prolonged. Both relations converge on the same clinical target — the prolonged operation — and describe when an additional or repeat dose of the prophylactic agent is indicated.

The first recommendation states that additional antibiotic doses apply to prolonged operations, with the population and conditions specified as obese patients and patients with severe blood loss; that is, the trigger for extra dosing is the combination of prolonged operative time, severe intraoperative blood loss, and obesity. The second recommendation adds timing specificity: a repeat antibiotic dose in prolonged operations should be given after an interval of 1–2 times the half-life of the chosen medication. Together they give quality-improvement leads a two-part rule — identify the at-risk case (long case, obese patient, significant haemorrhage) and time the repeat dose to the pharmacokinetics of the specific agent selected.

Only one guideline body contributes here: the ERAS Society (ERAS_Society T1, p1). Both statements come from the same source and page, so there is no cross-body disagreement, no competing threshold, and no opportunity to compare specificity between organisations. Within this single source, the "repeat antibiotic dose" statement is the more operationally specific of the two because it supplies a timing rule, whereas the "additional doses" statement is more specific about which patients qualify.

What this community does NOT establish: it names no specific antibiotic agent, dose, or route; it gives no numeric definition of "prolonged operation" (no minute or hour threshold), no BMI or weight cut-off defining obesity, and no volume threshold defining severe blood loss. It says nothing about timing of the initial preoperative dose, about postoperative continuation or discontinuation of prophylaxis, about surgical-site infection outcomes, allergy alternatives, or documentation and audit measures. Local protocols would need to supply agent-specific half-life values and operational definitions before this guidance can be implemented at the bedside.
key_entities: 1–2 times the half-life of the chosen medication

title: Surgical Antibiotic Prophylaxis Timing and Indications
summary: This community centres on preoperative antimicrobial prophylaxis — chiefly its timing relative to skin incision or umbilical cord clamping — and the infections it prevents. Core recommendation: prophylaxis should be given so a bactericidal serum and tissue concentration exists when the incision is made (CDC T1 p3, p13); operationally, within 60 minutes before incision (AUGS T2 p7; WHO T1 pp18, 60, 67, 117) and stopped within 24 hours of the end of surgery (WHO T1 p60). Drug-specific detail: cefazolin, adults, full therapeutic dose 1–2 g no more than 30 minutes before incision (CDC T1 p13); vancomycin infusion completed within 1 hour of incision (WHO T1 pp60, 67). Total joint arthroplasty is tightened to within 30 minutes of incision (WHO T1 p60). Populations and indications: routine use in clean-contaminated cases, considered in clean cases (WHO T1 p67); applies to hysterectomy and to both elective and non-elective caesarean section (WHO T1 p60); a single dose for women undergoing manual removal of the placenta (WHO T1 p10). Benefits include prevention of surgical site infection (with an antibiotic active against the bacteria expected for the procedure), postoperative infection after surgical or dental procedures, and — in caesarean section — post-caesarean infection, endometritis, wound infection and other infectious complications. WHO notes prophylaxis outperforms placebo whether given in the hour before incision or after cord clamping, but favours before skin incision (WHO T1 pp18, 60). Divergence: CDC advises giving the agent immediately after cord clamping in high-risk caesarean section (CDC T1 p21), and WHO also records a single dose after cord clamp/cut per its own guidance, so pre-incision versus post-clamp timing is not fully harmonised. A distinct, non-antibiotic item is intramuscular oxytocin for vaginal birth, given with delivery of the anterior shoulder or immediately after birth before cord clamping (RCOG T1 p11). Harms: incorrect or prolonged courses increase antibiotic-resistant and resistant bacteria (WHO T1 pp60, 211). Not established: specific agents/doses for gynaecologic or obstetric cases, weight-based or redosing rules, penicillin-allergy pathways, duration beyond 24 hours, or nursing documentation/audit measures.

title: Continuous Uterine Massage After Prophylactic Oxytocin
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused theme in third-stage labour management: whether continuous uterine massage should be used as a postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) prevention intervention in women who have already received prophylactic oxytocin. All four relations converge on one recommendation drawn from WHO Tier 1 guidance (pages 10, 19, 21): continuous uterine massage is NOT recommended as an intervention to prevent PPH in women who have received prophylactic oxytocin. The relation set expresses this both as a negated prevention claim (continuous uterine massage 'prevents' PPH only with the qualifier 'not recommended') and as an explicit contraindication/incompatibility between continuous uterine massage and prophylactic oxytocin (and oxytocin generally) when massage is used for PPH prophylaxis. The population is consistently and narrowly defined: women who have received prophylactic oxytocin. The condition is equally specific: the massage is being applied as a preventive intervention against PPH. For educators and QI leads, the practical teaching point is that routine, continuous fundal massage adds no recommended value once uterotonic prophylaxis with oxytocin has been given, and should not be built into standard post-delivery care bundles for that population.

Only one guideline body contributes here: WHO (Tier 1), appearing three times across pages 10, 19 and 21 with essentially identical wording, so there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile. The pages differ only in phrasing granularity ('when used as an intervention to prevent postpartum haemorrhage' on p19 versus 'as an intervention to prevent postpartum haemorrhage' on p10 and p21), and p10 uniquely names 'oxytocin' as well as 'prophylactic oxytocin'.

The community does NOT establish: any dose, route, or timing for prophylactic oxytocin; any threshold blood-loss volume defining PPH; whether uterine massage is appropriate as treatment of established PPH or as assessment of uterine tone; guidance for women who did NOT receive prophylactic oxytocin; alternative uterotonics; or any nursing monitoring frequency, staffing, or documentation requirements.
key_entities: women who have received prophylactic oxytocin

title: Bleeding Risk Assessment, Prophylaxis and Reversal
summary:
This community centres on bleeding as both a hazard of thromboprophylaxis and an outcome requiring structured assessment, monitoring and reversal. NICE contributes the assessment architecture: bleeding risk assessment for all medical patients and VTE risk assessment for all surgical and trauma patients, both done as soon as possible after admission or by the time of first consultant review; combined VTE and bleeding risk assessment for all acute psychiatric patients on admission using a published tool. Reassessment intervals are population-specific: daily in critical care, more than once daily if the patient's condition is changing rapidly; whenever clinical condition changes and at least daily in serious or major trauma; and at 24 hours after initial admission in spinal injury. NICE also warns that pharmacological prophylaxis increases bleeding risk in patients admitted at increased VTE risk, and that pharmacological thromboprophylaxis given unnecessarily exposes patients to bleeding without benefit. RCOG is more drug-specific for obstetric care: low molecular weight heparin increases bleeding risk (likely under 2% with prophylactic doses) in pregnant and postpartum women; unfractionated heparin carries greater bleeding risk than LMWH in obstetric patients; dextran increases bleeding risk. For reversal and monitoring, RCOG specifies protamine sulfate to prevent bleeding in women on subcutaneous unfractionated heparin when the aPTT is markedly prolonged near delivery, to treat haemorrhage in women receiving unfractionated heparin, and partially to treat LMWH-associated bleeding in some patients — noting it does not fully reverse the anti-Xa effect; aPTT monitoring applies to therapeutic subcutaneous unfractionated heparin if spontaneous labour occurs. WHO adds oral anticoagulants continued beyond planned duration as a bleeding risk, and surgical temporizing measures including intra-abdominal packing during damage control surgery to allow fluid resuscitation to catch up. ERAS links hypothermia to bleeding; OpenRN flags procedural sources — colonoscopy (rare), incorrectly prepared or injected parenteral medication, and arterial sampling versus venipuncture.

The community does not establish numeric bleeding-risk thresholds, protamine dosing, specific risk-assessment tool names, prophylaxis dosing regimens, or outcome data comparing assessment strategies.
key_entities: venous thromboembolism and bleeding risk assessment

title: Coagulation testing and FFP in PPH
summary:
This community represents the coagulation-monitoring and plasma-replacement thread of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) management: using laboratory clotting tests to detect and track haemostatic impairment, and using fresh frozen plasma (FFP) to correct it. All three relations are drawn from a single source, RCOG Table 1, page 20, so the theme reflects one guideline body's position rather than a cross-body consensus.

Main recommendations, with populations and conditions:

1) Detection — PT/APTT testing detects haemostatic impairment in women with postpartum haemorrhage. The stated interpretive threshold is that a PT or APTT greater than 1.5 times normal indicates severe and established impairment.

2) Monitoring — repeated PT/APTT testing is indicated for women with PPH whose initial PT/APTT is normal, specifically when bleeding persists. Normal early results therefore do not close the assessment; serial testing is the recommended safeguard.

3) Treatment — fresh frozen plasma treats haemostatic impairment in women with PPH when haemorrhage is ongoing and the most recent PT/APTT results are prolonged. The dose given is 12–15 ml/kg, titrated with the aim of maintaining PT/APTT below 1.5 times normal. Note the internal coherence: the same 1.5 × normal figure serves both as the diagnostic threshold for established impairment and as the therapeutic target for FFP.

Contributing bodies and differences: only RCOG contributes here (RCOG Table 1, p20). Because there is a single contributor, no inter-guideline disagreement or difference in specificity can be identified from this community; the RCOG entry is itself specific about population, trigger condition, dose and target.

What this community does NOT establish: it says nothing about fibrinogen or cryoprecipitate, platelet counts or platelet transfusion, tranexamic acid, red cell transfusion ratios, or point-of-care viscoelastic testing. It does not specify how frequently repeated PT/APTT should be performed, a turnaround-time expectation, when to give FFP empirically before results return, an upper limit on FFP volume, transfusion-reaction or fluid-overload monitoring, or any outcome data supporting the 1.5 × normal target. Populations outside PPH (e.g. non-obstetric surgical bleeding) are not addressed.

title: Suspected Pulmonary Embolism in Pregnancy
summary: This community centres on recognition, imaging and anticoagulation for suspected/confirmed pulmonary embolism (PE) in pregnancy and the puerperium, with peripheral links to sepsis chest imaging and perioperative VTE prophylaxis. RCOG (T1) dominates. Treatment: low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) is commenced immediately in pregnant women with clinically suspected PE until objective testing excludes it, unless strongly contraindicated (p11, p29); for confirmed DVT or PE, therapeutic subcutaneous LMWH continues for the remainder of pregnancy and at least 6 weeks postnatally, minimum 3 months total (p17). Anticoagulant treatment is continued until PE is definitively excluded (p2, p7). Thrombolytic therapy is reserved for severe pulmonary thromboembolism with haemodynamic compromise (p14). Temporary inferior vena cava filters prevent PE in iliac vein VTE in the peripartum period (p4, p17). ERAS Society adds pre-operative initiation of heparin to prevent PE after cancer surgery (p5). Risk factors: obesity (including overweight/obese women receiving LMWH doses appropriate for 50–90 kg), caesarean section (deaths 2–6 weeks post-delivery), antiphospholipid syndrome, untreated DVT, and IVF conception (VTE risk doubled overall, four-fold in the first trimester). Diagnostics: ECG (abnormal in only 41% of women with acute PE) and CXR (normal in over half of proven cases; abnormal features include atelectasis, effusion, focal opacities, regional oligaemia, pulmonary oedema) are first-line; CXR should precede decisions on further testing, since a normal CXR before V/Q scanning improves the likelihood of a definitive result. V/Q scan is used when there are no DVT signs; CTPA is preferred when the CXR is abnormal. V/Q carries a slightly higher childhood cancer risk and CTPA a slightly higher maternal breast cancer risk, both absolute risks very small. Bilateral compression duplex leg ultrasound is useful only if positive. Low-dose perfusion scan, echocardiography and angiography are also listed for antenatal PE. NICE contributes CXR to identify infection source in suspected sepsis and ECG only for ASA grade 2 patients with cardiovascular, renal or diabetes comorbidity before intermediate surgery; OpenRN covers CXR for suspected lower respiratory tract infection and ECG monitoring for dysrhythmia during airway suctioning. Not established: LMWH dosing regimens by weight band, diagnostic thresholds/D-dimer, filter removal timing, or gynecologic-surgery-specific PE pathways.

title: Deep Abdominal Palpation Contraindicated With Pulsatile Mass
summary:
Clinical theme: safe technique and sequencing of the abdominal assessment, specifically the safety stop that prevents deep palpation when inspection has already raised concern for a vascular or otherwise unstable abdomen. Both relations in this community converge on a single, narrow rule.

Main recommendations: Deep palpation of the abdomen is contraindicated when a pulsatile abdominal mass is present. The trigger for withholding deep palpation is what the nurse observes during inspection — the first relation states the contraindication applies if pulsatile masses, distension, rigidity, or other indications of suspected abdominal problems are noted on inspection; the second states it applies when a pulsatile mass is noted on inspection of the abdomen. The two statements are consistent, but the first is broader and more specific about the qualifying findings, extending the stop rule beyond pulsatility alone to distension, rigidity, and any other sign suggesting an abdominal problem. The implied sequence is inspection first, then a decision about whether deep palpation may proceed.

Contributing bodies: both statements derive from a single source, OpenRN (Nursing Skills, Volume 2, p. 1183); there is no second guideline body in this community and therefore no cross-body disagreement to reconcile. The only variation is in breadth of the triggering findings within the same page.

What this community does NOT establish: it names no population (no age, pregnancy, perioperative, or gynecologic-specific qualifiers), no perioperative timing (pre-, intra-, or postoperative), and no drugs, doses, or thresholds. It does not define mass size, pulsation criteria, or any measurement cutoff. It does not state a diagnosis (e.g., abdominal aortic aneurysm is not named), does not describe the harm expected from deep palpation, and does not specify escalation steps, imaging, provider notification, or documentation requirements. It is silent on whether light palpation, auscultation, or percussion remain permissible, and offers no guidance on reassessment intervals or on management once the contraindication is identified.

title: Pulse oximetry monitoring and cardiac arrest prevention
summary:
This community centres on continuous oxygenation monitoring as the pivot between early detection of hypoxia and prevention or management of cardiac arrest, together with the procedural and medication hazards that can precipitate arrest.

WHO (T1 pp.22, 25) is the most explicit on monitoring: pulse oximetry should be used for all patients undergoing anaesthesia to monitor for and prevent hypoxia, to detect and prevent cardiac arrest, to prevent anaesthetic mishap in surgical patients, and to prevent hypoxic brain damage. Intraoperatively it is applied continuously during surgery, monitoring hypoxia (as a secondary system) and providing continuous monitoring of both tissue perfusion and heart rate to flag inadequate tissue perfusion. OpenRN (T2) supplies concrete bedside thresholds and workflow: oxygen saturation less than 95% detects compromised respiration (p.616); pulse oximetry is gathered as a supply before tracheostomy suctioning (p.1307), and a repeat suctioning pass is timed only after pulse oximetry returns to baseline and if clinically indicated (p.1307).

Risk sources for arrest named here are procedural and pharmacological: nasotracheal suctioning increases risk of cardiac arrest (OpenRN p.1293), and potassium infusion increases risk of cardiac arrest in patients receiving intravenous electrolytes if administered too rapidly (OpenRN p.1329).

For treatment, CPR is indicated for pulselessness in a person with suspected opioid overdose if the individual becomes pulseless (OpenRN p.788), and RCOG (T1 p.14) specifies CPR for cardiac arrest in pregnant or puerperal women, performed with the woman in a left lateral tilt — the only obstetric-specific modification in the community.

The bodies are complementary rather than conflicting: WHO frames system-level anaesthetic safety, OpenRN gives skill-level thresholds and timings, RCOG adds the obstetric positioning caveat.

Not established: no oximetry thresholds for anaesthesia (only the <95% respiratory figure), no safe potassium infusion rate or concentration, no suction duration/pressure limits, no naloxone dosing, no compression rates or ratios, no degree of left lateral tilt, and no gynecologic-surgery-specific monitoring standard.

title: Wrist Band Recheck Prevents Identification Errors
summary:
This community represents a single, narrowly scoped patient-identification safety theme: the act of rechecking the patient's wrist identification band as a barrier against two distinct downstream errors — blood grouping (typing) error and specimen labelling error. Both relations are drawn from the same source, WHO Tool 1, page 81, and both are of the PREVENTS type, framing wrist-band verification as an error-prevention control rather than a diagnostic or therapeutic act.

The operative recommendation is therefore simple and repeatable: recheck the wrist identification band as the verification step whenever blood is grouped and whenever specimens are labelled, so that the sample and the resulting label or blood group result are tied to the correct patient. In a perioperative gynecologic nursing context this maps naturally onto pre-transfusion group-and-save/crossmatch sampling and onto labelling of surgical or laboratory specimens, but the graph itself does not narrow the recommendation further.

Guideline contribution is not diverse: WHO is the only contributing body in this community, and it supplies both edges. There is consequently no point of disagreement, no competing recommendation, and no instance of one body being more specific than another — the theme rests entirely on WHO Tool 1 p81, and any perceived consensus should not be over-read as multi-body corroboration.

Importantly, the community does not establish: (1) any population restriction — no age, parity, procedure type, emergency versus elective status, or gynecologic diagnosis is attached to either relation; (2) any condition, trigger threshold, or timing — it does not state how many times to recheck, at what point relative to venepuncture, specimen collection, or transfusion, or who must perform or countersign the check; (3) any effect size, error rate, or evidence grade for the preventive claim; (4) any alternative or adjunctive identifiers (barcode scanning, two-person verification, verbal name/date-of-birth confirmation) or what to do when a wrist band is absent, illegible, or removed for surgical access; and (5) any linkage to transfusion reaction outcomes, mislabelled-specimen rejection pathways, or documentation and incident-reporting requirements.

title: Blood products and rFVIIa in PPH
summary:
This community covers haemostatic resuscitation for postpartum haemorrhage (PPH), specifically the sequencing of blood transfusion before consideration of recombinant factor VIIa (rFVIIa). Two bodies contribute: RCOG (Tier 1, pp. 15, 22, 41) and WHO (Tier 1, p. 19).

Transfusion: RCOG states blood transfusion treats PPH in women with major obstetric haemorrhage or clinical shock, using O RhD-negative or group-specific blood as part of resuscitation (p41), and that blood should be transfused as soon as available if necessary, with the clinical picture — not a single laboratory trigger — as the main determinant of the decision (p15).

rFVIIa: RCOG (p22) positions rFVIIa for women with PPH in whom uterotonics have failed to arrest bleeding, where it reduces the need for second-line therapies; effective resuscitation towards normal physiology is a stated prerequisite. Its timing depends on prior management: rFVIIa is considered only after blood products and management of uterine atony, and is temporarily contraindicated until adequate blood/blood product administration and management of uterine atony have been undertaken. In women with life-threatening PPH, rFVIIa must not delay or substitute for a life-saving procedure such as embolisation, surgery or transfer to a referral centre. Off-label use in patients treated for life-threatening haemorrhage increases the risk of arterial thromboembolic events.

Differences in specificity: WHO is more restrictive and narrow — rFVIIa use "should be limited to women with specific haematological indications." RCOG is more operationally detailed, defining the sequence (blood products and atony management first), the physiological prerequisite, the uterotonic-failure population, the thromboembolic harm, and the rule against delaying definitive procedures.

Not established here: no transfusion thresholds (haemoglobin, fibrinogen, platelet counts), no rFVIIa dose, route, repeat dosing or weight-based regimen, no ratios or protocols for red cells, plasma, cryoprecipitate or platelets, no tranexamic acid or other uterotonic/haemostatic agents, no monitoring or nursing observation parameters, and no quantified magnitude of thromboembolic risk or benefit.

title: Preoperative Dexamethasone for PONV Prophylaxis
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused theme: preoperative dexamethasone as pharmacologic prophylaxis against postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) in women having reconstructive vaginal surgery, situated within enhanced recovery pathways for gynecologic surgery.

Main recommendations: (1) Dexamethasone applies to reconstructive vaginal surgery in women undergoing vaginal reconstructive procedures, with the timing specified as preoperative administration (AUGS T2 p10, p11, p14). (2) Administered preoperatively, dexamethasone prevents postoperative nausea and vomiting in this same population (AUGS T2 p11, p14), and is separately linked to prevention of postoperative nausea specifically (AUGS T2 p10). (3) More broadly, dexamethasone applies to gynecologic surgery when used as part of an enhanced recovery programme (ERAS Society T1 p4).

Contributing bodies and their differences: two sources contribute. AUGS (urogynecologic guidance, pages 10, 11 and 14) is the more specific contributor — it names the population precisely (women undergoing reconstructive/vaginal reconstructive surgery), states the condition (preoperative administration), and states the outcome (prevention of PONV, and nausea alone at p10). The ERAS Society (T1 p4) is broader and less population-specific: it places dexamethasone in gynecologic surgery generally, with the qualifying condition being that it is delivered as part of an enhanced recovery programme, and does not itself attach a PONV-prevention claim in these relations. The two are complementary rather than conflicting: ERAS provides the programmatic context, AUGS the procedure-specific PONV indication. Note a minor inconsistency in outcome wording across AUGS pages ("postoperative nausea and vomiting" vs "postoperative nausea").

What this community does NOT establish: no dose, no route, no exact timing interval relative to induction or incision, and no frequency or duration of therapy. It specifies no combination or comparison with other antiemetics, no contraindications, no glycemic, wound-healing or infection safety cautions, no monitoring requirements, and no thresholds or risk-scoring to select candidates. It does not address non-vaginal or non-gynecologic surgery, nor rescue treatment of established PONV.

title: Substance Use and Nutritional Risk
summary:
Clinical theme: This is a small, single-source community linking recreational drug or alcohol use to nutritional compromise. It represents the substance-use component of perioperative nutritional risk screening — the recognition that patients who use alcohol or recreational drugs arrive for gynecologic surgery at elevated risk of being nutritionally depleted, by two distinct mechanisms.

Main content and populations: Two relations are asserted, both from the same source (OpenRN Nursing Fundamentals/Management text, T2 p1015). Recreational drug or alcohol use increases the risk of (1) insufficient nutrient intake and (2) impaired nutrient absorption. Notably, neither relation carries a specific population qualifier, condition, threshold, quantity of alcohol or drug, named substance, or timing (e.g., no preoperative abstinence interval, no screening window, no defined 'units per week'). The practical teaching point for educators is therefore conceptual: substance use should prompt nutritional assessment because both the intake side (appetite suppression, calories displaced by alcohol, disorganised eating) and the absorption side (gastrointestinal/mucosal effects) can be affected — but the guideline text as captured here does not operationalise this further.

Contributing bodies and differences: Only one guideline body contributes — OpenRN — and both edges come from the same page, so there is no inter-body agreement or disagreement to adjudicate, and no instance of one body being more specific than another. Any perceived authority here rests on a single foundational nursing text rather than a specialty perioperative society.

What this community does NOT establish: it does not name specific drugs or alcohol thresholds; it does not specify screening tools, laboratory markers, or nutrient deficiencies (e.g., thiamine, folate, protein); it does not address perioperative or gynecologic populations explicitly; it says nothing about interventions, supplementation, referral to dietetics, surgical timing, withdrawal management, or postoperative outcomes such as wound healing or infection. It also does not quantify risk magnitude. Quality-improvement leads should treat this as a prompt to seek more specific, population-anchored guidance before building a screening protocol.

title: Route-Specific Contraindications: Thrombocytopenia and Rectal Administration
summary:
This community centres on situations where a medication route or agent must be withheld because of patient-specific vulnerabilities, with thrombocytopenia acting as the shared node linking anticoagulant and rectal-route cautions.

Two distinct recommendation streams appear. First, RCOG (Tier 1, p27) advises that low molecular weight heparin be temporarily contraindicated in women whose platelet count is fewer than 75 x 10^9/L; thromboprophylaxis is delayed while the platelet count remains low, implying reassessment and resumption once counts recover rather than permanent avoidance. Second, OpenRN (Tier 2) sets out contraindications to rectal medication administration: it is contraindicated after rectal surgery and after bowel surgery (p854), in patients with low platelet count (p854), and in patients with certain cardiac conditions (p905). OpenRN also notes that rectal administration increases the risk of bradycardia in some patients if unintended vagal stimulation occurs (p905), which explains the cardiac caution and supports monitoring pulse during and after suppository or enema administration.

Contributing bodies differ in scope and specificity. RCOG is the only source supplying a numeric threshold (platelets <75 x 10^9/L) and a temporal qualifier (delay while low), and it is population-specific to women receiving thromboprophylaxis. OpenRN is broader and route-focused, applying to general patient populations, but leaves "low platelet count" undefined numerically and describes "certain cardiac conditions" without naming them. The two sources do not conflict; they converge on thrombocytopenia as a bleeding-risk trigger reached from different directions (systemic anticoagulation versus mucosal trauma from rectal insertion).

The community does not establish: any platelet threshold for withholding rectal administration; which specific cardiac conditions preclude the rectal route; how long after rectal or bowel surgery the route remains contraindicated; alternative routes or agents to substitute; the platelet value or timeframe at which LMWH may be safely restarted; monitoring parameters or frequency; or whether the bradycardia risk warrants pre-procedure ECG or continuous observation. No dosing, gynecologic procedure-specific guidance, or outcome data are included.

title: FFP use in postpartum haemorrhage
summary:
This community centres on fresh frozen plasma (FFP) as the coagulation-directed component of transfusion in major obstetric haemorrhage, plus the emerging role of fibrinogen infusion. All relations derive from a single guideline body, RCOG (Tier 1, pp. 16-21); no other body contributes, so there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile, though specificity varies by page (p16 states the general principle, p18 and p20 give doses and thresholds).

Key recommendations: FFP treats clotting abnormality in women with major obstetric haemorrhage as part of blood products given during resuscitation (p41). In women with postpartum haemorrhage, FFP treats haemostatic impairment when haemorrhage is ongoing and the last PT/APTT are prolonged, dosed at 12-15 ml/kg, aiming to keep PT/APTT below 1.5 times normal (p20). Timing depends on haemostatic testing and whether bleeding continues (p16); where haemostatic results are unavailable and bleeding continues, FFP is given after 4 units of red blood cells at 12-15 ml/kg until test results are known (p16, p18, p20). Earlier-than-standard FFP is indicated for women with placental abruption or amniotic fluid embolism, because these situations are associated with early coagulopathy (p20).

Risks to teach: early FFP administration increases the risk of transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI); when PT/APTT exceeds 1.5 times normal and a larger FFP volume is required, transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) risk rises (p20). Fibrinogen infusion is described as preventing TACO in women with postpartum haemorrhage, but explicitly on observational evidence only, with RCTs required (p21).

What is not established: no cryoprecipitate, platelet, tranexamic acid or factor concentrate thresholds appear here; no paediatric, antenatal or non-obstetric populations; no monitoring intervals, repeat-dosing rules, or explicit fibrinogen thresholds/doses. The fibrinogen-for-TACO link is unproven by trial evidence, and no comparative effectiveness between FFP and fibrinogen is asserted. Nursing actions (consent, warming, infusion rates) are not specified.

title: Red Cell Antibodies and Transfusion Safety
summary:
This community represents a narrow but high-consequence transfusion-safety theme: the presence of red cell (atypical/irregular) antibodies in women who may require blood transfusion in the perioperative or obstetric setting, and the laboratory step that mitigates the resulting risk.

Two relations define the theme. First, red cell antibodies INCREASE the risk of haemolytic transfusion reaction, with the population explicitly scoped to mothers receiving transfusion. This frames antibody status as a risk marker to be identified before blood is given, not an incidental laboratory finding. Second, selection of antigen-negative red cell units for cross-matching PREVENTS haemolytic transfusion reaction; the population is women with red cell antibodies, and the stated condition is that the units selected are negative for the relevant antigen. The preventive claim therefore holds only when the specific implicated antigen is identified and matched against — antigen-negative selection is conditional, not generic.
