The practical implication for education and QI work is a two-step pathway: detect and characterise red cell antibodies in women who may be transfused, then ensure the transfusion laboratory cross-matches units negative for the relevant antigen. Both nodes converge on the same adverse outcome, haemolytic transfusion reaction, making that outcome the natural audit endpoint.

Only one guideline body contributes here: RCOG (both relations from RCOG Topic 1, page 18). There is consequently no inter-guideline disagreement to reconcile, but also no corroboration or alternative framing from other bodies in this corpus; the obstetric ('mothers', 'women') framing is RCOG-specific and is not generalised to all surgical patients.

The community does NOT establish: any antibody screening timing or interval, gestational or preoperative thresholds, which antibody specificities matter most, how long antigen-negative provision takes or how to manage urgent/emergency transfusion when antigen-negative units are unavailable, anti-D or immunoglobulin prophylaxis, any drug therapy, monitoring or recognition criteria for a haemolytic reaction, treatment once a reaction occurs, or effect sizes and incidence rates.
key_entities: selection of antigen-negative red cell units for cross-matching

title: Regional Anaesthesia Timing With Anticoagulation
summary: This community centres on regional (neuraxial) anaesthesia as both a therapeutic tool and a bleeding-risk decision point, with timing dictated by concurrent anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy. Benefits: RCOG-adjacent bodies aside, ERAS Society notes regional anaesthesia added to general anaesthesia prevents postoperative nausea and vomiting; WHO recommends it, if possible, as an adjustment to the anaesthetic approach in patients at high risk of a difficult airway (e.g. Mallampati 3 or 4) to prevent airway disaster; NICE states it can prevent VTE in individual surgical patients when used in addition to other VTE prophylaxis methods, taking account of patient preference and suitability. Timing/contraindications: RCOG is the most specific. For women on therapeutic LMWH, regional anaesthesia should not be undertaken until at least 24 hours after the last dose (stated as both a timing dependency and a temporary contraindication, pp5, 19, 20). For pregnant women on fondaparinux sodium, 36–42 hours should pass after the previous dose. Intravenous unfractionated heparin should be stopped 6 hours before induction of labour or regional anaesthesia. Regional anaesthesia is contraindicated in women receiving danaparoid for thromboprophylaxis because danaparoid's half-life is long (24 hours); danaparoid itself is used to prevent VTE in pregnant women intolerant of heparin, with persistent allergic skin reaction, or with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, i.e. when heparins cannot be used. NICE frames the same issue generically: pharmacological VTE prophylaxis timing depends on regional anaesthesia to minimise epidural haematoma risk, and for patients using or planned to use antiplatelet or anticoagulant agents, clinicians should refer to the summary of product characteristics for safety and timing rather than a stated interval. What is not established: no restart intervals after the block or catheter removal, no dosing regimens, no guidance for prophylactic (as opposed to therapeutic) LMWH intervals, no thresholds for platelet count or renal function, no monitoring or epidural-haematoma detection protocols, and no gynecologic-surgery-specific (as opposed to obstetric) timings.

title: ERAS Perioperative Care in Gynecologic Oncology Surgery
summary:
This community represents ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) perioperative bundle elements for gynecologic oncology surgery, spanning infection prevention, device/drain minimisation, and early return to oral intake.

Infection prevention: a first-generation cephalosporin should be administered within 60 minutes before skin incision. Skin cleansing with chlorhexidine-alcohol is preferred over aqueous povidone-iodine. Hair removal should be avoided unless mandatory; when it is mandatory, clipping (rather than shaving), performed in the operating room immediately prior to surgery, is recommended for surgical patients requiring hair removal and is stated to prevent surgical site infection.

Devices and drains: an indwelling urinary catheter should be used only for a short period, preferably removed within 24 hours postoperatively. Routine peritoneal drainage is not recommended, including in patients undergoing lymphadenectomy or bowel surgery.

Nutrition: patients undergoing gynecologic/oncology surgery should receive a regular diet within the first 24 hours after surgery; this is explicitly placed in the postoperative phase and is the operational definition of "early feeding" in this corpus (regular diet within the first 24 hours).

Guideline contribution: all relations derive from a single body, the ERAS Society (Table 1, pages 1, 2, 3 and 10), so no inter-society disagreement can be assessed. Internal granularity differs slightly: the early-diet recommendation appears both with an explicit population ("patients undergoing gynecologic/oncology surgery", p3) and without one (p2), and only the p3 statement anchors it to the postoperative phase; p10 restates it under the label "early feeding."

What this community does NOT establish: no antibiotic dose, redosing interval, or duration; no alternative agents for penicillin/cephalosporin allergy; no criteria or protocol for catheter removal beyond the <24 h preference, and no guidance on selective (non-routine) drain use or removal timing; no diet-advancement steps, tolerance thresholds, or management of nausea/ileus; no mechanical or pharmacologic thromboprophylaxis, analgesia, fluid, glycemic, temperature or mobilisation elements; no outcome magnitudes, evidence grades, or recommendation strengths; and no pediatric, obstetric, emergency or non-gynecologic populations.

title: Remote assessment detecting sepsis risk factors
summary:
This small community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: the use of remote assessment (telephone or other non-face-to-face contact) as a screening step to detect factors that increase a person's risk of sepsis, and the use of that information to decide whether a face-to-face assessment is needed and how urgently it should happen.

The relations captured are two closely parallel statements, both drawn from NICE (Tier 1 material, p6). In both, the population is people being assessed remotely (people undergoing remote assessment), and the condition attached is identical: the detection applies when deciding whether to offer a face-to-face assessment and on the urgency of that assessment. One relation frames the target as a 'risk factor for sepsis' and the other as a 'factor that increases risk of sepsis' — effectively the same construct expressed two ways, so the practical recommendation is that remote assessors should actively elicit and act on sepsis risk factors as part of triage, rather than treating remote contact as a passive information exchange.

Only one guideline body contributes here: NICE. There is therefore no cross-body disagreement to reconcile, and no point at which one organisation is more specific than another; the duplication of the two relations reflects wording variation within the same NICE source rather than competing guidance. For a nurse educator or QI lead, the teachable message is that remote triage pathways need a structured prompt for sepsis risk factors linked explicitly to a decision about face-to-face review and its urgency.

Importantly, this community does NOT establish which specific risk factors count (for example age, immunosuppression, recent surgery, indwelling devices, pregnancy or postpartum status), nor any numerical thresholds, physiological trigger values, early-warning scores, time targets for the face-to-face assessment, escalation routes, antibiotic choices or timings, or perioperative gynecologic-specific criteria. It also does not define who performs the remote assessment or what documentation is required. Those details must be sought from the fuller NICE sepsis guidance and local protocols.
key_entities: factor that increases risk of sepsis

title: Remote Infection Control and Surgical Prophylaxis
summary:
This community represents the theme of preventing surgical site infection (SSI) through two linked levers: eradicating infection at body sites remote from the incision before elective surgery, and delivering surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis around the operation itself. All four relations derive from a single guideline body, the CDC (CDC T1, pages 7, 11 and 19); no other guideline corpus contributes here, so there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile — but also no external corroboration.

Main recommendations and their attached populations/conditions: (1) A remote site infection increases the risk of SSI, qualified to patients undergoing certain kinds of operations (CDC T1 p7) — the guideline does not name which operations. (2) Consequently, elective operation is temporarily contraindicated in patients with remote site infections, with the condition that surgery is deferred until the infection has resolved (CDC T1 p19); the contraindication is explicitly temporary, not absolute. (3) Surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis applies to elective operations, specifically those in which skin incisions are closed in the operating room (CDC T1 p11). (4) Surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis prevents SSI in surgical patients, but only to the extent that it reduces intraoperative contamination; the guideline states it does not pertain to postoperative contamination (CDC T1 p11).

What this community does NOT establish: it names no specific antimicrobial agents, doses, redosing intervals, timing relative to incision, or duration of prophylaxis; it sets no thresholds (e.g., temperature, white cell count, or culture criteria) for judging a remote infection 'resolved'; it does not define which operations carry the elevated remote-infection risk; and it says nothing about emergency or non-elective surgery, wounds left open, obstetric or gynecologic procedures specifically, patient comorbidities, or postoperative wound care. Educators should therefore pair this material with agent-specific prophylaxis protocols and local preoperative screening criteria.

title: Contaminated Item Removal Prevents Environmental Contamination
summary:
This community represents a single, narrow infection-prevention theme: the technique used to remove and contain contaminated items at the point of care, so that neither the environment nor the wearer's clothing/skin becomes a vector. Two practices are captured, both drawn from OpenRN Nursing Skills (Open Resources for Nursing, Volume 2).

Main recommendations: (1) Removal of the isolation gown prevents environmental contamination, conditioned on the gown being removed BEFORE leaving the patient room (OpenRN T2 p203). The same action prevents contamination of the wearer's clothing or skin, conditioned on it being removed 'in a manner that prevents contamination' — i.e., technique, not merely timing, is the operative variable. (2) During dressing changes, wrapping the old inner dressing inside the glove as the glove is removed prevents environmental contamination, qualified as 'if feasible' (OpenRN T2 p1168). Both recommendations share the mechanism of containing the contaminated surface within the item being doffed, and both are stated at a general nursing-practice level.

Contributing bodies: OpenRN is the only guideline source represented here; there is no second body to compare or contrast, so no inter-guideline disagreement can be identified. Internally, the gown guidance is more specific than the dressing guidance: it names a hard spatial/temporal threshold (before leaving the room), whereas the dressing guidance is softened by a feasibility caveat ('if feasible'), implying clinician judgement when wound size, drainage volume or dressing configuration makes glove-wrapping impractical.

What this community does NOT establish: no population is specified — nothing here is restricted to, or validated in, gynecologic surgical patients, perioperative phases, or any age, immune-status or isolation-precaution category. It does not state which isolation precautions (contact, droplet, airborne) trigger gown use, the doffing sequence relative to gloves, masks or eye protection, hand hygiene requirements after removal, waste-stream or receptacle placement, outer-dressing handling, or any outcome data on infection rates, colonisation or compliance. No drugs, antiseptics, doses or timings beyond 'before leaving the room' are given, and no auditing or competency thresholds are defined.
key_entities: wrapping the old inner dressing inside the glove during removal

title: Nerve Stimulator Monitoring of Neuromuscular Block
summary:
This community represents perioperative neuromuscular monitoring: the use of a peripheral nerve stimulator in patients who receive neuromuscular blocking drugs, and the downstream airway/respiratory risk chain that follows incomplete reversal. Two recommendations converge on the same device. The ERAS Society (T1, p7) directs that a peripheral nerve stimulator be used in patients receiving neuromuscular block, with the stated condition that it is used to monitor the depth of block and to ensure correct reversal; in this population it both monitors for and prevents residual muscle weakness. The WHO (T1, p31) frames the same practice as intraoperative safety monitoring, stating that a nerve stimulator should be used to monitor for paralysis whenever neuromuscular blocking drugs are given. The clinical rationale is supplied by ERAS: residual muscle weakness increases the risk of postoperative respiratory complications, which makes confirmation of adequate reversal before emergence a patient-safety checkpoint rather than an optional refinement.

Contributing bodies are the ERAS Society and WHO. They do not conflict, but their emphasis differs. WHO is broader and more universal (any patient given a neuromuscular blocking agent, monitoring for paralysis), consistent with a global surgical-safety framing. ERAS is more specific about purpose and outcome: it names correct reversal as the monitoring endpoint, names residual muscle weakness as the target problem, and alone links that weakness to postoperative respiratory complications.

What the community does not establish: no specific neuromuscular blocking agent or reversal agent is named (no rocuronium, sugammadex or neostigmine), and no quantitative threshold is given — there is no train-of-four ratio, count, or timing interval for when to stimulate, how often, or how long before extubation. No monitoring site, stimulation mode, or documentation requirement is specified. The particular postoperative respiratory complications are unnamed and unquantified, and no gynecologic- or procedure-specific population, age group, or comorbidity qualifier is attached to either recommendation.

title: Escalating Interventions for Respiratory Acidosis
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: the treatment of respiratory acidosis through interventions that restore adequate alveolar ventilation and carbon dioxide elimination. All six relations converge on one target condition (respiratory acidosis) and describe a graded, escalating set of therapeutic options.

The recommendations, all drawn from OpenRN Nursing Fundamentals (Textbook 2, p. 1093), are: (1) improving ventilation and respiration; (2) removal of airway restrictions; (3) reversal of oversedation; (4) nebulizer treatment; (5) noninvasive positive pressure ventilation; and (6) mechanical ventilation. Only mechanical ventilation carries an explicit condition in the source relations — it is indicated 'if noninvasive interventions are not successful' — which establishes noninvasive measures as first-line and intubation/mechanical ventilation as the escalation step. The remaining five interventions are recorded without any population restriction or qualifying condition, meaning they are presented as general measures for patients with respiratory acidosis rather than being scoped to any specific perioperative, obstetric, or gynecologic subgroup.

Only one guideline body contributes here: the OpenRN open-education nursing textbook corpus. Because there is a single source, there are no inter-body disagreements, no competing thresholds, and no instance where one organisation is more specific than another. The only internal gradation in specificity is the conditional logic attached to mechanical ventilation versus the unconditioned status of the other five interventions.

What this community does NOT establish: it gives no numeric diagnostic or treatment thresholds (no pH, PaCO2, bicarbonate, or SpO2 cut-offs), no timing or reassessment intervals, and no named drugs — notably, 'reversal of oversedation' is stated without naming naloxone, flumazenil, or any agent or dose, and 'nebulizer treatment' is stated without naming a bronchodilator. It does not define which patients are at risk, does not address metabolic acidosis or mixed disorders, does not specify monitoring or documentation requirements, and does not link these interventions to any perioperative gynecologic population, procedure, or anesthetic technique. Educators should treat it as a conceptual escalation ladder requiring local protocol detail.

title: Nonpharmacologic Management of Hyperventilation-Induced Respiratory Alkalosis
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: the acute, nonpharmacologic nursing management of respiratory alkalosis arising from hyperventilation. All four relations converge on the same target condition (respiratory alkalosis), the same population (clients who are hyperventilating), and the same timing (acute management), making this a coherent bedside intervention bundle rather than a diagnostic or pharmacologic pathway.

The recommended interventions, each described as treating respiratory alkalosis in hyperventilating clients during acute management, are: (1) client reassurance; (2) explanation of symptoms, so the client understands what is happening physiologically; (3) removal of stressors contributing to the hyperventilation; and (4) breathing retraining, which is the most specific of the four — it is explicitly directed at abdominal (diaphragmatic) breathing. Together these emphasise anxiety reduction, environmental modification, and coached breathing mechanics as first-line nursing actions.

Only one guideline body contributes to this community: OpenRN (Nursing Skills / Nursing Advanced Skills, Volume 2, p. 1093). Because the corpus segment is single-source, there are no interbody disagreements to reconcile and no competing thresholds. The only internal gradation in specificity is that breathing retraining carries an explicit technique qualifier (abdominal/diaphragmatic breathing), whereas reassurance, symptom explanation, and stressor removal are stated generically without prescribed scripts, duration, or frequency.

What this community does NOT establish: it gives no arterial blood gas thresholds (no pH, PaCO2, or bicarbonate cut-points) to define or resolve the alkalosis; no respiratory rate trigger for initiating intervention; no timing, duration, or reassessment interval; and no escalation criteria or endpoint for when nonpharmacologic measures have failed. It names no drugs, no oxygen or rebreathing device, and no monitoring modality. It does not address underlying causes of hyperventilation (pain, sepsis, salicylate toxicity, mechanical ventilation settings), pediatric, pregnant, or perioperative gynecologic subpopulations specifically, nor does it link these interventions to documentation or handoff requirements. Educators should treat it as a starter intervention list requiring local specification of assessment parameters and escalation pathways.

title: Respiratory Arrest: Risk Factors and Rescue Breathing
summary:
This community centres on respiratory arrest — its precursors and the single treatment named in the corpus. Four entities are identified as increasing risk of respiratory arrest: severe acidosis, decreased level of consciousness, and respiratory distress (all OpenRN Nursing Skills, T2 p1425), plus nasotracheal suctioning as an iatrogenic/procedural risk (T2 p1293). Together these frame respiratory arrest as an anticipated deterioration endpoint that nurses should be screening for in patients who are acidotic, obtunded, or in distress, and as a procedural hazard to be monitored for during airway suctioning.

The one intervention captured is rescue breathing, which TREATS respiratory arrest. Its guideline attaches an explicit population and condition: a person with suspected opioid overdose, and only when the person is not breathing on their own (OpenRN T2 p788). This is the most specific statement in the community, pairing a defined population with a defined trigger for action.

All relations derive from a single guideline body — OpenRN (Open Resources for Nursing), Volume/Text 2 — drawn from three separate pages (p788, p1293, p1425). Because there is only one contributing source, there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile; however, the level of specificity differs sharply by page. The p788 rescue-breathing statement carries both population and condition qualifiers, whereas the risk relations at p1425 and p1293 are stated unconditionally, with no population, severity threshold, or timeframe attached.

What this community does NOT establish: no numeric thresholds (no pH or bicarbonate value for "severe acidosis," no GCS or sedation-scale cut-off for decreased level of consciousness, no respiratory rate or SpO2 criteria for respiratory distress); no suctioning duration, catheter size, or pre-oxygenation protocol to mitigate nasotracheal suctioning risk; no naloxone dosing, route, or repeat interval despite the opioid-overdose population; no rescue-breathing rate, ratio, or escalation-to-CPR criteria; no gynecologic or perioperative population specificity; and no monitoring frequency, documentation, or escalation pathway for at-risk patients.

title: Opioid-Induced Sedation and Respiratory Depression Monitoring
summary: This community centres on opioid- and sedative-induced sedation and respiratory depression in perioperative/postoperative analgesia, and the monitoring, pump safeguards and reversal agents that mitigate it. Risk relations: opioids and opioid analgesics increase risk of respiratory depression in all clients receiving opioids, including clients at the end of life; morphine dose-dependently raises sedation and respiratory depression (higher dose, higher level); analgesics, pain medication and antihistamines increase sedation risk; benzodiazepines or other sedatives taken concurrently with opioids increase respiratory depression risk. ERAS Society adds a distinct perioperative framing: opioid used as the sole post-operative analgesic increases sedation risk, implying multimodal analgesia, whereas OpenRN is the source of nearly all monitoring and pharmacologic detail. Recommendations: monitor sedation and respiratory status before administering opioids and at regular intervals thereafter; provide continual monitoring and monitoring for oversedation in all clients receiving opioids; use monitoring equipment for clients deemed highest risk (sleep apnea, continuous IV opioids, or supplemental oxygen); for PCA clients, nursing monitoring of respiratory rate, SpO2, sedation level and mental status. PCA pump settings prevent oversedation, overmedication, sedation and respiratory depression when the pump allows medication only every set number of minutes with a maximum hourly dose and only the client presses the button; overmedication itself raises sedation and respiratory depression risk. Around-the-clock analgesic administration after surgery, trauma or injury is temporarily contraindicated if sedation or respiratory status indicates otherwise. Monitor for sedative effects in clients receiving antihistamines such as diphenhydramine. Naloxone treats opioid-induced respiratory depression, opioid overdose (including unresponsive women and elderly clients), opioid toxicity and fentanyl-involved overdose; a second dose is indicated if no response within 2–3 minutes, because naloxone's duration is shorter than some opioids and potent/large-quantity overdoses may need more doses. Naloxone precipitates withdrawal symptoms in opioid-dependent clients. Not established: specific respiratory rate, SpO2 or sedation-scale thresholds; naloxone doses/routes; monitoring frequencies or durations; gynecology-specific protocols; and any comparative evidence between opioid-sparing strategies.

title: Preoperative cardiac testing sequencing before surgery
summary:
Theme: this small community represents the stepwise, indication-driven use of preoperative cardiac investigations — specifically resting electrocardiography (ECG) and resting echocardiography — in adults undergoing elective surgery, including elective gynecologic procedures. The organising principle is sequence and justification: echocardiography is not a routine screening test but a second-line study whose timing depends on a prior ECG and specialist interpretation.

Main recommendations with populations and conditions:
• Resting echocardiography is placed in the preoperative phase for people undergoing elective surgery, but only if the person has a heart murmur accompanied by a cardiac symptom, or has signs or symptoms of heart failure. Absent those findings, the relation gives no basis for ordering it.
• For people being considered for preoperative resting echocardiography, the timing of the echocardiogram depends on the resting ECG: the ECG must be carried out and its findings discussed with an anaesthetist before the echocardiogram is ordered.
• Correspondingly, the resting ECG itself sits in the preoperative phase for people being considered for resting echocardiography before surgery, performed before the echocardiogram is ordered.

Contributing bodies: all three relations derive from a single source, NICE (T1, p8). There is therefore no cross-body comparison available here — no ASA, AAGBI, AORN or specialty gynecologic society statements are represented, so no points of agreement or divergence can be characterised, and no body is shown as more specific than another.

What this community does NOT establish: it specifies no ASA physical status, age, surgery-grade or comorbidity thresholds; no numeric echocardiographic parameters (e.g. ejection fraction cut-offs) or ECG abnormality criteria; no timeframe in days or hours between ECG, anaesthetist discussion and echocardiography; no guidance on murmurs without cardiac symptoms, on emergency or urgent surgery, or on who performs or reports the studies. It also says nothing about downstream actions if the echocardiogram is abnormal, about stress testing, biomarkers, or anticoagulation, and nothing gynecology-specific. Local protocols must supply these operational details.
key_entities: heart murmur with a cardiac symptom
signs or symptoms of heart failure

title: Caesarean Section Prophylaxis and Uterotonic Management
summary: This community covers perioperative risk reduction for caesarean birth: infection prophylaxis, VTE prophylaxis, and uterotonic use for prevention and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH). WHO recommends antimicrobial/prophylactic antibiotics for all women undergoing caesarean section, elective and non-elective; CDC is more specific on timing, specifying administration before skin incision. WHO also recommends skin antisepsis for caesarean, with agent and method chosen on clinician experience, cost and local availability. For thromboprophylaxis, RCOG recommends LMWH for women undergoing caesarean section and for 10 days after delivery, with anti-embolism stockings combined with LMWH for hospitalised post-caesarean women at particularly high VTE risk, and discontinuation of maintenance LMWH 24 hours before planned elective delivery; NICE adds combined pharmacological plus mechanical prophylaxis for women likely to be immobilised or with significantly reduced mobility after surgery. Oxytocin is the dominant agent: WHO recommends 10 IU IM/IV for all births (vaginal or caesarean) as the single uterotonic and drug of choice in the third stage, with slow injection to avoid adverse haemodynamic effects; RCOG specifies 5 IU by slow IV injection at caesarean section, notes oxytocin is superior to misoprostol and is the prophylactic agent of choice, and warns that IV injection increases risk of profound hypotension. For treatment, oxytocin is first-line (WHO, including women who already had prophylaxis; RCOG 5 IU slow IV repeated, or 40 IU in 500 ml infusion for major PPH; preferred initially in hypertension or pre-eclampsia). Oxytocin 10 IU IV/IM with controlled cord traction treats retained placenta or third stage exceeding 30 minutes; it also treats confirmed delay in labour with amniotomy, and supports induction with a balloon catheter when prostaglandins are contraindicated/unavailable. Carbetocin is an alternative for vaginal or caesarean birth where oxytocin is unavailable or quality cannot be guaranteed; injectable uterotonics require skilled personnel trained to administer them. RCOG notes 40 or 80 IU did not reduce PPH treatment versus 10 IU after vaginal delivery. One WHO safety case notes oxytocin given in error instead of a tocolytic increased preterm birth risk. Not established: specific antibiotic agents or doses, LMWH dosing, antiseptic agent choice, or comparative superiority of carbetocin over oxytocin.

title: Ultrasound and surgical management of retained products
summary:
This community represents the diagnostic imaging and surgical management pathway for intrauterine and pelvic pathology after pregnancy — specifically retained products of conception (RPOC) and pelvic abscess — as described in RCOG guidance (Tier 1, pp. 6, 7, 30).

Diagnostic recommendations: pelvic ultrasound scan is used to detect retained products of conception, explicitly in women presenting with secondary postpartum haemorrhage and where clinical diagnosis of retained products is unreliable. Ultrasound findings cited as supporting RPOC in women with secondary postpartum haemorrhage are an echogenic mass in the uterine cavity and an anteroposterior diameter of the cavity above the 90th centile — the only quantitative threshold in this community. Pelvic ultrasound is also indicated to detect pelvic abscess in women following pregnancy and in women with suspected sepsis, in both cases conditioned on pelvic abscess being clinically suspected.

Treatment recommendation: surgical evacuation of retained placental tissue treats retained products of conception, and is repeatedly qualified — across p6 and p30 — with the requirement that it should be undertaken or supervised by an experienced clinician. This staffing/competency condition is the key operational point for QI leads and for theatre and ward nursing teams.

Guideline bodies: only RCOG contributes here (Tier 1), so there are no inter-body disagreements. Internal variation is one of specificity rather than conflict: p6 states the diagnosis–treatment pair in general terms, while p30 adds the population (secondary postpartum haemorrhage), the reliability caveat, and the sonographic criteria.

What is NOT established: no timing, interval or urgency window for scanning or evacuation; no antibiotic, uterotonic or other drug regimens; no drainage or surgical route for pelvic abscess (ultrasound is only linked to its detection); no definition of "experienced clinician", no anaesthetic, consent or blood-product guidance; no sensitivity/specificity or negative-scan pathway; and no follow-up, fertility or recurrence outcomes. Nursing roles, monitoring parameters and escalation criteria are likewise absent and must come from other communities.
key_entities: surgical evacuation of retained placental tissue

title: Preventing and detecting retained surgical items
summary:
This community centres on a single adverse outcome — the retained surgical item (RSI) — and the layered barriers used to prevent and detect it. All eight relations come from WHO Tool 1 (pages 78, 79 and 111), so the theme reflects one guideline body rather than a comparison across bodies; the differences are between pages, where p111 reads as the operational checklist-style articulation and pp78–79 as the narrative rationale.

Prevention recommendations: a surgical count is indicated for any procedure in which items could be retained in the patient (p78). Manual counting of sponges and instruments is named as a preventive practice even while the guideline acknowledges that counting is fraught with error (p79) — hence two complementary defences: a methodical examination of the wound by the surgeon before closure in every case, and clear communication among team members (p79, no population or condition qualifier attached to the communication item).

Detection recommendations: sponge and needle counts function as detection when verbally confirmed as complete by the scrub or circulating nurse (p111). An instrument count is specified for cases with an open cavity, with counts confirmed to be complete (p111). Radiographic imaging is the fallback — indicated if counts are not appropriately reconciled and if need be (p111) — and a radiograph taken at the completion of the procedure is indicated for surgical patients when a count ought to be performed but is not (p79).

What this community does not establish: no numeric thresholds, count timings or number of count cycles (e.g. before incision, at closure) are given; no specific imaging modality parameters, radiation dose, or interpretation responsibility; no drugs are involved. It does not define documentation requirements, escalation pathways when a discrepancy persists after imaging, RSI incidence rates, or gynecology-specific populations — "cases with an open cavity" is the only anatomic qualifier. No competing or corroborating guideline body (e.g. AORN, national bodies) is represented, so consensus across corpora cannot be inferred.
key_entities: manual count of sponges and instruments
methodical examination of the wound before closure

title: Braden Scale Pressure Injury Risk Screening
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: use of the Braden Scale as the screening instrument for detecting pressure injury risk and risk for skin breakdown in inpatient populations. All five relations converge on one assessment tool with one function — detection — and three closely related outcome concepts: pressure injury risk factor, risk of pressure injury, and risk for skin breakdown.

Main recommendations, with populations and conditions: (1) Perform Braden Scale assessment on hospitalised clients on admission, daily, and again if the client's condition deteriorates, or otherwise according to facility policy (OpenRN T2 p731). (2) Interpret the score against a threshold: a score of less than 23 indicates risk of pressure injury (OpenRN T2 p753). (3) Screen clients receiving inpatient care on admission for risk for skin breakdown, and continue to use the tool in clients already identified as at risk for skin breakdown (OpenRN T2 p753). (4) In patients with a wound, where the wound is a pressure injury, the Braden Scale is used to detect the contributing pressure injury risk factor (OpenRN T2 p1165).

Guideline bodies: all relations derive from a single corpus source, OpenRN Textbook 2 (pages 731, 753, 1165), so there are no competing bodies and no contradictions. Specificity differs by page rather than by organisation: p731 is the most specific on timing (admission, daily, deterioration, facility policy); p753 is the most specific on the numeric cut-off (<23) and on inpatient admission screening; p1165 is the most specific on the wound-care application.

What this community does NOT establish: no pressure-injury staging criteria, no prevention or treatment interventions (no repositioning schedules, support surfaces, dressings, nutrition, or drugs of any kind), no Braden subscale definitions or full score range, no risk stratification tiers below the <23 threshold, no validated alternative tools for comparison, and nothing specific to gynecologic or intraoperative positioning despite the perioperative context of the corpus. Escalation pathways and documentation requirements are also absent.

title: Infection, Antibiotics and Preterm Labour
summary:
This community represents the relationship between infection and preterm labour, and the resulting boundary on antibiotic use in women presenting in preterm labour. It links two ideas that nurses must hold together: infection is a genuine driver of preterm birth risk, yet antibiotics are not a blanket intervention for every woman in preterm labour.

Two recommendations sit in this theme. First, RCOG (T1, p4) establishes that severe infection increases the risk of preterm labour in pregnant women, with no further qualifying condition stated — this supports vigilance for infection as a risk factor in antenatal assessment. Second, WHO (T1, p17) states that routine antibiotic administration is contraindicated in women in preterm labour when the amniotic membranes are intact and there are no clinical signs of infection. The WHO statement is the more specific of the two: it names a defined population (women in preterm labour), two explicit conditions that must both be present (intact membranes; absence of clinical signs of infection), and the practice being restricted (routine, i.e. non-indicated, antibiotic administration).

The two bodies do not conflict; they operate at different levels. RCOG describes aetiological risk; WHO constrains a management response. Read together, they imply that clinical assessment for signs of infection and membrane status is the pivot for the antibiotic decision — documenting these findings is the practical quality-improvement target.

What this community does NOT establish: no specific antibiotic agents, doses, routes, timings or durations are named; no criteria, thresholds or vital-sign parameters are given for what constitutes "severe infection" or "clinical signs of infection"; no guidance is provided for women in preterm labour with ruptured membranes or with signs of infection (the inverse of the WHO condition is unaddressed here); no gestational-age boundaries are specified; and no quantified magnitude of the infection-related preterm labour risk is offered. It also says nothing about tocolysis, corticosteroids, screening tests, or postoperative/perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis.

title: Scopolamine for End-of-Life Secretions
summary:
This community represents a narrow but clinically important theme: the pharmacologic management of excessive upper-airway secretions ("death rattle") in dying and palliative care patients, with scopolamine as the single named agent. Although the surrounding corpus concerns perioperative gynecologic nursing, this cluster sits squarely in end-of-life/comfort care rather than intraoperative or postoperative recovery.

Two recommendations are captured, both drug-specific and both pointing to the same intervention:

1. Scopolamine treats terminal secretions in clients at the end of life (OpenRN Nursing Skills/Management, Tier 2, p. 1288). This relation is population-scoped (actively dying clients) but attaches no additional triggering condition, dose, route, frequency, or titration threshold.

2. Scopolamine treats high-volume secretions in palliative care clients, with the explicit condition "for high-volume secretions" (OpenRN Tier 2, p. 1269). This is the more specific of the two, because it names a symptom-severity trigger (high volume) rather than simply a phase of illness, and it broadens the population from actively dying to palliative care generally.

Only one guideline body contributes: the OpenRN open-access nursing textbook corpus, appearing at two separate page locations (p. 1269 and p. 1288). There is therefore no cross-body disagreement to reconcile. The two entries are consistent and complementary rather than conflicting; the difference is one of granularity, with p. 1269 supplying the secretion-volume qualifier and p. 1288 supplying the terminal-phase framing. Educators should note the corpus does not distinguish whether "terminal secretions" and "high-volume secretions" are the same phenomenon.

What this community does NOT establish: no dose, route (oral, transdermal patch, subcutaneous, IV), timing, or frequency; no titration or maximum dose; no comparison with alternative antimuscarinics such as glycopyrrolate, atropine, or hyoscyamine; no non-pharmacologic measures (repositioning, suctioning, family education); no contraindications, anticholinergic adverse effects, or monitoring parameters; no efficacy evidence, evidence grade, or outcome measure; and no guidance for non-palliative or perioperative gynecologic patients.
key_entities: clients at the end of life

title: Scrub Brush Harms in Surgical Hand Antisepsis
summary:
This small community represents a single, focused theme: the potential harms of using scrub brushes for surgical hand antisepsis (surgical hand scrub) among surgical personnel. Both relations in the community originate from one source, CDC Table 1, page 20, and both attach the same population — surgical personnel performing preoperative hand preparation. No other condition or qualifier (e.g., duration of scrub, agent used, first case of the day versus subsequent cases) is specified in the relations.

The two captured findings are: (1) scrub brushes increase the risk of skin damage in surgical personnel, and (2) scrub brushes increase the risk of increased bacterial shedding from the hands in surgical personnel. Taken together, the implied practice message is that brush use is counterproductive — the mechanical trauma to skin is linked to greater microbial shedding rather than a cleaner surgical hand, which is the outcome hand antisepsis is intended to achieve. For a nurse educator, these are usable teaching points when reviewing surgical scrub technique, skin integrity assessment of scrubbed staff, and rationale for brushless scrub practice.

Only one guideline body contributes here: the CDC. Because there is a single source, this community contains no inter-organizational agreement or disagreement, and no instance where one body is more specific than another; there is no AORN, WHO, or professional-association statement represented for comparison.

Important limits: the community does NOT recommend any specific alternative product, antiseptic agent (no chlorhexidine gluconate, povidone-iodine, or alcohol-based surgical hand rub is named), scrub duration, or number of brush strokes. It does not state a threshold of brush use at which harm occurs, does not quantify the magnitude of skin damage or bacterial shedding, and does not establish a link to surgical site infection or patient outcomes. It also does not prohibit brushes outright, address sponges or nail picks, cover non-surgical hand hygiene, or address patients — only surgical personnel.
key_entities: increased bacterial shedding from the hands

title: Preventing Secondary Infection: Devices and Gloves
summary:
This community centres on a single clinical outcome — secondary infection — and the two categories of nursing practice that modify it in perioperative gynecologic care: timely removal of indwelling devices/packing, and correct glove use with hand hygiene.

Four RCOG recommendations (RCOG T1 p3) are structurally identical: early removal of the urinary catheter, the surgical drain, the vaginal pack, and the intravenous drip each PREVENTS secondary infection, with the condition stated simply as 'removed as soon as possible.' The theme is therefore that every invasive or retained item is treated as an infection portal whose risk accrues with dwell time, and that removal decisions should be revisited continuously rather than at fixed intervals.

The countervailing relation comes from OpenRN (T2): gloves INCREASE the risk of secondary infection when gloves are not removed and hand hygiene is not performed before the next procedure. Gloves are thus framed not as protection in themselves but as a potential vehicle for cross-contamination between procedures or patients — a hand-hygiene-adjacent teaching point rather than a device-removal one.

Contributing bodies: RCOG contributes all four device-removal statements and is the more specific source on which items to remove (catheter, drain, vaginal pack, IV drip — the vaginal pack being distinctively gynecologic). OpenRN contributes the only practice-error relation and is the more specific source on the sequence of glove removal plus hand hygiene 'before the next procedure.' The two sources do not contradict each other; they address different links in the same chain.

What this community does NOT establish: no numeric thresholds or timings — 'as soon as possible' is never operationalised into hours or postoperative days for any of the four devices. No population is specified for any relation (no age, procedure type, comorbidity, or immunosuppression qualifiers), so these are undifferentiated recommendations. No antibiotic, antiseptic, or drug is named; no glove type or hand-hygiene agent is specified. No effect sizes, infection rates, surveillance definitions, or evidence grades are attached, and no relation addresses insertion technique, dressing care, or aseptic maintenance while a device remains in situ.

title: Peripheral IV Catheter Securement and Dressing
summary:
This small community represents a single clinical theme: mechanical protection of the peripheral intravenous (PIV) catheter site to prevent accidental dislodgement. Two interventions are named, both directed at the same outcome. First, a sterile transparent dressing is applied over the insertion site to prevent accidental dislodgement of the peripheral intravenous catheter; the population is explicitly patients with a peripheral intravenous catheter, with no further qualifying condition, implying it is the baseline expectation for every PIV. Second, a securement device may be added for the same population to prevent the same adverse event; the conditional phrasing ('may be added') marks this as an optional or adjunctive measure layered on top of the dressing rather than a substitute for it. The practical teaching point for a nurse educator is therefore a two-tier approach: transparent sterile dressing always, supplemental securement device as clinically indicated.

Only one guideline body contributes here — the OpenRN nursing skills text (Volume/Text 2, p.1329). Because the corpus contains a single source for both relations, there are no inter-guideline disagreements, no competing recommendations, and no instance of one body being more specific than another; the only internal gradation is the unconditional dressing recommendation versus the discretionary securement device.

The community does not establish a great deal that quality-improvement leads would need. It gives no dressing change frequency or dwell time, no catheter gauge or anatomical site preferences, no named securement product types (e.g., adhesive engineered stabilisation devices versus tape), and no criteria for deciding when a securement device should be added. It says nothing about infection prevention outcomes such as phlebitis, infiltration, extravasation, or catheter-related bloodstream infection — dislodgement is the sole outcome cited. It also omits any perioperative or gynecologic-specific qualifiers, paediatric or confused/agitated patient subgroups, documentation requirements, and any evidence grading or strength-of-recommendation rating. Any protocol built from this theme would need supplementation from vascular access guidelines outside this community.
key_entities: accidental dislodgement of the peripheral intravenous catheter
patients with a peripheral intravenous catheter

title: Securing Peripheral IV Catheters Against Dislodgement
summary:
This small community represents a single, focused theme: mechanical securement of peripheral intravenous (PIV) catheters to prevent accidental catheter dislodgement. Both relations converge on the same outcome node, indicating that the corpus treats dislodgement as a preventable device-related complication addressed by physical stabilization at the insertion site.

Two interventions are named for the same population — patients with a peripheral IV catheter — with no further qualifying condition (no restriction by age, vein site, gauge, infusion type, dwell time, or perioperative phase, and no stated frequency of reassessment or replacement): (1) application of a stabilization device, and (2) securing the peripheral intravenous catheter with tape. Both are presented as preventive measures for accidental catheter dislodgement, and the graph does not rank one above the other, does not state a preference hierarchy, and does not specify when a manufactured stabilization device should be chosen over tape or whether the two are used together.

Only one guideline body contributes here: OpenRN (Nursing Skills, Volume 2), with both relations traced to page 1363 of the same source. Because a single source underlies both statements, there are no inter-body disagreements, no differences in specificity between organizations, and no corroborating or conflicting recommendation from a perioperative or infusion-therapy specialty body within this community.

What the community does NOT establish: it names no products, adhesive types, dressing materials, or securement device brands; no thresholds (e.g., acceptable dislodgement rates), timings (e.g., dressing change intervals, catheter dwell limits), or drugs. It does not link securement to other downstream outcomes such as phlebitis, infiltration, extravasation, bloodstream infection, or infusion interruption, and it does not describe assessment, documentation, patient education, or actions to take once dislodgement has occurred. For QI purposes it supports only a basic practice standard — every PIV should be secured, by tape or a stabilization device — and would need supplementation from infusion-therapy standards to define technique, frequency, and product selection.
key_entities: securing peripheral intravenous catheter with tape
patients with a peripheral IV catheter

title: Suicide Risk Assessment and Continuous Observation
summary:
This small community represents the theme of acute suicide/self-harm risk assessment and immediate protective response within perioperative gynecologic nursing guidance — an inpatient safety concern that can arise in any patient population being screened for suicidal thinking, including surgical patients.

Two linked recommendations are captured. First, risk stratification: when a patient assessed for suicidal thinking can articulate a specific plan — naming how and when they intend to act, and particularly if the act is planned within the next 48 hours — this specificity is treated as increasing the risk of self-harm. The 48-hour window is the only explicit temporal threshold in the community and is the trigger for escalated concern. Second, the protective intervention: for patients believed to be at high risk of self-harm, continuous observation is described as preventing self-harm, with the operational conditions that the nurse does not leave the patient alone and collaborates on an immediate plan for emergency care.

Both relations derive from a single contributing source, OpenRN (Open Resources for Nursing) Volume/Text 2, page 138. Because only one guideline body contributes, the community contains no inter-guideline disagreement, no divergence in thresholds, and no instance where one body is more specific than another; the specificity present (the 48-hour planning horizon, the "do not leave alone" instruction) is internal to the OpenRN text.

The community does not establish: any validated screening tool or scoring instrument; who performs the assessment or documents it; what constitutes "continuous" observation in terms of staffing ratio, line-of-sight versus arm's-length, or duration; who the collaboration partners are (e.g., psychiatry, crisis team, provider); any pharmacologic management, restraint, seclusion, or environmental ligature-risk measures; criteria for de-escalating or discontinuing observation; or any gynecologic- or perioperative-specific modifications, such as handling during anesthesia, recovery, or discharge planning. It also does not quantify risk (no relative or absolute risk figures) or address protective factors, prior attempt history, or means restriction.
key_entities: patients believed to be at high risk of self-harm

title: Sensory Deprivation: Stimuli and Social Interaction
summary:
This small community represents a single clinical theme: nursing management of sensory deprivation through environmental and interpersonal intervention rather than pharmacologic means. Two relations anchor the theme, both drawn from the same source (OpenRN Nursing Fundamentals, Textbook 2, p521). First, the provision of meaningful stimuli is identified as treating sensory deprivation, with no population restriction or qualifying condition attached in the graph. Second, social interaction is identified as treating sensory deprivation, qualified by the condition 'as appropriate' — signalling nurse judgement about timing, patient tolerance, and situational suitability rather than a blanket directive. Both interventions point at the same target state (sensory deprivation), suggesting they are intended as complementary, non-pharmacologic measures.

Only one guideline body contributes here: OpenRN. Because the corpus segment contains no second source, there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile, no competing thresholds, and no instance of one guideline being more specific than another. The only difference in specificity is internal to OpenRN: the social interaction recommendation carries a conditional qualifier ('as appropriate'), whereas the meaningful stimuli recommendation is stated unconditionally.

What this community does NOT establish is substantial and should be flagged for any educator or QI lead building teaching material or an audit standard from it. It does not define sensory deprivation or specify assessment criteria or screening tools for detecting it. It names no population — no age group, no perioperative phase (pre-, intra-, or postoperative), no gynecologic surgical procedure, and no comorbidity such as visual or hearing impairment or delirium risk. It specifies no dosing, frequency, duration, or timing for either intervention, and gives no examples of what counts as a 'meaningful' stimulus or an appropriate form of social interaction. No drugs, monitoring parameters, outcome measures, or escalation pathways appear. It also states no contraindications, and does not address sensory overload as a counterpart condition. Any protocol would require supplementation from fuller source text.

title: Sensory Overload Prevention of Hospital Delirium
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: sensory overload in hospitalised clients as a modifiable environmental contributor to acute neurocognitive disturbance, and the nursing care-clustering strategies used to reduce it. Two causal claims anchor the theme: sensory overload increases the risk of delirium (stated both for hospitalised clients when sensory overload occurs, and unconditionally at OpenRN T2 p451) and increases the risk of acute confusion (for hospitalised clients, when sensory overload occurs). Delirium and acute confusion are presented as parallel outcomes rather than distinguished by severity or duration.

Two interventions are recommended, both nurse-controlled and non-pharmacological. First, limiting unnecessary awakenings and interactions treats sensory overload, with the population given broadly as 'clients' and the condition specified as when a client is experiencing sensory overload — i.e. it is framed as a responsive rather than universal measure. Second, combining nursing activities to avoid interrupting rest treats sensory overload; this relation carries no population or condition qualifier, so it reads as a general practice recommendation. Together they describe care clustering: batching assessments, medications, hygiene and monitoring so that rest periods are preserved.

Only one guideline body contributes: OpenRN (Nursing Fundamentals/Management, Volume 2), across pages 451, 510 and 521. Page 510 is the most specific source, attaching both the hospitalised-client population and the 'when sensory overload occurs' condition to the risk relations and to the awakening-limitation intervention. Page 451 states the delirium risk without qualifiers, and page 521 supplies the activity-combining intervention without qualifiers. There is no inter-body disagreement to reconcile, though the differing levels of specification across pages mean educators should default to the p510 phrasing when teaching populations and triggers.

The community does not establish any drugs, doses, thresholds, screening tools, timings, frequencies, or duration of rest periods; no delirium assessment instrument is named. It does not identify age, surgical, ICU or perioperative subgroups, does not address sensory deprivation as a counterpart risk, does not quantify effect size, and offers no evidence grading or outcome measures for the two interventions.
key_entities: combine nursing activities to avoid interrupting rest

title: Severe Hypertension: Drug Therapy and Activity Restriction
summary:
This community represents the management of severe hypertension across the pregnancy continuum and, separately, the safety gating of physical activity in people with poorly controlled blood pressure. Two distinct guideline bodies contribute, and they address different facets of the same core entity, severe hypertension.

WHO (T1) supplies the pharmacologic recommendations. Antihypertensive drugs are recommended to treat severe hypertension during pregnancy (stated twice, at p15 and p29), with p29 adding the specific qualifier that the choice of drug and route should be based on the prescribing clinician's experience with that agent, its cost, and local availability. WHO also extends treatment across the postpartum period in two ways: antihypertensive drugs are recommended for women with severe postpartum hypertension, and for women already treated with antihypertensive drugs antenatally, treatment should be continued postpartum. This gives a coherent antenatal-to-postpartum continuity message for nursing handover and discharge planning.

RNAO (T2 p48) contributes the activity-related recommendation: heavy physical activity is temporarily contraindicated for clients with severe hypertension or whose blood pressure is poorly controlled. The contraindication is explicitly temporary — activity should be discouraged or postponed until appropriate drug therapy has been instituted and found to be effective. RNAO is therefore more specific about the behavioural/activity dimension and the condition for lifting the restriction, whereas WHO is more specific about pharmacologic selection logic and the pregnancy/postpartum populations. The two are complementary rather than conflicting: RNAO's release criterion (effective drug therapy) presupposes the drug treatment WHO recommends.

What this community does NOT establish: no named antihypertensive agents, no drug classes, no doses or routes, and no numeric blood pressure thresholds defining "severe" or "poorly controlled." It does not define what counts as "heavy" physical activity, does not specify monitoring intervals, duration of postpartum therapy, or criteria for weaning. It also does not state whether RNAO's activity guidance applies to pregnant or postpartum clients specifically, nor does it address non-severe or non-pregnancy hypertension beyond the continuation statement.

title: Severe Pre-eclampsia: Timing of Delivery
summary:
This community centres on gestational-age-driven decision-making for severe pre-eclampsia — whether to deliver or to manage expectantly — plus one linked postpartum risk consideration.

Main recommendations (WHO T1 p29): For women with severe pre-eclampsia at term, early delivery is the recommended treatment. For women with severe pre-eclampsia at a gestational age when the fetus is not viable, or unlikely to achieve viability within one or two weeks, induction of labour is recommended. For women with severe pre-eclampsia and a viable fetus before 34 weeks of gestation, and separately for those between 34 and 36 (plus 6 days) weeks, expectant management is recommended — but only on the explicit conditions that uncontrolled maternal hypertension, increasing maternal organ dysfunction and fetal distress are absent, and that these parameters can be monitored. The same conditions apply to both gestational bands, so the practical nursing implication is a defined surveillance role (blood pressure control, organ dysfunction trends, fetal status) that legitimises continued expectant care and triggers delivery when breached.

RCOG T1 p22 contributes a distinct, non-overlapping point: severe pre-eclampsia increases the risk of venous thromboembolism in women after caesarean section — relevant to postoperative thromboprophylaxis risk assessment.

Contributing bodies: WHO (all delivery-timing and expectant-management guidance, with specific gestational thresholds of 34 weeks and 34–36+6 weeks) and RCOG (VTE risk after caesarean section). They do not conflict; they address different phases — WHO is far more specific on antenatal timing, RCOG on postoperative risk.

What this community does NOT establish: no drug therapies are named — no antihypertensive agents, no magnesium sulphate for seizure prophylaxis, no corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity, and no thromboprophylaxis agent, dose or duration despite the stated VTE risk. It gives no blood pressure or laboratory thresholds defining "severe", no definition of "uncontrolled" hypertension, no monitoring frequency or setting (inpatient vs outpatient), no mode-of-delivery preference, and no maternal or neonatal outcome data comparing expectant management with early delivery.

title: Head-of-Bed Limits to Prevent Shear
summary:
This community represents a narrow but high-yield pressure injury prevention theme: mechanical shear as a modifiable risk factor, and bed positioning as the countermeasure. The graph asserts one causal link — shear INCREASES_RISK_OF pressure injury — and two positioning interventions that PREVENT shear.

The main recommendations are: (1) elevate the head of the bed to 30 degrees or less, specified for clients rated '1–Problem' for friction/shear (i.e., patients scored as having an actual friction/shear problem on risk assessment), with the condition 'when feasible'; and (2) maintain the patient's position at 30 degrees or less, with the condition 'as appropriate'. The 30-degree threshold is the only numeric parameter in the community, and it is expressed as a ceiling (30 degrees or less), not a target angle.

Both statements come from a single contributing source, OpenRN Nursing Skills Volume 2 (p731 and p753); no second guideline body is represented, so there is no cross-body disagreement to reconcile. The two entries differ in specificity rather than substance: p731 attaches an explicit population (clients rated 1–Problem for friction/shear) and the feasibility caveat, making it the more actionable statement for protocol writing; p753 generalizes the same 30-degree ceiling to ongoing position maintenance with the softer qualifier 'as appropriate' and names no population.

What this community does NOT establish: it gives no repositioning frequency or timing, no surface, sling, lift-sheet, dressing, heel-offloading or barrier-product recommendations, and no drugs. It does not quantify how much pressure injury risk shear contributes, nor the effect size of the 30-degree limit. It does not define the friction/shear rating scale used to generate the '1–Problem' score, nor specify perioperative or intraoperative positioning despite the gynecologic surgical context. It also does not address exceptions where higher elevation is clinically required (e.g., feeding, respiratory or aspiration concerns) beyond the vague 'when feasible' and 'as appropriate' qualifiers, leaving local judgment to fill that gap.
key_entities: elevation of head of bed 30 degrees or less
maintaining position at 30 degrees or less

title: Shoe Covers and Caps as Barrier PPE
summary:
This community addresses non-gown personal protective equipment worn as a physical barrier in the operative and delivery setting — specifically shoe covers and surgical caps — and their role in protecting personnel from contamination rather than in protecting the patient from surgical site infection.

Main recommendations. WHO (T1 p211) positions shoe covers as protection for health-care workers against exposure to blood and bodily fluids, and is explicit about the triggering condition: situations in which splashing of blood or fluid is likely or expected, giving the labour room during delivery as a concrete example. CDC (T1 p15) makes a parallel but operative-team-focused recommendation: shoe covers prevent exposure of surgical team members to blood and other body fluids during an operation. CDC additionally specifies application to orthopedic operations for operating personnel, with the condition that gross contamination can reasonably be anticipated — and extends this same population and condition to the surgical cap.

Contributing bodies and differences. Two bodies contribute: WHO and CDC. They agree on the underlying principle (barrier PPE indicated when splash or gross contamination is anticipated) but differ in framing and specificity. WHO frames the population broadly as health-care workers and anchors the indication to an obstetric/labour-room example relevant to gynecologic and delivery practice; CDC narrows the population to surgical team members/operating personnel and names a procedure type (orthopedic operations). Only CDC brings the surgical cap into scope; WHO's contribution here concerns shoe covers alone.

What this community does not establish. It sets no thresholds, timings, durations of wear, donning/doffing sequence, or change frequency; it names no drugs or antiseptics. It does not claim that shoe covers or caps reduce surgical site infection or patient infection rates — the stated benefit is worker protection from blood and body fluid exposure. It does not specify shoe cover or cap materials, single-use versus reusable status, disposal requirements, or behaviour when gross contamination is not anticipated, and it offers no gynecologic-procedure-specific mandate beyond the labour-room delivery example.
key_entities: exposure to blood and bodily fluids
exposure to blood and other body fluids

title: Oral iron dosing frequency and tolerability
summary:
Clinical theme: this small community addresses tolerability of oral iron supplementation in the perioperative gynecologic setting — specifically how dosing frequency relates to gastrointestinal and other side effects, and therefore to adherence. Two linked relations frame the theme: daily oral iron supplementation increases the risk of side effects in 'some people', while an alternate-day oral iron regimen prevents (reduces) those side effects for people who experience unpleasant side effects from daily dosing, when alternate-day dosing is being considered as a means of reducing side effects and encouraging adherence.

Main recommendations with populations and conditions: (1) Recognise that daily oral iron carries a risk of side effects in some patients — the population is deliberately non-specific ('some people'), so nurses should screen all patients on daily oral iron for tolerability rather than assume universal problems. (2) For the subgroup who report unpleasant side effects on daily oral iron, consider switching to an alternate-day oral iron regimen, with the explicit dual aim of reducing side effects and improving adherence to therapy.

Contributing guideline bodies: only NICE contributes here (both relations from NICE Table 1, p21). There is therefore no cross-body agreement or disagreement to reconcile within this community, and no second source offering greater specificity. The NICE statements are conditional ('considered as a means of'), i.e. an option to weigh, not a mandate.

What this community does NOT establish: it names no specific iron salt or preparation, no elemental iron dose, no mg thresholds, no treatment duration or timing relative to surgery, and no haemoglobin, ferritin or transferrin saturation trigger for starting or stopping iron. It does not list which side effects occur, nor quantify how much alternate-day dosing reduces them. It makes no claim that alternate-day dosing is equally or more effective at correcting anaemia or raising haemoglobin, does not address intravenous iron as an alternative, and does not define contraindications, monitoring intervals, or pregnancy- or surgery-specific populations.

title: Preoperative skin antisepsis to prevent SSI
summary:
This community represents preoperative surgical skin antisepsis as a core infection-prevention intervention, linking the practice to its phase (preoperative), its target outcome (prevention of surgical site infection), a specific population (caesarean section), and a prerequisite condition (removal of gross skin contamination).

Main recommendations: WHO positions skin antisepsis as preoperative and preventive against surgical site infection at all levels of patient care (WHO T1 p11), before invasive procedures generally (p56), and for all surgical patients using an appropriate antiseptic agent selected for rapid reduction of skin microbial count and persistent efficacy throughout the operation (p67). For women undergoing caesarean section, WHO places antisepsis immediately prior to the procedure, with the choice of agent and method based on clinician experience, cost and local availability (p18). CDC likewise places skin antisepsis in the preoperative phase for surgical patients and is uniquely specific about sequencing: timing depends on prior removal of gross contamination — the skin should be free of gross contamination before skin preparation is initiated (CDC T1 p11). NICE reiterates that skin antisepsis before surgery prevents surgical site infection in patients undergoing surgery (NICE T1 p22).

Contributing bodies and differences: WHO, CDC and NICE all agree on the preventive intent and preoperative timing; they do not conflict. WHO is the most granular on population (caesarean section) and on agent-selection criteria (microbial count reduction, persistent efficacy, experience/cost/availability). CDC is the most specific on the pre-condition of gross decontamination. NICE contributes only the general preventive statement.

What this community does NOT establish: no specific antiseptic agents are named (no chlorhexidine, alcohol or povidone-iodine formulations or concentrations), no application technique, contact or drying times, no numeric intervals between antisepsis and incision, no dosing or volume thresholds, and no comparative effectiveness or strength-of-evidence grading. It also does not address hair removal, bathing, antibiotic prophylaxis, paediatric or neonatal populations, or non-surgical gynecologic procedures beyond the unspecified "invasive procedures" reference.
key_entities: removal of gross contamination from the skin

title: Preventing and Detecting Skin Breakdown
summary: This community centres on skin integrity: the risk factors for skin breakdown (and related pressure injury), the preventive interventions, and the assessments that detect it. Named risk factors are immobility (immobile clients), prolonged or excess moisture exposure, soiled/wet/wrinkled bed linen, pressure from a nasal cannula at the nares or over the ears in patients on oxygen therapy, and pressure from the tracheostomy tube flange. Preventive recommendations, with their populations/conditions: frequent repositioning for immobilized clients, turning at least every two hours on a specific schedule; frequent surveillance; removal of wet or soiled linens and keeping bed linens clean, dry and wrinkle free; protective skin barrier and moisture barrier ointment, including for clients with wounds and in skin areas subject to increased moisture — moisture barrier ointment is the only item credited with preventing both skin breakdown and pressure injury; skin protectant as appropriate for clients with diarrhea; protective products for clients with urinary incontinence; changing soiled incontinence pads, checking every two to three hours and changing as needed to keep dry; protective foam dressing at pressure points for patients on nasal cannula oxygen; condom catheter for males with incontinence as an alternative to an indwelling catheter; and regular cleaning of the suprapubic catheter insertion site per agency policy. Detection/monitoring: skin assessment at pressure points (behind ears/occipital area, elbows, sacrum, heels) — after oxygen therapy is initiated; perineal skin inspection for clients with incontinence; skin monitoring for clients with diarrhea; stoma assessment in tracheostomy patients (also detecting stoma infection); assessment for signs of complications in clients at risk of immobility complications; and limited comfort-focused physical assessment at end of life, which also monitors urinary retention. All relations derive from a single source, OpenRN Nursing Skills/Fundamentals (Volume T2, multiple pages), so no inter-body disagreement can be assessed, though page-level specificity varies (p753 and p771 give timings; p731 and p1421 are general). The community does not establish staging criteria, product brands or drug doses, treatment of existing breakdown, documentation requirements, comparative effectiveness of barriers versus dressings, or repositioning schedules outside the two-hour standard.

title: Sun Exposure, Mole Monitoring, Skin Cancer
summary:
This small community represents a skin-integrity and cancer-risk-surveillance theme rather than a directly perioperative one: it links an environmental exposure (sun exposure) to skin cancer risk, and pairs that risk with a surveillance behaviour (monitoring of moles for changes). Both relations derive from a single source, OpenRN Nursing Skills (Textbook 2, p806), so the theme is contributed by one guideline body only.

Two recommendations are captured. First, sun exposure increases the risk of skin cancer, with the condition explicitly stated as severe cases of excessive sun exposure causing DNA damage — i.e., the risk relationship is framed around cumulative/severe exposure and DNA damage as the mechanism, not around any single incidental exposure. No population restriction is attached to this relation, so it is stated generally. Second, monitoring of moles for changes is a surveillance measure for skin cancer, with the population specified as individuals with moles. This is the more population-specific of the two statements and gives the actionable nursing/patient-education task: assessing existing moles for change over time.

For a nurse educator or QI lead, the usable content is therefore: teach sun-exposure risk in terms of DNA damage from severe/excessive exposure, and teach or operationalise ongoing mole surveillance for patients who have moles. Because only OpenRN contributes, there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile, and no more-specific competing guidance to defer to.

The community does NOT establish: any screening interval or timing for mole checks; who performs the assessment (self-examination versus clinician skin exam); any assessment criteria or thresholds (no ABCDE-type change criteria, lesion size, or diameter cut-offs); any preventive interventions such as sunscreen SPF thresholds, protective clothing, shade, or avoidance hours; any drugs; any risk stratification by skin type, age, family history, immunosuppression, or prior skin cancer; any diagnostic pathway, biopsy indication, or referral trigger; and any explicit perioperative or gynecologic-surgical linkage. Outcomes of monitoring (e.g., earlier detection or mortality benefit) are also not asserted.

title: Skin colour inspection for pallor, cyanosis
summary:
This small community represents a single clinical theme: visual inspection of skin colour as a bedside assessment technique for detecting two signs of impaired oxygenation and perfusion — pallor and cyanosis — in the perioperative gynecologic nursing context. Both relations are DETECTS relations originating from the same assessment action (skin colour inspection), so the theme is essentially about where on the body the nurse should look, and for whom.

Two recommendations are established. First, skin colour inspection detects cyanosis, and the guideline specifies the assessment sites as the face, lips, and fingertips; no population restriction is attached to this recommendation, so it is stated generally. Second, skin colour inspection detects pallor, and here the guideline is explicitly population-specific: for patients with darker skin tones, assessment should be performed on the palms, the conjunctiva, or the inner aspect of the lower lip, rather than relying on general skin surface appearance. This is the more specific of the two recommendations and is the practical teaching point for educators — that pallor detection in darker-skinned patients requires deliberate use of mucous membrane and palmar sites to avoid missed or delayed recognition.

Only one guideline body contributes to this community: OpenRN (Nursing Skills, Tier 2), with both relations drawn from page 562. Because there is a single source, there are no inter-body disagreements, no competing site recommendations, and no reconciliation needed; the only asymmetry is internal, in that the pallor relation carries a defined population and named alternative sites while the cyanosis relation does not specify any population adaptation for darker skin tones.

The community does not establish: any numeric thresholds, timings, or frequencies for inspection (e.g., preoperative versus postoperative intervals); any link to pulse oximetry, SpO2 values, capillary refill, or laboratory measures; any drugs or interventions triggered by detecting pallor or cyanosis; escalation or documentation pathways; sensitivity or reliability of visual inspection; or population-adapted sites for cyanosis assessment in patients with darker skin tones.
key_entities: inner aspect of the lower lip

title: Skin Damage Risks and Surveillance
summary:
This community centres on skin integrity as a shared concern for both patients and health-care personnel, mapping the agents and mechanical forces that cause skin damage, irritation and dryness, plus the one active surveillance measure named: skin inspection.

Surveillance: NICE (T1 p11) recommends skin inspection to monitor for skin damage in people with a significant reduction in mobility, poor skin integrity or any sensory loss, performed 2 or 3 times a day, with particular attention to the heels and bony prominences. This is the only detection/monitoring recommendation in the community; no treatment or dressing choices are covered.
