Occupational risks (CDC, T1): non-antimicrobial soap increases risk of skin irritation and skin dryness (p10) and, in health-care personnel, of skin damage with frequent use compared with antiseptic preparations (p21). Soap and detergent applied on a regular basis increase skin damage risk in health-care workers (p23). Two surgical-specific practices are flagged: the 10-minute surgical hand scrub (surgical staff) and use of a scrub brush (surgical personnel) both increase skin damage risk (p20) — directly relevant to perioperative scrub protocols.

Patient-side mechanical risks: OpenRN (T2 p718) identifies friction as a cause of skin damage when skin is rubbed against a hard object such as a bed or wheelchair arm. WHO (T1 p163) is the most time-specific source: in infants, a bandage left in place can cause damage within 8 to 12 hours.

Contributors and contrasts: CDC dominates the hand-hygiene/occupational strand and is the only body comparing products (non-antimicrobial soap versus antiseptic preparations); NICE alone specifies inspection frequency and anatomical sites; WHO alone gives an hours-based threshold; OpenRN alone names a mechanical mechanism.

Not established: no recommended alternative products, moisturiser or emollient regimens, scrub durations to substitute for the 10-minute scrub, inspection frequency for staff hands, bandage-change intervals beyond the infant 8–12-hour warning, staging or grading of skin damage, or any gynecologic-surgery-specific population beyond "surgical staff/personnel".

title: Preventing Hand-Hygiene-Related Skin Dryness in Staff
summary:
This community addresses occupational skin dryness caused by hand hygiene practices in health-care workers, and the emollient strategies used to prevent it. All relations come from a single guideline body, the CDC hand hygiene guideline (Table 1 evidence, pages 10 and 27), so there is no cross-body disagreement in this theme; differences are only in level of specificity between the two source pages.

Risk relationships: non-antimicrobial soap increases the risk of skin dryness (no qualifying condition stated). Alcohol-based hand rub increases the risk of skin dryness specifically with frequent use, and only unless emollients, humectants, or other skin-conditioning agents are added to the formulation. At a more general level, page 27 states that hand-hygiene agents as a class increase risk of skin dryness in health-care workers when use is increased — a population-specific but agent-nonspecific framing, whereas page 10 is product-specific (soap vs. alcohol-based rub).

Preventive recommendations: glycerol prevents skin dryness when 1%–3% glycerol is added to alcohol-based formulations — the only numeric threshold in the community. Separately, skin-care lotion prevents skin dryness in health-care workers where use of hand-hygiene agents is increased. Practically, this supports two complementary QI levers: (1) product selection/procurement favouring alcohol-based rubs formulated with 1%–3% glycerol or other emollients/humectants/skin-conditioning agents, and (2) provision of skin-care lotions to staff in settings or periods of intensified hand hygiene.

What is NOT established: the community does not specify frequency, dose, or timing of lotion application; does not name particular lotion products, humectants other than glycerol, or brands; and does not compare the relative magnitude of dryness risk between non-antimicrobial soap and alcohol-based rub. It says nothing about antimicrobial soaps, dermatitis, irritant or allergic contact reactions, glove use, compatibility of lotions with glove or antiseptic products, patient (as opposed to worker) skin outcomes, effects on hand hygiene compliance, or infection outcomes. No pediatric, surgical-scrub, or intraoperative-specific conditions are attached.

title: Antimicrobial Prophylaxis Timing and Surgical Indications
summary:
This community centres on antimicrobial prophylaxis to prevent surgical site, wound, postoperative and selected obstetric/streptococcal infections, and on when in the perioperative pathway it should be given.

Timing is the dominant thread. CDC states dosing must be timed so a bactericidal serum/tissue concentration exists when the incision is made, and specifies no more than 30 minutes before skin incision in adults. WHO and AUGS use a 60-minute window before skin incision (WHO: most effective when serum/tissue levels are achieved within one hour prior to incision; redose if given longer than 60 minutes before). ERAS Society places prophylaxis intraoperatively, within 1 hour of incision, as a surgical site infection bundle element. CDC also limits prophylaxis to during the operation, with no additional doses after incision closure in clean and clean-contaminated procedures even with a drain in place (including prosthetic joint arthroplasty patients on systemic corticosteroids or other immunosuppression). WHO frames the timing as immediate preoperative/perioperative, before wound contamination occurs.

Indications: NICE specifies clean surgery involving a prosthesis or implant, clean-contaminated and contaminated surgery, given before surgery. CDC adds most neurosurgical operations, cardiac operations including pacemaker placement, vascular operations with prosthetic arterial graft or lower-extremity revascularisation, breast operations (advocated by some), operations entering a hollow viscus under controlled conditions, and clean operations where intravascular prosthetic material or a prosthetic joint is inserted or SSI would be catastrophic. WHO covers elective and emergency caesarean section, manual removal of the placenta, preterm prelabour rupture of membranes, and short-duration anti-staphylococcal prophylaxis in cardiac surgery. AUGS covers hysterectomy (cefazolin 2 g IV) and midurethral sling (Norwegian registry evidence).

A clear divergence: CDC (p13) times the caesarean dose immediately after umbilical cord clamping, whereas WHO and CDC p1/p8 recommend administration before skin incision. RCOG addresses non-surgical prophylaxis: for healthcare workers exposed to respiratory secretions of women with group A streptococcal infection, and routinely postpartum for their babies. WHO notes prophylaxis for recurrent UTI in pregnancy only within rigorous research.

Not established: specific agents or doses beyond cefazolin 2 g IV, weight-based or redosing regimens, duration limits in contaminated surgery, comparative effectiveness between the 30- and 60-minute windows, or paediatric guidance.
key_entities: clean surgery involving placement of a prosthesis or implant

title: Hand hygiene agents and skin irritation
summary:
This community centres on skin irritation as an occupational hazard of hand hygiene and skin antisepsis agents used by perioperative staff, and on the formulation strategies that mitigate it. Three agent classes are named as irritation risks: non-antimicrobial soap, iodine, and alcohol. For alcohol, the WHO guideline attaches an explicit condition — risk of skin irritation arises if alcoholic antiseptics are used repeatedly — which is the corpus's only dose/frequency-related qualifier. The CDC guideline lists non-antimicrobial soap and iodine as irritants without any stated frequency, concentration or population condition.

On the preventive side, the CDC guideline supports emollients. Two related recommendations appear: (1) adding emollients to soap preparations prevents skin irritation, conditioned on the emollients actually being added; and (2) emollients prevent skin irritation for health-care workers in clinical settings when contained in alcohol-based rinses or gels, compared with soaps or antimicrobial detergents. The second statement is the most population-specific in the community (health-care workers in clinical settings) and is explicitly comparative, positioning emollient-containing alcohol-based rinses/gels as gentler than soaps or antimicrobial detergents.

Contributing bodies are CDC (Table 1, p10) for all irritant and emollient statements except alcohol, and WHO (Table 1, p56) for repeated alcoholic antiseptic use. They are not in direct conflict, but they emphasise different things: CDC frames alcohol-based products favourably when emollient-containing, whereas WHO flags repeated alcoholic antiseptic exposure as itself irritating — a nuance educators should reconcile by stressing emollient-containing alcohol formulations.

What this community does not establish: no specific emollient ingredients, concentrations, or alcohol percentages; no thresholds for what counts as "repeated" use; no timings or frequency limits; no gynecologic- or surgical-patient-specific populations (the only named population is health-care workers); no comparative effectiveness for antimicrobial efficacy, dermatitis severity grading, product selection protocols, or skin-assessment monitoring. It also says nothing about chlorhexidine, glove-related irritation, or allergy versus irritant contact dermatitis.

title: Dressing selection and periwound maceration prevention
summary:
This community addresses a single, tightly focused wound-care theme: how dressing choice and application technique influence periwound skin maceration and secondary wound infection in surgical/perioperative wound management. Three of the four relations converge on maceration as the harm to be avoided, and one extends the concern to infection risk from retained exudate.

Key recommendations and their qualifiers: (1) Transparent film dressings increase the risk of skin maceration specifically when the wound has more than minimal drainage — the condition is exudate volume, so film dressings are positioned for dry or minimally draining wounds only. (2) For patients treated with hydrogel dressings, maceration is prevented by covering only the wound bed and not the surrounding intact skin; this is a technique-level recommendation tied to a defined population (hydrogel users). (3) Optilock polymer dressing prevents skin maceration, presented without a restricting population or condition. (4) The same optilock polymer dressing increases risk of wound infection when a drainage-filled pad is allowed to remain on the wound surface for extended periods — i.e., its protective effect is contingent on timely change once the pad is saturated.

Contributing bodies: all four relations derive from a single source corpus, OpenRN (Nursing Skills / Open RN, Textbook 2), from two separate passages — p1151 (film and hydrogel guidance) and p1423 (optilock polymer). There is no inter-organisational disagreement to reconcile; p1151 is more specific about conditions (drainage volume, application boundary), while p1423 is more specific about the temporal failure mode (prolonged retention of a saturated pad).

What this community does NOT establish: no numeric thresholds defining "minimal" versus excessive drainage, no stated dressing change interval or maximum wear time, no comparative ranking of film versus hydrogel versus optilock, no patient risk factors (diabetes, incontinence, obesity, age), no assessment or documentation standards for periwound skin, no treatment pathway once maceration or infection has occurred, and no evidence grading or gynecologic-procedure-specific application.
key_entities: covering only the wound and not surrounding skin

title: Skin Tear Risk and Adhesive Removal
summary: This community represents skin integrity risk in the perioperative gynecologic patient, specifically the causes of skin tears and the single protective intervention named in the corpus: adhesive remover. Three risk factors are established. First, older age increases skin tear risk in older adults whose skin is fragile and nonelastic. Second, long-term corticosteroid therapy increases risk in patients receiving such therapy (no dose, drug name, or duration threshold is specified). Third, adhesive bandages themselves increase risk, with the hazard attached specifically to the moment of bandage removal rather than to application or wear time. The one preventive recommendation is use of an adhesive remover, indicated for elderly patients when removing a transparent film dressing. Together these relations frame a simple practice message for staff education: patients who are elderly or on long-term corticosteroids should be flagged as skin-tear-prone, and any adhesive product — particularly transparent film dressings — should be taken down with an adhesive remover rather than by mechanical traction. All four relations derive from a single guideline body, OpenRN, drawn from two locations in the same volume (Nursing Skills/OpenRN T2 p1113 for the risk factors, p1423 for the adhesive remover recommendation). There is therefore no inter-body disagreement to reconcile; the only difference in granularity is that the p1423 recommendation is narrower in scope than the p1113 risk statements — it names a specific population (elderly) and a specific dressing type (transparent film), whereas the adhesive-bandage risk statement is generic to any adhesive on removal. The community does not establish: any age threshold defining 'older'; corticosteroid drug names, doses, routes, or minimum therapy duration; a validated skin tear risk assessment tool or scoring cutoff; the brand, formulation, or application technique for adhesive remover; timing or frequency of skin assessment; treatment or staging of an existing skin tear; whether adhesive remover mitigates risk in non-elderly or corticosteroid-treated patients; or any gynecologic-procedure-specific or intraoperative positioning guidance.

title: Risk Factors for Postoperative Small Bowel Obstruction
summary:
Clinical theme: This community is a single-outcome risk-factor cluster centred on postoperative small bowel obstruction (SBO) following gynecologic/pelvic surgery. All eight relations are of one type (INCREASES_RISK_OF) converging on SBO, so the theme is risk stratification and surveillance rather than treatment.

Risk factors and their conditions: Two factors carry explicit numeric thresholds and should be captured intraoperatively and from pathology: prolonged operating time, specified as operating time greater than 170 minutes, and increased uterine weight, specified as greater than 250 grams. Six additional factors are listed without thresholds or qualifying populations: perioperative blood transfusion, increasing age, pelvic adhesive disease, concurrent appendectomy performed at the time of the index procedure, non-white race, and prior abdominal or pelvic surgery. Practically, a QI lead could build a post-op SBO watch list flagging patients who received transfusion, had adhesive disease or a concurrent appendectomy, had prior abdominal/pelvic surgery, or crossed either the 170-minute or 250-gram threshold, and ensure nursing handoff and discharge teaching emphasise obstructive symptoms in those patients.

Contributing bodies: All eight relations derive from a single source, AUGS (American Urogynecologic Society) Table 2, page 10. Because only one guideline body contributes, there are no inter-body disagreements, no competing thresholds, and no instance of one society being more specific than another within this community. The specificity gradient is internal to AUGS: it quantifies operating time and uterine weight but leaves age, race, transfusion, adhesive disease, appendectomy, and prior surgery unquantified.

What this community does NOT establish: it gives no baseline or stratified incidence of SBO, no effect sizes, relative risks, or confidence intervals, and no ranking of which factor matters most. It specifies no age cut-off, no transfusion volume or unit threshold, and no definition of extent of adhesive disease. It offers no preventive interventions (for example adhesion barriers, minimally invasive approach, transfusion-sparing strategies), no diagnostic criteria, no monitoring interval or timeframe for SBO onset, and no management or escalation pathway. It also does not state the surgical population or procedure type to which these factors apply, nor does it establish causality as opposed to association.

title: Preventing Surgical Specimen Labelling Errors
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused patient-safety theme: preventing mislabelling of surgical specimens in the perioperative gynecologic setting. All three relations converge on one adverse outcome — specimen labelling error — and describe verification practices that guard against it.

The recommendations are: (1) patient identification using at least two identifiers, specified for the population of patients from whom a surgical specimen is taken; (2) rechecking the patient's wrist identification bands, stated without an attached population or qualifying condition; and (3) cross-checking the requisition form against the specimen, conditioned on being required by the facility and to be performed before the specimen is sent to the pathology department. That last item is the only relation in this community carrying an explicit timing anchor (pre-transfer to pathology) and the only one made contingent on local facility policy rather than applied universally.

Only one guideline body contributes here: WHO (WHO T1, p81), and all three relations originate from the same page. There is therefore no cross-body disagreement to reconcile, and no second source offering a competing or more granular specification. Within the WHO material itself, granularity varies: the two-identifier recommendation is population-scoped, the requisition cross-check is condition- and timing-scoped, and the wrist-band recheck is unscoped, which a QI lead may wish to clarify locally.

What this community does not establish: it names no specific acceptable identifiers (e.g., it does not state whether name, date of birth, or medical record number qualify); it sets no numeric thresholds beyond "at least two" identifiers; it specifies no responsible role (nurse, surgeon, circulator) for performing or witnessing verification; it does not address container labelling content, fixative or preservative choice, specimen handling, transport, or chain-of-custody documentation; it gives no timing for the wrist-band recheck or the two-identifier check relative to specimen collection; and it offers no gynecology-specific provisions, no error rates, no audit measures, and no escalation pathway when a discrepancy is found.
key_entities: patient identification with at least two identifiers
cross-checking requisition form against the specimen
patients from whom a surgical specimen is taken

title: Mobile Device Disinfection Prevents Disease Spread
summary:
Theme: mobile devices (phones, tablets) as fomites in health care facilities, and frequent disinfection as the mitigating control. This is an infection-prevention cluster rather than a perioperative medication or procedural cluster.

Risk statements: mobile devices increase the risk of transmission of pathogens (stated generally, without a specified population or condition) and increase the risk of spread of disease specifically for clients, staff and visitors in health care facilities, conditioned on the devices being brought into the facility.

Recommendations: (1) Wiping mobile devices with disinfectant prevents spread of disease for nurses, when performed frequently. (2) The same wiping recommendation is extended to clients, staff and visitors who bring mobile devices into health care facilities, again conditioned on frequent performance. (3) Phone disinfection prevents spread of disease for clients and visitors when performed frequently AND combined with avoiding touching the face after touching a mobile device — the only relation in this community that pairs disinfection with a behavioural adjunct.

Contributing bodies: all relations derive from a single source, OpenRN Nursing Skills (Text 2), with one edge pair traceable to p642. There is therefore no inter-guideline disagreement; the differences are in granularity within one source. The p642-anchored statements are the most population-explicit (clients, staff and visitors bringing devices in), the nurse-directed statement is the most role-specific, and the phone-disinfection statement is the most behaviourally specific.

Not established: no named disinfectant agent, concentration, or product class (e.g., alcohol or quaternary ammonium wipes); no contact/wet time; no numeric frequency or interval defining “frequently”; no cleaning technique or device-compatibility guidance; no named pathogens or outcome rates; no perioperative- or operating-room-specific rules (e.g., device restrictions in sterile fields); no policy or enforcement mechanism; and no evidence grading or effect size for the preventive claims.

title: Stage 1 Pressure Injury Detection Across Skin Tones
summary: This community represents early pressure injury identification, specifically stage 1 pressure injury, and centres on two linked ideas: causation by prolonged pressure, and detection through multimodal skin assessment when visual erythema is unreliable. The graph asserts that prolonged pressure increases the risk of stage 1 pressure injury; no population restriction or qualifying condition is attached to this causal relation, so it is stated as a general perioperative/positioning risk. The second relation is population-specific: assessment for pain, firmness, softness, temperature and colour changes detects stage 1 pressure injury in clients with dark pigmentation. The practical teaching point for educators is that in darkly pigmented skin, nurses should not rely on blanching or classic erythema alone but should palpate for firmness or boggy softness, compare local temperature, elicit reports of pain or discomfort, and look for any colour change relative to surrounding skin. Both relations derive from a single contributing source, OpenRN Nursing Skills (Volume 2, p718); no other guideline body is represented in this community, so there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile, and no source is more specific than another — the only specificity gradient is internal, with the assessment recommendation narrowed to dark-pigmentation clients while the pressure-risk statement remains unrestricted. Importantly, the community does not establish any thresholds or timings: no duration of pressure that constitutes 'prolonged', no repositioning interval, no reassessment frequency, and no intraoperative time limit. It names no drugs, dressings, support surfaces, offloading devices, or risk-assessment instruments (e.g., no Braden or Munro scoring). It does not describe stages beyond stage 1, does not address deep tissue injury or mucosal injury, does not specify anatomical sites or surgical positions, does not quantify sensitivity of the assessment techniques, and does not link detection to any documentation, escalation, or treatment pathway. Quality-improvement work would therefore need supplementary sources for repositioning schedules, device selection, and outcome measurement.
key_entities: assessment for pain, firmness, softness, temperature and colour changes

title: Staples versus sutures: wound closure risks
summary:
This community represents a narrow but practically important perioperative theme: the comparative risk profile of surgical staples versus sutures for skin/wound closure, and the consequent implications for closure-method selection and postoperative wound surveillance. Only one relationship type appears here — staples INCREASES_RISK_OF adverse wound outcomes — with two distinct outcomes attached.

The two recommendations are: (1) staples increase the risk of scarring, explicitly conditioned on comparison with sutures (OpenRN, T2 p1181); and (2) staples increase the risk of wound dehiscence when compared with sutures for wound closure, with the population stated broadly as patients having surgery across different types of surgery (NICE, T1 p25). Together they support counselling patients about cosmetic outcome and closure choice, and prioritising dehiscence assessment in stapled wounds during postoperative and discharge teaching.

Two guideline bodies contribute. NICE (T1) is the more specific source on population scope, generalising the dehiscence signal across surgical types rather than to a single procedure, and it names the comparison explicitly as sutures for wound closure. The OpenRN nursing text (T2) contributes the cosmetic outcome (scarring) and states the suture comparison but attaches no population qualifier. The two do not conflict; they are complementary, each naming a different harm, and both point in the same direction — staples carry higher risk than sutures on the outcomes named.

What this community does NOT establish: no magnitude of risk, relative risk, absolute event rate, or numeric threshold is given for either scarring or dehiscence. It specifies no gynecologic-specific population, no laparotomy versus laparoscopic distinction, no caesarean or obesity subgroup, and no BMI or wound-classification cut-off. It does not address staple removal timing, dressing regimens, antiseptic or antibiotic prophylaxis, negative-pressure wound therapy, or any drug. It offers no recommendation on speed of closure, cost, or infection risk, and does not state a formal preference or grade of recommendation for sutures over staples — only the directional risk comparisons above.
key_entities: patients having surgery across different types of surgery

title: Sterile Barriers Preventing Intraoperative Contamination
summary:
This community represents the theme of sterile barrier precautions — specifically sterile gowns and sterile drapes — as physical infection-prevention measures in the operative field. Two barrier items and two distinct outcomes are linked: prevention of surgical site infection (SSI) and prevention of bacterial contamination of the surgical field.

Recommendations, with populations and conditions:
• Sterile gown prevents surgical site infection for the operating team, with the explicit condition that the gown is worn during the operation (WHO, T1 p68). The population here is the operative team rather than the patient, and the benefit is conditioned on use throughout the procedure.
• Sterile gown prevents bacterial contamination of the surgical field for scrubbed surgical team members (CDC, T1 p15). CDC narrows the population from "operating team" generally to those who are scrubbed.
• Sterile drape prevents bacterial contamination of the surgical field for surgical patients (CDC, T1 p15). This is the only patient-directed barrier recommendation in the community.

Contributing bodies: WHO (T1 p68) and CDC (T1 p15). The two are complementary rather than contradictory. WHO frames the gown's benefit in terms of the harder clinical endpoint (SSI) and is more specific about timing (worn during the operation). CDC is more specific about population (scrubbed surgical team members) and adds the patient-side barrier (drapes), but frames the benefit at the intermediate endpoint of field contamination rather than SSI. There is no direct disagreement, and no source contradicts another on gown or drape use.

What this community does NOT establish: it specifies no gown or drape materials, impermeability standards, reuse versus single-use policy, number of layers, or draping technique; no thresholds, durations beyond "during the operation," or change/re-gowning intervals. It does not link sterile drapes to reduced SSI (only to field contamination), does not address gowning for unscrubbed circulating staff, and includes no gynecologic-procedure-specific qualifiers, no antimicrobial or antiseptic agents, and no data on effect size, comparative effectiveness, or evidence grading.
key_entities: bacterial contamination of the surgical field

title: Neuraxial anaesthesia safety: LMWH timing, asepsis
summary:
This community centres on procedural safety around spinal (neuraxial) anaesthesia in the perioperative gynaecologic setting, joining two distinct safety concerns: pharmacological thromboprophylaxis timing and aseptic technique for invasive procedures.

The dominant recommendation, repeated across four RCOG relations (Table 1, pages 5, 19 and 20), is that low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) should NOT be given for 4 hours after spinal anaesthesia, and equally not for 4 hours after removal of an epidural catheter. Two of these edges are framed as a timing dependency (LMWH dosing is scheduled relative to the neuraxial event), and one page (p19) frames the same 4-hour window as a temporary contraindication to LMWH following use of spinal anaesthesia. Functionally these agree: the 4-hour interval is the single explicit threshold in this community, applied to patients receiving both LMWH thromboprophylaxis and neuraxial anaesthesia or epidural catheterisation.

The second strand comes from WHO (Table 1, p25), which states that sterile practice applies to spinal anaesthesia and, in parallel, to insertion of a central venous line — extending the asepsis principle beyond neuraxial blocks to other invasive line placement.

Contributing bodies: RCOG (LMWH–neuraxial timing, most specific, with a numeric interval and inclusion of epidural catheter removal) and WHO (asepsis, stated as a general principle without technique detail, timing or population qualifiers). They do not conflict; they address different risk domains — spinal/epidural haematoma versus infection.

What the community does NOT establish: no LMWH dose, agent name, frequency or duration; no pre-procedure interval (i.e., how long before spinal anaesthesia LMWH must be withheld); no guidance on catheter insertion versus removal beyond the removal statement; no thresholds for renal impairment, weight, BMI or bleeding risk; no defined patient subgroups (e.g., caesarean, oncology, VTE history); no specification of what sterile practice comprises (hand hygiene, skin prep agent, drapes, checklists); and no monitoring, escalation or documentation requirements for suspected spinal haematoma.

title: Pelvic Floor Muscle Training for Incontinence
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: the role of pelvic floor muscle strength in urinary continence, and pelvic muscle (Kegel) exercise as both a preventive and therapeutic nursing intervention. Three relations, all drawn from the same source corpus (OpenRN Nursing Skills/Fundamentals, Volume T2), link one risk factor, one intervention, and two outcome states.

The causal premise is that weak pelvic floor muscles increase the risk of stress urinary incontinence (OpenRN T2 p1183); no population qualifier or threshold of weakness is attached. Against that risk, pelvic muscle exercise is recommended in two ways. First, as prevention: pelvic muscle exercise prevents stress urinary incontinence (OpenRN T2 p1162), stated without population or condition restriction — i.e., framed as a general preventive measure rather than one limited to postpartum, postmenopausal, or postoperative gynecologic patients. Second, as treatment: pelvic muscle exercise treats urinary incontinence specifically in clients who already have urinary incontinence (OpenRN T2 p1430). Note the difference in outcome specificity — the preventive claim names the stress subtype, while the therapeutic claim addresses urinary incontinence broadly, and only the therapeutic claim carries an explicit population condition.

Only one guideline body contributes here (OpenRN), so there are no cross-body disagreements to reconcile; the variation is internal, across three separate pages, where p1162 and p1183 speak to stress incontinence and p1430 to incontinence generally.

What this community does not establish: no exercise prescription — no number of repetitions, sets, hold times, daily frequency, or duration of therapy before reassessment; no instruction on verifying correct muscle isolation or use of biofeedback. It names no drugs, no pessaries, no surgical alternatives, and no perioperative timing (pre- versus post-hysterectomy or prolapse repair). It defines no measure or threshold of "weak" pelvic floor muscles, no expected effect size or continence outcome metric, and no populations for whom the exercises are contraindicated or ineffective (e.g., urge, overflow, or neurogenic incontinence). Educators should supplement with an explicit technique-and-dosing protocol.

title: Stroke and Death Risk from Medications
summary:
This community centres on stroke (plus associated death and downstream respiratory deterioration) as an adverse outcome that is partly modifiable and partly iatrogenic. Three strands appear. (1) Prevention and lifestyle: RNAO (Tier 2, p41) states that lifestyle modification prevents stroke when interventions are combined to achieve optimal blood pressure values; RNAO (p51) identifies binge drinking as increasing stroke risk specifically in young persons who consumed alcohol on weekends and holidays. (2) Medication-related risk: OpenRN (Tier 2) attributes increased stroke risk to all NSAIDs except aspirin, with risk higher when taken in greater doses or for longer than directed (p825 repeats the class caution without the dose qualifier). OpenRN p468 links antipsychotic medications generally, and brexpiprazole specifically, to increased risk of both stroke and death in older adults/patients with dementia or dementia-related psychosis. (3) Fatal administration error: WHO (Tier 1, p157) states vincristine is contraindicated with spinal administration and that accidental intrathecal/spinal administration in patients receiving chemotherapy increases risk of death. (4) Recognition and sequelae: OpenRN p368 supports BEFAST stroke assessment to detect stroke in individuals suspected of experiencing a stroke, and p1285 notes stroke increases risk of acute respiratory failure.

Contributing bodies: RNAO (primary prevention, population risk behaviours), OpenRN (pharmacologic risk, assessment, complications), WHO (high-alert medication safety). They are complementary rather than contradictory; RNAO is more specific about the modifiable-risk population (young weekend/holiday drinkers, blood-pressure targets), while OpenRN is more specific about drug classes and the geriatric dementia population, and WHO is the only source addressing route-of-administration error.

Not established: no numeric thresholds (blood pressure values, alcohol quantities, NSAID doses/durations), no timing for BEFAST use or treatment windows, no thrombolysis, imaging, or acute management pathway, no sensitivity/specificity for BEFAST, and no guidance on alternatives to antipsychotics in dementia. Nothing here is specific to perioperative gynecologic care, and no relation links these risks to surgery, anaesthesia, or pregnancy.

title: Subtotal Hysterectomy Choice in PPH
summary:
This community captures a single, tightly scoped surgical decision theme: which type of hysterectomy to perform when a woman with postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) requires hysterectomy as definitive management. The only contributing source is RCOG (Table/Section T1, p26).

Main recommendation: subtotal hysterectomy TREATS postpartum haemorrhage in the population of women with PPH requiring hysterectomy. The condition attached is important and should be taught verbatim: subtotal hysterectomy is the preferred procedure 'unless there is trauma to the cervix or a morbidly adherent placenta in the lower segment.' The paired relation states the corollary explicitly — subtotal hysterectomy is CONTRAINDICATED_WITH a morbidly adherent placenta in the lower segment, again for women with PPH requiring hysterectomy. Together these two relations mean the nurse's mental model should be: subtotal (supracervical) hysterectomy is the default, faster, lower-morbidity option; cervical trauma or a lower-segment morbidly adherent placenta are the two named exceptions that push the operation toward a more extensive procedure.

Guideline bodies: only RCOG contributes here, so there are no inter-body agreements or conflicts to reconcile within this community. RCOG is specific about the two anatomical exceptions but no other body is represented for comparison, and no differing level of specificity can be demonstrated.

What this community does NOT establish: it names no alternative operation (total hysterectomy is not named as the entity to substitute), no blood-loss threshold, transfusion trigger, haemodynamic parameter or timing/decision-to-incision interval for proceeding to hysterectomy. It specifies no preceding escalation steps — no uterotonics (e.g. oxytocin, ergometrine, misoprostol, carboprost), no tranexamic acid, no balloon tamponade, compression sutures, or arterial ligation/embolisation. It gives no consent, staffing, seniority, anaesthetic, cell-salvage, or postoperative/critical-care recommendations, no fertility-loss counselling content, and no outcome data or evidence grading. Educators should therefore use this community only to teach the procedure-selection rule and its two exceptions, drawing thresholds and escalation sequences from other communities in the corpus.
key_entities: morbidly adherent placenta in the lower segment

title: Airway Suctioning Risks and Oxygenation Management
summary:
This community represents airway clearance and oxygenation management, centering on suctioning as both a therapeutic intervention and a source of iatrogenic harm, with supplemental oxygen as a parallel treatment.

Therapeutic recommendations: both suctioning and supplemental oxygen are indicated as treatments for respiratory failure (OpenRN T2 p1285). In patients with a tracheostomy tube, suctioning performed through the tracheostomy tube to remove mucus prevents airway obstruction by mucus (OpenRN T2 p1285) — the only population-specific therapeutic indication stated here.

Risk profile: suctioning increases the risk of arrhythmia, trauma, hypoxemia, and atelectasis (OpenRN T2 p1296). A distinct population-conditioned harm is identified for clients with terminal secretions, in whom suctioning increases risk of agitation and distress (OpenRN T2 p1288) — implying suctioning may be inappropriate at end of life, though the graph frames this only as elevated risk, not as a contraindication.

Technique/timing: the single concrete threshold is a recovery period between suction catheter passes, applied to suctioning, with recovery of 30–60 seconds between passes (OpenRN T2 p1296). This sits alongside the p1296 risk list and functions as the mitigation for hypoxemia, arrhythmia, and atelectasis.

Contributing bodies: all relations derive from a single source corpus, OpenRN Textbook 2, across three pages. There is no cross-body disagreement to reconcile; instead there is a division of labour by page — p1285 supplies indications, p1296 supplies procedural risks and the 30–60 second recovery timing (the most specific guidance), and p1288 is the most population-specific, uniquely addressing terminal secretions.

Not established: no suction pressures, catheter sizes, maximum pass duration or number of passes; no oxygen flow rates, delivery devices, or SpO2 targets for supplemental oxygen; no pre-oxygenation protocol; no monitoring parameters or stop criteria; no explicit contraindications; no gynecologic or perioperative population specificity; and no comparative effectiveness between suctioning and supplemental oxygen in respiratory failure.
key_entities: recovery period between suction catheter passes

title: General Anaesthesia Risks and Oxygen Management
summary:
This community centres on the risk profile of general anaesthesia and the compensating role of supplemental oxygen in perioperative and obstetric care. General anaesthesia is repeatedly framed as a risk amplifier: for complications of anaesthesia even in healthy patients undergoing general anaesthesia (WHO T1 p8), for aspiration in patients undergoing anaesthesia (WHO T1 p37), and for venous thromboembolism in surgical patients specifically when compared with regional anaesthesia (NICE T1 p19). RCOG adds an obstetric layer: compared with regional anaesthesia, general anaesthesia increases maternal morbidity and maternal mortality in obstetric patients (RCOG T1 p24), and it is also linked to postpartum haemorrhage (RCOG T1 p10). The practical counterbalance is oxygen: WHO recommends supplemental oxygen for all patients undergoing general anaesthesia (WHO T1 p25, p31), and its use to treat oxygen desaturation in patients undergoing anaesthesia if oxygen saturation falls (WHO T1 p22). OpenRN extends oxygen therapy beyond theatre, as treatment for respiratory failure (p1285) and for hypoxaemia in clients at risk of pneumonia due to immobility, given as prescribed and especially during ambulation (p958). One preoperative caution appears: oral fluid intake is temporarily contraindicated in volume-depleted surgical patients when a general anaesthetic is impending (WHO T1 p42) — a fasting/aspiration-risk consideration that pairs with the aspiration relation.

Contributing bodies are WHO (intraoperative anaesthesia safety and oxygen; most specific on universal oxygen and fasting), RCOG (obstetric maternal outcomes), NICE (VTE risk and the regional-versus-general comparison), and OpenRN (ward-level oxygen indications). RCOG and NICE both favour regional over general anaesthesia comparatively, but for different outcomes; WHO does not make that comparison and instead focuses on mitigation.

The community does not establish oxygen flow rates, delivery devices, FiO2 targets, or a numeric saturation threshold defining 'falls'; nor fasting durations, VTE prophylaxis agents, PPH management drugs, or evidence that supplemental oxygen reduces the maternal, VTE or aspiration risks listed.

title: Surgical Care Raises Five Complication Risks
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: surgical care itself is a risk exposure, and the guideline corpus attributes five distinct postoperative complication categories to it. All five relations share the same subject (surgical care), the same population (surgical patients), the same relation type (INCREASES_RISK_OF), and the same source location (WHO Technical Manual 1, p228). The named risks are: respiratory complication, postoperative sepsis, thromboembolic complication, surgical site infection, and cardiovascular complication.

For a nurse educator, this cluster is best used as a framing or orientation model — it defines the domains that perioperative gynecologic nursing assessment and monitoring must cover for any patient undergoing surgery. It supports teaching a five-domain surveillance checklist (airway/breathing, infection at the wound, systemic infection/sepsis, venous thromboembolism, and cardiac/haemodynamic status) as the baseline scope of postoperative vigilance.

Only one guideline body contributes: WHO (Technical Manual, Volume 1, page 228). Because there is a single contributing source, there are no inter-body disagreements, no differences in specificity between organisations, and no competing thresholds to reconcile within this community.

Important limitations — what this community does NOT establish: it gives no incidence or absolute risk figures for any of the five complications; no risk stratification (no distinction by age, ASA class, comorbidity, procedure type, laparoscopic versus open, or emergency versus elective); and no gynecologic-procedure-specific qualifiers despite the corpus context. Critically, it names no preventive or therapeutic interventions — no antibiotic prophylaxis agents, doses or timing windows, no thromboprophylaxis drugs (e.g. no heparin or LMWH regimens), no mechanical prophylaxis, no mobilisation or incentive spirometry protocols, and no monitoring intervals, vital-sign thresholds, or escalation criteria. It also does not specify the perioperative phase (intraoperative versus early or late postoperative) in which each risk peaks, nor any conditions modifying the risk beyond the blanket condition "surgical patients." Any protocol built from this theme must draw thresholds, drugs and timings from other communities in the corpus.

title: Risk Factors for Severe Complication After Exenteration
summary:
This small community represents a single, narrowly scoped clinical theme: preoperative risk stratification for severe postoperative complications in patients undergoing total pelvic exenteration. Two risk relations are captured, both drawn from the same population (patients undergoing total pelvic exenteration) and both pointing to the same outcome node, severe complication. First, surgical complexity increases the risk of severe complication. Second, the presence of three or more comorbidities increases the risk of severe complication — this is the only explicit numeric threshold in the community, and it is a count of comorbid conditions, not a score or index. The practical implication for a nurse educator or QI lead is that exenteration candidates should be screened for comorbidity burden (with three or more as the flagged cut-point) and that the anticipated extent/complexity of the planned resection should be treated as an independent contributor to complication risk, supporting more intensive preoperative counselling, prehabilitation planning, and postoperative surveillance intensity.

Only one guideline body contributes: the ERAS Society (Table 1, p11). Because there is a single source, there are no inter-society disagreements, no competing thresholds, and no instance where one body is more specific than another; all specificity here (the population restriction to total pelvic exenteration, and the ≥3 comorbidities threshold) comes from ERAS Society alone.

The community does not establish a great deal. It defines no drugs, doses, fluids, antibiotics, thromboprophylaxis agents, or analgesic regimens. It gives no timings — no preoperative assessment window, no duration of monitoring, no length-of-stay or follow-up interval. It does not define what constitutes a 'severe complication' (no Clavien-Dindo grade or equivalent), does not quantify the magnitude of risk (no odds ratios, relative risks, or absolute event rates), and does not name which specific comorbidities count toward the three-or-more threshold. It does not define or grade 'surgical complexity.' Crucially, it recommends no intervention or mitigation strategy, and it does not extend these risk relations to gynecologic surgery populations other than total pelvic exenteration.

title: Surgical uterine evacuation: procedural risks
summary:
This small community represents the theme of procedural harm associated with surgical evacuation of the uterus in women with retained products of conception (RPOC). Both relations in the community are risk relations originating from a single intervention node — surgical evacuation of the uterus — and both are conditioned on the same population: women with retained products of conception. The two identified harms are uterine perforation (an acute intraoperative mechanical injury) and Asherman's syndrome (intrauterine adhesions, a longer-term consequence with implications for menstruation and future fertility). Practically, this means that when counselling or consenting a woman with RPOC for surgical management, and when planning post-procedure observation and follow-up, nurses should be alert to and document these two specific risks: signs suggestive of perforation in the immediate perioperative period, and later menstrual or fertility complaints that could indicate intrauterine adhesions.

Only one guideline body contributes here: the RCOG (Tier 1, page 30). Because the community draws on a single source and a single page, there are no inter-guideline disagreements, no competing risk estimates, and no instance of one body being more granular than another — the RCOG statements are the sole level of specificity available.

Importantly, the community does not establish a great deal that a QI lead might want. It gives no numerical risk magnitudes, incidence rates or thresholds for either perforation or Asherman's syndrome; no timing or gestational-age criteria; no named drugs or comparison with medical or expectant management of RPOC; no technique-specific detail (e.g. suction versus sharp curettage, ultrasound guidance, cervical preparation); and no operator-experience, parity, infection or prior-surgery modifiers. It also specifies no preventive measures, monitoring intervals, escalation criteria, consent wording, or follow-up schedule, and says nothing about outcomes such as haemorrhage, infection, subsequent subfertility or recurrence. Any protocol built from this theme must therefore return to the full RCOG text for actionable detail.
key_entities: women with retained products of conception

title: Surgical Escalation for Refractory Postpartum Haemorrhage
summary: This community centres on surgical intervention as the escalation step in the management of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH), plus one unrelated note on surgery as a risk factor for constipation. The core recommendation, repeated across two guideline bodies and four separate passages, is that surgical intervention treats PPH in women with postpartum haemorrhage when bleeding is not controlled by less invasive measures. WHO (T1 p19 and p28) frames the trigger as bleeding that 'does not stop in spite of uterotonics and other conservative interventions', explicitly naming uterotonic therapy and conservative measures as the prerequisites that must have failed. RCOG (T1 p6 and p26) frames the trigger as failure of 'pharmacological measures' to control the haemorrhage, and adds a timing qualifier that WHO does not: surgery should be 'initiated sooner rather than later' (RCOG T1 p26). RCOG T1 p6 states the condition without specifying a population, whereas RCOG T1 p26 and both WHO entries specify women with PPH. So the two bodies agree on the substantive escalation principle; WHO is more specific about which prior interventions define failure (uterotonics plus conservative measures), while RCOG is more specific about urgency of timing. A separate relation from OpenRN (T2 p1416) records that surgical intervention increases the risk of constipation, with no population, threshold or timeframe attached — a general postoperative consideration rather than a PPH-specific one. What this community does NOT establish: no named surgical procedures (e.g. no mention of balloon tamponade, uterine artery ligation, B-Lynch suture or hysterectomy), no named uterotonic drugs or doses, no blood-loss volume or haemodynamic thresholds defining 'bleeding does not stop', no defined time window for 'sooner rather than later', no sequencing or preference among surgical options, and no outcome data on effectiveness, mortality or morbidity. It also does not link the constipation risk to obstetric surgery specifically, nor offer any bowel-care or prevention guidance.

title: Surgical Mask Use Across Care Settings
summary:
This community centers on a single intervention — the surgical mask — and the several distinct protective purposes attributed to it across the corpus: source control of respiratory secretions, personal protection of health care personnel, protection of the sterile field during operations, and protection of immunocompromised clients.

Infection-prevention (OpenRN Tier 2, p203, p642) recommendations: apply a surgical mask to coughing persons as source control to contain secretions, preventing respiratory infection transmission; place masks on coughing patients in public areas as part of respiratory hygiene to prevent dissemination of infectious respiratory secretions; have health care personnel wear masks consistent with standard precautions and droplet transmission precautions to prevent contact with infectious material; and mask clients in reverse (protective) isolation during transport outside the room to prevent infection.

Perioperative recommendations (WHO Tier 1, p64, p68): the operating team should wear a surgical mask during the operation to prevent surgical site infection, framed at p64 as preventing surgical site contamination by surgical teams — with the explicit caveat that the association between mask use and surgical infections is less clear.

Contributing bodies: WHO covers the intraoperative/surgical-team application and is the only source that qualifies the strength of the evidence; OpenRN is more granular about non-operative populations (coughing persons and patients, health care personnel, reverse-isolation clients) and links mask use to named precaution categories (standard, droplet) and to respiratory hygiene and patient transport.

What this community does not establish: no mask type beyond "surgical mask" (no N95/respirator comparison), no thresholds for duration of wear, change intervals, or timing relative to incision or anesthesia induction; no specification of which surgical procedures, patient risk strata, or gynecologic populations require masking; no drugs, doses, or antiseptic co-interventions; no efficacy magnitude or outcome rates; and no resolution of the WHO uncertainty about whether operating-team mask use actually reduces surgical site infection. It also does not address eye protection, gowns, gloves, or removal/disposal technique.

title: Surgical Safety Checklist Across Perioperative Phases
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused theme: the WHO-style Surgical Safety Checklist as a perioperative harm-prevention tool, and where in the operative timeline its component pauses occur.

Main recommendations. For all surgical patients, the checklist is initiated in the preoperative phase — specifically before induction of anaesthesia (WHO T1 p106). Two further checkpoints fall in the intraoperative phase: after induction but before surgical incision, and during or immediately after wound closure before the patient leaves the operating room (WHO T1 p106). Framed at the level of the whole perioperative period, WHO T1 p87 describes the same three timings for operating teams: before induction of anaesthesia, before skin incision, and before the patient leaves the operating room. The claimed benefit is conditional on team behaviour: the checklist prevents avoidable surgical harm for surgical patients only when teams consistently follow the critical safety steps (WHO T1 p106). OpenRN T2 p378 states the outcome more bluntly for surgical clients — the checklist prevents surgical injury and death — without attaching a condition.

Contributing bodies and differences. Two sources contribute: WHO (Tier 1, pp. 87 and 106) and OpenRN (Tier 2, p. 378). WHO is markedly more specific: it names the three discrete timings, distinguishes preoperative from intraoperative placement, addresses operating teams as the actors, and qualifies effectiveness with the requirement of consistent adherence to critical safety steps. OpenRN contributes only a broad outcome claim (prevention of surgical injury and death) for surgical clients, with no timing, actor, or adherence condition — a stronger, unqualified benefit statement than WHO's conditional wording.

What is not established. Nothing here specifies checklist item content, who reads or signs it, documentation requirements, or escalation when an item fails. No gynecologic-specific adaptations, drugs, doses, or numeric thresholds (e.g., antibiotic timing minutes, VTE scores) appear. No effect sizes, compliance targets, audit methods, or postoperative/post-anaesthesia-care-unit checkpoints are given, and no pediatric, obstetric, or emergency-case exceptions are addressed.

title: Preoperative Surgical Hand Scrub Practices
summary: This community represents preoperative surgical hand hygiene — specifically the surgical scrub of the hands and forearms performed by surgical team members before entering the sterile field, and the nail-care step that precedes it. Two linked recommendations define the theme. First, the surgical scrub of the hands and forearms is situated in the preoperative phase: it applies to surgical team members and is to be performed for at least 2 to 5 minutes using an appropriate antiseptic. Second, cleaning underneath the fingernails is timing-dependent on the scrub: for surgical team members, subungual cleaning is done prior to the first surgical scrub of the day, establishing a sequence in which nail cleaning precedes (rather than accompanies or follows) that initial scrub. Together these define a minimum duration threshold (2–5 minutes), a defined population (surgical team members, not patients or unscrubbed circulating staff), a phase (preoperative), and an ordering rule tied to the first scrub of the day. The only contributing guideline body in this community is the CDC (CDC T1, p21); both relations derive from that single source and page, so there are no inter-body agreements, conflicts, or differences in specificity to reconcile here — no AORN, WHO, ACOG, or institutional guidance is represented. Importantly, the community does not establish which antiseptic agents qualify as "appropriate" (no chlorhexidine gluconate, povidone-iodine, or alcohol-based surgical rub products, concentrations, or comparative efficacy are named), nor does it specify scrub technique, brush versus brushless methods, tools for subungual cleaning, artificial nail or jewellery restrictions, duration requirements for subsequent scrubs after the first of the day, drying or gowning/gloving steps, or any monitoring, documentation, or compliance-audit expectations. It also does not link scrub practice to surgical site infection outcomes, gynecologic procedure types, or patient-level populations. Educators should therefore treat this as a narrow, duration-and-sequence anchor for scrub policy and source agent selection, technique, and audit criteria from other sections of the corpus.
key_entities: surgical scrub of hands and forearms
first surgical scrub of the day

title: Surgical Scrubbing for Perioperative Infection Prevention
summary:
This community represents a narrow but foundational perioperative theme: surgical hand scrubbing (surgical hand antisepsis) as a barrier to surgical site and theatre-acquired infection, and its placement within the preoperative phase of the operative timeline. Only two relations populate the community, both centred on the single intervention 'surgical scrubbing'.

Main recommendations. (1) WHO (Tool 1, p99) links surgical scrubbing to prevention of infection, with the population specified as staff entering theatres, and the condition framed as an access-control measure: the preventive effect is attached to staff being prevented from entering theatres until appropriate cleansing techniques have been followed. This is an environmental/behavioural control statement — scrubbing gates entry to the theatre. (2) CDC (Tool 1, p11) places surgical scrubbing in the preoperative phase, with a more tightly defined population — members of the surgical team who have direct contact with the sterile operating field or with sterile instruments or supplies — and a precise timing condition: immediately before donning sterile gowns and gloves.

Contributing bodies and differences. WHO and CDC both contribute, and they are complementary rather than contradictory. WHO is broader in population (all staff entering theatres) and frames scrubbing as an infection-prevention control with an enforcement condition. CDC is more specific on both population (scrubbed team members with direct sterile-field or sterile-supply contact) and timing (immediately before gowning and gloving), making it the better source for procedural sequencing in education and audit.

What this community does NOT establish. It names no antiseptic agents (no chlorhexidine gluconate, povidone-iodine or alcohol-based formulations), no scrub duration or minimum scrub times, no repeat/between-case scrubbing rules, no nail, jewellery or skin-condition requirements, and no water, sink or drying specifications. It gives no effect size, infection-rate threshold or evidence grade for the prevention claim, and does not address intraoperative or postoperative hand hygiene, gloving technique beyond the timing cue, or monitoring and compliance measurement methods.
key_entities: surgical team members with sterile field contact

title: Preoperative Staphylococcus aureus nasal decolonisation
summary: This community covers preoperative decolonisation to prevent Staphylococcus aureus surgical site infection (SSI), drawn entirely from NICE guidance (NICE T1, pages 6 and 20). The consistent recommendation is a paired intervention: nasal mupirocin plus a chlorhexidine body wash, given before the procedure — neither agent appears alone. Populations are specified three ways. First, patients undergoing procedures in which S. aureus is a likely cause of SSI should receive nasal mupirocin in combination with chlorhexidine body wash before the procedure, with the decision made locally taking account of procedure type, patient risk factors and the potential impact of an infection (p6). Second, people identified as carriers of S. aureus should have the mupirocin/chlorhexidine combination before surgery (p20). Third, more broadly, nasal mupirocin with chlorhexidine body wash is described for people having surgery as nasal decolonisation, and chlorhexidine body wash 'should be considered' before the procedure for people having procedures with an increased risk of S. aureus SSI (p20). Two procedure groups are named as increasing risk of S. aureus SSI: cardiac surgery and orthopaedic surgery, both regarded as high risk, with local decisions made jointly between surgical and infection control teams. Only one guideline body (NICE) contributes here, so there is no inter-body disagreement; however, page 20 is more specific than page 6, naming carrier status and the high-risk specialties, while page 6 frames the decision as locally determined by procedure type, patient risk and infection impact. Note the differing strength of language: the combination is recommended, whereas chlorhexidine body wash for increased-risk procedures is 'considered'. The community does NOT establish doses, formulations, application sites beyond 'nasal', number of days or exact timing before surgery, duration or frequency of washes, screening methods or thresholds for identifying carriers, what to do for mupirocin-resistant strains, alternative agents, gynecologic-specific applicability, or any outcome data quantifying SSI reduction. It also does not address intraoperative or postoperative antibiotic prophylaxis.
key_entities: surgical site infection caused by staphylococcus aureus

title: Caesarean skin closure and sepsis risk
summary:
This community links surgical wound closure technique at caesarean birth with the infection/sepsis risk that caesarean delivery itself confers, spanning two guideline bodies (NICE and RCOG).

Wound closure: NICE recommendations centre on suture use for skin closure at caesarean birth. For women having caesarean birth, sutures rather than staples for skin closure are stated to prevent superficial wound dehiscence (NICE T1 p12). The same source establishes that sutures apply to caesarean birth specifically for skin closure (NICE T1 p12), and NICE T1 p25 frames this as a 'consider' level recommendation — consider sutures rather than staples for women having caesarean births. Educators should note the wording difference across the two NICE pages: p12 asserts the dehiscence-prevention benefit, while p25 expresses the choice as something to consider, so it should be taught as a preferred but not absolute option.

Sepsis risk: RCOG contributes the risk side. Caesarean birth increases the risk of maternal sepsis in women during pregnancy/postpartum (RCOG T1 p4). RCOG is also more operationally specific for triage: in patients with suspected sepsis, an invasive procedure within the last 6 weeks — which includes caesarean birth — counts as an amber flag, i.e. moderate risk (RCOG T1 p4). This gives a concrete 6-week window for postoperative sepsis vigilance.

Division of labour: NICE addresses technique to reduce local wound complications; RCOG addresses recognition and risk stratification of systemic infection. They do not contradict one another, and neither cross-references the other.

Not established: these relations do not state that sutures reduce sepsis, surgical site infection, or maternal mortality — only superficial wound dehiscence. No suture material, gauge, technique (continuous vs interrupted), subcuticular versus interrupted approach, timing of removal, or antibiotic prophylaxis (drug, dose, timing) is specified. No red-flag sepsis criteria, physiological thresholds, escalation timings, staple-specific indications, or outcomes for other invasive gynaecologic procedures are given, and no evidence grading or effect sizes are attached.

title: Systemic Anticancer Treatment and Neutropenic Sepsis Risk
summary:
This community represents a small but high-acuity theme: the myelosuppressive consequences of systemic anticancer treatment (SACT) and the resulting risk of neutropenia and neutropenic sepsis in patients presenting for perioperative gynecologic care. Both relations originate from a single source, NICE (T1, p6), and both position systemic anticancer treatment as the causal exposure.

The first recommendation links systemic anticancer treatment to increased risk of neutropenia in people who have had past anticancer or immunosuppressant treatment, with the qualifier that risk depends on the individual's specific condition, medical history and the treatment actually received. This is a broad, history-based flag rather than a threshold-driven rule: it directs staff to elicit prior oncological and immunosuppressant exposure during preoperative assessment, but leaves risk stratification to individual judgement.

The second recommendation is more time-specific and more clinically actionable: systemic anticancer treatment increases the risk of neutropenic sepsis in people who become unwell, where treatment has been given within the last 30 days. The 30-day window plus the trigger of becoming unwell is the only concrete threshold in this community, and it is the operational teaching point for nursing staff — any patient who has had SACT in the preceding 30 days and who deteriorates should be treated as possible neutropenic sepsis.

Only one guideline body contributes (NICE), so there are no inter-body disagreements or divergences to reconcile here; the two NICE statements differ from one another mainly in specificity, with the sepsis relation supplying a timing threshold that the neutropenia relation lacks.

The community does not establish: any neutrophil count threshold defining neutropenia; named chemotherapy or immunosuppressant agents; antibiotic choice, dose or door-to-antibiotic timing; escalation pathways, observation frequency or sepsis screening tools; how surgery should be deferred or modified; or any gynecologic-procedure-specific guidance. No outcome, mortality or follow-up relations are present.
key_entities: people who have had past anticancer or immunosuppressant treatment

title: Systemic infection surveillance and VTE risk
summary:
This small community links systemic infection to two clinical concerns: it is a recognised risk factor for venous thromboembolism (VTE), and it is something nurses must actively monitor for at intravenous access sites. Together the relations frame infection as both a surveillance target at the bedside and a trigger for re-evaluating thromboprophylaxis decisions.

Recommendations, with populations and conditions:
1) Systemic infection increases the risk of venous thromboembolism in women during and after pregnancy (RCOG, Top guideline T1, p11). The attached condition is explicit: the presence of systemic infection should prompt reassessment for the correct thromboprophylaxis — i.e. an intercurrent infection is not a static observation but a cue to revisit the woman's VTE risk score and prophylaxis plan.
2) Monitoring for signs of systemic infection is indicated for patients with suspected local intravenous site infection (OpenRN, T2 p1363). Here the nursing action is escalation of assessment from local site findings to systemic involvement.

Contributing bodies: RCOG contributes the obstetric risk-factor and thromboprophylaxis-reassessment guidance, specific to the pregnant and postpartum population. OpenRN contributes the general nursing surveillance action, tied to a different and narrower trigger (suspected local IV site infection) with no population restriction to pregnancy. The two are complementary rather than conflicting: OpenRN is more specific about the assessment stimulus (local IV site infection), while RCOG is more specific about the population (women during and after pregnancy) and about the downstream decision (thromboprophylaxis reassessment). Neither cross-references the other.

What this community does NOT establish: it names no anticoagulant agent, dose, or duration; no threshold or timing for prophylaxis initiation or reassessment; no diagnostic criteria, vital-sign parameters, or laboratory markers defining "systemic infection"; no antimicrobial therapy; no guidance on IV catheter removal or replacement; and no evidence that monitoring for systemic infection alters VTE incidence. It also does not extend the IV-site monitoring recommendation explicitly to pregnant or postpartum women, nor quantify the magnitude of VTE risk conferred by infection.
key_entities: monitoring for signs of systemic infection

title: Tablet Crushing Contraindications for Modified-Release Formulations
summary:
This community represents a narrow but high-consequence medication-administration safety theme: which oral solid dosage forms must never be crushed. Two relations, both drawn from a single source (OpenRN Nursing Skills, Volume 2, p. 854), state that tablet crushing is contraindicated with (1) enteric-coated tablets and (2) sustained-release drugs. The clinical logic implied by the formulation types is that crushing defeats the coating or release mechanism, but the graph records only the contraindication itself, not the mechanism, consequences, or alternative actions.

Recommendations and their scope: crushing is contraindicated whenever the dosage form is enteric-coated or sustained-release. Notably, neither relation carries a qualifying population (for example, patients who are NPO, have dysphagia, are receiving enteral tube feeds, or are perioperative gynecologic surgical patients) and neither carries a condition, threshold, or timing. The contraindication is therefore recorded as unconditional and formulation-based rather than patient-specific.

Contributing guideline bodies: only one body contributes here — OpenRN (Open Resources for Nursing), Nursing Skills Volume 2, page 854. Because there is a single source and a single page, there are no points of disagreement, no differences in specificity between bodies, and no opportunity to compare a more granular recommendation against a broader one. Educators should treat this as an uncorroborated single-source statement within this corpus rather than a multi-body consensus.

What this community does NOT establish: it does not name any specific drug products or brands; it does not list other non-crushable categories (such as film-coated, buccal, sublingual, or cytotoxic agents); it specifies no alternatives (liquid formulations, orally disintegrating tablets, pharmacist consultation, or prescriber notification); and it gives no guidance for enteral feeding tubes, perioperative NPO status, dysphagia screening, or preoperative medication timing. It sets no thresholds, doses, or time windows, and states no harm outcome (dose dumping, mucosal irritation, therapeutic failure). Any local policy built from this theme will require additional sources to be actionable.

title: Temporary IVC filters in peripartum VTE
summary:
This community centres on a single, narrowly indicated mechanical intervention: the temporary inferior vena cava (IVC) filter, and the trade-off between its embolic protection and its device-related complications. The only benefit relation recorded is prevention of pulmonary embolism, and it is explicitly population- and time-qualified: patients with iliac vein venous thromboembolism, in the peripartum period. This appears twice in the corpus (RCOG Top Tips/guidance p4 and p17), suggesting it is stated as a summary point and then repeated in the body text, giving it emphasis but not broadening the indication. Nurses should therefore not extrapolate filter use to other VTE sites, to non-pregnant patients, or to routine antepartum or postoperative thromboprophylaxis on the basis of these relations.

The counterbalancing recommendations are the documented harms, all attached to the same device without further population restriction: caval thrombosis, filter migration, lower limb deep vein thrombosis, and infection, the last qualified as occurring rarely. Practically, this supports nursing surveillance for new or worsening lower-limb swelling and pain (suggesting caval thrombosis or new DVT), device-site and systemic signs of infection, and radiological confirmation of filter position; it also supports counselling that the filter is temporary and intended for retrieval.

Only one guideline body contributes here: RCOG. There is no ACOG, NICE, ASA or AAGBI content in this community, so no inter-body agreement or conflict can be assessed; the two RCOG page references are internally consistent rather than divergent, with p17 carrying all the complication detail and p4 carrying only the indication.

The community does NOT establish: any insertion or retrieval timing (gestational age, hours before or after delivery, dwell time limits); any anticoagulant regimen, drug, dose or threshold to accompany or replace the filter; comparative effectiveness against low-molecular-weight heparin or unfractionated heparin; contraindications; quantified complication rates beyond the word 'rarely'; imaging or monitoring schedules; or who should perform insertion. It also gives no guidance on filters in gynecologic surgical patients outside the peripartum iliac-vein VTE population.

title: Tubing Slack Prevents Traction Injury
summary:
Clinical theme: this small community addresses a single, transferable nursing technique — deliberately providing enough slack in tubing when securing indwelling catheters and surgical drains — as a mechanical safeguard against traction-related harm in the perioperative gynecologic patient.

Recommendations: (1) For patients with an indwelling urinary catheter, providing enough slack in the tubing prevents urethral injury (OpenRN Nursing Skills, T2 p1208). No condition qualifier is attached to this statement beyond the presence of the indwelling catheter, so it applies whenever a catheter is in situ. (2) For patients with surgical drains, providing enough slack prevents tension of the drainage system, explicitly conditioned on the slack being sufficient to accommodate patient movement (OpenRN T2 p1192). The second relation is therefore the more specific of the two: it names the mechanism (patient movement generating tension) and the object protected (the drainage system), whereas the catheter statement names only the injury outcome (urethral trauma).

Contributing bodies: both relations derive from a single source corpus, the OpenRN open-access nursing skills text (Tier 2, pages 1192 and 1208). There is thus no inter-organisational disagreement to reconcile; the two passages are complementary rather than conflicting, applying one principle to two device populations. Educators can safely teach it as a unified rule: secure the device, then check that tubing permits the patient's full range of expected movement (repositioning, ambulation, transfer) without traction on the insertion site.

What this community does NOT establish: no quantified threshold for “enough” slack (no centimetre or inch measure), no securement device or product named (no statlock, tape, leg strap or anchoring method), no frequency or timing for reassessment, and no perioperative phase specified (pre-, intra- or postoperative). It does not address catheter or drain size, drain type (Jackson-Pratt, Penrose, Hemovac), suction settings, dressing technique, infection risk, bladder spasm, accidental dislodgement rates, pain outcomes, or any pharmacologic adjunct. No pediatric, obstetric or high-BMI subpopulation is differentiated, and no evidence grade or outcome data support the two claims.

title: Anticholinergics: terminal secretions, continence, falls
summary:
This community centers on anticholinergic pharmacotherapy and its dual character as both a symptom-management tool and a source of iatrogenic risk, with the strongest cluster around management of terminal (end-of-life) respiratory secretions.

Main recommendations. (1) For clients at the end of life, anticholinergic medications are indicated to treat terminal secretions; two specific agents are named — scopolamine and atropine — both attached to the same end-of-life population (OpenRN Nursing Management and Professional Concepts/Nursing Fundamentals, p1288). (2) A nonpharmacologic measure accompanies drug therapy at the same page: repositioning the client onto the side to help manage terminal secretions, conditioned on feasibility ('if feasible'), which positions it as an adjunct or first-line comfort measure rather than a guaranteed intervention. (3) For clients with urinary incontinence, anticholinergic medication is described as an additional medical intervention treating incontinence (p1430) — framed as supplementary, implying behavioral or other measures precede it. (4) Counterbalancing this, anticholinergic medications increase risk of falls in older adults, specifically attributed to the side effects of dizziness and drowsiness (p1162).

Contributing bodies and differences. All relations derive from a single corpus, OpenRN (Open Resources for Nursing) textbook material, so there are no cross-body disagreements to reconcile; differences are instead in granularity. The end-of-life secretion guidance is the most specific, naming individual drugs (scopolamine, atropine) plus a positioning maneuver, whereas the incontinence and falls guidance stays at the drug-class level. The falls entry is the only one that specifies a mechanism and an age-defined population.

Not established. No doses, routes, dosing intervals, frequencies, or titration thresholds are given for scopolamine, atropine, or any anticholinergic; no age cutoff defines 'older adults'; no incontinence subtype (urge vs. stress) is specified; no comparative effectiveness between scopolamine and atropine, and no guidance on whether repositioning should precede or accompany drugs. It does not address deprescribing, anticholinergic burden scoring, fall-prevention offsets, monitoring parameters, contraindications, or perioperative gynecologic use specifically.
key_entities: clients at the end of life

title: Thiazide Diuretic Risks and Contraindications
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused pharmacologic safety theme: the adverse-effect profile and contraindications of thiazide diuretics, as documented in RNAO Tool/Table 2, page 140. All eleven relations originate from one entity (thiazide diuretic) and one source, making this a drug-monograph-style cluster rather than a multi-guideline consensus.

Risk relations: for patients treated with thiazide diuretics, the guideline flags increased risk of orthostatic hypotension, hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hyperglycemia, gout, and erectile dysfunction. The stated population for every risk edge is simply 'patients treated with thiazide diuretics' — no perioperative, gynecologic, age, or dose-specific subgroup is named.
