Contraindication relations: thiazide diuretics are contraindicated with hepatic impairment, renal impairment, predisposition to serious arrhythmia, gout, and fluid or electrolyte imbalance. Note that gout appears twice — both as a condition the drug can precipitate and as a pre-existing state contraindicating use — a useful teaching point about bidirectional risk. Similarly, the electrolyte adverse effects (hypokalemia, hyponatremia) mirror the contraindication of pre-existing fluid or electrolyte imbalance, giving educators a coherent monitoring rationale: baseline and ongoing potassium, sodium, volume status, glucose, uric acid, and standing blood pressure assessment in patients on thiazides.

Contributing bodies: RNAO alone (Tool/Table 2, p140). Because only one guideline body and one page contribute, there are no points of disagreement, no differences in specificity between organisations, and no corroboration from other guideline corpora within this community.

What the community does NOT establish: no specific drug names within the thiazide class, no doses, no laboratory thresholds (e.g., no potassium or sodium cut-offs), no monitoring intervals or timings, and no guidance on whether to continue, hold, or resume thiazides before or after gynecologic surgery. It does not grade evidence strength, does not name alternative antihypertensives, does not address drug–drug or drug–anaesthetic interactions, and does not link these risks to any perioperative outcome such as intraoperative hypotension or postoperative arrhythmia.

title: Preoperative VTE Prophylaxis in Gynecologic Surgery
summary: This community represents a single, narrow clinical theme: venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis in the perioperative gynecologic-oncology pathway, and specifically where in the care timeline it belongs and what outcome it is expected to prevent. Two relations define the theme. First, thromboembolism prophylaxis is placed in the preoperative phase, with the population qualified as patients at risk of VTE (ERAS Society, Table 1, p1) — that is, initiation is a pre-incision task, not solely a postoperative one, and it is targeted by risk status rather than applied indiscriminately. Second, thromboembolism prophylaxis prevents venous thromboembolism in patients undergoing pelvic exenteration or HIPEC (hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy) (ERAS Society, Table 1, p11) — an explicitly high-complexity, high-risk cytoreductive population in whom the preventive benefit is asserted. For a nurse educator, the teachable points are: identify VTE risk during preoperative assessment; ensure prophylaxis is ordered and documented before the operation; and treat pelvic exenteration and HIPEC cases as populations where prophylaxis is expressly indicated. Only one guideline body contributes here — the ERAS Society — so there are no inter-society disagreements to reconcile; however, the two statements differ in specificity, with the phase recommendation using a broad 'at risk of VTE' population and the prevention statement naming two concrete procedures. Critically, this community does not establish the modality or agent (no mention of unfractionated heparin, low-molecular-weight heparin such as enoxaparin or dalteparin, aspirin, intermittent pneumatic compression, or graduated compression stockings), no dose, no timing interval relative to incision or to neuraxial anaesthesia, no duration or extended post-discharge prophylaxis window, and no risk-stratification tool or scoring threshold (e.g. Caprini) to operationalise 'at risk'. It also says nothing about contraindications, bleeding risk, renal dosing, intraoperative or postoperative continuation, or monitoring. Local protocols must supply agent, dose, timing and duration; the graph supports only the phase placement and the preventive intent in the named populations.

title: Thrombolysis for Massive PE in Pregnancy
summary:
This community centres on thrombolytic therapy as a rescue intervention for life- or limb-threatening venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium, and on how it changes subsequent unfractionated heparin (UFH) dosing. All relations derive from a single source, RCOG Green-top guidance (RCOG T1, p14); no other guideline body contributes, so no inter-body disagreement can be assessed.

Indications: thrombolysis TREATS pulmonary embolism, but only in patients with severe pulmonary thromboembolism accompanied by haemodynamic compromise — it is explicitly reserved for that circumstance. For collapsed, shocked women who are pregnant or in the puerperium, thrombolysis is indicated when massive PE is confirmed, or, in extreme circumstances, before confirmation; the decision is to be made on an individual basis by a multidisciplinary resuscitation team. It also TREATS iliofemoral vein thrombosis when there are limb- or life-threatening ischaemic complications from extensive iliofemoral thrombus. In patients with massive PE, thrombolysis is also credited with PREVENTING recurrent pulmonary embolism.

Anticoagulation after thrombolysis: this is the most operationally specific element for nursing practice. A UFH loading dose is CONTRAINDICATED once thrombolytic therapy has been given. Instead, for patients who have received thrombolysis, the loading dose is omitted and the UFH infusion is started at 18 units/kg/hour. Both the timing of the UFH infusion and the decision to omit the loading dose depend on whether thrombolysis has been administered — a clear handover and prescribing checkpoint for perioperative and recovery nurses.

Not established: the community names no specific thrombolytic agent, dose, route or infusion duration; no bleeding contraindications, monitoring parameters (e.g. APTT targets), or duration of UFH therapy; no guidance on transition to LMWH or oral anticoagulants; no thresholds defining "massive" PE or haemodynamic compromise; and no recommendations for haemodynamically stable PE, surgical or catheter-based alternatives, or postoperative/perioperative timing restrictions. Composition of the multidisciplinary resuscitation team is likewise unspecified.

title: Thrombophilia Testing in Pregnancy-Related VTE
summary:
This community centres on selective thrombophilia testing/screening in pregnancy and the puerperium, and on thrombophilia as a driver of venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk. All relations derive from a single guideline body, RCOG (Tier 1, pp. 3, 6, 11, 16, 17, 21), so no inter-body disagreement is documented; differences are only in granularity across pages.

Main recommendations by population and condition: (1) For women who develop VTE during pregnancy or the puerperium, thrombophilia testing detects thrombophilia but its timing depends on anticoagulant treatment — testing should be performed only once anticoagulant therapy has been discontinued, and only if the results would influence future management (pp. 6, 21). (2) For women with previous VTE, test only if finding a thrombophilia would alter proposed management or influence thromboprophylaxis recommendations (p. 16). (3) For women with no personal VTE history or risk factors but a family history of unprovoked or estrogen-provoked VTE in a first-degree relative aged under 50 years, testing is more informative if the relative has a known thrombophilia (pp. 3, 17). (4) For asymptomatic pregnant women with a family history of VTE in a first-degree relative under 50 where the episode was unprovoked or provoked by pregnancy or combined oral contraceptive exposure, testing detects heritable thrombophilia as case finding in high-risk thrombophilic families, most informative when the proband's thrombophilic tendency is known (p. 17). (5) Interpretation caveat: in pregnant women, thrombophilia screening results may be influenced by the physiological changes of pregnancy and by acute thrombus (p. 11).

Risk relations: thrombophilia increases risk of VTE recurrence in pregnant women with VTE (p. 17), and increases VTE risk in women without previous VTE, stratified by the level of risk of the specific thrombophilia plus family history or other risk factors (p. 6).

Not established here: no named anticoagulant agents, doses, washout intervals, specific assays or thrombophilia subtypes, numeric risk thresholds, or nursing/perioperative workflow steps; no non-RCOG corroboration.
key_entities: family history of VTE in first-degree relative under 50

title: Thromboprophylaxis in Peripartum Thrombophilia Risk
summary: This community centres on preventing venous thromboembolism in the peripartum period, stratified by inherited/acquired thrombophilia and by bleeding risk, with almost all content from RCOG (Green-top thromboprophylaxis guidance, Tool 1, pp3-24). Risk factors named are heterozygous factor V Leiden, heterozygous prothrombin gene mutation, and antiphospholipid antibodies, each increasing thrombosis risk in asymptomatic women (p17); persistent antiphospholipid antibodies raise risk even without previous VTE (p4). RCOG grades duration and timing by the number of additional risk factors in asymptomatic heterozygous or antibody-positive women: postpartum thromboprophylaxis for 10 days if one other risk factor; thromboprophylaxis from 28 weeks if two other risk factors; antenatal thromboprophylaxis in the presence of three other risk factors (p3). For women with primary antiphospholipid syndrome but no previous VTE, pharmacological thromboprophylaxis is limited to 3-5 days postpartum only (p18). Where LMWH has been withheld, unfractionated heparin 5000 iu subcutaneously every 12 hours is recommended for undelivered women who have had no LMWH for 24 hours, continued until LMWH can be resumed after delivery (p24). Mechanical options are the fallback when chemical thromboprophylaxis is contraindicated after postpartum haemorrhage: anti-embolism stockings, intermittent pneumatic compression, and foot impulse devices (p23); chemical thromboprophylaxis is (re)started once bleeding is arrested and coagulopathy corrected (p23). Foot impulse devices are also endorsed for women at high risk of haemorrhage, explicitly as an alternative to pharmacological thromboprophylaxis (pp5, 20). OpenRN (T2 p562) contributes only a general pathophysiologic link: thrombosis increases risk of peripheral edema; it offers no dosing or population detail, so RCOG is far more specific on drugs, thresholds and timing. The community does not establish comparative efficacy among mechanical devices, LMWH agents or doses (beyond the UFH regimen given), aspirin or anticoagulant use in pregnancy loss, screening criteria for thrombophilia, homozygous or compound thrombophilia management, monitoring, or outcomes such as bleeding harms; no contradiction between bodies is evident.

title: Preventing Tissue Damage During Nursing Procedures
summary:
This small community centers on a single shared outcome — prevention of tissue damage — reached through two distinct mechanical-handling practices during device and wound care. Both relations converge on 'tissue damage' as the harm avoided, framing it as a theme of atraumatic technique rather than pharmacologic or infection-control management.

Recommendation 1: For patients with a tunneling wound, gentle probing with a sterile cotton-tipped applicator prevents tissue damage, with the explicit condition that the clinician insert the swab only until resistance is felt and never force it. The threshold here is tactile (resistance), not a measured depth, and the equipment is specified as a sterile cotton-tipped applicator.

Recommendation 2: For patients with an indwelling urinary catheter, securing the catheter after insertion prevents tissue damage. The timing condition is explicit — immediately after catheter insertion — though no securement device, anchoring site (thigh versus abdomen), or tension threshold is named.

Both statements derive from a single guideline body, OpenRN (Open Resources for Nursing), Text 2, at pages 1136 (wound assessment/tunneling) and 1226 (urinary catheter care). Because only one source contributes, there are no interbody disagreements to reconcile. The two entries differ in specificity: the wound-probing guidance supplies both a technique-limiting rule and a stop criterion, whereas the catheter guidance states the action and timing only, leaving securement method to local policy.

What this community does not establish: it does not define or grade tissue damage (no distinction among pressure injury, urethral erosion, false tract creation, or bleeding); it names no drugs, dressings, lubricants, or antiseptics; it gives no frequency for reassessment of securement, no catheter dwell-time limits, and no measurement protocol for tunnel depth. It does not address gynecologic surgery populations specifically, pediatric or obstetric patients, infection prevention (CAUTI), pain management, or documentation requirements. No outcome data, evidence grades, or comparative effectiveness between securement devices or probing tools are provided.
key_entities: gentle probing with sterile cotton-tipped applicator
patients with an indwelling urinary catheter

title: Lactate-Guided Sepsis Detection and Fluid Resuscitation
summary:
This community represents the sepsis recognition-and-resuscitation pathway in obstetric/gynecologic care: using urgent serum lactate measurement to detect sepsis and tissue hypoperfusion, and intravenous fluid bolus administration as the immediate treatment response.

Detection (RCOG): serum lactate should be measured urgently in women with features indicating a high risk of sepsis, to detect sepsis and guide care. RCOG is specific about the actionable threshold: a serum lactate of 4 mmol/l or more indicates tissue hypoperfusion and prompts immediate escalation of care.

Treatment: RCOG links the same 4 mmol/l or more threshold to intravenous fluid bolus administration for tissue hypoperfusion. NICE contributes two population-specific recommendations: (1) for people aged 16 or over at high risk of severe illness or death from sepsis, give an IV fluid bolus within 1 hour of identifying high risk, unless contraindicated; and (2) for people with suspected sepsis who are or have recently been pregnant and meet any high risk criterion, consider giving an IV fluid bolus when lactate is below 2 mmol/litre (a weaker 'consider' recommendation at a lower lactate value).

Contributing bodies and differences: RCOG frames both lactate testing and fluids around a single high threshold (≥4 mmol/l) in women at high risk of sepsis, without specifying a time-to-fluid target. NICE is more specific on timing (within 1 hour) and on age (16 or over) and adds explicit obstetric framing (currently or recently pregnant), plus guidance for the low-lactate (<2 mmol/litre) scenario. They are complementary rather than contradictory, but the strength of wording differs (RCOG's escalation directive versus NICE's 'consider').

What is NOT established here: no antibiotic, vasopressor, or other drug is named; no fluid type, volume, or rate is specified; contraindications to fluid boluses are referenced but not defined; management for lactate between 2 and 4 mmol/l is not addressed; no repeat-lactate interval, escalation destination, monitoring plan, or outcome/mortality evidence is provided; and nothing addresses paediatric or non-pregnant gynecologic subgroups beyond the stated populations.

title: Hyperglycemia as Perioperative Wound Risk
summary:
Clinical theme: this small community captures a single causal mechanism relevant to perioperative gynecologic nursing — elevated blood glucose as an upstream risk factor for impaired surgical healing. Two relations are asserted, both from the same source: elevated blood glucose increases the risk of tissue hypoxia, and elevated blood glucose increases the risk of infection.

Recommendations, populations, conditions: the graph records no explicit recommendation text, threshold, target glucose value, timing (preoperative, intraoperative, postoperative), drug, or insulin protocol. Notably, the two relations carry no attached population and no attached condition — they are stated as general physiologic risk associations rather than as guidance qualified to, for example, diabetic patients, patients undergoing hysterectomy, or a defined glycemic range. Educators should therefore present these edges as mechanistic teaching points (hyperglycemia → tissue hypoxia; hyperglycemia → infection) that justify glucose surveillance and wound-risk assessment, not as an actionable protocol with numeric cut-points.

Contributing bodies: only one source contributes — OpenRN (Open Resources for Nursing), Text 2, page 696. Because there is a single contributor and a single page, there are no inter-body agreements, contradictions, or differences in specificity to reconcile within this community. No professional society guidance (e.g., surgical-site-infection or enhanced-recovery bodies) is represented here, so the theme cannot be triangulated across corpora.

What this community does NOT establish: it does not define what glucose value counts as "elevated"; it does not specify monitoring frequency or sampling method; it does not name any pharmacologic or nonpharmacologic intervention (no insulin regimen, no supplemental oxygen strategy for the tissue-hypoxia pathway); it does not state effect size, relative risk, or strength/quality of evidence; it does not link tissue hypoxia and infection to each other or to downstream outcomes such as dehiscence, delayed healing, or length of stay; and it does not restrict applicability to diabetic versus nondiabetic or to any specific gynecologic procedure. Any quality-improvement metric or glycemic target must be sourced elsewhere.

title: Preventing Tissue Injury: Fever and Injections
summary:
This community represents a narrow prevention theme: protecting patients from tissue injury, approached from two unrelated clinical directions — systemic hyperthermia and local injection-site selection. The shared outcome node is 'tissue injury'; both recommendations are framed as preventive interventions rather than treatments.

Recommendation 1: Fever management prevents tissue injury in clients with toxic shock syndrome or scarlet fever, specifically when fevers exceed 42 °C. The 42 °C threshold is the only numeric parameter in the community and is the trigger tied to tissue-damage risk in these two infectious/toxin-mediated conditions.

Recommendation 2: Skin and tissue quality assessment of the injection site prevents tissue injury in patients receiving an injection. The stated technique is to avoid bruised, nonintact, abraded or scarred areas and to choose another recommended location instead.

Guideline contribution: both statements derive from a single source body, Open RN (OpenRN Nursing Skills / fundamentals text, Volume T2), at pages 603 (fever) and 1053 (injection site assessment). Because only one corpus contributes, there are no cross-body disagreements to reconcile. The two entries differ in specificity: the fever entry is more specific about population and threshold (named conditions, 42 °C) but does not name any antipyretic drug, dose, cooling method or timing; the injection entry is more specific about assessment criteria and the corrective action (select an alternative recommended site) but leaves the population broad — any patient receiving an injection — with no route, needle length, gauge, or named medication.

What this community does NOT establish: no drugs, doses, or antipyretic agents; no monitoring intervals, reassessment timing, or duration; no perioperative or gynecologic-specific application despite the corpus context; no severity grading or definition of 'tissue injury'; no evidence levels or strength-of-recommendation ratings; no guidance for fevers below 42 °C; no named acceptable injection sites; and no link between the two pathways (i.e., no claim that febrile patients require different injection-site handling). It should be treated as two isolated single-source prevention statements, not a validated bundle.
key_entities: skin and tissue quality assessment of the injection site

title: Preoperative Tobacco Cessation to Prevent SSI
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused theme: preoperative tobacco cessation as a modifiable patient-level risk reduction measure in elective gynecologic surgery. Two relations anchor it. First, tobacco cessation is placed in the preoperative phase of care, for patients undergoing elective surgery, with the condition that cessation begin at least 30 days before the elective surgery 'if possible' (WHO, T1 p68). Second, tobacco cessation is identified as preventive against surgical site infection (SSI), for the narrower population of patients undergoing an elective operation who use tobacco, under the condition that they abstain for at least 30 days before the elective operation (CDC, T1 p19). The practical takeaway for education and quality improvement is consistent across both bodies: screen for tobacco use early enough in the elective surgical pathway that a 30-day abstinence window is achievable, and frame cessation explicitly as SSI prevention rather than only general health advice.

Two guideline bodies contribute: WHO and CDC. They agree on the 30-day threshold, the elective-surgery population, and the preoperative timing. They differ in emphasis and specificity. WHO situates cessation within the phase structure of perioperative care and softens the timing with the qualifier 'if possible,' acknowledging that scheduling may not permit a full 30 days. CDC is more specific about the population (patients who actually use tobacco) and about the outcome, naming SSI prevention as the stated benefit of abstinence. Neither is contradicted by the other.

The community does not establish several things a nurse educator should not infer: no cessation method is named (no nicotine replacement, varenicline, bupropion, counselling model, or referral pathway), no dose or intensity of tobacco use is defined, and no guidance is given for emergency or non-elective surgery, for patients presenting fewer than 30 days before operation, or for vaping/smokeless products specifically. It also gives no effect size or strength-of-evidence grading for SSI reduction, no postoperative abstinence duration, and no gynecologic-procedure-specific detail.

title: Routine tracheostomy care prevents airway contamination
summary:
This community represents a single, narrow clinical theme: routine tracheostomy care as an infection-prevention intervention for the artificial airway and lower respiratory tract. Both relations in the community are causal-preventive claims linking the nursing activity of tracheostomy care to reduced bacterial burden.

Main recommendations and their scope:
1) Tracheostomy care prevents bacterial entry into the artificial airway and lungs. Population: patients with a tracheostomy. Condition: care is provided on a routine basis (OpenRN Nursing Skills Text 2, p1314).
2) Tracheostomy care prevents bacterial contamination of the trachea and lungs. Population: patients with a tracheostomy tube. Condition: care is performed routinely to keep the flange, dressing, ties or straps, and surrounding area clean (OpenRN Text 2, p1285).

The second statement is the more operationally specific of the two: it names the concrete targets of cleaning — the tracheostomy flange, the dressing, the ties/straps, and the peristomal skin — whereas the p1314 statement asserts only that care be routine, without specifying components. The two are otherwise consistent, differing mainly in the anatomical scope of the harm prevented ("artificial airway and lungs" versus "trachea and lungs").

Guideline bodies: only one source corpus contributes here — OpenRN (Open Resources for Nursing), Text 2, at two separate page locations. There is therefore no cross-body disagreement to reconcile, and no external society or perioperative-specific guidance in this community.

What the community does NOT establish: no frequency or timing is specified ("routine" is undefined — no shifts, hours, or per-day interval); no technique detail (sterile versus clean technique, suctioning, inner cannula handling, tube change intervals); no named cleaning agents, antiseptics, saline, or drugs; no dressing products; no thresholds or assessment criteria for escalating care; no outcome data on pneumonia, ventilator-associated infection rates, or mortality; and no perioperative or gynecologic-surgery-specific qualifiers despite the surrounding corpus. Educators should supplement with local policy for frequency, technique, and supplies.
key_entities: bacterial entry into the artificial airway and lungs
bacterial contamination of the trachea and lungs

title: Preoperative Anemia Treatment Prevents Transfusion
summary:
Clinical theme: this small community represents preoperative patient blood management in gynecologic surgery — specifically, identifying and correcting anemia before the operation so that perioperative allogeneic blood transfusion can be avoided. Both relations in the community point to the same outcome node, transfusion, framing transfusion as an avoidable harm rather than an inevitable consequence of surgery.

Recommendations and their populations/conditions: (1) Treating anemia preoperatively prevents transfusion — stated generally, with no population restriction or condition attached in the graph (ERAS Society, Table 1, p1). (2) Prompt identification and treatment of iron deficiency anemia prevents transfusion, explicitly scoped to patients with iron deficiency anemia (ERAS Society, Table 1, p1). The second relation is the more specific of the two: it names the anemia subtype, attaches an eligible population, and adds a timing/process element (“prompt identification”), implying screening must occur early enough in the preoperative pathway for treatment to take effect before surgery.

Contributing bodies and differences: only one guideline body contributes here — the ERAS Society — and both statements come from the same source location (T1, p1). There is therefore no inter-society disagreement to reconcile; the two statements are consistent, differing only in granularity (general anemia versus iron deficiency anemia specifically). Educators should note the corpus offers no competing or contradictory recommendation on this point.

What this community does NOT establish: it specifies no hemoglobin or hematocrit diagnostic threshold, no ferritin or transferrin saturation cutoff, and no screening interval. It names no specific therapy — no oral or intravenous iron formulation, no erythropoiesis-stimulating agent, no vitamin B12 or folate, and no dose. It gives no timing window (e.g., number of weeks before surgery), no re-testing plan, no transfusion trigger threshold, and no outcome data on length of stay, morbidity, or mortality. It also does not address non-iron-deficiency anemias, gynecologic-cancer-specific or benign-surgery-specific populations, or intraoperative and postoperative blood-conservation measures.
key_entities: prompt identification and treatment of iron deficiency anemia

title: Managing Transient Mechanical Phlebitis at IV Sites
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: the conservative, symptom-directed management of transient mechanical phlebitis in patients with peripheral intravenous access. All five relations converge on one condition (transient mechanical phlebitis) and one population (patients with transient mechanical phlebitis), forming a bundled care set rather than competing options.

The recommended interventions are: (1) catheter stabilisation, to reduce ongoing mechanical irritation of the vein wall; (2) limb elevation of the affected extremity; (3) heat application to the site; (4) an analgesic, given 'as needed' for discomfort; and (5) an anti-inflammatory agent, described as an additional pharmacologic intervention to be used 'if needed.' The first three are non-pharmacologic and are stated without conditional qualifiers, implying they are baseline measures for any patient with the condition. The two pharmacologic entries carry explicit conditionality — analgesia as needed, anti-inflammatory therapy only if further intervention is required — signalling a stepped approach in which mechanical and physical measures precede or accompany drug therapy.

Only one guideline body contributes: OpenRN (Open RN Nursing Skills, Volume 2, p1363). Because the corpus here is single-source, there are no inter-body disagreements, no divergent thresholds, and no instance where one organisation is more specific than another; the specificity gradient exists only within the OpenRN text itself, between unconditional physical measures and conditional pharmacologic ones.

What this community does NOT establish: no named drugs, drug classes, doses, routes, or frequencies are specified for the analgesic or anti-inflammatory agent; no temperature, duration, or frequency is given for heat application; no degree or duration of limb elevation is defined; and no stabilisation device or technique is named. It does not define diagnostic criteria, grading scales, or thresholds for phlebitis severity, nor does it address catheter removal or resiting, escalation criteria, expected time to resolution, infective or chemical phlebitis, thrombophlebitis, prophylaxis, or any gynecologic- or perioperative-specific modifications. Contraindications (for example to heat or anti-inflammatory use) are likewise absent.

title: Invasive Device Handling and Microorganism Transmission
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused infection-prevention theme: the risk of transmitting harmful microorganisms during contact with invasive devices, and the two behavioural safeguards that mitigate that risk. Three device categories are named as risk-increasing exposures: indwelling urinary catheters, vascular access systems, and drainage systems. Each is asserted to increase the risk of transmission of harmful microorganisms; no qualifying population or condition is attached to these risk relations, so they are stated as general device-related hazards.

Two preventive actions are recommended. First, careful preparation before device contact prevents transmission of harmful microorganisms, with an explicit condition: when inserting a catheter, or when opening a vascular access system or a drainage system. Second, hand hygiene prevents transmission of harmful microorganisms, specified for the population of students and conditioned on the moments when preparing food, medications and dressings. Notably, the hand-hygiene recommendation in this community is framed around food, medication and dressing preparation rather than around device insertion itself, while device insertion and system opening are covered by the 'careful preparation' recommendation.

Only one guideline body contributes: WHO (Tool 1, page 211). Because the corpus segment is single-source, there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile; however, the relations differ in specificity. The preventive relations carry conditions (and, for hand hygiene, a defined learner population of students), whereas the three device risk relations are unconditioned and unpopulated, i.e. less specific.

What the community does not establish: no drugs, antiseptic agents, concentrations, contact times, catheter dwell-time thresholds, or removal timings are named. It does not quantify the magnitude of risk for any device, rank urinary catheters against vascular or drainage systems, or specify which organisms are involved. It defines no infection outcomes (e.g., CAUTI or CLABSI rates), no surveillance or audit measures, no aseptic-technique steps constituting 'careful preparation', and no recommendations for populations other than students, nor any perioperative-phase-specific or gynecologic-procedure-specific guidance.

title: Preventing infection transmission during patient transport
summary:
This community represents infection prevention and control as it applies to moving clients within the healthcare facility, plus the foundational role of hand hygiene. All three relations converge on a single outcome node — transmission of infection — approached from two directions: protective practices that prevent it, and a lapse that increases its risk.

Two transport-specific recommendations are drawn from OpenRN (Nursing Skills, T2 p642), both scoped to the same population: clients requiring transmission-based precautions. First, barrier use during transport prevents transmission of infection, with the stated condition that the barriers be consistent with the route and risk of transmission for that particular client (i.e., barrier selection is matched to the precaution category rather than applied uniformly). Second, notification of receiving area personnel prevents transmission, with the timing condition that notification occurs before the impending arrival of the client — advance warning, not handoff on arrival. Together these frame transport as a two-part intervention: containment at the source and readiness at the destination.

The WHO guideline (T1 p163) contributes the complementary risk relation: failure to perform hand hygiene increases the risk of transmission of infection. Notably, this relation carries no population or condition qualifier, making it a universal statement, whereas the OpenRN transport recommendations are explicitly conditional on precaution status and on transport timing. WHO is therefore broader in applicability; OpenRN is more specific in operational detail (who to notify, when, and how to select barriers). The two bodies do not conflict — they address different points in the transmission chain.

What this community does not establish: it names no specific barrier types (no mention of gowns, gloves, masks, or respirator classes), no precaution categories (contact, droplet, airborne), no hand hygiene agents, durations, or moments, no distance or route restrictions for transport, and no patient outcome data, thresholds, or effect sizes. It also says nothing about staffing, documentation, receiving-area room preparation, equipment decontamination after transport, or pediatric, obstetric, or perioperative-specific adaptations, despite the perioperative gynecologic framing of the corpus.

title: Aseptic Technique for Microorganism Transmission Prevention
summary:
This community centres on infection prevention through aseptic and sterile practice during nursing and perioperative procedures. The unifying claim, repeated across OpenRN Tier 2 (including p201), is that both aseptic technique and sterile technique prevent transmission of microorganisms when performing nursing procedures. Adjunct barrier and hygiene measures sit alongside these: nonsterile gloves prevent transmission of microorganisms when used according to agency policy (OpenRN T2 p1192), and proper hand drying after hand hygiene prevents transmission of microorganisms in health-care workers (WHO T1 p211).

Device-specific recommendations are the most concrete. For patients receiving an indwelling urinary catheter, aseptic technique during insertion — using sterile gloves and equipment — prevents catheter-associated urinary tract infection (OpenRN T2 p1226). CDC T1 p12 makes the parallel structural point that aseptic technique applies to urinary catheter insertion for patients in the acute care hospital setting, with sterile equipment. CDC T1 p21 extends aseptic technique to surgical site infection prevention for patients receiving intravascular devices, spinal or epidural anesthesia catheters, or intravenous drugs, applied when placing those devices or when dispensing and administering intravenous drugs. WHO T1 p211 states the broadest, least qualified claim: aseptic technique prevents infection, with no population or condition attached.

Contributing bodies are OpenRN (Tier 2), CDC (Tier 1) and WHO (Tier 1). They do not conflict but differ in granularity: OpenRN is most specific about the nursing act and its equipment (sterile gloves and equipment at insertion) and about glove selection deferring to local agency policy; CDC is most specific about settings and device types (acute care hospital, intravascular, spinal/epidural catheters, IV drug administration); WHO is most general, contributing only broad infection prevention and the hand-drying step.

The community does not establish any drugs, antiseptic agents, doses, timings, durations, thresholds, or audit measures; it does not distinguish when sterile technique is required versus aseptic technique, does not specify catheter dwell time or removal criteria, and offers no gynecologic- or pregnancy-specific populations, no outcome magnitudes, and no evidence grading.

title: MRSA prevention and treatment in perioperative care
summary:
This community centres on methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) as a perioperative and inpatient infection risk, spanning three angles: antimicrobial treatment, staffing-related risk, and antiseptic prevention.

Treatment: RCOG (T1 p11) recommends vancomycin for MRSA infection when MRSA is likely. It is more specific for one population — women with life-threatening sepsis — where vancomycin should be added to the empirical antibiotic combination if there is any suspicion of MRSA. This is the only drug named for treatment in the community.

System/staffing risk: CDC (T1 p8) identifies understaffing of nurses as increasing the risk of MRSA infection for patients in intensive-care settings, with the stated mechanism being relaxed attention to basic control measures such as hand hygiene. This makes nurse staffing levels a legitimate quality-improvement target for MRSA rates, not merely a workforce issue.

Prevention: Triclosan is credited with preventing MRSA in two distinct populations. WHO (T1 p57) addresses patients, where triclosan is used both for hand hygiene and as a bathing cleanser. CDC (T1 p18) addresses hospital personnel, where triclosan is supplied as a triclosan-containing preparation for hand antisepsis. WHO is therefore broader in application (patient bathing plus hand hygiene), while CDC is narrower and staff-directed. The two bodies do not contradict each other; they cover complementary populations, and both converge with CDC's staffing relation on hand hygiene as the common control measure.

What this community does NOT establish: no dose, route, duration or timing for vancomycin; no de-escalation or stop criteria once MRSA is excluded; no concentration, contact time or frequency for triclosan; no numeric nurse-to-patient staffing ratio or threshold below which MRSA risk rises; no comparative effectiveness of triclosan against chlorhexidine or other agents; no MRSA screening or decolonisation protocol; and no explicit surgical-site-infection or gynecologic-procedure-specific MRSA data. Resistance risk from triclosan use is not addressed.

title: Tricuspid Area Auscultation for Murmurs
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: cardiac auscultation of the tricuspid area as a physical-assessment technique for detecting right-sided and septal cardiac abnormalities. It sits within the broader cardiovascular assessment skills that support perioperative gynecologic nursing, where baseline cardiac findings inform surgical risk and postoperative monitoring.

The substantive recommendation is anatomical and technique-specific: auscultate the tricuspid area at the fourth and fifth intercostal spaces along the left sternal border. Under that condition, three findings are attributed to this listening post — tricuspid stenosis, tricuspid regurgitation, and ventricular septal defect. All three relations share the identical positional condition, so the landmark itself is the operative teaching point: incorrect placement (e.g., too high or at the apex) would shift the expected findings. For educators, this makes the tricuspid site the appropriate location to characterise murmurs suspected to arise from the tricuspid valve or an interventricular septal shunt.

Only one guideline body contributes: OpenRN Nursing Skills (Open Resources for Nursing), Volume/Text 2, page 562. Because the corpus contains a single source for this theme, there are no inter-body disagreements, no competing landmark descriptions, and no more- or less-specific parallel recommendations to reconcile. Quality-improvement leads should note that the evidence base here is a foundational nursing skills text rather than a specialty cardiology or perioperative society statement.

The community does NOT establish: any patient population or subgroup (no age, pregnancy, gynecologic-procedure, or comorbidity qualifiers are attached); no timing or frequency of assessment (preoperative, intraoperative, or postoperative); no diaphragm-versus-bell selection, patient positioning, or breath-holding manoeuvres; no murmur grading, timing within the cardiac cycle, radiation patterns, or intensity thresholds; no distinguishing features separating tricuspid stenosis from regurgitation from ventricular septal defect at the same site; and no downstream actions such as escalation criteria, echocardiography referral, anticoagulation, antibiotic prophylaxis, or any drug therapy. It also does not address the other auscultatory landmarks (aortic, pulmonic, mitral/apical) or the sensitivity and specificity of this maneuver.
key_entities: fourth and fifth intercostal spaces along the left sternal border

title: Preventing Enteral Feeding Tube Clogging
summary:
This small community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: nursing techniques that prevent enteral feeding tube occlusion (clogging) during medication administration. Both relations converge on the same adverse outcome — tube clogging — and identify two distinct preventive nursing actions.

Recommendation 1: Administer each medication separately rather than combining or co-mingling drugs in one dose. Population: patients receiving multiple enteral medications. Condition: applies when more than one medication is being administered through the tube.

Recommendation 2: Flush the enteral tube with water. Population: patients receiving medication via an enteral tube. Conditions: flush both when beginning and when ending medication administration, and only when water flushing is not contraindicated for that individual patient (for example, a documented fluid or free-water restriction would need to be honored, per the stated 'unless contraindicated' caveat).

Guideline contribution: both relations derive from a single source, OpenRN Nursing Skills (Open RN, Volume/Text 2, p. 908). Because only one guideline body contributes, there are no cross-body disagreements to reconcile; however, the two recommendations differ in specificity. The flush recommendation is the more specific of the two, naming the flush medium (water), the timing (beginning and end of administration), and an explicit exception clause. The separate-administration recommendation names no volumes, sequence, or dwell time between drugs.

What this community does NOT establish: it names no specific drugs, drug classes, or high-risk formulations (e.g., crushed tablets, viscous suspensions); it specifies no flush volumes (no mL thresholds), no water temperature or type (tap vs. sterile vs. purified), and no flush frequency between individual medications or during continuous feeding. It does not define tube types or sizes (nasogastric, gastrostomy, jejunostomy, French size), does not address what to do once a tube is already clogged (declogging agents or techniques), and does not identify which patients have contraindications to water flushing. It also makes no perioperative or gynecologic-surgery-specific claims, and offers no outcome data, effect sizes, or evidence grading.

title: Blood Pressure Cuff Sizing Measurement Accuracy
summary:
Clinical theme: this small, tightly focused community addresses measurement accuracy in noninvasive blood pressure monitoring, specifically how blood pressure cuff size relative to the patient's arm biases the recorded value. Both relations in the community converge on a single outcome entity — underestimation of blood pressure — making cuff selection a technique-dependent source of measurement error rather than a drug- or procedure-related risk.

Recommendations and conditions: (1) An undersized blood pressure cuff increases the risk of underestimation of blood pressure, with the stated condition being when the cuff is too small for the arm. (2) An oversized blood pressure cuff likewise increases the risk of underestimation of blood pressure, when the cuff is too large for the arm. The practical implication for educators is that cuff-to-arm mismatch in either direction is flagged as a hazard, so staff should size the cuff to the individual arm circumference at every measurement rather than defaulting to a single ward cuff.

Contributing bodies: only one guideline source contributes here — RNAO (Registered Nurses' Association of Ontario), Table 2, page 30. Because a single body supplies both relations, there is no inter-guideline disagreement to reconcile and no instance where one body is more specific than another; the corpus offers no corroborating or competing statement from another organisation on cuff sizing.

What this community does NOT establish: no population is specified for either relation — there is no restriction to gynecologic surgical patients, adults, obese patients, or any perioperative phase. No numeric thresholds are given (no arm circumference ranges, no bladder-width-to-arm-circumference ratio, no mmHg magnitude of the underestimation). No timing or frequency of measurement is stated, no correct cuff-selection procedure is described, and no downstream clinical consequences (missed hypertension, undetected hypotension, delayed intervention, medication decisions) are linked. Notably, the graph attributes underestimation to both directions of mismatch and does not describe any overestimation effect, nor does it name devices, drugs, or alternative monitoring methods.

title: Heparin thromboprophylaxis: agent choice and timing
summary: This community centres on pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis with heparins in obstetric and gynecologic surgical patients, and specifically on the trade-off between unfractionated heparin (UFH) and low molecular weight heparin (LMWH), plus the timing interface with regional analgesia/anaesthesia. RCOG (Green-top, T1) contributes most detail: UFH carries higher risks than LMWH of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (pregnant women; risk substantially lower with LMWH), heparin-induced osteoporosis (2% vs 0.04%), bleeding in obstetric patients, and — with prolonged pregnancy use — osteoporosis and fracture; osteoporosis in turn predisposes to fracture from minor injury (OpenRN T2). Both LMWH and UFH increase bleeding/bruising after caesarean section versus no heparin. UFH is nonetheless recommended as an alternative to LMWH for women at high risk of haemorrhage, and peripartum for women at very high thrombosis risk where haemorrhage risk is raised or regional anaesthesia may be needed; a prophylactic 5000 iu subcutaneous dose every 12 hours can bridge women not yet delivered who have had no LMWH for 24 hours until LMWH resumes. UFH is also preferred where anticoagulation is needed but bleeding is a concern (antepartum haemorrhage, coagulopathy, progressive wound haematoma, suspected intra-abdominal bleeding, postpartum haemorrhage). Apparent heparin resistance leading to excessive dosing raises haemorrhage risk in late pregnancy, and thromboprophylactic dosing (5000 iu q12h) after IV UFH was associated with VTE recurrence in nonpregnant patients. Timing rules: 12 hours between prophylactic LMWH and regional analgesia, 4 hours for prophylactic UFH; regional techniques avoided for at least 24 hours after a therapeutic LMWH dose; the first postpartum LMWH dose is given as soon as possible after delivery only if regional analgesia was not used. ERAS Society (T1) is narrower, endorsing UFH as chemoprophylaxis with mechanical prophylaxis for patients at increased VTE risk and as dual prophylaxis throughout hospital stay for gynecologic oncology major surgery >30 minutes. Not established here: LMWH dosing/weight bands, prophylaxis duration, HIT monitoring or management, direct oral anticoagulants, or comparative efficacy data; OpenRN adds only that IV catheter placement is contraindicated in a fractured extremity.

title: Universal Glove Use in Epidemic ICUs
summary:
This community represents a narrow but well-defined infection-prevention theme: the use of universal gloving as a barrier precaution to interrupt transmission of multidrug-resistant organisms in critical care settings. Both relations in the community come from a single source, the CDC (T1, p31), and both make the same structural recommendation with different target organisms.

Recommendations, with populations and conditions: (1) Universal glove use prevents vancomycin-resistant enterococcus (VRE) outbreaks for all patients in intensive-care units, under the condition that VRE has been epidemic in that unit or facility. (2) Universal glove use prevents methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) outbreaks for all patients in intensive-care units, under the condition that MRSA has been epidemic in that setting. Note that the population is universal within the ICU — gloves are applied to contacts with all patients, not only those known to be colonized or infected — and the trigger for adopting the practice is documented epidemic activity of the specific organism rather than routine baseline conditions.

Guideline bodies: only the CDC contributes here; both statements trace to the same page of the same CDC document. There is therefore no inter-body disagreement to reconcile, and no competing or more granular recommendation from another organization within this community. The two statements are parallel in specificity, differing only in the resistant organism named.

What this community does NOT establish: it specifies no glove material, donning/doffing sequence, or duration of the universal gloving intervention; no threshold or case-count definition of what makes VRE or MRSA "epidemic"; and no criterion for de-escalating back to standard precautions once an outbreak resolves. It does not address non-ICU wards, operating rooms, or perioperative gynecologic patients specifically, nor does it cover other resistant organisms (for example Clostridioides difficile or resistant Gram-negatives). It also says nothing about accompanying measures such as hand hygiene, gowning, cohorting, active surveillance cultures, or environmental cleaning, and provides no efficacy magnitude or outcome data supporting the preventive claim.

title: Universal Precautions Prevent Bloodborne Pathogen Transmission
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: universal (standard) precautions as the core infection-prevention intervention against bloodborne pathogen transmission in perioperative and delivery-room care. Every relation in the community radiates from one intervention node — universal precautions — to a set of transmission-risk outcomes, indicating that the corpus treats this as a foundational, non-negotiable practice rather than a conditional or risk-stratified one.

Recommendations and their populations/conditions: (1) Universal precautions prevent HIV transmission for health care workers at all deliveries, explicitly including deliveries involving mothers known to be HIV-positive (WHO T1 p31) — the guideline's framing is that precautions apply universally at every delivery, not selectively when maternal HIV status is known. (2) Universal precautions prevent hepatitis B virus transmission, bloodborne pathogen transmission generally, and human immunodeficiency virus transmission for both health-care workers and patients, with the condition specified as during the administration of first aid or health care (WHO T1 p211). (3) Universal precautions prevent occupational exposure to human immunodeficiency virus for health-care workers (WHO T1 p211).

Contributing bodies: all relations derive from a single source, WHO (Tier 1 document, pages 31 and 211). There is therefore no inter-body disagreement to reconcile. There is a difference in specificity within WHO itself: p31 is population- and setting-specific (health care workers at all deliveries, mothers with HIV), while p211 is broader — covering both workers and patients, naming HBV alongside HIV, and extending the setting to any first aid or health care encounter. The p211 material is also the only place that names occupational exposure as a distinct outcome.

What this community does NOT establish: it names no specific components of universal precautions (no gloves, gowns, eye protection, sharps handling, or hand hygiene steps), no drugs, no post-exposure prophylaxis regimens, no timings or thresholds, and no testing or serostatus criteria. It does not address hepatitis C, does not quantify risk reduction or efficacy, does not describe management after a needlestick or exposure, and offers no guidance on vaccination (including HBV immunisation) or on patient-to-patient transmission mechanisms.
key_entities: occupational exposure to human immunodeficiency virus

title: Coude Catheter Use in Male Patients
summary:
This small community represents a single, focused clinical theme: selection and safe insertion technique for the coude (curved-tip) urinary catheter in male patients. Two relations anchor the theme. First, the coude tipped catheter applies to urinary catheterization specifically for male patients, and the stated condition for choosing it is when the patient has an enlarged prostate — i.e., the curved tip is the device of choice when prostatic enlargement obstructs passage of a straight catheter (OpenRN Nursing Skills, T2 p1241). Second, the same catheter increases the risk of urethral damage in patients undergoing coude catheter insertion, with the qualifying condition that the risk arises if the tip is not pointed anteriorly during insertion (OpenRN T2 p1208). Practically, the two statements combine into one teaching point for competency training and QI audit: when a coude catheter is indicated for an adult male with an enlarged prostate, the inserter must orient the curved tip anteriorly (upward) throughout advancement to avoid urethral trauma.

Only one guideline body contributes here — the OpenRN open-access nursing skills text — drawn from two separate pages. There is no inter-organisational disagreement to reconcile; p1241 is more specific about the indication and population (male patients, enlarged prostate), while p1208 is more specific about the procedural hazard and the technique-dependent condition (tip orientation).

The community does not establish several things a educator should not infer: no catheter French size, balloon volume, lubricant, anaesthetic gel (e.g., lidocaine), or antiseptic agent is named; no timing, dwell duration, or number of insertion attempts is specified; no threshold defines "enlarged prostate" (no prostate volume, PSA, or IPSS value). It does not state who may insert a coude catheter, whether urology consultation or escalation is required after failed attempts, and gives no guidance for female patients, children, or perioperative gynecologic patients specifically. Outcomes beyond urethral damage — bleeding, false passage, stricture, CAUTI — are not addressed, nor is any management pathway once urethral damage occurs.

title: Aseptic Urinary Catheter Insertion Practices
summary:
This community centers on a single clinical theme: the technique and personnel competency required for urinary catheter insertion, with all three relations converging on catheter insertion as the shared procedural node. It bundles three complementary elements: (1) aseptic technique, which applies to urinary catheter insertion for patients in the acute care hospital setting, with the condition that sterile equipment be used; (2) sterile single-use lubricant jelly, specified as the lubricant for insertion (no population or qualifying condition attached in this graph); and (3) periodic in-service training, directed not at patients but at healthcare personnel and others who take care of catheters, with the condition that it stress correct techniques and procedures for insertion, maintenance, and removal. Notably, the training relation is the broadest in scope, extending beyond insertion to maintenance and removal, whereas the aseptic technique and lubricant relations are confined to the insertion event itself.

Only one guideline body contributes here: the CDC, drawing from a single document (Table/Section T1, pages 12 and 45). Because the corpus for this theme is monolithic, there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile; differences are only in specificity. The aseptic technique recommendation is the most population-specific (acute care hospital patients) and equipment-conditioned (sterile equipment); the lubricant recommendation is the least qualified, naming a product type without population, timing, or frequency; the training recommendation is the most specific about audience and curricular content but not about interval.

What this community does NOT establish: no interval or frequency is defined for "periodic" in-service training; no competency assessment, credentialing, or documentation standard is specified; no catheter type, size, material, or indication criteria are given; no duration-of-dwell, insertion-site antisepsis agent, hand hygiene product, or glove/drape specification appears; no lubricant volume, anesthetic-containing lubricant, or brand is named; and no outcome measure (e.g., CAUTI rate), non-acute-care setting (long-term care, home, outpatient), pediatric or obstetric population, or intermittent versus indwelling distinction is addressed.
key_entities: healthcare personnel and others who take care of catheters
patients in the acute care hospital setting

title: Urinary Catheterization: Indications and Routine Care Limits
summary: This community centres on indwelling urinary catheterization — its legitimate clinical indications, device selection, and the routine care practices that should NOT be performed once a catheter is in situ. Two recommendations define appropriate use: catheterization TREATS urinary retention, including specifically when the client is unable to void (OpenRN T2 pp. 825, 1183); and catheterization serves a monitoring function for hypovolaemia in volume-depleted surgical patients, as part of fluid status monitoring and depending on the clinical situation (WHO T1 p. 42). For device selection, a coude (curved) tipped catheter applies to male patients when an enlarged prostate is present (OpenRN T2 p. 1241). Two practices are flagged as inappropriate routine care. Periurethral cleansing with antiseptics is contraindicated once the catheter is in place — stated by OpenRN T2 p. 1226 for patients with an indwelling catheter after the catheter is in place, and echoed by CDC T1 p. 13 as temporarily contraindicated while the catheter is in place. Bladder irrigation is likewise temporarily contraindicated in catheterized patients unless obstruction is anticipated, with CDC T1 p. 13 giving the concrete exemplar of bleeding after prostatic or bladder surgery. Contributing bodies are OpenRN (nursing skills text), CDC (infection-prevention guidance), and WHO (surgical safety/perioperative). They agree substantively on periurethral antiseptic cleansing; CDC frames it as temporary (duration-of-catheter) rather than absolute, and CDC alone addresses bladder irrigation and names the obstruction exception. OpenRN alone addresses catheter type selection and retention indications; WHO alone addresses haemodynamic monitoring. The community does NOT establish: any named antiseptic agent, irrigation solution, or drug; catheter sizes, materials, or dwell/removal timings; frequency or method of acceptable perineal hygiene as an alternative to antiseptics; criteria or thresholds for diagnosing urinary retention or hypovolaemia (no urine-output thresholds are given); indications for intermittent versus indwelling catheterization; CAUTI rates or outcome data; or any gynecologic-surgery-specific catheterization protocol.

title: Urinary Incontinence Risk, Prevention, Treatment
summary: This community centres on urinary incontinence (UI) in adult females across the perioperative and postpartum continuum: its risk factors, conservative and pharmacologic management, and postnatal surveillance. Three risk factors are named for adult females: pregnancy, menopause, and vaginal hysterectomy (OpenRN T2 p1150) — the last making UI a directly relevant gynecologic surgical outcome. Prevention is framed as nurse-delivered education: bladder control training prevents UI in clients when delivered through nurse education (OpenRN T2 p1162). Treatment for clients already diagnosed with UI is a bundle of behavioural and lifestyle measures: pelvic muscle exercise, timed voiding (specifically to assist in regaining bladder control), avoidance of caffeine, weight control, and avoidance of heavy lifting (OpenRN T2 p1430), plus biofeedback (OpenRN T2 p1162). Anticholinergic medication is positioned not as first-line but as an additional medical intervention for clients with UI (OpenRN T2 p1430). Notably, avoidance of heavy lifting does double duty in the corpus: for surgical patients it also prevents wound dehiscence when advised (OpenRN T2 p1113), so a single discharge instruction serves both incision integrity and continence goals. WHO contributes the only timed monitoring recommendation: assessment of urinary incontinence and micturition in postpartum women at each subsequent postnatal contact beyond 24 hours after birth (WHO T1 p23). Thus WHO is more specific on timing and population (postpartum, repeated contacts), while OpenRN is more specific on intervention content; neither contradicts the other, and OpenRN does not attach a screening schedule while WHO does not name any treatment. The community does NOT establish: any named anticholinergic drug, dose, route or duration; UI subtypes (stress vs urge) or severity thresholds; frequency, repetitions or duration for pelvic muscle exercise or timed voiding intervals; caffeine or weight/BMI thresholds; a lifting weight limit or time period after surgery; comparative effectiveness or sequencing of behavioural versus pharmacologic therapy; referral criteria for surgical management; or any evidence-grade, outcome measure, or male/non-obstetric population data.
key_entities: assessment of urinary incontinence and micturition

title: Pessary Use and Urodynamic Bladder Assessment
summary:
Clinical theme: this small community addresses lower urinary tract dysfunction in gynecologic/perioperative nursing care, pairing one mechanical management device (the pessary) with one diagnostic modality (urodynamic testing) around two shared outcome entities — urinary leakage and urinary retention. It spans both the intervention side (containing leakage) and the assessment side (identifying whether the underlying problem is leakage from involuntary bladder contractions or incomplete emptying/retention).

Main recommendations with populations and conditions:
1) A pessary prevents urinary leakage in clients with urinary incontinence or vaginal prolapse, and the relation is explicitly conditioned on the device being professionally fitted (OpenRN Nursing Skills Tome 2, p1162). The 'professionally fitted' qualifier is the key teaching point: the preventive effect is not attributed to a self-selected or unfitted pessary.
2) Urodynamic testing detects urinary retention (OpenRN T2 p1169) and detects urinary leakage when there are involuntary bladder contractions causing leakage (OpenRN T2 p1183). Thus urodynamic testing serves a dual diagnostic role, distinguishing overactive/involuntary-contraction leakage from retention.

Contributing guideline bodies: all three relations derive from a single source corpus — OpenRN (Nursing Skills, Tome 2), at pages 1162, 1169 and 1183. There is therefore no cross-body disagreement to reconcile; differences are only in specificity. The pessary relation is the most specific, carrying both a population (incontinence or prolapse) and a procedural condition (professional fitting). The retention-detection relation at p1169 is the least specified, listing no population or condition, whereas the leakage-detection relation at p1183 adds the mechanistic condition of involuntary bladder contractions.

What this community does NOT establish: no drugs, doses, thresholds, volumes, pressures, or timings are given; no perioperative sequencing (pre- vs post-operative testing) is specified; no population is attached to urodynamic testing at all, including no age, parity, surgical or pregnancy-related criteria. It does not state that urodynamic testing should precede pessary fitting, does not link pessary use to retention, and offers no comparative effectiveness, contraindications, complications, follow-up interval, or alternative therapies (e.g., pelvic floor training, surgery, catheterization).

title: Urinary retention detection and management
summary:
This community centers on recognizing, measuring, and managing urinary retention in the perioperative and post-catheter period. Risk factors: opioids increase retention risk generally, and specifically in clients taking opioids, in opioid-naive clients, and when opioids are given via the spinal route; other contributors are an enlarged prostate (adult males) and blockage in the urinary tract. Retention is not benign — the ERAS Society links it to delayed discharge in gynecologic minimally invasive surgery patients, attributing 30% of delayed discharges to it.

Detection recommendations (OpenRN Nursing Skills/Fundamentals T2): bedside bladder scanning with an ultrasound bladder scanner to obtain post-void residual after the client voids (supine position), and to confirm bladder fullness in patients being assessed for catheterization per agency policy; post-void residual measurement by bladder scanner or straight catheterization in clients with suspected retention; urodynamic testing also detects retention. After indwelling catheter removal, scan patients unable to void within 4–6 hours and/or complaining of bladder fullness, or when voided volume is less than 180 mL; if no scanner is available, straight catheterization is used to detect incomplete emptying. Management: urinary catheterization treats retention when the client is unable to void, and straight catheterization is indicated when post-void residual exceeds 300 mL. Monitoring: continual monitoring for retention in clients receiving opioids; focused physical assessment in end-of-life clients, limited to comfort.

AUGS adds timing specificity absent from OpenRN: post-void residual monitoring following catheter removal within 3 to 48 hours, and PVR monitoring prior to discharge for patients undergoing an early trial without catheter (postoperative voiding difficulty). OpenRN supplies the volumetric thresholds (180 mL, 300 mL); ERAS supplies the outcome rationale.

Not established: no medication (e.g., alpha-blocker) treatment pathways, no catheter type/duration choices, no specific gynecologic-surgery risk factors beyond opioids and obstruction, no PVR threshold from AUGS or ERAS, and no evidence grading or infection-risk trade-offs of repeat catheterization.

title: Urinary Tract Infection Prevention, Detection, Treatment
summary:
This community centres on urinary tract infection (UTI) across the perioperative and general nursing continuum: risk factors, detection, prevention, treatment and monitoring.

Detection: OpenRN (T2 p1159) pairs urinalysis, urine dip and urine culture for clients presenting with UTI symptoms; a culture reported as 'no growth' at 24 or 48 hours usually indicates no infection (p1183). Urine dip is also ordered for clients assessed for incontinence after review of the voiding diary and physical assessment (p1162). Culture site is chosen by suspected infection site (p663). NICE (T1 p8) is more restrictive and preoperatively specific: microscopy and culture of a midstream urine sample in elective surgery patients only if a UTI would influence the decision to operate.

Risk: prolonged urinary catheterization raises UTI risk in postoperative patients versus shorter duration (ERAS Society T1 p6); retained urine in urinary retention (OpenRN p1183); urostomy (p1232); chronic disease and incontinence in older adults (p1241). RCOG (T1 p12) uniquely links UTI to increased venous thromboembolism risk in pregnant women.

Treatment (OpenRN): antibiotics; increased fluid intake for clients with a UTI; phenazopyridine for pain, frequency and burning in patients with UTI.

Prevention (OpenRN p1159): urination after sexual activity, adequate hydration and regular urination, showering instead of bathing, minimizing douching/sprays/powders in the genital area, and wiping front to back for females; keeping the collection bag off the floor for patients with indwelling catheters (p1208).

Monitoring (OpenRN): specific post-removal assessment after recent indwelling catheter removal; monitoring for signs of UTI in urinary retention; ongoing urine output monitoring (clarity, color, amount) in catheterized patients, with specimen collection if urine is cloudy, concentrated, malodorous, dark amber, or contains sediment, blood or pus.

Not established: no antibiotic agents, doses, durations or phenazopyridine dosing; no numeric fluid-intake targets; no catheter duration threshold defining 'prolonged'; no diagnostic colony-count thresholds; no guidance on treating asymptomatic bacteriuria or deferring surgery; and no VTE prophylaxis pathway linked to UTI beyond the RCOG risk association.
key_entities: microscopy and culture of midstream urine sample

title: ERAS pathway elements in urogynecologic surgery
summary:
This community represents a single coherent theme: the components of an enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) pathway for patients undergoing urogynecological surgery, spanning the preoperative, intraoperative and discharge phases. All relations derive from one guideline body, the American Urogynecologic Society (AUGS) Table 2 document, drawn from pages 4-12.

Preoperative recommendations: structured preoperative fasting guidance, explicitly extrapolated from oncological, abdominal and gynecological surgery protocols rather than urogynecology-specific evidence (p4); routine carbohydrate loading with a ≤ 50-g clear liquid for patients undergoing urogynecologic surgery, also extrapolated — here from non-gynecological surgery data (p4); and preoperative counseling specifically for patients being planned for same-day discharge, delivered when same-day discharge is being planned (p12).

Antibiotic prophylaxis: cefazolin 2 gm intravenously within 1 hour of skin incision, increased to 3 g for patients weighing more than 120 kg (p6) — the most numerically specific recommendation in the community.

Intraoperative and anesthetic care: a standardized anesthetic protocol (p5) and multimodal analgesia for patients undergoing urogynecological/urogynecologic surgery, appearing on both p5 and p8, indicating reinforcement across sections. A minimally invasive surgical approach is preferred over abdominal approaches when feasible (p7).

Discharge: same-day discharge for properly selected patients undergoing urogynecological surgery, as part of an ERAS pathway (p12), paired with the preoperative counseling above.

Because only AUGS Table 2 contributes, there are no inter-body disagreements to reconcile; differences are instead in specificity — cefazolin dosing and carbohydrate volume carry explicit thresholds, whereas the standardized anesthetic protocol, multimodal analgesia and minimally invasive approach are stated without named agents, doses, techniques or timing.

What this community does NOT establish: which analgesic drugs or anesthetic agents comprise the recommended protocols; specific fasting time intervals; criteria defining "properly selected" or "feasible"; alternatives for cefazolin allergy; content or timing of counseling; postoperative outcomes, complication rates, or any urogynecology-specific evidence supporting the extrapolated fasting and carbohydrate-loading recommendations.

title: Uterotonics for postpartum haemorrhage prevention
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: the use of uterotonics to prevent and treat postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) around the time of birth, including in women undergoing caesarean section. All 15 relations derive from one guideline body — WHO (WHO T1, pp. 9-36) — so the corpus shows convergence rather than disagreement, though the level of specificity varies by page.

Core prophylactic recommendation: uterotonics prevent PPH in all births / all women giving birth, administered during the third stage of labour (pp. 9, 10, 19, 21, 26), or more loosely 'after birth as prophylaxis' / 'for women after birth' (pp. 10, 19). Two pages add an important qualifier for practice and audit: only one uterotonic — and on p. 9 only one *effective* uterotonic — should be used during the third stage (pp. 9, 26). Uterotonics are named as the main intervention within the active management of the third stage of labour (AMTSL) package for women in the third stage (p. 19).

Treatment recommendation: for women who already have PPH, oxytocin alone is the first choice (p. 19) — the only drug named anywhere in this community.

Safety/quality conditions: use should be monitored (p. 19); correct dosage and safe use are required for women giving birth (p. 36). For women undergoing caesarean section, injectable uterotonics require skilled health personnel trained to administer them (p. 26).

What this community does NOT establish: no doses, units, routes, timing windows (e.g. within one minute of birth), or blood-loss thresholds defining PPH; no named agents other than oxytocin (no misoprostol, ergometrine, carbetocin, tranexamic acid); no comparative effectiveness or hierarchy among uterotonics; no contraindications, adverse effects, or storage/cold-chain requirements; no guidance for women with prior caesarean, anaemia, or other high-risk subgroups; no non-pharmacological adjuncts (uterine massage, cord traction) beyond the AMTSL label; and no contribution from non-WHO bodies for triangulation.
key_entities: active management of third stage of labour

title: Vaginal bleeding and antenatal LMWH
summary:
This community centres on vaginal bleeding as a clinical trigger point in the perioperative/peripartum period, linking it both to the withholding of pharmacological thromboprophylaxis and to the expected consequences of routine obstetric assessment.

The dominant recommendation, contributed twice by RCOG (Top Tip / p20 and p5), is that low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) is temporarily contraindicated in the presence of vaginal bleeding. The population is specifically women receiving antenatal LMWH. The condition is stated in two closely aligned forms: women should be advised to withhold further LMWH if they have any vaginal bleeding or once labour begins, until they are reassessed on admission (p20); and p5 adds a further operational detail — the interruption continues until the woman is reassessed on admission and further doses are prescribed. The p5 phrasing is therefore the more specific of the two, making explicit that resumption requires an active prescribing decision rather than simply clinical review. Note the threshold is 'any' vaginal bleeding — no volume or duration cut-off is applied — and labour onset is an equally sufficient trigger, independent of bleeding.

WHO (p103) contributes the second, distinct strand: vaginal examination increases the risk of vaginal bleeding in pregnant women, with the qualifier that a small amount of bleeding after examination is regarded as normal. This is useful for educators because it establishes that not all post-examination bleeding is pathological.

The two bodies do not conflict, but they are not integrated: the community does not establish how WHO's 'small amount of bleeding regarded as normal' after vaginal examination should be reconciled with RCOG's instruction to withhold LMWH for 'any' vaginal bleeding. No relation states whether examination-related spotting should trigger LMWH interruption. Also absent: LMWH doses, agents or brand names, timing intervals between last dose and regional anaesthesia or delivery, criteria for reassessment on admission, management of the bleeding itself, mechanical thromboprophylaxis alternatives during interruption, postpartum restart timing, and any explicit VTE-risk stratification for the women concerned.

title: Vaginal Hysterectomy: Analgesia and Incontinence Risk
summary:
This community centres on vaginal hysterectomy as an index gynecologic procedure, linking it to two distinct concerns: a downstream urologic complication and regional/neuraxial analgesic strategies used to limit opioid exposure.

Risk theme: OpenRN (Textbook 2, p1150) establishes that vaginal hysterectomy increases the risk of urinary incontinence in adult females. No qualifying condition, timeframe, or incontinence subtype (stress vs. urge) is attached, so the relation should be read as a general postoperative risk to include in preoperative counselling and discharge teaching rather than a graded or time-bound prediction.

Analgesia theme: the ERAS Society (Text 1, p2) contributes two interventions that apply to vaginal hysterectomy under the same stated condition — to reduce pain and opioid consumption: paracervical nerve block and intrathecal morphine. Both are presented as applicable options for the same procedure and the same goal; the corpus does not rank them, combine them, or state that one is preferred.

Contributing bodies and differences: only two sources appear, and they address non-overlapping aspects. OpenRN speaks to complication risk and is the only source that specifies a population (adult females). ERAS Society is the more specific source on intervention naming (two named techniques) but attaches no population — only a therapeutic condition — so age, comorbidity, and contraindication boundaries for paracervical block or intrathecal morphine are not defined here.

What this community does NOT establish: no doses, concentrations, volumes, or local anesthetic agents for the paracervical block; no intrathecal morphine dose, timing relative to incision, or monitoring interval for respiratory depression or pruritus; no magnitude of opioid or pain-score reduction; no incidence, severity, or duration of postoperative urinary incontinence, and no link between the analgesic techniques and incontinence risk in either direction. Nothing is stated about alternative surgical routes, non-opioid multimodal adjuncts, catheter management, pelvic floor rehabilitation, or preoperative screening for baseline urinary symptoms. Educators should therefore treat this as a two-strand awareness theme requiring local protocol detail before bedside implementation.

title: Vaginal antisepsis and packing in vaginal surgery
summary:
This community represents preoperative vaginal antisepsis and postoperative vaginal packing practice for vaginal-route gynecologic and obstetric surgery, framed by the infectious risks of that route. The WHO guideline (T1 p57) establishes the rationale: vaginal surgery increases the risk of both endometritis and wound infection, making the vagina a target site for preparatory antisepsis.
