Main recommendations: (1) Vaginal cleansing with povidone-iodine applies to patients undergoing vaginal surgery (AUGS T2 p7). (2) AUGS T2 p14 broadens the agent choice, stating that vaginal cleansing with either chlorhexidine gluconate or povidone-iodine applies to women undergoing hysterectomy or vaginal surgery, performed before surgery. (3) WHO T1 p18 extends povidone-iodine vaginal cleansing to a distinct obstetric population — women undergoing caesarean section — with a specific timing condition: immediately before caesarean section. (4) AUGS T2 p14 also addresses postoperative care: vaginal packing should not be used routinely following vaginal surgery.

Contributing bodies and differences: two bodies contribute — WHO (T1) and AUGS (T2). WHO is the source of the risk statements and of the caesarean-section application, and is the more specific on timing ("immediately before" the caesarean). AUGS is the more specific on population breadth and agent choice within gynecologic surgery, naming hysterectomy alongside vaginal surgery and permitting chlorhexidine gluconate as an alternative to povidone-iodine; the earlier AUGS entry (p7) names only povidone-iodine for vaginal surgery. AUGS alone addresses vaginal packing.

What is not established: no concentrations, volumes, contact/scrub times, or number of applications are given for either povidone-iodine or chlorhexidine gluconate; no preference between the two agents is stated, and no timing interval is specified for vaginal surgery (only for caesarean section). The relations do not quantify the magnitude of endometritis or wound-infection risk, do not state that vaginal cleansing reduces those specific outcomes, and give no exceptions or indications for when vaginal packing would be appropriate non-routinely. Antibiotic prophylaxis, skin preparation, and postoperative surveillance are absent from this community.
key_entities: vaginal cleansing with chlorhexidine gluconate or povidone-iodine

title: Validated Guidelines Preventing Perioperative Never Events
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused theme: the use of validated clinical guidelines by health professionals as a preventive control against perioperative 'never events' and surgical site infection in gynecologic care. Four relations, all drawn from the same source (WHO T1, p228), converge on one causal claim: a validated clinical guideline PREVENTS (1) procedural site infection, (2) wrong person treatment, (3) wrong site treatment, and (4) wrong procedure treatment. The population attached to every relation is identical - health professionals - and no narrower subgroup (e.g., scrub nurse, circulating nurse, surgeon, anaesthetist) or patient population is specified. No additional condition, qualifier, timing, or clinical trigger is attached to any of the four relations; they are stated unconditionally for health professionals.

Only one guideline body contributes: the World Health Organization (WHO T1 p228). Because the corpus segment contains no second body, there are no points of disagreement, no differences in specificity, and no opportunity to compare stricter versus more permissive phrasing. Educators should note that the evidence here is uniform in source and therefore cannot be triangulated within this community.

For a nurse educator or QI lead, the usable message is conceptual rather than procedural: adherence to validated clinical guidelines is positioned as the shared safeguard for both infection prevention and correct-patient/correct-site/correct-procedure verification, allowing these four safety outcomes to be taught as one bundle under a single behavioural expectation for all health professionals.

What this community does NOT establish: it names no specific guideline instrument (no surgical safety checklist, time-out, or site-marking protocol), no drugs or antimicrobial prophylaxis agents, no doses, no thresholds, and no timings (e.g., minutes before incision, pre-induction versus pre-incision verification). It does not specify who performs verification, how compliance is audited, what documentation is required, or effect sizes and evidence grades. It does not address gynecologic procedure types individually, patient risk factors, or postoperative follow-up, and it offers no guidance on what to do when a guideline is unavailable or conflicts with local practice.

title: Blood Pressure Cuff Venous Congestion Prevention
summary:
Clinical theme: this small community addresses an iatrogenic risk of non-invasive blood pressure monitoring in the perioperative gynecologic setting — limb venous congestion caused by the blood pressure cuff itself, and the timing interval used to prevent it. It is a monitoring-technique safety theme rather than a drug or diagnostic theme.

Recommendations and conditions: (1) The blood pressure cuff is identified as increasing the risk of venous congestion when it is left partially inflated for too long — that is, when the cuff does not fully deflate between measurements. (2) Allowing a one-minute interval between successive blood pressure readings prevents venous congestion; the stated condition is explicitly 'between successive blood pressure readings.' Practically, this supports teaching staff to confirm full cuff deflation and to space repeat cycles at least one minute apart, particularly where frequent or automated cycling occurs.

Contributing guideline bodies: only RNAO (Registered Nurses' Association of Ontario) contributes here, with both relations traced to a single source location (RNAO Tool 2, p32). Because there is a single contributing body and a single page, there is no inter-guideline disagreement to reconcile, and no second body offering a more specific threshold or an alternative interval. Any perceived consensus should therefore be attributed to RNAO alone, not to the wider corpus.

What this community does NOT establish: it specifies no population — no age group, no gynecologic procedure type, no comorbidity (e.g., lymphedema, prior axillary or pelvic node dissection, arteriovenous fistula), and no perioperative phase (pre-, intra-, or post-operative). It gives no maximum permissible inflation duration, no cuff pressure threshold, no cuff size or placement guidance, no limb-rotation or contralateral-alternation instruction, and no maximum number of cycles. It does not describe how venous congestion is recognised, graded, or managed once present, nor any downstream harms (e.g., petechiae, nerve injury, measurement inaccuracy). It also does not address invasive arterial monitoring or automated oscillometric devices specifically. Local protocols must supply these details.
key_entities: one minute interval between blood pressure readings

title: VTE Prophylaxis Across Surgical Populations
summary: This community centres on venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis as a cross-cutting perioperative intervention: which surgical and inpatient populations it applies to, which phases of care it spans, and when it should be withheld. Two guideline bodies contribute. ERAS Society (T1 p1) is the gynecologic-oncology-specific voice: prophylaxis applies to major gynecologic oncology surgery when surgery exceeds 30 minutes, and it is explicitly placed in both the preoperative and postoperative phases, signalling continuity across the episode of care rather than a single dose. NICE (T1, multiple pages) is broader and organised by surgical specialty and risk balance: prophylaxis prevents VTE in people admitted to hospital at increased risk (p9); abdominal surgery including gastrointestinal, gynaecological and urological, for those at increased risk (p27); thoracic surgery at increased risk (p29); bariatric surgery (p28); other knee surgery such as osteotomy or fracture surgery, where VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk (p23); and people taking antiplatelet agents for other conditions, again where VTE risk outweighs bleeding risk (p13). For upper limb surgery, NICE is the most conditional: prophylaxis is generally not needed with local or regional anaesthetic, but should be considered if total general anaesthetic time exceeds 90 minutes or the operation is likely to impair mobilisation (p24). NICE also defines when to stop or hold: prophylaxis is contraindicated in people in the last days of life (p16) and temporarily contraindicated in women admitted to hospital or a midwife-led unit while in active labour (p34). Note the differing time thresholds — ERAS uses >30 minutes of surgery in gynecologic oncology, NICE uses >90 minutes under general anaesthetic for upper limb surgery — so thresholds are population-specific, not interchangeable. The community does not specify any pharmacological or mechanical agents, doses, start or stop times, duration of extended prophylaxis, risk-assessment tools, or how 'increased risk of VTE' is defined or measured, and it names no outcomes beyond VTE prevention.

title: Preventing VTE Recurrence in Pregnancy
summary:
This community centres on recurrent venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk in pregnancy and the postpartum period, and the anticoagulant strategies used to prevent it. All relations derive from a single guideline body, RCOG (Thromboembolic disease in pregnancy, T1, pp. 6-38); no other body contributes, so no inter-body disagreement can be shown, though specificity varies by page.

Treatment recommendations: low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) prevents recurrence in pregnant women managed for VTE, specifically when therapeutic (not prophylactic) doses are used and continued throughout the remainder of the pregnancy (pp. 11, 17); LMWH is also preferred over unfractionated heparin in patients with DVT or PE during the initial treatment period (p. 11). Conversely, unfractionated heparin at thromboprophylactic doses (5000 iu every 12 hours) after initial intravenous unfractionated heparin increased recurrence risk in nonpregnant patients (p. 17). At term, intravenous unfractionated heparin is favoured because its shorter half-life minimises time without anticoagulation (p. 19). Postpartum thromboprophylaxis is recommended for all women with prior VTE, the postpartum being the period of greatest risk (p. 13). In non-pregnant patients with a first unprovoked VTE, low-dose aspirin after completing warfarin gives a modest reduction versus placebo (p. 25).

Risk factors for recurrence: previous VTE (pregnancy and postpartum; classed high risk in pregnancy except a single VTE related to major surgery, pp. 6, 13, 38); pregnancy itself versus the nonpregnant period (relative risk 3.5, p. 13); thrombophilia and reduced venous flow velocity in pregnant women with VTE (p. 17); antithrombin deficiency, particularly type 1 with family history (p. 14); antiphospholipid syndrome with previous VTE in pregnancy (p. 14); and family history of VTE, including in the absence of an identifiable thrombophilic tendency (pp. 14, 17).

Not established: specific LMWH agents, mg/kg or weight-based dosing, monitoring or anti-Xa thresholds, duration of postpartum prophylaxis, timing of peripartum interruption/neuraxial anaesthesia intervals, breastfeeding safety, and any quantified recurrence rates beyond the RR 3.5 for pregnancy.

title: VTE Risk Assessment Across Care Phases
summary:
This community represents the theme of structured venous thromboembolism (VTE) risk assessment as a screening activity that detects risk factors before thromboprophylaxis decisions are made. Three guideline bodies contribute, each anchoring the assessment to a different population and timing.

AUGS (T2 p13) places VTE risk assessment in the preoperative phase, where it is performed as part of the preoperative assessment to detect risk factors for venous thromboembolism.

RCOG (T1 p2, p10) extends the same assessment into the antenatal phase, specifying that all women should be risk-assessed in early pregnancy or prepregnancy to identify risk factors for VTE; the generic 'risk assessment' entity carries the identical population and timing (RCOG T1 p10), indicating the assessment is not surgery-specific but a routine maternity activity.

NICE (T1 p7) is the most specific on timing, tooling and scope: for all surgical and trauma patients, risk assessment should occur as soon as possible after admission to hospital or by the time of the first consultant review. NICE alone requires the use of a tool published by a national UK body, professional network or peer-reviewed journal, and NICE alone makes the assessment explicitly dual — detecting both venous thromboembolism risk and bleeding risk, rather than VTE risk factors only.

Points of difference: AUGS and RCOG frame the output as 'risk factors for VTE'; NICE frames outputs as VTE and bleeding risk. AUGS ties assessment to a surgical phase, RCOG to pregnancy timing, NICE to admission/consultant-review milestones and surgical/trauma populations.

What this community does NOT establish: no named risk-assessment tool or scoring system, no numeric thresholds or score cut-offs, no drugs, doses or mechanical prophylaxis options, no reassessment intervals, and no linkage from a given risk level to a specific prophylactic action or contraindication. It also says nothing about intraoperative or postoperative reassessment, discharge planning, or documentation requirements.

title: Vitamin K Antagonists Contraindicated in Pregnancy
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused theme: the fetal safety hazards of vitamin K antagonists (VKAs), including warfarin, when used for antenatal venous thromboembolism (VTE) treatment. All relations derive from RCOG (Green-top guidance on thromboembolic disease in pregnancy), pages 4 and 18 of the same trimester-1 tagged source, so the theme is contributed by one guideline body only, with no cross-body agreement or conflict available to assess.

Core recommendations: warfarin is contraindicated for antenatal VTE treatment in pregnant women because of adverse effects on the fetus (p4). The same contraindication is stated more broadly for the drug class — vitamin K antagonists are contraindicated both for antenatal VTE treatment and in pregnancy itself, specifically for pregnant women requiring antenatal VTE treatment, again on the grounds of fetal harm (p4, p18). Page 18 is the more specific of the two passages, enumerating the fetal and neonatal risks that justify the contraindication: embryopathy following fetal exposure in the first trimester (condition explicitly timed to the first trimester, population = fetus); and, for pregnant women generally, miscarriage, prematurity, low birth weight, neurodevelopmental problems, and fetal and neonatal bleeding. Page 4 gives the practical prohibition without the mechanism; page 18 supplies the rationale — useful for teaching the "why" behind the rule.

What this community does NOT establish: no alternative anticoagulant is named (no LMWH, heparin, dose, weight band, anti-Xa monitoring or INR threshold appears), so it cannot be used to teach substitution therapy. It gives no postnatal or breastfeeding guidance, no advice on women already on VKAs who become pregnant (no switching timing or preconception counselling), no mechanical prophylaxis, no quantified risk magnitudes or incidence rates, and no gestational cut-offs beyond "first trimester" for embryopathy. It also says nothing about VKA use for mechanical heart valves or other indications, nor about surgical/perioperative timing of anticoagulation. Educators should pair it with dosing and peripartum-management guidance from elsewhere in the corpus.

title: Volume Overload Risk in Uncontrolled Hypertension
summary:
This small community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: identifying contributors to volume overload in patients whose blood pressure remains above target despite treatment. Two risk relations are captured, both drawn from the same source context (RNAO Table 2, p71) and both conditioned on the same population — patients whose target blood pressure is not being reached. In that population, (1) high sodium intake increases the risk of volume overload, and (2) renal insufficiency increases the risk of volume overload. Practically, this frames volume overload as a reason to reassess why a patient's BP target is not being met, and directs assessment toward dietary sodium and renal function as two candidate explanations. For a nurse educator or QI lead, this supports teaching that in the perioperative gynecologic patient with persistently elevated blood pressure, dietary sodium history and evidence of renal insufficiency should be explicitly reviewed rather than escalating antihypertensive therapy alone.

Only one guideline body contributes: RNAO (Registered Nurses' Association of Ontario), Table 2, p71. There is therefore no cross-body agreement or disagreement to report, and no instance where one guideline is more specific than another — the corpus offers a single, undifferentiated statement of risk for both factors, with no ranking of which contributes more.

The community does NOT establish: any numeric thresholds (no sodium intake limit in mg or g per day, no blood pressure target value, no eGFR, creatinine, or CKD stage defining 'renal insufficiency'); no timing or frequency for assessment or reassessment; no named drugs, including diuretics, ACE inhibitors, or other antihypertensives; no diagnostic criteria or clinical signs for volume overload itself (no weight change, edema, or fluid balance parameters); and no recommended interventions, monitoring plan, or escalation/referral pathway once risk is identified. It also says nothing about perioperative timing, gynecologic surgery specifically, or outcomes if volume overload occurs. Local protocols would need to supply all operational detail.
key_entities: patients whose target blood pressure is not being reached

title: Warfarin timing and bleeding risk
summary: This community centres on warfarin as an oral anticoagulant in women's perioperative and maternity care, specifically its bleeding and fetal harms, its contraindication in pregnancy, and the heparin-to-warfarin transition. Recommendations: warfarin is contraindicated in pregnancy and for antenatal VTE treatment because of adverse fetal effects (RCOG T1 p4, p18); in pregnant women it increases risk of fetal and maternal haemorrhage, spontaneous miscarriage and stillbirth (p25), and women on long-term warfarin or other oral anticoagulants in pregnancy face fetal harm (p2, p15). Postpartum, warfarin should be avoided until at least the fifth postnatal day, and longer in women at increased risk of postpartum haemorrhage, with administration delayed while that risk persists (p5, p20); given before day 5 it increases PPH risk (p20), and compared with LMWH it increases PPH and perineal haematoma in women following delivery and breastfeeding mothers (p25). Transition rules are explicit: heparin is continued until the INR exceeds 2.0 for at least 24 hours (p20); women who choose warfarin postpartum have daily INR monitoring during transfer from LMWH (p20); women on long-term anticoagulation convert from LMWH when haemorrhage risk falls, usually 5–7 days after delivery (p7); and in women with recurrent VTE on long-term oral therapy LMWH continues until switched back to warfarin or another oral agent (p21). Warfarin prevents VTE for at least 6 weeks postpartum in women with previous confirmed VTE, regardless of mode of delivery (p6, p21). WHO T1 p15 contributes only a general statement that warfarin prevents VTE in surgical patients when indicated, and OpenRN T2 p825 adds that concurrent NSAIDs increase gastrointestinal bleeding risk. RCOG is far more specific on populations, day-5 thresholds, INR targets and LMWH bridging; WHO and OpenRN are generic. The community does not establish warfarin doses, target INR ranges beyond >2.0, duration of long-term therapy, safety of alternative oral anticoagulants, breastfeeding transfer data, reversal or perioperative-interruption protocols, or comparative effectiveness against LMWH for VTE prevention.

title: Hand jewelry and bacterial colonization risk
summary:
This community represents a narrow but practically important perioperative hand-hygiene theme: the relationship between wearing rings on the hands of health-care personnel and increased bacterial colonization of the skin. Two relations, both drawn from CDC Table 1 (p32), anchor the theme.

First, wearing rings increases the risk of skin bacterial colonization in health-care personnel, with the condition specified as the skin underneath rings compared with fingers without rings on the same or comparable hands. Second, wearing rings increases the risk of carriage of gram-negative bacilli and Staphylococcus aureus, specifically in intensive care unit nurses, with the condition that the concentration of organisms correlated with the number of rings worn — a dose-response observation that supports counselling staff to minimize the number of rings, not merely to consider ring removal in principle.

Only one guideline body contributes here: the CDC (hand hygiene evidence summarized in Table 1, p32). There is therefore no inter-body disagreement to reconcile in this community, and no second source that is more or less specific. Within the CDC material itself, the ICU nurse finding is the more specific of the two: it names the organism groups (gram-negative bacilli, S. aureus), names a defined population (ICU nurses), and describes a quantitative relationship with ring number, whereas the first relation is a more general anatomical comparison (skin under rings vs. bare fingers) across health-care personnel broadly.

What this community does NOT establish: it makes no claim that ring wearing causes surgical site infection, postoperative wound infection, or patient-to-patient transmission; colonization and carriage are the only outcomes described. It sets no threshold for an acceptable number or type of ring (no distinction between plain bands and stone-set rings), specifies no timing for removal relative to scrubbing, hand antisepsis, or gloving, and names no antiseptic agent, product, or scrub protocol. It also offers no data on artificial nails, nail polish, wristwatches, or bracelets, and no evidence on whether ring removal reduces colonization.
key_entities: carriage of gram-negative bacilli and Staphylococcus aureus

title: WHO Surgical Safety Checklist Universal Application
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused theme: the World Health Organization (WHO) Surgical Safety Checklist as a universal perioperative safety intervention. All five relations centre on one entity, and all derive from a single guideline source (NICE T1, pages 10 and 25).

Main recommendations. First, scope of application: the checklist applies to surgical procedures, with the condition that it be used 'for each surgical procedure, including dental procedures' (NICE T1 p10). Dental procedures are named explicitly as a separate APPLIES_TO relation, signalling that the checklist is not limited to major theatre surgery and should not be omitted for procedures perceived as minor. Second, outcomes: in the population of surgical patients, the checklist is credited with preventing mortality, preventing postoperative complications, and preventing never events (NICE T1 p25). The never-event benefit carries an explicit condition — it applies 'when the checklist is completed' — which is the key operational message for educators and QI leads: partial or ritualistic use is not what the guideline links to harm prevention; completion is the stated condition.

Contributing bodies and differences. Only NICE contributes here (NICE T1). There are therefore no cross-body disagreements to reconcile, and no second guideline offering a more or less specific formulation. Internally, p10 supplies the scope/applicability statement while p25 supplies the outcome claims, so the two pages are complementary rather than conflicting; p10 is the more specific of the two in naming procedure types.

What this community does NOT establish. It specifies no checklist content — no named sign-in, time-out or sign-out items, no team-briefing or debriefing steps. It gives no timings (when in the pathway each phase occurs), no thresholds, no audit or compliance targets, and no effect sizes or risk reductions for mortality, complications or never events. It names no drugs, no gynecologic-specific populations or procedures, no roles or professional responsible for completion, and no documentation, escalation or exception process. Any local protocol detail must come from outside this community.
key_entities: world health organization surgical safety checklist

title: Wound Cleansing Agents and Dressing Sequence
summary:
This community represents a single, tightly focused clinical theme: safe wound cleansing practice and its place in the wound care sequence, specifically which cleansing agents are contraindicated and when cleansing must occur relative to dressing application.

Main recommendations. (1) Wound cleansing is an intervention for impaired skin integrity, to be performed per facility protocol or as ordered (OpenRN T2 p753) — the guideline defers dosing/frequency to institutional policy or a provider order rather than specifying an interval. (2) Timing: wound cleansing depends on and must precede dressing application — the stated condition is 'prior to applying a dressing' (OpenRN T2 p1423). (3) Agent selection: three named agents are flagged as contraindicated for wound cleansing in patients undergoing wound cleansing — hydrogen peroxide, betadine (povidone-iodine), and acetic acid (OpenRN T2 p1145). Each contraindication appears twice, once with the explicit population qualifier 'patients undergoing wound cleansing' and once unqualified, so the prohibition should be read as general to the cleansing task rather than restricted to a subgroup.

Contributing bodies. All relations derive from a single source corpus, OpenRN Nursing Skills (Text 2), across three page loci: p753 (indication/impaired skin integrity), p1145 (contraindicated agents), and p1423 (cleansing-before-dressing sequence). There is therefore no inter-body disagreement to reconcile; the only variation in specificity is internal — p1145 is the most concrete (naming three specific agents), p1423 supplies the only explicit timing, and p753 is the least specific, delegating protocol to the facility.

What this community does NOT establish. It names no recommended or preferred cleansing solution (e.g., no saline or commercial cleanser is endorsed here), no concentrations, volumes, pressures, temperatures, or frequencies, and no gynecologic- or perioperative-specific population qualifiers (no cesarean, laparotomy, or vaginal-cuff wounds; no age, pregnancy, or immunosuppression strata). It gives no rationale for the contraindications (e.g., cytotoxicity to granulation tissue is not stated), no exceptions or supervised-use scenarios, no dressing-type guidance, and no assessment, documentation, or escalation criteria. Educators should pair it with dressing-selection and wound-assessment content.

title: Wound Dehiscence: Risk, Prevention, Monitoring
summary: This community centres on surgical wound dehiscence — its risk factors, prevention, detection, and immediate management — chiefly during closure-device removal. Risk factors: obesity (in obese individuals), smoking, and coughing or straining in patients with abdominal wounds (OpenRN T2 pp.696, 1113). NICE T1 (p25) adds a device-level risk: staples increase dehiscence risk compared with sutures for wound closure, stated broadly for patients having surgery across different types of surgery. Prevention for surgical patients: adherence to postoperative instructions, avoidance of heavy lifting as advised, and protecting skin from being pulled around the wound site (OpenRN T2 p1113). Detection: wound assessment detects dehiscence, particularly in wounds becoming increasingly painful (p1145). During intermittent suture removal, observe the wound line for separations and stop the procedure if there are any concerns; assess wound healing after removal of each suture; delay removal of remaining sutures if there are concerns about approximation (p1176). Steri-strips have three distinct roles: applied prior to suture removal they prevent dehiscence; applied when wound edges are open in patients undergoing intermittent suture removal they treat dehiscence; and they are applied after removal of the remaining staples following staple removal (pp.1176, 1181). Contributing bodies: NICE T1 (single relation, closure-material comparison, no population subgroup or threshold beyond 'different types of surgery') and OpenRN T2, which supplies all patient-level risk factors, education, monitoring, and steri-strip technique — clearly the more procedurally specific source. The two do not conflict; they address different levels (device choice vs. bedside practice). Not established: any gynecologic-specific or perioperative-population-specific guidance; no drugs, dosing, BMI or pack-year thresholds, timing intervals for suture/staple removal, or quantified dehiscence rates; no criteria defining 'concerns about approximation'; no escalation, dressing, antibiotic, or return-to-theatre pathway once dehiscence occurs beyond steri-strip application; and no evidence grading or comparative effectiveness among the preventive measures.
key_entities: observation of the wound line for separations
protecting skin from being pulled around the wound site

title: Surgical Wound Infection Prevention, Detection, Treatment
summary: This community centres on wound infection across the perioperative continuum: risk factors, prophylaxis, surveillance/detection, and treatment. Prevention: antimicrobial prophylaxis prevents wound infection in surgical patients, most effective when serum and/or tissue levels are achieved and given within one hour prior to incision (WHO T1 p109); prophylactic antibiotics are recommended for women undergoing elective and non-elective caesarean section (WHO T1 p60). ERAS Society adds thermal management—hypothermia increases risk, and active warming reduces wound infection with a 13% absolute risk reduction versus conventional methods. Nursing measures include changing saturated dressings, wound dressing, protection from contamination for wounds healing by secondary intention, and draining irrigation fluid into a basin during indicated wound irrigation (OpenRN). Specific products: hydrofera blue antimicrobial foam applied to a cleansed wound under an occlusive cover for pressure injuries, diabetic/venous stasis/arterial ulcers, superficial burns, donor sites, post-surgical incisions, trauma wounds, abrasions and lacerations; silver hydrofiber dressing requires silver to remain in place at least 24 hours; silver sulfadiazine treats infected wounds under a secondary dressing. Conversely, super sponge gauze, abdominal pads, optilock polymer dressing and kerlix gauze rolls increase risk if drainage-filled and left on the wound surface for extended periods. Risk factors: obesity, vaginal surgery (WHO T1 p57), hypothermia, and healing by secondary intention where wounds cannot be approximated. Detection: wound culture (including drainage specimens and swabs) when infection is suspected, unhealthy granulation tissue is present, or new signs are reported to the provider; wound assessment every shift/at each dressing change, comparing with previous assessment, noting fever, altered consciousness, drainage type, odor, dark red granulation tissue, periwound redness, warmth, tenderness, and increasing pain (which also suggests dehiscence). Antibiotic therapy must match wound culture results and the bacteria present. RCOG uniquely links persistent wound infection lasting more than 10 days postpartum to venous thromboembolism risk. Not established: specific antibiotic agents, doses, or redosing intervals; thresholds for obesity or temperature; dressing change frequency; gynecologic-specific bundles beyond caesarean and vaginal surgery; and comparative effectiveness among dressings.

title: Saline Wound Irrigation Before Wound Procedures
summary:
This community centres on a single, recurring nursing intervention: wound irrigation with sterile normal saline performed as a preparatory step immediately before other wound-related procedures. Across three separate guideline passages the irrigation is positioned not as a therapeutic end in itself but as a pre-procedure cleansing measure whose purpose changes with the procedure that follows.

Main recommendations, with population and timing:
1) In patients undergoing staple removal, sterile normal saline irrigation prevents infection when performed before staple removal, specifically to remove surface debris or exudate from the incision line (OpenRN T2 p1181).
2) In intermittent (alternate) suture removal, saline irrigation applies as a step to be carried out before removing sutures; here the guideline states the applicability and timing but does not attach an explicit outcome such as infection prevention (OpenRN T2 p1176).
3) In patients undergoing wound culture collection, saline irrigation performed before specimen collection prevents specimen contamination — i.e., the goal is diagnostic accuracy of the culture rather than infection control (OpenRN T2 p1172).

Guideline bodies: all three relations derive from a single source corpus, OpenRN Nursing Skills (Text 2), across pages 1172, 1176 and 1181. There is therefore no inter-body disagreement to reconcile. The passages differ in specificity: the staple-removal (p1181) and wound-culture (p1172) entries name a concrete outcome and rationale (debris/exudate removal; contamination avoidance), whereas the suture-removal entry (p1176) is the least specific, giving only the timing ("before removing sutures").

What this community does NOT establish: no irrigation volume, syringe size, pressure, temperature, or number of passes; no alternative solutions (e.g., antiseptics, povidone-iodine, chlorhexidine) or comparisons against saline; no guidance for continuous/full suture removal, drain sites, or surgical debridement; no patient-level contraindications, timing intervals relative to surgery, or dressing choices afterward; and no outcome data, effect sizes, or evidence grading supporting the claimed prevention of infection or specimen contamination.
key_entities: wound irrigation with sterile normal saline

title: Verbal Identity Confirmation Prevents Wrong-Site Surgery
summary:
This community centres on a single, high-leverage safety practice: verbal confirmation of patient identity, the intended procedure and the surgical site, as a barrier against the three classic never events — wrong site surgery, wrong procedure and wrong patient surgery. All relations derive from the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist material (WHO T1, pages 11 and 107), so the theme reflects one guideline body applied at two distinct checkpoints.

Two complementary recommendations appear. First (WHO T1 p107), the checklist coordinator verbally confirms identity, procedure and site with the patient before proceeding; where the patient cannot confirm (e.g. is unable to participate), a guardian or family member may confirm on their behalf. This step is credited with preventing wrong site surgery, wrong procedure and wrong patient surgery. Second (WHO T1 p11), for all surgical patients, the same confirmation is repeated and confirmed by the whole operating room team — not the coordinator alone — immediately before the skin incision, and is placed explicitly in the intraoperative phase. The p11 relations name prevention of wrong site and wrong patient surgery; the p107 relations are broader in the harms covered (adding wrong procedure) and more specific about who speaks and the surrogate-confirmation fallback, while p11 is more specific about population (all surgical patients), team participation and exact timing (before skin incision). Educators can therefore teach the practice as a two-stage redundancy: an early coordinator-led check with the patient or surrogate, then a team-wide restatement at the moment of incision.

The community does not establish anything gynecology-specific, nor any drugs, doses, thresholds or timings beyond "before proceeding" and "immediately before skin incision." It does not address site marking, imaging or consent-document verification, laterality rules, documentation requirements, escalation when team members disagree, effectiveness data or compliance rates, and it names no contributing body other than WHO — so no inter-guideline conflict can be assessed from these relations.
key_entities: verbal confirmation of patient identity, procedure and surgical site

title: Preventing Wrong Site Surgery Through Verification
summary:
This community centres on prevention of wrong site surgery through layered preoperative verification, site marking, and team communication. The dominant recommendation is surgical site marking: performed preoperatively, 'if appropriate,' before induction of anaesthesia, by the surgeon performing the operation, usually with a permanent felt-tip marker, and specifically indicated for cases involving laterality or multiple structures or levels (WHO T1 p106-107). Marking the incision site with a permanent marker is also cited preoperatively for orthopaedic surgical patients (p16). WHO is explicit that marking works only in combination with a verification process, not alone, and that it forms part of a five-step verification process for patients undergoing surgery or other invasive procedures (p17). Complementary elements include verbal confirmation of patient identity, procedure and surgical site — by the checklist coordinator before proceeding, with a guardian or family member permitted to confirm if the patient cannot, and confirmed by the whole operating room team before skin incision for all surgical patients (p11, p107); a surgical time out immediately before incision in the operating theatre; patient or caregiver participation in verification; patient involvement in preoperative planning; informed consent (preoperative, surgical patients); accurate patient identification and labelling; improved communication among team members; a universal protocol; and a broader verification process (p228). Named risk factors are inadequate handoff communication (OpenRN T2 p159) and, for orthopaedic and spinal patients, absence of radiographic images or wrong site labelling on radiographic images (WHO T1 p16).

Contributing bodies: WHO Tier 1 supplies nearly all content, including populations, timing and technique; OpenRN Tier 2 adds only the handoff-communication risk link, without population or condition detail. WHO is far more specific on who marks, with what, and when.

The community does not establish efficacy for several measures: WHO explicitly notes surgical checklists rest on preliminary data with evidence still being gathered, and that evidence for preoperative verification protocols is lacking. No gynecologic-specific populations, drugs, doses, numeric thresholds, audit metrics, or outcome rates are provided, and no comparative effectiveness among the listed strategies is stated.
key_entities: verbal confirmation of patient identity, procedure and surgical site
wrong site labelling on radiographic images

title: Xeroform Gauze for Surgical Incision Dressing
summary:
This community represents a narrow wound-care theme: the use of Xeroform gauze as a non-adherent, occlusive contact layer on surgical incisions in the perioperative gynecologic setting. All three relations derive from a single source, OpenRN Nursing Skills (T2, p1423), so this theme is supported by one guideline body only and there are no competing or divergent recommendations to reconcile.

The substantive recommendations are: (1) Xeroform gauze applies to the surgical incision — i.e., it is the indicated dressing surface for an operative wound; (2) Xeroform gauze prevents wound contamination, but only under an explicit condition — it must be placed directly over the wound and covered with a secondary dressing. The primary layer alone is not represented as sufficient; the two-layer construction is the stated condition for the contamination-prevention benefit. (3) Xeroform gauze prevents bacterial buildup at the incision, stated without a qualifying condition.

For teaching or audit purposes, the actionable checkpoints are therefore placement (directly on the wound bed, not offset or over an intervening layer) and coverage (a secondary dressing applied over the Xeroform). These are the only two verifiable process elements the community supplies.

What this community does NOT establish is extensive. There is no specified population beyond "surgical incision" — no gynecologic procedure type, age group, wound classification, or risk stratum (e.g., diabetic, immunosuppressed, obese patients). No timing is given: no interval for first dressing change, frequency of change, or duration of use. No thresholds are provided for drainage volume, wound size, or signs prompting discontinuation. The composition of Xeroform (e.g., any antimicrobial constituent) and the nature of the required secondary dressing are unspecified. No comparative effectiveness against alternative contact layers is asserted, no outcomes such as surgical site infection rates or healing time are quantified, and no contraindications, allergy cautions, or adverse effects are described. Nothing here addresses documentation, sterile technique specifics, or who may perform the dressing change. Local policy must supply these gaps.
